questions.prompt: A publisher signs a game patch, and Windows checks the signature on your machine. Which key does each side use?
questions.explanation: Only the private key can make a signature that the matching public key accepts, so it never leaves the publisher. The public key travels inside the certificate, where anyone can use it to check. If checking needed the private key, every user would hold the secret needed to sign malware.
options: The publisher signs with its private key; Windows checks with the public key in the certificate
The publisher signs with its public key; Windows checks with the private key in the certificate
Both sides use one shared secret key that was exchanged when the patch was first released
Windows uses no key at all, because the file's hash alone shows who made the file

questions.prompt: What does a SHA-256 hash do for trust?
options: It moves trust from where the hash came onto the bytes on your disk
It creates trust by proving which person originally wrote the file
It removes the need to trust any source of the file or of the hash
It proves the program is free of bugs and of any hidden behavior
questions.explanation: A hash says only that bytes match a recorded value. How far you can trust that depends on how the hash reached you.

questions.prompt: You download a file and its published SHA-256 hash from the same web page, and an attacker can edit that page. You hash the file and it matches. What have you learned?
options: Little, since the attacker could have changed the file and the hash together
That the file is genuine, since matching hashes are practically impossible to fake
That the file is safe, since SHA-256 detects any malicious code inside a file
That the page is trustworthy, since the hash would not match if it were not
questions.explanation: A hash only shows that two copies of the bytes agree. When both the file and its hash come from the same place an attacker controls, the match says nothing about who made them.

questions.prompt: When is comparing a downloaded file with a hash worth doing?
options: The hash reached you by a route the attacker does not control
The hash sits on the same page as the download link itself
Both files show the same upload date in the download listing
The hash is a shorter string than the name of the download file
questions.explanation: A separate channel, a signed release, or a value you recorded yourself from a trusted copy keeps one attacker from changing both.

questions.prompt: An attacker controls the download page and replaces both the file and its hash. Why can't they also replace the signature?
options: They lack the publisher's private key, so a new signature would not verify
Signatures are stored on a server that the attacker cannot reach
A signature is just a longer hash, so the same hash rules protect it
Windows refuses to open any file whose download page was modified
questions.explanation: Only the private key can produce a signature that the publisher's public key accepts.

questions.prompt: An attacker signs a modified game file with their own key pair. Why does Windows not accept it?
options: It matches only the attacker's key, whose certificate is untrusted
The signature has too many digits for Windows to read it in full
The attacker's private key is shared with the game's own publisher
The file hash no longer matches the length stored in the signature
questions.explanation: A signature can verify against its own public key, but the policy asks whether the certificate chain is one Windows trusts.

questions.prompt: Given only 119, you try divisors in order 2, 3, 5, and so on. Which is the first that divides it?
questions.explanation: 119 ÷ 7 = 17, so 7 is the first to work, while checking a proposed answer takes one division. RSA uses this gap with enormous numbers.

questions.prompt: A publisher's private key is stolen. What can the thief do?
options: Sign anything until the certificate is revoked
Nothing, since a signature cannot be reused
Only sign files the publisher already released
Read all files the publisher has encrypted
questions.explanation: The signature says who approved the bytes, not that they are safe. A stolen key lets the thief approve anything until revocation.

questions.prompt: A tool reports that a downloaded installer has no embedded digital signature. What is the sensible reading?
options: It is one fact, not a verdict; look for other evidence like published hashes
It is malicious, since legitimate software always carries a signature
It is safe, since only dangerous files are left without signatures
The signature was stripped, which proves that someone tampered with it
questions.explanation: Many legitimate open-source builds are unsigned. A missing signature is a reason to ask the next question, not an answer in itself.

questions.prompt: Windows reports a file is explicitly distrusted. What is the reasonable next question?
options: Why did Windows policy reject this publisher or signature?
Does the project publish a hash that I can compare against?
Was the file damaged in transit from the download server?
Is the save format of this game supported by the editor?
questions.explanation: Each result in the table leads to a different next question. An explicit distrust is a policy decision.

questions.prompt: A function documents that it returns an error code where exactly zero means success and any other number describes a problem. A reader writes a test that treats any code that is not negative as success. What is wrong?
options: Positive codes are errors, so the test counts real failures as successes
Nothing, since any code that is not negative means the call worked
Zero means failure here, so the test accepts only the wrong value
The test is too strict, since negative codes are also successes
questions.explanation: Return conventions differ between APIs. With a zero-means-success status, only the exact documented value is success, and everything else must be treated as a failure.

questions.prompt: A tool translates numeric status codes into messages, and it receives a code it has no message for. What is the safest behavior?
options: Treat it as a failure and print the raw code so it can be looked up
Treat it as success, since it did not match any known error
Ignore it and carry on as if nothing had been reported
Replace it with the nearest known code and print that message
questions.explanation: Unknown results must fail closed. Showing the raw value keeps the information so someone can look it up later.

questions.prompt: Why might a command-line verification tool ask a security API to suppress any dialog boxes?
options: A pop-up would block a non-interactive tool, which needs a status code back
Dialogs make the check slower by recalculating the file's hash twice
Dialogs are the step that actually performs the signature verification
Dialogs are shown only to administrators, so ordinary users would never see them
questions.explanation: A tool run from a terminal or a script cannot wait for someone to click a window. It should get its answer as a returned status instead.

questions.prompt: An API call can allocate internal state while it works, and a second call with a 'close' action frees it. Why must a caller make the second call even after the first reports its result?
options: Otherwise the allocated state leaks, since the first call does not release it
The second call re-checks the result in case the first call was wrong
The second call is what writes the final result into the status variable
The second call signs the data so that others can verify it later
questions.explanation: Some APIs split work into acquire and release phases. Skipping the release leaks whatever the first call created.

questions.prompt: A signature check is run without contacting the internet to see whether the signing certificate has been revoked. What is the trade-off?
options: It is repeatable and works offline, but a recently revoked certificate may go unnoticed
It is more secure, since skipping network lookups removes a place for attackers to interfere
It is equally strong, since revocation only matters for certificates that have expired
It makes the check fail for every file, so no useful results are produced
questions.explanation: Offline checks give reproducible results but cannot learn about a revocation that happened recently. A release process should use a stricter policy.

questions.prompt: A native call receives a raw pointer into a buffer owned by the caller. Why must that buffer stay alive until the call has finished?
options: The pointer does not own the data, so a freed buffer would be read after release
Native code deletes the buffer itself, so the caller must not touch it earlier
The compiler refuses to build calls that pass pointers to temporary values
Freed buffers are cleared to zero, so the call would silently read nothing
questions.explanation: A raw pointer only points at data and does not keep it alive. If the owner is dropped first, the pointer dangles and the native code reads freed memory.

questions.prompt: A system file has no signature embedded in the file itself. Why is it risky to simply call it 'unsigned'?
options: Some files are covered by signed catalogs stored elsewhere, which an embedded check misses
System files keep their signatures in the registry, so file checks cannot find them
Embedded signatures can only be read after the file has been executed once
Files without embedded signatures have no trust information of any kind
questions.explanation: Trust can be recorded outside the file, such as in a signed catalog of hashes. A complete check has to look there as well.

questions.prompt: After you install a mod, the checker reports new hashes for several game files. Which are expected?
options: Only the files the mod replaced; any others need explaining
All of them, since installing a mod reinstalls the whole game
None of them, since a file's hash never changes after install
Only the main executable, since it is the file that loads the mod
questions.explanation: A SHA-256 value belongs to one exact file. A change in a file the mod did not touch is unexplained.

questions.prompt: A trusted Authenticode signature is shown on a game's EXE. What does it not prove?
options: That the software has no bugs, or that you meant this version
That the bytes match what the publisher originally signed
That a certificate chain which Windows trusts was involved
That the file was not changed at any point after signing it
questions.explanation: Signatures speak about who approved the bytes under a policy. They do not say the software is bug-free.

questions.prompt: Hashing a 4 GiB file by reading it 128 KiB at a time needs roughly how much memory for the file data?
options: About 128 KiB, regardless of how big the file is
About 4 GiB, since the whole file must be loaded before hashing
About 512 MiB, one eighth of the file at a time
About 4 KiB, one small block for each gigabyte
questions.explanation: Hashing can be done incrementally, feeding each chunk into the hash state and then reusing the buffer. Memory use stays at the chunk size.

questions.prompt: A `GSAV` save has `05` in its name-length byte at offset 11. At which offset does its checksum start?
questions.explanation: The fixed fields fill offsets 0 to 11, which is 12 bytes. The name takes the next 5 bytes, offsets 12 to 16, so the checksum starts at 12 + 5 = 17 and the file ends at 17 + 4 = 21 bytes.

questions.prompt: Nia's save is valid, with stored checksum 842. You change only the level byte at offset 10 from `03` to `04`. What sum does the loader compute, and what happens?
questions.explanation: The level byte used to add 3 and now adds 4, so the total rises by one: 842 − 3 + 4 = 843. The stored checksum still says 842, so the file is refused until the checksum bytes are rewritten as `4B 03 00 00`, because 843 = 3 × 256 + 75 and 75 = 4 × 16 + 11 = 0x4B.
options: 843, so it refuses the save
842, so it accepts the save
846, so it refuses the save
4, because only the level byte is summed

questions.prompt: Why is a plain text editor a poor tool for changing a binary save?
options: Saving can quietly change bytes, such as converting line endings
It cannot open any file that is larger than a few kilobytes in size
It displays each byte in decimal, which hides the real stored value
It refuses to save any file that lacks a `.txt` extension on its name
questions.explanation: A hex editor in overwrite mode writes the exact bytes you typed. A text editor treats the file as characters, so it can alter bytes you never touched.

questions.prompt: In a hex dump, a byte sits on the row labelled 00000030, under column 07. What is its offset?
questions.explanation: Add the row offset and the column number: 0x30 + 0x07 = 0x37. Joining the digits as 307 is a common slip, and the column alone ignores the row.

questions.prompt: In a hex dump, a byte 4B shows as the letter K in the character column, but it is the low byte of a score. What does that tell you?
options: Every byte is drawn as a character, so numbers can look like letters
The score is stored as text, since the dump found a letter
The dump has shifted the columns, so the byte is in the wrong place
The file is text only, since a letter appears in its dump
questions.explanation: 4B is 75, the ASCII code for K, but nothing in the file marks which bytes were meant as text.

questions.prompt: Gold sits at file offset 6. Where will you find it in the game's memory once the save is loaded?
options: At an address unrelated to 6 that usually changes between runs
At address 6, since the loader keeps every file offset as its address
At the file offset added to the module's base address in memory
At the same offset, but inside the graphics card's own memory
questions.explanation: The game copies fields into its own structures at addresses of its choosing. An offset is a distance within a file, not a memory address.

questions.prompt: You change byte 6 of the save on disk while the game is running. What happens to the gold on screen?
options: Nothing until the next load; the game may overwrite the edit on exit
It updates at once, since the game rereads the file on every frame
It updates only once the checksum bytes at the end are rewritten too
It resets to 250 because the loader restores the first value it saved
questions.explanation: The running game uses the copy in its own memory. Editing a file changes it only for the next load, and a save on exit can erase the edit.

questions.prompt: What job does a magic number at the start of a file do?
options: It identifies the format, so a loader can refuse other files
It stores the file's size, so a loader knows where it ends
It protects the file, so only the right program can open it
It holds the file's checksum, so changes can be detected
questions.explanation: A fixed pattern at the start tells the loader what it was given. Without it, the bytes of some other file would be misread as real fields.

questions.prompt: An editor supports version 1 of a save format and finds a file marked version 2. What should it do?
options: Refuse it with an unsupported-version error, since fields may move
Change the version byte to 1 and edit it anyway
Edit it anyway, since the versions are usually almost the same
Delete it and create a new save with the version it knows
questions.explanation: A new version means the layout may have changed. Forcing the version byte would hide the mismatch and risk corrupting the save.

questions.prompt: A save stores a number lowest byte first. The bytes read 34 12 00 00. What is the value?
questions.explanation: Lowest byte first means 0x34 + 0x12 × 256 = 52 + 4,608 = 4,660, which is 0x1234. Reading the bytes in the written order would give 13,330.

questions.prompt: The bytes 64 00 00 00 are read with the most significant byte first. What value results, and what does it suggest?
options: 1,677,721,600, so huge that the order is probably wrong
100, which is modest, so the order is probably right
6,400, which is modest, so the order is probably right
64, which is small, so the order is probably wrong
questions.explanation: Read that way it is 100 × 16,777,216 = 1,677,721,600. When one order gives billions and the other a modest number, the modest one is probably right.

questions.prompt: A save has 10 fixed bytes, then a name whose length is given by a byte, then a 2-byte checksum. The length byte is 06. How long is the file?
options: 18 bytes
16 bytes
12 bytes
6 bytes
questions.explanation: Ten fixed bytes, plus 6 name bytes, plus 2 checksum bytes gives 18. Forgetting the checksum gives 16.

questions.prompt: A 20-byte save has 10 fixed bytes, a variable-length name and a 2-byte checksum, and its name-length byte reads FF. What should a careful loader do?
options: Compare 10 + 255 + 2 = 267 with the file size and fail
Read the 255 bytes anyway, since the length byte is trusted
Read up to the end of the file, and ignore the length byte
Replace the length byte with 8, the largest sensible name
questions.explanation: FF is 255, so the file claims to be far longer than it is. A careful loader checks the claim against the real size instead of reading past the end.

questions.prompt: In an unfamiliar save, a byte just before some text equals the number of characters after it. What is that pattern?
options: The fingerprint of a length-prefixed string
The marker of a string ended by a `00` byte
The version number of the file format
The first byte of a checksum field
questions.explanation: Storing the length first lets a loader read exactly that many bytes. Strings that end with a `00` byte have no count in front of them.

questions.prompt: Between two saves, the gold bytes differ and so does one byte near the end. Why did the other byte change?
options: It is a checksum, which changes when any covered byte does
It stores the gold's sign, so it follows the gold
It is a random value that the game rewrites at each save
It marks the end of the file, so it moves with the data
questions.explanation: A byte that changes whenever any other value changes is the sign of a checksum or similar protection.

questions.prompt: A gold value changes from 100 to 2,000, two bytes change, and the next two bytes stay 00. Why can't you yet say the field is two bytes wide?
options: They could be the upper bytes of a wider field that are still zero
Zero bytes are never part of a number, so they are padding
A field always has an even width, so the next two are another field
Unchanged bytes belong to the next field, by the rules of the format
questions.explanation: A larger value, above 65,535, would show whether those bytes change. Until then, unchanged zeros prove nothing about the field's width.

questions.prompt: A save stores a checksum equal to the sum of its other bytes, which is 600. The gold changes from 300 (bytes 2C 01 00 00) to 1,000 (bytes E8 03 00 00) and nothing else. What sum does the loader compute, and what happens?
options: 790, which does not match 600, so it refuses the save
600, which matches the stored checksum, so it accepts the save
835, which does not match 600, so it refuses the save
235, which does not match 600, so it refuses the save
questions.explanation: The old gold bytes add 44 + 1 = 45 and the new ones add 232 + 3 = 235, so the sum is 600 − 45 + 235 = 790. It no longer matches the stored value.

questions.prompt: In the loader's flow, which check comes first?
options: Whether the first four bytes are `GSAV`
Whether the sum matches the stored checksum
Whether the version byte is 1
Whether the gold is under 65,535
questions.explanation: The magic number is checked before anything else, since a file that is not a `GSAV` save has no meaningful fields. The checksum is the last gate.

questions.prompt: Why do real formats often use a CRC-32 or a hash rather than a plain sum of bytes?
options: A sum cannot notice two bytes being swapped, as the total is the same
A plain sum always takes four more bytes of space than a CRC-32 does
A CRC-32 can be edited without changing any of the bytes it covers
A plain sum is too slow to compute for files larger than 19 bytes
questions.explanation: Addition ignores order, so swapped bytes go unnoticed. A CRC-32 is designed to change when bytes are reordered.

questions.prompt: Why can't you recompute a MAC or a digital signature the way you recomputed this checksum?
options: It depends on a secret key you do not have
It is stored in a different byte order than the game
It needs the file to be compressed with gzip first
It covers only the gold bytes, which cannot be changed
questions.explanation: A plain sum needs nothing secret, so anyone can redo it. A keyed check or signature can be produced only by the holder of the key.

questions.prompt: Why should you use overwrite mode rather than insert mode when changing gold?
options: An inserted byte would shift every later field, including the checksum
Insert mode refuses to accept hexadecimal digits that are typed in
Overwrite mode updates the checksum for you when the file is saved
Insert mode makes the game read a new version number from the file
questions.explanation: Gold fills exactly four bytes, so you replace those four. Inserting shifts everything after them and the file ends up one byte too long.

questions.prompt: A save stores a name-length byte, then the name, then a checksum. Changing the name from 3 bytes to 5 bytes needs which steps?
options: Insert two bytes, set the length to 5, and recompute the checksum, now two bytes later
Overwrite the next two bytes, and leave the length and checksum alone
Insert two bytes and set the length, since the checksum is only checked at load time
Pad the name with spaces up to 5 bytes, and leave the length alone
questions.explanation: A longer name is the one edit that must add bytes. Everything after it moves, so the length and the checksum must both be right.

questions.prompt: Why is editing a gzip-compressed save in a hex editor unlikely to work?
options: One changed compressed byte upsets all that follows, so unpack, edit, repack
Compressed files cannot be opened in a hex editor at all
The editor shows compressed bytes in a different order than they are stored
Compression encrypts the data, so only the game can read it
questions.explanation: The values are not stored as plain bytes. A gzip stream, which begins with 1F 8B, has to be decompressed before the value can be edited.

questions.prompt: A code pattern matches six executable locations in the exact supported build. What is the safest next step?
options: Refine the signature and verify the surrounding instructions until one meaning is proven
Patch all six locations, since at least one of them must be the instruction you wanted
Choose the first match, because the scanner returns addresses in sorted order
Turn every byte into a wildcard so the pattern is guaranteed to match something real
questions.explanation: Several matches mean the pattern is not a unique identity. Add stable surrounding bytes, reduce needless wildcards, and disassemble each candidate; a scanner should refuse ambiguity rather than make six writes.

questions.prompt: After a game update, why can the old module-base-plus-RVA calculation point at the wrong code even when the base is correct?
options: The instruction may have moved within the module, so the old RVA lands on different bytes
The loader refuses to add a base to an RVA once the executable has been rebuilt by its developer
The module base is always recalculated as zero after an update, so the sum is no longer valid
Updates convert every RVA into a file offset, which cannot be added to a live base address
questions.explanation: An RVA is only correct for the exact build it was measured on. A pattern searches the current module instead of trusting an old position.

questions.prompt: What does a byte pattern match give you by itself?
options: A candidate location that still needs checking in each supported build
Proof that the instruction is the gold-changing one in every version of the game
A guaranteed unique address, because the bytes of a pattern cannot appear twice in a module
A decoded instruction with its operands and meaning, ready to be patched in place
questions.explanation: The pattern shows where matching bytes sit; it does not prove what the instruction means. Semantic verification is a separate step.

questions.prompt: A near call instruction stores the distance from the next instruction to its target. Why should a byte signature wildcard that distance?
options: The same call lands on a different distance whenever surrounding code shifts between builds
The distance is a random value the compiler picks for each call site, so it never repeats
The distance is padding that the processor skips, so it carries no useful information at all
The distance holds the version number of the game, so it differs in every release
questions.explanation: A relative call stores how far away the target is, not where it is. When code moves, the distance changes even though the same function is still called.

questions.prompt: What separates a justified wildcard from "a shrug" in a signature?
options: A written reason, such as "relative call displacement, changes when code moves"
A count showing that the wildcard appears in fewer than four positions of the signature
A test run proving that the pattern still matches after the wildcard bytes are removed
A rule that wildcards may only replace bytes whose value is zero in the design build
questions.explanation: The lesson says each wildcard needs a stated reason. Without one, you cannot tell whether you hid a changing byte or just an inconvenient one.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of putting wildcards over many positions in a signature?
options: The pattern becomes common and ambiguous, matching ordinary code in many places
The pattern becomes too long, so the matcher returns false near the end of every buffer
The pattern stops working on the build used to design it, because wildcards remove its anchors
The pattern gets copied to the target process, which can overwrite the instruction it was meant to find
questions.explanation: Too few wildcards make a signature fragile; too many make it match unrelated code. The skill is placing them where bytes truly vary.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when a pattern "overfits"?
options: It memorizes accidental details of one executable instead of describing the instruction you meant
It matches so many places that the scan runs out of memory before it reaches the module end
It grows longer than the module's executable section, so no window can ever fit inside it
It uses wildcards that were written down without a reason, so reviewers must reject the pattern
questions.explanation: An exact 30-byte sequence may work on one build and fail after an unrelated compiler layout change. Looseness that matches everywhere is the opposite mistake.

questions.prompt: A pattern matches exactly once in the build used to design it. What should you do before calling it version-tolerant?
options: Test it against another build you actually intend to support
Nothing, because a single match is enough proof that it will work in every other build
Add wildcards at random positions until the pattern also matches an unknown build
Lengthen the scan to every section of the module, so more locations are checked
questions.explanation: One match in the design build may simply mean the pattern is overfitted. A second supported build shows whether it finds the same kind of instruction.

questions.prompt: Why is it wrong to keep weakening a pattern until it matches an unknown build?
options: It can return success on the wrong code; the goal is the same instruction in every named build
It makes the pattern longer, which would exceed the limit the lesson sets for byte signatures
It changes the module's fingerprint, so the supported builds are then rejected by the scanner
It is allowed, as long as the final pattern matches at least one location in that build
questions.explanation: The pattern should find the same instruction in the builds you named, not any build at all. For a single supported build, an exact fingerprint plus signature is more honest.

questions.prompt: A pattern format treats the byte value 0x00 as meaning "match anything". What is the main drawback of this design?
options: A pattern can no longer ask for a real zero byte, because zero is already taken
Zero bytes are reserved by the operating system, so no scanner may compare against them
The scanner slows down, since zero must be converted to a register value before comparing
Wildcards can only be applied to single bytes, so longer patterns stop working entirely
questions.explanation: If a special value means "anything", you lose the ability to mean that value literally. A separate explicit wildcard marker keeps the two ideas apart.

questions.prompt: A matcher tries a pattern starting at a position where fewer bytes remain in the buffer than the pattern needs. What is the correct result for that position?
options: No match, since a full comparison is impossible there
A match on the available bytes, treating the missing ones as wildcards
A crash with an out-of-range error, so the caller learns the buffer was too small
A wrap-around to the start of the buffer to finish the comparison
questions.explanation: A partial pattern is not a match. Treating the position as a plain non-match keeps the scan safe near the end of the buffer.

questions.prompt: A buffer holds 10 bytes and the pattern is 4 bytes long. Which start offsets must be tried?
options: 0 through 6
0 through 5
0 through 7
0 through 9
questions.explanation: The last start with room for 4 bytes is 10 - 4 = 6, and that position must be included. Stopping at 5 would miss a match at the very end; going past 6 would run off the buffer.

questions.prompt: A scanner computes the last valid start position as buffer length minus pattern length, using unsigned integers. What goes wrong if the pattern is longer than the buffer and nothing checks for that?
options: The subtraction underflows, giving a panic or a huge wrapped number instead of "no room"
The scanner quietly compares only the first bytes of the pattern against the buffer
The result is a negative number, which the loop then handles like zero iterations
The pattern is shortened automatically so that it fits inside the buffer
questions.explanation: Unsigned integers cannot go below zero, so subtracting a larger number from a smaller one wraps or panics. A guard that returns an empty result first avoids that.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many comparisons does the simple scan do at most for a 1,000-byte buffer and a 4-byte pattern?
options: About 4,000
About 1,004
About 250
About 16,000
questions.explanation: The lesson says at most roughly `n × m` comparisons: 1,000 × 4 = 4,000. Faster algorithms matter only after measurement shows this loop is the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: A function turns text like "29 47 ZZ" into a byte pattern, and "ZZ" is not valid hexadecimal. Which behavior is safest?
options: Reject the whole pattern with an error, so a typo never becomes a different search
Treat the bad token as a wildcard and keep parsing the remaining tokens as usual
Skip the bad token and return a pattern one byte shorter than was written
Stop at the bad token and return the bytes parsed so far as the final pattern
questions.explanation: A silently altered pattern searches for something other than what the writer meant. Failing early and loudly turns a typo into an error before any memory is scanned.

questions.prompt: Why is it usually better to restrict a signature scan to a program's executable code section than to scan every readable region?
options: Data and heap bytes can match a pattern by coincidence, and a smaller range gives fewer false hits
Operating systems refuse to let anyone read data sections, so scanning them always fails
Signatures are rewritten by the loader inside data sections, so they never match there
Scanning more regions makes each individual match less accurate, so the first match is always wrong
questions.explanation: Code signatures describe instructions, so searching only where instructions live keeps the scan focused. Random data elsewhere can look like the same bytes and cause misleading matches.

questions.prompt: Why copy a region of another process's memory into a local buffer once, then search that buffer, instead of reading the remote memory piece by piece during the comparison?
options: A local snapshot cannot change or fail partway through a comparison, and one bulk read is cheaper
Remote memory cannot be compared against wildcards, so a local copy is required for them
The copy hides the scan from the other process, so it cannot notice that it was searched
Reading a region twice is not allowed, so the first read has to be kept for every later one
questions.explanation: Matching against a stable local copy means no read can fail in the middle of a comparison, and fewer calls are needed. The cost is that the snapshot can go stale if the target changes.

questions.prompt: A signature that worked on one build of a program finds no matches on another build. What is the most sensible first conclusion?
options: One of its assumptions does not hold, such as the build, the scanned range, or the bytes themselves
The signature is perfect, because a truly unique pattern should not be found by a scanner
The scanner is faulty, so it should be run again until it eventually reports one match
The target is hiding its code, so the scan range should be widened to every region in memory
questions.explanation: Zero hits means something you assumed is wrong, so verify the exact build, architecture, range and pattern first. Widening the search blindly tends to hide the real mistake.

questions.prompt: A pattern is ambiguous. What is the right way to fix it?
options: Extend the pattern into surrounding instructions until only the intended one matches
Lengthen the scan to another unrelated section until only one match is left in total
Take the first match and write down that the scanner chose it by address order
Replace the leading bytes with wildcards so that the matcher accepts a smaller set of windows
questions.explanation: The lesson says not to fix ambiguity by changing the search area. Add identity to the pattern, because several matches mean it does not contain enough.

questions.prompt: After the scanner reports exactly one match, which step still comes next?
options: Disassemble the neighboring bytes and confirm whole instructions and the build fingerprint
Patch the address right away, because a unique match proves the instruction's meaning
Copy the match offset into the process as the new module base for later lookups
Rescan the entire process once more, so the pattern can be shown to match nowhere else
questions.explanation: One match locates a candidate; semantic checks decide whether it is the right one. Unknown builds should be rejected.

questions.prompt: A test builds a two-item list in its own setup and then asserts that the list has length two. Why is this considered a weak test?
options: It only restates the setup, so no mistake in the code under test could ever make it fail
It tests the code too deeply, so it would break whenever the implementation is refactored
It only compiles in optimized builds, so it is skipped during normal debug test runs
It counts items instead of values, which testing guidelines forbid for list structures
questions.explanation: A useful test is one that a wrong implementation would fail. Checking the size of a list you just wrote cannot catch any bug in the matcher.

questions.prompt: A tutorial shows a made-up signature with wildcards to teach the idea. Before trusting a signature on a real build, what should you do?
options: Measure the bytes in that exact build with a disassembler and confirm they match the instruction you want
Use the tutorial's bytes unchanged, since a sample signature is valid for every build of a program
Replace every byte with a wildcard, so that the pattern cannot fail on any build
Search for the tutorial bytes in data sections first, because they are most stable there
questions.explanation: A sample is only an illustration of the technique. A real signature must come from the actual bytes of the build you target, checked against the instruction you meant to find.

questions.prompt: A code signature reports a hit that sits inside a data section. Which question is most useful to ask first?
options: Did the scan range include data memory, where the same bytes can appear by chance?
Was the pattern too long, so that the scanner crossed into the next section by mistake?
Did the loader rewrite the data section into code while the scan was still running?
Is the pattern missing a leading call opcode that every valid hit has to start with?
questions.explanation: Code signatures should only be searched in executable memory. A hit in data usually means the range was too wide, and the bytes matched by chance.

questions.prompt: A first scan finds every address containing 100. You spend points and the visible value becomes 75. What should the next scan keep?
options: Only the old candidates that now contain 75
Every address that has ever contained 100
Every readable address that contains 75, ignoring the first scan
Only addresses that sit in executable pages
questions.explanation: The first scan creates a candidate set, and the second asks which members of that same set changed to the new value. Rescanning all memory for 75 would bring back unrelated copies.

questions.prompt: In a memory search, a filter step re-reads only the addresses already on the candidate list. After one filter pass the list is larger than before. What most likely happened?
options: A fresh search of memory was run instead of re-checking the existing candidates
The filter found extra matching addresses next to the existing ones and added them
The target allocated more memory, and the filter added each new page to the list
The filter compared values in the wrong byte order, so it kept every candidate twice
questions.explanation: Re-checking a list can only drop entries, never add them. A list that grows means a brand-new scan of memory took place.

questions.prompt: Which statement best separates asking the operating system to describe a memory region from reading that region?
options: Describing reports a region's size, state and protection, while reading copies out its bytes
Describing copies the bytes out in a compact form, while reading only reports the region's size
Describing changes the region's protection to readable, while reading then copies the bytes
Describing works on any process, while reading is only possible inside your own process
questions.explanation: Describing a region tells you what it is and whether it can be read, without copying any contents. Keeping the two steps separate makes failures easier to explain.

questions.prompt: The four bytes 2A 00 00 00 stand for the number 42 under which interpretation?
options: As a little-endian 32-bit unsigned integer, with the lowest byte stored first
As a big-endian 32-bit unsigned integer, with the highest byte stored first
As four separate characters, each of which is read as its own small number
As any four bytes in memory, since hexadecimal 2A always means 42 in every context
questions.explanation: Bytes have no meaning until you choose how to read them. The same four bytes could be a pointer, part of an instruction, or unrelated data, which is why a first scan only finds candidates.

questions.prompt: A scanner looks for the value 500 stored as a little-endian 32-bit integer. Which byte sequence does it search for?
questions.explanation: 500 is 0x1F4, so the lowest byte F4 comes first, then 01, then two zero bytes. The reversed order is big-endian.

questions.prompt: With 400 MiB of readable memory, about how many bytes does the first scan read?
options: About 419 million
About 400 thousand
About 160 thousand
About 72
questions.explanation: 400 × 1,048,576 = 419,430,400 bytes, because the first scan reads every readable byte once. Later passes read only the candidates.

questions.prompt: The first scan found 40,000 candidates of 4 bytes each. How many bytes does the second scan read?
questions.explanation: The second pass re-reads only the survivors: 40,000 × 4 = 160,000. It no longer depends on how large the game's memory is.

questions.prompt: The first scan is O(n) in the size of memory. What happens if the game uses twice as much memory?
options: The scan reads about twice as many bytes
The scan reads about four times as many bytes
The scan reads the same number of bytes
The scan reads about half as many bytes
questions.explanation: O(n) means the cost grows in step with the input. O(n²) is the case where doubling the input makes the work four times worse.

questions.prompt: Comparing every one of 40,000 candidates with every other candidate costs how many comparisons?
questions.explanation: 40,000 × 40,000 = 1,600,000,000, which is O(n²) and 40,000 times the work of reading the list once. Doubling the candidates would make it four times worse.

questions.prompt: Why is finding one candidate's previous value in a hash table keyed by address called O(1) on average?
options: Hashing the address picks a bucket directly instead of reading the whole candidate list
The table keeps candidates sorted, so a lookup always finds the value in the first position
The table copies every candidate into memory next to the target, so no search is needed
The table's lookups are guaranteed to take identical time no matter how many collisions occur
questions.explanation: The lesson says collisions and an overloaded table can slow individual lookups, so this is not a promise of equal timing. It is a statement about average growth.

questions.prompt: Which regions should the scanner keep when looking for a visible value such as gold?
options: Committed regions with readable protection, skipping guard and no-access pages
Reserved regions that have never been committed, because gold is stored in unused address space
Only regions marked executable, because every game value is stored next to its code
Free regions, since the game has not yet claimed them and their bytes cannot change
questions.explanation: State tells whether a range is committed, reserved, or free, and protection tells what can be done to it. Reading a guard or no-access page would fail or have side effects.

questions.prompt: A loop walks through a process's memory by moving to start plus size for each region. Why should it check that the position really advanced?
options: A region reporting size zero would leave the position unchanged and loop forever
Large regions can be reported twice, so each step must prove the region is new
Position values must always increase by a power of two, or the walk would stop early
Memory regions are checked in random order, so the walk must confirm the order is sorted
questions.explanation: The walk moves forward only by region size. A zero-sized region, or an arithmetic overflow that wraps around, would make it repeat the same spot endlessly.

questions.prompt: Why does a memory scanner describe another process's region with plain numbers and flags, such as start, size and protection, rather than with a reference to its bytes?
options: That memory sits in another address space, so locally you can only hold a description
References are not allowed to be stored in structures, so numbers are the only choice
Numbers are faster to compare than references, which matters more than correctness here
Region sizes are too large to be held by a reference, so they must be split into numbers
questions.explanation: A local reference can only point into your own address space. For another process you keep a description and copy the bytes only when you ask for them.

questions.prompt: A scanner searches a copied buffer for a 4-byte value. Why might it test every byte offset instead of every fourth offset?
options: The value is not guaranteed to start at a multiple of four, so unaligned positions may hold it
Stepping by four would skip past the last bytes of the buffer, which cannot be checked otherwise
Every byte offset holds a different encoding of the value, so each must be tried in turn
The processor can only read values that overlap with the previous one, so steps must be one
questions.explanation: Aligned scans can step by the value size, but data packed into a structure may start anywhere. Checking every offset is slower yet finds those values too.

questions.prompt: A block of memory was copied from target address 0x7000. A match is found at local offset 20 inside the copy. Which target address should be reported?
questions.explanation: The target address is the base plus the offset, and 20 is 0x14 in hexadecimal, giving 0x7014. The offset alone is only a position inside the local copy.

questions.prompt: Why do adjacent 1 MiB chunks overlap by three bytes?
options: A four-byte value can begin in the last three bytes of a chunk and would otherwise be split
The overlap gives the scanner a safety margin, so that Windows never returns a short read
Three bytes is the size of the header that every chunk carries from `ReadProcessMemory`
The overlap lets the scanner compare each chunk with the one before, to detect changed pages
questions.explanation: Without it, a value straddling the boundary would never exist as a complete four-byte window in either buffer.

questions.prompt: A search narrows its list with filters such as "increased" and "unchanged". Why must each candidate remember its last value as well as its address?
options: Those filters compare the new read of that exact address with the earlier read of it
The address can change between reads, so the old value is used to find it again
Values are stored in the list in order, so the previous value gives the candidate's rank
The earlier value is needed to undo a write if the final change goes wrong
questions.explanation: A filter such as "changed" is a comparison between two reads of the same address. Without the earlier value there is nothing to compare against.

questions.prompt: A candidate address read as 80 last time and reads as 65 now. Which filters keep it?
options: "Decreased" and "changed"
"Increased" and "changed"
"Unchanged" only
"Decreased" only
questions.explanation: The value went down, so it satisfies "decreased", and it differs from before, so it also satisfies "changed". It fails "increased" and "unchanged".

questions.prompt: Which candidate survives an "unchanged" filter?
options: One that read 7 last time and reads 7 now
One that read 7 last time and reads 8 now
One that read 7 last time but cannot be read this time
One that read 7 last time and also reads 7 at a different address
questions.explanation: "Unchanged" keeps a candidate only when the current read equals the previous read of the same address. An address that cannot be read is dropped rather than counted as unchanged.

questions.prompt: Why is a fixed set of named options, such as an enumeration, safer than passing filter names as free text?
options: A misspelled option fails at compile time, and every case can be checked for being handled
Free text cannot hold letters, so options must be stored as numbers
Named options run faster, since the processor compares them without looking at memory
Free text is rejected by the operating system when it is sent to another process
questions.explanation: With text, a typo can silently act like an unknown mode. With a closed set of options, the compiler catches typos and flags every place that needs updating when a new option is added.

questions.prompt: During a filter pass, a candidate address can no longer be read. How should the scanner treat it?
options: As removed from the list, without crashing the scan
As a successful match, since an unreadable value cannot have changed
As proof the whole scan is invalid, so every candidate must be discarded
As a reason to pause the target process until the memory becomes readable again
questions.explanation: The game can free or re-protect memory at any time. A robust tool drops that candidate, reports skipped work, and continues.

questions.prompt: What does "the scanner's snapshot is always slightly behind the running process" mean?
options: The game keeps running between queries, reads, and later checks, so memory may change meanwhile
The scanner reads memory in the order it was allocated, so older pages are always seen first
Windows delays each `ReadProcessMemory` result by one frame so that the game can finish writing
The snapshot is a saved file on disk, which the game overwrites only when it exits
questions.explanation: Between the region query and the read, the game can free an allocation or change its protection. This is a normal race, not necessarily a bug.

questions.prompt: A first scan for the value 0 returns millions of candidates. Why is that a poor starting search?
options: Zero appears in countless unrelated places, so the list is huge and barely narrows
Zero is a reserved value that the operating system hides from every scanner
Zero can only be stored in code sections, so the scan reads the wrong memory
Scanning for zero changes the value being searched, which makes later filters fail
questions.explanation: A very common value matches almost everywhere. A less common starting value gives a much smaller list that later filters can narrow quickly.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of chunk, region, candidate, output, and time limits?
options: They keep a memory-safe program from becoming unusable by exhausting memory, time, or the terminal
They remove the need for bounds checks, since a limited program can never read out of range
They make the scanner invisible to the game, because it then performs only small reads
They let the scanner write more quickly, because the limits switch the process into a faster mode
questions.explanation: The lesson says that without limits, perfectly memory-safe code can still make an unusable program. Safety from panics and usability are separate concerns.

questions.prompt: Why does the guarded write re-read the value just before writing four bytes?
options: The game kept running after the scan, so the address could hold a newer value now
Writing without a read first is not permitted by the Windows memory manager
The read lets the program save a copy of the region for the next full scan
The read proves that the address belongs to the executable, so it is safe to modify
questions.explanation: This closes a time-of-check/time-of-use gap. If the value no longer equals `candidate.previous`, the write stops instead of overwriting newer state.

questions.prompt: A tool refuses to write to an address because the value there no longer matches what it last read. What is the safeguard preventing?
options: Overwriting a spot that changed since it was checked and may now hold something else
Writing a value that is too large to fit in the memory page at that address
Writing to memory that belongs to the tool's own process instead of the target
Writing the same value twice, which would waste time and show up in the target
questions.explanation: A stale reading means the candidate may no longer be the value you wanted. Refusing and asking for a fresh scan is the safety check working as intended.

questions.prompt: Why can exact byte equality be misleading when scanning floating-point values?
options: `NaN` does not equal itself, `-0.0` equals `0.0`, and the displayed text may be rounded
Floats are stored big-endian, so the byte order of every float differs from integers
Floats cannot be stored at four-byte addresses, so every scan must use eight-byte windows
Visible decimals are always exact, so only the sign bit can ever cause a mismatch
questions.explanation: `-0.0` and `0.0` compare equal despite different bit patterns, and visible text may round the stored value. A `ValueKind` should say whether it compares bits, values, or a tolerance.

questions.prompt: The first pass finds zero candidates. Which phase should you inspect first, according to the troubleshooting table?
options: Value type, endianness, range permissions, or the target build
The guarded write, since it runs before the first candidate is stored
The output limit, since the terminal prints at most 25 results
The overlap size, since three bytes is too few for four-byte values
questions.explanation: Zero first-pass candidates point at how the value was searched for. Things like the guarded write only happen after a single survivor exists.

questions.prompt: Why is it good practice for a scanner that only reads memory to open its handle to the target without write rights?
options: A tool that cannot write cannot damage the target by mistake, so it holds what it needs
Write rights make every read slower, so leaving them off speeds the scanner up
Handles with write rights are rejected by the operating system for every ordinary program
Without write rights, the scanner can read memory that is normally protected from reading
questions.explanation: This is the principle of least privilege: ask for only the access a task needs. A read-only tool then cannot overwrite the target through a bug.

questions.prompt: After an `int3` breakpoint fires, why restore the original byte, rewind `EIP`, set the trap flag, and continue for one instruction?
options: To let the real instruction run once before putting `0xCC` back
To make the process permanently single-threaded while the breakpoint is installed
To turn the game's x86 instructions into readable source code on the debugger's side
To skip the instruction that was replaced, so the program resumes at the next one
questions.explanation: The CPU pauses after consuming the one-byte `0xCC`, so `EIP` points just past it. Rewinding and restoring lets the displaced instruction execute, and the trap flag pauses right afterward so the debugger can reinsert the breakpoint.

questions.prompt: Which sequence matches the debugger's event loop?
options: Wait for an event, decode it, inspect or update state, continue it, then wait again
Continue the event, decode it, wait for the next one, then inspect the state afterward
Decode the event, wait for it to arrive, update state, then stop the loop until detach
Inspect the state, wait for any event, continue it once, then decode what was received
questions.explanation: The loop is `WaitForDebugEvent`, decode, inspect or update, `ContinueDebugEvent`, and back to waiting. Continuing before decoding would resume the target too early.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a kind of event that Windows reports to a debugger?
options: A DLL being loaded into the target
A change in the player's gold value
A write to a file by the debugger
A mouse click inside the debugger's window
questions.explanation: Windows reports process creation, DLL loading, exceptions, and process exit. A breakpoint is one exception that the tool deliberately causes and handles.

questions.prompt: Why is it good design to convert raw operating system event structures into your own typed values right where they enter your code?
options: Awkward unsafe layouts stay at the edge, and the rest of the code uses safe typed data
The operating system refuses to deliver the next event until the first one is converted
Typed values make the operating system send events faster than raw structures do
Converted values remove the need to ever release the handles that came with them
questions.explanation: Converting at the boundary keeps unsafe or platform-specific details in one place. Handles that arrive with an event also have to be closed or handed over so a long session does not leak them.

questions.prompt: A software breakpoint overwrites one byte of an instruction with a special trap byte. Why must the debugger remember the byte it replaced?
options: It has to be put back so the real instruction can run correctly
The trap byte is only valid while it matches the saved byte beside it
The saved byte tells the processor which instruction comes next
The operating system compares it to the trap byte before delivering an event
questions.explanation: Without the original byte the instruction stays damaged. The debugger restores it to let the real code execute, and again when the breakpoint is removed.

questions.prompt: A debugger may hold dozens of breakpoints at once. Why is a table keyed by address a natural way to store them?
options: When a trap fires, the exception address finds that breakpoint and its own saved state
Addresses are sorted by the table, so breakpoints always trigger in ascending order
Only one entry per address is allowed, which prevents a program from having several threads
The table moves each breakpoint when the target code is relocated in memory
questions.explanation: Keying by address gives every breakpoint its own record, so there is no single global slot. On an exception the debugger looks up the address to see whether it owns that trap.

questions.prompt: Which order correctly installs a software breakpoint?
options: Save the original byte, write the trap byte, then flush the instruction cache
Write the trap byte, save the byte that was there, then flush the instruction cache
Flush the instruction cache, write the trap byte, then save the original byte
Write the trap byte, flush the instruction cache, then save the byte that was there
questions.explanation: The original byte must be saved before it is overwritten or it is lost. The cache flush comes after the write so the processor sees the modified code.

questions.prompt: What is the trap flag used for in the breakpoint cycle?
options: It makes the CPU raise a single-step exception after one instruction so `0xCC` can be reinserted
It stops every other thread in the process from running while the original byte is restored
It marks the exception as belonging to Windows, so the debugger knows to pass it onward
It tells the instruction cache to flush, so the restored byte is the one that executes
questions.explanation: After the original instruction runs once, the single-step exception gives the debugger a safe moment to put `0xCC` back and clear the trap flag.

questions.prompt: A debugger tracks each breakpoint as disabled, armed, or temporarily stepping over. What does "armed" mean?
options: The trap byte is currently written into the target's code at that address
The original byte is restored while one thread single-steps past the spot
The breakpoint has been hit at least once and is waiting to be reported
The breakpoint has been removed from the table but still shows in the log
questions.explanation: Armed means the trap is live in the target. The stepping phase has the original byte restored for a moment, and disabled means nothing is installed.

questions.prompt: Why check an exception's address against your breakpoint map before treating it as yours?
options: Windows and the target may use breakpoints internally, and those must be passed onward
Every exception that carries a code of breakpoint is created by the debugger's own writes
An address outside the map means the process has exited, so the loop should stop
Addresses in the map are the only ones that Windows will report as first-chance exceptions
questions.explanation: The lesson lists the exception code, address, map membership, first-chance status, and current phase and thread. Unhandled exceptions are passed on with the correct continue status.

questions.prompt: What does the term instrumentation bias describe?
options: The tool used to measure a program changes what the program does
A debugger's tendency to show only the first instruction of each function it meets
The extra memory used by a debugger when it stores a copy of the whole target
The gap between the compiled instructions and the source code they came from
questions.explanation: Pausing a thread, writing `0xCC`, or single stepping all affect the target. A difference seen only while attached comes from the measurement, not the game's normal logic.

questions.prompt: A behavior appears both with the debugger attached and when running without it. What does that suggest?
options: It is probably part of the target rather than an artifact of the pause
It was caused by the breakpoint byte, since attached runs always change the code
It proves the target can observe the debugger and is acting on what it sees
It is a timing difference, since only elapsed time can change while attached
questions.explanation: The table says a behavior that happens both ways is probably part of the target. Behavior that appears only attached points at scheduling or at the target noticing the debugger.

questions.prompt: A debugger receives an exception it did not cause, such as one from the target's own code. Why should it report it as not handled when continuing?
options: The target's own error handling can still see it, instead of the debugger swallowing it
Reporting it as handled would make the processor skip the next instruction
Not handled tells the operating system to remove the exception from the target
Handled exceptions cannot be continued, so every exception must be marked otherwise
questions.explanation: A debugger should only consume events it owns, such as its own breakpoints. Passing the rest back keeps the target's behavior unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which milestone is wise to reach first when building a new debugger?
options: A loop that waits for events, prints them and continues each until the target exits
A full interface with stepping, symbol names and a graphical view of every thread
A breakpoint system that supports many breakpoints, before any events are printed
A memory editor that writes values into the target before the loop is working
questions.explanation: The wait, print and continue loop with a clean exit is the foundation. Breakpoints, stepping and symbols are easier to add once that is solid.

questions.prompt: A debugger stops at the instruction add dword ptr [ebx+8], ecx. Which register holds the amount being added?
options: ecx, while ebx plus 8 locates the memory that is changed
ebx, while ecx plus 8 locates the memory that is changed
Neither one, since the amount added is the number 8
Both, since the instruction adds ebx and ecx together first
questions.explanation: The memory operand in brackets is the destination, formed from ebx plus 8. The register after the comma is the value added to it.

questions.prompt: A debugger stops at mov ecx, [esi+0x10] and esi holds 0x00800000. At which address does the instruction read?
questions.explanation: The memory operand is the register value plus the offset, so 0x00800000 + 0x10 = 0x00800010. The register alone is only the base of the record.

questions.prompt: Which action belongs in a debugger's cleanup when it detaches or exits?
options: Restore every armed breakpoint, flush the cache, continue pending events, and close handles
Leave the breakpoint bytes installed, so the game can reuse them on the next run
Keep the pending event unresolved, so the target stays safely paused after detach
Close the handles first, then restore the breakpoint bytes through those same handles
questions.explanation: A debugger that pauses correctly but cannot cleanly detach is not finished. Leaving `0xCC` in the target would crash it the next time that instruction ran.

questions.prompt: A PE section reports an instruction RVA of `0x1200`, and Windows loads the module at `0x7FF600000000`. What is the live virtual address?
questions.explanation: An RVA is a distance from the module's live base. Add the two: `0x7FF600000000 + 0x1200 = 0x7FF600001200`. A file offset answers where bytes sit on disk; it is not automatically the address the CPU executes.
options: 0x7FF600001200, the live base plus the RVA
0x1200, since an RVA is already the final live address
The file offset of the section, since that is where bytes sit
0x7FF600000000, the module base without adding the RVA

questions.prompt: What is a Portable Executable, or PE?
options: The Windows `.exe` format; headers say where code and data live
A file holding only raw CPU instructions with no separate sections
A format that stores the full memory contents of a running process
A header block that exists only inside the debugger while it runs
questions.explanation: An EXE is not one solid blob of instructions. Its headers describe where code, data, imports, resources, and relocation information are.

questions.prompt: What do a file offset and an RVA each measure?
options: Offset: a spot in the file; RVA: a distance from the loaded base
Offset: a spot in the loaded image; RVA: a spot in the file
Offset: a live address; RVA: a distance from the preferred base
Offset: a distance from the module base; RVA: a spot in the file
questions.explanation: The same section has two places, numbered differently. A section row converts between them; the numbers are related but not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Why can an executable's layout in its file on disk differ from its layout in memory after loading?
options: Separate alignments, zero-filled data, and fixes after mapping
The file is encrypted on disk and then decrypted when it is loaded
The CPU reorders sections to make a game run much faster
The file is compressed on disk and then expanded by the loader
questions.explanation: Sections have separate file and memory alignments, zero-initialized data may need no file bytes, and relocations and imports are applied after mapping.

questions.prompt: Which order does a parser follow through the headers?
options: DOS header, PE signature, COFF header, optional header, section table
Section table, optional header, COFF header, PE signature, DOS header
COFF header, DOS header, section table, PE signature, optional header
PE signature, section table, DOS header, optional header, COFF header
questions.explanation: Each structure confirms the image or says where the next one begins. A section row cannot be trusted before the headers that locate it have passed their checks.

questions.prompt: An old DOS-compatible header at the start of a Windows executable has a field telling a parser where the modern header begins. What kind of value is it?
options: A file offset to the signature of the modern header
A live memory address of the signature after loading
An RVA that is relative to the load address
A section number that counts from the first section
questions.explanation: It is a file offset, not an RVA or a live address. It is how a parser leaves the old header and finds the signature of the modern one.

questions.prompt: Why must a parser never jump to a later header using a guessed offset?
options: A wrong header should stop the parse before its numbers are trusted
Later headers are encrypted until the earlier ones have been read
The guessed offset would be an RVA, which Rust would then reject
Guessing an offset makes the file larger when it is saved to disk
questions.explanation: Each header tells where the next begins or how large it is. Following that chain is what keeps invalid numbers from being trusted.

questions.prompt: Why is the "optional" header not optional for an executable?
options: The name comes from object files, which can omit it; images need it
Executables need it only when they have more than 96 sections
It becomes required only when the program runs as administrator
It is truly optional, though every Windows game happens to include it
questions.explanation: The image base and entry-point RVA live there. Object files can omit it, which is where the old name comes from.

questions.prompt: A file format stores multi-byte numbers with the least significant byte first. How should a parser read a 32-bit field?
options: Assemble the four bytes in little-endian order
Read the bytes in the order written, as big-endian
Reverse the bits inside each of the four bytes
Read just the first byte, since it carries the value
questions.explanation: Little-endian puts the least significant byte first. Reading the bytes in the order written would give a very different number.

questions.prompt: Which facts does the COFF header give a parser?
options: The target CPU, the section count, and the next header's size
The image base address and the entry-point RVA of the program
The name and the permission flags of every section in the file
The file offset where the old DOS header begins in the image
questions.explanation: The COFF header follows the `PE\0\0` signature. The image base and entry point are in the optional header, and section details are in the section table.

questions.prompt: Why does the parser reject a section count above 96?
options: A wild count means a wrong offset or a damaged file
Windows refuses to load any image that has over 96 sections
Each section row would stop fitting in its fixed 40 bytes
The `u16` type cannot hold a number that is above 96 at all
questions.explanation: The cap is deliberately boring. It is a sanity check on the data, not a rule of the loader.

questions.prompt: An executable's header has a magic number that marks the file as 32-bit or 64-bit. Why does that matter to a parser?
options: Some later fields differ in size, so offsets shift between them
It sets the compression that is used for the whole file
It chooses the language that the operating system displays to users
It shows whether the file has been digitally signed by its maker
questions.explanation: The two formats have fields of different sizes, so the position of everything after them changes. A parser has to look at the magic before it reads further.

questions.prompt: A table starts at byte T, and each row is 24 bytes long. Where does the row with index 5 start?
options: T + 144, since counting starts at one
T + 29, since the index is added to the size
T + 5, since the index is the offset
questions.explanation: Row number i starts at T + i x 24, so index 5 gives 120. Counting starts at 0, so index 5 is the sixth row.

questions.prompt: A format stores a name in a fixed 8-byte field padded with zero bytes. Why can a parser not assume the name ends with a zero byte?
options: An eight-character name fills the field with no terminator
Names are stored backward, so the zero byte comes first in the field
Names are stored as two-byte characters in a different layout in the file
Zero bytes are not allowed to appear in a field of text like that one
questions.explanation: The fixed field need not end in a terminator. A parser looks for a zero byte and uses all eight bytes if there is none.

questions.prompt: What does the loader use to set a section's page protection?
options: The characteristic flags; names are only conventions
The section name, such as `.text` or `.data`, read by the loader
The position of the section within the section table
The size of the section's data as stored on the disk
questions.explanation: `.text` is normally readable and executable, but the flags are what is enforced. A strangely named section can still be executable.

questions.prompt: Which pairing matches the normal permissions of sections in an executable?
options: Code is readable and executable; variables are readable and writable
Code is writable and executable; constants are readable and writable
Code is read-just and not executable; variables are executable too
Every section is readable, writable and executable together at once
questions.explanation: Code sections are read and execute, writable variables are read and write, and constant data is read-only. Keeping them apart limits what a mistake can do.

questions.prompt: A game was built as a 32-bit program for Windows on x86. Which kind of header does its executable have?
options: The 32-bit format, usually called PE32
The 64-bit format, usually called PE32+
A DOS-just header with no modern header after it
A header that has no optional header
questions.explanation: A 32-bit build has the 32-bit form of the header. A good parser supports both forms so that it can say which one it found.

questions.prompt: Your encoder's output can be decoded by your decoder. Why is one real captured fixture still valuable?
questions.explanation: An encoder and decoder written from the same mistaken idea can agree perfectly with each other. A known real frame anchors the test to the actual protocol and exposes shared mistakes in lengths, byte order, compression, or field layout.
options: Both halves might share one wrong assumption and still agree
Captured bytes make bounds checks and size limits unnecessary
A fixture switches TCP into a mode that keeps message boundaries
Real data guarantees every later game version stays compatible

questions.prompt: The 4-byte header of a length-prefixed frame says 0x2A, and the length does not count the header itself. How many bytes is the whole frame on the wire?
options: 46 bytes
42 bytes
50 bytes
38 bytes
questions.explanation: 0x2A is 42, and the whole frame is that plus the 4 header bytes, so 46.

questions.prompt: Which wire bytes announce a 100-byte body in a format with a 32-bit big-endian length?
questions.explanation: 100 is 0x64, written as a 32-bit number with the most significant byte first. Little-endian order would put 64 first.

questions.prompt: A complete frame is 70 bytes long on the wire, header included, and the 4-byte length does not count itself. Which header does it carry?
questions.explanation: The length excludes the 4 header bytes: 70 − 4 = 66, which is 0x42. 0x46 is 70, the mistake of counting the header.

questions.prompt: A frame header claims a length of about four gigabytes, but only a few payload bytes follow. What should the parser do first?
options: Reject the claim because it exceeds the configured maximum
Allocate the full size, since the header says that much is coming
Wait for the rest of the data, since networks can be slow
Read the few bytes that are there, and guess the rest of the message
questions.explanation: The header is a claim, not permission. Checking it against a limit comes before allocating or waiting.

questions.prompt: A header claims 4 payload bytes (well under the limit), but only 2 have arrived so far. What does this tell the parser?
options: Nothing is wrong yet; TCP may deliver the rest later
The frame is forged and the connection should be closed
The header is invalid and its length must be read again
The two bytes are the whole payload and TCP lost the rest
questions.explanation: Having fewer bytes so far does not prove a frame is false. The reader keeps buffering, within its limits and timeouts.

questions.prompt: Framing found a complete frame, but decompressing its payload fails. Which layer should you inspect?
options: The compression wrapper and the payload inside it
The transport layer, since the bytes arrived through it
The game-meaning layer, since that is the last one to read the data
The framing layer, since the length decides how much is decompressed
questions.explanation: Each layer has its own failures. A decompression error points at the compressed data, not at TCP or the later layers.

questions.prompt: The WML parses cleanly but the game ignores the message. Where should you look next?
options: At the expected message fields and the connection state
At the length prefix, checking its byte order again
At the gzip header and its magic bytes `1F 8B`
At the capture interface that recorded the bytes
questions.explanation: Valid WML only means the text structure is fine. Whether the game acts on it depends on the schema fields and where the session is.

questions.prompt: A parser's "take n bytes" operation fails because fewer than n bytes remain. Where should its position be afterward?
options: Unchanged, so no field is left half-read
At the end of the input, so nothing more can be read
Moved forward by the bytes that were available
Reset to the start, so the parse begins again
questions.explanation: The operation checks the whole range before it moves the position, so an error leaves the parser exactly where it started.

questions.prompt: Why use checked addition for position plus count when the count comes from the input?
options: A hostile count could overflow and wrap to a small, wrong position
Checked addition is faster than plain addition for large numbers
The count is always negative in hostile input, so it needs a sign check
Plain addition cannot add two numbers of the same type together
questions.explanation: A huge count could wrap around and look like a valid position. Checked addition turns the overflow into an error.

questions.prompt: Why return an error value for bad network input rather than panic?
options: Bad input is normal, so it should be handled, not crash like a bug
A panic is slower than an error, which matters for every packet
A panic is not allowed in code that handles network connections
An error value always repairs the data, so the parse can continue
questions.explanation: Bad input from a network is expected. It should be a result the caller can handle, not a crash that looks like a programmer's mistake.

questions.prompt: What does a lifetime parameter on a cursor over a byte slice express?
options: The slices it hands out borrow from the input, so cannot outlive it
The cursor itself is copied each time it moves, so it lives only briefly
The cursor keeps the input alive, so the input is never freed
The slices it hands out are independent copies of the input bytes
questions.explanation: The cursor holds only a position number. Everything it returns points into the borrowed input, so it cannot outlive that input.

questions.prompt: Why cap both the compressed size and the decompressed output size?
options: A small compressed input can expand into an enormous output
Compressed and decompressed data always have the same size, so one cap is enough
The decompressed cap speeds up the compressed data, which is read first
A compressed cap is not needed, since compressed data is never read
questions.explanation: Capping only the compressed size would not stop a tiny, highly compressible input from filling memory after decompression.

questions.prompt: A decoder enforces a maximum output size. Why read up to one byte more than the maximum?
options: Reaching the extra byte proves the output is over the limit
The extra byte is a terminator that every compressed stream must end with
One extra byte is always needed to hold the length of the output
The extra byte is dropped, so the output is exactly the maximum size
questions.explanation: Reading one byte past the limit separates "exactly at the limit" from "too large" while keeping memory bounded.

questions.prompt: A peer announces a legal frame length and then sends one byte every few seconds. Which protection addresses this?
options: A read timeout or cancellation, plus a cap on buffered data
A smaller maximum frame size, since the announced one was legal
A faster decompressor, since slow data is a decompression problem
A checksum on every frame, since slow data is probably corrupt
questions.explanation: Parsing limits protect against bad completed inputs. The transport must also bound the time and memory spent waiting for a frame to finish.

questions.prompt: A decoder parses one complete value and finds extra bytes left over. Why report that as an error?
options: Extra bytes could hide ignored data, so exact frames should be split first
Extra bytes are always padding, so reporting them keeps the logs tidy
The decoder cannot ignore bytes, since it must read every byte it is given
Extra bytes mean the next frame has already started, which is fine
