questions.explanation: A valid prefix with something appended is suspicious. A stream reader should first split the stream into exact frame slices.

questions.prompt: A game update renames a required WML field. Why is this riskier than adding an optional field?
options: It can break old and new readers on each other's messages
Optional fields are not allowed in tagged text formats
Renaming a field changes the length prefix of the message
A tolerant format ignores renames but rejects new fields
questions.explanation: A tolerant tree format may skip an unknown optional field, but a missing required field can break both directions.

questions.prompt: Why might a serializer reject quote characters and newlines in a value written to a quoted text field?
options: They could end the field early or start a new line and change the structure
Quotes and newlines take too many bytes, so they would make the message too long
Quotes and newlines cannot be stored in memory, so they are never valid
Quotes and newlines are only used by compression, so they are reserved
questions.explanation: In a quoted format, a quote ends a field and a newline starts a line. A value containing them could rewrite the message layout.

questions.prompt: Why convert a length to a 32-bit number with a checked conversion instead of a plain cast?
options: A cast silently drops high bits, so the header and payload disagree
A cast is slower, since it checks the size of the number first
A cast rounds the length up to the next multiple of four bytes
A checked conversion adds the header length to the result
questions.explanation: A truncated length produces a header that does not match the data. A checked conversion turns that case into an error.

questions.prompt: Gzip and zlib both wrap DEFLATE data. Why can't one be swapped for the other when a protocol specifies gzip?
options: They use different headers and checksums, so the wrapper is part of the wire format
They use different compression algorithms, so one cannot read the other's data
The two differ only in file extension, so a protocol has to name one
Gzip uses a larger window, so zlib data would fit inside it
questions.explanation: The wrapper around the compressed data is part of the format. A correct gzip stream begins with the bytes 1F 8B.

questions.prompt: A frame header announces a length of 8,388,608 bytes, and the configured maximum is 4,194,304. What happens, even if all of those bytes are already in the buffer?
options: It is refused as too large before slicing or decompressing
It is accepted, since the bytes are already present
It is accepted, but only the first 4,194,304 bytes are used
It is refused only after decompression shows the real size
questions.explanation: The announced length is checked against the cap as soon as it is read. Having the bytes available does not change that.

questions.prompt: A socket closes in the middle of a read. Which category of failure is this?
options: A transport failure
A framing failure
A content failure
A game-rule failure
questions.explanation: Closed or timed-out sockets are transport problems. Framing is about impossible lengths, and content is about things like compression, text encoding or markup.

questions.prompt: A length-prefixed message claims 6 payload bytes, but only 3 follow. What kind of error is this?
options: Truncated input: the claim cannot be met with the bytes there
Oversized input, since the claim is larger than the data
Malformed content, since the payload is not valid text
Trailing bytes, since there is data after the header
questions.explanation: The header says 6 bytes but only 3 remain, so reading the payload fails before any decompression or parsing is attempted.

questions.prompt: Why can one call to `read` not be assumed to return one complete application message?
questions.explanation: TCP preserves ordered bytes, not message-shaped chunks. One read may return part of a frame or several frames together. Your protocol must define a length, delimiter, or fixed size, and the reader must loop until that rule is satisfied.
options: TCP is a byte stream and does not keep the sender's write boundaries
TCP converts each message into UDP datagrams of random size
Windows trims the first byte from each read result it returns
Ports force each message on one connection to be the same size

questions.prompt: In a client-server game, what is a client's "move north" message?
options: An intent, a request that the server may accept or reject
A command, which the server must carry out exactly as sent
A fact, which the server records as already true
A reply, which confirms what the server has decided
questions.explanation: The server applies the shared rules, so the client's message is only a request until the server's reply says what was accepted.

questions.prompt: A client predicted that it moved into a new cell, but the server's reply reports the old cell because a wall blocked the move. What should the client do?
options: Correct its display to the position the server reported
Keep showing its own prediction, since the client knows its own input best
Resend the same move until the server finally accepts it
Hide the reply, since a blocked move is not worth showing
questions.explanation: The reply reports what the server actually accepted. The client's prediction is a guess and is not authoritative.

questions.prompt: A sender writes two messages back to back over a TCP connection. Which result can a single read call return?
options: The whole first message plus the start of the second one
Exactly the first message, since each write is delivered as its own unit
The second message before the first, since the network may reorder the bytes
Only the body of the first message, since headers are removed on delivery
questions.explanation: TCP keeps the bytes in order but ignores the boundaries between writes, so a read can end anywhere. It never reorders bytes or strips headers.

questions.prompt: Two framed messages total 13 bytes on the wire. Read #1 returns 8 bytes. How many bytes are still to come?
options: 5 bytes
4 bytes
6 bytes
13 bytes
questions.explanation: 13 - 8 = 5. In the lesson those 5 bytes finish the second length field and the second payload.

questions.prompt: A receiver is reading a 4-byte length prefix, but only 2 of those bytes have arrived. What should it do with them?
options: Keep them in a buffer until the other two arrive
Treat them as the full length, since two bytes are enough to be a number
Throw them away and wait for a fresh message to start over
Pass them on to the next layer, which can finish reading the length
questions.explanation: A message cannot be parsed until its header is complete, so the receiver holds the leftover bytes and appends what arrives next.

questions.prompt: Why read a fixed-size length prefix in a loop that continues until every byte has arrived, rather than with one read call?
options: A single read may return fewer bytes than requested
A single read always waits for the full count, so a loop is just a habit
A loop reads faster, since it asks the network for the data in smaller pieces
A single read can only return one byte at a time, so a loop is needed
questions.explanation: A plain read returns whatever is available, which may be less than you asked for. The reader must wait for the whole header before trusting the length.

questions.prompt: Why compare a received length with a maximum before allocating a buffer of that size?
options: The length comes from an untrusted peer and could demand huge memory
A buffer must be sized in powers of two, so the length is rounded up first
Allocating before the check would make the length arrive more slowly
The maximum is the exact size of the message, so the buffer can be reused
questions.explanation: A corrupt or hostile length could ask for gigabytes. Bounding it first keeps the allocation under the receiver's control.

questions.prompt: A length-prefixed reader receives the header 00 00 00 03 followed by 58 59 5A. What does a successful read return?
options: Just the payload 58 59 5A
The whole thing, 00 00 00 03 58 59 5A
The length and the first byte, 03 58
The number 3, the size of the payload
questions.explanation: The header gives the payload length and is consumed. The function returns one complete payload without it.

questions.prompt: The four bytes 00 00 02 03 are read as a big-endian 32-bit number. What value results?
questions.explanation: Big endian puts the most significant byte first, so the value is 2 × 256 + 3 = 515. Reading the same bytes in the opposite order gives 50,462,720.

questions.prompt: Why should network code decode integers with an explicit byte order instead of casting raw bytes to an integer?
options: The protocol fixes the wire order, which may differ from the CPU's
A cast is rejected by the network card, which checks the byte order
An explicit order makes the data smaller, since it removes padding
A cast only works for numbers that are written in text form
questions.explanation: A cast uses the host's byte order, which is little endian on common processors. Network code must follow the protocol, not the CPU.

questions.prompt: TCP delivered every byte of your request to the server's socket. What does that prove about the request?
options: Only that the bytes reached the receiving socket in order
That the server parsed a complete message from them
That the server accepted the request and updated its state
That a meaningful reply has already been sent
questions.explanation: TCP reliability stops at the ordered byte stream. Acknowledgments, request IDs, and retries belong to the application protocol.

questions.prompt: A login reply arrives before any login request. Which of the protocol's four questions does this problem belong to?
options: Which messages are allowed right now
Where one message ends and the next begins
What each part of a message means
How the bytes are encoded in memory
questions.explanation: Message order is part of the protocol. The bytes may be well formed and still illegal at this point in the conversation.

questions.prompt: Bytes just arrived from the TCP stream carrying a gzip-compressed WML chat message. What does the receiver do first?
options: Split off one frame using the big-endian length
Parse the WML tags to find the sender's name
Gunzip the whole buffer, header bytes included
Build the typed `Message` value and hand it over
questions.explanation: The receiver undoes the layers in reverse order: framing first, then decompression, then serialization, then meaning.

questions.prompt: The TCP connection works and gunzip succeeds, but the parser reports unbalanced tags. Which layer failed?
options: Serialization: the WML text is not well formed
Transport: TCP lost part of the stream
Framing: the length prefix used the wrong byte order
Compression: the gzip magic bytes were missing
questions.explanation: Each layer has its own failure. A valid connection and valid gzip say nothing about the tagged text inside.

questions.prompt: What is WML in this chapter?
options: Wesnoth's tagged text format, written with `[tag]` blocks
The 4-byte length prefix that is placed before each frame
The compression scheme that produces the gzip payload bytes
The Rust enum that models the decoded message kinds
questions.explanation: WML is the serialization layer: structured data written as bracketed tags. Compression and framing wrap it, not the other way round.

questions.prompt: Why might a fast game send frequent position updates over UDP?
options: A newer update makes an old one useless, so freshness wins
UDP guarantees each datagram arrives exactly once and in order
UDP merges datagrams into one long stream for the receiver
UDP encrypts positions so a lost one cannot be read later
questions.explanation: UDP keeps datagram boundaries but promises no delivery or order. That is acceptable when later data replaces earlier data.

questions.prompt: A message is sent again because an acknowledgment was lost, so the receiver sees the same event twice. What must it do?
options: Recognize the repeated event identifier and not apply it twice
Apply it again, since the sender repeated it on purpose
Close the connection, since a repeated message is a protocol violation
Rely on TCP to remove the duplicate, since it never delivers one twice
questions.explanation: Retries are an application concern, since TCP cannot know what a message means. An event identity lets the receiver treat a repeat as the same event.

questions.prompt: A server replies "queued" when a request enters a work queue. What does that reply establish?
options: Received only; it may not be validated, applied, or saved yet
It passed validation and was already applied to the match
It was written to the database and can no longer be lost
It will be handled before any request queued after it
questions.explanation: Asynchronous work means the sender continues early. The protocol must say which stage each reply confirms.

questions.prompt: Recomputing a leaderboard from a collected set of finished-match results is an example of what?
options: Batch processing
Stream processing
Framing
Byte-order conversion
questions.explanation: A batch waits for a group of data and processes it together. Stream processing handles events one by one as they arrive.

questions.prompt: Why should a service bound its queue as well as its message size?
options: An unbounded queue eats memory and makes results staler
A bounded queue lets TCP keep message boundaries intact
A bigger queue speeds up the slowest job in the chain
Fixed-size queues are the sole way to parse length frames
questions.explanation: If input arrives faster than it is processed, the backlog grows. The lesson says what to drop is a decision about message meaning.

questions.prompt: What makes a program a server in a multiplayer connection?
options: It receives clients’ requests and provides a service to them
It draws each player’s screen and reads that player’s keyboard
It must run on a separate computer with a special processor
It stores every client’s variables in one shared memory space
questions.explanation: Server describes a program’s role: serving connected clients. Its service might simulate a match, host a lobby, or forward inputs. Client and server can run on the same machine.

questions.prompt: A game server stores a player at a wall. The client requests a move through it. Who decides the accepted position in a server-authoritative match?
options: The server checks the destination and reports the accepted position
The client changes its displayed position and overwrites server memory
TCP compares the destination with the map before delivering the request
The nearest player accepts the move because their connection is fastest
questions.explanation: In this model the server calculates movement and checks collisions. A client may predict a move, but it corrects its display to the server’s result. Sending a request does not make it valid.

questions.prompt: During a local test, the client and server run as separate processes on one computer. What happens when the client changes a local position variable?
options: The server keeps its own value until it processes a message or other input
The server receives the write immediately because both use the same machine
Both processes change together because loopback connects all their variables
The server must restart before it can receive any more movement requests
questions.explanation: Separate processes have separate memory. A loopback network connection carries messages; it does not turn their variables into shared storage. The server changes its state according to what it processes.

questions.prompt: A player runs the program that checks movement and tells all clients the accepted position. What arrangement does this describe?
options: Client/server with a player-hosted server.
Lockstep just because a player owns the PC.
No server because the machine also draws.
A relay that can only forward raw inputs.
questions.explanation: A server is a program providing the service. It can run beside a client on a player’s computer.

questions.prompt: Two players exchange messages directly. What must you still determine before changing a stored gold value?
options: Which monitor displays that player’s gold.
Which program’s result the game accepts.
Which keyboard sent the first key press.
Which cable joins the two computers.
questions.explanation: Communication topology does not identify authority. Directly connected peers can divide responsibility in several ways.

questions.prompt: In deterministic lockstep, why do peers exchange an ordered input history?
options: To replace their local map with a screenshot.
To let each peer invent a different position.
To let each simulation compute the same result.
To avoid keeping any match state in memory.
questions.explanation: Given the same starting state and ordered inputs, deterministic simulations calculate matching results. This is one peer design, not every peer design.

questions.prompt: `ConnectNamedPipe` reports `ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED` immediately after the server creates its pipe. What does that result mean here?
questions.explanation: A fast client can connect after `CreateNamedPipeW` but before the server calls `ConnectNamedPipe`. Windows reports that race as `ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED`. The server should treat this specific result as a successful connection, not tear down a healthy client.
options: A client already connected in the small window before the call
The pipe name is invalid, so the server must create it again
The client must be disconnected before the server carries on
Message mode has changed to byte mode on this pipe handle

questions.prompt: In a named pipe exchange, who creates the pipe name?
options: The server creates it and waits; the client opens that name
The client creates it and the server later opens it
Both create it at the same instant
The operating system creates it once a message is written
questions.explanation: A server creates a known pipe name and waits. After the client opens the name, both sides read and write with ordinary calls.

questions.prompt: What does a named pipe give a one-request, one-reply exchange that a shared memory region does not?
options: A connection where the order of reads and writes is explicit
Faster access, since pipes are always quicker than shared memory
Access from other computers, since shared memory is limited to one
Larger messages, since shared memory has a very small size limit
questions.explanation: Shared memory needs an extra agreement about timing when a writer is active. With a pipe, the request and the reply simply follow one another.

questions.prompt: In byte mode, what can a single read return?
options: Part of one write, or data from several writes
One complete write, exactly, on every single read
The length header of a write, and nothing beyond it
Nothing at all until the pipe has been closed
questions.explanation: Byte mode is a stream like TCP. Message mode is the one that preserves write boundaries.

questions.prompt: A channel keeps message boundaries and also adds a length header to each frame. Why use both?
options: Boundaries keep messages apart, and the header lets the receiver validate
The header replaces the boundaries, so message mode is just a backup
Boundaries are needed for large messages, and headers for small ones
The header is only for the sender's benefit, to count what it has sent
questions.explanation: The receiver can reject a damaged or unexpected frame instead of trusting every byte the system delivered.

questions.prompt: A frame consists of a 4-byte length header followed by the word "hello". How many bytes is the frame?
options: 9 bytes
5 bytes
4 bytes
10 bytes
questions.explanation: A 4-byte length plus 5 text bytes makes 9.

questions.prompt: A message is the word "naïve", where the letter ï takes 2 bytes in UTF-8. What length belongs in a frame header that counts bytes?
questions.explanation: The header counts UTF-8 bytes, not characters: n, a, v and e take one each and ï takes two, giving 6. The visible character count of 5 would be wrong.

questions.prompt: A received frame declares a text length of 2000 bytes. Which check rejects it?
options: The check that the declared length is at most 1024
The check that the header holds at least four bytes
The check that the text bytes are valid UTF-8 text
The check that the client is on this same machine
questions.explanation: `MAX_TEXT_BYTES` is 1024. The check for the header being too large comes before the size comparison.

questions.prompt: A read returns only 3 bytes, but each frame needs a 4-byte header first. What should the reader do?
options: Reject it, since there is no complete length header
Treat the 3 bytes as the length, since three bytes are enough
Wait for 4 bytes silently, since a short read is always complete
Pad the 3 bytes with zero, and then carry on reading
questions.explanation: A header needs all four bytes before its value can be trusted, so a shorter read fails the first check.

questions.prompt: A frame header declares 20 bytes of text, but the read returned 28 bytes in total, counting a 4-byte header. What should happen?
options: The frame is rejected, since 28 is not 4 + 20
The frame is accepted, since 28 is larger than 20
The frame is cut to 20 bytes, and the rest is dropped
The extra 8 bytes are kept for the next frame
questions.explanation: The received size must equal the header size plus the declared length, here 24. Anything else means the frame is damaged or wrong.

questions.prompt: Why should a parser check that the header exists before looking at the declared length?
options: Later checks rely on facts that the earlier ones have proven
The order does not matter, so it is chosen to look neat
The length is stored before the header, so it must be read first
Checks run faster when the header is verified last
questions.explanation: Checks run in dependency order: header present, length within limit, size matching, then text validity.

questions.prompt: Why is "local" not the same as "trustworthy" for a pipe?
options: Another program in the account might guess the pipe name
Local pipes are not able to carry UTF-8 text at all
The pipe name is announced to every remote computer
Local clients are the same program as the server
questions.explanation: The receiver treats IPC data as untrusted input and validates everything before making a `String`.

questions.prompt: What does refusing remote clients on a named pipe do?
options: Only programs on the same computer can connect
The pipe is faster, since it skips encryption on local connections
Only the creator of the pipe can connect to it
The pipe accepts only one message at a time
questions.explanation: Named pipes can support clients on other computers. Refusing them keeps a local channel local.

questions.prompt: Why does a simple message channel have no need to impersonate its clients?
options: It only exchanges framed messages, and has no need to change privileges
Impersonation is not possible on pipes, since they carry no identity
Impersonation is needed only for long messages, so a short exchange avoids it
The channel already runs as every client, so it needs no extra step
questions.explanation: Identity features solve other problems. A channel that only passes messages should not take on extra power.

questions.prompt: A write call succeeds but reports fewer bytes than the frame holds. Why check for that?
options: A short write sends a frame whose header disagrees with its body
A short write means the receiver has already read the frame
A short write is faster, so it is preferred for large frames
A short write means the connection was closed cleanly
questions.explanation: A successful call still reports how much it wrote. Accepting less would break the protocol.

questions.prompt: A connect call can report "already connected" when a client connects before the server starts waiting. How should that be handled?
options: As success, while other unexpected errors are returned
As a failure, since the connection should have been waited for
As a signal to retry forever, since the client will leave
As an error to ignore, along with every other connect error
questions.explanation: This race is documented and harmless, so it counts as success. Unexpected errors still need to propagate instead of being buried.

questions.prompt: A local tool receives a command string over a pipe. What is a safer design than passing the string to a shell?
options: Define a small set of allowed message types and reject any other
Limit the string's length, since a short string cannot do any harm
Remove spaces from the string, so a shell cannot split it into parts
Run the string with lower privileges, so it cannot change anything
questions.explanation: Data should select one defined action rather than become code. A length limit alone does not make a string safe to execute.

questions.prompt: For a message-mode named pipe, which statement is right?
options: The server sets the type at creation, and the client sets its own read mode
The client chooses the type when connecting, and the server sets its read mode
Both ends get message mode automatically, whichever mode each one asks for
The server sets both ends' read modes, so the client never has to
questions.explanation: The pipe's type is fixed by the server at creation, but each end's read mode is set separately after opening.

questions.prompt: The client runs before any server exists. What happens?
options: `CreateFileW` fails, with advice to start the server first
The client makes the pipe itself and waits for a server
The client writes into a pipe that fills up and stalls
The client falls back to shared memory automatically
questions.explanation: `OPEN_EXISTING` needs a pipe with that name. The lab adds context telling you to start the server in another window.

questions.prompt: Which measure helps a larger local tool built on pipes stay safe?
options: Rate-limit messages and keep queues bounded
Accept messages as fast as they arrive, so none are ever lost
Let queues grow as needed, so no message is ever refused
Trust every local client, since local programs are always safe
questions.explanation: Rate limits and bounded queues stop a flood from using up resources. Versioning, an allowed message set, authentication of sensitive clients and an explicit security descriptor also help.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit game holds a `*const f32` and a `*const u8`. How many bytes does each pointer itself take up?
questions.explanation: These plain raw pointers in a 32-bit process each hold a 32-bit address, so both are 4 bytes. The pointee types decide what gets read at the destination: 4 bytes as a float, or 1 byte.
options: 4 and 4, because a pointer's own size is set by the process
4 and 1, because each pointer matches what it points to
8 and 8, because pointers are always 8 bytes
It depends on the value stored at the destination

questions.prompt: Which kind of storage does this book mean by "memory" when it talks about a game's health value?
options: RAM, which holds the running game's state until power-off
The storage drive, which keeps saves and art between sessions
CPU registers, which hold every value the game ever used
The CPU cache, which keeps a permanent copy of each value
questions.explanation: RAM holds the running game's code, objects, and current state, and it is wiped at power-off. The drive keeps files, and registers and caches only hold what the CPU is working on right now.

questions.prompt: Why does saving a game have to write a file to the drive?
options: RAM loses its contents at power-off, while a drive keeps them
RAM can only hold numbers, so saved text must go on a drive
The CPU empties RAM whenever the game window loses focus
A drive is faster to read than RAM, so saves belong there
questions.explanation: Health and other live state sit in RAM, which does not survive a power-off. A drive is slower than RAM, so the last option has the speed relationship backwards.

questions.prompt: A byte has its bits set as 0110 0100 (place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1). What decimal value does it hold?
questions.explanation: Add the place values of the positions holding a 1: 64 + 32 + 4 = 100. Mixing up which positions are set gives the other totals.

questions.prompt: What is the largest value one byte can hold, and why?
options: 255, because all eight place values added together make 255
256, because a byte has 256 patterns and the last one is 256
128, because the leftmost bit is the biggest single place value
99, because a byte can show only two decimal digits
questions.explanation: With every bit set a byte holds 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255. There are 256 patterns, but they start counting at 0.

questions.prompt: Why does exactly one hex digit describe half of a byte?
options: Four bits hold 0 to 15, the same range as one hex digit
Four bits hold 0 to 9, the same range as one decimal digit
Eight bits hold 0 to 15, the same range as one hex digit
Hex digits ignore bit positions, so any split of a byte works
questions.explanation: A half byte has place values 8, 4, 2, and 1, which reach 15 when all are on, and one hex digit covers 0 to 15. That is why two hex digits are always one byte.

questions.prompt: What does "little endian" mean for a multi-byte number on x86 Windows?
options: The least-significant byte sits in the lowest-numbered box
The most-significant byte sits in the lowest-numbered box
The bytes are stored in a random order picked at each launch
Each byte's own bits are written in reverse inside its box
questions.explanation: On x86 the byte worth the least comes first in memory. Big endian is the opposite order, and neither reorders the bits inside a byte.

questions.prompt: Four bytes sit in memory as 10 27 00 00 (hexadecimal) and are read as a little-endian 32-bit whole number. What is the value?
options: 10,000, since the first byte counts ones and the next counts 256s
270,991,360, since the first byte is the most significant one
55, since the two nonzero bytes are simply added together
4,135, since just the first two bytes count, read as written
questions.explanation: The first byte is the least significant: 0x10 + 0x27 x 256 = 16 + 9,984 = 10,000 (hexadecimal 2710). Reading the bytes in the order written would give a huge wrong number.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit unsigned number 500 is 0x01F4 in hexadecimal. Which bytes would a hex dump show for it on a little-endian x86 machine?
options: F4 01 00 00, with the low byte first
01 F4 00 00, with the high byte first
00 00 01 F4, with the zero bytes first
F4 01, since the two zero bytes are not stored
questions.explanation: The low byte F4 comes first, then 01, then zero bytes to fill all four boxes. A 32-bit number always occupies four bytes.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a location, a byte pattern and an interpretation in memory?
options: Location says where, the pattern says which bits are stored, interpretation says what they mean
Location says what they mean, the pattern says where, interpretation says which bits are stored
Location says which bits are stored, the pattern says what they mean, interpretation says where
All three describe the same thing, and just the name changes between tools
questions.explanation: An address says where to look, the bytes there are the stored pattern, and only the reading step turns that pattern into a number, a decimal or something else.

questions.prompt: A type tells a program which two things about some stored bytes?
options: How many bytes to read, and what the bits inside them mean
Where the bytes are kept, and when they will be freed again
Who owns the bytes, and which parts of a program may read them
How fast the bytes can be read, and how often they get changed
questions.explanation: A type is the instruction for reading bytes: a size and a meaning. Location and lifetime are separate ideas.

questions.prompt: What does the type name i16 tell you?
options: A signed whole number using 16 bits, which may be negative
An unsigned whole number using 16 bytes, which cannot be negative
A decimal number using 16 bits of precision after the point
A text character that is stored using 16 bits of space in total
questions.explanation: The i stands for signed integer and the number is the size in bits. A u would mean unsigned and an f would mean floating point.

questions.prompt: A signed and an unsigned integer both use 8 bits. Why can the signed one reach -128 while the unsigned one starts at 0?
options: Both have 256 patterns; the signed one spends half of them on negatives
The signed type has an extra bit to hold its sign, so it has more patterns
The unsigned type wastes half of its patterns on values that not occur
The signed type stores two numbers, one for the sign and one for the size
questions.explanation: The same number of bits gives the same number of patterns. A signed type uses half of them for negative values, shifting the range around zero.

questions.prompt: The same four bytes in memory are read first as a 32-bit integer and then as a 32-bit float. What changed in memory between the two readings?
options: Nothing; only the type used for reading the bytes changed
The bytes were rewritten into a different pattern for the second reading
The bytes were copied to a new address for the second reading
The bytes were rounded to the nearest valid float for the second reading
questions.explanation: Both readings are valid and the bytes never change. A type is just a way of interpreting the same pattern.

questions.prompt: Why can a scan for the whole number 10 not find the float 10.0?
options: They are different byte patterns: `0A 00 00 00` versus `00 00 20 41`
The scanner skips any address that holds a value above 9
Floats live in CPU registers and are never written to RAM
Whole numbers are stored big endian while floats are little endian
questions.explanation: A scanner searches for one specific byte pattern, so it must know the type first. 10 and 10.0 are stored as different patterns.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit float is asked to store 0.1. What does it actually hold?
options: The nearest value its bits can express, which is very slightly off
Exactly 0.1, since floats store the decimal digits one by one
Exactly 0, since floats cannot hold fractions that small
The characters 0, a dot and 1, stored as one character per byte
questions.explanation: Most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly in binary, so a float keeps the closest representable number. That is why scanners accept a small range when searching for floats.

questions.prompt: A position is four 32-bit floats in a row (x, y, z, w), with x at offset +0x00. At which offset does w begin?
options: +0x0C, since each float takes four bytes
+0x03, since w is the fourth item and offsets count by one
+0x10, since w begins after all four floats have ended
+0x04, since w follows directly after the first float
questions.explanation: Each 32-bit float is four bytes, so x is at +0x00, y at +0x04, z at +0x08 and w at +0x0C. Offsets are distances in bytes, not item numbers.

questions.prompt: What makes an ordinary number a pointer?
options: The code treats the number as the address of something else
Its size: pointers always fill exactly four bytes
A marker bit that is set inside the stored bytes
Its location: pointers are only ever stored on the stack
questions.explanation: Nothing in the bytes marks a pointer. It is a pointer only because the code that reads it uses it as an address.

questions.prompt: The little-endian bytes 00 30 00 00 make the number 12,288 (0x3000). What other reading can the same bytes have?
options: A pointer to address 0x3000, if code uses the number to find data
A float with the value 0.3, since the second byte is hexadecimal 30
A negative number, since the high bytes are all zero
Nothing else, since each byte pattern has one valid reading
questions.explanation: The same pattern is just a number until code uses it as an address, and then it is a pointer. The code that reads the bytes decides which reading applies.

questions.prompt: A pointer stored at address 0x2000 holds the value 0x5000. Which statement describes reading the thing it points to?
options: Read 0x2000 to get 0x5000, then read at 0x5000 to reach the target
Reading 0x2000 gives the target directly, with no second step needed
Read 0x5000 first, which then gives back the address 0x2000
Read 0x2000 twice, since the second read repeats the first one
questions.explanation: The first read returns the pointer's own value. Following it, which is called dereferencing, is a second read at that address.

questions.prompt: A library card says a book is on shelf 12. Later a different book is placed in that spot. What does this model in memory?
options: A stale pointer that looks valid but now leads to a different object
A null pointer that points at nothing, so it can be spotted easily
A pointer whose type changed, so it now reads fewer bytes
A corrupted pointer whose stored number was changed by mistake
questions.explanation: Nothing about the card looks damaged, yet it sends you to the wrong book. A non-zero pointer can still be wrong.

questions.prompt: Why would a game keep a pointer to an object instead of using one fixed address?
options: The object can be rebuilt elsewhere and the pointer updated
A pointer lets the object use less RAM than a direct field would
Windows forbids reading any object except through a pointer
A pointer keeps the object at one address even after a restart
questions.explanation: When the game updates the pointer, code that reads it again follows the new address. A pointer does not make an address permanent.

questions.prompt: Two pointers hold the same address, but one is typed for 32-bit floats and the other for single bytes. What differs when each is followed?
options: How many bytes are read there and how they are interpreted
Which address each one reads, since types change the address
How large each pointer itself is, since the type changes its size
Which process each one can read from, since types pick the process
questions.explanation: The pointee type describes the data at the destination. The pointer's own size comes from the machine architecture, not from what it points to.

questions.prompt: An object starts at address 0x8000 and its mana field sits at offset 0x24. At which address is mana read?
options: 0x8024, the base plus the offset
0x0024, the offset on its own
0x7FDC, the base minus the offset
0x8240, the offset appended to the base
questions.explanation: An offset is a distance, not a place. The base says where the object starts and adding the offset says where the field sits.

questions.prompt: Why can a field offset keep working after a restart when an object's address may not?
options: It is a distance inside the layout, while the base may move
Offsets are saved on the drive, while addresses exist only in RAM
Windows rewrites each offset to match the new base on launch
The game re-checks every offset before it finishes loading
questions.explanation: Health can stay 48 bytes into the same layout for that build while the object's base moves. Recheck the offset if the game or layout changes.

questions.prompt: How does a stack frame differ from a heap object in how long it lasts?
options: A stack frame lasts through one call; a heap object may outlive many calls
A heap object lasts for exactly one call; a stack frame lasts the whole run
Both last until the game restarts, and then both are freed together
Stack bytes are never reused, but heap bytes are reused instantly
questions.explanation: Later calls can reuse a finished frame's bytes. A heap object lives until the game removes it, and its address may then be reused.

questions.prompt: Two different programs each show the address 0x5000. Why might they not refer to the same bytes?
options: Virtual addresses belong to one process, and each process has its own space
One of them must be displaying the address in reverse byte order
Addresses are random numbers that change each time they are displayed
The operating system hides one of them behind a duplicate address
questions.explanation: Each process sees its own virtual address space. That is why an outside tool opens a handle to a specific process and asks Windows to read an address in that process's space.

questions.prompt: Why is a memory scan described as a snapshot gathered over a short stretch of time?
options: The game keeps updating bytes while the scanner copies them
The scanner copies only half of the bytes to save time
Windows freezes the game, so every copied value is out of date
A scan records only values that changed since the last scan
questions.explanation: A scan copies selected memory while the game runs, so fields may describe slightly different moments. It is not a frozen picture of the whole game.

questions.prompt: You read an enemy pointer, the game removes that enemy and reuses its address for another, and then you read health. What can happen?
options: Both reads succeed, but the answer describes the wrong enemy
The second read always fails because the address was freed
Windows returns the first enemy's health from a cache
The pointer automatically updates to follow the new enemy
questions.explanation: Both reads can succeed and still mislead you. Recheck a promising candidate and its object identity before trusting it.

questions.prompt: A tool only maps regions and reads bytes. Which handle design best follows least privilege?
options: Request query and read rights, without write or operation rights
Request every process right now, in case a later feature needs them
Request write and remote-thread rights as a safety net, then leave them unused
Open no handle and infer the memory map from the PE section table
questions.explanation: Permissions should match the operation the tool performs now. Query-and-read rights are enough for a read-only mapper, make intent clear, and are less likely to fail under ordinary Windows security rules.

questions.prompt: How do a page and a region differ?
options: A page is a fixed unit, commonly 4 KiB; a region is a run of pages with matching rules
A page is a run of regions with matching state; a region is a fixed 4 KiB unit
A page belongs to the EXE file on disk; a region exists after the process starts
A page holds code and a region holds data, and the two do not overlap in memory
questions.explanation: A 200 KiB read-only region is many pages sharing the same rules, not one enormous hardware page.

questions.prompt: With 4 KiB pages, what is the offset within its page of the address 0x0052_3A7C?
options: `0xA7C`
questions.explanation: A 4 KiB page is 0x1000 bytes, so the low three hex digits are the offset, 0xA7C, and the rest is the virtual page number.

questions.prompt: In virtual-to-physical translation with 4 KiB pages, which part of an address does translation replace?
options: The page-number part; the low 12-bit offset stays the same
The offset part, while the page number stays the same
Both parts, since a new address replaces the old one
Neither part, since translation only checks permissions
questions.explanation: The offset picks one byte inside a page, so translating from a virtual page to a physical frame leaves it untouched.

questions.prompt: Two different processes both use the virtual address 0x0040_0000. What does that show?
options: An address is a position in one process's own map only
The two processes share the same physical memory at that spot
One of the processes must be reading the other's memory
Virtual addresses are unique across the machine, so one is a copy
questions.explanation: A virtual address belongs to a process's own map. It does not directly name a cell in RAM, and another process may have nothing mapped at that number.

questions.prompt: Why must an API that reads another process's memory be told which process to use?
options: The same number can mean different things in each process
Addresses are encrypted per process and need a process key
Windows reads memory more slowly when no process is named
Only handles can hold addresses larger than 32 bits
questions.explanation: A given number may be mapped in one process and absent in another. The handle chooses which map interprets the address.

questions.prompt: A page is committed. Does that mean it is currently held in physical RAM?
options: No; it may be paged out and restored on access, which is normal
Yes, committed pages stay pinned in RAM until they are freed
Yes, but only while the process is the foreground one
No, committed pages are kept on disk and never held in RAM
questions.explanation: A page fault is ordinary operating-system behavior. Commit says that backing storage is ready, not that the page is resident.

questions.prompt: In virtual memory, what does it mean for an address range to be reserved but not committed?
options: Addresses are set aside, with no storage behind them yet
The range is filled with zeros and is ready to use at once
The range is locked in RAM and protected from paging out
The range is shared with every other process on the machine
questions.explanation: Free ranges have nothing reserved, reserved ranges hold addresses without storage, and committed ranges are usable according to their protection.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of memory type and meaning is correct?
options: Image is a mapped EXE or DLL; private is process-owned, like heap
Image memory is heap data; private memory is a mapped library file
Private memory is a shared file; image memory is a thread stack
Image memory is a graphics texture; private memory is video RAM
questions.explanation: The type says where committed pages came from. Mapped memory is a different type again, for mapped files and shared sections.

questions.prompt: A page is marked as a guard page. Why should a memory scanner skip it?
options: The first access raises an exception and clears the guard
Guard pages are always empty, so reading them is pointless
Guard pages are encrypted by Windows, so reads return nonsense
Reading one permanently locks it, so the process cannot use it
questions.explanation: Guard pages implement things like growing thread stacks. Touching one changes its state, so a scanner should leave it alone.

questions.prompt: A region of memory is both writable and executable. How should an analyst treat it?
options: As a lead to investigate, since some runtimes generate code
As proof that something malicious wrote code into it
As normal, since all code regions are writable and executable
As irrelevant, since permissions do not matter once loaded
questions.explanation: Ask who created it, whether it is inside the expected image, whether a clean run shows it, and whether its lifetime fits a known feature. It is a lead, not a verdict.

questions.prompt: What does 'write xor execute' suggest about normal memory?
options: It should be writable or executable, not both at once
It should be writable and executable so the loader can patch it
It should be readable or writable, but not both at once
It should be executable after every guard flag has been cleared
questions.explanation: Normal compiled code is readable and executable, and data is writable but not executable. Keeping the roles separate is the point.

questions.prompt: A memory-region query at address 0x7000 reports a region with base 0x6000 and size 0x2000. At what address should the next query start?
questions.explanation: The walk moves from the reported base to the first address after the whole run: 0x6000 + 0x2000 = 0x8000. Adding to the query address would skip into the next region.

questions.prompt: A loop walks memory regions by repeatedly asking the system to describe the next one. One call returns 0, meaning nothing was described. What should the loop do?
options: Stop, since nothing was described by that call
Continue with the previous region's data as a fallback
Retry the same address until the call finally succeeds
Skip ahead by one byte and ask again from there
questions.explanation: A zero return means no region was described. Using the leftover result structure would invent a phantom region.

questions.prompt: A loop advances by adding a region size to an address, and requires the new address to be greater than the old one. What does that protect against?
options: Address wraparound, and an endless loop with no progress
Reading the same region twice, since sums can repeat
Running out of memory from storing too many regions
The target changing its protections during the walk
questions.explanation: Checked addition stops a huge region from wrapping around to a low address, and the progress check stops a loop that never moves forward.

questions.prompt: A region query reports a base address and a size. What is true of every page in that run?
options: They share the same state, type and protection
They are all committed and readable
They all hold similar data to each other
They were all touched recently by the process
questions.explanation: A new run starts wherever the state, type or protection changes. Pages within one run are uniform in all three.

questions.prompt: A tool that only inspects a process opens it with a 'read-only' setting. What does that mean?
options: It asks only for query and read rights, not write rights
It opens the process but suspends all of its threads
It reads the process's memory from disk instead of live
It prevents every other tool from opening the process
questions.explanation: The handle should match the question being asked. A tool that only inspects has no need for rights to change things.

questions.prompt: Which kind of address is measured from the start of a module's image, regardless of where the module is loaded?
options: A relative virtual address
A physical address in RAM
A file offset on disk
A live virtual address
questions.explanation: A file offset is a position in the file on disk. A live virtual address is the image base plus the relative address in one run, and a physical address is a hardware memory location after translation.

questions.prompt: A scanner checks that a memory region is committed and readable, then reads it, yet the read fails. How is that possible?
options: The process kept running, so state can change before the read
Readable regions can be read once, and then they are locked
Reads fail on the first attempt, as a built-in safety feature
The scanner's handle expired between the check and the read
questions.explanation: This is a time-of-check to time-of-use race. A robust scanner treats a failed read as a normal event, reports it, and continues when safe.

questions.prompt: A region has base 0x2000 and size 0x6000, but the module it is being compared with ends at 0x5000. What size results when the region is clipped to the module's end?
questions.explanation: The clipped end is the smaller of the region end (0x8000) and the module end (0x5000), so the size is 0x5000 - 0x2000 = 0x3000.

questions.prompt: Which parallel scanner design gives workers the most stable input?
options: Copy bounded readable code regions once, then scan immutable local buffers
Let every worker repeatedly query and read arbitrary remote pages as it goes
Give every byte its own operating-system thread and merge the results at the end
Patch matches as soon as any worker finds one, so the next worker sees new bytes
questions.explanation: Remote memory changes and Windows reads can fail. Copying once keeps that unstable boundary in one stage, and workers then compare over immutable slices.

questions.prompt: In a parallel scanner for another process, why should only one stage copy memory out of the target while workers search local buffers?
options: It keeps the unstable cross-process step in one place, and workers search stable private data
Workers cannot run on more than one core if they share a handle to the target process
Operating systems only allow a single thread to ever read from another process
Local buffers are always faster to read, so the target must never be touched again
questions.explanation: Reading another process can fail or change under you. Doing that once, then scanning private copies, keeps the risky boundary small and lets workers run safely in parallel.

questions.prompt: Which benefit comes from scanning copied snapshots instead of live memory?
options: A page cannot disappear halfway through a worker's comparison
The scan reads fewer bytes in total, because copies are compressed in memory
The workers can write matches directly back into the live game safely
The scan no longer needs a pattern, since a snapshot knows its own contents
questions.explanation: Copied bytes can also be saved and replayed in tests. The copy does not reduce what is read, and the lab never writes to the game.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes safety and progress promises?
options: Safety says what bad result must never happen; progress says what must eventually finish
Safety says every thread finishes in time; progress says no thread reads a byte twice
Safety is about speed on large inputs; progress is about memory used by each worker
Safety only applies to code using `unsafe`; progress applies to code that uses atomics
questions.explanation: The lesson gives rules such as "the result cap is never exceeded" for safety and "the main thread joins every worker" for progress.

questions.prompt: Why is "it uses atomics" not a complete concurrency argument?
options: You must name which safety fact each atomic protects and what lets each loop finish
Atomics are slower than locks, so they make a scanner unsafe on large inputs
Atomics cannot be shared between threads, so they must be cloned for each worker
Atomic operations are only valid on integers that are smaller than a pointer
questions.explanation: The lesson wants a reason for each atomic: for example, the index hands out regions once and the counter bounds the results.

questions.prompt: Why does the real tool cap all copied executable bytes at 128 MiB?
options: Memory safety stops corruption but not an unbounded allocation exhausting the machine
Windows refuses to read more than 128 MiB from any one process at one time in total
The pattern is only valid inside the first 128 MiB of a module's code, so more is wasted
Rust cannot index a `Vec<u8>` larger than 128 MiB when building for 32-bit Windows
questions.explanation: Safe code can still be logically unbounded. A limit on the total snapshot makes memory use predictable.

questions.prompt: A page of the target changes while a scanner is copying it, so the copy comes back incomplete. What is the safest handling?
options: Skip that region and report a diagnostic, so no partial buffer is ever scanned
Scan the partial buffer anyway, since most of the bytes were read correctly
Retry the read forever until the page stops changing, then continue with the scan
Fill the missing part with zeros and scan, since zeros never match a pattern
questions.explanation: A partial copy can give wrong or missing matches. Skipping one region and saying so keeps the other snapshots trustworthy.

questions.prompt: Several worker threads pick their work by atomically incrementing a shared counter and using the old value as their item number. What does this guarantee?
options: Each worker gets a distinct item, so none is handed out twice
The items are processed strictly in order, one after another
The workers all wait until every worker has taken an item
The counter itself becomes immune to being read by other threads
questions.explanation: An atomic increment returns the previous value and advances the counter in one indivisible step. Two threads can never receive the same number.

questions.prompt: Why is dynamic scheduling, where workers fetch the next index when free, better than fixed quarters?
options: A worker that gets small regions can keep helping while another scans a large one
It guarantees that every worker scans exactly the same number of bytes in total
It removes the need for an atomic counter, because each worker owns its own range
It makes the order of results fixed, so the final sort is no longer needed
questions.explanation: Fixed shares can leave one worker idle while another is stuck with big regions. Sorting is still needed, since completion order varies.

questions.prompt: A large buffer is split into chunks that are scanned independently for a 6-byte pattern. By how many bytes must neighboring chunks overlap so that no match is lost at a boundary?
options: 5 bytes
6 bytes
3 bytes
0 bytes
questions.explanation: Overlapping by pattern length minus one lets any boundary-crossing match appear whole in one chunk. Results from the overlap must then be deduplicated.

questions.prompt: Why cap the number of worker threads at the available cores and at the amount of work?
options: Extra threads cost memory and scheduling time, and ones with no work only sit idle
The operating system refuses to create more threads than there are processor cores
More threads than work items always change the results of the scan
Each core can only hold a single thread's data, so extra threads are discarded
questions.explanation: Threads are not free, and more of them than cores or tasks adds overhead without adding speed. A worker with nothing left to claim does no useful work.

questions.prompt: Why is a per-thread result limit of 4,096 not enough with eight workers?
options: The workers together could still produce 32,768 items
Eight workers would each skip 4,096 items, so no result would ever be recorded
The limit would be applied eight times, so only 512 items could ever be kept
Each worker would reset the limit when it claimed another region from the queue
questions.explanation: 8 × 4,096 = 32,768. A bound across every worker needs one shared counter, not one limit per thread.

questions.prompt: With a global cap of three, worker 1 has two matches and worker 2 finds two more. How many can be published?
options: Three in total, because only one of worker 2's matches gets the last slot
Four in total, because each worker checks the counter at the same time
Two in total, because the second worker is cancelled after its first match
Five in total, because the cap applies only to matches that came from worker 1
questions.explanation: Each match must reserve a slot through the shared counter. Reading "2 of 3 used" and then appending would publish four.

questions.prompt: Why must a shared match counter check the cap and increment in one atomic step, rather than loading the count and adding to it separately?
options: Otherwise two threads could both see room for the last slot and exceed the cap
Separate steps would make the counter slower, though the result would be the same
Atomic operations are the only way to add numbers inside a thread
Loading and adding would reset the counter to zero after every thread finishes
questions.explanation: A check followed by a separate update leaves a gap in which another thread can slip in. Doing both as one indivisible step closes that gap.

questions.prompt: In atomics, what is the purpose of pairing a release store with an acquire load?
options: Writes made before the release become visible to a thread that sees the value
It locks the variable so that only one thread can read it at a time
It forces the threads to take turns, running one after another
It copies the value to every processor immediately, bypassing all caches
questions.explanation: Release and acquire order memory operations so one thread can safely publish a signal, such as a stop flag, to another. They do not lock anything or serialize the threads.

questions.prompt: Why do the snapshot bytes need no mutex or atomic?
options: They are immutable, so many workers can read them without conflict
They are stored in a different process, so the workers cannot touch them
They are read one at a time by the main thread, so the workers only get copies
They are marked executable, and Windows serializes every read of executable pages
questions.explanation: Shared reads of data that never changes are safe. The shared mutable pieces are only the index, the counter, and the flag.

questions.prompt: Why might code sort results and remove duplicates even when the design says duplicates should not occur?
options: Correctness should not rely on an assumption, such as no overlapping chunks, that may break
Duplicates always occur in parallel code, so this step is required for every result
Sorted results run faster, so removing duplicates is a performance requirement
The operating system returns each address twice, so a cleanup is always needed
questions.explanation: Defensive cleanup protects the output if a later change, such as overlapping chunks, begins reporting an address twice. The result stays correct without relying on hope.

questions.prompt: Capture takes 80% of a run and scanning takes 20%. What is the best overall speedup from parallelizing the scan perfectly?
options: Roughly 1.25x
Roughly 5x
Roughly 10x
Roughly 0.8x
questions.explanation: The 80% that stays serial remains, so the best case is 1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25. More workers shrink only the 20% part.

questions.prompt: A signature scan expected to find exactly one match finds zero or many. Does adding more worker threads help?
options: No, the cause is a wrong assumption about build, range or pattern, not speed
Yes, since more threads cover more memory and will find the missing match
Yes, since extra threads filter out the duplicate matches before they are counted
No, because parallel scans are not allowed to report more than one match
questions.explanation: Parallelism changes how fast a scan runs, not what it finds. Zero or many hits point to the same causes as in a single-threaded scan.

questions.prompt: What should happen if one scanner worker panics?
options: The main thread's join reports it as an error instead of waiting forever
The other workers continue silently, and the missing region is left out of the results
The panic is hidden by the sort step, so the final list still looks complete
The process under test is stopped, since a worker panic corrupts its memory
questions.explanation: One progress promise is that a worker panic becomes an error rather than an endless wait. The main thread joins every worker before publishing.

questions.prompt: A guard faces (1, 0). The unit direction to the player is (0.6, 0.8). With VIEW_CONE_COS = 0.5, can the guard see the player, ignoring walls and distance?
questions.explanation: For unit vectors the dot product is the cosine of the angle between them. 0.6 is at least cos 60° = 0.5, so the player is less than 60° from the facing (about 53°) and inside the cone.
options: Yes: 0.6 × 1 + 0.8 × 0 = 0.6, which is at least 0.5
No: 0.8 is larger than 0.6, so the target lies mostly to the side
Yes: any direction with a positive y part falls inside the cone
No: 0.6 + 0.8 = 1.4 is above 1, so the dot product is invalid

questions.prompt: A guard stands at (2, 1) and a player at (7, 13). What is the offset from the guard to the player, and what does it mean?
options: (5, 12), the arrow from the guard to the player
(9, 14), the sum of the two positions
(-5, -12), the arrow from the player to the guard
13, the single number for the distance
questions.explanation: The offset is the target's position minus the guard's: (7 - 2, 13 - 1) = (5, 12). It is a vector, an arrow, not a single number.

questions.prompt: A guard sees up to a distance of 13. One player is at offset (5, 12) and another at offset (12, 9). Which pass the distance check?
options: Only the first, at 13; the second is 15 away
Only the second, since its parts are larger than the first one's
Both, since each separate part of each offset is below 13
Neither, since both of them lie right on the limit of sight
questions.explanation: The square root of 25 + 144 is 13, which is within the limit. The square root of 144 + 81 is 15, which is not.

questions.prompt: For two unit vectors, what does the dot product equal?
options: The cosine of the angle between them
The angle between them in degrees
The distance between their tips
The product of their lengths added together
questions.explanation: For unit vectors, `a.x × b.x + a.y × b.y` is the cosine of the angle. For a guard facing east it is simply the other vector's x part.

questions.prompt: A vision rule uses a cosine threshold of 0.5. What angle does that correspond to?
options: 60 degrees, since unit vectors that far apart have tips 1 apart
30 degrees, since the cosine is half of the angle in degrees
45 degrees, since half is the middle of the way up to 90 degrees
90 degrees, since a quarter turn is half of a half turn in angle
questions.explanation: Two unit vectors 60 degrees apart form an equilateral triangle, so their tips are 1 apart, and the cosine is 0.5. The constant is a cosine, not a fraction of the cone.

questions.prompt: A vision rule rejects targets whose direction has a dot product below 0.5 with the facing direction. What does it reject?
options: Directions over 60 degrees from the facing, on either side
Directions less than 60 degrees away from the facing direction
Directions that are behind the character, and no others
Directions that are farther than half a unit away from the NPC
questions.explanation: Cosine falls steadily as the angle grows, so a dot product below 0.5 means an angle above 60 degrees. The cone is 60 + 60 = 120 degrees wide.

questions.prompt: A guard at the origin faces east (1, 0). A player stands due north at (0, 5). Does a 60-degree cone rule see them?
options: No: the dot product is 0, which is a 90-degree turn
Yes: the player is well within the distance range of sight
Yes: the dot product of the unit directions is exactly 1
No: the dot product is negative, since the player is behind
questions.explanation: The unit direction is (0, 1), and 0 x 1 + 1 x 0 = 0, below 0.5. Distance passes, but the cone check fails.

questions.prompt: Why does the code compare the dot product with a constant instead of computing the angle?
options: Getting an angle needs a slower inverse cosine
An angle cannot be stored in an `f32` value
The dot product is already measured in degrees
An angle would change the guard's own facing
questions.explanation: Comparing with a cosine worked out once gives the same answer using two multiplications and one addition.

questions.prompt: Line of sight is checked by stepping along the line and testing whether a sample point is inside a wall's box. A wall spans x 5 to 7 and y -1 to 1. Why does a sample at (6, 0) stop the check?
options: It lies inside the wall's bounds, so the view is blocked
It lies too far from the guard for the check to continue
It lies on top of the player, so the check has finished
Its y value is zero, which means a wall
questions.explanation: A point is inside a box when each coordinate lies between the corners. The check stops at the first such sample.

questions.prompt: A sight line runs from (0, 0) to (4, 2), and a wall covers x 2 to 3 and y 2 to 3. Does the wall block sight?
options: No: across the wall's x range the line is below the wall
Yes: the line shares the same x range as the wall does
Yes: the line ends inside the area that the wall covers
Yes: the wall lies between the two points when measured in x
questions.explanation: The line has y = 0.5 x, so over the wall's x range it passes below the box. Sharing an x range is not enough.

questions.prompt: A line-of-sight check samples every 0.2 units across a view distance of 12. How many samples does it need?
options: 60, from 12 divided by 0.2
2.4, from 12 multiplied by 0.2
12, one for each unit of distance
240, from 12 multiplied by 20 and again by 1
questions.explanation: Each sample is tested against every wall, so line of sight costs more with distance and with finer steps. Engines often use exact ray casts instead.

questions.prompt: What does utility AI do each time it chooses?
options: Scores every option for the situation and runs the highest
Walks through a priority list and runs the first that succeeds
Moves between named states along fixed arrows
Picks randomly among options that score above 0
questions.explanation: A state machine asks which mode it is in. Utility scoring asks which option is best right now. Priority lists belong to behaviour trees.

questions.prompt: A fighter at health 0.3 has an enemy in view, no cover, and one potion. Which option scores highest?
options: Take cover, at 0.72, ahead of heal at 0.70 and attack at 0.58
Heal, at 0.70, which beats both attack and take cover
Attack, at 0.58, since it scores best when an enemy is in view
Attack, at 0.58, since it is the first option in the match
questions.explanation: Take cover scores 0.9 − 0.6 × 0.3 = 0.72, ahead of healing at 1.0 − 0.3 = 0.70 and attacking at 0.4 + 0.18 = 0.58.

questions.prompt: Option A scores 0.8 - 0.5h and option B scores 1.0 - h, where h is health from 0 to 1. At what health do they tie?
options: 0.2, since the difference of the two constants is 0.2
0.8, since that is the starting constant in option A
0.1, since the two slopes differ by about a tenth in size
questions.explanation: Setting 0.8 - 0.5h = 1.0 - h gives 0.5h = 0.2, so h = 0.4. Below that health, B scores higher.

questions.prompt: Hurt (health 0.3), in cover, and out of potions, which option does the fighter choose?
options: Attack, since cover and heal both score 0
Take cover, since it was chosen last time
Heal, since low health always means heal
Nothing, since no option scores above 0.58
questions.explanation: Once in cover, taking cover scores 0, and healing with no potions scores 0. Attack, at 0.58, is all that is left.

questions.prompt: A utility chooser keeps only options with a score above 0 and picks the highest. If every option scores 0, what does it return?
options: Nothing, so another behavior like patrol keeps control
The first option in the list, used as a default choice
A random option picked from the whole list of options
An error that stops the whole game from running
questions.explanation: With no option worth doing, the chooser returns nothing and leaves control to another system.

questions.prompt: Near a switch point, a tiny health change can flip the choice every tick. How do games damp this?
options: Add a small bonus to whatever the NPC is already doing
Round health to the nearest whole number before scoring
Run the scoring only once every second instead of each tick
Remove the option that scored lowest on the last tick
questions.explanation: A rival option must then beat the current action clearly before the NPC switches, so the choice stops flickering.

questions.prompt: In a behaviour tree, what is the difference between a selector and a sequence?
options: A selector stops at the first success; a sequence at the first failure
A selector runs every child; a sequence runs only its last child
A selector holds a score; a sequence holds the current state
A selector runs children right to left; a sequence left to right
questions.explanation: The guard's tree is one selector of sequences, tried in priority order. At 20 health the first sequence reaches flee and the rest are never inspected.

questions.prompt: Where does a behavior tree keep remembered values between ticks, such as how long it has seen the player?
options: In a shared store beside the tree, often called a blackboard
Inside each node of the tree, which remembers its own history
In the player's own data, which the tree borrows
Nowhere, since the tree recomputes everything from scratch
questions.explanation: A tree keeps no memory between ticks by itself, so engines store these values in a blackboard.

questions.prompt: How did the guard's four arrows into Flee appear in the behaviour tree?
options: As one child placed first, since priorities restart at the top
As four separate sequences, one for each of the other four states
As a blackboard value that every node in the tree must read first
They disappear, since a behaviour tree has no way of making a guard flee
questions.explanation: Because priorities are re-checked from the root each tick, the single first child covers every state.

questions.prompt: A structure holds four 4-byte floats, then a 4-byte integer, then a 1-byte flag, then another 4-byte integer. With typical alignment, where does the last integer start?
options: 0x18, after three padding bytes
0x15, right after the flag
0x14, on top of the flag
0x1C, after four padding bytes
questions.explanation: The floats fill 0x00 to 0x0F, the first integer 0x10 to 0x13, and the flag sits at 0x14. A 4-byte field must start at a multiple of 4, so bytes 0x15 to 0x17 are padding.

questions.prompt: A structure's fields add up to 33 bytes, but its size is 36. What explains the difference?
options: Padding bytes that the compiler inserts for alignment
A hidden header that the compiler adds to every structure
A rounding error made when the size was measured
Debug information that is stored inside the structure
questions.explanation: Alignment makes the compiler insert padding so each field starts at a suitable address, and the total is rounded to the alignment of the largest field.

questions.prompt: In a toy C++ program, you write 9 into the state byte. What can happen, and why?
options: It depends on the `switch`: a range check gives a default branch, a bare jump table may crash
It goes to Patrol, since every out-of-range value is treated as state 0 by the compiler
It crashes at once, since one byte cannot hold a value that lies past the last real state
It becomes Chase, since 9 wraps around to 1 when it is stored inside a single byte
questions.explanation: Compilers often turn a switch into a jump table. With a range check, 9 takes the default branch; without one, the code reads past the table and usually crashes. In Rust, safe code cannot store 9 in a `GuardState`.

questions.prompt: The tool captured a valid gold address, but the second snapshot has a different side pointer. What should the advanced pipeline do?
questions.explanation: A remote address has meaning only while the object path and target profile still support it. A changed side pointer invalidates the earlier destination, so the correct transaction outcome is no write.
options: Stop without writing because the object identity changed
Write to the old address because it was valid earlier
Search all writable memory for the old gold number
Ignore the pointer and compare only the PID

questions.prompt: What is the central idea of splitting a tool's work into phases separated by gates?
options: Data is rechecked before the tool acts, since earlier reads may be stale
Each phase adds more code, so the finished tool looks more advanced to users
Gates make the game pause between each of the phases of the tool
Gates encrypt the data as it moves between the phases
questions.explanation: The point is not extra code. A single long function trusts earlier facts after the game may have changed, while gates check them again.

questions.prompt: A snapshot stores the whole chain of pointers that was followed plus the final value, not just the value. Why?
options: Comparing the chain catches a changed link, not just a changed value
It makes the snapshot smaller than storing the value alone would do
Each pointer holds a backup copy of the game's saved data on disk
A value on its own cannot be stored by a tool
questions.explanation: Equality then asks whether the whole chain and its value stayed the same, which is stronger than comparing the final address only.

questions.prompt: A snapshot records the intermediate objects of a pointer chain. What can a changed intermediate object mean?
options: The chain now leads elsewhere, so an action based on it is invalid
The final value became larger, so the old value can still be reused
The game saved its state, so nothing else has changed
The tool's handle expired, so the whole chain was deleted
questions.explanation: A change in an intermediate link means the root reaches another object or the match moved on. Either invalidates a proposed action.

questions.prompt: How can a tool decide that a read result is stable enough to act on?
options: Capture twice and accept only if both captures match, otherwise retry
Capture once and wait a second before acting on the result
Capture repeatedly until the value happens to be zero
Capture once and compare it with the result of the previous run
questions.explanation: Equal consecutive captures suggest a quiet moment. A capped retry loop then gives up with an error if it never sees one.

questions.prompt: Why are two matching reads not a mathematical proof that nothing changed in between?
options: A change could happen and be undone between reads without showing
Reads of memory give random results, so they do not match exactly
A match says nothing about the first read, just about the second one
Reading memory changes it, so a match cannot be trusted fully
questions.explanation: It is an optimistic consistency check that assumes a short read sees a quiet moment, then verifies the assumption. It does not lock the running game.

questions.prompt: What can give a real guarantee that a larger structure did not change while it was being read?
options: Pausing the target, a game-made snapshot, or a version counter
Reading it three times in a row and comparing all three of the reads
Reading it from a faster loop so that less time passes in between
Reading it with extra privileges so that the game cooperates fully
questions.explanation: These give a real guarantee. Two equal reads are only a practical gate for a small structure in a safe, offline setting.

questions.prompt: Why should a retry loop have a maximum number of attempts?
options: An endless loop makes a broken tool look frozen; an error is clearer
Retrying more than a few times damages the target's own memory
Each retry runs more slowly than the one that came before it
The operating system forbids loops that run for a long time
questions.explanation: If the pointer path keeps changing, waiting forever helps nobody. Stopping with an error is more useful than appearing frozen.

questions.prompt: When the tool runs with no arguments, what rights does it request, and why?
options: Query and read only, so a tool that only looks has a handle that cannot write
Query, read, operation, and write, since the handle must be the same for every run
Write only, since reads are allowed for every process by default
No rights at all, since the operating system chooses them after the handle opens
questions.explanation: The command decides what access it needs before opening the process. The `--set` mode adds the operation and write rights.

questions.prompt: Why decide whether write access is needed before opening another process, rather than after?
options: Rights are fixed when the process is opened, so ask for write if needed
A process cannot be reopened later with different access rights
Read-just handles are slower than handles that have write rights
The operating system asks the user again whenever any rights change
questions.explanation: The decision about write rights happens before the process is opened, so write access is requested only when the user actually asked for a change.

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes a careful guarded write?
options: Capture again and require a match, write, then read back and compare
Write the new bytes, capture again, then compare with the old values
Read once, write the new bytes, and then trust the call's success
Write the new bytes twice and keep the result of the second write
