questions.explanation: Parity makes the count of 1s among APnDP, RnW, A2, A3 and itself even. One 1 plus the parity 1 gives two. Sent with Start = 1, Stop = 0 and Park = 1, the byte is `0xA5`.

questions.prompt: A shift routine places the incoming bit at position 'top', the register's highest bit. Why is top 0 for a bypass register but 31 for a 32-bit ID register?
options: The bypass register has one bit, so one cell is bottom and top
The bypass register is wider, so it needs fewer shifts
The ID register shifts right, and the bypass register shifts left
The bypass register is read before the ID register
questions.explanation: The top position is the register length minus one. A one-bit register has only one cell, while the ID register has 32.

questions.prompt: A phone's kernel marks a page holding a key as readable only in kernel mode. An engineer halts the processor through an open JTAG port and reads that page. Why did the kernel's protection not stop the read?
questions.explanation: Memory protection is enforced by the running processor as it executes code. A halted core executes nothing, and the debug unit performs its own bus reads. That is why production devices lock the port in hardware, with fuses and authentication, instead of relying on software running on the chip.
options: The debug logic reads memory over the bus itself, and the kernel's rules need a running core
The kernel always lets debuggers read any page, since debug access has special rights in kernel mode
JTAG reads memory faster than the kernel can check it, so the protection arrives too late to matter
The page was never really protected, because a kernel-only marking is only advisory to the hardware

questions.prompt: Why did the bed-of-nails test fixture become hopeless for many modern boards?
options: Packages like a ball grid array hide connections underneath, out of any probe's reach
Modern boards use no copper traces at all, so there is nothing for a spring pin to touch
Spring-loaded pins cannot carry a signal fast enough to test chips with high clock speeds
Boards are now built in single copies, so a custom fixture for each one costs too much
questions.explanation: Surface-mounted chips already squeezed their pins closer together in the 1980s. A ball grid array joins through solder balls on its underside, which is why the Joint Test Action Group built the probes into the chips.

questions.prompt: What was JTAG's original job, before it became a debugging path?
options: Testing board connections for bad solder joints, using probes built into the chips
Locking a chip's debug logic so that only the maker's lab could halt the core
Loading a new operating system into a device over a four-wire serial link
Measuring how fast each chip on a board could run at its highest clock rate
questions.explanation: The group formed in 1985 to find bad joints such as solder bridging two pins. The standard, IEEE 1149.1, came in 1990, and the debugging use came later.

questions.prompt: What can a boundary-scan cell do in test mode that it does not do in normal operation?
options: Capture the level on its pin, or drive a chosen level onto the pin
Copy the chip's flash contents onto the wire without involving the processor
Reset the TAP controller whenever it sees a 1 on its pin
Hold the pin's level steady while the chip's own logic keeps driving it
questions.explanation: In normal operation the cell is transparent, so signals pass straight through. In test mode it can record the pin's level or override the chip's own logic.

questions.prompt: What happens on each clock tick in a shift register?
options: Each cell takes its neighbour's value; a bit enters at one end and one falls out the other
Each cell is cleared to 0, and the new pattern is loaded into all the cells at once
Every cell copies the value of the first cell, so the whole row ends up holding the same bit
The cells swap places in pairs, so each bit moves two places along the whole row
questions.explanation: That is how captured levels can leave through a single wire while a new pattern arrives through another. Chips linked this way form a scan chain.

questions.prompt: Which of the TAP's four signals steers the controller from one state to the next?
options: TMS, Test Mode Select
TCK, Test Clock
TDI, Test Data In
TDO, Test Data Out
questions.explanation: TCK ticks every action, and TDI and TDO carry the data bits in and out. TMS is the one wire that gives orders, by choosing between the controller's two next states.

questions.prompt: Why would a board test apply a pattern with a 1 on each trace and then repeat it with a 0?
options: Each pattern alone misses a trace stuck at that same level
The second pattern confirms the first was measured correctly
A trace conducts only when driven both high and low in turn
Testing both patterns doubles the speed of the test
questions.explanation: A trace stuck at 1 passes the 1 test and a trace stuck at 0 passes the 0 test. Only the two patterns together expose both faults.

questions.prompt: How can the debugger give orders such as capture, shift and update using only the one wire TMS?
options: The TAP controller is a state machine, and TMS picks one of its two next states each tick
The debugger sends each order as a number in a packet, which the chip decodes from the wire
Each order has its own wire inside the chip, and TMS only selects which wire gets used
TMS changes how fast the clock ticks, and each tick speed stands for a different order
questions.explanation: A sequence of TMS levels walks the controller wherever the debugger needs it, through Capture, Shift and Update. SWD is the design that sends packets instead.

questions.prompt: What does the Update state do after a shift?
options: It copies the final pattern to the outputs in one step, hiding the in-between patterns
It loads the register from its inputs, such as the levels currently seen on the pins
It moves the register one place toward TDO, so the old bits leave and new ones arrive in
It returns the controller to Test-Logic-Reset, so the test logic is switched off again
questions.explanation: While bits ripple along during Shift, the register passes through many in-between patterns. Update makes the pins change once, to the final pattern.

questions.prompt: A debugger is unsure what state the TAP controller is in. What can it do?
options: Send five 1s on TMS, which reaches Test-Logic-Reset from any state
Pulse TCK once with TMS at 0, which returns the controller to Run-Test/Idle
Send 32 clocks with TMS at 0, so any shift in progress runs to its end
Switch the chip off and on, because the controller cannot be reset by signals alone
questions.explanation: From any state, five clocks with TMS at 1 reach Test-Logic-Reset, so the debugger can start again from a known place.

questions.prompt: What does the BYPASS instruction do?
options: It selects a one-bit register, so the chip adds only a single bit to the chain
It selects a 32-bit register that holds the chip's manufacturer and part number
It selects the boundary-scan register, so the chip's pins can be driven for a board test
It disconnects the chip's TDO wire, so the chip drops out of the chain entirely
questions.explanation: BYPASS lets the debugger reach other chips without shifting through this one's long registers. The 32-bit identifying register belongs to IDCODE.

questions.prompt: With every chip on a chain in BYPASS, why does timing a single 1 from TDI to TDO count the chips?
options: Each chip adds exactly one bit to the chain, so the delay in clocks reveals the number of chips
Each chip adds its IDCODE length to the chain, so the delay reveals the total of the ID bits
Each chip inserts one clock of delay in its TAP controller, regardless of its register
The 1 is copied by every chip, so the number of copies that return equals the chip count
questions.explanation: After reset a data scan can also read the ID of every chip that has one. Together these two small registers let a debugger explore a board it knows nothing about.

questions.prompt: How does a JTAG debugger's request differ from a Windows debugger's request?
options: It stops the whole processor, kernel included, and the OS has no say because it stopped running
It pauses one thread through the OS, but over a hardware link the OS cannot monitor
It asks the kernel to halt every thread, using a driver with the highest privilege level
It stops the processor only while user-mode code runs, since the chip protects the kernel
questions.explanation: A Windows debugger asks the OS to pause one thread, and the rest of the system runs on. A JTAG debugger works through on-chip debug logic wired to the test pins.

questions.prompt: How do on-chip hardware breakpoints and watchpoints work?
options: Comparators halt the core when it fetches from or accesses a chosen address, set from outside
The debugger overwrites the instruction at that address with a special halting instruction
The debug unit single-steps the core and compares each address in software before it goes on
The operating system watches the chosen address and then signals the debugger via a driver
questions.explanation: They work like the x86 debug registers of Lesson 2.4, except that they are set through the chip's test pins rather than by code running on the core.

questions.prompt: Why did Arm design Serial Wire Debug?
options: Four or five signals are a lot for a twenty-pin chip, and SWD needs only two
JTAG cannot halt a core or read memory at all, and SWD is the design that adds both
JTAG's clock is too slow for modern chips, so SWD was made with a much faster clock
JTAG sends no error checking at all, so SWD adds a parity bit to each of its wires
questions.explanation: SWD uses SWCLK and a single data wire, SWDIO, which the debugger and the chip take turns driving. Behind either protocol sits the same debug port, so halting and memory access work alike.

questions.prompt: In one SWD read, how many bits does the chip itself send, counting its acknowledgement, the data and the parity bit?
options: 36: a 3-bit acknowledgement, 32 data bits, and 1 parity bit
44: the 8-bit request, a 3-bit acknowledgement, 32 data bits, and 1 parity bit
35: a 3-bit acknowledgement and 32 data bits
33: 32 data bits and 1 parity bit
questions.explanation: The debugger sends the 8-bit request. After the turnaround, the chip answers with 3 + 32 + 1 = 36 bits.

questions.prompt: An SWD read delivers 32 data bits that contain seven 1s. What must the parity bit be?
options: 1, so the total number of 1s is eight, which is even
0, so the total number of 1s stays at seven
1, so the total number of 1s is eight, which is odd
0, because seven is an odd number of 1s and no parity bit is needed
questions.explanation: The parity bit is chosen to make the count of 1s even. A single bit damaged on the wire then shows up as an odd count.

questions.prompt: Why is a fuse that disables debug stronger than turning debug off in early boot code?
options: Hardware reads the fuse at power-on, before software runs; boot code protects only from then on
A fuse can be reset by the debugger once authenticated, while boot code can never be undone
A fuse is readable by the kernel at any time, while early boot code cannot be read later
A fuse protects the whole product line at once, while early boot code protects one unit
questions.explanation: An eFuse is a one-time programmable bit that nothing can change back from 1 to 0. Early boot code protects only if nothing can run before it.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that the hardware reading the debug fuses is built to fail closed?
options: Any fuse reading other than a clean "open" leaves debug off, in case the check is disturbed
If the fuse reading is unclear, debug is left on, so the maker can still repair the unit later
If the fuse reading is unclear, the chip is erased at once, so no stored secret can remain
A fuse that is read twice with different results is then treated as a clean "open" reading
questions.explanation: Failing closed means an attacker who disturbs the check gains nothing by making it confusing. The lock follows the chip through its life as one-way fuse changes.

questions.prompt: Why can an open debug port undermine secure boot, even if the boot checks passed?
options: The debugger can write memory, so it can change code that secure boot checked a moment earlier
The debugger can reset the fuses that hold the boot ROM's key hash to any value
The debugger can sign its own boot image, using the maker's private key stored on the chip
The debugger can remove the boot ROM from the chip, so the chain starts from the next stage
questions.explanation: The debug logic does not care what software the chip runs. A debugger that can halt the core can also read keys and decrypted code.

questions.prompt: A flaw is found in one stage of a console's boot chain. Which stage's flaw cannot be fixed by a system update on consoles that are already sold?
questions.explanation: The boot ROM is written into the chip at the factory and cannot be rewritten, and nothing runs before it to check it. Every later stage can be replaced by an update, because the stage before it verifies the new version's signature like any other. A boot ROM flaw is fixed only in new chips.
options: The boot ROM, which is written into the chip when it is manufactured
The bootloader, which the boot ROM checks before running it
The system kernel, which the bootloader checks before running it
The game partition's OS, which the hypervisor starts above the system

questions.prompt: A console's anti-rollback fuses record a minimum security version of 3. It is offered a boot image that the platform holder genuinely signed, with security version 2. What happens?
questions.explanation: A signature proves who made the code, not that it is current. Version 2 may contain a hole that version 3 fixed, so the boot code compares the image's security version with the count of blown fuses and refuses anything lower, however genuine its signature.
options: The boot code refuses it, because 2 is below the fused minimum of 3
It runs, because its signature is valid and the maker really did sign it
It runs, and the console blows another fuse to record the new version
It runs, but only while the console is offline and not signed in

questions.prompt: What is a system on a chip (SoC)?
options: One chip holding most parts, such as CPU cores and a GPU
A circuit board that holds several separate chips and a fan
A memory chip that stores the system software for the console
A chip that is dedicated to security checks and nothing else
questions.explanation: In a console the CPU cores and GPU sit on the same piece of silicon. A gaming PC has a separate graphics card with its own video memory.

questions.prompt: How does a graphics buffer get from the CPU to the GPU on a console with unified memory?
options: The CPU writes it to the shared pool, and the GPU reads the same bytes
The CPU copies it across a PCI Express bus into the GPU's own video RAM
The security processor copies it between two separate memory pools
The hypervisor encrypts it in the game partition and decrypts it for the GPU
questions.explanation: On a gaming PC the textures and buffers are copied across the PCI Express bus. A console's CPU and GPU share one pool, so no copy is needed.

questions.prompt: The PlayStation 5's memory bus is 256 bits wide and each wire carries 14 billion bits per second. How many bytes per second is that?
options: 448 GB: 256 x 14 = 3,584 billion bits, divided by 8 bits per byte
3,584 GB: 256 x 14 = 3,584 billion, counting each bit as a byte
1,792 GB: 256 x 14 = 3,584 billion bits, divided by 2 for the two directions
1.75 GB: 14 billion bits divided by 8 bits per byte, for a single wire
questions.explanation: Multiplying the width by the rate gives total bits per second. Dividing by 8 turns bits into bytes, which gives 448 GB every second shared by the CPU and GPU.

questions.prompt: At 60 frames per second, roughly how much time does the console have for all of one frame's work?
options: About 16.7 ms, from 1,000 ms divided by 60
About 60 ms, since each frame uses the full number of frames
About 33.3 ms, from 1,000 ms divided by 30
About 6.0 ms, from 1,000 ms divided by 60 and then by 3
questions.explanation: A second has 1,000 ms, so 60 frames each get 1,000 / 60, which is about 16.7 ms. A background task that takes 2 ms at the wrong moment makes a visible stutter.

questions.prompt: Why can console developers spend a frame's time budget almost to the last millisecond?
options: Every console of one model has the same chip, memory and clocks, so one measurement holds for all
The console's hypervisor stretches a frame when a game runs late, so a late frame never shows up
Console games skip all operating system calls, so nothing else uses time in a frame
Unified memory removes the frame limit, because the GPU can simply wait for the CPU
questions.explanation: A PC game must run on thousands of part combinations, while a console game targets exactly one. Developers can even compile shaders ahead of time for the single GPU.

questions.prompt: The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X use the same x86-64 instruction set as many PCs. Why is moving a console game to PC still porting work?
options: The game's code calls the console's own operating system and graphics interfaces
The console CPU cores store numbers in the opposite byte order from a PC
The console encrypts its machine code with an instruction set that PCs do not run
The console GPU cannot be addressed by a PC's graphics driver at all
questions.explanation: The instruction set is shared, but machine code calls into the console's OS and graphics interfaces, such as a console version of Direct3D 12 on Xbox.

questions.prompt: A malformed save file crashes a game on a console with a hypervisor and two partitions. Why does the damage stay inside the game partition?
options: System partition memory, which holds account tokens, is not mapped into the game
The security processor restarts the whole console, so any damage is erased on reboot
The game partition is read-only, so a crash cannot change any of the saved data on disk
The hypervisor rewrites each save file with a checksum before the game can open it again
questions.explanation: A partition is a virtual machine that sees only the cores, memory and devices the hypervisor gives it. The game partition can still make narrow, checked requests of system services.

questions.prompt: Which description fits the console's security processor?
options: A small separate processor that starts before the main cores and holds keys they never see
A main CPU core reserved for the hypervisor, which runs keys on behalf of the game partition
A chip on the network adapter that scans all incoming data for modified software
A fuse bank that counts the security version and refuses old boot images itself
questions.explanation: Most console chips contain such a processor. It performs the checks and, later, decrypts game content without handing the keys to the game or the system software.

questions.prompt: Why does the chain of trust need no check on the boot ROM itself?
options: It is written into the chip at manufacture and nobody can change it, so it is where trust starts
It is signed by the bootloader, which lets the chain check itself in a loop
It is rechecked by the hypervisor every time a game starts, so it never needs a first check
It is stored in flash, where the owner can replace it with a signed update
questions.explanation: Every later stage is trusted only because an earlier stage checked it. The chain ends at the one piece of code that cannot be altered.

questions.prompt: An RSA-2048 public key would need 2,048 fuses. How do chips avoid this?
options: They fuse a 256-bit SHA-256 hash of the key, and the key itself travels in flash with the bootloader
They fuse only the first 256 bits of the key, and the rest is guessed from the signature
They fuse a 256-bit SHA-256 hash of the signature, and the key is read from the security processor
They fuse the key once at the maker and use a different 256-bit key for every boot stage
questions.explanation: A 256-bit hash costs 256 fuses. The boot ROM hashes the key that came with the image and compares it with the fused value, so the full key can safely live in flash.

questions.prompt: What does the boot ROM do first with the public key that came with the boot image?
options: It hashes the key and compares the result with the hash held in fuses
It uses the key to check the image's signature straight away
It compares the key with the previous image's key stored in flash
It sends the key to the online service for approval
questions.explanation: A mismatch means someone supplied their own key. Only once the key is trusted does the ROM check the signature, then the security version, and then jump to the code.

questions.prompt: Three of eight anti-rollback fuses are blown. An update that fixes a security hole raises the version to 4. What is true afterwards?
options: Fuse 3 is blown, and version-3 images are refused from then on
Fuse 2 is unblown, and the old image is kept for recovery purposes
Four fuses are blown, but version-3 images are still accepted for older games
Fuse 7 is blown, so the console now counts down from eight
questions.explanation: The minimum accepted security version equals the number of blown fuses, and it only ever rises because a fuse cannot be unblown.

questions.prompt: Why do makers raise the security version only for updates that fix a security flaw?
options: A bank of eight fuses can only count to 8, and each increase spends a fuse forever
Raising the version slows the console's boot by one check for each increase
Raising the version needs a new signature key from the maker for each update
A higher version makes the hypervisor refuse every game released before the update
questions.explanation: A fuse cannot be unblown, so the counter is a limited resource. Spending it on every update would use it up.

questions.prompt: A console game package is both signed and encrypted. What does each protection do?
options: The signature proves it came unchanged from the platform holder; the encryption hides its contents
The signature hides the contents; the encryption proves who made the package
The signature stops the game from being downloaded; the encryption stops it being installed
The signature protects the keys; the encryption protects the security version
questions.explanation: The two protections do different jobs. Encryption keeps code from being read or copied to run elsewhere, and its keys stay inside the security processor.

questions.prompt: Why do consoles generally not let ordinary games mark memory as both writable and executable?
options: Code a game writes for itself at run time was never signed, but all code must be
Writable memory is kept on a different chip from executable memory on a console
A game that runs its own code would slow the hypervisor's scheduling of the partitions
Executable memory is kept encrypted, so a game could not write bytes into it
questions.explanation: Everything a console runs must carry the platform holder's signature, so memory that is both writable and executable is a place where unsigned code could appear. An emulator's fastest technique needs exactly that combination.

questions.prompt: The owner of a Windows PC and the owner of a retail console each try to run an unsigned program. What happens?
options: Windows warns, then runs it as the owner decides; the console refuses to run it
Both refuse, because every operating system rejects code that has no signature
Both run it after a warning, because the owner is the administrator on each
Windows refuses, and the console runs it only when it is offline
questions.explanation: On a PC an Authenticode signature is optional for ordinary programs. On a console the platform holder decides which code may run, through signatures.

questions.prompt: How does a game console's security goal differ from a PC's?
options: It also protects the platform holder from the owner
It is identical to a PC's, since both defend the owner
It is weaker, since consoles hold no valuable data
It protects the hardware from physical damage
questions.explanation: A PC's security defends its owner against other people, and the owner is the administrator who can switch protections off. A console is built so that the owner cannot.

questions.prompt: In remote attestation, what does the security processor sign?
options: The service's nonce plus the boot measurements, using a key unique to that console
A hash of the whole game library, using the platform holder's one shared key
The owner's account name together with the console's printed serial number
A list of the games last played, using a key stored in the boot image file
questions.explanation: The measurements are hashes recorded by each boot stage of the next stage before it ran. The service checks the signature and compares them with the values genuine software produces.

questions.prompt: Why does an online service ban a console that fails attestation, instead of just ignoring the report?
options: A modified console can cheat, run pirated games, or send odd messages, so nothing it says is trusted
The console's report damages the service's servers, so a ban is technically necessary to stop it
Console makers publish their attestation protocols, so any console that fails is seen as hostile
A failed report proves the owner copied games, which is the offence the ban would punish
questions.explanation: The ban is the service's decision under its terms of service, not a technical malfunction. It protects other players and the store.

questions.prompt: Even with remote attestation, why do well-designed online games still check every action on the server?
options: No client check is perfect, so trusting a console's claim is as weak as trusting a PC's
Attestation works only for the store and cloud saves, never for matchmaking itself
The server cannot read the measurements, so it has to rely on checking actions instead
Consoles send actions too slowly for the client to check them without any server help
questions.explanation: Attestation is one layer, not the whole defence. The server's own checks do not rely on the console telling the truth.

questions.prompt: Under copyright law, how is playing pirated copies of games on a modified console generally treated?
options: As infringement, whatever way the console was modified
As legal, if the owner modified the console personally
As legal, if the games are played only at home
As a warranty issue rather than a legal one
questions.explanation: Anti-circumvention laws and their exemptions vary by country and device, and this is not legal advice. Copying and using pirated games is generally infringement however the console was modified.

questions.prompt: At step 11 of the trace, `JNZ 0x02` does not jump. Why not?
questions.explanation: `JNZ` jumps only while Z is 0, and Z records whether the last result was zero. The instruction just before it, `DEX`, computed X = 1 − 1 = 0, so Z became 1. `ADD` sets Z too, but `DEX` ran after it, and neither `STA` nor `JNZ` changes Z.
options: DEX at step 10 made X zero, so Z became 1
A holds 20 at that point, which is not zero
0x02 is not a valid jump target in this memory
JNZ can jump only once for each run of a program

questions.prompt: In a typical simple CPU, which kinds of instructions leave the zero flag unchanged?
options: Stores and jumps, which produce no result
Loads and additions, which produce a result
Decrements and comparisons, which produce results
None, since every instruction changes the flag
questions.explanation: Instructions that compute or load a value set the zero flag when the result is zero. Stores and jumps do not produce such a result, so they leave it alone.

questions.prompt: A toy CPU spends one cycle per memory access. A 2-byte load instruction fetches both bytes and then reads one data byte. What does it cost?
options: 3 cycles: two fetches and a data read
2 cycles: only the fetches count
1 cycle: the opcode alone is enough
4 cycles: each fetch costs two
questions.explanation: Each memory access costs one cycle, so two instruction-byte fetches plus one data read make three. A store costs the same, writing the data byte instead of reading one.

questions.prompt: A conditional jump costs 2 cycles when it is not taken and 3 when it is taken. What is the extra cycle for?
options: Loading the target address into PC
Re-reading the condition flag a second time
Fetching the next opcode early, ahead of time
Clearing the zero flag after the jump is made
questions.explanation: Both cases fetch the two instruction bytes. The extra cycle is spent only when the jump is taken, to load the target into the program counter.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an immediate operand like #5 and an operand written as an address?
options: An immediate is the value itself; an address says where it is
An immediate is stored in a register, and an address is stored on disk
An immediate is signed, and an address is unsigned
An immediate takes more cycles than an address
questions.explanation: An address operand needs another memory read to get the value, which is why an instruction using one costs more cycles than one using an immediate.

questions.prompt: An 8-bit register holds 1, and a decrement-by-one instruction runs twice in a row. What does it hold afterward, and is the zero flag set?
options: 255, and the zero flag is clear
0, and the zero flag is set
-1, and the zero flag is clear
1, since a decrement applies only once
questions.explanation: The first decrement makes 0 and sets the flag. The second wraps around to 255, because registers are 8 bits wide, and the flag is clear since the result is not zero.

questions.prompt: An 8-bit accumulator holds 200 and an add of 100 runs. What does it hold afterward, and is the zero flag set?
options: 44, and the zero flag is clear
300, and the zero flag is clear
255, since it stops at the maximum
44, and the zero flag is set
questions.explanation: Eight bits hold 0 to 255, so 200 + 100 = 300 wraps around to 300 - 256 = 44. The result is not zero, so the zero flag stays clear.

questions.prompt: A program's last instruction is a 1-byte halt at address 0x1F, and it starts at address 0. How many bytes does it occupy?
options: 32, since addresses 0 to 31 count
31, the address of the last byte
30, since the halt is not counted
33, since the halt takes two bytes
questions.explanation: 0x1F is 31, and counting from address 0 gives 32 bytes. A count is the last address plus one.

questions.prompt: In a toy CPU an immediate instruction costs 2 cycles, a store 3, a decrement 1 and a load 3. How many cycles do these four take in a row: immediate, store, decrement, load?
questions.explanation: 2 + 3 + 1 + 3 = 9. Each instruction costs its fetches plus its data accesses.

questions.prompt: A loop body costs 12 cycles when its closing conditional jump is taken (3 cycles) and 11 when it falls through (2 cycles). Why is the final pass cheaper?
options: A jump that is not taken skips the target-loading cycle
The data is cached after the first pass through the loop
The loop counter is smaller on the last pass through
The instructions are decoded just once on the first pass
questions.explanation: The jump's extra cycle loads the target address, and that is spent only when the jump is taken. The last pass falls through, saving one cycle.

questions.prompt: A CPU fetches an opcode by reading the byte at PC and then adding 1 to PC. After fetching a 1-byte halt at address 0x2A, what is PC?
questions.explanation: Each fetch reads the byte at PC and adds 1, so after fetching the halt the counter sits one past it.

questions.prompt: An emulator's write routine has cases for RAM and the display, and a catch-all that does nothing. What happens to a write to a read-only input register?
options: The catch-all discards it; the register is read-only
It changes the register, since all writes take effect
It crashes the emulator with an error
It is saved and applied at the next frame
questions.explanation: Only RAM and the display accept writes. The final arm covers read-only and unused addresses, so a write there has no effect, while a read returns the buttons.

questions.prompt: Why would an emulator report an unknown opcode as an error instead of guessing what it means?
options: Guessing would hide bugs in the guest code and the emulator
Unknown opcodes are harmless, so errors help nobody
Guessing makes the emulator slower than reporting errors
Real CPUs always stop when they meet an unknown opcode
questions.explanation: An emulator that guessed would hide mistakes. Real CPUs might raise an exception or do something undocumented, so the emulator should say clearly what it does not know.

questions.prompt: What does an emulator's fetch routine do each time it is called?
options: Reads the byte at PC and advances PC by one
Reads the byte at PC and leaves PC alone
Executes the instruction at PC and returns its cost
Reads the whole instruction, however many bytes long
questions.explanation: Each call consumes one byte of the instruction, so an opcode fetch and an operand fetch together move the counter by 2.

questions.prompt: A console has 2 KiB (2,048 bytes) of RAM mirrored through the addresses 0x0000 to 0x3FFF (16,384 bytes). How many copies of the RAM does that range hold?
options: 8 copies, since 16,384 ÷ 2,048 = 8
4 copies, since 8,192 ÷ 2,048 = 4
2 copies, since the RAM is mirrored once
questions.explanation: The address decoder ignores the top address bits for RAM, so the same bytes answer again and again through the range.

questions.prompt: An emulator runs whole instructions while the cycles used are below a budget, never stopping mid-instruction. If the longest instruction takes 4 cycles, by how much can a frame overshoot the budget at most?
options: By 3 cycles, since the last instruction can start at budget minus 1
By 4 cycles, since the longest instruction can start at the budget
By 0 cycles, since the check happens before each instruction
By 1 cycle, since only the last cycle can overshoot
questions.explanation: The check runs before each instruction, so the last one can begin when one cycle is still left. A 4-cycle instruction then ends 3 cycles past the budget.

questions.prompt: A frame ends after an instruction that added to register A but before the store that copies A into memory. What does memory hold?
options: The old value; the new total is only in register A
The new total, since an add updates memory directly
Zero, since a frame boundary clears memory
A mix of the old and new values
questions.explanation: The store has not run, so a snapshot of memory alone would lose the new total. That is why a save state needs the registers as well.

questions.prompt: A toy save state holds 5 bytes of registers, a 64-bit cycle counter, 100 bytes of RAM and 2 bytes of I/O registers. How many bytes is it?
options: 171 bytes, counting the counter as 64 bytes
107 bytes, leaving the counter out
119 bytes, counting the counter as 12 bytes
questions.explanation: A 64-bit counter is 64 ÷ 8 = 8 bytes, so the total is 5 + 8 + 100 + 2 = 115.

questions.prompt: Why does loading a save state refuse a Z or halted byte that holds a value such as 7?
options: No real run of the machine could have produced it, so the data must be damaged
A value above 1 would overflow the register, so the emulator has to protect itself
A Z byte must always equal the halted byte, so any other value is a mismatch
The emulator can store a flag only as 0 or 1 in a file, since the others are reserved
questions.explanation: Reading a state back is parsing input from outside the program. The lab also refuses anything that is not exactly 255 bytes long.

questions.prompt: Frame 1 ends after step 8 and the cheat writes 99 to gold. What does step 9 do to that 99?
options: It stores A's 20 over it, because A already held the new total
It leaves the 99 alone, because the cheat wrote it later than the game did
It adds 5 to the 99, because `ADD #5` runs against gold
It stops the program, because gold changed behind the game's back
questions.explanation: The game had already loaded gold into A and added 5 before the cheat wrote to RAM. A cheat can lose a race against a value held in a register.

questions.prompt: Frame 2 has a budget of 17 cycles. Why does it finish the whole program?
options: Steps 9 to 13 cost 3 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 10 cycles, well inside the budget
Steps 9 to 13 cost 3 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 3 = 12 cycles, which is just inside the budget
Frame 2 gets an unlimited budget, because the program has already halted
The cheat adds cycles to the budget, because it writes to RAM at the end
questions.explanation: Steps 9 to 13 are `STA 0x80`, `DEX`, `JNZ` falling through, `STA 0xF0` and `HLT`. The display shows 20 at step 12, and the cheat writes 99 to RAM again at the frame's end.

questions.prompt: In unsigned arithmetic, what does a saturating subtraction do when the true result would be negative?
options: It stops at 0 instead of wrapping around
It wraps around to the largest possible value
It panics and ends the whole process at once
It returns a negative number in its place
questions.explanation: Unsigned values cannot be negative, so a saturating subtraction clamps at 0. A frame that ends early has no overshoot to report.

questions.prompt: A watchpoint records the PC register inside the write routine. A 2-byte store instruction sits at address 0x10. Which PC value does the watchpoint record?
questions.explanation: The step routine fetches the opcode and then the operand before it calls write, so the counter has already advanced by 2. The recorded value is not the instruction's own address.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit game running on 64-bit Windows shows `cs` = `0023` in x64dbg. At which privilege level is its code running?
questions.explanation: Only the lowest two bits of `cs` hold the privilege level. `0x23` is 2 × 16 + 3 = 35, or `0010 0011` in binary, and its lowest two bits are `11` = 3. The upper bits pick a different code segment (a 32-bit one), but the level is still ring 3, user mode.
options: Ring 3, because `0x23` is `0010 0011` and its lowest two bits are `11`
Ring 0, because `0x23` is smaller than the 64-bit value `0x33`
Ring 2, because the hex value `0x23` begins with the digit 2
None; the value of `cs` only picks a segment and says nothing of privilege

questions.prompt: A tool opened a game with `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION` (`0x0400`) and `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION` (`0x1000`), so its handle's rights are `0x1400`. It calls `ReadProcessMemory`, which needs `PROCESS_VM_READ` (`0x0010`). What happens?
questions.explanation: `0x0400` is 4 × 256 = 1,024 = 2¹⁰ (bit 10) and `0x1000` is 2¹² (bit 12), so `0x1400` has bits 12 and 10 set. The read needs bit 4, which is 0, so the AND is 0 and the kernel returns an error status. Nothing faults: the system call returns normally with `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED`, and `kernelbase.dll` reports error 5. Running as administrator affects what `OpenProcess` may grant; it cannot add rights to a handle that already exists.
options: The kernel refuses with `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED`, because `0x1400` AND `0x0010` is 0
The kernel copies the bytes, because a handle that can query a process can also read it
The processor raises a general-protection fault inside the tool when it makes the call
The read succeeds if the tool runs as administrator, since that adds missing rights

questions.prompt: Why are there exactly four privilege rings on x86?
options: The level is stored in two bits, and two bits give 2 × 2 = 4 patterns: `00`, `01`, `10`, `11`
The level is stored in one byte, but the processor defines only the first four of its 256 values
The page-table flag byte has four permission bits, and each one stands for one ring
Windows ships four kinds of driver, and each kind needs its own ring to run in
questions.explanation: The current privilege level is the lowest two bits of `cs`. Two bits can hold four patterns, which is exactly the four rings. Windows uses only 0 and 3.

questions.prompt: On x86, the current privilege level sits in the lowest two bits of the code segment value. A code segment value is 0x08. Which ring is that?
options: Ring 0, since the lowest two bits are 00
Ring 8, since the value written is 8
Ring 3, since the value is not zero
Ring 1, since bit 3 is set in 0x08
questions.explanation: Only the lowest two bits give the level, and 0x08 is 1000 in binary, so they are 00. The higher bits select the segment, not the ring.

questions.prompt: User code tries to load a kernel-level code segment value into the code segment register to give itself kernel privilege. What does the processor do?
options: Refuses; privilege rises only through kernel-prepared entry points
Allows it, if the code is running as an administrator
Allows it, but the kernel notices later and ends the process
Allows it, but only for the length of one instruction
questions.explanation: The processor refuses any segment change that raises privilege, except through a few kernel-prepared entry points. Administrator rights live in the access token, not in the processor ring.

questions.prompt: Two page-table entries are identical except for one bit: the user/supervisor bit is set in one and clear in the other. What difference does that make to code running at the least-privileged level?
options: It can access the page where the bit is set, but not where it is clear
It can access both, but the page where the bit is clear is slower
It can write where the bit is set, but only read where it is clear
It can access neither, since that level has no page access at all
questions.explanation: The user/supervisor bit decides whether ring 3 may touch the page at all. Kernel pages have it clear, so user code that touches them faults.

questions.prompt: A page-table entry has an 'accessed' bit and a 'dirty' bit that the processor sets by itself. When does each get set?
options: Accessed on first use of the page, dirty on first write to it
Accessed on first write, dirty on first read
Both when the kernel first maps the page
Accessed when the page is swapped out, dirty when it is freed
questions.explanation: The processor sets accessed the first time a page is used and dirty the first time it is written. The kernel uses them to decide which pages are in use or need saving.

questions.prompt: A system-call instruction overwrites one register with the return address, but the calling convention puts the first argument in that register. What does a stub do about it?
options: It copies the argument to another register first so the kernel can find it
It pushes the argument on the user stack and passes nothing in registers
It waits until the kernel returns, then passes the argument along
It encrypts the argument before it makes the call to the kernel
questions.explanation: Moving the argument to another register first keeps it from being overwritten. The service number goes in yet another register.

questions.prompt: System service numbers change between Windows builds. What does that mean for a tool that hard-codes one?
options: It may call a different kernel routine on another build, so the book never copies a number
It works on any build, because the number is looked up by name in the kernel's table at run time
It still works on the same build, but Windows blocks it from reading memory without the right
It fails only on 32-bit programs, since WoW64 renumbers services but 64-bit programs keep theirs
questions.explanation: The numbers index the kernel's internal routine table and are not a stable interface. A hard-coded number can point at a different routine, or none, on another build.

questions.prompt: Why does the kernel's entry code switch to a kernel stack that belongs to the thread, instead of using the program's stack?
options: The program's stack pointer could point anywhere, and everything from user mode must be assumed hostile
The program's stack is stored on disk, so the kernel cannot reach it quickly enough to save registers
The kernel needs a much larger stack than the program has, and user stacks cannot be grown
The program's stack is in the user half of memory, which the processor locks while ring 0 code runs
questions.explanation: Everything user mode supplies, including the stack pointer, could be hostile. A kernel stack under its own control makes sure the saved registers have a safe place.

questions.prompt: A kernel service checks a user-supplied range, a start plus a length. Why must it reject a range whose end wraps past the largest address to a small value?
options: A wrapped range can pass a naive check while the copy reaches the kernel
Wrapped ranges are far too slow to copy in practice, so they are refused
The hardware would trap on every wrap automatically anyway
A wrapped range points at unmapped memory, so it would fail alone
questions.explanation: The kernel's own check must catch wrap-around and ranges that reach its half. The page-table protection bit cannot do this job, since the copy runs at full privilege.

questions.prompt: A handle holds rights 0x0D, and an operation needs rights 0x05. The kernel takes the bitwise AND of the two. What is the result, and what happens?
options: `0x05`, equal to the requirement, so the operation is allowed
`0x0D`, the handle's rights, so the operation is refused
`0x00`, so the operation is refused
`0x08`, the leftover rights, so the operation is allowed
questions.explanation: AND keeps only the bits set in both values. Every required bit survives, so the requirement is covered.

questions.prompt: The same handle holds rights 0x0D, and a different operation needs rights 0x02. Why is it denied?
options: `0x02` is a bit that is 0 in `0x0D`, so the AND is `0x00`
`0x02` is covered, so the AND is `0x02` and it is allowed
`0x02` is covered, so the AND is `0x0F` and it is allowed
`0x0D` is larger than `0x02`, so the AND is `0x0D`
questions.explanation: 0x0D is 1101 in binary and 0x02 is 0010. They share no set bit, so the AND is 0 and the right is missing.

questions.prompt: A memory-copy API is asked for 4 bytes, but a page becomes unavailable partway through. What should the caller do?
options: Check the returned count of bytes copied; do not assume all arrived
Assume all 4 bytes arrived, since the call itself has returned
Retry with a count of 8 so that it covers the missing gap
Treat the failure as harmless and go on using the buffer
questions.explanation: A mid-copy failure can be reported as a failed or partial read. The caller must inspect the byte count instead of assuming success.

questions.prompt: Many system status codes use their top two bits as severity: 00 success, 01 information, 10 warning, 11 error. A status begins with hex digit 4. What severity is it?
options: Information, since 4 is 0100 and the top two bits are 01
Warning, since 4 is 0100 and the top two bits are 10
Success, since 4 is 0100 and the top two bits are 00
Error, since 4 is 0100 and the top two bits are 11
questions.explanation: The top hex digit 4 is 0100 in binary, so the top two bits are 01, which means information.

questions.prompt: After a system call finishes, the return instruction resumes the thread. Where does user code continue, and at what privilege?
options: Right after the call, at the least-privileged level again
At the start of the function, at kernel privilege
At the entry point of the process, at user privilege
Right after the call, but still at kernel privilege
questions.explanation: The return address saved by the call instruction is reused, and the processor drops back to user privilege.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit program runs on 64-bit Windows. Why does its system call take an extra step compared with a 64-bit program's?
options: A translation layer converts the 32-bit call to the 64-bit path
The kernel emulates each 32-bit instruction in software, step by step
The call is sent over the network to a separate 64-bit service
32-bit programs run inside a virtual machine with its own kernel
questions.explanation: The 32-bit program uses a different code segment, and a compatibility layer translates its calls, converting pointer-sized arguments and structures along the way.

questions.prompt: The input samples are false, true, true, true. How many times does this lesson's controller toggle the lamp?
questions.explanation: The controller remembers whether the previous sample was pressed. Only the first true follows a false; the other true samples describe the same held press. This assumes already debounced logical input, not a bouncing physical contact.
options: Once, when `false` first becomes `true`
Three times, once for every `true` sample in the list
Four times, because every sample counts as an event
Zero times, because the controller ignores a button that stays held

questions.prompt: What is firmware?
options: Software that runs a device, usually stored in flash
Any software that happens to be written in assembly language
The driver that runs on a PC to talk to a device
A file format that is used for operating-system images
questions.explanation: Firmware is a role, not a file type or a language. The flash it lives in can be erased and programmed again.

questions.prompt: Which statement about flash memory is correct?
options: It keeps its contents without power and can be reprogrammed
It loses its contents when power is removed, like working RAM
It can be written once and can never be changed
It is where the call stack lives while the code runs
questions.explanation: Flash is nonvolatile and reprogrammable. Working state and the call stack sit in SRAM, which does not retain its contents without power.

questions.prompt: A USB game controller involves firmware, a PC driver and a game. Which piece samples the buttons and prepares the reports?
options: The controller's firmware, on its own processor
The PC driver, running on the computer's main processor
The game, as soon as it receives a button press
The connector chip at the end of the USB cable
questions.explanation: Firmware, driver and game cooperate across a device boundary but run in different places. The driver exchanges reports, and the game turns a press into an action.

questions.prompt: An application runs on a small embedded Linux system inside a camera. Is it bare-metal firmware?
options: No; bare-metal means no operating system at all
Yes; anything inside a device is bare-metal
Yes; embedded Linux is a kind of bare-metal
No; bare-metal requires the code to be written in assembly
questions.explanation: Bare-metal programming uses no operating system, though firmware can also use a real-time OS or embedded Linux. Those are different arrangements.

questions.prompt: The modelled board has 256 KiB of flash. How many bytes is that?
options: 262,144 bytes, which is 256 x 1,024
256,000 bytes, which is 256 x 1,000
65,536 bytes, which is 64 x 1,024
131,072 bytes, which is 128 x 1,024
questions.explanation: A KiB is 1,024 bytes, so 256 KiB = 256 x 1,024 = 262,144. The 64 KiB figure belongs to the board's SRAM, not its flash.

questions.prompt: A microcontroller's stack grows toward lower addresses. Where should the stack pointer start?
options: Just past the top of RAM, so the first push lands inside it
At the lowest RAM address, so it can grow upward
At the middle of RAM, to leave room in both directions
At address zero, inside the flash memory
questions.explanation: Pushing onto a downward-growing stack moves the pointer back inside RAM, starting from one past the last byte.

questions.prompt: RAM starts at 0x2000_0000 and is 32 KiB long, which is 0x8000 bytes. What is the last valid address inside it?
questions.explanation: The last byte is the start plus the length minus one: 0x2000_0000 + 0x8000 - 1 = 0x2000_7FFF. The address 0x2000_8000 is the first one after the region.

questions.prompt: A simulator models a board with flash at a particular address. What do such addresses refer to?
options: The emulated device's own address space, not the PC's
Addresses in the PC's real memory where the simulator keeps its data
Physical flash chips attached to the PC
File offsets in the operating system's disk image
questions.explanation: These are the model's addresses. Loading an image into modelled flash does not reproduce the electrical procedure for programming a real flash chip.

questions.prompt: After the lamp controller is powered off and on again, what has survived?
options: Its instructions in flash; the lamp state is rebuilt by the program at each boot
Its instructions and also the last lamp setting, because both are held in flash
Its last lamp setting only, because the instructions are reloaded from the PC each time
Nothing, because flash is wiped whenever the board loses power
questions.explanation: Instructions survive in flash. The lamp state is working state that the program starts again, so remembering it needs an explicit storage design.

questions.prompt: Why would writing the lamp state to flash on every main-loop pass be a poor way to remember it?
options: Flash has erase and program constraints and finite endurance that RAM does not
Flash loses its contents quickly, so the stored state would vanish before the next boot
Flash can be read only by the debugger, so the firmware could never see the saved value
Flash writes overwrite the vector table, which would stop the board starting
questions.explanation: Flash is nonvolatile but wears with repeated erase and program cycles, so a loop that writes every pass would burn through its endurance.

questions.prompt: What do the first two entries of the Cortex-M vector table contain?
options: The initial stack pointer, then the reset-handler address
The reset-handler address, then the initial stack pointer
The address of `main`, then the address of the first interrupt handler
The first instruction of the application, then its checksum
questions.explanation: The table holds values and addresses, not instructions. The core loads the stack pointer from the first entry and jumps to the address in the second after reset.

questions.prompt: A writable static variable must start with the value 7 on a microcontroller. How does it get its initial value?
options: The 7 is stored in flash, and start-up code copies it into RAM
The 7 is written into RAM at the factory and survives power loss
The compiler writes 7 when the function is first called
RAM starts each run with the value from the previous run
questions.explanation: The initialized-data section has an initial value stored in the image and a working place in RAM, so start-up copies one to the other. The zero-initialized section is the one that starts as zeros.

questions.prompt: A writable static counter starts at zero. What does the image need for it?
options: A reserved RAM range that startup fills with zeros, so no zero bytes are stored
A run of zero bytes stored in flash, which startup copies into RAM on every boot
A copy of the counter in `.rodata`, which startup reads and writes back to RAM
Nothing at all, because the hardware always clears SRAM when the chip is reset
questions.explanation: `.bss` reserves a range and startup writes the zeros, so the image stays smaller. The runtime and linker agree on where the range begins and ends.

questions.prompt: Where do a function's local variables live on a microcontroller?
options: In registers or on the stack, as the compiler chooses
In the data section, copied from flash at start-up time
In the zero-initialized section of RAM at start-up time
In the flash memory next to the application's code
questions.explanation: Locals are separate from the static sections. The compiler may keep one in a register or place it on the stack.

questions.prompt: Why is a source file with only a main function not a complete firmware image for a microcontroller?
options: It also needs a vector table, start-up code and memory layout
The chip accepts only programs that are named by the vendor
Main functions cannot be compiled for a microcontroller
Firmware must always include an operating system
questions.explanation: Reset starts from the vector table, not from a function called main. A runtime prepares static data and then calls the application's entry function.

questions.prompt: What is a bootloader?
options: Software that selects, checks or loads the next application
The memory that holds the chip's very first instructions
The cable that loads firmware onto a board
The language runtime that initializes static data
questions.explanation: A boot ROM is start-up software in read-only memory. A bootloader may support updates and recovery, and its work stays distinct from a language runtime's initialization.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a logical change from false to true, and how can code detect it?
options: A rising edge, found by remembering the previous sample
A falling edge, found by remembering the previous sample
A rising edge, found from the current sample alone
A debounce, found by waiting a fixed amount of time
questions.explanation: A press counts as new only when the current sample is pressed and the remembered one was not.

questions.prompt: A lamp starts off and toggles on each rising edge of a button. The samples are false, true, true, false. What is the lamp state after the fourth sample?
options: On, since only a false-to-true change toggles
Off, because the release toggled it back
Off, because the held sample toggled it again
On, but it toggled twice on the way
questions.explanation: Only a false-to-true change toggles. Sample 2 turned the lamp on, sample 3 was still the same press, and the release at sample 4 does not toggle it.

questions.prompt: A lamp starts off and toggles on each rising edge of a button. The samples are false, true, false, true, true, true, false, true. How many times does it toggle, and what is the final state?
options: Three times, ending with the lamp on
Five times, ending with the lamp on
Four times, ending with the lamp off
Two times, ending with the lamp off
questions.explanation: The rising edges are at samples 2, 4 and 8, so it toggles three times and ends on. Samples 5 and 6 are the same press still held.

questions.prompt: A rising-edge detector updates its stored previous sample on every call, not only when it toggles. Why?
options: The next call needs it, or a held press looks new
It saves energy by avoiding repeated comparisons
It debounces the switch by averaging samples
It lets the lamp toggle twice for each press
questions.explanation: Rising-edge detection compares the current sample with the last one. Skipping the update would leave stale information behind.

questions.prompt: Does rising-edge detection also cure switch bounce?
options: No; the controller expects a stable logical press, so firmware must debounce the raw input first
Yes; only the first contact of a bounce counts as a rising edge, so the rest are ignored
Yes; a bounce is just a held button, which the edge rule already handles
No; bounce is cured by writing the lamp state to flash after each sample
questions.explanation: Bounce briefly makes and breaks contact several times, which would look like several presses to an edge detector. A debounce policy, often several stable samples over time, comes first.

questions.prompt: In bare-metal Rust that uses only the core library and has no allocator, which of these still works?
options: Option and Result, which come from the core library
Vec and String, which grow automatically as needed
File and thread operations from the operating system
Printing text to a terminal from any function
questions.explanation: The core library is kept, but the OS-oriented standard library is left out. Growable collections need allocation support, and files, threads and terminal printing do not appear automatically.

questions.prompt: Why is a microcontroller's entry function typically declared so that it never returns?
options: No caller is waiting for it, so it ends in a loop
The compiler cannot compile functions that return
Returning would erase the flash memory
Entry functions return only when an error occurs
questions.explanation: On a microcontroller nothing is waiting for the entry function to finish, so a typical one ends in a loop.

questions.prompt: What does semihosting let a program on an emulated target do?
options: Ask the emulator to do a host-side job, like printing text
Run faster by using the PC's own processor directly
Access the real network card through the target's pins
Replace the operating system on the host
questions.explanation: Semihosting is a request channel to a debugger or emulator. It suits a short trace but not timing measurements.

questions.prompt: The built ELF file is much larger than 256 KiB. Does that mean the firmware cannot fit in the board's flash?
options: No; the file includes debug metadata that never loads into flash, so size is not usage
Yes; the loader copies the whole ELF file into flash, so its full size must fit
Yes; ELF files always count their sections twice, so the true size is even larger
No; ELF files are compressed, so the loader can unpack them into a larger flash
questions.explanation: ELF carries sections, addresses, and other information a loader or debugger can use. Only the loaded sections occupy the microcontroller's flash.

questions.prompt: A button is wired active-low. Which electrical change matches a logical press?
options: A high-to-low change on the input pin
A low-to-high change on the input pin
The pin floating between the two levels
The pin staying high for a while
questions.explanation: Active-low means a low level represents a press. A pull resistor keeps the unpressed input at a defined level.

questions.prompt: On a real board a lamp reacts to the button's release instead of its press. What is the sound approach?
options: Compare expected and seen transitions; check pin polarity
Change the control rule to react to falling edges
Add a delay so that the release comes later
Replace the button, since the rule is proven correct
questions.explanation: Changing the control rule to compensate for a wiring mistake hides the cause. The tests check the rule, so the boundary to inspect is polarity, debounce timing, timer rate or register setup.

questions.prompt: What is a watchdog on a real microcontroller?
options: A timer that resets a stalled device unless firmware services it
A tool that finds every bug in the firmware without needing to run it
A peripheral that copies the stack into flash when the program panics
A debugger feature that stops the processor at each GPIO write it sees
questions.explanation: A watchdog needs a careful configuration and recovery policy on real hardware. It is not a cure for an unexplained bug.

questions.prompt: A recompiler has translated a guest loop into host code and stored it. The guest program then writes a new byte into the middle of that loop, over the operand of an `ADD` instruction. What must the emulator do before the loop runs again?
questions.explanation: The stored host code still adds the old number, which no longer matches the guest's memory. Code is data, and a guest may legally rewrite its own instructions, so the recompiler has to watch for writes to translated addresses and discard those translations. Otherwise the emulated program runs code that no longer exists.
options: Discard the stored translation that covers the changed address and translate it again
Nothing, because the stored translation is still correct for the guest's memory now
Run the old translation one more time, and only then translate the block again
Stop the guest, because guest code is never allowed to change its own bytes at all

questions.prompt: A toy CPU's PC register holds 0x10, the bytes at 0x10 and 0x11 are `03 07` (add 7), and register A holds 20. After one pass of the fetch-execute loop, what do A and PC hold?
options: A = 27 and PC = 0x12
A = 27 and PC = 0x11
A = 20 and PC = 0x12
A = 7 and PC = 0x12
questions.explanation: Fetching the opcode moves PC to 0x11, and fetching the operand moves it to 0x12, the first byte of the next instruction. Executing sets A = 20 + 7 = 27.

questions.prompt: A toy CPU spends one cycle on every byte it reads or writes in memory. What does a 2-byte instruction that also reads one data byte from memory cost?
options: 3 cycles: two fetches and one data read
2 cycles, since only instruction bytes count
1 cycle, since the data byte is free
4 cycles, since a data read costs two
questions.explanation: Two instruction bytes plus one data byte are three memory accesses. Counting cycles tells an emulator how long the real chip would have taken.

questions.prompt: Nothing in memory marks where one instruction ends. How does the CPU find the start of the next one?
options: The opcode gives the instruction's length, and fetching its bytes moves PC past them
A special marker byte follows every instruction, and the CPU scans for it
The emulator keeps a table of every instruction's address, which it reads in order
Each instruction is padded to the same length, so PC always moves by two
questions.explanation: Some instructions carry an operand byte and some do not. Because the opcode tells the CPU how many bytes to fetch, PC lands on the next instruction automatically.

questions.prompt: A loop of five guest instructions runs 1,000 times. How many instructions does an interpreter decode, compared with a dynamic recompiler?
options: 5,000 against 5, since the recompiler translates the block once and then runs it
5,000 against 1,000, since the recompiler decodes once per pass of the loop
1,000 against 5, since the interpreter decodes only the loop's first instruction
5 against 5,000, since the interpreter keeps stored translations of each block
questions.explanation: The interpreter pays 5 x 1,000 = 5,000 decodes, although only five different instructions exist. The recompiler pays 5 decodes and then runs the stored host code 1,000 times.

questions.prompt: Why must an emulator on a console or some phone platforms fall back to interpreting instead of recompiling?
options: A recompiler writes machine code to memory then runs it, which those platforms refuse to allow
A recompiler needs the platform's graphics driver, which these platforms do not provide at all
A recompiler needs more RAM than those platforms can offer to run the original game
A recompiler can only run code for processors that were built back in the 1980s era
questions.explanation: Code that a program writes for itself at run time was never signed, so these platforms generally do not allow it to run.

questions.prompt: In a toy console, RAM occupies addresses 0x00 to 0xBF. How many bytes is that?
options: 191, since 0xBF is 191
193, since both ends are counted twice
256, since an 8-bit bus has 256 addresses
questions.explanation: The count is the last address plus one, so 0xBF + 1 = 0xC0 = 192. The other addresses of the 8-bit space belong to devices or are unused.

questions.prompt: On a console that uses memory-mapped I/O, the CPU stores a byte to an address assigned to the display. What happens?
options: The byte goes to the display; the address picks it
The byte goes to RAM, and the display reads it later
The store faults, since the display is not memory
The byte is discarded, since displays are read-only
questions.explanation: In hardware, address-decoding circuits choose the device. In an emulator, the write function does the same job.

questions.prompt: How does an emulator imitate a console's address-decoding circuits?
options: Every access goes through a read or write function that picks the target by address
The emulator gives each device its own host thread, which watches the address lines
The emulator maps each device into the host's own address space for the host to decode
The game code is rewritten to call each device by name, instead of by address
questions.explanation: In the lesson's diagram the bus checks which range holds the address and sends the access to RAM, the display register, the buttons register, or nothing.

questions.prompt: The toy console's clock runs at 1.2 MHz and the screen redraws 60 times a second. How many cycles does each frame last?
options: 20,000, from 1,200,000 divided by 60
72,000,000, from 1,200,000 multiplied by 60
2,000, from 1,200,000 divided by 600
1,200, from 1.2 MHz read as 1,200 cycles
questions.explanation: The emulator runs instructions until the frame's 20,000 cycles are used, draws the frame, and then waits until 1/60 of a second of real time has passed.

questions.prompt: A game changes a picture-chip register partway down the screen. What goes wrong if the emulated CPU reaches that write too early?
options: The split lands on the wrong line of the screen
The game's save file is corrupted when the frame ends
The picture chip skips the next frame to catch up
The host's GPU refuses to draw the texture
questions.explanation: Older games depended on exact timing, so emulators run the CPU for a slice of cycles and advance the other chips by the same amount of time.

questions.prompt: For an 8-bit or 16-bit console, what does the emulator do with the pixels its picture-chip imitation produces?
options: It writes them into a framebuffer array and hands that array to the host's GPU as a texture
It sends each pixel to the host display directly, one at a time, as the CPU writes it
It compiles them into shaders, which the host GPU then runs to draw the frame
It stores them in the guest's RAM, where the host operating system reads them
questions.explanation: The emulator imitates the chip's rules for tiles and sprites. A 3D console is harder because the emulator must translate the guest's GPU commands into Vulkan or Direct3D.

questions.prompt: Why can an emulated 3D game stutter the first time a new effect appears on screen?
options: The emulator translates the guest's shaders at that moment, then caches the result
The emulator has to decrypt that effect's data from the disc image first
The host GPU must warm up to the guest's clock speed before it draws a new effect
The guest's sound chip pauses the video until enough samples have been made first
questions.explanation: The original console never had this problem, because its games shipped shaders already compiled for its one GPU.

questions.prompt: A host plays 48,000 audio samples per second and the emulator runs at 60 frames per second. How many samples must it produce every frame?
options: 800, from 48,000 divided by 60
80, from 48,000 divided by 600
8,000, from 48,000 divided by 6
1,200, from 48,000 divided by 40
questions.explanation: If the samples run out, the speakers click and crackle, while a late video frame just leaves the previous picture up a moment longer. That is why many emulators pace themselves by the audio device.

questions.prompt: How does a save state differ from a game's own save file?
options: A state captures the whole machine at any instant; a save file holds what the game chooses
A state holds only RAM contents; a save file holds registers and RAM together as one
A state works only at the start of a frame; a save file can be written at any instant
A state is stored in the game's own format; a save file uses the emulator's own format
questions.explanation: A save state includes every register, all of RAM, the I/O registers and the emulator's own timing position, so it works for any game, even in the middle of a frame.

questions.prompt: Why must a save state include the CPU's registers as well as RAM?
options: A new value may exist only in a register and not yet in memory
The registers hold the game's graphics, which RAM does not contain at all
RAM is rebuilt from the registers whenever a state is loaded
The registers record which version of the emulator saved the state
questions.explanation: A snapshot of RAM alone would lose such a value. Emulators also store a version number, because the layout changes as the emulator does.

questions.prompt: A RAM search on an NES game covers 2 KiB of guest RAM. How many bytes is that?
questions.explanation: A RAM search is the scan of Lesson 1.9 run over the guest's RAM, so it covers a few thousand bytes instead of the gigabytes a PC game can occupy.

questions.prompt: How can an emulator provide a watchpoint on a guest variable without any debug registers?
options: An `if` in the write function checks the address and records PC
The emulator pauses the host operating system and lets the debugger read the host's registers
The emulator rewrites the game's code so it calls a debugger routine before each store
The emulator scans the guest's whole RAM after every frame and compares it with the last scan
questions.explanation: Every guest memory access passes through the emulator's read and write functions, so a check there sees every store.

questions.prompt: How did a Game Genie differ from an Action Replay or GameShark code?
options: It changed the byte read from a cartridge address; the others wrote a value to RAM each frame
It wrote a value to RAM each frame; the others changed the byte read from a cartridge address
It replaced the console's BIOS with its own copy; the others left the BIOS in place
It decrypted the game from its package; the others ran the encrypted package as it was
questions.explanation: A RAM-writing code is just an address and a value. Such a code can lose a race if the game stores its own number back over the cheat's.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the legal side of emulation is closest to the truth in many countries?
options: Writing an emulator is generally lawful; copying games is not
Emulators are illegal everywhere, whatever they contain
Downloading games is lawful if you own the matching console
Copyright does not apply to old games
questions.explanation: Court cases have treated reverse engineering for compatibility as fair use, and many emulators replace original firmware with their own code. This is not legal advice.

questions.prompt: A guest runs on an Intel processor with hardware virtualization and second-level address translation. Which of these guest actions causes a VM exit?
questions.explanation: Ordinary instructions and system calls run natively inside the guest, and a fault on a page the guest's own tables do not map is delivered to the guest kernel, which handles it as it would on real hardware. `cpuid` always exits on Intel processors, so the hypervisor controls what the guest learns about its processor.
options: A `cpuid` instruction asking about the processor
An `add` instruction on two registers in a guest program
A system call from a guest program into its own guest kernel
A page fault on a virtual page the guest kernel has not mapped yet

questions.prompt: In virtualization vocabulary, what is the guest?
options: The operating system running inside the virtual machine
The real computer whose hardware is being shared out
The software that creates machines and shares the hardware
The file on the host that holds the virtual disk
questions.explanation: The guest is the OS inside the VM and the host is the real computer. The hypervisor, also called a virtual machine monitor, is the software that creates VMs and shares the hardware.

questions.prompt: Hyper-V is turned on, and the PC is restarted. What has happened to the user's own Windows installation?
options: It has become the root partition, a privileged guest that manages the other guests
It keeps running straight on the hardware, with Hyper-V as an ordinary application
It has been replaced by Hyper-V's own kernel, and the old files are unreachable
It has become a normal guest with no more rights than any other virtual machine
questions.explanation: Hyper-V is type 1: the hypervisor starts first at boot and everything runs above it. Windows is still there, but as the root partition with extra privileges for managing guests.

questions.prompt: How does a hypervisor's virtual machine differ from a bytecode virtual machine such as a scripting language's?
options: It offers the real processor's instruction set, run directly
It interprets every instruction in software, one at a time
It translates guest code into bytecode before running it
It runs only text scripts and cannot run machine code
questions.explanation: A scripting VM carries out bytecode that no processor runs in silicon. A hypervisor's VM offers the processor's own instruction set, so it steps in only when the guest touches something the host must control.

questions.prompt: With Intel VT-x, in which ring does the guest's kernel run, and why does that help?
options: In the guest's own ring 0, so it runs unmodified and each instruction behaves as it expects
In ring 3, with the hypervisor emulating every privileged instruction that faults
In ring 1, a middle ring that the guest kernel was written to expect on virtual machines
In the host's ring 0, shared with the hypervisor but separated by the page tables
questions.explanation: VMX non-root operation gives the guest its own complete set of rings 0 to 3. Running the kernel in ring 3 is the old approach that failed because some instructions did not fault there.

questions.prompt: The hypervisor keeps a VMCS (Intel) or VMCB (AMD) for each virtual processor. Which list matches what it holds?
options: The guest's saved state, the host's state, and the exit controls
The guest's disk blocks, the delta file, and the snapshot index
The stage-2 tables, the guest's RAM, and the list of host processes
The guest's registers and a log of every instruction it has executed
questions.explanation: The structure holds the guest's registers, the host state to reload when the guest stops, and the list of guest actions that must hand control to the hypervisor.

questions.prompt: On a processor with hardware virtualization support, how does a hypervisor start and continue a guest?
options: Dedicated instructions: one to launch, one to resume
With an ordinary jump into the guest's first instruction
By booting the guest from disk each time
With a system call into the guest's kernel
questions.explanation: Hardware virtualization provides special entry instructions, with one to start a guest and another to continue one that has run before.

questions.prompt: After handling an exit caused by a guest instruction, what does the hypervisor usually do before the VM entry?
options: It moves the guest's saved instruction pointer past the instruction it just handled
It restarts the guest at the beginning of its boot code with a clean register set
It rewrites the guest's own page tables so the instruction cannot exit again
It clears the exit reason so the guest can read that the exit happened
questions.explanation: The exit saves the guest's state and gives the hypervisor an exit reason. After dealing with the cause, the hypervisor steps the saved instruction pointer forward so that, from inside the guest, the instruction just seems to have taken effect.

questions.prompt: A guest network driver writes 1 to its virtual card's START register and a VM exit follows. What caused the exit?
options: The register's guest-physical page has no second-stage mapping, so the processor hands the address to the hypervisor
Every memory write from a guest exits, so the hypervisor can check each one before it happens
The guest's own page table marks the page not present, so the guest's kernel reports the error to the host
The write is a ring-0 instruction, which always faults in the guest and is passed up to the host
