questions.prompt: Why shouldn't acknowledged commands be replayed again?
options: The returned state already includes their effects
An acknowledgment proves no commands changed position
Replaying old input replaces every version check
Every input record has a different interface contract
questions.explanation: Replaying covered commands repeats work already represented by the server state.

questions.prompt: What does interpolation use for another player's visible position?
options: Intermediate positions between received states
That other player's newest unreceived input record
The local player's final authoritative inventory
Arbitrary server states beyond the available history
questions.explanation: Received snapshots support smooth presentation on a slightly older timeline.

questions.prompt: What happens after a lag-compensated hit check?
options: The current simulation state is restored
The whole world remains permanently at the old time
The client becomes owner of the server's accepted state
Every player receives an extra simulation tick
questions.explanation: The server temporarily uses eligible recorded state, then restores the present.

questions.prompt: What does FCVAR_REPLICATED describe in this lesson?
options: A server-controlled setting enforced on connected clients
A client setting that decides all server movement rules
A variable guaranteed to contain every game's entity state
A command that returns a rendering frame immediately

questions.prompt: What does StartQueryCvarValue return immediately?
options: A cookie matching the later query reply
The client's final variable value synchronously
Every server-side rule about the queried setting
A complete record of the client's installed software

questions.prompt: Which distinction correctly describes VPK and BSP?
options: Resource package versus compiled map with data lumps
Game input record versus accepted server movement command
Client object pointer versus optional interface status output
Prediction history versus the renderer's received snapshot list
questions.explanation: VPK bundles resources; BSP organizes compiled map data in sections called lumps.

questions.prompt: A learner wants to truly absorb an unfamiliar idea from a reference page. Which routine builds the most real understanding?
options: Read the part you need, hide it, explain it from memory, then compare and fix gaps
Read the part you need several times over until all of its words feel familiar and clear
Copy the part you need into your notes word for word, then reread those notes the next day
Skim several pages quickly, then move on once nothing seems confusing anymore
questions.explanation: Hiding the source forces you to rebuild the idea yourself, and comparing afterwards shows exactly what you missed. Rereading or copying only rehearses recognition.

questions.prompt: Why can rereading the same paragraph many times leave someone feeling that they know it when they do not?
options: Familiar words feel like understanding, but that does not show you can rebuild the idea
Each rereading slightly changes the meaning that is stored in the reader's own memory
Repeated reading uses up attention, so new details stop being noticed or stored
A paragraph read several times becomes less accurate as a source of evidence
questions.explanation: Recognition (it looks familiar) is different from understanding. Explaining the idea without the page tests whether you can actually reconstruct it.

questions.prompt: Which study goal is specific enough that you can tell when you have finished it?
options: Explain what I saw after one jump and separate it from my guess about why
Understand game hacking well enough to feel confident in later chapters
Collect facts about every game engine before looking at any one game
Read the whole chapter twice so that every term feels familiar to me
questions.explanation: A recognizable goal ends with something you can show: a short explanation and a repeatable observation. Vague goals such as understanding a whole field never tell you when you are done.

questions.prompt: Which question is small enough to answer with an experiment?
options: If I press jump while standing still, does the character rise and then land?
How do games work, and which parts of them matter most to a player?
What is the best way to understand how every kind of game handles input?
Why do some games feel better to play than others on the same computer?
questions.explanation: A good question names the object (jump button), the change to look for (rise and land), and a check you can repeat. The broad versions have no single observation that could answer them.

questions.prompt: Which set lists what a useful technical question usually names?
options: The object, the relationship you want, and evidence you can check
The tool, the file format, and the person who will review the result
The answer you expect, the time you have, and the source you trust most
The game's engine, its version number, and a screenshot of the menu
questions.explanation: The lesson's jump example names the button, the change after one press, and a repeatable observation. Tools and engines may matter later, but they are not the three parts of the question itself.

questions.prompt: A player presses a key to make a character jump and nothing happens. Which next question is most useful for narrowing down the cause?
options: Did the key press reach the game, or did a rule block the jump here?
Is the whole game broken, so should it be reinstalled from the very beginning?
Which stored value controls jumping, so it can be forced to a new number now?
Does a different game built on the same engine allow the jump to happen too?
questions.explanation: No visible jump leaves two separate possibilities: the input was missed, or a rule prevented the action. Testing them one at a time beats guessing a fix for a cause you have not confirmed.

questions.prompt: In the jump example, which item is an assumption until you check it?
options: The character was standing on the ground at that moment
You pressed the jump button on the keyboard at that moment
The character visibly did not rise after your press
You wrote down the starting position of the character
questions.explanation: Pressing the button and seeing no rise are things you observed. Whether the character was grounded is a guess until you check the starting position.

questions.prompt: In games and other software, what does the word "state" mean?
options: The information a program holds right now that describes how things stand
The things that are currently visible on the screen to the player at that moment
A copy of the player's progress that is kept on disk between separate play sessions
The list of every key the player has pressed since the game was started
questions.explanation: State is what a program currently remembers, such as health or position. It can matter before it is drawn, so it is not limited to what is visible, and it exists in memory even if nothing is saved to disk.

questions.prompt: A tutorial explains a gold search, but it was written for another game version and another processor architecture. What should you check first?
options: Whether its target, version, and conditions match your experiment
Whether the tutorial has many comments and has been shared widely
Whether the steps look short enough to repeat in one sitting
Whether the author used the same operating system theme as you
questions.explanation: A source can be accurate and still answer a different question. It may explain the general mechanism yet give the wrong steps for your build.

questions.prompt: You watched the character jump once from one spot. What does that establish?
options: It shows what happened under those conditions, not from every position
It proves that jumping works from every position in the game
It proves that the game received every button press you made
It shows the rule that decides whether jumping is allowed at all
questions.explanation: One repeatable observation is evidence for the conditions you recorded. It cannot cover other starting positions, and it does not reveal the rule behind the jump.

questions.prompt: Five websites all say the same thing about a game setting, but they quote one original post. How many independent checks do you have?
options: One, because repeating a claim does not check it again
Five, because each website published its own copy of the text
Two, because the post and the group of sites count separately
Zero, because anything found on a website is automatically unreliable
questions.explanation: Several sites repeating one original claim are not several independent checks. Checking the code, the documentation, or a repeatable observation gives independent evidence.

questions.prompt: A jump fails. What makes a test useful when you have two competing explanations?
options: The two explanations predict different results for it
It is the first test that occurs to you after the failure
It confirms the explanation you already prefer in all cases
It changes several conditions at once to save time
questions.explanation: A test that gives the same result whichever explanation is true tells you nothing. Resetting to a known position and varying one condition separates, for example, a missed input from an airborne character.

questions.prompt: Two explanations fit a bug: one needs a single cause, the other needs three unproven coincidences. How should Occam's razor guide you?
options: Test the simpler explanation first, but be ready to revise it if new evidence disagrees
Treat the simpler explanation as settled and stop collecting any further evidence
Discard any explanation that involves more than one cause working together
Choose whichever explanation more people online happen to repeat to each other
questions.explanation: Occam's razor is a rule for deciding what to investigate first, not a proof. A more complicated cause may fit later observations better.

questions.prompt: After comparing your own explanation with a trusted source, why mark each part as correct, missing, wrong or unclear instead of just "good" or "bad"?
options: It shows which exact parts need work, so you fix only those instead of redoing everything
It produces a score that you can compare with other learners who studied the topic
It proves the source is mistaken whenever your answer happens to differ from it
It lets you skip every part that you marked as unclear and keep going
questions.explanation: Specific marks turn a vague verdict into a to-do list. Each label points at a different kind of repair: add what is missing, fix what is wrong, clarify what is fuzzy.

questions.prompt: A tutor marks your answer wrong and only hands you the right sentence. What would help you most that is missing?
options: An explanation of why your answer fell short, so you can fix the misunderstanding
A longer replacement sentence, since more words carry more detail about the topic itself
A count of how many other people made the same mistake that you have just made
A reminder to memorize the corrected sentence exactly as it was written for you today
questions.explanation: A sentence you only copy teaches little. Knowing why your answer failed lets you repair the misunderstanding that produced it.

questions.prompt: Which answer shows you can explain an idea a different way, as opposed to just answering accurately?
options: If a character loses health, the stored number drops and the bar may follow
Game state describes what is happening now in the game world
State is the information that describes what is happening at the moment
A game's state is information describing what is occurring currently
questions.explanation: Explaining it differently keeps the meaning but changes the example or comparison. The other three only reword the same sentence, which checks precision rather than whether you can use the idea.

questions.prompt: A game shows 100 gold, and an item costs 25. After one purchase, what should you predict a second 25-gold purchase leaves?
options: 50 gold, because 100 minus 25 is 75 and 75 minus 25 is 50
75 gold, because the second purchase works the same as the first
0 gold, because buying twice uses everything the player had
25 gold, because the item cost stays in the display after buying
questions.explanation: The lesson follows 100 to 75 first, then asks you to predict the next step before checking in the game. Each purchase subtracts 25 from whatever is left.

questions.prompt: A student's code compiles after an assistant filled in a line. What does the successful compile tell them?
options: The code is accepted, but not that they understand it or that it does the intended job
That they understand every line, since they could not have compiled it otherwise
That the new line produces exactly the intended behavior when the code runs
That any warnings or error output can be safely ignored from this point on
questions.explanation: Compiling only means the code is well-formed enough to build. Explaining each line yourself is the real check that you understand it and that it solves your problem.

questions.prompt: A beginner keeps hitting the same error. Which response best helps find the cause?
options: Save the exact message, go back to the last step that worked, and try something smaller
Rewrite everything from scratch so that the old error disappears along with all the rest
Change several settings at once and watch whether anything starts to improve
Decide the topic is too hard and skip ahead to material that seems easier
questions.explanation: An error is information about one attempt, not a verdict on you. Shrinking the task to a small known case makes the cause findable.

questions.prompt: Which help request gives someone enough to reproduce your problem?
options: I expected a rise; the input was logged but the position stayed put. What next?
It does not work. Could you tell me what is wrong with my game and how to fix it?
Jumping is broken in my game and I tried everything I could think of to fix it.
My game is bad and nothing responds to me. Do you know of a fix for this one?
questions.explanation: A reproducible request states what you expected, what happened, the code or error, the version, and what you already tried. Complaints like it does not work give another person nothing to inspect.

questions.prompt: An AI answer states a fact about a game's setting but cannot say where it came from. How should you treat it?
options: As a lead to verify against the program, documentation, or source code
As evidence, because it was written in a confident and clear tone
As settled, provided the AI also repeated the same fact twice
As worthless, so no AI answer is ever worth following up on
questions.explanation: AI can suggest tests and simplify text, but important claims are checked against the real program or documentation. A fact with no visible source is a lead, not evidence.

questions.prompt: While a game runs, which part holds the current gold value?
options: RAM, the fast working storage for the running program's values
The storage drive, which keeps the live number between frames
The GPU, which keeps every number the game has to calculate
The keyboard, which supplies and then stores the changing value
questions.explanation: The drive keeps the game files when the game is closed; RAM holds code and current values while it runs. The GPU helps draw the picture rather than keeping gold.

questions.prompt: What kind of work does one CPU instruction do?
options: A small specified operation, such as adding two numbers or comparing them
A whole game action, such as understanding what collecting a coin means
The drawing of one finished picture frame to the player's screen
The loading of the game file from the storage drive into memory
questions.explanation: The CPU does not understand a game the way a person does. It executes small operations; meaning and drawing come from the program and other hardware.

questions.prompt: A register holds 100 and an add-one instruction runs. What has happened?
options: The register's value is now 101, and nothing else has been decided
The register now holds 101 and the screen already shows 101
The register holds 100 still, and a new register holds the 101
The register's value is 101, and the game knows a coin was collected
questions.explanation: An add-one instruction changes only that working value. It does not decide what a coin means or draw the number; later steps store and display it.

questions.prompt: In the tiny program that takes 100 and gives back 101, which word names the 100?
options: Input, the value supplied to the calculation
Output, the result that the calculation produces
State, which is a name for the final stored answer
Branch, the point where the program picks one path
questions.explanation: The input is what comes in and the output is the result. State is the information describing what is happening now, such as the gold count.

questions.prompt: How does a program relate to the individual instructions inside it?
options: It arranges many simple instructions so that together they do a larger job
It is one single long instruction that the computer runs all at once
It is the remembered information, such as health, that a game keeps
It is a named step that other code can ask to run again and again
questions.explanation: A program combines instructions to do a bigger job than any one could. Named reusable steps are functions, and remembered information is state.

questions.prompt: Why do programmers package a piece of behavior as a named function?
options: So other code can reuse that behavior by name instead of repeating its steps
So that the behavior runs by itself without any other code asking for it
So that the behavior is forced to take an input and return a useful number
So that the computer can store the behavior as plain data, not instructions
questions.explanation: Naming a behavior lets different parts of a program ask for it again instead of rewriting its steps. A function still needs to be called, and it does not have to take or return anything.

questions.prompt: A function takes a number, doubles it, adds 3, and gives back the result. What does it give back for an input of 10?
options: 23, because doubling gives 20 and then 3 is added
26, because 3 is added first and then the sum is doubled
13, because just the 3 is added to the input number
30, because the input number is multiplied by three
questions.explanation: Follow the steps in order: 10 doubled is 20, and adding 3 gives 23. Changing the order of the steps would change the result.

questions.prompt: For one action, what does a branch do?
options: It compares the action and follows exactly one path
It runs the add path and the subtract path one after the other
It repeats the same path until the number is zero
It waits for the next action before it chooses a path
questions.explanation: A branch lets the same program respond differently to different input. It does not run both outcomes for a single action.

questions.prompt: Which digits does binary use?
options: Only 0 and 1, with each place worth twice the place to its right
The digits 0 to 9, with each place worth ten times the place to its right
The digits 0 to 7, with each place worth eight times the place to its right
Only 1 and 2, with each place worth twice the place to its right
questions.explanation: Binary has two digits, called bits. Decimal has places worth ten times the one to the right, which is a different base.

questions.prompt: A byte's bits are 0 1 1 0 0 1 0 0, with place values 128 down to 1. What number is it?
questions.explanation: The set bits are in the 64, 32, and 4 places. Adding only those place values gives 100.

questions.prompt: How many bits does one hexadecimal digit represent, and how many digits describe one byte?
options: Four bits, so two hex digits per byte
Eight bits, so one hex digit per byte
Two bits, so four hex digits per byte
Sixteen bits, so one hex digit per two bytes
questions.explanation: Hex has sixteen digits (0-9 and A-F), which is exactly four bits per digit. A byte is eight bits, so it takes two hex digits.

questions.prompt: What does the prefix in 0x64 tell you, and what is its value?
options: The prefix marks hex, and the value is 6 x 16 + 4 = 100
The prefix marks binary, and the value is 6 + 4 = 10
The prefix marks hex, and the value is 6 x 10 + 4 = 64
The prefix marks decimal, and the value is 0 x 64 = 0
questions.explanation: Hex digits are worth 16 per place, so 0x64 is 6 sixteens plus 4. It is still the decimal number 100, only written a different way.

questions.prompt: Decimal 100, binary 01100100, and hex 0x64 are what, relative to each other?
options: Three ways to write the same number
Three different amounts that happen to look alike
Three kinds of gold that a game could hold
Three results that depend on which CPU you use
questions.explanation: Decimal, binary, and hex only change how a number is written. They are not different kinds of gold or different values.

questions.prompt: One byte can represent which range of values?
options: 0 through 255, with larger values using several bytes
1 through 256, with larger values using two bytes only
0 through 127, with larger values using signed bytes
0 through 100, with larger values using the next byte
questions.explanation: Eight bits give 256 patterns, from 0 to 255. Larger values spread across several bytes.

questions.prompt: How does assembly language differ from a high-level language?
options: Assembly names single CPU operations; high-level code expresses bigger ideas
Assembly is what a graphics card runs, while high-level code is what the CPU runs
Assembly is a newer style that was invented to replace all high-level languages
Assembly works on every kind of CPU unchanged, while high-level code is tied to one
questions.explanation: A CPU runs patterns of bits. Assembly names those individual operations so people can read them, while a high-level language lets you write larger ideas without spelling out each CPU step.

questions.prompt: Many languages have a type called u8, an unsigned 8-bit whole number. Which value can it not hold?
options: 300, since eight bits can only count up to 255
0, since unsigned numbers start counting from one
255, since that is above what eight bits can hold
17, since odd numbers need extra bits to be stored
questions.explanation: A type's bit width fixes its range of values. Eight bits give 256 patterns, so an unsigned value runs from 0 to 255 and 300 does not fit.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of an operating system for a game?
options: It provides common services, like files and windows, for programs
It supplies the game rules, such as the coin price and the damage dealt
It takes over from the CPU when the program is too large to run
It stores every game's saved values together in one shared place
questions.explanation: A program can ask Windows to read a file or show a window rather than controlling each device itself. The game still brings its own rules and state.

questions.prompt: What is a process?
options: One running instance of a program, with its own memory
The game file kept on the storage drive while the game is closed
A single CPU instruction that the running program has just finished
The part of the screen where the game draws its main picture
questions.explanation: Starting the game file creates a process. The file on storage is not the process; it is what Windows loads into memory.

questions.prompt: What is a thread?
options: A path that executes instructions inside a process
A copy of the game file kept on the storage drive
A cable that connects the CPU to a graphics card
A kind of value that stores gold during the game
questions.explanation: Windows starts a thread in the process to run instructions. A process may have more than one, but one is enough to picture the first example.

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes the repeating cycle at the heart of most games?
options: Take input, update the state, draw the new state, then repeat
Draw the frame, update the state, read input, then stop for good
Load the save file, draw the screen, then close and reopen the game
Update the state, wait for the window to close, then draw once at the end
questions.explanation: The loop collects what the player did, changes the stored state, shows the result, and goes around again for the next action.

questions.prompt: A number shown in a game does not change after an action. Which set of questions best finds where the change failed?
options: Did the input arrive, did the stored value change, and did the display show it?
Did the player click, did the monitor refresh, and did the CPU overheat?
Did the game save, did the file close properly, and did the window resize?
Did the code compile, did the engine start, and did the level finish loading?
questions.explanation: Splitting a change into input, stored value and display shows which stage failed. Each stage can fail independently of the others.

questions.prompt: Why does editing a number on the screen not change how much gold a game thinks a player has?
options: The screen only reports the state; the stored state and rules decide the outcome
The screen is drawn before the state exists, so it can just show old numbers there
The screen runs on a separate computer that not talks to the game itself
The screen can just change numbers that are smaller than the stored value
questions.explanation: Input leads to rules, rules change the stored state, and the screen then shows that state. The display reports the result; it does not decide it.

questions.prompt: What does a game engine typically provide, compared with the game built on top of it?
options: Reusable common jobs such as the loop and drawing; the game adds its own rules
The game's own rules and levels; the game adds just the window and title
The art and sounds; the game adds the loop and the drawing code
A finished game that the developer can rename but cannot change
questions.explanation: An engine is reusable software for jobs most games share, like the repeating loop, drawing and loading files. Rules such as what an item costs belong to the particular game.

questions.prompt: A player holds 120 coins and 50 health, then takes 15 damage. What does the player hold afterward?
options: 120 coins and 35 health, since damage changes only health
105 coins and 50 health, since damage is paid out of the coins
105 coins and 35 health, since damage is split across both values
120 coins and 65 health, since damage is added to the health
questions.explanation: Each rule touches a particular part of the state. Damage lowers health, and the coin count stays as it was.

questions.prompt: What question does an identifier such as player ID 17 answer?
options: Which player or entity is this?
How much gold does this player have?
What does this entity look like?
Where is this entity in the world?
questions.explanation: The ID says which entity; fields such as gold say what is true about it now. Two players called Ada can still have different IDs, so a display name need not identify anyone.

questions.prompt: When modeling a game character, what is a component?
options: One part of the model that has a single job, such as health or position
A physical piece of computer hardware that the game needs in order to run
A bug that appears when two separate rules disagree about the same value
A saved copy of the character that is written into a file on the disk
questions.explanation: Components split a character into parts with distinct responsibilities, like health, wallet, position and appearance.

questions.prompt: What is an entity's lifetime?
options: The interval from its creation to its removal
The number of seconds that a player spends in a round
The largest value its health field can hold
The count of frames that are drawn for it each second
questions.explanation: A coin's lifetime ends when Ada picks it up. A later coin may reuse its storage without being the same coin.

questions.prompt: Ten enemies in a level share one picture file. One enemy is defeated. What happens to the picture and to the other enemies?
options: The other nine stay in the world and the shared picture remains available
The picture is unloaded, so the other nine enemies disappear along with it
The ten enemies shared one position, so all ten are removed together
The picture is copied again so that each remaining enemy owns its own version
questions.explanation: A shared asset is a resource, while each enemy is its own instance with its own identity, position and availability. Removing one instance does not affect the others.

questions.prompt: A character type says its maximum health is 100. One character in play currently has 40. What is that 40?
options: The current state of that one running character, not part of the shared type
A new maximum, since the type has to follow whatever damage the character took
A mistake, since a running character's health has to match its type's value
A backup of the type's settings that was saved when the game first started
questions.explanation: A definition describes what something is by default, and an instance's current values can start equal and then drift apart. The 40 belongs to that one running instance.

questions.prompt: Why keep several player records in a collection rather than fields like gold2 and health2?
options: One rule can then handle any number of players
Collections store each value in fewer bytes than fields
A collection makes every player's gold the same value
A collection stops a player from ever being removed
questions.explanation: With separate field names, each new player demands more special-case code. A collection plus a loop keeps the rule the same when the group grows.

questions.prompt: A loop visits each of three players in a list and adds 2 points to each. They start with 10, 20 and 30. What do they hold after one full loop?
options: 12, 22 and 32, since the same rule is applied once to each
12, 20 and 30, since the loop ends after handling the first one
16, 26 and 36, since each player gets 2 points for every player
10, 20 and 32, since a loop just changes the last item in a list
questions.explanation: A loop runs the same rule once for each item in a collection. Each player's own value changes by 2.

questions.prompt: A rule says health must be at least 0 and at most a maximum of 100. Which value breaks the rule?
options: 120, since it is higher than the allowed maximum
100, since a value equal to the maximum is too high
0, since a value has to be greater than zero
50, since it is lower than the allowed maximum
questions.explanation: The boundaries 0 and 100 are allowed, so a value exactly on either edge is fine. Only values outside that range, such as 120, break the rule.

questions.prompt: A tool finds the memory address that holds a character's gold. Later the character is removed from the game. Why can the address not be trusted to mean that character afterward?
options: An address says where data sits now, and that memory can be reused for something else
Addresses change every time a character picks up or spends any amount of gold
Addresses are just copies that update when the game saves its progress to disk
Addresses are random labels that the operating system rewrites every second
questions.explanation: A memory address is a location, not an identity. Once an object is removed, that spot can be given to a different object.

questions.prompt: A buy button is held down and the purchase rule runs on every update. What could go wrong?
options: One press could accidentally buy many items
The purchase rule would never be allowed to run
The game would draw the screen in black and white
The held button would reset the player's gold to zero
questions.explanation: The lesson separates a button being pressed now from being held. One press of the buy button requests one purchase, while holding movement requests continued movement.

questions.prompt: In a 2D world where x grows to the right and y grows upward, an object at (5, 1) moves two units left. Where does it end up?
options: (3, 1), since moving left lowers x by two
(7, 1), since moving left raises x by two
(5, 3), since moving left raises y by two
(5, -1), since moving left lowers y by two
questions.explanation: The axis directions are a convention. Moving left reduces x and leaves y unchanged, so (5, 1) becomes (3, 1).

questions.prompt: A camera follows a character so it stays near the middle of the window while it walks right through a long level. What changes?
options: Its world position keeps increasing while its screen position stays near the middle
Its screen position keeps increasing while its world position stays near the middle
Neither position changes, because just the size of the level is changing
Both positions increase by the same amount for as long as it keeps walking
questions.explanation: World coordinates say where something is in the game world, and screen coordinates say where its picture is drawn. Moving the camera changes the view without changing the character's world location.

questions.prompt: An object moves at 6 units per second for 0.5 seconds, starting at x = 10. What is its new x?
options: 13, since distance is speed times time, which is 3 units
16, since the speed is simply added to the position
10.5, since just the elapsed time is added to the position
12, since the speed is divided by the elapsed time
questions.explanation: Distance equals speed multiplied by elapsed time: 6 x 0.5 = 3. Adding that to 10 gives 13.

questions.prompt: Which job belongs to the simulation rather than to rendering?
options: Moving a projectile and counting a timer down
Turning the current world into one picture on the screen
Choosing which image to load for the player's appearance
Showing the text Gold: 76 on the display
questions.explanation: Simulation advances movement, health, timers, and other rules. Rendering makes an image of the current world; one displayed picture is a frame.

questions.prompt: A game moves a character 2 units every frame it draws. What happens on a computer that draws 120 frames per second instead of 60?
options: It moves twice as far each second, so movement should be tied to elapsed time instead
It moves the same distance each second, since the engine adjusts the step per frame
It moves half as far each second, since each frame lasts a shorter time
It moves the same distance each second, since frames are measured in game time
questions.explanation: Tying movement to the number of frames makes speed depend on the drawing rate. Scaling movement by elapsed time gives the same distance per second at either rate.

questions.prompt: A point at x = 2 asks to move to x = 8, and a thin wall stands at x = 5. Why must collision testing look at the path and not only the destination?
options: The destination lies beyond the wall, so only the path shows that it was crossed
Walls can just be detected while a point is moving at a very slow speed
A path is shorter than a destination, so it is cheaper for the game to test
The destination check cannot read the wall's position from the game world
questions.explanation: Checking only where the point lands misses a wall that it jumped over. Testing the whole movement lets the game stop the point just before the wall.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between detecting contact and deciding its consequence?
options: A contact test can start all three, then each follows its own rule
A coin, a wall, and a trap each need their own kind of contact test
The contact test itself already knows to award gold, block, or hurt
The contact test and its consequence are one step and cannot be split
questions.explanation: A wall blocks movement, a coin awards gold and removes itself, and a trap applies damage. The contact test is only the first step.

questions.prompt: In a state machine, what is a move from one mode to another called, and what is the whole set of modes and rules called?
options: Transition for the move, state machine for the set of modes and rules
Frame for the move, game loop for the set of modes and rules
Instance for the move, asset library for the set of modes and rules
Component for the move, engine for the set of modes and rules
questions.explanation: A change between modes, such as alive to defeated, is a transition. The allowed modes together with the rules for moving between them make up the state machine.

questions.prompt: In a game, how does an action request differ from an event?
options: A request asks for something to happen; an event reports that it already happened
A request reports the new state of the game; an event asks the game to change that state
They are the same kind of message, and the name just depends on who is sending it
A request is saved to disk, while an event lives just in the computer's memory
questions.explanation: Requests are asks and events are reports. The game can reject a request that no longer makes sense, such as picking up an item that was already collected.

questions.prompt: Someone changes only the display text from Gold: 76 to Gold: 999. What does the purchase rule still see?
options: 76, because it reads the gameplay gold, not the display text
999, because the rule reads whatever text the screen shows
0, because changing the text clears the gameplay value too
1075, because the rule adds the two values together first
questions.explanation: The text is derived from the number but is not necessarily what the rule reads. This is why a matching number in memory is only the start of an investigation.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that the gameplay gold is authoritative for the purchase?
options: The purchase rule accepts it as the amount Ada actually has
It is stored in a special numeric type that cannot be changed
It is the copy that is drawn first on the player's screen
It is the value that is written to the save file first
questions.explanation: Authority describes a role, not a numeric type. The display copy reports the result and does not decide it.

questions.prompt: In an online game the server holds 50 gold for a player, while a modified client displays 999. The player asks to buy a 20-gold item. What happens in a sound design?
options: The server checks its own 50, accepts, and leaves the player with 30
The server believes the client's 999 and leaves the player with 979
The server rejects the request, since the two numbers do not match
The server accepts it, then copies the client's 999 back as its own
questions.explanation: In a sound design the server keeps authoritative state and checks requests against it. The displayed 999 never gave the server any more gold.

questions.prompt: A player saves with 60 gold, then spends 25 without saving again. What do the live state and the save file hold?
options: Live state holds 35 and the file still holds 60, since a save captures one moment
Both hold 35, since a save file updates itself whenever the state changes
Live state holds 60 and the file holds 35, since spending is recorded on disk first
Both hold 60, since spending is just applied the next time a save is made
questions.explanation: Saving copies chosen state at one moment. Afterward the live state and the file can disagree because they describe different moments.

questions.prompt: After a game is restarted and a save is loaded, a tool still holds a memory address from the earlier run. What is true?
options: Loading rebuilds the data in new memory, so the old address need not hold the same record
The save file stores memory locations along with the values, so the old address is still valid
The old address is still valid as long as the same save slot is loaded again
The old address is still valid because the operating system keeps locations fixed
questions.explanation: Saved data keeps its meaning across runs, not its memory locations. Each run builds fresh records in whatever memory it is given.

questions.prompt: In the toy format, one byte of player ID then one byte of gold, what are the bytes for ID 17 and gold 76?
questions.explanation: 17 is 1 x 16 + 1 = 0x11 and 76 is 4 x 16 + 12 = 0x4C, written ID first. The bytes alone do not label themselves; the format says which byte means what.

questions.prompt: A number stored as four bytes might be gameplay gold, a display copy, a saved value, or a server result. What does its byte pattern alone tell you?
options: How it is represented, but not its role or authority
Its role, because the bytes name what they are for
Its authority, because the bytes say who set them
When it was last updated, since bytes keep a timestamp
questions.explanation: Representation and role are separate questions: how is it represented, and what role does it have? Bytes alone do not establish authority.

questions.prompt: Ada and Bo use the same damage method. Why can only Ada lose health on Ada.damage(20)?
options: The receiver selects Ada’s own fields.
The class replaces both player records.
The method gives every player one field.
The picture selects the stored result.
questions.explanation: A shared method operates on the receiver supplied by that call. Separate instances retain separate fields.

questions.prompt: A Player class has been declared, but no player has been created. What exists at this point?
options: A picture already placed in the world.
A definition of fields and operations.
One shared object for all later players.
The saved health of every future player.
questions.explanation: A class describes a kind of object. An instance must be created before there is a particular player with current values.

questions.prompt: A server receives an item ID while the client shows 999 gold. Which check decides this example’s purchase?
options: Compare the client’s pixels with the item.
Compare the frame count with the player.
Compare the server’s gold with its price.
Compare the display text with its width.
questions.explanation: The server looks up the item price and uses its own stored player gold. Display text does not supply the accepted amount.

questions.prompt: Holding Buy for several ticks should buy once in this example. What must the input handler distinguish?
options: A shared asset from a disk file name.
A saved player from a drawn health bar.
A decimal number from a binary number.
A new press from a button still held.
questions.explanation: A press event requests one purchase; repeated held-state updates would otherwise request several purchases.

questions.prompt: A wall, a coin, and a trap can all use contact detection. Why can the resulting updates differ?
options: Each contact handler applies its own effect.
Every contact test directly subtracts health.
The picture chooses a random stored effect.
Each object must use a different bit width.
questions.explanation: Detection reports contact. The consequence may block movement, award gold, or apply damage.

questions.prompt: How are data, a value and a type related?
options: Data is stored bytes, a value is what they mean, and a type says how to read them
Data is what the screen shows, a value is the stored bytes, and a type is a name
A value is the raw bytes, data is their meaning, and a type is a variable's label
Data and value are two words for the same thing, and a type is a storage location
questions.explanation: The same bytes can mean different things depending on the type used to read them, so bytes and meaning are separate levels of the same information.

questions.prompt: Four bytes sit in memory in this order, written in hexadecimal: 2A 00 00 00. Read as one 32-bit little-endian whole number, what is the value?
options: 42, because the first byte is the least significant
704643072, because the first byte is the most significant
2, because just the first hexadecimal digit is kept
168, because each of the four bytes adds 2A again
questions.explanation: Little-endian puts the least significant byte first, so only 2A counts. Hexadecimal 2A is 2 x 16 + 10 = 42.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a literal from a variable?
options: A literal is a value written directly in code, and a variable is a name holding a value
A literal is a name holding a value, and a variable is a value written directly in code
A literal is a value that changes while running, and a variable is fixed forever
A literal and a variable are the same thing, named differently in different languages
questions.explanation: A literal such as 100 is written straight into the code. A variable is a name that refers to a stored value, and its value may change.

questions.prompt: In many languages a statement such as total = total - fee runs with total at 80 and fee at 30. What happens?
options: The right side is worked out as 50 first, then stored back into total
The statement is an error, since total cannot equal itself minus the fee
Both sides are compared first, and nothing is stored unless they match
The fee is subtracted twice, once for each side of the equals sign
questions.explanation: Here the equals sign means assign, not compare. The right side is calculated first and the result goes into the variable on the left.

questions.prompt: A game screen shows the label "Gold: 75". How does that label relate to the stored gold amount?
options: The label is built from a stored value, and the rules might check another one
The label is the stored amount itself, so editing the label edits the amount
The label is the just copy of the amount, so the rules read it directly
The label and the stored amount are the same, so they cannot differ
questions.explanation: The path runs from input to calculation to stored state to display. Displayed text is derived output, and it may not come from the value the next rule check reads.

questions.prompt: A balance stored as an unsigned whole number is 10 and the price is 25. Why check before subtracting?
options: The purchase should be refused, and an unsigned number cannot go negative
Subtraction is slower than comparison, so checking first saves a little time
Unsigned numbers cannot be subtracted, so the check switches to addition
The check raises the balance first so that the price is guaranteed to fit
questions.explanation: A guard turns the rule into code: only subtract when the balance covers the price. Without it, 10 - 25 has no valid unsigned representation.

questions.prompt: What is an algorithm?
options: A repeatable procedure made of ordered steps that solves a problem
A particular programming language that is used to write game code
A value kept in memory that can change while a program is running
A saved result that a program remembers from one run to the next
questions.explanation: The plan is the algorithm, and code is one exact way of writing it down. The same procedure can be run on different inputs.

questions.prompt: Which three building blocks can be combined to express almost any procedure?
options: Sequence (steps in order), selection (choosing), repetition (looping)
Input (reading keys), output (drawing frames), storage (saving files)
Variables (naming data), types (shaping data), values (holding data)
Compile (building code), link (joining parts), run (executing it)
questions.explanation: Sequence runs steps in order, selection picks a path with a condition, and repetition repeats work. Larger programs are built by combining them.

questions.prompt: In a function definition such as fn price(base: u32, tax: u32) -> u32, what are base and tax?
options: Parameters: names for the input values the function receives
Return values: results the function hands back to whoever called it
Types: descriptions of how many bits each of the values will use
Literals: numbers written directly into the body of the function
questions.explanation: Parameters are the names in the parentheses that stand for inputs. The arrow and the type after it describe what is returned.

questions.prompt: A function checks a condition and returns early when it is true, with another return line written after the check. When the condition is true, what happens to that last line?
options: The early return ends the call, so the last line is never reached
Both returns run, and the caller receives the later value
The last line runs first, and then the early return runs
The function fails to build, since it contains two return lines
questions.explanation: A function does not have to run every line. A return ends the call at once and hands the value back.

questions.prompt: A function computes a new balance and gives it back. A caller calls it but ignores the result. What happens to the caller's own balance variable?
options: It is unchanged, since the caller must store the returned value
It becomes the returned value as soon as the function call finishes
It is reset to zero until the next time that the function is called again
It is updated just when the variable and the function share the same name
questions.explanation: A call produces a value. The caller decides whether to store it, for example by assigning it back to the variable.

questions.prompt: After a purchase attempt a balance is unchanged. Why can that alone not prove that no purchase happened?
options: An item costing zero leaves the balance the same even when it is bought
Balances are just updated when the game saves, so any changes show up late
A purchase changes the displayed number but does not change the stored balance
Purchases are logged in a separate counter that the balance ignores
questions.explanation: A result that does not separate success from failure is ambiguous. Representing the outcome explicitly removes the doubt.

questions.prompt: A shop sells an item for 40 coins. Which set of balances best tests the buying rule at its boundary?
options: 39, 40 and 41: just below, exactly at, and just above the price
0, 80 and 160: spread out evenly across a large range of balances
1, 2 and 3: the smallest balances that a player could possibly have
40, 40 and 40: the price repeated to confirm the same result each time
questions.explanation: Bugs cluster where a decision changes. Testing just below, exactly at and just above the threshold checks the comparison itself.

questions.prompt: A shop accepts a purchase when balance >= price, and a developer changes this to balance > price. What changes when the balance exactly equals the price?
options: A purchase that used to succeed is now refused
A purchase that used to be refused now succeeds
The balance goes negative once the purchase is made
Nothing changes, since equal values not reach the check
questions.explanation: With >= an exact match is allowed, and with > it is not. The boundary value shows which comparison was intended.

questions.prompt: Which input combines unusual conditions and is called a corner case?
options: Zero gold and a zero price together
A purchase of 25 with exactly 100 gold
An item priced just below the player's gold
Two players who each have the same gold
questions.explanation: A corner case combines unusual conditions, here zero gold and a free item. An edge case is one unusual end of the range, such as zero gold alone.

questions.prompt: In many languages, what does dot notation such as hero.health do?
options: It selects the health field that belongs to that particular record
It divides the hero by its health to get a ratio of the two
It creates a new record named health inside the hero record
It searches every record in the game for a field with that name
questions.explanation: The dot picks one named part out of a specific record, so hero.health and other.health can hold different values.

questions.prompt: Which player record breaks the rule that health should be between zero and the maximum?
options: Health 120 with a maximum of 100
Health 80 with a maximum of 100
Health 100 with a maximum of 100
Health 0 with a maximum of 100
questions.explanation: A health of 120 is above the maximum of 100. The lesson later names such a rule an invariant.

questions.prompt: Two accounts hold 90 and 30 coins. A loop charges each a fee of 35 using a rule that refuses when funds are too low. What are the balances afterward?
options: 55 and 30, since the second cannot afford it and is left unchanged
55 and -5, since the loop charges both whether or not they can pay
55 and 0, since a refused charge drains the account instead
90 and 30, since a loop changes nothing unless every item succeeds
questions.explanation: The loop applies the same rule to each account in turn, and the guard decides each one separately. The first pays and the second is refused.

questions.prompt: A loop visits each record in a list. How does looping over copies of the records differ from looping over the records themselves with permission to change them?
options: Changes to copies are lost, while changes to the records themselves stay in the list
Copies change faster, since they skip the extra work of reaching the original
Both keep their changes, since a list syncs itself with copies of its items
Looping over the records themselves forbids reading the values that they hold
questions.explanation: A copy is a separate value, so editing it leaves the list untouched. Changing the records in place needs a way to reach the originals.

questions.prompt: Gold starts at 100 and the prices are 25, 90, and 10, each bought only when affordable. What is the final gold?
options: 65, because 90 fails after gold falls to 75
0, because every price in the list gets paid
35, because 25 and 90 are paid but 10 is not
75, because only the first price is paid
questions.explanation: The passes go 100 to 75, then 75 is below 90 so it stays 75, then 75 - 10 = 65. Following the stored gold, not just the prices, gives the answer.

questions.prompt: In the three-price example, what would change if the 90-gold purchase came first?
options: It could succeed, and the later 25-gold purchase would then fail
Nothing, since the total is the same whatever the order
Both would fail, because 90 is more than the cost
The program would repeat the 90 purchase until gold is zero
questions.explanation: With 100 gold, 90 is affordable and leaves 10, so the following 25 fails. This is why order matters when reading logic.

questions.prompt: When is a while-style loop a better fit than a for-style loop over a collection?
options: When a condition, not a known list, decides whether another pass is needed
When the loop has to visit every item in a known list one time each
When the loop should run exactly one time whatever the conditions are
When the collection is too small to be worth using a loop for
questions.explanation: A for loop suits a known collection. A while loop keeps going while a condition holds, which fits cases where you do not know in advance how many passes are needed.

questions.prompt: A list of scores is empty. Why can a program report its count but not its minimum?
options: The count is zero, but no item exists to supply a minimum
Counting needs a sorted list, and an empty list cannot be sorted
A minimum needs at least two items, since it compares one with another
Counting reads each value, so an empty list gives a read error
questions.explanation: Zero is a sensible count of nothing, but a minimum or maximum has to come from an actual item. A missing answer needs a way to be represented explicitly.

questions.prompt: A game must quickly find a player's record using the player's name. Which collection fits best?
options: A hash map, where each key points to its value
A queue, which hands back items in the order they arrived
A stack, which hands back the item that was added last
A set, which just records whether a name is present
questions.explanation: A hash map answers "what value belongs to this key?" A key might be missing, and the order of entries is not part of its promise.

questions.prompt: Commands from players must be processed in the exact order they arrived. Which structure fits?
options: A queue, adding at the back and removing from the front
A hash map, which finds an item quickly from its own key
A set, which stores each distinct item a single time here
A stack, which adds and removes items at the same end
questions.explanation: A queue answers "what arrived next?", handing items out first in, first out. It is not built for looking up arbitrary items.

questions.prompt: What characterizes a procedural style of writing a rule?
options: Writing ordered steps that check conditions and change the state
Describing the rule just as a calculation from inputs to a result
Reacting to announced events by running handlers attached to them
Bundling data with the functions that work on it into objects
questions.explanation: The procedural style spells out steps that change state. Functional, event-driven and object-oriented styles organize the same rule differently.

questions.prompt: What makes a function an example of a functional style?
options: It computes a result from its inputs and does not secretly change anything else
It changes a shared record and gives back nothing to the code that called it
It runs just when an event handler calls it in response to a notice
It stores its data and its behavior together inside one object
questions.explanation: A function that only turns inputs into a result is easy to check with other inputs, and the caller decides whether to store the result.

questions.prompt: What is an abstraction in programming?
options: A simpler interface that hides inner steps behind a name
A comment that explains the inner steps in plain language
A copy of some code that is stored somewhere else for safety
A shortcut that skips the checking of the values given to it
questions.explanation: Other code can use the rule without repeating its steps. The name still has to keep its promise, so it does not fix inputs that do not fit.

questions.prompt: A check returns the result of the comparison health <= maximum. What does it return for health 130 and maximum 100?
options: false, because 130 is above the maximum
true, because 130 is a valid whole number
130, because it hands back the larger of the two
30, because it hands back the difference between them
questions.explanation: A comparison produces a boolean. 130 is not less than or equal to 100, so the result is false.

questions.prompt: In Rust's build tool, how does checking a project differ from running it?
options: Checking finds errors fast without making a program; running builds it and starts it
Checking runs a program in slow motion to find bugs; running skips all error detection
Checking just tidies the layout of the code; running tests that the code is correct
Checking builds and starts a program; running just builds it and then stops again
questions.explanation: A check is a fast way to catch compile errors without producing something runnable. Running compiles the code and then executes the result.

questions.prompt: In most languages, why can a later line use a name created by an earlier line, but not the other way around?
options: Lines run from top to bottom, so earlier names exist by the time later lines run
Names are shared across a file in alphabetical order, from the first to the last
Names marked as changeable can be seen by the lines that come after them
Later lines run first and then copy their names back up to the earlier lines
questions.explanation: Statements run in sequence. A name has to be created before the code that uses it runs.

questions.prompt: In Rust, a line says ready = stamina >= cost, comparing two whole numbers. What type does the compiler infer for ready?
options: A boolean, since a comparison produces true or false
The same number type as stamina, since stamina appears in it
A string of text that describes how the two numbers compare
A number that is 1 for a yes and 0 for a no
questions.explanation: A comparison does not return one of the numbers; it returns a true-or-false answer. The compiler works out the type from what the expression produces.

questions.prompt: An unsigned 8-bit counter holds 2 and 4 is subtracted with no check, in a setting where overflow wraps around. What does the counter hold?
options: 254, since it wraps past zero to the top of its range
-2, since the counter keeps the sign of the true answer
0, since an unsigned counter stops once it reaches zero
2, since the subtraction is refused and nothing changes
questions.explanation: An unsigned number cannot be negative, so going below zero wraps to the largest values. A 32-bit counter does the same, ending near four billion, and Rust debug builds stop with an error instead. That is why a check should come first.

questions.prompt: A rule says: if there is enough energy, spend it; otherwise report a shortage. Energy is 3 and the cost is 5. What happens?
options: The otherwise branch runs, and the energy stays at 3
The spending branch runs, and the energy drops to -2
Both branches run, one after the other, in that order
Neither branch runs, because the two numbers differ
questions.explanation: A condition selects exactly one path. 3 is less than 5, so the shortage branch runs and nothing is spent.

questions.prompt: Stamina starts at 12 and the loop tries costs 4, 10, and 2 in order, paying only if it can. What is the final stamina?
options: 6, because 10 is skipped when only 8 remains
0, because 4, 10, and 2 are all paid in turn
8, because only the first cost is ever paid
-4, because 12 - 4 - 10 - 2 is computed
questions.explanation: The trace is 12 to 8, then 10 is more than 8 so stamina stays 8, then 2 leaves 6.

questions.prompt: A counter starts at 0. A loop repeats while counter < 4, adding 1 at the start of each pass and then printing the counter. What is printed?
options: 1, 2, 3 and 4, on four separate lines
0, 1, 2 and 3, on four separate lines
1, 2 and 3, on three separate lines
1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, on five separate lines
questions.explanation: The condition is checked before each pass. Passes start at counter 0, 1, 2 and 3, printing 1 through 4, and the loop ends when the counter reaches 4.

questions.prompt: A loop construct has no built-in condition. How does it ever stop?
options: Code inside its body checks something and explicitly breaks out
It stops itself after a fixed number of passes chosen by the language
It stops once the body has printed something to the screen
It stops when every variable in the body has been used once
questions.explanation: A plain loop repeats until the body decides to leave it. The programmer has to put the exit check inside.

questions.prompt: What is the job of a struct, a record type with fields such as name and stamina?
options: It groups related values so code knows which values belong to the same thing
It applies the rules that decide how those values are allowed to change
It makes the values permanently unchangeable once the record is created
It repeats the same values for every item that is stored in a list
questions.explanation: A struct only groups values. The rules that use them are written in functions.

questions.prompt: In a language with ownership, a function is given a borrowed reference to a record. Who owns the record while that function runs?
options: The caller keeps ownership, and the function only borrows it for a while
The function becomes the owner, and the caller loses the record for good
Ownership is split equally between the caller and the function
Nobody owns the record until the function has finished running
questions.explanation: A borrow lends access without changing the owner. After the call, the caller can keep using the record.

questions.prompt: In Rust, code tries to hand out editable access to a variable that was declared without permission to change. What happens?
options: The compiler rejects the code before a program ever exists
It runs, but any edits made through it are silently ignored
It runs, then crashes the first time any value is edited
It runs normally, since the permission is just a suggestion
questions.explanation: Mutability is checked at compile time. The compiler message points out which part of the code breaks the promise made by the declaration.

questions.prompt: In a language with ownership, a growable text value is assigned to a second name. Why can the first name no longer be used?
options: Ownership moved to the second name, so the first no longer owns the value
Assigning deletes the old value, so the second name is left holding nothing
A name can be used just once, even when it holds a plain number
The value became a number, and the first name just accepts text values
questions.explanation: Moving transfers ownership. Small plain numbers are copied instead, so both names stay usable.

questions.prompt: Why would a language move a growable value to a new owner instead of letting two names own it at once?
options: Two owners could each release the same memory, causing a double-release bug
Two owners would double the amount of memory that the value takes up in total
Two owners would stop either name from being able to read the value
Two owners would force the value to become unchangeable from then on
questions.explanation: Exactly one owner is responsible for releasing a growable value's memory. A visible transfer lets the compiler track who that is.

questions.prompt: Two characters have 15 and 9 stamina. Each tries an action that costs 6 and is allowed when stamina covers the cost. What do they have afterward?
options: 9 and 3, since both can afford it
9 and 9, since just the first one acts
15 and 9, since the cost is checked but not charged
9 and 0, since an action uses up all remaining stamina
questions.explanation: Both have at least 6, so each pays 6: 15 becomes 9 and 9 becomes 3.

questions.prompt: An action subtracts its cost only when stamina covers it. If the cost is raised so that nobody can afford it, what happens to the stamina values?
options: They stay unchanged, since a refusal leaves state as it was
They fall to zero, since a refused action drains all of them
They go negative, since the cost is subtracted all the same
They are halved, since refused costs are split in two parts
questions.explanation: A guard that refuses must also leave the state untouched. Refusal is a different outcome from payment.

questions.prompt: In an object-style method definition, what does a receiver marked as a mutable reference to self mean?
options: The method gets temporary editable access to the value it is called on
The method receives a private copy of that value that it can edit
The method takes ownership of that value and removes it from the caller
The method can read that value but it is not allowed to change it
questions.explanation: The receiver is the value the method is called on. A mutable borrow lends editable access without giving the value away.

questions.prompt: What can an enum with several shapes express that a plain true-or-false result cannot?
options: Why something failed, or what is left, as shapes carrying data
A faster result, since enums are executed quicker than booleans are
More than two numbers, since a boolean is just able to hold digits
A result that does not have to be checked by the code calling it
questions.explanation: A boolean says only whether something worked. An enum can give each outcome its own shape and details, such as what remains or what is missing.

questions.prompt: A function reports either success with the amount left, or failure with the amount missing. With 3 available and 8 needed, what does it report?
options: Failure, with 5 missing
Success, with 5 left
Failure, with 3 missing
Success, with 11 left
questions.explanation: Since 3 is less than 8, the failure shape is built with 8 - 3 = 5 as the missing amount.

questions.prompt: Why do some languages force a match over alternatives to cover every possible case?
options: So that no outcome is silently forgotten, even when a new one is added
So that the match runs faster by trying every one of its cases at once
So that the match is guaranteed to print something each time it runs
So that the same match can be reused unchanged in other programs too
questions.explanation: If alternatives are part of a type, the compiler can point out any case that is not handled, instead of letting it fall through unnoticed.

questions.prompt: A growable list holds 12 and 8, then 6 is added at the end. Which value is at position 1?
options: 8, since positions are counted from zero
12, since positions are counted from one
6, since the newest item takes position 1
1, since the position is the value itself
questions.explanation: The list holds 12, 8 and 6. Position 0 is 12, so position 1 is 8.

questions.prompt: Why does looking up a key in a map often return a possibly-empty result, such as Some or None, instead of a plain value?
options: The key might not be present, so there may be no value to give back
Map values are locked until the caller unwraps them with a code
The map has to wait for another thread before it can answer
Returning plain values would be slower than wrapping each one
questions.explanation: A lookup can fail to find anything, so the return type forces the caller to handle that case. Removing an item from a queue is similar.

questions.prompt: Items are added to a queue in this order: A, then B, then C. One item is taken from the front. What is still waiting?
options: B and C, since the oldest item leaves first
A and B, since the newest item leaves first
A and C, since the middle item leaves first
B alone, since taking one item removes two
questions.explanation: A queue hands out items first in, first out, so A leaves and B and C remain.

questions.prompt: A pipeline takes the values 9, 2, 7 and 4, keeps those that are at least 5, then counts them. What does it produce?
options: 2, since only 9 and 7 pass the filter
3, since all but the smallest value pass
4, since counting ignores the filter step
16, since counting adds up the kept values
questions.explanation: The filter keeps 9 and 7. Counting reports how many values were kept, not their total.

questions.prompt: A list holds two items. What does a safe lookup that returns an optional result give for position 5?
options: No value, so any code guarded by the lookup is skipped
The last item in the list, since out-of-range positions wrap around
Zero, since a missing item is treated as the number 0
An error that halts everything as soon as it is asked
questions.explanation: Direct indexing past the end would fail at runtime, while a safe lookup returns None. The guarded block then does not run.

questions.prompt: A checked subtraction on unsigned numbers returns a value only if the result fits. What does it give for 12 - 4, 2 - 4 and 4 - 4?
options: Some(8), None and Some(0)
Some(8), Some(0) and Some(0)
Some(8), None and None
Some(8), Some(-2) and None
questions.explanation: 12 - 4 fits, 2 - 4 does not fit, and 4 - 4 is a valid zero. A missing answer needs a different shape from zero.

questions.prompt: When is a result type that carries an error better than an optional value?
options: When the caller needs to know why an operation failed
When something may simply be absent and no reason is needed
When the operation not fails, so nothing needs checking
When the value has to be stored inside a list instead
questions.explanation: An optional value says there is nothing. A result carries either success or an error, which suits cases where the reason for failure matters.

questions.prompt: A function tries to convert the word "tired" into a whole number. What should a well-designed conversion do?
options: Report an error, so invalid input is not mistaken for a valid zero
Return zero, since a word without any digits has no number value
Return five, since the word has five letters in it, which is a number
Return the word unchanged, so the caller can decide what to do later
questions.explanation: Text that is not a number should produce an explicit error. Returning zero would hide the problem.

questions.prompt: In Rust, what does a question mark placed after an operation that might fail do?
options: Continues with the success value, or returns the error to the caller
Retries the operation over and over until it finally succeeds at last
Ignores the error and carries on with a default value instead of it
Asks the user whether the code should continue running or stop now
questions.explanation: The question mark unwraps a success, and on failure it hands the error back to the calling function immediately.

questions.prompt: A test starts with 2 stamina and requests an action costing 4. It checks that the action reported failure and that stamina is still 2. What bug does that guard against?
options: A rule that spends the cost without first checking that it can be paid
A rule that refuses actions which it should have allowed to happen
A display that shows the wrong stamina number on the screen
A loop that not ends after stamina runs out
questions.explanation: The test sits right at the boundary where the player cannot afford the action. It would fail if the code subtracted first and checked later.

questions.prompt: After a 25-gold purchase the display falls from 100 to 75. Which statement is a hypothesis rather than an observation?
options: A four-byte value stores the gold the purchase rule uses
The display changed from 100 to 75 after the purchase happened
The item cost 25 gold when the player bought it one time
The player started the test with 100 gold showing on screen
questions.explanation: What you can see is an observation. A guess about where the amount is stored is a hypothesis to test, and the game may keep a display copy or let a server decide.

questions.prompt: Which order describes a careful four-step approach to studying how a game behavior works?
options: Pick a repeatable behavior, work out its rule, find where it lives, change one thing
Change a value at random, watch what breaks, work out the rule, pick a behavior
Find a value in memory, change many things at once, then work out why it broke
Work out a rule, change it, find where it lives, then pick a behavior to study
questions.explanation: Choose something you can repeat, understand its rule, locate the data and code involved, then change one thing and measure. A failed change can send you back to an earlier step.

questions.prompt: A guessed rule says: if the balance is at least the price, the new balance is the balance minus the price; otherwise nothing changes. What is the new balance for a balance of 60 and a price of 45?
options: 15, since the balance covers the price and so the price is subtracted
60, since the price is checked against the balance but not charged
105, since the price is added to the balance when it can be covered
45, since the leftover balance equals the price that was paid
questions.explanation: The condition is true because 60 is at least 45, so the first branch gives 60 - 45 = 15. A written rule is a prediction you can check against what the game really does.

questions.prompt: A guessed damage rule says new health = max(0, old health - damage). What is the new health for 12 health and 30 damage?
options: 0, since max keeps the result from dropping below zero
-18, since the subtraction is applied exactly as it is written
12, since damage larger than the health is simply ignored
18, since a negative result is flipped into a positive one
questions.explanation: 12 - 30 is -18, and max(0, -18) is 0. Clamping explains why health never shows a value below zero.

questions.prompt: In the damage chain, the health bar is resized after health becomes 55. What role does the bar have?
options: Derived display, not the state the rules read
Game state that the rules compare with max health
The temporary result of the subtraction 80 - 25
The input that triggers the damage event
questions.explanation: The chain is damage event (input), calculate 80 - 25 (temporary result), store health 55 (state), resize bar (derived display). The calculation, stored result, and bar need not be one stored value.

questions.prompt: A program copies a stored number into a display variable, then lowers the original by 20. If the original was 90, what do the two hold afterward?
options: The display copy holds 90 and the original holds 70
Both hold 70, since a copy follows the original around
The display copy holds 70 and the original holds 90
Both hold 90, since the copy blocks the original's change
questions.explanation: A copy is a separate value made at one moment. Changing a displayed copy would not change the value that the game's rules read.

questions.prompt: What is the point of writing the tool's small contract before touching another process?
options: It limits what the tool may read, change, and when to stop
It makes the tool faster at scanning big memory regions
It lets the tool skip the checks of the game's version
It records the tool's own address for the later runs
questions.explanation: The contract names the target, input, read, change, stop conditions, and restore step. It prevents a small experiment from quietly turning into an unbounded tool.

questions.prompt: A tool fails to read the gold field. What should it conclude?
options: Stop at that step and keep the error; do not assume zero gold
The player has zero gold, so the next step may use that zero
The value must be 75, since that was the last number we knew
The address must be correct, so the write should go ahead now
questions.explanation: A successful write depends on a successful read of the intended field in the intended build. A failed read is not a value.

questions.prompt: What is a module-relative pointer path, and when does it stay valid?
options: A chain of lookups from a fixed starting point, valid across runs of one exact build
A single fixed address that keeps working across every build of the same game
A copy of the target value that is updated each time the game is restarted
A list of every candidate address that a scan has found for a value
questions.explanation: A temporary address changes between runs, so a path of lookups from a stable starting point can replace it. It still only holds for the build in which it was found.

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes a typical scan-and-filter search for a value in memory?
options: Scan for the known value, change it in a controlled way, filter the candidates, repeat
Scan for the known value, delete every candidate, then guess the address from memory
Change the value several times, scan once at the end, then take the first result
Filter first, scan for the value afterward, then write to every candidate found
questions.explanation: Each controlled change lets you throw away candidates that did not respond the same way. Repeating the filter narrows the list down.

questions.prompt: What does the scanner know about the number it is searching for?
options: Nothing about gold: it compares bytes with your value and type
That the number is the player's gold, because of its label
Which instruction in the game code writes that number
Whether the game keeps a display copy of that number
questions.explanation: The scanner does not know what gold means. Even checking every fourth byte could miss a value that starts between those checks.

questions.prompt: A first scan finds 5,000 candidate addresses. After changing the value in a known way and filtering, 40 remain. What happened to the other 4,960?
options: They did not change in the same way as the target, so the filter removed them
They were freed by the game, so they no longer exist anywhere in memory
They were moved to different addresses by the filtering step itself
They were all confirmed as the target and merged into the remaining 40
