questions.explanation: Candidates that did not follow the controlled change are dropped. 5,000 - 40 = 4,960 were ruled out as coincidental matches.

questions.prompt: What does a write breakpoint do?
options: Pauses the game when an instruction writes to an address
Stops the scanner from reading the address that was chosen
Saves the original bytes found at the address that was chosen
Pauses the game whenever its display text is redrawn on screen
questions.explanation: It shows which instruction changed the candidate, tying it to the game's own code. Chapter 2 teaches how to use one.

questions.prompt: A candidate address worked once. Why restart the game and check again?
options: To see whether it repeats, as one find is only one run's lead
To reset the scan so that the address becomes a permanent one
To remove the display copy from the memory of the game
To confirm the address uses the same type as the display text
questions.explanation: An object can even disappear before the run ends. A module-relative path, not the absolute address, is what may carry over, and only for the same build.

questions.prompt: Why scan again after buying an item with a different price?
options: It rules out an unrelated value that matched once by chance
It makes the scanner cheaper because it reads fewer bytes
It changes which instruction in the game writes the gold field
It refreshes the display copy of the gold on the screen
questions.explanation: Each kind of check rules out a different mistake. A second scan with a different amount removes a coincidental match.

questions.prompt: You change a value and only the on-screen text changes; the next purchase still uses the old gold. What did you probably find?
options: A display copy
The gameplay gold field
A server-owned value
A value of the wrong width
questions.explanation: If only the text changes you probably found a display copy. If the value snaps back, another system owns or recomputes it.

questions.prompt: A tool writes a new value into a game, and a moment later the old value reappears. What does this suggest?
options: Something else in the game owns or recomputes it, so its rule needs more study
The operating system undid the write because the new number was far too large
The game rejects every write from outside tools, whatever address it is given
The game's screen is lagging behind and will catch up with the write later on
questions.explanation: A value that snaps back is being decided by something other than your write. That sends you back to understanding the rule.

questions.prompt: Several steps in an investigation do not match what you predicted. Which mismatch should you examine first?
options: The earliest one, since later failures may follow from it
The most dramatic one, since it is the easiest one to notice
The last one, since it sits closest to the final result seen
The smallest one, since it is the quickest one to explain away
questions.explanation: Later symptoms can follow from an earlier divergence. Explaining the first mismatch often explains the rest.

questions.prompt: A bug stops appearing as soon as logging is added. What does that most likely indicate?
options: A change in timing worth investigating, not proof that the bug is fixed
The logging fixed the bug, so the logging should be kept as the fix
The bug was imaginary, since it cannot be seen while logging runs
The logging output is wrong, so the log should simply be ignored
questions.explanation: Pausing and printing both change how long things take. A failure that vanishes under diagnostics is a lead pointing at timing.

questions.prompt: A safe write rule allows a write only when the current value equals the expected value and the replacement is at most 500. The current value is 12, the expected value is 10, and the replacement is 50. Is the write allowed?
options: No, because the current value does not match the expected one
Yes, because the replacement is below the limit of 500
Yes, because passing either one of the conditions is enough
No, because the replacement is too small to be accepted
questions.explanation: Both conditions must pass. 12 differs from 10, so the check fails even though 50 is within the limit.

questions.prompt: A rule allows a write only if the current value equals the expected value and the replacement is at most 500. Which attempt is rejected because of the limit, not because of a mismatch?
options: Current 10, expected 10, replacement 501
Current 10, expected 10, replacement 500
Current 10, expected 10, replacement 0
Current 9, expected 10, replacement 50
questions.explanation: 500 is allowed and 501 is not. The last attempt is also rejected, but for a different reason: the current value does not match.

questions.prompt: Which problem can a passing logic test, run on its own, still leave undetected?
options: A live address that points at the wrong field in the running game
A type mismatch that stops the code from building
A misspelled name that the compiler would refuse to accept
A function that gives the wrong answer for an example it was tested on
questions.explanation: A test checks examples of the logic. The compiler catches build errors, and only the running game and a debugger can show whether an address is really the field you want.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in an experiment record for a reader to repeat the work?
options: Game build, architecture, and the save or map used
Only the final address that the scanner found
A screenshot of the result with no values written out
The tool's name, with no mention of its version
questions.explanation: The record lists the reference environment, the reproduction steps, the evidence, and decisions. A screenshot alone is not enough; write down the value and condition too.

questions.prompt: Why predict an affordability check and subtraction before a memory search?
options: They give observations that can reject a guess.
They guarantee the first address is correct.
They replace every check of the running game.
They make a display copy own later purchases.
questions.explanation: A prediction supplies contrasting cases and expected changes. A matching number alone does not identify the purchase input.

questions.prompt: A tool expected 75 gold but read 74 before writing. What follows from the example’s write decision?
options: Change the expected value without recording it.
Reject the write and investigate that mismatch.
Treat the failed comparison as a zero balance.
Write first and inspect the display afterward.
questions.explanation: The expected-value check prevents the tool from acting on a changed sample; diagnostics should begin at that mismatch.

questions.prompt: A displayed_gold variable copied gold before a purchase. Why can it remain 100 when gold becomes 75?
options: The display variable owns the purchase decision.
The purchase must restore gold on every tick.
The assignment stored a separate earlier value.
The compiler forbids every subtraction on gold.
questions.explanation: The copied number is a snapshot. Later changes to gold do not automatically update that independent copy.

questions.prompt: What does a virtual machine snapshot give you, and what does it not give you?
options: A saved point to roll back to, not a promise that every action is safe
A promise that nothing inside the machine can affect the host
A permanent backup that still exists after the machine is deleted
A faster copy of the host that shares all of its files with it
questions.explanation: A snapshot is a recovery point, and you should test that you can really restore it. It does not make risky actions harmless.

questions.prompt: What is a virtual machine?
options: A simulated computer running inside a real one, with its own operating system
A program that speeds up the graphics of whatever computer it is installed on
A folder on the main computer that holds copies of all of its own programs
A remote server that runs your own programs for you over the internet
questions.explanation: A virtual machine can run its own operating system and be reset without touching your everyday system.

questions.prompt: What makes a free trainer that gives you gold while it copies saved browser passwords a trojan?
options: It does what it advertises and something else at the same time
It changes game files instead of reading the game's memory
It runs inside a virtual machine instead of on the host
It needs a debugger before it can start
questions.explanation: The cheat working is exactly what makes people trust it. The lesson's rule is to use tools only from official project pages or ones you build yourself.

questions.prompt: Why start a practice virtual machine with modest resources instead of giving it nearly all of the host's CPU and memory?
options: The host needs its own CPU and memory, and small practice tasks need little
Extra CPU or memory given to a virtual machine cannot be taken back later
A virtual machine refuses to start when it gets over half of the host
Programs inside a virtual machine run more safely when they have little memory
questions.explanation: A reasonable starting point is a couple of cores, a few gigabytes of memory and some disk space. Starving the host or oversizing the guest gains nothing.

questions.prompt: Why are shared folders, clipboard sharing and USB passthrough usually left off in a practice virtual machine at first?
options: Each one is a path between host and guest, so enable one only when needed
They make a virtual machine run slower than any other setting does
They are not supported by any virtual machine software on the market
They permanently link the two systems so that snapshots stop working
questions.explanation: The separation between host and guest is the point of the setup. Every connection weakens it, so turn one on only when needed and know what can cross it.

questions.prompt: Which kind of account should you normally work in on a practice machine, and when are extra rights justified?
options: A normal account, with extra rights only for a tool that really needs them
An administrator account, since extra rights make tools more accurate
A guest account with no password, since it is easiest to get into
A normal account that launches everything with extra rights
questions.explanation: Giving a tool only the rights it needs limits what a mistake can do. Raise rights for one tool when its operation requires it.

questions.prompt: Why does a Rust toolchain for Windows need a separate set of build tools installed?
options: A linker and Windows libraries turn compiled code into a runnable program
The compiler alone cannot translate any Rust code into machine instructions
The tools make the finished program run much faster than it otherwise would do
Windows refuses to run any program that was not built with a full code editor
questions.explanation: Compiling produces pieces of machine code, and a linker joins them with system libraries into an executable. The full code editor is not needed.

questions.prompt: In a target name like x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, which part says what kind of CPU instructions are produced?
options: x86_64, the first part
unknown, the second part
linux, the third part
gnu, the last part
questions.explanation: The first part of a target name is the CPU architecture. The remaining parts describe the vendor, the operating system and the toolchain conventions.

questions.prompt: A 64-bit library is built for a game that runs as a 32-bit process. Can it be loaded into that process?
options: No, since loaded code has to match the architecture of its process
Yes, since the operating system translates the library for the process automatically
Yes, as long as the library file has been given a valid digital signature
Yes, but it runs at half the speed that it would normally manage
questions.explanation: A loaded library shares the process's address space and instruction set, so the two must match. An outside tool can differ because the operating system copies bytes across the process boundary.

questions.prompt: A build tool has a quick check mode that type-checks code without producing a final optimized build. When is it useful?
options: For catching compile errors quickly before a full build
For producing the smallest and fastest final version of a whole program
For running tests against a game that is already open on screen now
For attaching to a running process in order to read all of its memory
questions.explanation: A check is the fastest first test for a compiler or dependency problem. A separate release build produces the final result.

questions.prompt: A build for a certain target succeeds. What does that prove?
options: It compiles for that target, not that it can attach to a running game
It proves the tool can attach to any running game of that same kind too
It proves the addresses used inside the tool are correct for a game too
It proves the tool is safe to run directly on the host machine itself
questions.explanation: A successful build only shows that the code compiles and links. Whether it works with a running game has to be tested separately.

questions.prompt: A build prints dozens of errors. Which one should you read and fix first?
options: The first one, since later errors are often follow-up effects of it
The last one, since it describes whatever is left over at the end
The longest one, since it has the most detail about the problem
The one that mentions the most files, since it is the biggest
questions.explanation: One missing type or bracket can cause many follow-on messages. Fix the earliest and rebuild.

questions.prompt: Why should snapshots be named by what they contain, such as Clean Windows and Ready for lessons?
options: A date alone does not say which state is safe to restore
Snapshots with a date in the name cannot be restored later
The VM requires each snapshot name to be a unique word
Names make each snapshot take up less space on the disk
questions.explanation: Clean Windows is taken after updates and before the lab tools; Ready for lessons is taken after tools, the target, and course code work.

questions.prompt: How does exporting a virtual machine as an appliance file differ from taking a snapshot?
options: It is a slower, portable backup, while a snapshot is a quick local rollback
It is faster to restore than a snapshot and also works as a rollback point too
It is just a list of settings with none of the disk contents stored in it
A snapshot can be moved to another computer, but an appliance file cannot
questions.explanation: Snapshots give quick recovery on the same machine. An exported file can be imported again later, even elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Why record a file's hash alongside the notes about an address found in it?
options: A hash fingerprints a file's bytes, so a match suggests the same build
A hash is the address of the file, so it tells a tool where to look for it
A hash encrypts the file, so the addresses inside it cannot move
A hash shrinks the file, so it loads more quickly the next time it starts
questions.explanation: A hash is a short fingerprint computed from every byte of a file. If it differs, the file is different and an old address may no longer apply.

questions.prompt: A memory offset was found during one session. What does it depend on?
options: The exact build of the game, since another build can move fields around
The monitor resolution that was in use at the moment it was found
The name of the folder that the game happens to be installed in
The player's own account name inside the game while it was found
questions.explanation: Offsets describe layout inside one build. A different build, tool version or starting state can change where things sit.

questions.prompt: Before a first memory experiment on a practice machine, which step best protects your work and keeps results comparable?
options: Restore a known clean snapshot so you start from a known state
Turn on every connection to the host so files can be copied out easily
Skip checking the toolchain, since any errors will appear later anyway
Run the target with extra rights so that nothing gets blocked
questions.explanation: Starting from a named clean state makes results repeatable and easy to undo. Extra connections or rights only add risk.

questions.prompt: You need to rewind one existing VM after an experiment. Which choice directly provides that recovery point?
options: A snapshot of that VM’s starting state.
A network name copied from another VM.
A host folder opened by both machines.
A second adapter using the same address.
questions.explanation: A snapshot records a recovery point for one VM. A clone serves the different purpose of making a second VM.

questions.prompt: A linked clone records separate disk writes. Which dependency still matters?
options: Its display must use the host’s exact frame rate.
Its source base disks must remain available.
Its guest must share every baseline file edit.
Its memory address must match the baseline.
questions.explanation: Differencing disks record clone changes, but unchanged content still comes from the source base disks.

questions.prompt: What does a full clone’s copied virtual disk provide in this lesson?
options: A guarantee that host shared files are recovered.
A proof that every guest connection is isolated.
A disk copy without that source-base dependency.
A promise that copied network names are unique.
questions.explanation: Full cloning copies dependent disks. Network settings and host sharing need their own review.

questions.prompt: A test edits a file in a shared host folder. Why may restoring a guest snapshot leave that edit in place?
options: The snapshot always deletes every host-side file.
The guest display stored the host folder’s bytes.
The clone moved that file into a CPU register.
The host file is outside the guest disk snapshot.
questions.explanation: Guest disk recovery does not rewind an external host file accessed through sharing.

questions.prompt: Why review network settings before starting the baseline and its clone together?
options: Copied settings may reuse names or fixed addresses.
Separate disks force every network packet to fail.
A new VM can never open a connection to its host.
A snapshot changes all peers’ addresses at once.
questions.explanation: The clone has separate VM state, but copied guest configuration and adapter policies may retain identities that need review.

questions.prompt: What does attaching a memory scanner to a running process accomplish?
options: It selects which process's memory the scanner reads
It reports the address of every value that the process stores
It copies the process into the scanner so it can be paused
It protects the process from being changed by other programs
questions.explanation: Attaching only chooses the process. The scans afterward work out where a value lives and how it is stored.

questions.prompt: The first scan for 100 returns many addresses. What is the correct reaction?
options: Expected: 100 can appear in timers, fields, and unrelated data
A sign the scan failed, so restart Cheat Engine and scan again
Proof that gold is stored in many copies, each equally real
A sign the game guards its gold with decoy values on purpose
questions.explanation: A value like 100 shows up all over memory by coincidence, so many matches are normal. More than one result does not mean several gold values.

questions.prompt: After the first scan, what does each result prove?
options: Only that four bytes there read as the integer 100 at scan time
That the address controls how much gold the player really has
That the address belongs to the player object's own fields
That the address stays valid until the whole match has ended
questions.explanation: A first-scan hit says nothing about gold control. It only says the bytes matched at that moment.

questions.prompt: The screen shows 100 gold and the unit you recruit costs 15. What should you enter for the next scan?
options: 85, because the price is subtracted from 100
115, because gold and the price are added together
15, because that is the unit price shown on the button
100, because the first scan's value is simply kept
questions.explanation: Gold drops by the price, so 100 − 15 = 85. The next scan checks the old candidates against that new number.

questions.prompt: How does Next Scan treat the earlier results?
options: It checks only previous candidates and keeps those holding the new value
It scans the whole process again and merges the two result lists
It deletes the earlier results and keeps the lowest address
It checks only addresses lying near the previous results in memory
questions.explanation: A value scan filters an existing candidate set instead of searching everything again.

questions.prompt: The first scan finds addresses A, B, and C holding 100. After a purchase, only B and C hold 85. Which addresses does the next scan check?
options: B and C
A, B, and C
Only A
Every address in the process
questions.explanation: The candidates are the intersection: addresses that matched before and also match now. A no longer holds 85, so it is dropped.

questions.prompt: When narrowing scan results, why change a value by several different amounts instead of repeating one back-and-forth pattern?
options: An unrelated value that follows the same pattern could stay in the list
Different amounts make the game store the value at a brand new address
Repeating one pattern makes a scanner run slower on each pass
A scanner will not accept a scan unless the amounts are different
questions.explanation: A varied pattern is harder for coincidental addresses to match, so more false candidates drop out of the list.

questions.prompt: The list is down to a few addresses. What should you do with the first one?
options: Test it, because it is still only a candidate
Treat it as the gold address, since it is first in the list
Delete the others from memory so the game uses that one
Skip testing, because a short list already proves the result
questions.explanation: The lesson says not to assume the first remaining address is correct. A few survivors still need a test.

questions.prompt: After writing a replacement value to a candidate, why restore the original?
options: A leftover value makes the next test start from a different state
The game crashes if a candidate stays modified for ten seconds
Cheat Engine only lets you test one candidate per session
The original value is required to make the next scan succeed
questions.explanation: If the state differs, two test results can no longer be compared. Restoring it keeps every test starting from the same place.

questions.prompt: You write a new number to a candidate and only the on-screen text changes. A real purchase still uses the old gold. What is the likely meaning?
options: Probably a display copy, not the game-play value
The strongest candidate for the real game-play state
Proof the scanner used the wrong scan type for gold
A sign that Wesnoth encrypts its real gold value
questions.explanation: If the number and the purchase rules both changed, the candidate would be strong. Only the text changing points to a copy used for display.

questions.prompt: Why can several gold-related addresses all be legitimate in one game?
options: The game may keep simulation, animation, text, and network copies
Wesnoth duplicates gold on purpose to catch cheating attempts
Every unit on the map owns its own private pool of gold
Windows copies each value into RAM twice as a precaution
questions.explanation: A game can legitimately hold several related values, such as the current value, previous value, display text, and temporary calculations.

questions.prompt: What is the usual next step after a value scan finds a strong candidate?
options: A write breakpoint to find which instruction changes it
Scan again until the list holds only one single candidate
Restart the game and reuse the same address from before
Overwrite the value with zero and leave it there for good
questions.explanation: Value scanning is the start of reverse engineering. A write breakpoint shows which instruction changes the value, and the instructions around it reveal the object and its other fields.

questions.prompt: After a game is restarted, what should you expect about an address you found in the earlier run?
options: It may differ, since the process layout and heap can change between runs
It stays the same, since the game files on disk have not changed
It stays the same unless the game receives an update from its publisher
It moves by exactly the same distance every time the game starts
questions.explanation: An address belongs to one run of the process. Later techniques rely on distances that stay fixed within one build instead.

questions.prompt: A game never shows a number for a value you want to find. Which scanning approach fits best?
options: Scan for an unknown value, then filter by whether it rose, fell or stayed
Scan for the exact number zero, since hidden values usually start at zero
Scan for the label words that the game uses to describe that value
Wait until the game eventually displays the number, then scan for it
questions.explanation: With no visible number, filter by how the value changes after each action rather than by an exact number.

questions.prompt: What is the main practical benefit of embedding Lua in a compiled game engine?
options: Designers can change a quest or rule without rebuilding the engine
Lua code runs faster than the compiled engine code it replaces
Scripts can reach any engine function without host permission
Lua checks every variable's type before the script runs
questions.explanation: The engine is compiled ahead of time, but Lua text scripts are loaded at run time, so rules can change without a rebuild. Lua is not claimed to be faster, and it only sees what the host exposes.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that Lua is commonly embedded inside a larger program?
options: The game owns a Lua interpreter and asks it to run scripts
The Lua source is compiled into the game's machine code first
Lua scripts start as separate processes with their own handles
The game is rewritten in Lua so no host code remains
questions.explanation: An embedded Lua is a library the host program owns and drives. It does not become a separate process or replace the host.

questions.prompt: A script calls a function that lives in a table the embedding application passed in. Where does that function's code actually run?
options: In the host application, so the call crosses from the script into host code
Inside the scripting language's standard library, which every interpreter includes
Inside the script itself, since the script can see the function's code
In a separate process that the interpreter starts for each call
questions.explanation: An embedded script only has what the host puts in front of it. A host-supplied function is native code, so calling it crosses back out of the scripting language.

questions.prompt: In a dynamically typed language, a variable first holds a number and later is assigned a string. What happens?
options: It runs; the variable can refer to either, and type mistakes appear at run time
It is rejected before the script runs, since the variable's type was fixed
It runs but converts the string to a number automatically on assignment
It stops with an error at the second assignment, since a variable cannot change meaning
questions.explanation: In dynamic typing, values carry types and variables do not. That is flexible, but mistakes that a compiler would catch early show up only when the code runs.

questions.prompt: What cost comes with Lua's flexible, dynamic typing?
options: More mistakes surface at run time, so tests matter more
Every script must declare each variable's type up front
Numbers cannot be stored inside a table at all
The host must recompile the engine after a type change
questions.explanation: A statically typed host language catches type mistakes at compile time. Lua defers them to run time, so clear names, validation, and small APIs help.

questions.prompt: Why should a scripting tutorial name the exact language version it uses?
options: Games embed different versions or custom dialects, so features may differ
Scripts written for one version refuse to start on any other version
Version numbers decide how fast scripts run on any given computer
The version tells the game which operating system it should use
questions.explanation: Embedded languages are often frozen at an old version or modified. Readers should check the target's own version before assuming a feature exists.

questions.prompt:
What does this Lua code print?
```lua
local a = { hp = 40 }
local b = a
b.hp = 10
print(a.hp)
```
options: 10, because both names refer to the same table
40, because assigning to b made its own copy of the table
nil, because b.hp created a new field only on b
An error, because a table cannot be given two names
questions.explanation: Assigning a table copies the reference, not the table. There is one hp field, so a change through b is seen through a.

questions.prompt: What is the name for two variables reaching the same table through copied references?
options: Aliasing
Interning
Shadowing
Hashing
questions.explanation: Aliasing means one table with several names. Shadowing is a different idea (a new local hiding an older name), and interning is about string storage.

questions.prompt: In Lua, which line creates a global variable that other scripts could overwrite?
options: `count = 0`
`local count = 0`
`local count`
`local count = nil`
questions.explanation: A plain assignment with no local keyword writes into the shared global environment. The local forms stay private to their scope.

questions.prompt: Why do scripting style guides say to declare variables local unless you mean to share them?
options: Globals can be overwritten by other scripts, and typos create new globals
Local variables are the only kind that can hold tables or functions
Globals are cleared automatically at the end of each script run
Local variables are always stored in a faster part of the processor
questions.explanation: A misspelled name quietly becomes a new global instead of an error, and separate scripts can clobber shared names. Locals keep state private.

questions.prompt: A game host wants scripts to change game state. Why is a general function that writes arbitrary bytes at any address a poor design?
options: A script could pick any address and value, like full process control
Byte-writing functions are too slow to call from a script every frame
Scripting languages cannot represent addresses or byte values at all
The function would write correctly but could not report errors back
questions.explanation: A host should expose narrow, validated operations. A raw write function hands the script almost the same power as a process handle.

questions.prompt: A host gives a script a snapshot of game data by copying it into script tables. What does this protect against?
options: The script gets no handle or pointer into the game, so it cannot reach live memory
It makes the data in the script update automatically whenever the game changes
It guarantees that the copied data is still current at the moment the script uses it
It lets the script change the game's values directly, only more slowly
questions.explanation: A copy is just data. Because the script never receives a handle or pointer, reading it cannot damage or control the game.

questions.prompt: A script asks the host to act on object 5, but that object was removed since the script last looked. Why can the host still handle this safely?
options: The host validates every request on arrival, so a stale ID can be rejected
The host trusts the request, since the script only asks about objects it has seen
The host keeps removed objects alive so that old requests still succeed
Scripts are paused until every object they know about has been deleted
questions.explanation: Scripts only describe what they want. The host owns the game state and checks each request against what is true now.

questions.prompt: In capability-based design for scripting, what limits what a script can do?
options: Only the functions and data its environment hands to it
The comments in the script that declare what it intends to do
A list of forbidden words that the host scans for in the source
The host's trust in the script author, set when the script is installed
questions.explanation: A script that was never given a function cannot call it. The environment, not the script's intent, sets the limit.

questions.prompt: In many languages, a loop over indexed items yields a position and a value. What is the purpose of naming the position `_` when only the value is needed?
options: By convention it signals that the position is deliberately unused
It makes the interpreter skip the position, so the loop runs faster
It tells the interpreter to walk the items in reverse order
It stores the position in a special global variable for later
questions.explanation: The underscore is a conventional name for a value the loop body does not need. It documents intent and does not change behavior.

questions.prompt: In Lua, what does the expression `nil or 5` evaluate to?
options: true
nil
false
questions.explanation: The or operator returns its first operand if that is truthy, and otherwise its second operand. Here nil is falsy, so the result is 5, not a boolean.

questions.prompt: Which difference between games changes how a Lua script's failures show up or what it can do?
options: Its CPU, memory, and action limits
The color theme of the in-game console
The length of the script file's name
The number of comments inside the script
questions.explanation: Hosts differ in version, libraries, API rules, trust, resource limits, and error handling, so a script may behave differently from game to game.

questions.prompt: What does a call frame record?
options: Where the caller resumes, plus locals and function
The full text of the function's source file
Every value the game has ever stored in memory
Which host callbacks the script may use later
questions.explanation: A call frame is the VM's bookkeeping for one call: the function, its base, where to continue afterward, and where results should go.

questions.prompt: A callee's frame starts at base 5 on a shared value stack, and its locals are numbered from 0. Where does its local slot 2 sit in the stack vector?
options: Index 7
Index 5
Index 2
Index 8
questions.explanation: A local operand means base plus local index, so slot 2 is at 5 + 2 = 7.

questions.prompt: Why do bytecode operands for locals say 'base plus a small number' instead of holding a raw stack index?
options: The same code works at any frame position and stays inside its own frame
Small numbers are decoded faster than large ones by the processor
Raw indexes cannot be stored inside bytecode instructions at all
Base-relative operands let a frame read its caller's locals directly
questions.explanation: A frame can sit at different depths on the shared stack on different calls. Relative slots keep working at any depth and stay inside their own frame.

questions.prompt: A caller wants exactly 2 results from a function that returns 3 values, in a language with multiple returns. What happens to the extra value?
options: It is discarded without an error
The call fails with an error
It is stored in a global variable
It replaces the second result
questions.explanation: With multiple returns, the caller picks how many results it wants. Extras are dropped and missing ones become nil.

questions.prompt: A caller asks for three results but the function returns two. What is the third?
options: nil
An error
The second value, repeated
questions.explanation: Missing results become nil; unwanted extras are discarded.

questions.prompt: A function returned from another function keeps using a variable that belongs to the outer function. What is that variable called from the inner function's point of view?
options: An upvalue, captured from an enclosing scope
A global, since it outlives the outer call
A parameter, since it is passed in at call time
A constant, since the inner function does not own it
questions.explanation: The inner function keeps using the variable after the outer one returns, so it is captured rather than being a local of its own.

questions.prompt: When is an upvalue 'open'?
options: While it refers to a live slot in an active frame
After the closure has returned some value
Whenever a host callback is currently running
Once the garbage collector has marked it
questions.explanation: Open means a stack index; closed means the value now lives in a cell the closure owns. The identity of `count` is unchanged, only its storage moves.

questions.prompt: While the outer function's frame is still running, what does the upvalue for a captured variable refer to?
options: The variable's slot on the stack, as an open upvalue
A private copy of its value, as a closed upvalue
A global entry with the variable's name in it
The location of the function's bytecode in memory
questions.explanation: While the frame is alive, the upvalue points at the live stack slot. After the frame returns, the value moves into the upvalue's own cell.

questions.prompt: When the outer function returns, why must an upvalue be closed, with its value moved into its own storage, before the stack slot is reused?
options: Otherwise the closure would read whatever new data fills that slot
Closing makes the variable constant so closures cannot change it
Open upvalues use too much memory to be kept after a return
Stack slots cannot be reused until the garbage collector has run
questions.explanation: Closing copies the value somewhere permanent, so the closure keeps reading and writing the right variable.

questions.prompt: Two closures capture one counter, but each gets its own private copy when it closes. Closure A is called twice, then closure B once. What do the three calls return?
options: 1, 2, then 1
1, 2, then 3
1, 1, then 1
2, 3, then 4
questions.explanation: The second closure increments its private copy from 0, so it returns 1. With one shared cell the third call would return 3, which is what Lua promises.

questions.prompt: Why must several closures capturing one local share a single upvalue cell?
options: One closure's updates must be seen by the others
Each closure needs a separate memory region
Cells cannot be copied inside the interpreter
The collector will only free shared cells
questions.explanation: If every closure copied the number independently, their updates would disagree and the language behavior would be wrong.

questions.prompt: A binding layer wraps a host function so that scripts can call it. Which step belongs in that wrapper?
options: Convert host errors into script errors with context
Copy the host's entire memory into the script's state
Disable the garbage collector while the host function runs
Start a new process for the host function on every call
questions.explanation: The wrapper checks argument counts and types, converts values, calls the function, converts the results, and turns failures into script errors.

questions.prompt: In the Lua C API, how does native code receive its arguments and return values?
options: Through an indexed value stack
Through global variables with fixed names
Through shared files on disk
Through the return value of `main`
questions.explanation: A native callback reads arguments from stack slots, validates them, pushes results, and reports how many it returned.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to treat a host function exposed to scripts like a small parser of its inputs?
options: Specify accepted types and ranges, and reject bad input early
Convert every input to text first, then split it into words
Trust the script's input, but parse the host's output carefully
Accept any input and quietly repair it into something valid
questions.explanation: Validate up front and return a clear error instead of acting on half-checked data.

questions.prompt: Why can a Lua instruction budget not stop a host callback that blocks?
options: The budget counts VM instructions, not native work
Callbacks always run before the script starts
Blocking calls use no CPU time at all
The hook only fires on odd-numbered instructions
questions.explanation: An instruction hook fires inside the VM. Arbitrary blocking work in native code is outside its reach, so callbacks must be short and bounded.

questions.prompt: What is re-entrancy at a script-host boundary?
options: A host call that runs script code which calls the host again
A script running the same line of code twice by accident
The host restarting a script that has stopped working
Two separate scripts sharing the same global variable name
questions.explanation: Host and VM frames nest inside each other. Holding a mutable engine lock while running script code is risky because the script may call back into the engine.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in a debug record for a misbehaving call?
options: Active function, frame base, and open upvalues
The player's account password for the game
The full contents of every snapshot taken
The computer's desktop wallpaper image
questions.explanation: The lesson lists the bytecode position, frame base, argument tags, result count, open upvalues, callback name, and error chain. It warns against printing secrets or whole snapshots by default.

questions.prompt: Some scripting languages use one built-in structure for lists, records and maps. What is the idea behind that design?
options: A single key-to-value mapping is flexible enough to play all three roles
Lists, records and maps are checked against a fixed shape when created
Each role gets its own hidden structure that the script cannot see into
The language forces every key in every table to be a piece of text
questions.explanation: One mapping that accepts several kinds of keys can act as a list (keys 1, 2, 3), a record (names) or a map. Sequence behavior is just a convention on top.

questions.prompt: In Lua, a list is written `{ "a", "b", "c" }`. What does reading index 0 give?
options: nil, since the first position is key 1 and a missing key reads as nil
"a", because indexes start at zero as they do in most languages
An error, because index 0 is outside the valid range of the list
"c", because index 0 wraps around to the end of the list
questions.explanation: Keys 1, 2 and 3 exist, but key 0 does not. A missing key reads as nil instead of raising an error.

questions.prompt: A hash table has 8 slots and picks a key's starting slot as the hash value modulo 8. A key's hash value is 29. Which slot does it start in?
options: Slot 5
Slot 3
Slot 7
Slot 1
questions.explanation: 29 divided by 8 is 3 remainder 5, and the remainder is the slot. Slot 3 is the quotient, which is not what modulo gives.

questions.prompt: Why is the remainder after dividing by a power-of-two slot count simply the hash's lowest bits?
options: The slot count is 2^k, so the remainder is the last k bits
Lua throws away the lowest k bits before it picks a slot
Every hash value is already smaller than the slot count
The slot count is kept in the hash value's top bits
questions.explanation: Dividing by 4 keeps the last two bits, and dividing by 8 keeps the last three. 22 is `10110`, so with 4 slots the answer is `10`, or 2.

questions.prompt: What happens when two keys hash to the same starting slot?
options: Lua links the displaced key so both can be found
Lua overwrites the first key with the second key
Lua raises an error and refuses to add the second key
Lua moves both keys into the array part instead
questions.explanation: A collision is handled by chaining the displaced key. Long chains cost extra comparisons, so hashing narrows lookup but is not one comparison every time.

questions.prompt: A language's loop over all fields of a key-value table has no documented order. What should you do if a script needs a stable order?
options: Keep an explicit ordered list of keys, or sort the keys before looping
Insert the fields in the wanted order, since loops follow insertion order
Trust the order seen in testing, since every machine will repeat it
Use numbers as keys, which makes the loop run in increasing order
questions.explanation: If order matters, the script has to create it. Hash-based storage can change its order after a resize, so observed order is not a promise.

questions.prompt: A Lua list has three items, and the value at key 2 is set to nil. How many items does a loop using `ipairs` visit?
options: One, since it stops at the first missing key
Two, since the third item shifts down into key 2
Three, with a nil in the middle of the sequence
None, since a list with a gap is considered broken
questions.explanation: ipairs counts up from key 1 and stops at the first key with no value, so everything after a gap is never reached.

questions.prompt: A Lua list has values at keys 1 and 3 but nothing at key 2. Why is the length operator not a dependable way to count the entries?
options: It may return 1 or 3, since only some border is promised
It counts every key, including text keys, so the answer is inflated
It reports 2 by counting only the keys that currently hold values
It raises an error as soon as the interpreter detects a gap
questions.explanation: A border is a key with a value whose next key has none. Both 1 and 3 qualify, so tables with holes give unpredictable lengths.

questions.prompt: A record has text keys such as `hp`, `mp` and `speed`. Which Lua loop visits every field?
options: `pairs`, since the keys are names and not positions 1, 2, 3
`ipairs`, since it handles every kind of key in a table
`ipairs`, since the record's fields are stored in a sequence
Neither, since text keys cannot be looped over at all
questions.explanation: ipairs walks only integer keys from 1, so it would visit nothing here. pairs visits all keys, though in no promised order.

questions.prompt: In a language where functions are values, a function named `compute` exists. What does `local f = compute` do?
options: Gives the function a second name, without calling it
Calls compute once and stores its result in f
Copies compute's source into a new independent function
Raises an error, because functions cannot be assigned
questions.explanation: Functions are ordinary values, so assigning one gives another name for something callable. A call happens only when parentheses follow.

questions.prompt: A ranking function returns the squared distance between two points, the x difference squared plus the y difference squared, with no square root. What does it return for (2, 1) and (7, 13)?
questions.explanation: The differences are 5 and 12, so 25 + 144 = 169. The true distance, 13, would need a square root.

questions.prompt: Why does the ranking function return squared distance instead of true distance?
options: It keeps the nearest-to-farthest order without a square root
It makes every distance come out as an exact integer
It lets the function accept position tables with no fields
It converts the result into a new position table
questions.explanation: Squaring preserves the ordering of non-negative distances, so ranking works without calculating a square root. Squared values are not always integers.

questions.prompt: What is a closure?
options: A function plus the outer variables it keeps using after the outer one ends
A function that automatically closes the files that it has opened for you
A function stored in a table so that it can be called with a colon
A function that can be called one time before it expires for good
questions.explanation: A closure captures surrounding variables, so they stay alive and usable as long as the inner function exists.

questions.prompt: A function creates a local counter and returns an inner function that uses it. You call the outer function twice and keep both results. How do their counters relate?
options: Each call creates its own counter, so they change independently
They share one counter, since both inner functions have the same code
The second call resets the first counter back to its start
Only the most recent call's counter survives, and the other is lost
questions.explanation: Every call to the outer function makes a fresh local variable. Each returned function keeps its own copy unless the code deliberately shares it.

questions.prompt: A closure keeps a hidden counter that starts at 0. On each call, if the counter is 0 it returns true and sets the counter to 2; otherwise it subtracts 1 and returns false. What are the results of six calls in a row?
options: true, false, false, true, false, false
true, false, false, false, true, false
true, false, true, false, true, false
true, true, false, false, true, true
questions.explanation: Call 1 fires and sets the counter to 2. Calls 2 and 3 count it down while returning false, and call 4 fires again, so the pattern repeats every three calls.

questions.prompt: In Lua, `obj:act(5)` is shorthand for which call?
options: `obj.act(obj, 5)`, passing the table on the left as the first argument
`obj.act(5)`, with the table made available to the function as a global
`act(obj, 5)`, calling a global function that happens to be named act
`obj.act(5, obj)`, passing the table on the left as the last argument
questions.explanation: The colon adds the table on its left as a hidden first argument, conventionally called self.

questions.prompt: A class table has a method that writes `self.mode`, and an instance table inherits from it through a metatable. Calling the method as `Cls:set(1)` on the class itself instead of `inst:set(1)` changes which table?
options: The class table, since the colon passes whatever is on its left
The instance table, since instances and classes share their fields
Both tables, since the metatable links them together
Neither, since the call fails when the class is not an instance
questions.explanation: Self is just the table to the left of the colon, so the method writes into the class. Calling it on the instance writes into the instance.

questions.prompt: In Lua's metatable mechanism, what does the index field of a metatable control?
options: Where Lua looks next when a key is missing from the table
Which kinds of keys are allowed to be created in the table
How many entries the table is permitted to hold at one time
The order in which the table's keys are visited by a loop
questions.explanation: Attaching a metatable alone changes nothing. When a lookup fails, Lua checks the metatable's index field and repeats the lookup there.

questions.prompt: A script attaches a metatable to an instance table but never sets the metatable's index field. It then calls a method that lives only in the class table. What happens?
options: A run-time error, since the lookup finds nothing and Lua tries to call nil
It works, since attaching a metatable is enough to inherit methods
It works, but only the first time the method is called
A compile-time error, since the missing field is found before running
questions.explanation: Without the index field, a failed lookup just yields nil, and calling nil is an error that appears only when the line runs.

questions.prompt: Why do many guides advise beginners to prefer plain tables and functions over heavy use of metatables and metamethods?
options: Metamethods can hide control flow, so it is hard to tell what a line does
Metatables are not supported by most embedded interpreters in games
Metatables stop a script from using closures in the same file
Metamethods run slower than every other feature of the language
questions.explanation: Plain data and functions are easier to read and debug. Metamethods run code behind ordinary-looking operations.

questions.prompt: A Rust crate offers an option to compile its own bundled copy of a C library instead of finding one already installed. What is the benefit?
options: The build works without having to locate or install a separate library
The library runs in a sandboxed process, so its crashes cannot spread
The bundled copy is guaranteed to be the newest version available
The final program is smaller because the library is left out
questions.explanation: Bundling, or vendoring, a dependency removes a setup step. It keeps beginners from hunting for a matching library file.

questions.prompt: Why do programs wrap a lower-level error inside a higher-level error with added context, instead of replacing it with a plain message?
options: The original details are kept while the context says what was being done
Wrapping makes an error cheaper to create than a message string is
Wrapped errors are sent to the developer over the network automatically
Plain messages cannot be printed by a program at all
questions.explanation: Chained errors keep the root cause and add where it happened, so the final report is both specific and traceable.

questions.prompt: When a host embeds a scripting interpreter, how are the two related?
options: A separate subsystem with its own state, memory and call stack, reached through a bridge
The interpreter shares the host's memory and type system, as one merged language
It is only a parser, and scripts are merged into the host's own compiled code
It is a set of host objects that scripts can modify directly in memory
questions.explanation: Embedding does not merge the languages. A binding layer converts values and controls exactly when execution crosses from one side to the other.

questions.prompt: When a script asks the host to perform a game action, what should the host check?
options: That the request is well formed and legal under the game's rules right now
That its types are correct, since game rules are the script's job
That the script's author is trusted, since trusted scripts send valid requests
Nothing, since the interpreter already guarantees that every request is safe
questions.explanation: Type checks catch malformed input, but the host must also confirm the request makes sense in the current game state. Scripts are not trusted to enforce rules.

questions.prompt: In the two-phase boundary, what does the host do during the commit phase?
options: Checks target, snapshot version, IDs, and rules before acting
Lets Lua write directly into the live game state
Rebuilds the Lua interpreter from the saved script
Skips validation because planning already checked everything
questions.explanation: During planning, Lua reads an immutable snapshot and proposes actions. At commit time the host confirms the proposals still hold and rejects a plan based on an old snapshot.

questions.prompt: In Rust, what does the `?` operator after a call that returns a Result do when the result is an error?
options: Returns that error to the caller at once instead of continuing
Ignores the error and quietly substitutes a default value instead
Panics and aborts the whole program with a short message
Retries the call over and over until it finally succeeds
questions.explanation: The question-mark operator unwraps a success value and early-returns the error otherwise, so a failed setup does not continue with a broken state.

questions.prompt: A callback interface hands every callback a handle to its runtime, though many callbacks do not need it. What is the usual way to write one that ignores it?
options: Name the parameter with an underscore to show it is deliberately unused
Leave the parameter out, since the interface adapts to any signature
Reuse the handle anyway, since unused values cause errors
Wrap the callback in an error handler, as the compiler demands
questions.explanation: The callback signature is fixed, so the parameter must be present. An underscore name says it is intentionally ignored and avoids warnings.

questions.prompt: In stack-based calling between a script and a host, what happens when the script calls a host function with two arguments?
options: The function, then each argument, are pushed in order and read by position
The arguments are written into global variables that the host reads by name
The host receives a copy of the script's whole stack, including its locals
The arguments are placed in shared memory, in reverse order, for the host
questions.explanation: A call pushes the function value, then the arguments in order. The receiving side finds each argument by its position on the stack.

questions.prompt: A host function expects two tables as arguments, but a script passes a number in the second position. In a typed binding layer, what happens?
options: The conversion fails and a script error is raised before the body runs
The function runs, treating the number as an empty table
The host crashes with a memory fault, since the types do not match
The number is turned into a one-entry table automatically
questions.explanation: A binding layer converts arguments to the declared types before calling. A mismatch becomes an ordinary error in the script, not a crash.

questions.prompt: A host function returns the true 3D distance, with a square root, between two points. What does it return for (1, 1, 1) and (3, 7, 4)?
questions.explanation: The differences are 2, 6 and 3, so the square root of 4 + 36 + 9 = 49 is 7. Forgetting the square root gives 49.

questions.prompt: Why might a host group all the functions it exposes to scripts under one named table instead of many separate global names?
options: One table makes a visible, documentable boundary showing what the host supplies
Global names cannot be created by a host program at all in most interpreters
Scripts run faster when functions sit in a table than when they are globals
An interpreter requires a table before it will accept any native function
questions.explanation: A namespace keeps the exposed surface in one place, so readers can see what the host offers and what is script-defined.

questions.prompt: A host converts a zero-based Rust list into a Lua list. Under which Lua key does the first item go, and why?
options: Key 1, since Lua sequences conventionally count from one
Key 0, since the host index is kept as it is
Key 2, since key 1 is reserved for the table's length
Key -1, to mark that the item came from the host
questions.explanation: The host's zero-based index plus one gives Lua's conventional first key, so loops and the length operator work as scripts expect.

questions.prompt: A game entity has an identifier number stored as data, and it is placed in a list at some position. Why can the identifier and the position differ?
options: The id is data about the entity, while the position is where it sits in the list
The list renumbers its ids to match positions every time the list changes
A list position is assigned by the entity itself at the moment it spawns
Ids are generated only at the moment an entity is added to a list
questions.explanation: The identifier belongs to the entity and survives reordering. The position is a property of the collection and may change.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to give a chunk of script code a name, such as its file path, before running it?
options: Error messages can then point to the script that failed
The interpreter runs named chunks faster than unnamed ones
Naming a chunk protects its code from being modified
The name decides which functions the chunk may call
questions.explanation: A chunk name is attached to errors and tracebacks, so a failure points at the right file.

questions.prompt: Why should the host not hold a mutable game-state lock while a script runs?
options: Give Lua a copied snapshot and collect requests instead
Locks cannot be created inside an `mlua` host
Scripts run so fast that locks would never matter
The script needs the lock so it can edit state directly
questions.explanation: Holding the lock during untrusted script work invites trouble. The two-phase design runs Lua on a copy and applies validated requests afterward.

questions.prompt: A binding library converts values between a host language and a script safely. What does it NOT do for you?
options: Decide whether a requested action or ID is valid under your game's rules
Check that argument types match what a host function expects to receive
Prevent a script from corrupting the memory of the host program
Report a script's run-time errors back to the host application
questions.explanation: The library handles safe conversion and memory safety. Whether a request makes sense in your game is your code's job.

questions.prompt: Why does the host print accepted actions only after the script returns?
options: Lua proposes data, and the host decides what happens
Scripts cannot run until the host has printed
Printing earlier would delete the script's requests
The accepted list is computed by Lua's garbage collector
questions.explanation: The delay is deliberate. A script's output is only a proposal until the host checks it.

questions.prompt: Why is giving scripts general read and write functions over raw memory addresses worse than giving them a small set of meaningful operations?
options: Every layout rule and bound leaks into every script, and a typo gains great power
Raw memory functions cannot be called from a script at all in most designs
Raw access is slower than meaningful operations, which can be inlined
Scripts cannot hold numbers large enough to be used as addresses
questions.explanation: With raw access, every script has to know offsets and validate pointers, and one mistake can damage the target. Narrow operations keep that knowledge in one place.

questions.prompt: In the host's collection steps, which single step is the one that crosses into Lua?
options: Creating ordinary owned records from copied fields
Opening the target with the least rights required
Resolving versioned roots and the pointer paths
Verifying the game build and its architecture
questions.explanation: Only step 5, building ordinary owned records, crosses into Lua. Addresses, handles, and versioned paths stay in the host.

questions.prompt: A copied record of an entity's id, name, position and alive flag contains no memory address. Why is that deliberate?
options: A script cannot keep a stale pointer that it was never given
Addresses take more memory than names, so they are left out to save space
Addresses change on every frame, so they are not worth storing
Records that include addresses cannot be copied at all
questions.explanation: The record carries meaning, not locations. If an entity dies, a remembered address might later belong to something else.

questions.prompt: What is the main danger of giving a script light userdata that wraps a raw pointer?
options: The address may belong to another object later
Light userdata cannot be compared inside Lua code
The pointer is duplicated every time a script reads it
A script cannot store the value in any table field
questions.explanation: Light userdata is essentially an unowned pointer value. A dead entity's address can be reused, so a retained pointer may reach whatever lives there now.

questions.prompt: Lua remembers slot 3, generation 6. The entity dies and slot 3 is reused at generation 7. What does the host do with the old handle?
options: Rejects it, because 6 does not match 7
Accepts it, because slot 3 still exists
Updates it silently to generation 7
Accepts it, but logs a warning only
questions.explanation: A generation counter changes every time a slot is reused, so a stale pair no longer matches and the host refuses to act on the new occupant.

questions.prompt: Which extra field would a real snapshot carry besides its list of entities?
options: A sequence number telling how old the data is
The target process's raw handle, kept for later reads
The script's last error text, kept for debugging
The total bytes the game has allocated so far
questions.explanation: `GameSnapshot` holds `sequence`, `captured_at_ms`, and `profile` as well as the entities, so snapshots have a time and a version.

questions.prompt: In an object layout, three consecutive 4-byte floats start at offset 0x18. At what offset is the third float?
questions.explanation: The floats sit at 0x18, 0x1C and 0x20. Each offset is the previous one plus 4.

questions.prompt: A struct has a 1-byte flag at offset 0x1C, followed by an 8-byte pointer. Typically, where does the pointer start, and why?
options: At 0x20, since an 8-byte pointer must start on a multiple of 8
At 0x1D, since fields are packed back to back with no gaps between them
At 0x1C, since a flag and a pointer can share the same bytes
At 0x24, since padding comes in whole multiples of 4 bytes
questions.explanation: The flag ends at 0x1D, and the next multiple of 8 is 0x20, so three padding bytes are left unused. Alignment rules make this padding common.

questions.prompt: A byte in game memory holding 1 means 'alive'. How should a well-designed snapshot present it to a script?
options: As a named boolean field, with no offsets or pointers visible
As the raw number 1 plus the offset where it was found
As a pointer to the byte so the script can re-read it later
As a text string containing the byte's hexadecimal value
questions.explanation: A snapshot translates raw memory into named, typed values. Layout details stay on the host side.

questions.prompt: What does the abstraction barrier let you do when a new game build moves the position field?
options: Change only the observer, not every script
Skip the observer and edit each Lua script by hand
Keep old scripts working by guessing the new offset
Move the barrier into the Lua standard library
questions.explanation: Lua knows only `id`, `name`, `position`, and `alive`. The observer below the barrier knows offsets and encodings, so it is the only place that changes.

questions.prompt: A script-facing layer reads game data through an interface that both a live reader and a recorded replay can implement. What does that give you?
options: The same script logic can be tested on recorded data without a live game
Scripts can write changes back into the recorded replay afterwards
Scripts run faster because replays skip every validation step
Live data is replaced permanently by the recording on disk
questions.explanation: An abstraction lets two sources provide the same shape of data, so automation can be tested repeatably without running the game.

questions.prompt: A host copies a variable-length list into a script and has a published maximum size. What should it do when the list exceeds that maximum?
options: Fail with a clear error naming the limit, not silently truncate
Copy as many as fit and quietly drop the rest of the list
Copy everything anyway, since the limit is only a guideline
Pick random entries so that the whole list will fit
questions.explanation: A documented bound is enforced loudly. Silent truncation would give scripts a wrong view of the game without telling anyone.

questions.prompt: A script sends a request marked as based on snapshot 41. By the time it arrives the game is at snapshot 42, and the target despawned in 42. How should the host respond?
options: Refuse it, since the target no longer exists in the current state
Perform it on the nearest remaining object, to be helpful
Perform it anyway, since the script was correct at snapshot 41
Crash the script, since stale requests are always a script bug
questions.explanation: The script did nothing wrong, since it was right about snapshot 41. Tagging requests with their basis lets the host see that the moment has passed.

questions.prompt: Why is sending a structured request with a kind and fields safer than building a command string for the host to interpret?
options: A string needs parsing and can be manipulated; a request has a fixed shape
Strings are slower to send between a script and a host than tables are
Structured requests are encrypted, while strings are sent as plain text
Strings cannot hold numbers, so any ids inside them would be lost
questions.explanation: Building command strings creates an injection boundary. A fixed shape with an explicit set of kinds makes unknown or malformed requests fail cleanly.

questions.prompt: Why must the host validate again when it processes a request?
options: Checking at snapshot time says nothing about later state
Checks made at snapshot time are skipped for speed
Scripts are unable to see the values that were checked
The first check always ran against a different map
questions.explanation: This is a time-of-check/time-of-use issue: an entity may disappear between the snapshot and the request. Check recency, existence, state, finite numbers, bounds, and budget.

questions.prompt: How should the host handle permissions for an observer script versus an automation script?
options: The host picks the API first; observers get no requests
The script names its own permission level at the top
One API for all scripts, which agree to behave
Permissions come from the script's file name
questions.explanation: Do not decide permissions from a script-provided name. An observer gets snapshot and log only; automation gets those plus two bounded requests.

questions.prompt: Which input belongs in a test of the Lua-to-host request boundary?
options: A coordinate of `0/0` or infinity
A request that the host has approved before
A snapshot with every field filled in
A script that only logs one line
questions.explanation: The tests should send missing IDs, non-finite coordinates, unknown actions, too many actions, and expired sequences. The host must reject each usefully and stay alive.

questions.prompt: A script sends the same request to its host inside an endless loop with no other logic. What is the main design problem?
options: It keeps no state, never checks the request worked, and has no way to stop
Scripting languages refuse to compile any loop that never ends
Each repeat overwrites the previous request, so only the last one acts
The loop works, but it uses more memory than a timed loop does
questions.explanation: With no named phase, no confirmation and no stop rule, the script can flood the host and never respond to a stop signal.

questions.prompt: In a finite state machine used for automation, what does one update step compute?
options: The next state, and maybe an action, from the current state and input
The full list of every state the machine could ever reach
The input, worked out from the current state and the previous action
A new set of rules, chosen from the current state and the clock
questions.explanation: An update maps the current state and a new input to a next state and, optionally, one action.

questions.prompt: Which job belongs to the host rather than the state machine?
options: Delivering a request and checking the target
Deciding that a living candidate was found
Moving the bot from Choose to Request
Counting down the `wait_ticks` value each update
questions.explanation: The state machine is policy: whether a request is appropriate. The host is mechanism: how it is delivered and whether the current target allows it.

questions.prompt: Why should a state machine name phases like 'waiting for a result' instead of creating a new state for every specific target it handles?
options: A state names a phase of control; specifics like the target are separate data
Machines are limited to about ten states, so names must be general
State names that contain numbers cannot be compared by the interpreter
Targets are stored by the host, so the script has no place for them
questions.explanation: The state says what the machine is doing. Details such as the chosen target, a request number or a timeout are data carried alongside it.

questions.prompt: Why define all state names once as constants in a table, instead of typing raw strings throughout the code?
options: There is one place listing every state, and typos are easier to catch
Strings stored in a table are compared faster than any raw string is
The interpreter refuses to compare raw strings inside conditions
Constants in a table are hidden from every other script
questions.explanation: A table of constants documents the states in one place, and a misspelled name yields nil instead of a silently different string.

questions.prompt: Why should one call of a script's update function perform only one transition and propose at most one action?
options: Bounded work is measurable, so the host can stop between calls
The interpreter can only return one value from each function call
Doing more work per call makes the machine run out of states
The host has room to store only one action per game session
questions.explanation: Small, bounded steps make scheduling visible, so the host can interleave rendering and input and stop a script between calls.

questions.prompt: Who should own the main loop that repeatedly calls a script's update function, and why?
options: The host, since it controls the rate and a script cannot flood actions
The script, so it can decide when it is ready to run again
The operating system, which schedules scripts the way it does threads
The player, who triggers each update by hand when needed
questions.explanation: If the script had its own endless loop it could flood actions between frames. The host chooses when each update runs.

questions.prompt: Before a state machine moves from sending a request to waiting for the result, what two things should it record?
options: The snapshot the request used, and a countdown for how long to wait
The expected result, and a copy of the host's whole game state
The script's file path, and the number of states in the machine
The host's memory address, and a list of every earlier request
questions.explanation: Tagging the request with its basis lets the host spot stale requests, and a timeout counter ensures the wait cannot last forever.

questions.prompt: A machine enters a waiting state with a timeout counter of 8, and the counter drops by 1 on every update that sees no confirmation. If no confirmation ever arrives, what happens?
options: After 8 updates the counter is 0, and the next update gives up and stops
After 7 updates the counter is 0, and the next update gives up and stops
After 8 updates the counter is 0, and the machine keeps waiting at zero
After 9 updates the counter is 0, and the next update gives up and stops
questions.explanation: Eight unconfirmed updates take the counter from 8 to 0. On the next update the counter is already 0, so the machine stops safely instead of waiting forever.

questions.prompt: A script remembers the snapshot it used to choose a target, and later receives newer snapshots while waiting. Why keep the old one separate from the newer ones?
options: The request can be tagged with its basis, so the host can detect staleness
Old snapshots are smaller than new ones, so keeping them saves memory
A newer snapshot cannot be read until the older one has been deleted
The script can undo its actions later by replaying the older snapshot
questions.explanation: The request records what the choice was based on, and newer snapshots are used to look for confirmation. Keeping them apart makes staleness checks meaningful.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a helper function that picks a target to be 'pure'?
options: It reads its inputs and returns a result, with no side effects
It does not use any numbers and works on nothing but text values
It is written in the host language instead of in the script
It runs once per game session and then caches its own result
questions.explanation: A pure function depends only on its inputs and changes nothing else, which makes it easy to test with fixed tables.

questions.prompt: A helper skips the local player and any dead entities, then returns the nearest of the rest. The player is at distance 0, living candidates are at 7.0 and 4.0, and a dead entity is at 2.0. Which does it return?
options: The living entity at 4.0
The dead entity at 2.0
The player at 0
The living entity at 7.0
questions.explanation: Filtering comes first: the player and the dead entity are skipped. Of the living candidates, 4.0 is nearer than 7.0.

questions.prompt: Which of these should move the host to Stopped even if the Lua script wants to continue?
options: The user pressing the stop hotkey
The script choosing a new state name
The bot finishing its CHOOSE phase
A snapshot containing a living entity
questions.explanation: The script is a guest, not the authority over shutdown. Hotkey, process exit, profile mismatch, an error limit, a rejected action, or an invalid snapshot all stop it.

questions.prompt: What should the update function do on an unknown state string?
options: Raise an error containing the bad state name
Treat it as Observe and carry on quietly
Move to Request to retry the last action
Return true without changing anything at all
questions.explanation: The final `else` calls `error("unknown bot state: " .. tostring(bot.state))`. A readable error is better than silently continuing from a nonsense state.

questions.prompt: What stance should an embedded interpreter take toward script failure?
options: Treat it as a normal result; keep the game running
Treat it as impossible once scripts pass a review
Close the whole game so the error cannot spread
Retry the failing line until it finally succeeds
questions.explanation: One script error should not crash the game, leak resources, or leave input stuck.

questions.prompt: A script has a block that is opened but never closed. At which stage does the failure appear?
options: When the source is compiled, before any of it can run
At run time, when execution reaches the unclosed block
During a call to the host, when arguments are validated
In gameplay, as a unit that behaves in an odd way
questions.explanation: A syntax error means the source never became a runnable function. Run-time, host-API and gameplay errors all need code that already compiled.

questions.prompt: A script runs without raising any error but selects the wrong unit. Which kind of error is this?
options: A gameplay error, where nothing is raised
A syntax error, caught when the file loads
A runtime type error, from unsuitable values
A host-API error, from a broken contract
questions.explanation: Every layer ran correctly; the requested action was simply wrong. It needs a test that asserts expected behavior, not an error message.

questions.prompt: A script calls a host function but leaves out a required field in the request. Which kind of failure is that?
options: A host API error, since the script broke the function's contract
A syntax error, since part of the source is missing
A budget error, since the call used too many resources
A gameplay error, since the result was not what the player expected
questions.explanation: The script ran, called the engine, and violated what the engine requires. The source itself was fine, so it is not a syntax error.

questions.prompt: Why might a sandbox limit call depth separately from the number of instructions a script may run?
options: Endless recursion can exhaust stack space before the instruction budget does
Recursive calls do not count as instructions, so they escape the budget
Call depth only matters for scripts that run on more than one thread
Instruction counts cannot be measured while a loop is running
questions.explanation: Different resources are exhausted in different ways. A script that recurses endlessly can fill the stack long before it executes many instructions.

questions.prompt: When a budget is exceeded mid-update, what should the host do with the update's queued actions?
options: Discard them and report which budget was hit
Commit them, since they were valid when queued
Keep them for the script's next update
Commit the first half and discard the rest
questions.explanation: Do not quietly continue with half-produced output. Stop the update, drop uncommitted actions, and name the exact budget.
