questions.prompt: A memory limit is written as 16 * 1024 * 1024 bytes. How many bytes is that?
questions.explanation: 1,024 × 1,024 = 1,048,576 bytes is one mebibyte, so sixteen of them is 16,777,216. Using 16,000,000 mixes decimal and binary units.

questions.prompt: Does the Lua memory limit cover everything a host callback allocates?
options: No; only Lua-managed memory, so callbacks need bounds
Yes; any allocation during a script call counts
Yes; Rust heap memory is counted through `mlua` too
No; it covers only the size of the script's source
questions.explanation: The limit applies to Lua-managed memory. A host function can allocate other memory, so it needs its own limits.

questions.prompt: A hook fires every 500 VM instructions, and the script is stopped once the hook has fired more than 40 times. Roughly how many instructions can one update run?
options: About 20,000
About 540
About 2,000
About 200,000
questions.explanation: The budget is the interval times the number of allowed firings: 500 × 40 = 20,000 instructions, give or take one interval.

questions.prompt: A callback that may run on another thread and the code that created it must share one counter in Rust. Which pairing fits?
options: An Arc for shared ownership and a Mutex so that updates do not overlap
A Box, which gives each closure its own private copy of the counter
An Rc, which is meant for sharing a value across several threads
A plain reference, which lets every closure keep it alive forever
questions.explanation: Arc lets several owners hold the same value, and a Mutex lets only one of them change it at a time. Cloning an Arc shares the counter instead of copying it.

questions.prompt: Why is an instruction-count hook not a stopwatch?
options: Instruction costs differ, and callbacks run between hooks
The hook counts seconds instead of instructions
Hooks fire only once, at the moment a script ends
Instructions always cost the same number of nanoseconds
questions.explanation: Different instructions cost different real time, and host callbacks can do work between hooks, so the hook is one defense against runaway bytecode, not a timer.

questions.prompt: Who should reset the instruction allowance?
options: The host, at a controlled boundary
The script, when it runs low
The hook, after each call
The user, by restarting the game
questions.explanation: Reset from the host side, not from inside the script, which could otherwise grant itself unlimited work.

questions.prompt: A test script contains an endless loop that does nothing. A correctly configured sandbox should produce what result?
options: An error that stops the script and says which limit was hit
A normal finish, since the loop does no real work
A syntax error, since endless loops are not valid code
A crash of the whole host, which then restarts itself
questions.explanation: A budget limit must interrupt a runaway script and report it with context. If the host hangs forever, the limit is not working.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in a host callback's input checks?
options: Numeric finiteness, range, and referenced IDs
Whether the script file is long enough to run
Which Lua version wrote the script's comments
The colors the log output will be shown in
questions.explanation: Validate argument types, string lengths, sequence lengths, numeric finiteness and range, referenced IDs, permissions, and rate budgets.

questions.prompt: Which detail should NOT appear in a public error report?
options: Account tokens or dumps of process memory
The script path or a stable identifier
The line number and the traceback if known
The validation rule that failed on the call
questions.explanation: Development builds should report path, traceback, API function, and rule. Do not leak memory, tokens, private logs, or arbitrary host paths.

questions.prompt: How should a host usually respond to the first error a script raises during an update?
options: Stop that update, report the error, and keep the host running
Disable the script forever and delete all of its saved state
Ignore it and continue the same update from where it failed
Shut down the whole game so that the error cannot spread
questions.explanation: One failed update is a contained event. The host reports it and carries on, and only repeated errors justify disabling the script.

questions.prompt: Why should the host not catch a script error and keep going from the same state?
options: Host state may be half-changed; commit only afterward
Lua errors always repair themselves by next frame
Lua requires every error to close the interpreter
Catching errors always makes the script run faster
questions.explanation: Lua requests should be queued and committed only after the script returns successfully, so a failure cannot leave half-mutated host state.

questions.prompt: Which list names the four parts of a Turing machine?
options: A tape, a head, a current state, and a table of rules
A register file, a clock, a stack, and a program counter
A compiler, an interpreter, a linker, and a loader
A keyboard, a screen, a memory, and a processor
questions.explanation: A tape of cells, a head that reads and writes one cell, a current state, and a rule table are the whole model.

questions.prompt: What does one step of a Turing machine do?
options: Look up a rule, write, move one cell, switch state
Read the whole tape, then rewrite every cell at once
Jump to any cell by its address and swap two symbols
Compile the rule table and then run the compiled result
questions.explanation: One step is lookup, write, move one cell or stay, and a state change. The head walks one cell at a time; it does not jump.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when a Turing machine 'halts'?
options: It stops because no rule applies to its state and symbol
It erases the whole tape and restarts from its first state
It reaches the right end of the tape and cannot move on
It finds an error in its rule table and reports it to you
questions.explanation: Halting is simply stopping. A machine that has no rule for its situation has nothing left to do.

questions.prompt: A machine adds 1 to a binary number: starting at the rightmost digit, it turns each 1 into 0 and moves left until it finds a 0, which it turns into 1, then halts. What is on the tape after it runs on 10111?
questions.explanation: The three right-hand 1s become 0s, and then the 0 becomes 1, giving 11000. That turns twenty-three into twenty-four.

questions.prompt: Using the add-one method of turning 1s into 0s and then writing a 1 over the first 0 or blank, what happens on 111?
options: The carry reaches blank tape and writes a new 1, giving 1000
Every digit becomes 0 and nothing writes a 1, giving 000
The 1 is added at the right end instead, giving 1110
There is no 0 to turn into a 1, so the tape stays 111
questions.explanation: The carry runs past the leftmost digit into blank tape, where the machine writes a leading 1. Seven becomes eight.

questions.prompt: Which pair matches a Turing machine part to its closest counterpart in a real computer?
options: The tape and memory
The head and the power supply
The rule table and the file system
The state and the monitor
questions.explanation: Tape maps to memory, head position to an address, state to registers including the instruction pointer, rules to the program, and a step to an instruction.

questions.prompt: Why does a real computer only approximate the Turing machine model?
options: Its memory is a fixed size; the tape never runs out
Its CPU cannot read a symbol before writing one
Its hardware can only use binary, never other symbols
Its programs cannot be stored as bytes in memory
questions.explanation: A finite machine eventually runs out of memory or states. The Turing machine says what could be computed with as much time and storage as needed.

questions.prompt: What makes a universal Turing machine special?
options: It reads another machine's rules from tape and imitates it
It runs any program on any input in one single step
It has an unlimited supply of different states to use
It never halts, whatever input sits on its tape
questions.explanation: A rule table is just symbols, so it can sit on a tape like data. To change what the machine does, change the tape, not the machine.

questions.prompt: What does 'stored-program computer' mean for the tools in this book?
options: Instructions and data are both bytes in memory
Programs live on a separate chip from the data
Programs cannot be changed once they are loaded
Data bytes are run whenever the CPU reads them
questions.explanation: Because code is bytes, tools can inspect code as well as data, subject to memory protections. Only bytes the instruction pointer reaches run as instructions.

questions.prompt: Which action treats code as data by writing it?
options: A debugger writing `0xCC` over an instruction byte
A disassembler naming the instructions it reads
A game loading a texture file in order to draw it
A script printing a log message to the console
questions.explanation: A software breakpoint is a one-byte write of `int3` (`0xCC`). The disassembler reads code as data; the other two are not about code.

questions.prompt: What stops a program from overwriting its own instructions?
options: Page protections set by the OS and enforced by the CPU
The Turing machine model, which forbids the write
Comments in the program marking its code read-only
The instruction pointer, which erases every change
questions.explanation: Nothing in the model forbids it. The OS marks pages readable, writable, or executable, and the CPU refuses forbidden accesses. A writable-and-executable page deserves a second look.

questions.prompt: What is true of a Turing-complete system, given enough time and memory?
options: It can compute anything a Turing machine can
It will halt on every program it runs
It can only run programs written in Rust or C++
It needs a graphical screen to work
questions.explanation: In idealized form Rust, C++, Lua, and assembly qualify, and so do Conway's Game of Life and redstone circuits. Real builds are limited by their actual resources.

questions.prompt: Why is a downloaded script mod a different kind of concern from a downloaded image file?
options: A script computes, so the host must limit what it can do
Scripts are larger than images, so they take longer to check
Images cannot hold mistakes or hidden data, but scripts can
Scripts run in a separate process, but images run inside the game
questions.explanation: An image is read in one fixed way. A script computes, so the safety of running it depends on the limits and the interface the host provides.

questions.prompt: In the halting-problem argument, a program is built to do the opposite of whatever a hypothetical checker predicts for it. If the checker says it will halt, what does it do?
options: It loops forever, so the checker was wrong
It halts, which shows the checker was right
It crashes, so the checker's answer is never used
It asks the checker again and waits for a new answer
questions.explanation: Whichever answer the checker gives, the program does the opposite, so the checker is wrong. Therefore no checker can be right about every program.

questions.prompt: Which kind of question about arbitrary programs is undecidable in general?
options: What a program does when run, like ever writing to an address
How many characters are contained in its source text file
Whether its source text contains one particular chosen word
Whether its file begins with a given signature of bytes
questions.explanation: Questions about the behavior of a program are undecidable in general. Questions about the text or bytes are plain checks.

questions.prompt: Why can a disassembler produce a plausible but wrong listing on x86?
options: Lengths vary, so a start one byte off misreads
Disassemblers cannot read bytes held in memory
Every x86 instruction is exactly four bytes long
Disassemblers run the program and guess output
questions.explanation: It must decide which bytes are instructions. Starting too early or late gives a convincing wrong listing, so check odd output against the debugger.

questions.prompt: Why can a signature scanner miss code it has never seen?
options: It matches known patterns, not behavior
It scans only files under one megabyte
It runs each file and waits for a halt
It cannot read executable files at all
questions.explanation: Since behavior is undecidable in general, scanners use known byte patterns and behavior. They can miss the unknown and occasionally flag something harmless.

questions.prompt: A machine reaches its halting condition on exactly the last step of its allowed budget. A runner that looks for a rule before it checks the budget reports what?
options: Halted, since the missing rule is noticed first
Out of budget, since the budget was just spent
An error, because two limits were reached at once
Still running, because it needs one more step to be sure
questions.explanation: The order of checks matters at the edge. Looking up the rule first returns Halted if none exists, before the budget is considered.

questions.prompt: A simulator takes its rules as data. Why should it still validate a rule table before running it?
options: Running a table is running a program, so bad data can misbehave
Rule tables are encrypted and must be decoded before use
Data files cannot contain mistakes, but programs can contain them
Validation makes the rules run faster once they are checked
questions.explanation: A rule table is a program in data form, so treat it as untrusted input and check it before it runs.

questions.prompt: A machine flips each binary digit it reads, moving right, and halts at the first blank. How many rule steps does it take on 10110?
options: 5, and it stops at the blank without a sixth step
6, counting one more step on the blank
4, because the first digit does not need a step
10, one step to read and one to write each digit
questions.explanation: One rule is applied to each of the five digits, giving 01001. At the blank no rule matches, so the machine halts.

questions.prompt: In what order do the stages of a typical interpreter process a line of source code?
options: Lexer, then parser, then compiler to bytecode, then virtual machine
Parser, then lexer, then virtual machine, then compiler to bytecode
Compiler to bytecode, then lexer, then parser, then virtual machine
Lexer, then virtual machine, then parser, then compiler to bytecode
questions.explanation: Characters become tokens, tokens are checked against the grammar, the meaning is turned into bytecode, and the virtual machine executes it.

questions.prompt: What is the lexer's job in the pipeline?
options: Group characters into tokens like name or integer
Check the token order against the grammar
Turn the program's meaning into bytecode steps
Run the bytecode using a stack of values now
questions.explanation: The lexer produces tokens like name, equals, integer, plus, integer. Grammar checking is the parser, and compiling and running are later stages.

questions.prompt: Does every interpreter use the lexer, parser, bytecode, VM pipeline?
options: No; one may walk a syntax tree or add a JIT
Yes; bytecode is part of the definition of Lua
Yes; every interpreter must emit native code
No; only compiled languages have a parser
questions.explanation: The stages are common but not definitional. The language's meaning can stay the same while its implementation changes.

questions.prompt: Which is a language rule, as opposed to an implementation detail?
options: `+` adds two numbers and produces a number
Pop two VM values, check variants, push the sum
The host's native code runs on the CPU
A bytecode listing has eleven instructions
questions.explanation: The source rule is the contract. Stacks, bytecodes, and native instructions are replaceable ways to carry it out.

questions.prompt: A bytecode instruction says 'push constant 2'. What does the 2 refer to?
options: A position in a table of constants stored alongside the code
The literal number two, which is pushed onto the stack directly
The second instruction in the code, which holds the value
The memory address where the constant was loaded
questions.explanation: Instructions usually point into a constant pool by index, which keeps instructions small and lets constants be shared.

questions.prompt: A virtual machine's code is a numbered list, and its jump instructions take an absolute position. A conditional jump with operand 9 is taken. What happens next?
options: Execution continues at the instruction in position 9
Nine instructions are skipped, and then execution continues
The value 9 is pushed onto the stack and execution continues
Execution returns to the start and repeats nine times
questions.explanation: A jump operand names a place in the bytecode, so taking the jump just sets the instruction pointer to that position.

questions.prompt: A conditional compiled to bytecode has a 'then' part followed by an 'else' part. Why does the 'then' part end with an unconditional jump past the else part?
options: Otherwise execution would fall through and run the else part too
To return to the start of a loop and test the condition again
To free the stack values that the then part created
To tell the virtual machine that the then part may be deleted
questions.explanation: Bytecode runs in sequence. After finishing the then part, execution must skip over the else part instead of falling into it.

questions.prompt: A virtual machine's loop fetches an instruction and advances its instruction pointer by one before executing it. Why?
options: That sets the default next instruction, which a jump can overwrite
Instructions are deleted once they run, so the pointer must move on
It prevents any single instruction from being run twice by mistake
The pointer is defined to point at the instruction that just ran
questions.explanation: Advancing first makes straight-line code work by default, and a jump simply overwrites the pointer with a new target.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT part of a small virtual machine's own state?
options: A handle to the operating-system process of the game around it
The position of the next instruction that will be run
The stack of values that are being worked on at the moment
The remaining instruction budget for the current run of code
questions.explanation: The VM's state is its instruction pointer, code, constants, stack, budget and output. A process handle belongs to the host, not to the VM.

questions.prompt: A stack machine pushes 6, pushes 7, then runs Multiply, which pops two values and pushes their product. What is on the stack afterward?
options: The single value 42
The single value 13
The two values 6 and 7
The single value 67
questions.explanation: Multiply consumes both operands and leaves one result, 6 × 7 = 42.

questions.prompt: A stack machine pushes 8, then 3, then runs a greater-than instruction, which pops the right-hand value, then the left, and tests left > right. What is left on the stack?
options: The single value true
The single value false
The two values 8 and 3
The single value 5
questions.explanation: It pops 3 and then 8 and tests 8 > 3. The one value left is the Boolean true, which a conditional jump can test.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the constant pool and the value stack?
options: The pool holds constants; the stack holds temporaries
The pool holds temporaries; the stack holds constants
Both hold identical values, just in a different order
The pool holds code; the stack holds output text
questions.explanation: Adding two values removes both from the stack and leaves one result, while the pool is only read.

questions.prompt: A stack machine computes 'left minus right' by pushing left first, then right. For Subtract, which operand must it pop first, and why?
options: The right one, since it was pushed last and a stack returns the newest first
The left one, since it is the first operand that the expression mentions
Either one, since the result is identical in both orders of popping
The larger one, so that the answer never goes negative at all
questions.explanation: A stack is last-in, first-out. The most recently pushed value, the right operand, comes off first, so the machine must keep track of which is which.

questions.prompt: What happens if the tiny VM is told to add a Boolean to an integer?
options: A VM error from the variant check
The Boolean quietly becomes the integer 1
The integer quietly becomes the Boolean true
The VM adds the two values' raw bytes
questions.explanation: `pop_integer` checks the variant. Dynamic typing means the check happens at run time, not that types do not exist.

questions.prompt: A script's jump target points outside the program. Which kind of failure is this?
options: Bytecode validation
Lexing of the source
Parsing of the grammar
Execution of the code
questions.explanation: The lesson separates lexing, parsing, bytecode validation, and execution failures. A jump outside the program is invalid bytecode, a different stage from a type error at run time.

questions.prompt: Why keep the four failure kinds separate in error messages?
options: The host can tell bad Lua from a budget stop
Short messages make every script run faster
Lexing errors can only be fixed by the host
Each stage writes its errors to a different file
questions.explanation: If everything becomes 'script failed', no one can tell whether the author wrote invalid Lua, the compiler made bad code, or a valid script exceeded resource policy.

questions.prompt: Why does a virtual machine count down a step budget on every instruction and stop when it reaches zero?
options: So a program that loops forever ends in an error, not a hang
So that instructions run in a faster order near the end of the run
To measure how long each instruction takes in real seconds
So that every program is forced to finish in the same number of steps
questions.explanation: Each instruction consumes one step, so even an endless jump loop is stopped with a clear error.

questions.prompt: Why does each interpreter value carry a tag beside its payload?
options: An operation reads the tag to learn the value's type first
The tag stores the value's address in memory
The tag makes the payload immune to garbage collection
The tag lets the host skip type checks in Rust
questions.explanation: Lua decides many operations at run time, so `+` checks both tags before touching payloads. Two Integer tags can add; an Integer with a Table is a type error.

questions.prompt: An interpreter represents a table value as a small ID for storage it owns, rather than as a raw pointer. What is the benefit?
options: Objects stay under one memory manager, with no raw pointers in scripts
IDs make table lookups faster than any pointer-based lookup could be
Tables can be copied between scripts without using any extra memory
The ID keeps its table alive forever, whatever else the script does
questions.explanation: Handles keep every object under the interpreter's control and avoid handing scripts raw native pointers.

questions.prompt: Many table implementations keep densely numbered keys 1, 2, 3, ... in a compact array and other keys in a hash structure. A table has items at keys 1, 2 and 3 plus named keys `title` and `count`. Which keys use the compact array?
options: Keys 1, 2 and 3, the densely numbered ones
The named keys title and count
All five keys, since they share one table
Only key 1, since arrays hold one item
questions.explanation: Dense integer keys fit an array part, and named keys use the hash part. These are implementation strategies behind one table value.

questions.prompt: Why does a hash-based table loop promise no meaningful order?
options: Entries are visited by where hashing placed them, not when they were added
The interpreter shuffles the entries each time to stop scripts relying on order
Entries are visited from the newest to the oldest, which has no real meaning
Entries are visited in alphabetical order, but only for text keys
questions.explanation: Position follows the hash values of the keys, so adding or resizing can change it. A script that needs order must keep its own list.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to intern strings?
options: Keep one canonical copy and let values carry an ID
Make every string a fresh copy for each table
Store each string inside the table that uses it
Convert each string into its integer length
questions.explanation: Repeated names and keys share one stored string, so values hold a small ID or shared reference.

questions.prompt: Why is comparing two interned strings fast?
options: It is one integer comparison, whatever the length
The text is compared one letter at a time
Interned strings are always one letter long
The collector compares them while it is running
questions.explanation: If both values carry `String(0)`, equality is `0 == 0`. The cost moves to lifetime work: the VM must know when no live value still needs the string.

questions.prompt: Three tables P, Q and R are linked in a ring: P points to Q, Q points to R, R points to P. One local variable also refers to P. What are the reference counts of P, Q and R?
options: P is 2, Q is 1, R is 1
P is 1, Q is 1, R is 1
P is 2, Q is 2, R is 2
P is 3, Q is 2, R is 2
questions.explanation: P is held by the local variable and by R. Q is held only by P, and R is held only by Q.

questions.prompt: In a ring of three tables that point to each other, the last outside reference is dropped. Why does plain reference counting never free them?
options: Each table is still pointed at by the previous one, so no count hits zero
Reference counts can never go below 1 for any table in a ring
The counts go negative, and the interpreter ignores negative counts
Counting only works for strings, not for tables of any kind
questions.explanation: A cycle keeps every member's count at 1 even though nothing outside can reach it. A tracing collector avoids that by asking what is reachable.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between unreachable and unreferenced?
options: Unreachable means no root path; unreferenced means count zero
Unreachable means count zero; unreferenced means no root path
Both mean the same thing for a table
Unreachable is for strings; unreferenced is for tables
questions.explanation: In a cycle the objects are unreachable from any root but still referenced by each other, and counting alone cannot tell those apart.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a root in a tracing collector?
options: The global environment, which holds live names
A table that is found only through an unreachable cycle
A string whose reference count has already hit zero
A function that the script never defined anywhere
questions.explanation: Roots include the global environment, active frames, VM stack values, open upvalues, and intentionally retained host references. The collector marks everything reachable from them.

questions.prompt: What does a tracing collector do with objects the mark step did not reach?
options: It sweeps them, cycles included
It keeps them until the script ends
It counts them and frees any whose count is 0
It moves them to the nearest root
questions.explanation: It asks about reachability, not owner counts, so two tables in an unreachable cycle are both reclaimed.

questions.prompt: What risk comes from a host API that retains a Lua table?
options: It may keep a large graph of objects alive
It stops the script from using that table
It converts the table into a string
It forces a collection every frame
questions.explanation: Anything reachable from a retained table stays alive, which is why limits should measure interpreter memory and not the source size.

questions.prompt: A host builds the table of functions that a script can see. Why is leaving a dangerous function out of that table a form of security?
options: A script can only call what its environment actually contains
The interpreter scans scripts and deletes calls to missing functions
A missing function is replaced by a safe stub that does nothing
Scripts see everything, but the table slows down dangerous calls
questions.explanation: A function that is not in the environment cannot be called, so the environment itself is part of the security boundary.

questions.prompt: In a debug build of an embedded VM, which structure hints at a VM instruction pointer separate from the CPU's?
options: An index into an array of bytecodes
A pointer into the Windows kernel's thread list
A string table that holds only file paths
An array of GPU shader constants
questions.explanation: The lesson suggests looking for tagged-value dispatch, a central table lookup, a VM instruction pointer, bytecode or constant arrays, roots, and callbacks under readable names.

questions.prompt: Why is the first code run at a program's entry point usually not the developer's own main function?
options: Startup code prepares the runtime first, then it calls main
The operating system chooses the entry point at random on each launch
The main function is run by the kernel before the file is loaded
Entry points refer to resource data, never to runnable code
questions.explanation: Startup code can set up security state, global constructors and thread storage before main runs. Calling the first address 'main' hides that chain of steps.

questions.prompt: Which pair of things do all threads of one process share?
options: The virtual address space and the handle table
The instruction pointer and the general-purpose registers
The stack and the saved return addresses
The thread ID and the thread-local storage slots
questions.explanation: Address space and handles are process-wide. Each thread needs its own registers, stack, and TEB so Windows can pause and resume it independently.

questions.prompt: Why does every thread need its own registers and stack?
options: So Windows can pause it and later resume exactly where it stopped
So the process can hold a separate address space for each thread
So each thread can keep its own private copy of every loaded DLL
So each thread has a separate handle table that other threads cannot see
questions.explanation: A paused thread's place in the code and its call history live in registers and the stack. The address space and handle table stay shared.

questions.prompt: What does the PEB (Process Environment Block) mainly describe?
options: Process-wide user-mode data: image base, loader lists, process parameters
The registers, stack bounds, and error code of the one thread that is running now
The kernel-mode page tables Windows uses to translate this process's addresses
The list of files on disk that the game's installer copied into its folder
questions.explanation: The PEB is a root for process-wide metadata. Per-thread details such as stack boundaries live in each thread's TEB.

questions.prompt: How do the TEB and PEB relate?
options: Every thread has a TEB, and each TEB leads to the one shared PEB
Each process has many PEBs, one per thread, and the TEB is the shared copy
The PEB sits inside the kernel while the TEB sits inside the game's EXE file
The TEB lists the loaded modules and the PEB lists the current thread's stack
questions.explanation: TEB is one per thread, PEB is one per process. Thread-specific facts such as stack boundaries come from the TEB, and the loader lists hang off the PEB.

questions.prompt: Disassembly of 64-bit Windows code shows a read through the `gs` segment at a small fixed offset. What is it most likely doing?
options: Reading per-thread bookkeeping, such as process information
Reading a player's health value from the game world's memory
Reading the keyboard state from a hardware register
Reading the launch arguments of the game from the disk
questions.explanation: On 64-bit Windows the gs segment helps locate the current thread's data, and from there the process's environment block. It is operating-system bookkeeping, not game data.

questions.prompt: A structure field sits at offset 0x30 in the 32-bit layout and at 0x60 in the 64-bit layout. What should a learner conclude?
options: Each layout has its own offsets, taken from the real layout and not from a rule
64-bit offsets are twice the 32-bit ones, so the rule works for any field
The offsets are the same on both, so one of the numbers is a typo
Offsets change only when the Windows version number changes
questions.explanation: Wider pointers and alignment help explain why layouts differ, but the real offsets must be observed for one architecture and one build. No doubling rule exists.

questions.prompt: A tool copies a PEB field offset from an old 32-bit article and uses it on a current 64-bit process. What is the main risk?
options: Layout depends on architecture and Windows build, so it may hit another field
Windows will refuse to run any program that uses a number copied from an article
The offset will be too small by exactly one pointer width, so a +4 fix works
The PEB is encrypted on 64-bit systems, so every read returns random bytes
questions.explanation: PEB and TEB internals are not a stable public API contract. An old offset can still read plausible-looking bytes, which is what makes the mistake hard to notice.

questions.prompt: Why is a documented snapshot API a better way to list a process's modules than walking its internal loader structures by hand?
options: It is a supported, read-only, point-in-time copy of the module list
It freezes the target process so that nothing changes while it is read
It reads the modules directly from disk instead of from memory
Internal structures are encrypted, so they cannot be read at all
questions.explanation: Internal structures are fine to study in a debugger, but a documented API gives a supported copy. A snapshot is stable, but the process itself keeps running.

questions.prompt: Many Windows APIs ask the caller to fill in a size field of a structure before the call. What is that field for?
options: The size and version of the structure the caller prepared
It tells the system how many items it should return in total
It holds the size of the module or file that is being described
It reserves how much memory the system may use during the call
questions.explanation: The size field identifies which version of the structure the caller built, so old and new callers can both work. It is different from fields that describe the data itself.

questions.prompt: A tool lists a process's modules from a snapshot, then a read at one module's base address fails. Which explanation fits best?
options: The process kept running, so the module may have unloaded after the snapshot
The snapshot froze the process, so memory cannot be read until it resumes
Snapshots contain made-up addresses that are not real
Modules can be read only at the instant their names are listed
questions.explanation: A snapshot is a consistent copy, but the process is not paused. Any later read has to be allowed to fail, and a Result type makes that explicit.

questions.prompt: What does 'enumeration tells you what existed during the snapshot' mean for later reads?
options: An address seen earlier may still fail to read and should give a normal error
Any address seen in the snapshot stays valid until the program exits
A read should be retried in a loop until Windows finally allows it
The tool should cache the address and skip checking the result next time
questions.explanation: Seeing an address earlier does not guarantee it is valid now. The tool reports an error rather than assuming a previously seen address must remain valid.

questions.prompt: When enumerating items with a 'next' call, the call fails with the documented 'no more items' error. How should the loop treat it?
options: As the normal end of the list, while other errors are real failures
As a crash of the target process, so the tool should abort
As a sign the list is corrupted, so enumeration should restart
As a permission problem, so the tool should retry with more access
questions.explanation: That error is the documented end-of-list signal. Anything else is a genuine failure that should be returned to the caller.

questions.prompt: A module's file says it prefers base 0x400000, but this run loads it at 0x730000. A function has RVA 0x1A2B0. Where is it in this run?
options: `0xB4A2B0`
questions.explanation: An RVA is measured from the module's start, so the live address is the live base plus the RVA: 0x730000 + 0x1A2B0 = 0x74A2B0. The preferred base only matters if the module loaded there.

questions.prompt: If ASLR moves the whole module, why does the same RVA still name the same position?
options: It is measured from the module's start, which moves along with every byte inside
It is an absolute address that Windows rewrites in the lab tool's output
It is stored in the PEB, and the PEB is left unchanged when a module moves
It is a file offset on disk, which does not depend on where the module loads
questions.explanation: An RVA is a relative position. That is why the lab adds it to the live base instead of reusing a displayed absolute address after a restart.

questions.prompt: Why is editing operating-system process structures, or unlinking modules from loader lists, a poor way to gather information?
options: It can break loader assumptions and hide activity from tools
It is slower than using documented APIs, but otherwise equivalent
It works on 32-bit processes only, so it is not portable
It makes the module unloadable until the machine is restarted
questions.explanation: Those structures are good for explaining how Windows works, but documented APIs are the supported route. Tampering is fragile and conceals activity from tools.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly separates mechanism from policy?
options: A context switch is mechanism; picking the next ready thread is policy
A context switch is a policy; the thread's saved registers are the mechanism
A handle is a policy; the access check on a request is the mechanism
Choosing the next thread is a mechanism; stopping one thread is a policy
questions.explanation: A mechanism is how something is done and a policy decides what should be done. Mixing them makes an implementation detail sound like a guarantee.

questions.prompt: Why is copying a game's executable file not the same as copying a running game session?
options: A process also holds live memory, register state and handles
The executable is compressed, while a process is stored uncompressed
A process is the executable plus a longer, more specific file name
The file holds only code, and the running process holds only data
questions.explanation: The file supplies code and initial data. The process adds an address space, register contexts, handles and bookkeeping, which is why a crash dump reveals more than the file.

questions.prompt: Which of these can make a live process differ from its EXE file?
options: Applying relocations, resolving imports, and zero-filling data
Rewriting the PE section names so they match the process's heap names
Deleting the import table from the file once the game starts running
Renumbering every function so RVAs match the preferred base exactly
questions.explanation: The process is not simply a copy of the file. Windows may place sections at different virtual addresses and also creates private memory that never existed in the EXE.

questions.prompt: Why is walking the PEB's live loader lists risky compared with a snapshot?
options: Another thread may load or unload a module while the list is being walked
The lists are stored encrypted and each entry needs a key from the TEB
The lists exist while a debugger is attached to the process
The lists contain 32-bit modules, so 64-bit DLLs would be missed
questions.explanation: The loader lists are live linked lists. A walker needs the correct layout at every step and must tolerate the list changing underneath it.

questions.prompt: x86 processors define four privilege levels. Which two does Windows actually use, and for what?
options: Ring 0 for the kernel and drivers, ring 3 for games, browsers, debuggers, and every tool in the book
Ring 0 for games and debuggers, ring 3 for the kernel and the drivers that talk to hardware
Ring 1 for drivers and ring 2 for services, with ring 3 for the kernel's scheduler and memory manager
Ring 0 for administrator programs and ring 3 for standard user programs, with the kernel in between
questions.explanation: Windows uses ring 0 (kernel mode) and ring 3 (user mode). Administrator versus standard user is a security-token matter, not a processor ring: an administrator's game tool still runs in ring 3.

questions.prompt: Why does the user/kernel privilege rule have to be enforced by the processor instead of by ordinary operating-system code?
options: A restricted program could overwrite protections kept in ordinary code or data, so the rule must live beyond its reach
Ordinary operating-system code runs too slowly to check every instruction a program executes on a busy core, so hardware must
Software checks cannot read the page tables, so only the processor knows which memory belongs to which running program
Every game is compiled with its own copy of the rules, so a shared software rule could not apply to all of them
questions.explanation: If the protections were just code and data, the program being restricted could rewrite them, the way a debugger rewrites an instruction. Only the processor sits beyond a ring-3 program's reach. Speed and page-table visibility are not the reason.

questions.prompt: A user-mode program tries to execute an instruction reserved for the kernel, such as one that disables interrupts. What happens?
options: The processor raises a fault, and the kernel usually ends the process
The instruction runs, but the kernel undoes its effect afterward
The processor silently ignores it and carries on running the code
The instruction runs if the user has administrator rights
questions.explanation: Privileged instructions are refused outside the most privileged level. The refusal becomes an exception that normally ends the program, so a program cannot take over the processor.

questions.prompt: A control register holds the address of the top-level page table, and loading it changes how every virtual address is translated. Why is that register kept from user-mode code?
options: Changing it would let user code view memory it was never given
It would slow the processor down for every other process
It would erase the data that is currently stored in RAM
It would switch off the processor's caches for the whole machine
questions.explanation: The register selects a process's whole view of memory. Only the kernel loads it, for example when switching between processes.

questions.prompt: A page-table entry for a present page has its user/supervisor bit (bit 2) set to 0. A ring-3 instruction tries to read that page. What happens?
options: A page fault occurs, because the page is reserved for ring 0 even though it is present
The read succeeds, because a present page can be read by any code that knows its address
The processor sets the page's dirty bit and then lets the read finish normally
The kernel copies the page into the program's own memory so the read can finish
questions.explanation: Bit 2 equal to 0 on a present mapping means supervisor-only, so a ring-3 access causes a page fault. Being present only says the page is in memory; it does not say who may use it.

questions.prompt: A fast system-call instruction saves the address of the instruction after it in a register before entering the kernel. Why?
options: So the kernel can later resume user code right after the call
So the kernel can read the call's arguments from that address
So the kernel can tell which service has been requested
So user code can jump into the kernel's code directly
questions.explanation: The saved return address lets the matching return instruction resume the user program at the right place.

questions.prompt: When user code executes a system-call instruction, how is the kernel's entry address determined?
options: From a processor setting that only privileged code can change
From an operand chosen freely by the calling code each time
From a table that sits inside the calling code's own memory
From the address of the most recent function call it made
questions.explanation: The kernel configures the entry point at boot. A program picks when to ask for a service, never which kernel instruction runs, and that is what makes the crossing controlled.

questions.prompt: A system-call stub puts a small number in a register before the system-call instruction. What is that number for?
options: It tells the kernel which of its services to run
It tells the kernel how many bytes to copy
It identifies the target process to operate on
It gives the priority of the calling thread
questions.explanation: The stub is only a few instructions: place the service number, then enter the kernel. The kernel uses the number to choose the routine.

questions.prompt: A tool with a fully privileged handle asks the kernel to read from an address in the kernel's own half of the address space. Why does it fail?
options: The kernel checks the range is user space, whatever the handle allows
The handle's rights are ignored, so the processor blocks the read
Kernel memory can be read only by the processor, never copied
The read succeeds, but it returns nothing except zeros
questions.explanation: The kernel validates the requested ranges itself before copying, since the copy runs at full privilege. Rights on a handle cannot override that check.

questions.prompt: A handle was opened with query and read rights only. The tool asks the kernel to write through it. What happens, and can the tool fix it afterward?
options: The write is denied at the rights check, and rights cannot be added to that handle
It is denied, but a later call can add the missing right to the same handle
It succeeds, because administrators can write through any handle
It succeeds, because the kernel ignores rights for local processes
questions.explanation: The right needed for writing was never granted. Rights are fixed when the handle is opened, so the tool must open a new one.

questions.prompt: Which kind of instruction returns from a system call, dropping back to user privilege and resuming right after the call?
options: A system-return instruction
A breakpoint instruction
A halt instruction
A no-operation instruction
questions.explanation: The kernel places its status in a register and executes the return instruction, which restores user privilege at the saved address.

questions.prompt: A library call that asks the kernel to do work fails, and the thread's last-error value is a small number. Where does that number typically come from?
options: A kernel status that a library converted to an error number
A register the processor filled in when the fault occurred
A value the code calculated itself from the failing address
A report sent by the graphics driver to the application
questions.explanation: The kernel returns a status, and a library translates it into the numbers that applications see. An access-denied status, for example, becomes the access-denied error number.

questions.prompt: A game is running when the player presses a key. Which way does execution reach the kernel's key-handling code?
options: An interrupt from the device arrives between two of the game's instructions
A `syscall` that the game must execute first before the key press is noticed
An exception raised by the game's own instruction, such as a page fault
The kernel polls the keyboard by running its own loop in the middle of the game's code
questions.explanation: The three ways into the kernel are system calls, exceptions raised by the running instruction, and interrupts that arrive between instructions whether or not the program expects them. A key press is a device interrupt.

questions.prompt: The interrupt descriptor table is indexed by a one-byte vector number. How many entries can it have at most, and what is vector 14?
options: 256 entries, numbered 0 to 255; vector 14 is the page fault
128 entries, numbered 0 to 127; vector 14 is the page fault
256 entries, numbered 0 to 255; vector 14 is the breakpoint
65,536 entries, numbered 0 to 65,535; vector 14 is the page fault
questions.explanation: One byte holds 2⁸ = 256 values. The processor fixes vectors 0 to 31: 3 is the breakpoint (`int3`), 13 the general-protection fault, 14 the page fault. Devices get vectors from 32 up.

questions.prompt: What must the kernel do when it moves the processor from a thread of one process to a thread of a different process?
options: Save old registers, load new ones, and switch to the new page tables
Copy the old process's memory to disk and then load the new one's
Restart the new process from its entry point each time
Pause every other thread in the system until the switch completes
questions.explanation: A context switch saves one thread's registers and loads another's. If the process differs, it also installs that process's top-level page table.

questions.prompt: After a page is committed, Windows may assign its physical frame only on first access. Why does the kernel hand the game a zeroed page then?
options: So old data from another process cannot leak into the new page
So the first read always returns a recognizable pattern that the game can test for
So the page fault finishes faster than if the kernel copied real data
So the game's variables start at the default values written in its executable file
questions.explanation: The first access faults, and the kernel supplies a zeroed page, updates the mapping, and retries the instruction. Zeroing prevents data left in a reused frame from showing up in another process.

questions.prompt: Why must interrupt handlers be short?
options: Other work on that core waits while they run, so long handlers delay everything
The processor ends any handler that runs for longer than one timer tick
Interrupt vectors are only 32 bytes apart, so handler code cannot be longer
A handler's registers are kept only in a small buffer that overflows if it runs too long
questions.explanation: While a handler runs, other work on that core waits. Lesson 12.4 shows how drivers split the work so the urgent part stays brief. There is no hard time cut-off that ends handlers.

questions.prompt: A game follows a bad pointer in user mode. What is the normal outcome?
options: The kernel handles the page fault and raises an access violation for that one process; everything else keeps running
The kernel stops the whole computer with a bug check, since a bad address cannot be told apart from kernel damage
The processor silently fixes the pointer by mapping a zeroed page, and the game carries on unaware
The kernel ends every process that shares a module with the game, because they might hold the same pointer
questions.explanation: At ring 3 the kernel checks its records, finds nothing valid at that address, and turns the fault into an access-violation exception for that process. The program's handler, a debugger, or Windows Error Reporting deals with it; at worst that one process ends.

questions.prompt: Why does Windows stop the whole machine on an unexpected fault inside kernel code, rather than just ending the offender?
options: Kernel code and drivers share data structures, and a fault mid-update leaves records Windows cannot trust
The kernel cannot tell which process was running when the fault struck, so it has no single process to end and must stop everything
Ending a driver would require restarting the hypervisor, and that takes the whole machine down anyway
Windows cannot write a crash dump unless the whole system stops completely first
questions.explanation: Kernel state such as scheduler lists, page records, and locks is shared, and a fault may leave one half updated with a lock held. Windows cannot generally prove what is still sound, and carrying on could write corrupted data to disk.

questions.prompt: A computer shows a blue screen with a stop code. What is that screen?
options: A deliberate stop after an unrecoverable kernel failure
A fault in one application that the kernel has already cleaned up
A warning that the disk is nearly full and needs attention
A request to press a key before the machine continues
questions.explanation: The system halts on purpose when kernel code fails, because continuing could damage data. An ordinary access violation ends only one process.

questions.prompt: How can kernel-mode security software make a tool's read of a protected process fail, even though the tool asked for read rights?
options: By stripping rights from handles at the moment they are opened
By moving the tool to a higher privilege ring on the processor
By marking the tool's own memory as unreadable to the tool
By replacing the read call's service number with another one
questions.explanation: Callbacks run while a handle to the protected process is being created and may remove rights. The tool then holds a handle without read rights, so the read fails at the rights check.

questions.prompt: What is a real cost of putting anti-cheat code in the kernel?
options: Its bugs become bug checks on players' machines, and a flaw in it exposes every installed machine
It makes the game slower only while the player is not in a match, so the cost is easy to avoid entirely
It cannot see process creation, because only user-mode code receives such notifications from Windows
It lets cheat tools run at ring 0 as well, because Windows lowers its checks for every signed driver
questions.explanation: Kernel code has the authority of the whole kernel, so its mistakes are bug checks and its vulnerabilities spread widely. It also asks players to trust a company with ring-0 code. Process notifications are in fact one of the things it gains.

questions.prompt: Why does this book keep its labs in user mode and inside a virtual machine?
options: A user-mode crash ends one process, and a bug check inside a virtual machine stops only that machine
User mode is the only mode in which a debugger is able to read the memory of another process
A virtual machine runs at ring 0, which makes every instruction in the lab run noticeably faster
Windows refuses to write crash dumps for any programs that do not run inside a virtual machine
questions.explanation: Failures in user mode are contained to one process, and a bug check inside a VM stops only that VM. A debugger can attach in the way the book describes without needing a VM.

questions.prompt: A dump from a crashed game shows the failing thread. A teammate asks what happened ten seconds earlier. What can the dump tell you?
options: Little, because it records one instant; pair it with logs or an ETW trace when history matters
Everything, because a dump keeps a timeline of every call the process made before it was captured
The last ten seconds, because dumps always include a rolling buffer of recent events
Only the earlier module loads, since those are the one event type a minidump records over time
questions.explanation: A dump saves selected state at one capture moment, not a timeline. The history must come from logs or an event trace.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to post a crash dump file in a public chat to ask for help. What is the right concern?
options: It may contain paths, arguments and memory, so treat it as private
Dump files are too large to post in any chat or ticket
Small dumps are harmless, and only full dumps hold private data
A dump cannot be read without the original machine it came from
questions.explanation: Even a 'mini' dump is a selected subset of a process's state, not a harmless log. Paths, arguments and stack contents can be private.

questions.prompt: A reader opens a dump and cannot find a particular heap object. What is the safest conclusion?
options: It may not have been captured, since the dump type decides which streams and pages are saved
The object never existed, because a dump lists every object that was alive at the capture time
The object was freed just before the capture, because dumps list every freed object by name too
The dump is corrupt, since a valid minidump must always contain the whole heap of the process
questions.explanation: A missing object or exception record can mean not captured, not never existed. The dump type chooses the optional streams.

questions.prompt: Dump options are bit flags: one is 0x0800, another is 0x0040, and the baseline is 0. What value results from combining all three with bitwise OR?
questions.explanation: OR sets both bits, and the baseline 0 adds nothing: 0x0800 | 0x0040 = 0x0840. OR adds bits and does not clear them.

questions.prompt: In a set of bit flags, a flag named 'normal' has the value 0. What does OR-ing it into a combined value do?
options: Nothing; it sets no bit, so it just names the baseline
It clears every other flag that is already in the combined value
It doubles the combined value, which changes the meaning of the flags
It marks the whole combined value as invalid
questions.explanation: OR-ing in 0 changes nothing. The other flags are the bits that add extra data.

questions.prompt: A dump option that copies all of a process's private memory is left off in a learning exercise. Why?
options: A smaller dump is enough, and full copies are large and sensitive
The option does not work on a process's own memory at all
The option corrupts the process that is being dumped
Windows forbids full dumps for accounts that are not administrators
questions.explanation: The exercise only needs the workflow, and copying every private page makes a very large, sensitive file.

questions.prompt: A learning exercise dumps only the process that runs it. What does that avoid?
options: Searching for another process or opening a handle to it
Writing any file to disk during the whole exercise
Needing any permissions at all to run the tool itself
Capturing the thread stacks of the process it is in
questions.explanation: Limiting the exercise to the current process means it never touches any other process.

questions.prompt: A tool writes its output using an open mode that fails when the file already exists. What does this protect?
options: An earlier capture, which a repeat run cannot overwrite
The dump's size, which is capped automatically at creation
The file's owner, which is locked to the account that made it
The dump's contents, which are encrypted when it is created
questions.explanation: The open fails if the file exists, so a previous capture is never silently replaced.

questions.prompt: A program passes a file's raw handle to a system call that writes into it. Why must the file object stay alive until the call returns?
options: The file object owns the handle, and closing it early leaves a stale number
The system call closes the file itself, so the file object must exist
The raw handle is a copy that needs a live original to refresh it
Files are deleted as soon as their owner is dropped from memory
questions.explanation: Borrowing a raw handle does not keep the owner alive. The owner must outlive the call, so the drop belongs after it.

questions.prompt: When analyzing a crash dump, which question does a list of loaded modules with their address ranges answer?
options: Which executable files were mapped, and where in memory
Which functions were executing at the moment of capture
Which values the registers held in each of the threads
Which exception was the one that ended the process
questions.explanation: A module list shows what was loaded and where. Thread lists, call stacks and registers answer other questions.

questions.prompt: The self-dump is captured during a normal function call, not a crash. Why is that useful for learning?
options: You can practice module, thread, register, and stack navigation without any undefined behavior
`!analyze -v` can only run on dumps that were written by a healthy, non-crashing process
WinDbg refuses to open any dump that holds a real exception record from a crash
A dump from a crash is always smaller, so it gives the learner less to practice on
questions.explanation: With no crash exception in the file, `!analyze -v` has nothing to summarize, but the navigation commands all work. No crash is needed to learn them.

questions.prompt: A call stack listing for a thread shows the most recently entered function at the top and thread start-up code at the bottom. What does the top frame represent?
options: Where the thread was when captured, with its callers below
The first function the thread ever ran, with later ones below
The function that will run next, with finished ones below
The function that crashed, even if the thread was healthy
questions.explanation: The top frame is the thread's position at capture, and the frames below are its callers. Reading from the bottom up replays the calls in order.

questions.prompt: With no symbols available, a debugger shows a location as a module name plus an offset, such as `game+0x1234`. What does that identify?
options: A spot 0x1234 bytes into that module, for one exact build
The function name, which the debugger could not print for you
A fixed address that stays the same in every build of the game
The size of the module in bytes as it sits on the disk
questions.explanation: It is a module plus an offset from where the module loaded. Paired with the exact build, it picks out one specific instruction.

questions.prompt: A learner wants a crash dump to practice on. What is a good source?
options: A tiny test program that crashes on purpose, run in a disposable VM
A running game whose memory has been corrupted by hand
A dump that another user posted publicly for the community
A dump made by deliberately crashing the host operating system
questions.explanation: Do not damage a running game just to get a dump. Your own test program in a disposable VM is a safe source.

questions.prompt: A Rust program built with the default settings panics with a message and exits with code 101. Why is there no dump from Windows Error Reporting?
options: The default panic is caught by the runtime and ends as an ordinary exit; nothing crashed
Windows Error Reporting only watches programs that return an error from `main` with code 1
Exit code 101 is reserved for programs that ran out of memory, so no dump is ever allowed
The panic message goes to the console instead, and the console process blocks dump capture
questions.explanation: Returning an error from `main` exits with code 1 and a default panic exits with 101; both are ordinary exits, so there is nothing to dump.

questions.prompt: In Rust, how does a program built so that a panic aborts end differently from the default, which unwinds the stack?
options: It ends right away in a fail-fast crash the system can record
It continues running after it prints the panic message to the console
It restarts itself automatically after the panic has been printed
It unwinds more slowly, so that cleanup code runs twice
questions.explanation: An abort ends in a fail-fast exception that Windows error reporting can capture, instead of unwinding and running cleanup code.

questions.prompt: Why can a dump help with a crash that disappears when a debugger is attached?
options: It saves state close to the failure without a debugger attached, so timing is left alone
It lets the process keep running while the debugger sets a breakpoint on the failing line
It replays the crash from the beginning, so the debugger sees the same timing as before
It forces the crash to happen again whenever the dump file is opened in WinDbg
questions.explanation: Attaching a debugger can change timing and hide a reproducible crash. A dump saved near the failure keeps the state with no debugger. A dump does not replay events.

questions.prompt: A Unity game's data folder holds its gameplay code as a managed assembly of intermediate language. Which backend does that suggest?
options: Mono, which runs C# as managed intermediate language
IL2CPP, which turns C# into native code at build time
A native C++ engine with no managed code
Godot, which uses only its own scripting
questions.explanation: A managed assembly of the game's logic is the clue for the Mono backend. IL2CPP builds ship a native library instead.

questions.prompt: Which pair of files best suggests a Unity game built with IL2CPP?
options: A native game-logic DLL plus a separate metadata data file
A managed assembly of the logic plus a small settings file
A Java archive plus a launcher script
A packed data file plus an engine library
questions.explanation: IL2CPP converts C# to C++ and compiles it into a native library, keeping type information in a metadata file.

questions.prompt: A large data package with a custom extension sits beside a small executable. How should you treat that as evidence about the game engine?
options: As a starting hypothesis, to check against loaded modules and behavior
As proof of the engine, since file layouts identify engines uniquely
As irrelevant, since data packages look the same in every engine
As proof the game is unmodded, since packages are always signed
questions.explanation: Folder clues begin an investigation. A game can add native extensions or use another arrangement, so confirm with the loaded-module list before deciding.

questions.prompt: Why confirm a folder-based guess against the process's loaded-module list?
options: The folder shows what is installed; the module list shows what the running process mapped
The module list is generated before launch, so it matches the folder in every case
The folder lists files ending in `.dll`, which hides any executable beside them
The loaded modules appear for native games, so they separate native from managed
questions.explanation: A launcher can start a different executable than the one you inspected. The module list reflects the real process, not the install directory.

questions.prompt: What changes for a Unity Mono build compared with a native one?
options: A decompiler shows near-original C#, like a `health` field and the `TakeDamage` that writes it
The code is encrypted at rest, so the sole evidence is offsets found by scanning memory
The collector moves objects so often that field names can be read after a pause
The assemblies hold plain C++ source files, so no decompiler step is needed
questions.explanation: `Assembly-CSharp.dll` holds intermediate language that keeps class, method, and field names. The Chapter 3 recovery skills become confirmation rather than discovery.

questions.prompt: Why can't you open a .NET decompiler on the gameplay code of a Unity build compiled ahead of time to native code?
options: The C# was compiled into machine code, so it is disassembly again
The logic is encrypted, so only the game itself can ever read it
The logic is stored in a database file instead of in code
The logic lives on the publisher's servers, not on the disk
questions.explanation: Ahead-of-time compilation removes the managed intermediate language, so ordinary managed-code tools no longer show the logic. Metadata may still help with names.

questions.prompt: A build ships a metadata file listing type and method names. How far should you trust those names?
options: It helps, but names can be stripped, so cross-check the build
Completely, since a metadata file matches every build of the game
Not at all, since metadata names are random labels
For types only, since method names are never included in it
questions.explanation: Metadata can reveal useful names and relationships, but stripping and packaging change what remains. Check it against the exact build in front of you.

questions.prompt: Unity's collector is non-compacting. Why is a pointer chain still not a permanent identity?
options: The game can destroy and recreate it, reuse its storage, or change layout in a new build
The collector shuffles survivors at random each frame when the scene is under load
The pointer chain is invalidated whenever the executable's PE checksum is read
Unity re-encrypts each object address whenever the player pauses the game
questions.explanation: Not moving removes one reason an address might change. It does not stop destruction, storage reuse, or a layout change in a new build.

questions.prompt: In a runtime with a compacting garbage collector, an object was at address 0x5000 and later sits at 0x5A00. What does that show?
options: A raw address is valid only until a collection moves the object
The object was copied, so two live copies now exist at once
The object was corrupted, so its old data is now lost
The first address was wrong, and the second one is permanent
questions.explanation: A compacting collector relocates live objects, so a raw address is not a durable identity. Use a runtime reference, a validated handle, or a fresh lookup.

questions.prompt: A game is written in Java. What should you conclude about whether its objects move?
options: Nothing yet; many JVM collectors, G1 included, move objects, so check them
They stay put, because Java guarantees one fixed address for each object
They stay fixed on 64-bit Windows, because that platform pins JVM heaps
They move when a `.jar` file is replaced, and not during a normal match
questions.explanation: The word 'Java' alone does not give a permanent address. The collector and its configuration decide, and G1 is an example of a collector that moves survivors.

questions.prompt: A native game engine registers its classes and properties in a reflection system. What does that give an analyst?
options: Class and property names, though some fields may be unlisted
A complete, verified map of every value in every object
Permission to modify any object safely at run time
Nothing, since reflection data does not survive compilation
questions.explanation: Reflection data is a useful directory of types and properties, but it is not a guarantee that every value is described.

questions.prompt: A tool reads a value at 'object base plus a fixed offset' to find a stat. Which three assumptions does that make?
options: The right object type, the same layout, and an object still alive
The right operating system, graphics driver, and a 64-bit processor
That the stat is stored as text, the object is cached, and ASLR is off
That the offset is the same in every game, version and object
questions.explanation: An offset means something only for the right object, in the right build, while that object exists. That is why the runtime question comes first.

questions.prompt: A studio switches a Unity project from Mono to IL2CPP between early access and release. What should you do?
options: Re-read the folder and loaded modules for the new build, not reuse the old class
Keep the old classification, because the scripting backend cannot change after launch
Reuse the old offsets, because both backends share one object layout
Check the executable's file name, since it records the backend
questions.explanation: A runtime classification is true for the exact build inspected, just like an offset. A new build means checking again.

questions.prompt: In a game whose C# was compiled ahead of time to native code, a pointer found today identified an object. Could it identify the same object after a scene reload?
options: Not necessarily; objects can be recreated, so verify identity again
Yes, since native code never moves or recreates its own objects
Yes, since metadata names keep identity stable across all reloads
No, since pointers cannot be read at all in native code
questions.explanation: A pointer found today may point at freed or reused storage after a reload. Names may be stripped too, so check the identity again.

questions.prompt: A game switches to a runtime whose collector compacts memory. What earlier assumption should you revisit before reusing a raw object address?
options: That objects stay at one address, since compaction can relocate them
That addresses can be read at all, since compaction blocks reads
That object sizes stay fixed, since compaction shrinks every object
That module names stay the same, since compaction renames modules
questions.explanation: Runtime, build and object lifetime must each be checked. A move from a non-compacting to a compacting collector breaks the stable-address assumption.

questions.prompt: In every branch of the runtime flowchart, what does an offset actually describe?
options: A layout in one particular build; it does not keep the object alive
A permanent identity that survives collection, scene reloads, and later builds
The distance from the executable's start to the object, fixed by the runtime
A reference the collector tracks, which blocks the object from being freed
questions.explanation: The branches differ in what evidence is available and whether an object can move. An offset still only says where a field sits, in that build, if the object exists.

questions.prompt: Some designs store a slot number plus a generation counter in a handle. What problem does that solve?
options: A slot reused for a different object, which the generation reveals
Objects moving to new addresses after a compacting collection
Objects being too large to fit inside a single storage slot
Two threads reading the same slot at exactly the same moment
questions.explanation: If the slot's generation no longer matches the handle's, the handle is stale. It is an identity problem much like a moving collector, solved without raw addresses.

questions.prompt: Two installs of a game carry the same version label. Why is that not enough to reuse an address offset between them?
options: Their bytes can differ after a rebuild, a mod or one patched file
Version labels are random numbers assigned when each install is made
Offsets depend on the install folder's path, not on the files in it
Version labels are encrypted, so they cannot be compared
questions.explanation: An offset belongs to one module layout, so it needs the exact bytes rather than a claimed release name.

questions.prompt: What does a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 produce for a file?
options: A fixed-size fingerprint of all its bytes that changes sharply if one byte does
A copy of the file compressed to 256 bytes that can be unpacked to restore it
A list of the function names inside the file, sorted by their RVAs
A signature naming the author, which Windows checks before it runs the file
questions.explanation: The digest is a fingerprint, not a compressed copy or an author record. That is why changing even one byte of a game file shows up as a different digest.

questions.prompt: Today's digest equals a trusted earlier digest. What have you learned?
options: The file's bytes match that earlier file, but not who made it or whether it was safe
The file is safe to run, because matching digests prove the original was clean
The file was signed by its publisher, because the digest embeds the signer's name
The live process mapped this file, because the digest records the module path
questions.explanation: A hash compares bytes with a baseline. It says nothing about the baseline's origin or safety, and it cannot say which copy a running process mapped.

questions.prompt: Why does the word 'trusted' matter in 'compare with a trusted manifest'?
options: If both the file and manifest can be replaced, a match shows the replacements agree
A manifest that is not trusted refuses to open, so the verifier would stop at line one
An untrusted manifest uses a weaker hash than SHA-256, so digests cannot be compared
Trusted manifests are signed by Windows, which then checks the file's bytes for you
questions.explanation: The baseline must be kept somewhere the experiment does not rewrite, such as a read-only lab snapshot or version control. Otherwise the comparison is circular.

questions.prompt: Which fact answers 'which file did this process map?', and what is its limit?
options: The live module path, which does not identify the file's bytes
The SHA-256 digest, which does not reveal the file's location on disk
The version label, which does not reveal the architecture of the module
The PE fields, which do not describe the module's section layout
questions.explanation: A path tells you where the file was, not what it contained. The digest tells you whether the bytes match, but only against a trusted record.

questions.prompt: The manifest line holds a digest, a byte count, and a path. What is the byte count for?
options: Extra context that makes a mismatch easier to explain; it does not replace the digest
A cheaper check that proves identity, so the digest is optional when sizes agree
A limit on how many bytes the hasher reads from each file during verification
A counter of how many times the manifest line has been verified successfully
questions.explanation: Two different files can have the same length, so size cannot establish identity. Together with the digest it helps a person see what changed.

questions.prompt: Why does the tool reject tabs and newlines inside file paths?
options: They would make the one-line, tab-separated manifest format ambiguous to parse
Windows forbids those characters in any file name, so the files could not exist
The hasher stops reading a file whenever its path contains a control character
Those characters change the digest of the file stored at that path
questions.explanation: The format uses tabs as separators and newlines as record ends. If a larger format is needed, the lesson suggests JSON, CBOR, or a signed catalog.

questions.prompt: Why do hashing tools read a file in fixed-size chunks instead of loading it all into memory first?
options: Memory use stays small and constant, and the digest is the same
A chunked digest is more secure than one from the whole file
Whole files cannot be hashed by a function such as SHA-256
Chunking changes the digest, so copies can be told apart
questions.explanation: Hashing can be done incrementally. The digest is identical to hashing the whole file, but a multi-gigabyte file needs only a small buffer.

questions.prompt: A read call fills a buffer and returns how many bytes it wrote. What does a return value of zero mean?
options: End of file: no bytes remain, and this is not an error
An error occurred, and the buffer contents are invalid
The buffer was too small, so the call should be repeated with a bigger one
The read is unfinished, so the call should be repeated immediately
questions.explanation: Zero bytes means the file has no more data. Real errors come back through a separate error path.

questions.prompt: A loop hashes a file in chunks using one reusable buffer. On the last, shorter chunk, why must it hash only the bytes the read filled?
options: The rest of the buffer holds stale data, which would give a wrong digest
Hashing a partly empty buffer is slower, but gives the same digest
The hash function refuses inputs that differ in length from the buffer
The rest of the buffer is zeros, so it has no effect on the digest
questions.explanation: After a short final read, the bytes past the count are left over from earlier chunks. Including them would make the digest disagree with the file.

questions.prompt: A tool writes a baseline file of trusted checksums, opening it in a mode that fails if the file already exists. What is the purpose?
options: To keep a trusted baseline from being silently replaced later
To make writing faster by skipping a check for existing files
To keep a second copy of the baseline file for redundancy
To make sure the new file is created as read-only
questions.explanation: Updating a baseline should be a deliberate, reviewed step. A verifier should never overwrite its own reference after noticing a change.

questions.prompt: Why does the verifier return a non-zero exit status when a file changed?
