options: A colored message is for a person; the exit status is how another program or script learns of failure
Windows requires a non-zero status whenever a program has printed text to the console
The status is the number of bytes that differ, so scripts can compute the size of the change
A non-zero status makes Windows restore the changed file from the manifest
questions.explanation: The verifier prints OK or CHANGED for humans and exits with status 1 if anything changed. Scripts can then block a patch run automatically.

questions.prompt: A supported mod deliberately changes some game files. How should checksum manifests be handled?
options: Keep the clean one and add a reviewed one for the modded state
Update the clean one so the changed files verify as clean again
Delete the manifest, since checks would now report failures
Hash only the files that the mod did not change at all
questions.explanation: Each known state gets its own list of digests. Overwriting the clean baseline until everything looks clean erases the evidence.

questions.prompt: A tool keeps a backup of an original file before changing it. What should that backup's checksum equal?
options: The checksum recorded for the original before the tool ran
The checksum of the modified file, since the two are linked
A fresh value that differs, since copying updates a checksum
Nothing in particular, since backups are not verified
questions.explanation: A backup is meant to be the untouched original, so it should match the clean state. The changed file has a new digest of its own.

questions.prompt: A verifier confirms a file's digest, and then another tool opens the file a moment later. What is the risk?
options: The file could change between check and use, so the used file is not the checked one
The verifier's digest becomes invalid after a minute and has to be recomputed
The second tool would double the file's size by hashing it a second time
Opening a verified file removes its manifest line, so later checks would fail
questions.explanation: This is a time-of-check/time-of-use race. For the lab, closing the game and mod tools while verifying is enough; a launcher needs a stronger design.

questions.prompt: Why should a live patcher still check the original bytes at the final address after the on-disk hash matches?
options: The disk hash cannot show which copy was mapped or if memory changed after loading
The disk hash expires when the game starts, so the process must be hashed again
The disk hash covers the PE header, leaving the code sections unchecked
The original-byte check replaces the digest, so keeping both is redundant
questions.explanation: Each check covers a gap the others leave. The patch proceeds only when the module name and range, architecture, RVA or pattern, and original bytes all pass.

questions.prompt: Why should save files, logs, and configuration files not be added to the baseline manifest?
options: They change every run, so verification would report CHANGED without tampering
Their digests are too long to store in a manifest line with the path and size
Hashing them would modify their contents, so the game could not load them again
Windows refuses to open files that the game itself wrote during a match
questions.explanation: A manifest is for files expected to stay identical, such as the exact executable and important DLLs. A baseline full of volatile files produces noise that hides real changes.

questions.prompt: Analysis notes say 'offset 0x58 is mana'. What is missing for that to be a complete, correct statement?
options: Which exact build, which kind of object, and how many bytes are read
Which compiler vendor, linker version and debug symbols were used
Which monitor resolution, graphics API and player level applied
Which Windows user account, folder and file name were involved
questions.explanation: An offset is true for one exact build, one kind of object and one access width. Without that scope it is only a number.

questions.prompt: Why can an old offset point at the wrong field after a game update?
options: The class may be recompiled with fields added, removed, or reordered, so it lands elsewhere
Windows renumbers every byte of heap memory when the game's version label changes
ASLR rewrites the offsets inside objects each time the executable file is replaced
The old offset is cleared by the loader whenever a new section is added to the PE file
questions.explanation: That is why an offset must be re-verified after every update. Memory at the old offset is still mapped, which is what makes a stale layout look plausible.

questions.prompt: The target invariant for using a layout has four demands. Which list is right?
options: Right build, confirmed object, bounded read, and a sensible returned value
Right build, fast scan, writable page, and a value that changes each frame
Right object, big buffer, repeated read, and a value that matches the old layout
Right engine, same offset, signed manifest, and a value that is nonzero
questions.explanation: A four-byte read that succeeds is not the same as a read that returned health. Each demand guards against a different failure.

questions.prompt: Why can one memory scan not settle an object's structure?
options: A four-byte 100 at some offset fits health, ammunition, or a coincidence equally well
A scan reads two-byte values, so a four-byte field is invisible to it
A scan returns every offset in the object, which is too many to compare
A scan changes the object's layout while it runs, so the result is out of date
questions.explanation: Static access patterns, runtime value changes, identity, and field relationships each rule out different wrong answers. Agreement among them is what accepts a layout.

questions.prompt: Code makes an indirect call through a pointer loaded from the start of an object, and that pointer leads to read-only data whose entries are code addresses. What is that pointer most likely?
options: A pointer to a table of virtual functions
A pointer to the object's name string
A pointer to the object's position vector
A pointer to the next object in a list
questions.explanation: An indirect call through a table of code addresses is the signature of a vtable. A vtable pointer is also the first piece of an identity check for the object.

questions.prompt: A 12-byte field is read by three adjacent 4-byte floating-point loads, and its contents change as an entity moves. Why does it look like a position vector?
options: Three 4-byte floats fill 12 bytes, like x, y, z, and track movement
Any field that changes while an entity moves must be a position
Floating-point values are used for coordinates and nothing else
Three loads in a row always indicate a vector of coordinates
questions.explanation: Size and type fit three coordinates, and the runtime observation agrees with that static reading. Both kinds of evidence together are what make it convincing.

questions.prompt: Code stores a value into a field after clamping it to no more than a bound read from the next field. Why does that strengthen the guesses 'current health' and 'maximum health'?
options: One piece of logic ties them together, so each guess supports the other
The two fields are adjacent, and nearby fields are always related
Clamping appears only in code that handles health values
The two values happen to have the same size in memory
questions.explanation: A relationship such as 0 <= value <= max is much stronger evidence than two numbers that merely look reasonable. Closeness alone proves nothing about roles.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a shape check and an identity check?
options: Shape: bytes resemble a player. Identity: it is the player reached by the expected path
Shape says the object is alive; identity says the object has the right number of fields
Shape compares file hashes; identity compares addresses with the module base
Shape is done once per build; identity is done once per game launch
questions.explanation: Two objects can have similar bytes but different roles. Identity needs signals such as entity ID, generation, and the ownership path.

questions.prompt: An analysis tool stores a table of offsets, one per field, for one specific build. What does that table represent?
options: Analysis notes about candidate locations, not data from the game
A copy of the game's object stored in the tool's own memory
A guarantee that every offset works in all builds of the game
The live values of each field at the moment of reading
questions.explanation: The numbers are offsets that locate fields, not the values stored in them. They are tied to one build.

questions.prompt: Why record a confidence level next to each discovered offset?
options: A candidate should not be trusted just because its name sounds right
Confidence levels make offset values faster to look up later
The compiler requires a confidence before a constant can be used
Higher confidence changes an offset into a more accurate value
questions.explanation: The level records which accesses and value changes earned it. That keeps uncertainty visible when the build changes again.

questions.prompt: When migrating to a new build, why collect member accesses again instead of adding a constant to each offset?
options: A field inserted in the middle shifts what follows it and nothing before it
Every field moves by the same constant, but the constant is hard to measure
Windows relocates the whole object, so each offset changes by the new base address
The compiler re-sorts the fields alphabetically, so offsets are unpredictable
questions.explanation: Layouts do not move uniformly. Fields before an insertion stay put, and alignment can absorb part of the shift.

questions.prompt: In an old build a field sits at offset 0x90. A new build inserts an 8-byte field at offset 0x40. Where is the field in the new build?
questions.explanation: The field lies after the insertion, so it shifts by 8: 0x90 + 8 = 0x98. Fields before the insertion do not move.

questions.prompt: A tool assumes every field moved by +8 in a new build and adds 8 to every old offset. What happens to a field located before the point where space was inserted?
options: It reads 8 bytes too far, possibly returning plausible but wrong data
It still works, since all offsets shift together
It fails safely with an error, since the address is invalid
It reads the correct field, because the shift cancels itself out
questions.explanation: A field before the insertion did not move, so a blanket shift reads the wrong bytes. They can still look like reasonable values, which makes the mistake hard to notice.

questions.prompt: The tool meets a build it has no layout record for. What should a reader do?
options: Reject it as unsupported, not fall back to the nearest known layout
Use the nearest known build's layout and hope the object is similar
Subtract the version numbers and shift each offset by that difference
Retry the read with a larger size until the values look sensible
questions.explanation: A wrong layout produces believable but false data. Failing closed is safer than guessing.

questions.prompt: One candidate has a matched controlled health transition (+4), a damage function storing there (+3), and a holding range relation (+2). Another merely holds a plausible number (+1). What are the totals?
options: 9 for the first candidate and 1 for the second
7 for the first candidate and 1 for the second
9 for the first candidate and 3 for the second
10 for the first candidate and 1 for the second
questions.explanation: 4 + 3 + 2 = 9 against 1. The lesson stores the score with the list of checks that produced it, so a high score can be audited.

questions.prompt: A new build no longer contains an old byte pattern for a field access. What follows?
options: Nothing certain; optimization can inline or reorder accesses, so the concept may remain
The field was deleted from the game, so the feature it supported can no longer exist
The binary was tampered with, so the build fingerprint should be set aside
The field moved to offset zero, so the reader should try that offset next time
questions.explanation: A missing old pattern does not prove the underlying concept disappeared. Find the behavior again through call relationships and controlled tests.

questions.prompt: What status does an old offset have on a new build?
options: A hypothesis to test, not a migrated layout
A verified layout that needs its confidence label updated
A fingerprint of the new build once the hash matches
A value that Windows keeps valid until the process exits
questions.explanation: The new fields must be recovered from access patterns and relationships, with their shape and identity checked and the evidence stored beside each confidence score.

questions.prompt: You have found a running game's PID. What does that give you?
options: A way to name the process in `OpenProcess`, but no access to its memory
A handle with read rights, because the PID proves the process is visible to you
Permission to read memory, until the process's integrity level changes
A copy of the process's access token that you can reuse for later calls
questions.explanation: The PID is like a catalogue number, and the handle is the claim ticket. Finding and opening are separate steps with different permissions.

questions.prompt: What is a process handle, conceptually?
options: A system-managed reference to a process plus granted permissions
The memory address of the process, which any code can then use
A copy of the process's memory and threads, made on demand
A password that any code can present to take over the process
questions.explanation: The handle is not the process itself. APIs compare the rights they need with the rights recorded on the handle.

questions.prompt: When opening a handle to another process, a tool declines handle inheritance. What does that mean?
options: Child processes it launches do not get the handle automatically
The handle is destroyed as soon as the first call returns
The handle cannot be used from more than one thread at once
The target process loses its own access to itself
questions.explanation: Inheritance would pass the handle and its rights to a child process. Declining keeps the capability inside the tool meant to hold it.

questions.prompt: The same PID is opened twice with different access masks. What follows?
options: Two handles with different capabilities; closing one does not close the other
One handle that merges both masks and stays valid until both calls end
Windows rejects the second call because the PID is already open
Both handles carry the larger mask, so the smaller request is ignored
questions.explanation: Rights belong to the handle, not permanently to the PID. That lets a tool keep a read-only handle and create a separate write-capable one deliberately.

questions.prompt: What does a process's access token describe?
options: Its security context: identity, privileges, restrictions, integrity level
Its loaded modules, command line, and heap layout, kept inside the PEB
Its handle table, listed by object type and granted access mask
Its thread priorities and base scheduling state shown in ToolHelp
questions.explanation: When you sign in, Windows creates security information for your account and groups. A process receives a token representing that context.

questions.prompt: What is an integrity level used for?
options: Limiting which processes can influence others; it is one input to access checks
Scoring whether software is good or bad, so safe programs get more access
Counting how many handles a process may open before Windows refuses more
Naming which user account created the process for the Task Manager list
questions.explanation: A normal desktop program commonly runs at medium integrity, and an approved administrator program at high. The level is a boundary, not a rating of trustworthiness.

questions.prompt: What does the target's DACL describe?
options: Which trustees may receive which rights to the process object
Which DLLs the process is allowed to load from its folder
Which memory pages the process marked as guarded or executable
Which handles the process has already granted to other programs
questions.explanation: A process object has a security descriptor, and its Discretionary Access Control List is part of it. `OpenProcess` checks the requested rights against that.

questions.prompt: A beginner says: 'I found the PID, so why did reading memory fail?' What is the best answer?
options: Finding a process and getting a read handle are separate steps with different permissions
PIDs refer to the parent process, so the tool needed the child's PID instead
Memory reads fail until the game is paused, because it holds a lock on its pages
The PID changed when the game window lost focus, so it no longer names the process
questions.explanation: The handle needs `PROCESS_VM_READ`, and Windows decides whether to issue it based on the token and DACL.

questions.prompt: Why can requesting a broad set of access rights when opening a process cause the open to fail, even though a narrower request would work?
options: The system checks the requested rights against what is permitted
Broad requests exceed the number of handles allowed per program
Windows refuses any request that asks for more than one right
Broad requests take longer, so they time out before finishing
questions.explanation: The check happens when the handle is created. A narrower request for only what you need might have been allowed.

questions.prompt: A process handle was opened with only a right to query basic information. Can it be used to read that process's memory?
options: No; reading memory needs a handle that carries the read-memory right
Yes, since any handle to a process can read its memory
Yes, but only the first page of the process's memory
No, since Windows never allows reading another process's memory
questions.explanation: Rights are recorded on the handle. A query-limited handle can report things like the image path but cannot copy bytes out of the target.

questions.prompt: Why is requesting every possible right a poor habit when a tool only needs a few?
options: It requests many unrelated powers and hides what the tool needs
It makes the handle slower on every call made afterward
It is rejected for all programs, even those run by administrators
It causes the target process to restart itself afterward
questions.explanation: A broad request could quietly obtain write, thread-creation or termination rights. A narrow request documents what the tool actually does.

questions.prompt: A tool replaces a request for all rights with a narrow query-only right to read a process's image path. What does a successful open now tell you?
options: That the tool did not quietly gain extra powers like writing memory
That the target process is trustworthy and safe to inspect fully
That the tool can now read the memory of the target process
That the target runs at the same integrity level as the tool
questions.explanation: The small request documents the tool's purpose. If Windows grants it, no extra authority came along with it.

questions.prompt: A Windows call fills a large buffer with characters and reports how many it wrote. Why should code use that count when building a string from the buffer?
options: The rest of the buffer is unused and would add junk or zero characters
The count is the only part of the buffer that Windows lets you read
The buffer is always exactly the same size as the characters written
The count says how many more calls are needed to finish the job
questions.explanation: Output buffers are usually bigger than needed. Only the reported number of units is meaningful.

questions.prompt: A call to open another process fails. What is a good first troubleshooting step?
options: Record the exact error code and the rights that were requested
Request every possible right to see whether that makes it work
Restart the computer to clear the handle table completely
Run the tool again repeatedly until the error goes away
questions.explanation: Failures can come from another account, a higher integrity level, an access control list, or a reused ID. The error and the requested rights narrow it down.

questions.prompt: A tool lists processes, then tries to open one by its ID and fails. Which cause is about timing rather than permissions?
options: It exited after being listed, or its ID went to another process
The target runs at a higher integrity level than the tool does
The target's access control list denies the tool's account
The tool asked for rights that the target never grants to anyone
questions.explanation: A process list is a snapshot, so the target can vanish and its ID can later belong to a different process. Checking the image path helps catch that.

questions.prompt: A library that opens processes defaults to read-only access, with write rights behind an explicit flag. What does this achieve?
options: Asking for write power becomes a visible, deliberate decision
Write operations become faster than when they are always requested
Read operations are blocked until the write flag has been set
The target process is told that it is being written to
questions.explanation: A scanner can open read-only, while a patcher has to opt in on purpose. The default stays minimal.

questions.prompt: Permission bits are: view 0x0040, edit 0x0004, share 0x0200. A mask that grants view and share is built with a bitwise OR. What is the result?
questions.explanation: 0x0040 | 0x0200 = 0x0240. Adding the edit bit as well would give 0x0244.

questions.prompt: A base mask of 0x0240 gains an 'edit' bit, 0x0004, and a 'delete' bit, 0x0001, both joined with OR. What is the final mask?
questions.explanation: 0x0240 | 0x0004 | 0x0001 = 0x0245. Leaving out the delete bit gives 0x0244, and leaving out the edit bit gives 0x0241.

questions.prompt: In a design that separates observing a process from patching it, how can types help?
options: Give observers a read-only handle type and patchers a separate write-capable one
Use one handle type for both and note in comments which functions may write
Hide the handle in a global so only trusted functions can find it
Make every function check the player's name before it writes
questions.explanation: Then observer functions cannot grow into writers without changing their inputs and call sites. That makes the architecture, not just manners, enforce the limit.

questions.prompt: A file handle was opened for reading only. Code that knows the file's path tries to write through that handle. What happens?
options: The write is refused, since the handle has only its original rights
It succeeds, since the code knows the path of the file
It succeeds once, and then the handle is closed automatically
It silently turns the handle into a read-write handle
questions.explanation: Knowing a name does not add rights to a handle that already exists. The same logic explains why a query-only process handle cannot read memory.

questions.prompt: What is the numeric value of a handle that a program holds?
options: An index-like token the system looks up in a per-process table
The memory address of the kernel object that it refers to
A global ID that means the same thing in every process
A pointer to a structure that the process may read directly
questions.explanation: Reading memory at the handle's number reveals nothing. The value works only through the handle table of the process that holds it.

questions.prompt: Between a handle value and the kernel object it refers to, what does the operating system consult?
options: The process's own handle table, which records granted access
A system-wide list of every name that any process has used
The target process's page tables and its full memory map
The file system, where each handle has its own file entry
questions.explanation: A handle value is only an entry key. The handle table maps it to a kernel object and the access rights that were granted.

questions.prompt: What is a handle leak, and why does it matter?
options: Forgetting `CloseHandle`; repeats can exhaust resources or keep objects alive
Closing a handle twice; repeated closes corrupt the page table of the process
Passing a handle to another thread; repeated passes slow the scheduler's queue
Reading memory at a handle's number; repeated reads corrupt the object
questions.explanation: The owner must call `CloseHandle` once it is done. A leak keeps files and processes alive longer than expected.

questions.prompt: Code closes a handle, the system later reuses that number for a different object, and then the code closes the old number again. What happens?
options: It closes the new, unrelated object, and nothing reports an error
It fails harmlessly with an invalid-handle error
It closes the original object a second time, which is ignored
It crashes immediately, so the mistake is easy to find
questions.explanation: The second close lands on a perfectly real object, just not the intended one. That is why double-close bugs are so hard to trace.

questions.prompt: Why do double-close bugs show up far from their cause?
options: It depends on handle allocation order, so it appears later in unrelated code
Windows delays every close request until the next frame, so errors arrive late
The second close succeeds, but the log of the failure is written when the game exits
The handle value changes at each call, so the debugger cannot match the two closes
questions.explanation: Step 4 reports no error and the damage happens at a moment that depends on allocation order. That timing dependence makes them easy to blame on the wrong component.

questions.prompt: What may a borrower of a handle do?
options: Use it temporarily but never close it
Close it if the owner is slow, because someone must
Duplicate it and then close the original
Close it when the borrower's function returns
questions.explanation: Only the single owner reaches the cleanup path. Borrowing allows an API call without taking responsibility for cleanup.

questions.prompt: What does RAII mean in languages like Rust and C++?
options: A value owns a resource and frees it automatically at end of scope
A background thread releases resources on a timer instead
Every resource must be released by hand when the process exits
A resource may be released once, by the first function that finds it
questions.explanation: Cleanup is tied to scope, including early returns and error exits, so it cannot be skipped by accident the way a manual close at the end of a function can.

questions.prompt: Why would a wrapper that owns a resource deliberately not allow itself to be copied or cloned?
options: Two owners would both release it, freeing the same resource twice
Copies would use too much memory to be practical in most cases
The compiler cannot copy values that hold plain numbers inside
Clones would keep the resource alive forever after the process ends
questions.explanation: Moving transfers ownership, so only one owner remains. Copies would each run cleanup on the same number.

questions.prompt: In Rust, how can a function use an owned resource temporarily without taking over its cleanup?
options: It borrows a reference to the owner and leaves cleanup to the owner
It takes the owner by value and gives it back when it is done
It copies the raw value and releases that copy afterward
It stores the owner in a global so any function can free it
questions.explanation: Borrowing allows temporary use, while only the owner runs the cleanup. Taking the value by move would take ownership away from the caller.

questions.prompt: What does RAII not guarantee?
options: That the contract is right; a borrowed handle wrapped as owned still double-closes
That cleanup runs when an early return or a `?` error leaves the current function
That the handle is closed at the moment its owning value leaves its scope
That a handle cannot be used by the old variable after it moved to another owner
questions.explanation: RAII connects lifetime to scope but does not decide whether the value should be owned in the first place. A wrong wrapper only automates the bug.

questions.prompt: A cleanup routine that runs automatically when a value is dropped cannot return an error to a caller. If closing a resource fails there, why is the failure usually ignored?
options: It means ownership was already wrong, so the fix is design, not retry
Close failures are harmless and do not point to any real bug
The operating system retries the close on its own at a later time
Ignoring the error causes the resource to be released twice
questions.explanation: Cleanup often runs while another error is unwinding. A failing close usually points to a design mistake, and retrying it on an unknown number would only add risk.

questions.prompt: A test counts open handles before (25), creates 64 new ones, and requires the count while they are owned to be at least before + 64. What is the smallest passing count?
questions.explanation: The count must grow by at least 64 from 25, so 89 is the smallest passing value. A test checks direction, not exact equality, since background handles can appear.

questions.prompt: Code creates 100 owned resources in a loop and collects them into a result, and creation fails on the 40th. What happens to the 39 already made?
options: They are dropped and released as the error returns, so nothing leaks
They leak, since the error stops the cleanup code from running
They stay alive until the process exits, then are released
They are handed to the caller along with the error value
questions.explanation: Every earlier owner is dropped when a later creation fails, so adding an early-return error path does not create a leak.

questions.prompt: Some APIs return a special constant that stands for 'the current process' rather than a real new handle. How should a program treat it?
options: As a constant to use directly, never wrapped as owned or closed
As a normal owned handle that must be closed after each use
As a handle to duplicate before the original is closed
As an error value meaning that the call failed
questions.explanation: A pseudo-handle does not refer to a new handle you own, so closing it would be wrong.

questions.prompt: How do you decide whether a returned handle is yours to close?
options: Read the API's documented contract; holding the number is not ownership
Any nonzero handle value is yours to close, whatever the API says
Handles returned by system calls belong to the system, not to you
If the handle works when you use it, then you own it
questions.explanation: Some APIs hand you a new handle to wrap, while pseudo-handles and borrowed ones must never reach the close call. Only the contract tells you which.

questions.prompt: Before wrapping a returned handle in an owning type, which question matters most?
options: Does success give me a new owned handle, and what frees it?
Does the handle's value look like a pointer into memory?
Can the handle's value be turned into a number for logging?
Is this the first handle that was created by the process?
questions.explanation: The checklist also asks which values mean failure, whether the handle can be shared across threads, and whether a callback transfers ownership.

questions.prompt: Why model owned and borrowed handles with different types?
options: A type that always closes fits where the contract says the caller owns the handle
Different types make Windows store the two kinds of handle in separate tables
A borrowed type makes `CloseHandle` run faster because it skips the access check
Different types let the compiler choose which of the two values is the real handle
questions.explanation: One universal wrapper cannot express the difference between handles you own and those you only use. The type documents the cleanup rule.

questions.prompt: Which split of responsibilities between a process and its threads is right?
options: The process supplies address space, handles, and modules; a thread is a path of execution
The process is a path of execution; each thread supplies its own address space and handles
The process holds registers and a stack; each thread supplies the loaded modules
The process schedules itself on a core; its threads store its security token
questions.explanation: Every process begins with at least one thread, and games commonly add more for rendering, audio, networking, and loading.

questions.prompt: Which list contains only things each thread has its own copy of?
options: Thread ID, registers, stack, thread-local storage, and TEB
Thread ID, handle table, loaded modules, stack, and heap blocks
Instruction pointer, access token, address space, stack, and TEB records
Registers, handle table, thread-local storage, PEB, and loaded modules list
questions.explanation: Threads share code and most data but need private execution state. Handles, modules, and the address space belong to the process.

questions.prompt: What must a correct program assume about how threads run?
options: It may interleave on one core or truly run in parallel on several, and must work in both
It runs in parallel on any machine, so interleaving problems cannot occur
It runs on one core at a time in a fixed order chosen when the thread was created
It gets exclusive control of the CPU until its thread voluntarily yields
questions.explanation: Windows schedules runnable threads onto cores. The scheduler may choose a different order on the next run.

questions.prompt: One thread updates a record's x and y fields while another thread reads both. If the reader runs between the two writes, what does it see?
options: New x with old y, a mixture that never existed as one state
The old x and y, since a read sees only the last complete state
A hardware error, since the processor detects the race
Nothing, since the reader waits until the writer finishes
questions.explanation: This is an interleaving problem. It can pass many test runs and still fail under a different scheduler order.

questions.prompt: A counter starts at 200. Thread A reads it, then thread B reads it. A writes back 200 + 50, and then B writes back 200 - 30 last. What is the final value, and what should it have been?
options: 170, though the correct result is 220
250, though the correct result is 220
220, which is also the correct result
230, though the correct result is 220
questions.explanation: Both changes should combine to 200 + 50 - 30 = 220. B's write came from the stale value 200, so it replaced A's update and left 170.

questions.prompt: Two threads each read the same starting value, compute a new value, and write it back. Which thread's change survives?
options: Only the change of whichever thread writes last
Both changes, since the hardware merges writes
Only the change of whichever thread read first
Neither change, since conflicting writes are discarded
questions.explanation: The last writer wins, with a value computed from the stale read. Either way, one of the two changes is lost.

questions.prompt: How does a mutex fix the gold race?
options: It makes read, add, and write one unit, so the purchase waits, reads 1,500, then writes 1,200
It runs the reward and the purchase on two cores at once so neither thread waits
It lets the purchase read first and skips the reward whenever the two threads overlap
It copies gold into each thread, then averages the two results at the end of the frame
questions.explanation: The mutex protects a group of operations as one critical section. For a single number, an atomic add does the same job more cheaply.

questions.prompt: What does an atomic read-modify-write instruction guarantee?
options: One small value is read, changed and written as a single step
Every field of the surrounding object is updated consistently
Other threads are paused until the instruction finishes
The update is saved to disk immediately afterward
questions.explanation: An atomic operation makes one small value indivisible. It does not make the larger object around that value consistent.

questions.prompt: Thread 1 locks player A then waits for B, while thread 2 locks B then waits for A. What is this, and how can it be prevented?
options: A deadlock; take locks in one agreed order, such as the lower player ID first
A starvation case; give thread 1 a higher priority than thread 2 to break it
A race condition; replace both locks with one atomic flag for the pair of players
A torn read; make each thread copy both players before it takes any lock
questions.explanation: Each holds what the other needs, so neither continues. A fixed lock order makes the cycle impossible.

questions.prompt: A tool checks that an enemy pointer is non-null, then reads health through it. What problem can occur?
options: An atomicity violation: the enemy can die and be freed between check and read
An order violation: the render worker reads a snapshot before it is built
A deadlock: the check and the read each wait on the other's lock to free
A starvation case: the check keeps losing to other threads' later reads
questions.explanation: A true check does not reserve the object for the next line. The read returns whatever occupies that memory now.

questions.prompt: A render worker reads a snapshot before initialization finishes. What kind of bug is that?
options: An order violation: one action assumes another already ran, with nothing enforcing it
An atomicity violation: two steps meant to be one were split by a second thread
A deadlock: the worker waits on a lock that the initializer still holds
A leak: the snapshot was not freed after the worker finished with it
questions.explanation: An event, condition variable, or channel can establish that initialization completed before consumption begins. Making the timing less likely is not a fix.

questions.prompt: Which statement about safety and progress is right?
options: A mutex may improve safety but deadlock, and a safe thread may be starved
A mutex guarantees both safety and progress, so no thread can starve
Progress is about torn states and safety is about threads waiting forever
A spin loop is a safe design, because it makes progress
questions.explanation: Safety asks whether something bad can happen. Progress asks whether intended work can eventually happen. A spin loop may pass a test and waste a whole core in the game.

questions.prompt: A network thread spends most of its time waiting. What should you conclude?
options: Nothing is broken; waiting means blocked until I/O, a timer, a lock, or an event
It is hung, because a healthy thread is either running or ready to run
It has been starved, because waiting threads get no turn on any CPU core
It has leaked its stack, because waiting means the stack is not reachable now
questions.explanation: A CPU profiler mainly samples running work, so wait analysis is the tool for why a thread is not running.

questions.prompt: Why is a thread's context meaningful only at a controlled instant?
options: Reading or writing registers of a running thread would race with the CPU
Registers are encrypted while a thread runs and decrypted at breakpoints
Windows keeps one context per process, so a running thread would overwrite it
The context exists for threads with a TEB that has a priority above normal
questions.explanation: A debugger gets an event while Windows has stopped the relevant threads. The course does not randomly freeze a game thread and hope cleanup succeeds.

questions.prompt: A stack trace lists function A at the top, then B, then C. Which statement is right?
options: A was called from B, and B from C; the newest frame is listed first
A called B, and B called C; the oldest frame is listed first
A, B and C were running in parallel on different threads
A is the last function that will run before the process exits
questions.explanation: A stack trace walks from the current frame toward older callers. Optimized code can inline or omit frames, so the neat picture is a guide.

questions.prompt: Why is a platform's stack-walking library better than a hand-written walker that follows saved frame pointers?
options: It uses unwind data and symbols, so inlining does not break it
Hand-written walkers cannot read memory belonging to another thread
Library walkers are faster because they skip some of the frames
Frame pointers are not saved by any compiler in any build
questions.explanation: A walker built from raw pointers breaks when the compiler omits frame pointers or reuses stack slots. Unwind data describes how each function really lays out its frame.

questions.prompt: 90 tasks of 5 ms each are run by 8 worker threads, each doing one task at a time. Assuming perfect parallelism and counting partial rounds as full ones, how long do the workers take?
options: 60 ms, from 12 rounds of 5 ms
56 ms, from 11.25 rounds of 5 ms
450 ms, from 90 rounds of 5 ms
5 ms, since all tasks run at once
questions.explanation: 90 divided by 8 is 11.25, which rounds up to 12 rounds, since a partial round still takes a full 5 ms. One thread alone would need 450 ms.

questions.prompt: Each thread reserves 1 MiB of address space by default. Why not start a thread per job with 1,000 jobs?
options: That reserves about 1,000 MiB, and the scheduler must juggle all the threads
That reserves 1 MiB in total, but the threads would all share one stack
Windows refuses any process with more than eight threads on an 8-core CPU
Each thread then needs its own PEB, which doubles the process's memory use
questions.explanation: A fixed thread pool, often one fewer than the cores, takes tasks from a queue instead.

questions.prompt: A path task finishes after entity 42 was despawned and its slot reused. How does the main thread avoid applying the result?
options: It compares its remembered generation with the slot's and drops a differing result
It checks that the worker thread's ID is still alive and applies the result if so
It locks the slot until the worker finishes, so the slot cannot be reused
It applies the result and relies on the next frame to correct the entity
questions.explanation: Workers send results through a channel, and the main thread picks them up at one known point. The generation check is the Lesson 3.6 idea reused.

questions.prompt: A thread-list snapshot call covers the whole system, whatever process ID is passed in. What must the caller do to see only one process's threads?
options: Filter the entries by each thread's owner process ID
Nothing, since the snapshot already holds only that process
Pass the process ID again in every thread entry
Suspend the process before the snapshot is taken
questions.explanation: The caller compares each entry's owner process ID with the target's and keeps only the matches.

questions.prompt: Why should a TID not be stored as a version-specific constant?
options: It is temporary and can eventually be reused, and thread counts change between runs
It changes with every game frame, so reads would fail after one tick
It is the same across games, so it carries no information about any one process
It is derived from the base priority, which Windows recomputes at each launch
questions.explanation: Games create and retire worker threads. Look for threads that appear and disappear before assigning any ID a permanent role.

questions.prompt: How can you work out a thread's role?
options: Combine start address, stacks sampled over time, CPU and wait activity, and a description
Read its base priority, since higher priorities mean rendering and lower ones mean audio
Take one paused stack and treat it as the thread's permanent job in the game
Use its TID, since TIDs are assigned in order of role at launch time
questions.explanation: One paused stack shows only what the thread was doing at that instant. A job-system worker can mix audio and decompress textures in consecutive samples.

questions.prompt: A debugger replaces an instruction's first byte with a one-byte breakpoint. After the breakpoint is hit, why does it move the instruction pointer back and single-step?
options: To run the original instruction, then re-arm the breakpoint
To skip the original instruction and carry on after it
To remove the breakpoint for good so the game runs normally
To reset the thread's stack pointer to its starting value
questions.explanation: The breakpoint byte overwrote part of the real instruction, so the pointer returns to it. A single step lets the original run, and then the breakpoint is re-armed.

questions.prompt: Which three ideas describe how a documented API call reaches the kernel?
options: A contract, a library path, and a privilege transition
A compiler, a linker, and a loader working in sequence
A cache, a request queue, and a thread scheduler
A handle, a thread, and a memory page for each call
questions.explanation: The API documents the contract, user-mode libraries implement or forward it, and a system-call instruction performs the transition for work that needs kernel privilege.

questions.prompt: Where does the operating system's user-mode library code run when an application calls it?
options: Inside the application's own process, mapped into its address space
In a separate service process that the application sends messages to
Inside the kernel, mapped into kernel memory
On a hardware coprocessor reserved for the system
questions.explanation: These libraries are software layers mapped into the same process as the caller. They are not separate processes.

questions.prompt: Why can a bug in user-mode code usually not overwrite the kernel or another process?
options: The CPU enforces user mode, so privileged work must go through a defined entry point
Windows scans every user-mode write and cancels any that lands near the kernel
User-mode code runs interpreted, so it cannot issue the writes that would do harm
Each process is sandboxed inside a virtual machine that blocks the kernel's pages
questions.explanation: Kernel mode manages page tables, devices, and scheduling, so a bug there can affect the whole computer. That is why the course avoids kernel-driver experiments.

questions.prompt: How does a system call differ from a normal function call?
options: It changes privilege through a defined entry point, not a call to a named function
It jumps to a function by name inside the kernel's module with no privilege change
It copies the caller's stack into kernel memory and runs it with user rights
It runs inside the same privilege level, with a different calling convention
questions.explanation: The CPU enforces the border, so the transition is controlled and validated rather than an ordinary jump.

questions.prompt: What does 'limited direct execution' mean for a running game?
options: Most instructions run natively in user mode, while timers and system calls give Windows control
Windows interprets each game instruction in software so it can check it first, then runs it
The game runs in kernel mode for speed, and Windows limits it with a lower thread priority
The game is paused after every function call so Windows can inspect its registers
questions.explanation: Most instructions execute natively. Hardware privilege, address translation, interrupts, and controlled entries provide the limits.

questions.prompt: A learner says 'Windows interprets every ordinary game instruction'. What is the correction?
options: Most instructions run directly on the CPU; Windows regains control through interrupts and system calls
Windows interprets the first thousand instructions after launch, then steps aside
Windows interprets instructions in kernel mode and runs user-mode ones natively on another core
Windows interprets all instructions, but its interpreter is built into the CPU
questions.explanation: Windows is not in the path of each instruction, but timers and interrupts let it schedule, and system calls give a validated entry path.

questions.prompt: A library lists an exported function that only forwards to another library's function. What is stored for that export?
options: A text name of the target, not a code address
A copy of the target function's machine code
A system-call number for the function
A null entry that callers must fill in themselves
questions.explanation: The entry holds a string, and the loader resolves it to a real address in the target library. Callers never notice the redirection.

questions.prompt: When a lookup routine is asked for the address of a forwarded export, what does it do?
options: Follows the forward and returns the real address there
Returns the address of the forwarder's text string
Fails, since forwarded exports have no usable address
Returns a stub that restarts the lookup each time
questions.explanation: Callers get a usable address in the target library. That is why an implementation can move between libraries without breaking imports.

questions.prompt: Why is calling low-level, undocumented system entry points usually worse for normal applications than calling the documented API?
options: They are undocumented and may change between operating-system builds
They are slower, since they skip optimizations in the documented path
They cannot be called from user-mode code at all
They are protected by passwords that applications lack
questions.explanation: The documented interface is the stable contract for applications. Closer to the kernel means closer to details that can change.

questions.prompt: Why is copying a system-call number from one Windows build into a tool a poor idea?
options: Numbers and structures can change, which makes the tool fragile on other builds
The CPU rejects numbers that were not issued by `ntdll.dll` at the same address
System-call numbers are random for each process, so a copy is meaningless
Windows checks the numbers against the PE checksum of the calling program
questions.explanation: The course does not call a native function or build a direct-syscall bypass. A documented Win32 contract is the stable route.

questions.prompt: A lookup routine returns the address of a library function. Where is that address meaningful?
options: Only in this process during this run
In every process on the machine
In every future run of the same process
On any machine that has the same library
questions.explanation: The returned address is process-local, and it can change on the next run.

questions.prompt: ASLR may map a DLL at a different base after a reboot. What should a tool store as stable identity?
options: The export name, or an RVA when that is the stable identity
The absolute address that `api_layers` printed in the earlier run
The module base address from the last time the DLL was loaded
The address of the first instruction found in the DLL's import table
questions.explanation: A displayed absolute address is not safe to paste into tomorrow's program. Names and RVAs survive relocation.

questions.prompt: A learning tool looks up a system function's address by name in a loaded library and prints it, without calling the function. What does the printed address show?
options: Where the function lives here; it was not called
That the function ran successfully once
That the function is safe for applications to call
The system-call number that the function will use
questions.explanation: Resolving a name only finds the address inside a library that is already loaded. No call is made and nothing is opened.

questions.prompt: When a library is already loaded in a process, why prefer asking for its existing handle over loading it again?
options: No new load happens, so there is no extra reference to release
Loading it again would replace the earlier copy with a new one
Existing handles run faster than newly loaded ones
Loading twice maps the library at two addresses permanently
questions.explanation: Borrowing the handle of an already-loaded module keeps cleanup simple, since nothing new was acquired.

questions.prompt: Why might an API take library file names as wide (UTF-16) strings but exported function names as plain byte strings?
options: File names use Windows wide strings, while export names are stored as ASCII bytes
Wide strings are for names over 255 characters, and bytes for shorter ones
Function names must be short, so bytes are enough for them
Both are wide strings, and one is just a different alias
questions.explanation: The two encodings really are different. Types that make the difference visible prevent silently mixing them.

questions.prompt: After a reboot, a library function is found at a different address. What does that mean?
options: Expected with ASLR; names and behavior stay stable
The library file was changed on disk between the two boots
The earlier lookup was wrong and the new one is correct
The system is under attack and the library was moved
questions.explanation: ASLR can map a library at a different base each boot, so addresses are not safe to treat as permanent identifiers.

questions.prompt: One tool lists the DLLs loaded in a process, and another looks up a function inside one loaded DLL. How are those jobs related?
options: One lists modules; the other looks up exports in a module
Both return the same data, but in different formats
The second loads DLLs that the first reports as missing
The first lists exports, and the second lists modules
questions.explanation: Both are views of the same loader idea. One names the modules, and the other asks a loaded module for one of its exports.

questions.prompt: A process reports that it loaded a library named `compress.dll`. Why is that name alone weak evidence about which code ran?
options: Many files share one name, so path, hash and signer say more
Windows randomizes library names each time a process starts
Names are shown only for libraries that failed to load properly
The loader renames each library to match its host process
questions.explanation: A name does not say which file supplied the bytes. Path, hash, signer, architecture and loaded range give stronger identity.

questions.prompt: A tool built for one version of a legitimate DLL is run against a different version. Which problem is most likely?
options: Missing exports, changed structure layouts, or code patterns that no longer match
The loader refuses every DLL whose version differs, so the game never starts
The tool runs but reports the old version number, with the same layouts as before
The game's PE import table is rewritten by the loader to point at the newer file
questions.explanation: Loading the wrong version of a legitimate DLL can cause missing exports, crashes, changed layouts, or patterns that stop matching. The loader does not reject versions by number alone.

questions.prompt: What does the loader do after it finds a DLL named in the game's import table?
options: Maps it, resolves its imports, and repeats the process for that DLL's own dependencies
Maps it and stops, since only the executable's direct imports are ever needed at run time
Copies it into the game's folder, so that later loads of the same name find it first
Marks it as trusted, so its own imports are skipped to keep the start-up quick and short
questions.explanation: The import table starts a dependency graph: locate, map, resolve imports, and repeat for dependencies. Final module lists can also include DLLs requested later with `LoadLibrary`.

questions.prompt: A tool lists the loaded modules of a process from a snapshot. What should it do with those entries?
options: Treat them as observations, not ownership of the mappings
Unload any entry that it considers unwanted or suspicious
Use each entry as proof that the module is still loaded now
Edit entries to change what the process will load next
questions.explanation: A snapshot observes the loader's published records. It does not own the mappings, and it never grants permission to unload them.

questions.prompt: What is an API set, in the DLL search rules?
options: A virtual DLL name that Windows redirects to whichever real DLL implements it on that build
A list of exports that every game must declare in its import table before it will run
A folder of system DLLs that the loader always searches before looking in the game's directory
A signed bundle of DLLs that Windows installs once and shares across all running games
questions.explanation: API sets are virtual names redirected to the real implementing DLL. They are one of the checks that happen before any folder is searched.

questions.prompt: Why can a planted file in the game's folder not stand in for a DLL listed in KnownDLLs?
options: KnownDLLs are checked before any folder search, and load from the trusted system copy
KnownDLLs files are marked read-only on disk, so no other file may share their names
The game's folder is searched last for KnownDLLs, after every system directory is tried
KnownDLLs are loaded at boot into every process, so no later load ever looks for them
questions.explanation: The KnownDLLs list is consulted before the numbered folder searches, so a core system DLL always comes from the trusted system directory.

questions.prompt: What does safe DLL search mode change?
options: It moves the current directory later in the order, so a file planted there is less likely to win
It checks every DLL's signature before the loader maps it, and refuses any unsigned file outright
It makes the application's directory the last place searched, behind the system directories
It limits each bare-name search to the system directory, so no other folder is read at all
questions.explanation: Safe mode (on by default) places the current directory after the system directories, at step five. With it off, the current directory moves to second place.

questions.prompt: A library is requested by bare name, and two folders on the search list both contain a file with that name. Which file supplies it?
options: The one in the folder searched first
The newer of the two files, judged by date
The larger of the two files, judged by size
Both files, merged into one module
questions.explanation: A search runs in order and stops at the first match. That is why the order, and what sits in each searched folder, matters.

questions.prompt: A process asks the loader for a library that is already loaded in it. What does the loader do?
options: Reuses the loaded module instead of searching folders again
Loads a second copy from the first folder it finds
Searches the folders and replaces the loaded copy if newer
Fails with an error, since duplicates are not allowed
questions.explanation: Before searching folders, the loader checks whether a module with that name is already loaded and reuses it.

questions.prompt: Which design choice makes an application's DLL loading safer?
options: Loading its own plug-ins by absolute path from an install directory with controlled permissions
Placing its plug-ins in the current working directory, which the loader always checks first
Passing bare names everywhere, so the loader can pick the newest matching file it finds first
Making the install folder writable by all users, so that updates can drop new files in easily
questions.explanation: Safer design uses controlled install directories, manifests, `LoadLibraryEx` flags, absolute paths, and no writable current directory in the dependency search.

questions.prompt: Why might a 64-bit inspector tool need an extra option to list the 32-bit modules of a 32-bit target?
options: By default it lists its own architecture, so 32-bit needs an option
32-bit modules are hidden from every tool for safety reasons
32-bit modules are stored inside a separate helper process
The target must be restarted as 64-bit before it can be listed
questions.explanation: Module lists default to the tool's native architecture. An extra flag adds the 32-bit modules for a 64-bit inspector.

questions.prompt: Why must a caller set a structure's size field before the first call that fills the structure in?
options: The API needs the caller's structure size, which varies by build
The size field is the first output value that the call returns
The call fails if the structure holds more than one field
The size tells the call how many items to list
questions.explanation: A structure has a fixed shape, but its size can vary by build, so the caller states which version it prepared before the API writes into it.

questions.prompt: A structure begins with six 4-byte fields, followed by a text field of 128 UTF-16 units (2 bytes each). At what offset does the next field start?
questions.explanation: The six fields take 24 = 0x18 bytes, and the text field takes 128 × 2 = 256 = 0x100 bytes, so the next field begins at 0x118. Forgetting the 2 bytes per unit gives 0x98.

questions.prompt: A structure has a text field starting at offset 0x118 that holds 130 UTF-16 units. What is the structure's total size if nothing follows the field?
questions.explanation: 130 units × 2 bytes = 260 = 0x104. Adding the start offset gives 0x118 + 0x104 = 0x21C, which is 540 bytes.

questions.prompt: The module list taken in the main menu is shorter than one taken during a match. What is the most likely reason?
options: Some games delay-load graphics, audio, or networking parts, so a later list may be longer
The first snapshot was corrupted, since a correct module list never changes during play at all
A cheat tool injected the extra modules, since normal games load every DLL on start-up
Windows lists modules only after the player has spent their first 60 seconds in a match
questions.explanation: Games often delay-load components. A longer list later is not automatically suspicious; compare against a baseline.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in an approved baseline entry for a non-system module?
options: The full path, SHA-256 hash, size and version, publisher, reason it loads, and game build
Only the short module name and the time of day that it was first loaded by the game process
The module's base address, which is the same on every run so it can identify the file
The name of the player who last ran the game, plus the module's short name and its size
questions.explanation: A baseline needs identity details that survive restarts: path, hash, version, source, reason, and build. A base address changes between runs.

questions.prompt: A new module appears in a game's list and is absent from the baseline. What is the right conclusion?
options: Not necessarily malicious: it may be a capture layer or an update, so investigate first
It is malicious, since any DLL missing from the baseline was added by a cheat program
It is a Windows system DLL, since only system DLLs ever load after the baseline is made
It is harmless, because baselines list only those DLLs that cannot be changed by anyone
questions.explanation: A different module may be a graphics capture layer, accessibility tool, language pack, supported mod, or updated dependency. Investigate before removing anything.

questions.prompt: A helper DLL loads and unloads between two ToolHelp snapshots. What do the snapshots show, and what source catches it?
options: Neither lists it; an ETW trace of image-load and unload events shows it came and went
Both list it, since ToolHelp keeps unloaded modules until the process exits
Only the second lists it, as an unloaded entry; ETW would miss it for the same reason
Neither lists it, and no other source can see it, since the module is gone
questions.explanation: A snapshot is a moment-in-time view of loader records. ETW image-load events cover mappings and unmappings over time.

questions.prompt: A module is mapped into the game without being registered with the loader. Why might the ToolHelp list miss it, and what source can still show it?
options: The list shows only registered modules; the memory map shows executable regions no module covers
The list shows every mapped image, so such a module cannot exist in a normal process
The list misses it only on 32-bit games; a 64-bit inspector always lists it correctly
The list misses it because it hides names under 8 letters, and a file hash would reveal it
questions.explanation: ToolHelp reports the loader's registered modules. The memory map lists every committed region, including executable memory with no listed module.

questions.prompt: Why does the course refuse to hide modules or unlink loader entries, even as an experiment?
options: Those actions corrupt loader records that this chapter's tools, debuggers, and crash reporters read
They are slow on the lab's 32-bit builds, which makes the experiments hard to repeat reliably
They would raise the process's integrity level, which the labs deliberately keep fixed at one value
They only work on 64-bit games, so the 32-bit lab games could not show the effect at all
questions.explanation: The course observes and baselines modules; it does not alter loader state, which other tools read too.

questions.prompt: Why does an operating system loader hold a process-wide lock while initializing a library, and where does the library's start-up callback run relative to that lock?
options: So no thread sees a half-built module; the callback runs while it is held
So two processes cannot load one library; the callback runs after release
So loading can be cached for speed; the callback runs on a new process
So file reads are blocked briefly; the callback runs before the lock
questions.explanation: The loader serializes important steps so that no thread observes a half-initialized module, and it calls the entry point while that lock is held.

questions.prompt: Which list best describes what the loader does while loading a DLL?
options: Maps sections, applies relocations, resolves imports, sets up TLS, updates bookkeeping, calls entry points
Copies the file into the game's folder, signs it, resolves imports, then asks the game to call its entry
Reads the export table, deletes the relocation data, hands the module to the kernel, and waits for a reply
Maps the first page only, resolves imports lazily at each call, and never runs an initialization entry point
questions.explanation: Loading is a coordinated operation, not a byte copy. Initialization entry points such as `DllMain` are part of it.

questions.prompt: A library's entry-point callback is told why it is being called. Which reason announces that a new thread has started in the process?
options: A thread-attach notification
A process-attach notification
A process-detach notification
A thread-detach notification
questions.explanation: Process attach is for the library joining the process, thread attach is for each new thread, and the two detach reasons are for a thread ending or the library unloading.

questions.prompt: When a library is loaded by one thread, on which thread does its start-up callback run?
options: On the thread that caused the load
On a new thread that the loader creates just for the callback
On the process's main thread, whichever thread asked
On a system thread that runs inside the kernel
questions.explanation: The callback runs in the context of whichever thread caused the load or unload. These are loader notifications, not ordinary application events.

questions.prompt: Thread A holds lock X and waits for lock Y, while thread B holds lock Y and waits for lock X. What happens?
options: Neither continues, since each waits on a lock the other holds
One of them times out, and the other one proceeds normally
They alternate, taking turns on both of the locks
The operating system breaks the tie by releasing one lock
questions.explanation: A deadlock needs a cycle of waits. Following one global lock order, or avoiding the wait, prevents it, while a timeout only hides it.

questions.prompt: Library start-up code starts a new thread and then waits for that thread to finish. Why can this hang forever?
options: The new thread needs the loader lock, which the waiter holds
Threads cannot be created while a library is still loading
A waiting thread cannot be woken by a newly created thread
The new thread finishes too quickly for the wait to notice
questions.explanation: The waiter holds the loader lock and waits for the thread, but the thread needs that same lock to run its start-up notification. The cycle is the hidden second lock.

questions.prompt: In that hang, thread creation reported success. Why does nothing look wrong at the creation call?
options: The thread exists, but it blocks before it reaches your own code
The creation call is skipped until the wait has finished
The new thread runs your code, but its output is lost
The creation call returns success before the thread is real
questions.explanation: The thread exists, but the loader makes it run attach notifications first, and those need the lock. Nothing fails at creation, so the wait never ends.

questions.prompt: Which kind of work is acceptable inside a library's start-up callback?
options: Tiny work that never waits, like turning off thread notices
Loading other libraries and initializing large subsystems
Waiting for worker threads to finish their own setup first
Scanning memory for patterns before the callback returns
questions.explanation: Keep the entry point tiny. Loading libraries, waiting on workers, scanning and installing changes all belong to later stages.

questions.prompt: What does a library do when it tells the system to stop sending it per-thread attach and detach notifications?
options: It opts out of thread notifications it does not use
It releases the loader lock early so other threads can proceed
It stops its own worker threads from running any further
It unloads the library from the process once start-up ends
questions.explanation: It is a documented optimization during process attach: no allocation, waiting or scanning. It does not release any lock.

questions.prompt: Why might a library do its real start-up in an exported function called after loading finishes, instead of in its load callback?
options: It runs after the load completes, so outside the loader lock
Exported functions run faster than load callbacks do
Load callbacks cannot call any exported function at all
The load callback is skipped when libraries load by name
questions.explanation: Once the load has returned, the loader lock is no longer held, so complex work can begin on an ordinary thread, with each stage's failure visible on its own.

questions.prompt: A start function might be called twice by mistake. What protects against starting two workers that race over the same state?
options: A once-only guard that returns early if already started
A longer timeout on the second call to the start function
A second lock that the new worker thread must acquire
Letting both workers run and merging their results later
questions.explanation: A once-only guard prevents duplicate start-up. A second worker would race over the same hooks and cleanup state.

questions.prompt: Why might a stop function only set a flag and return, rather than waiting for its worker to finish?
options: Waiting in a loader callback could cause a deadlock
Waiting would let the worker skip its own cleanup steps
A flag is faster, so the worker finishes sooner than before
The operating system forbids waiting on any thread at all
questions.explanation: A request-only stop keeps waits out of loader callbacks. The worker owns restoration and cleans up at its next checkpoint.

questions.prompt: Shutdown should reverse the order of ownership. Which order is sound?
options: Stop work, stop the worker, wait outside the lock, restore, release
Release resources, restore changes, then ask the worker to stop
Unload first, then ask the worker to stop and restore changes
Wait for the worker inside the loader lock, then restore changes
questions.explanation: Stop new work first, wait without the loader lock, restore changes before releasing resources, and only then allow unload.

questions.prompt: A tool with a lock-order bug passes ten test runs. What does that prove?
options: Very little, because deadlocks depend on timing and may need an unlucky ordering to appear
The lock order is correct, since ten clean runs on one machine rule out a cycle of waits
The bug is limited to 32-bit builds, since a 64-bit run would have shown it already
The loader lock is released early on that machine, so the bug cannot occur anywhere else
questions.explanation: “It worked on my machine” does not prove the ordering is safe. Write the lock edges down and check for cycles instead.

questions.prompt: A game hangs while loading the DLL. A teammate suggests adding a ten-second timeout to the wait. What is the better first step?
options: Inspect lock order and the work in entry points, since a timeout hides a deadlock instead of repairing it
Raise the timeout to a full minute, since the hang is just slow disk access and will end by itself
Retry the load in a loop until it works, since the deadlock depends on timing and may not recur
Move the wait into `DLL_THREAD_ATTACH`, which runs after the loader lock has already been released
questions.explanation: A timeout leaves the wait cycle in place. Remove the wait from the loader callback or establish one global lock order.

questions.prompt: Which step belongs in a lifecycle test for a library that starts a worker?
options: Start and stop it, then confirm changes were restored and freed
Start it and confirm that it runs, leaving stopping for later
Start it twice and confirm that both workers are running
Stop it while the game is paused and ignore any leftover state
questions.explanation: A good test runs the full cycle, checks restoration and release, and repeats it to catch assumptions that only hold on the first run.

questions.prompt: Verification of the target fails before any patch is installed, and the DLL starts cleanup. What should cleanup do?
options: Skip restoring the patch, since nothing was installed and the lifecycle makes that state visible
Restore the patch's original bytes anyway, to be safe, even though nothing was ever written there
Wait for the loader lock and then retry the verification, since the failure is probably just timing
Call `gha_start` again, so the lifecycle begins from the first step and every patch is rechecked
questions.explanation: An explicit lifecycle makes partially initialized states visible. Cleanup should not pretend a patch exists when it was never installed.

questions.prompt: In a sound start-up order for a library, what comes right after the library has been mapped?
options: Finish the loader's notifications, then call the explicit start
Install features immediately, before the load has completed
Verify the target and create all resources in the load callback
Call the explicit start from inside the load callback itself
questions.explanation: Each step may begin only after the one before it has completed: map, finish notifications, explicit start, verify the target, create resources, install features.

questions.prompt: What are sensible steps for resolving an optional operating-system function at run time?
options: Get the library, find the export, check it, then call or fall back
Scan memory for the function's bytes, patch it, and then call it
Call the address blindly and catch any crash that results from it
Copy the function's code into your own program and run it there
questions.explanation: Dynamic resolution turns an optional API into a checked capability, and nothing is patched or scanned for.

questions.prompt: Why should a tool not decide that an API exists just because the Windows version string is new enough?
options: Compatibility settings, servicing changes, and alternative implementations can make version checks lie
Version strings are stored in the PE header and are changed whenever a DLL is loaded dynamically at run time
Version strings only describe the 64-bit kernel, so a 32-bit tool cannot learn anything useful from them
Windows publishes the version string only after the export has been resolved, so it cannot guide the lookup
questions.explanation: Look up the documented export, validate the result, and take the fallback when it is absent.

questions.prompt: A function was successfully found by name at run time. Does that guarantee a later call to it will succeed?
options: No; handles, buffers and targets can still cause errors
Yes, since finding it proves that the call is valid
Yes, but only on the version of Windows that exports it
No, since found functions can be called only once each
questions.explanation: Feature detection chooses a code path, while normal error handling still applies inside that path.

questions.prompt: In the 32-bit stdcall convention, who removes the arguments from the stack after a call?
options: The called function, as it returns
The caller, right after the call returns
The operating system's scheduler
Nobody; they stay until the thread ends
questions.explanation: In stdcall the caller pushes the arguments, and the function removes them with a return instruction that also pops them.

questions.prompt: In 32-bit stdcall, on entry the stack pointer addresses the return address, and the arguments follow in 4-byte slots. At what offset from the stack pointer is the third argument?
options: `[esp+0x0C]`
questions.explanation: The return address is at +0, the first argument at +4, the second at +8, and the third at +0xC (12).

questions.prompt: On x86-64 Windows, the first four integer or pointer arguments are passed in registers. Which register holds the fourth, and where does the return value come back?
options: R9, with the result in RAX
R8, with the result in RAX
R9, with the result in RCX
RDX, with the result in RDX
questions.explanation: The first four arguments go in RCX, RDX, R8 and R9, and the result returns in RAX.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit caller declares a function pointer type with fewer parameters than the real function, which pops all its real arguments on return. What goes wrong?
options: The caller pushes fewer bytes than the function pops
The function reads garbage from a register, but the stack is fine
The call fails to link, since the two types differ
Nothing happens, since extra pops are quietly ignored
questions.explanation: A mismatch of bytes between what was pushed and what is popped moves the stack pointer away from where the caller expects it.

questions.prompt: On x86-64, the same under-declared signature is used: three parameters for a function that takes four. What goes wrong?
options: It still reads the fourth register, whatever it holds
Nothing, since the missing argument defaults to zero safely
The call fails to compile, so there is no real risk at all
The stack pointer is shifted, just as it is on 32-bit
questions.explanation: Registers are not cleared between calls, so the function acts on whatever the fourth register contained. A close-enough signature fails whatever the pointer size.

questions.prompt: A lookup by name finds no address for an optional function. How should a robust resolver report that?
options: As a normal 'not available' result, with a fallback
As address zero, which the caller then goes on to call
As a fatal error that ends the whole process at once
As a guess at a similar function that does exist
questions.explanation: An absent export is a supported state, not necessarily fatal. Returning an optional value makes the caller handle the missing case.

questions.prompt: A plug-in resolver caches a function pointer from a module that can later unload. What is the risk?
options: The address becomes invalid once the module unloads, so keep module ownership and pointer lifetime together
The pointer is valid only until the next `GetProcAddress` call, which overwrites the previously stored address
The cached pointer is read-only, so a later call from another thread will write through it and fault at once
The module's exports are renumbered at unload, so the pointer calls the wrong function when it loads again
questions.explanation: System modules used for the whole process lifetime are simpler. A module that can unload leaves the cached address dangling.
