questions.prompt: An API takes a buffer size going in and, on success, writes back the number of characters it wrote, not counting the terminator. A buffer of 4,096 is given and the result text is 20 characters. What is the size value afterward?
questions.explanation: Going in, the value is the buffer size; coming back it is the number of characters written without the terminator.

questions.prompt: A buffer of 16-bit units must hold the longest allowed path of 32,767 characters plus a terminator. How many units does it need, and how many bytes is that?
options: 32,768 units, which is 65,536 bytes
32,768 units, which is 32,768 bytes
32,767 units, which is 65,534 bytes
65,536 units, which is 131,072 bytes
questions.explanation: 32,767 + 1 = 32,768 = 2^15 units. Each unit is 2 bytes, so the buffer is 65,536 bytes.

questions.prompt: After an API reports how many units it wrote into a buffer, why check that the number fits the buffer before slicing it?
options: The length is untrusted, and slicing past the end panics
Slices must have the same size as the whole buffer
The check makes the API write faster the next time
Buffers shrink automatically after each call returns
questions.explanation: A returned length is data that must be checked. An invalid length is an error, not a slice.

questions.prompt: The export is present but the call fails because the handle lacks rights. What should the code do?
options: Handle the call error, because a failed call does not automatically choose the fallback
Take the fallback anyway, since a failed call proves the API is not really available
Resolve the export again under another name, since the first lookup was wrong
Panic at once, since a failed call means the function pointer type is wrong
questions.explanation: The API can exist while the handle, buffer, or target state is invalid. Keeping those cases apart stops compatibility logic from hiding an ordinary error.

questions.prompt: A fallback source supplies similar data to the primary one. How should results from it be presented?
options: As a different observation, labeled with its source and its limits
As identical to the primary result, since the data is similar
As more trustworthy than the primary one, since it is simpler
Not at all, since fallback data is discarded
questions.explanation: A fallback is not just a shorter path to the same answer. It can fail in different ways and may be a moment-in-time view, so say where it came from.

questions.prompt: Which action is an unsafe way to handle a function that could not be found at run time?
options: Calling address zero, or an unresolved address, as a function
Checking for the missing function and choosing a fallback
Reporting that the feature is unavailable on this system
Testing the code path with the function absent
questions.explanation: Never call an unresolved address and never turn 'absent' into zero. The other options are the recommended ways to handle it.

questions.prompt: In analyzing code, a name string is passed to a lookup routine and a later instruction calls the returned pointer. What does recognizing that pattern give you?
options: A way to link an indirect call to a documented function
Proof that the code is malicious or hiding something
A guarantee that the function never fails when called
The address the function will have on every machine
questions.explanation: Dynamic resolution is a common pattern. Reconstructing the chain ties the indirect call to a documented API and signature. It is not evidence of bad intent.

questions.prompt: Why does Windows not let two programs drive the same disk controller directly?
options: Devices hold shared state, so one program could overwrite another's command or aim a copy engine at it
Disk controllers run only in 16-bit mode, so a user-mode program cannot form the commands the hardware needs
Programs would be too slow at setting registers, so the controller would time out and lose the request
Each controller has a unique signature, and only the kernel is allowed to carry a certificate to use it
questions.explanation: If programs shared the controller, one could change the sector another had just chosen, or aim the copying engine at another process's memory. The operating system coordinates who may operate devices and which buffers they may reach.

questions.prompt: The I/O manager has checked that a caller's handle may write to a device. Why must the driver still validate the request?
options: A handle check does not prove the operation, lengths, and buffers inside the request are safe for the device
The handle check happens only for read requests, so every write arrives with no check of any kind
The I/O manager forgets the handle once it builds the IRP, so the driver has to look it up again
Handle rights apply only to user-mode drivers, so a kernel-mode driver must do all the checks itself
questions.explanation: The I/O manager checks the handle; the driver must still validate the operation, lengths, and buffers it uses. An access check does not prove the request's contents are safe.

questions.prompt: In a driver stack, which driver knows the device itself and does the real work?
options: The function driver
The bus driver
A filter driver
The I/O manager
questions.explanation: A bus driver talks to the bus (USB or PCI Express), the function driver knows the device and does the work, and optional filter drivers watch or adjust requests. The I/O manager is part of the kernel, not a driver in the stack.

questions.prompt: Driver code runs at the highest privilege, so a user program cannot call it directly. How does a program send a numbered, device-specific command to a driver?
options: It opens a handle to the device and sends a device-control request
It jumps to the driver's code address inside the kernel directly
It writes the command into the driver's file on the disk
It loads the driver into its own process before sending it
questions.explanation: The driver is in the kernel, so requests travel through a handle using read, write, or a general-purpose device-control call for everything else.

questions.prompt: What is an I/O request packet (IRP)?
options: A kernel data structure serving as a request's work order, with its operation, buffers, and result
A hardware signal on the interrupt line that tells a device the next queued request is ready to start
A processor instruction that switches from user mode into the driver's dispatch routine for the call
A file on disk that stores each driver's list of supported control codes and the rights they require
questions.explanation: The I/O manager builds an IRP, which travels down the driver stack and comes back up carrying the result. It is a data structure, not a signal.

questions.prompt: A driver's dispatch routine receives a read IRP, but no key events are ready. What does it do?
options: Keeps the IRP, returns `STATUS_PENDING`, and completes it later from the interrupt-driven code
Completes the IRP at once with zero bytes, so the program can simply retry the read when it likes
Spins in the dispatch routine, reading STATUS repeatedly until an event finally arrives from the device
Hands the IRP back to the I/O manager to be rebuilt and re-sent when a key is pressed
questions.explanation: If the dispatch routine has to wait for the hardware, it parks the IRP and returns pending; the program's thread waits inside `ReadFile` until the DPC completes it.

questions.prompt: A device-control request is described as checked twice. What are the two checks?
options: The system checks the handle's rights; the driver checks parameters
The compiler checks the types, and the linker checks the names
The user checks the device, and the vendor checks the signature
The hardware checks the rights, and the firmware checks the buffer
questions.explanation: Each control code declares the rights it needs, and the I/O manager refuses a mismatched handle before the driver runs. The driver still distrusts the parameters it receives.

questions.prompt: What does memory-mapped I/O mean for a device driver?
options: Registers sit at physical addresses used with ordinary loads and stores
Device registers are copied into files that the driver reads from disk
Device data lives only in the device's own firmware memory space
Registers are reached through a separate set of special instructions
questions.explanation: Most modern devices expose registers as a range of physical addresses that the kernel maps. Port I/O with special instructions is the older mechanism.

questions.prompt: A toy device has five 2-byte registers in order: A, B, C, D, E. At what offset is register E, and how big is the block?
options: At +0x08, in a block of 10 bytes
At +0x0A, in a block of 10 bytes
At +0x08, in a block of 8 bytes
At +0x10, in a block of 20 bytes
questions.explanation: Each register starts 2 bytes after the previous one: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Five registers of 2 bytes fill 10 bytes.

questions.prompt: Why is reading the keypad's DATA register different from reading ordinary memory?
options: Reading it removes the event it returns, so the next read gives the next event
Reading it flips the device off, so the driver must write CONTROL again afterward
Reading it always returns the A key's scan code, `0x1E`, whatever key was pressed
Reading it is slower than ordinary memory but changes nothing inside the device
questions.explanation: DATA holds the front event; a read removes it. A tool that read DATA just to look would silently swallow a key press.

questions.prompt: STATUS can change between two consecutive reads with no instruction in between. Why does that matter for how reads are compiled and mapped?
options: The device changes it, so accesses must never be cached, merged, or skipped; the memory is uncacheable
Windows rewrites it between reads, so the driver must lock the page that holds the register in memory
The compiler may reorder reads freely, since the device checks the order of the values on its own side
It only changes when interrupts are off, so the driver turns them off around each of the register reads
questions.explanation: Register accesses are never cached, merged, or skipped. Drivers use dedicated read-register and write-register routines that the compiler must carry out exactly as written.

questions.prompt: Why does the keypad driver use interrupts rather than polling STATUS over and over?
options: Polling wastes a processor core on a device that sits idle almost all the time
Polling is not possible, since STATUS can be read only from inside an interrupt handler
Polling would let two programs read the same event, which the keypad does not allow
Polling needs port I/O, and the toy keypad has only memory-mapped registers
questions.explanation: An interrupt makes the processor stop between instructions and run the registered handler when the device has news.

questions.prompt: How is the work split between the ISR and the DPC for the toy keypad?
options: The ISR confirms the interrupt and writes ACK; the DPC drains events, fills the buffer, and completes the IRP
The ISR drains events and completes the IRP; the DPC runs later and does nothing except write to ACK
The ISR runs at low priority and does the real work; the DPC runs first and only queues up the ISR
Both run at the same priority at once, and each of them handles one half of the waiting key events
questions.explanation: The ISR runs immediately while other work waits, so it does the minimum. The DPC runs moments later at lower priority with interrupts enabled again.

questions.prompt: Why does the ISR read STATUS before doing anything else?
options: Several devices can share one interrupt line, so it must confirm its own device raised the interrupt
STATUS holds the IRP's buffer address, which the ISR needs before it can fill it
Reading STATUS turns the interrupt line off, so the ISR can safely enable interrupts again
STATUS tells the ISR which process owns the key press, so it can wake that process directly
questions.explanation: Because an interrupt line can be shared, the ISR reads STATUS to confirm the interrupt came from its device, then writes ACK so the device lowers the line.

questions.prompt: A user presses and releases A. How does the DPC complete the parked read?
options: It collects two events, A pressed and A released, and completes the IRP with 2 bytes
It collects one event, A pressed, and completes the IRP with 1 byte, leaving the release for the next read
It collects two events and completes the IRP with 8 bytes, the size of the program's buffer
It completes the IRP with zero bytes and lets the program read DATA itself
questions.explanation: The lesson's example: the DPC collects *A pressed* and *A released* and completes the read with those 2 bytes, even though the program's buffer was 8 bytes.

questions.prompt: Why do a disk or network card use DMA instead of register reads?
options: They move megabytes, and copying them by register reads would keep a core busy doing only that
They have no registers at all, so DMA is the only way that a driver can tell them what to do
DMA lets them skip the driver stack entirely, so the program talks to the hardware directly instead
DMA lets the device write to any virtual address in the program, so that no buffer has to be set up
questions.explanation: With DMA the driver gives the device a buffer's address and size; the device copies the data into or out of RAM and interrupts once when the transfer is done.

questions.prompt: What kind of address does a driver give a DMA device?
options: A physical address or, with an IOMMU, a device address that the IOMMU translates and limits
A virtual address from the process's page tables, which the device resolves on its own
A segment number, which the device combines with the process's `cs` value
A handle to the buffer, which the device exchanges for an address through the I/O manager
questions.explanation: A device has no access to any process's page tables. The IOMMU limits it to the buffers the driver approved.

questions.prompt: A USB host controller asks a keyboard for news 125 times a second. How often is the keyboard asked?
options: Every 1,000 ÷ 125 = 8 milliseconds
Every 125 ÷ 1,000 = 0.125 milliseconds
Every 125 × 8 = 1,000 milliseconds
Every 1,000 × 125 = 125,000 milliseconds
questions.explanation: A USB device never speaks first; the host asks on a schedule. Many gaming keyboards are asked every millisecond.

questions.prompt: A key press passes through layers: the device reports a usage code, a driver maps it to a scan code, and the system maps that to a virtual-key code using the keyboard layout. Why is the last step layout-dependent?
options: One physical key can yield different characters per layout
Scan codes are different on every computer that is used
Usage codes are valid for only one spoken language
Virtual-key codes are chosen at random in every session
questions.explanation: The scan code names a physical key, and the layout decides what that key means. That is why the final mapping depends on the layout.

questions.prompt: Synthetic input injected through a high-level system API enters the input path above the keyboard drivers. What follows for a tool watching input at a lower level?
options: It can see real hardware key presses but not the synthetic ones
It sees both kinds identically, since all input shares one path
It sees only the synthetic input, since that is newer
It sees nothing, since low-level watching is blocked
questions.explanation: Synthetic input joins above every driver, so input observed at lower levels does not include it. Where you watch decides what you see.

questions.prompt: A driver carries a valid digital signature. What does that tell you?
options: Who published it and whether it has changed since signing, but not whether its code is safe
That its code is safe, since Microsoft reads and tests every signed driver before signing
That it can never be on the vulnerable driver blocklist, since that list holds only unsigned code
That it runs at ring 3, since only user-mode drivers need signatures
questions.explanation: A signature answers who published it and whether it changed. A correctly signed driver can still expose a control code that reads or writes any memory.

questions.prompt: What is the vulnerable driver blocklist for?
options: It lists signed drivers known to be exploitable, which Windows refuses to load
It lists unsigned drivers that Windows allows for testing on disposable machines
It lists drivers that Secure Boot has already loaded, so they can be unloaded in order
It lists devices that cannot use DMA, so their drivers are loaded with the IOMMU off
questions.explanation: Attackers load old, legitimately signed drivers to borrow their bugs. The blocklist is Microsoft's answer; it is always enforced when memory integrity is on.

questions.prompt: A cheat seller says to turn off Secure Boot and memory integrity before loading their driver. What does that advice cost the user?
options: It lowers the machine's defense against all kernel malware, not only against cheats
It affects only the game, since those protections guard games and nothing else on the machine
It costs nothing once the cheat has loaded, since both features re-enable on the next restart
It lowers the defense only for 32-bit drivers, so 64-bit software stays protected as before
questions.explanation: Each of those protections protects the machine against all kernel malware. Turning one off lowers the defense for everything, and the driver's author is anonymous.

questions.prompt: Why is kernel-mode code held to a different standard of trust than ordinary application code?
options: It helps enforce system checks, so a flaw can break them everywhere
It runs faster, so mistakes cost the system more time overall
It is written in lower-level languages, so it is less readable
It is signed more often, so it deserves more trust than others
questions.explanation: User code is confined by privilege and page-table checks. Kernel code takes part in enforcing those checks, so a bug can change mappings, device state and security decisions.

questions.prompt: A user-mode program follows a bad pointer, and a driver follows a bad kernel pointer. How do the outcomes usually differ?
options: The user-mode crash normally ends one process; the kernel one can crash the computer or corrupt any process
Both end only the program that made the mistake, since Windows isolates each of them from the rest equally
The user-mode crash takes the computer down, while the kernel one is contained by the driver stack above it
Both end one process, but the driver's process always restarts itself automatically afterward in the kernel
questions.explanation: A bad kernel pointer can take the whole machine down, or corrupt data belonging to any process.

questions.prompt: A teammate says that moving a tool's code into a kernel driver makes it better engineering. What is the right response?
options: More privilege enlarges both its authority and the damage a bug can do
Correct, since kernel code is faster and therefore safer
Correct, since drivers are checked more thoroughly when they load
Correct, since drivers cannot crash the whole system
questions.explanation: Moving code into a driver enlarges its authority and the damage a bug can cause alike. It is not an engineering improvement in itself.

questions.prompt: Why is the documented API boundary useful?
options: Callers get no kernel authority just by asking; the kernel checks the request and a sound driver checks again
Callers gain kernel authority for the length of each call, so they can then check the work for themselves
The kernel trusts the caller's handle completely, so the driver can skip any further checks of its own now
The boundary hides drivers from user mode, so callers never learn which drivers are loaded on the machine
questions.explanation: The kernel checks handles, rights, and buffers, and a sound driver checks again before touching device or privileged memory.

questions.prompt: When studying an offline single-player game, why is a kernel driver usually unnecessary?
options: User-mode APIs, a debugger and reversible changes are enough
Drivers cannot interact with the processes of games at all
Offline games run entirely inside the kernel, out of reach
User-mode tools can see everything that kernel tools can see
questions.explanation: An offline process can be studied with ordinary tools, so the extra authority of a driver is not needed.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the course deliberately not build?
options: Arbitrary kernel or physical-memory read/write commands
A read-only inventory of the drivers Windows has loaded
A user-mode DLL that is started in a separate, explicit second stage
A hash baseline of the modules a game has loaded
questions.explanation: The course avoids arbitrary kernel read/write, privilege escalation, security or anti-cheat bypasses, hidden drivers, and loaders for vulnerable drivers. The inventory is read-only and defensive.

questions.prompt: What design question does Microsoft's driver security guidance begin with?
options: Whether a kernel driver is actually required, since a service or application is the lower-risk boundary
Whether the driver can be signed by its developer, since unsigned drivers will not load on any Windows machine
Whether the driver can avoid using IOCTLs, since every IOCTL raises the privilege of the driver that serves it
Whether the driver supports 32-bit games, since most drivers for such games will have to run in ring 3 instead
questions.explanation: If a service or application can do the job, it is the lower-risk boundary.

questions.prompt: A driver is correctly signed. Why is that not enough to call it safe?
options: It may expose a badly protected command that lets another program read or write arbitrary privileged memory
Signed drivers are never checked at load time, so the signature only helps after a crash has already happened
The signature covers only the driver's file name, not its code, so changes to the code itself are missed
Signatures expire after a day, so every signed driver must be reloaded with a brand new signature each morning
questions.explanation: A signature says who published it and whether it changed; a signed driver can still be vulnerable.

questions.prompt: A new driver appears on a machine. Which investigation order is sensible?
options: Check signature and hash, check block lists, find the installer
Delete it, reboot, and then check who installed it afterward
Load it in a test, watch what it does, and then check the hash
Check its file size, run it, and then check its signature
questions.explanation: Driver loading is a rare, high-impact event, so identify the file, compare it with what is known, and trace what introduced it before acting.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to load a suspicious driver on their daily computer to see what it does. What is the better approach?
options: Use an isolated, disposable VM and vendor analysis guidance
Load it, but only briefly, then restart the daily computer
Load it with the network unplugged on the daily computer
Load it as an ordinary user instead of an administrator
questions.explanation: A disposable VM contains the impact of anything a suspicious driver does. A daily computer should never be the test bed.

questions.prompt: A read-only tool lists loaded drivers. What kind of API calls should it use?
options: Query-only calls that change nothing on the system
Calls that load each driver again to test how it behaves
Calls that unload any driver that looks unfamiliar to you
Calls that enable extra privileges to see more of the system
questions.explanation: An inventory observes and prints names. It enables no privileges and changes no driver state.

questions.prompt: A call reports it needs 4,096 bytes to list pointers that are each 8 bytes wide, while the buffer holds 256 pointers. What should the caller do?
options: Resize to 512 pointers (4,096 ÷ 8) and call again
Resize to 4,096 pointers and call again, one per byte
Use only the first 256 pointers and ignore the remainder
Resize to 32,768 pointers and call again, eight per byte
questions.explanation: The number of pointers is the byte count divided by the pointer size: 4,096 ÷ 8 = 512, which is more than 256, so the buffer must grow and the call be repeated.

questions.prompt: A loop that grows a buffer until a list fits also refuses counts above a sane maximum. Why?
options: To refuse an absurd count instead of allocating hugely
Because lists over that size cannot exist on Windows
To make the loop run faster on very large machines
Because buffers above that size cannot be resized again
questions.explanation: The check guards against an unreasonable value from the API. Without it, the loop could allocate far more memory than any real list needs.

questions.prompt: On a hardened Windows installation, the inventory shows fewer details. What should you do?
options: Treat it as the security boundary working, and do not weaken the machine to lengthen the list
Enable the debug privilege for the program so that it can see every driver on the whole machine
Turn off memory integrity for the run, since that feature hides driver names from user programs
Run the lab as ring 0 code inside a driver, so that the list matches what the kernel itself sees
questions.explanation: The program does not enable debug privileges. Fewer details are not a failure to fix by lowering defenses.

questions.prompt: Which item does a useful driver baseline record besides the file name?
options: Version, publisher, signature result, hash, why it is installed, and the approved update source
The driver's base address in memory, since that stays the same after every restart of the machine
The player's account name, since drivers are installed separately for each user of the machine
The game that was running when the driver was first loaded, and nothing else about the driver
questions.explanation: A baseline lists Windows build and capture time, file name, version, publisher, signature result, hash, reason, and update source.

questions.prompt: An older hardware driver conflicts with a kernel protection feature. What is the sound course of action?
options: Look for a supported update; do not just switch protection off
Turn the protection off, since compatibility must come first
Turn it off temporarily, then back on after the experiment
Rename the driver so the feature does not detect it at all
questions.explanation: Kernel code-integrity protections are there for a reason. Fix the dependency instead of turning protections off to run an experiment.

questions.prompt: Which Sysmon event can record a loaded driver's hash and signature information, and how should a hit be handled?
options: Event ID 6; confirm the file, service, signature, source, and owning software before acting
Event ID 1; delete the file with the unexpected name before looking at anything else
Event ID 6; assume it is malicious, since every driver load is a high-risk event
Event ID 3; block the network connection of the driver before checking its signature
questions.explanation: Alert on unknown publishers, missing signatures, hashes not in the baseline, and drivers introduced outside normal updates. Detection is not just deleting one weird filename.

questions.prompt: What does DMA stand for, and what does it do?
options: Direct memory access: a device moves data without the CPU copying each byte
Dynamic memory allocation: a program asks its allocator for space and gets an address
Debug memory analysis: a debugger reads the pages of another process
Data mapping array: a table the CPU uses to track free physical pages
questions.explanation: DMA is a hardware feature for device transfers. It shares the word memory with allocation, but that is a different operation done by a program's allocator.

questions.prompt: A classmate says any DMA transfer is automatically a cheat. What is the better statement?
options: It is a normal hardware feature; trouble starts when a device reaches memory it should not
It is an attack by design, since the transfer skips the CPU and so cannot be logged
It is harmless on every machine, so a device reaching extra memory is never a concern
It is used by storage controllers; network and graphics hardware copy bytes via the CPU
questions.explanation: Storage, networking, and graphics hardware all use DMA for speed. Security problems come from a device reaching memory it should not, or from software trusting a device too much.

questions.prompt: Two processes both read virtual address 0x1000 and see different bytes. Why?
options: Each has its own page tables, so one number maps differently
One of the two reads a cached copy of the other's data
The second process overwrote the bytes of the first process
Virtual addresses are randomized again on every read
questions.explanation: A virtual address only has meaning together with an address space. Each process has its own page-table root, so the translations differ.

questions.prompt: On a CPU with multi-level paging, what does the control register used for translation identify?
options: The physical base of the top-level translation table
The virtual address of the running code
The physical address of the next instruction to run
The size of the process's address space
questions.explanation: The register is where the walk starts. Without the right value, a walk follows some other address space.

questions.prompt: Which bits of a 48-bit virtual address select the byte inside a 4 KiB page?
options: Bits 11 to 0
Bits 47 to 39
Bits 20 to 12
Bits 63 to 48
questions.explanation: A 4 KiB page is 2^12 bytes, so the lowest twelve bits are the offset. Bits 20 to 12 pick the page-table entry instead, and bits 63 to 48 are the sign extension.

questions.prompt: How big is one translation table, and how are its entries laid out?
options: 512 entries of eight bytes each
256 entries of 16 bytes each
1,024 entries of four bytes each
512 entries of 16 bytes each
questions.explanation: Nine index bits select among 512 entries, and each entry is eight bytes, so a table fills exactly one 4 KiB page.

questions.prompt: How many bits of a 64-bit virtual address do the four table indices and the offset use together, and what about the rest?
options: 48 bits (4 x 9 + 12); the top 16 must copy bit 47
52 bits (4 x 10 + 12); the top 12 must copy bit 51
36 bits (4 x 9, no offset); the top 28 must be zero
64 bits (4 x 16); no bits are left over for copying
questions.explanation: Four 9-bit indices plus a 12-bit offset make 48 bits. The remaining 16 carry no information and must repeat bit 47, which makes an address canonical.

questions.prompt: How can a translation finish before reading all four levels?
options: A PDPT entry can map 1 GiB, or a page-directory entry can map 2 MiB
A page-table entry can map 2 MiB, or a page-directory entry can map 4 KiB
A PML4 entry with a clear present bit maps the whole address as one block
Large pages still walk four levels but use a 13-bit offset field instead
questions.explanation: Large pages stop the walk early at the PDPT (1 GiB) or page-directory (2 MiB) level, and the skipped index bits become part of the offset.

questions.prompt: A CPU with 48-bit virtual addresses requires bits 63 to 48 to equal bit 47 (a canonical address). Is 0x0001_0000_0000_0000 canonical?
options: No; bit 47 is 0, but bit 48 is 1
Yes; bit 48 is within the allowed 48 bits
Yes; all of its lower bits are zero
No; it is not a round power of two
questions.explanation: Bit 48 is the lowest of the upper sixteen bits, and it must match bit 47. Here bit 47 is 0 while bit 48 is 1, so the address is noncanonical.

questions.prompt: Why validate an address's form before using it to read from a capture file?
options: It gives a clear error rather than following bad offsets
It makes the read faster by skipping the file lookup
The capture file refuses to open without validation
It converts the address into a physical address first
questions.explanation: Impossible input cannot lead anywhere real. Failing fast with a named error is clearer than reading nonsense bytes that look plausible.

questions.prompt: What does an IOMMU do for DMA-capable devices?
options: It translates device addresses so the OS can confine a device to approved regions
It compresses RAM pages so a device can fit much more data into each transfer it makes
It encrypts each transfer so a device cannot read the plain bytes that it fetches from RAM
It replaces the CPU's page tables so that processes stop using virtual addresses entirely
questions.explanation: An IOMMU does for devices what page tables do for processes: it sits between device and RAM and blocks requests outside approved regions.

questions.prompt: A protected machine blocks a DMA device during your experiment. What is the right response?
options: Treat it as the defense working and use the synthetic or offline capture
Turn off the IOMMU in firmware for the whole length of the experiment
Disable Kernel DMA Protection temporarily so the device can finish its work
Mask extra address bits in the walker until some output finally appears
questions.explanation: A blocked path is a successful defense, not a translation failure. The labs use synthetic or offline captures so no protection has to be weakened.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an offline capture is accurate?
options: Pages may have changed right after capture, and some may be absent or omitted
Threads keep running inside the image, so values update while you read
CPU caches and device memory are included in every RAM image
Any CR3 value works, because pages are stored by virtual address
questions.explanation: A capture is a frozen snapshot. It can miss pages, caches, and device memory, and you need the correct CR3 and architecture details to interpret it.

questions.prompt: Why do origin, build, capture time, and a hash travel with a capture file?
options: Numbers like CR3 only mean something for their source machine; the hash shows no changes
The hash lets the tool repair any pages that changed after the capture was taken
Provenance lets the walker skip the present-bit check when the file is trusted
The capture format requires a header holding the machine name and nothing else
questions.explanation: The file alone does not say where it came from. The record plus a cryptographic hash tells you what the numbers mean and whether the bytes are still the original ones.

questions.prompt: A RAM capture file is no longer needed after an exercise. What should happen to it?
options: Keep it secure, then delete it; it may hold private data
Keep it forever, since captures can never be recreated
Post it publicly so that others can reproduce the result
Rename it so that it is much harder for others to find
questions.explanation: A capture holds whatever was in RAM, including private data unrelated to the exercise. Keep it secure and remove it when it is no longer needed.

questions.prompt: In the apartment-number analogy, what plays the part of the building?
options: The page-table root (CR3) chosen for the address space
The physical RAM chip that holds the final byte
The byte offset inside the final 4 KiB page
The access type: read, write, or instruction fetch
questions.explanation: Apartment 1000 means nothing without the building, just as `0x1000` means nothing without the page-table root. The analogy is limited, because real mappings can change and carry permissions.

questions.prompt: A software page-table walker over a capture returns a physical address for a virtual one. What does that show?
options: Entries lead there, but live access is not proven allowed
The CPU would allow any read or write to that address
The page is writable and executable by user code
The capture contains the whole address space
questions.explanation: The walker checks presence and file bounds. It does not emulate every read, write, execute and user/supervisor check that the CPU makes.

questions.prompt: Why wrap addresses in distinct types for physical and virtual instead of using plain 64-bit integers?
options: The compiler rejects mixing them unless you convert explicitly
Distinct types make address arithmetic run faster
Distinct types allow larger addresses than a plain integer
Plain integers cannot hold addresses on 64-bit systems
questions.explanation: Both kinds are 64-bit numbers underneath, so mixing them is an easy logic error. Distinct types turn that into a compile error without adding speed or range.

questions.prompt: When computing start + length for a read, which failure does a checked addition guard against?
options: The sum overflowing and wrapping around to a small number
The sum coming out as an odd number rather than an even one
The length being zero, which would make the read empty
The start address not being aligned to a page boundary
questions.explanation: A wrapped sum could look like a valid small range. Checked addition reports the overflow instead.

questions.prompt: The eight bytes of a page-table entry in memory are 03 40 00 00 00 00 00 00, stored little-endian. What is the entry's value?
options: `0x4003`, with the next table at 0x4000 and the low bits as flags
`0x0340_0000_0000_0000`, since the first byte is the highest
`0x0340`, since only the first two bytes count
`0x4003`, with the next table at 0x4003 and no flags
questions.explanation: Little-endian puts the lowest byte first, so 0x40 in the second byte is worth 0x4000 and 0x03 sets the low flag bits. Clearing the flag bits leaves the address 0x4000.

questions.prompt: Why does each table index take exactly nine bits?
options: A table holds 512 entries, and 512 is 2^9
A page is 4,096 bytes, and 4,096 is 2^9
Each entry is eight bytes, and eight is 2^9
Four levels share 36 bits, and nobody chose the split further
questions.explanation: Nine bits can choose among 512 entries. The 4,096-byte page size fixes the 12-bit offset, a different field.

questions.prompt: A 9-bit page-table index sits at bits 38 to 30 of an address. Which expression extracts it?
options: `(value >> 30) & 0x1FF`
`(value >> 38) & 0x1FF`
`(value >> 30) & 0xFFF`
`(value << 30) & 0x1FF`
questions.explanation: Shift right so the field's lowest bit moves to bit 0, then keep nine bits with 0x1FF. A mask of 0xFFF would keep twelve bits.

questions.prompt: For the address 0x0000_7FFA_BCDE_1A30 and 4 KiB pages, which byte of the final page does a walk end up reading?
options: Byte 0
questions.explanation: The last twelve bits, 0xA30, are the page offset: 10 × 256 + 3 × 16 = 2,608. The remaining bits are table indices.

questions.prompt: The address 0x0000_7F00_0000_0000 is nonzero only in its upper bits. Which top-level table entry number does it use, from bits 47 to 39?
options: Entry 254
Entry 127
Entry 255
Entry 508
questions.explanation: 0x7F in bits 47 to 40 shifts to 0xFE when the field is moved down to bit 39, which is 254. Entry 127 would come from shifting one bit too far.

questions.prompt: A 100-byte read starts at page offset 4,000 in a 4,096-byte page. How many of those bytes lie in the first page?
options: 96, since 4,096 minus 4,000 is 96
100, since the whole read fits in the page
4, the number of bytes that spill over
4,000, the offset itself
questions.explanation: 4,096 - 4,000 = 96 bytes fit. The other 4 bytes lie in the next virtual page, which needs its own translation.

questions.prompt: A reader translates only the start address and then copies 32 consecutive physical bytes across a page end. What goes wrong?
options: The last 24 bytes come from whatever follows physically, maybe unrelated memory
The CPU raises a fault at the page boundary, so the read stops with an error code
The reader returns zeros for the second half until it later translates once again
The copy repeats the first page, because the offset wraps around back to zero
questions.explanation: Nothing warns you. The bytes look ordinary but belong to an unrelated allocation, another process's data, or nothing mapped at all.

questions.prompt: A page-table entry holds flag bits in its low and high bits as well as an address. Why mask it before using it as the next table's address?
options: To keep just the address bits as a page-aligned base
To clear the present bit before following the entry
To convert a virtual address into a physical one
To make the table's size a power of two
questions.explanation: The low bits store flags like present and writable, and high bits hold more flags. Only the middle bits are the address.

questions.prompt: With 4 KiB pages, what does masking an address with 0xFFF keep?
options: The 12-bit offset within the page
The page-table index at the lowest level
The page number
The flag bits of the entry
questions.explanation: 0xFFF is 4,095, so the mask keeps exactly twelve bits, which is the byte position inside the final page.

questions.prompt: How does the walk recognize a 1 GiB or 2 MiB page?
options: Bit 7 of the PDPT or page-directory entry is set, so the walk stops early
Bit 0 of the PML4 entry is clear, so the walk skips two levels
The virtual address has bit 47 set, which marks it as a large page
The capture file is larger than 2 MiB, so the reader switches modes
questions.explanation: Bit 7 (`0x80`) is the large-page flag at those two levels. When set, the index fields that were skipped become part of the offset.

questions.prompt: A mapping covers a 2 MiB page (2^21 bytes). Which mask extracts the offset inside it?
options: `value & 0x1F_FFFF`
`value & 0x3FFF_FFFF`
`value & 0xFFF`
questions.explanation: An offset mask is one less than the page size. 2^21 is 0x20_0000, so the mask is 0x1F_FFFF. The 0x3FFF_FFFF mask belongs to a 1 GiB page.

questions.prompt: A synthetic capture file is 0x5000 bytes. How many 4 KiB pages is that?
options: Five pages, since each 0x1000 is one page
Four pages, since the last 0x1000 is padding
Twenty pages, since 0x5000 is 20,480 in decimal
Fifty pages, since 0x5000 is 5,000 bytes
questions.explanation: Each 0x1000 bytes is one page, and 0x5000 is five of them, which is 20,480 bytes.

questions.prompt: In a toy setup where every index is 0 because the address is below 0x1000, and the final page base is 0x6000, what physical address does virtual 0x0456 translate to?
questions.explanation: The walk follows each table's first entry to the page base 0x6000, and the offset 0x456 is then added, giving 0x6456.

questions.prompt: A page-table walk fails because an entry's present bit is clear at one level. Which is a likely meaning?
options: Page unmapped, wrong root, or an incomplete capture
The address is not in canonical form, so the walk never began
The read length is too long to fit within a single page
The page is mapped but marked as read-only by its entry
questions.explanation: A clear present bit means that level has no valid next table. Noncanonical addresses and out-of-range reads produce different errors.

questions.prompt: A walk succeeds and returns bytes that look sensible, but the object is not the one you meant. What is a likely cause?
options: A wrong address space, a stale pointer, or a wrong build model
A noncanonical address that the reader forgot to reject
A present bit that the walker failed to check at the PML4
A bounds check that was too strict for the capture file
questions.explanation: A successful translation only says the page tables lead somewhere. The somewhere can still be the wrong object, which is why Lesson 12.9 adds provenance and independent checks.

questions.prompt: A page translation fails with an error. Which response is sound?
options: Check entries and layout, and keep the failure visible
Mask off the failing bits so the walk can continue
Skip the failing check and use the bytes that come back
Retry with random root values until it succeeds
questions.explanation: Forcing output by masking or skipping checks hides the real problem. A visible failure with context is more useful than bytes from the wrong place.

questions.prompt: Why does the command-line tool limit the byte count to 1 through 4,096?
options: A learning tool should make unexpectedly huge reads impossible
The page-table walk can only translate a single 4 KiB page per command run
The capture file format cannot store more than 4,096 bytes at one address
Larger reads would need CR3 to change partway through the printed output
questions.explanation: The limit is a deliberate safety choice, not a technical necessity. `read_virtual` does handle page crossings, so a limit is not there to avoid them.

questions.prompt: Why might a function that reads virtual memory from a capture return a new buffer rather than a slice of the capture?
options: Adjacent virtual pages need not be physically adjacent
Slices cannot be returned from functions in Rust
The capture is encrypted and must be decoded first
Returning a copy always makes the read faster
questions.explanation: Neighboring virtual pages can sit anywhere in physical memory, so the result has to be assembled from separate pieces.

questions.prompt: Why does a wrong CR3 value usually not make the page-table walk fail?
options: It is still a valid page-table root for some other address space
The walker silently falls back to the correct CR3 stored in the file
Every CR3 value leads to the same top-level table in the capture
The present bits are ignored whenever the CR3 does not match
questions.explanation: A clean walk only means the tables in the file lead somewhere. With the wrong root, the somewhere belongs to a different process.

questions.prompt: The capture's SHA-256 no longer matches the digest in its provenance record. What is the right move?
options: Stop, because every earlier translation assumed the recorded bytes
Continue, since the page-table walk will report any damaged pages itself
Recompute the digest and overwrite the old one in the record
Continue on a copy, since only the original file is affected by the change
questions.explanation: A changed file means the bytes are no longer the ones the record describes. Nothing translated from it can be trusted until the change is explained; overwriting the digest would hide the problem.

questions.prompt: Why keep the original capture read-only and experiment on a working copy?
options: A mistake then cannot change the only copy of the evidence
The walker refuses to open a file that is writable by anyone
A read-only file loads into RAM faster than a copy does
The hash can only be computed for a file that is marked read-only
questions.explanation: The original must keep matching its digest. Experiments on a copy leave the evidence intact.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in a capture's provenance record?
options: The CR3 source and the process it belongs to
The current health value read from the first object found
The decoded `PlayerSnapshot` from the first translation
The names of all other files stored on the source machine
questions.explanation: Provenance records where and how the file was made: tool, build, architecture, UTC time, included ranges, CR3 source, and the digest. Decoded values come later and are not provenance.

questions.prompt: A capture translator and a debugger give the same physical address, yet the object is still wrong. Which mistake can remain?
options: Both translated the wrong thing correctly, such as a stale pointer
The first translator contains a bug that the debugger happens to share by luck
The hash of the capture file was computed using the wrong hashing algorithm
The IOMMU blocked one of the two translations while the capture was recorded
questions.explanation: A second translator catches a bug in the first. Agreement says the translation is right, not that the target is the intended object, which is what semantic structure checks are for.

questions.prompt: Why run several checks on different fields rather than trusting one plausible health value?
options: Random memory often holds small integers, yet several checks rarely all pass by chance
A single check cannot be written in Rust code without also writing all of the others
The health field is stored in a different physical page than the other fields are
Each additional check lowers the digest size, so the hash is faster to verify later
questions.explanation: One field can look right by accident. A wrong address usually fails at least one of several checks that examine different bytes in different ways.

questions.prompt: A record layout has an 8-byte pointer, a 4-byte integer, two 4-byte floats and two 8-byte pointers, with no padding. What is its total size?
questions.explanation: 8 + 4 = 12, plus 8 for the floats makes 20, plus 16 for the pointers makes 36, which is 0x24.

questions.prompt: What does the semantic check on the vptr verify?
options: That it points into the expected module's read-only section
That it equals the virtual address where the object was found
That it is a multiple of 4,096 so it sits at a page start
That it matches the CR3 value stored in the provenance record
questions.explanation: A vtable normally lives in read-only data of the expected module. A pointer elsewhere suggests the bytes are not the object you meant.

questions.prompt: A growable list stores three pointers: begin, end of the used items, and the end of its reserved space. Which order must a valid list satisfy?
options: `begin <= end <= capacity`
`end <= begin <= capacity`
`begin <= capacity <= end`
`capacity <= begin <= end`
questions.explanation: The list starts at begin, holds items up to end, and has room up to capacity, so the three pointers must be in that order.

questions.prompt: The capture layer, layout layer, and presentation layer are kept separate. What is the main benefit?
options: A layout mistake cannot corrupt translation code; each layer tests alone
The presentation layer can skip decoding whenever the hash already matches the record
Page tables can be walked without any CR3 once the object layout is already known
The layout layer can repair the physical ranges that the capture tool omitted from the file
questions.explanation: The capture layer knows physical ranges and page tables; the layout layer knows fields and invariants; the presentation layer prints. Splitting them keeps each mistake local.

questions.prompt: Which step is part of defensive validation for DMA exposure?
options: Check Windows Security or System Information for the protection state
Turn off Kernel DMA Protection for a moment so the check runs faster and more simply
Plug in an unknown device and watch whether the machine reacts to the new hardware
Disable Secure Boot so the firmware reveals much more of its diagnostic output
questions.explanation: Defense means confirming protections are on, keeping software updated, and using trusted devices. The lesson says not to disable protections to make an experiment easier.

questions.prompt: A control validates something and acts on it a moment later. A 'time gap' targets which assumption?
options: That the checked state stays the same until it is used
That the check itself is implemented correctly
That the user who started the action is the same person
That the code was compiled by a trusted compiler
questions.explanation: A time gap is the assumption that trusted state does not change between check and use, so the test changes the state in that interval.

questions.prompt: A function runs several checks in order, and each returns an error with an early exit on failure. Two of the checks would fail. Which error is returned?
options: The error from the first failing check
The error from the last failing check
A combined error that lists both of them
The most severe of the two errors
questions.explanation: Each early exit ends the function, so the first failing check decides the named reason.

questions.prompt: The byte comparison is the last check, right before the toy write. What does that achieve?
options: It shortens the time gap but does not make a remote read and write atomic
It guarantees no other code can change the bytes before the write happens
It replaces the need for the build and range checks that came earlier
It proves the bytes belong to the intended process and object
questions.explanation: A tool needing a true guarantee must own the state exclusively, or have the owner validate and apply the request as one operation.

questions.prompt: What is an invariant in program design?
options: A condition that must hold every time
A value that never changes during execution
A function that cannot fail
A variable with a fixed type
questions.explanation: Stating an assumption as an invariant makes it testable. A value that never changes is a constant, which is a different idea.

questions.prompt: Which assumption defines a telemetry gap?
options: A blocked action needs no event of its own
Every execution path passes the point being observed
The name or handle a control trusted cannot change
A crash cannot leave hooks or handles in a bad state
questions.explanation: The safer test asserts that every allow, deny, timeout, and parse failure produces an event. The other assumptions describe the coverage, identity, and recovery gaps.

questions.prompt: A control trusts a name, a signer or a process ID. An 'identity gap' targets which assumption, and how can it be tested?
options: That identity cannot change; restart or rebuild and recheck
That the control is fast; flood it with repeated checks
That the check is correct; give it unusual inputs
That the log is complete; delete part of it
questions.explanation: An identity gap assumes the trusted name, signer, PID or handle stays the same. Restarting or rebuilding the target tests exactly that.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an invariant?
options: An entity ID names at most one live entity in a snapshot
Entity 7's health changed from 6 to 0 during tick 900
The player pressed the heal button during tick 41 once
The damage routine was called twice within one frame
questions.explanation: An invariant is a statement that must be true in every valid state. The other options describe single events, which can happen and still leave the state valid or invalid.

questions.prompt: Health is 5 and a request asks for 20 damage. What should a correct damage routine produce?
options: Health 0, because the range rule `0 <= health <= max_health` must hold
Health -15, because the subtraction is exact and the bar clamps it later
Health 5, because a request larger than the current health is ignored
Health 20, because the larger number replaces the current one
questions.explanation: The invariant forbids negative health, so the control limits the transition and leaves 0. A display that hides -15 would not fix the stored value.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a detector rather than a control?
options: A scan that logs any entity whose health exceeds its maximum
A damage routine that stops health at 0 instead of going negative
A heal routine that applies `.min(max_health)` before storing
A command handler that refuses a change in read-only mode
questions.explanation: A control keeps an invariant true by limiting or refusing a transition. A detector only reports that the invariant may already have failed.

questions.prompt: A detector stays quiet for a whole play session. What can you conclude about the control it watches?
options: Nothing certain, since the control can still be incomplete
The control is complete, because the detector would have noticed any gap
The invariant is no longer needed, because nothing has broken it
The control must have run on the authoritative copy of the state
questions.explanation: Detector and control are separate code that fail separately. A quiet detector may simply not cover the path that was used.

questions.prompt: A game state shows health 120 while max health is 100. Which statement fits the idea of an invariant?
options: The state is invalid, whichever check or code path failed to prevent it
The state is valid until some check happens to notice it
Only the field that holds health is wrong, so only it needs a fix
The state is valid as long as the display shows a value under 100
questions.explanation: An invariant is a property of the whole state, not of one address or one piece of code. A clamp, a limit field and a log line are places where it is kept or reported.

questions.prompt: In security design, what is a 'bypass'?
options: A path to an outcome that skips its guarding control
A faster route that makes a control run more quickly
An alarm that fires for harmless behavior
A control that is turned off for testing
questions.explanation: A bypass is a mismatch between a convenient proxy and the real rule. It is about the path and the control, not about speed or false alarms.

questions.prompt: A menu button is greyed out unless the player may heal. In the proxy table, what real property does that button stand in for?
options: The engine policy actually permits the state change
The health bar's cache currently matches the entity
The game build matches the one the tool was made for
The telemetry queue has not dropped any events
questions.explanation: A greyed-out button answers how the screen should look. Whether the simulation may perform the effect is a separate question that must be checked where the effect happens.

questions.prompt: A checksum over one field matches. Which real property does it fail to establish?
options: That the complete object relation is current and valid
That the field was copied from memory without any error
That the build number is recorded in the provenance file
That the entity is drawn on screen this frame
questions.explanation: A matching one-field checksum says only that field is unchanged. Other fields can still make the whole relation invalid.

questions.prompt: In a single-player game, which copy of health is usually authoritative?
options: The simulation's entity object
The health bar's cached copy
The snapshot handed to a script
The copy shown in a debugger window
questions.explanation: The authoritative copy is the one whose value decides what happens next. The others are copies that catch up afterward.

questions.prompt: In a networked game with an authoritative server, what is a client's copy of health?
options: A prediction that the server can overwrite
The record that the server must copy before each tick
A second authoritative value, equal in rank to the server's
An integrity tag the server checks against its record
questions.explanation: The server's record decides, and each client's value is only a prediction. That is why requests from clients are validated against the server's own record.

questions.prompt: Why does a server validate every client request against its own record?
options: Anything a client computed can be altered on its machine before sending
Clients send values in a binary format that the server cannot decode directly
Servers are faster than clients, so they can recheck every single computation
The network always changes numbers while they travel over the wire to the server
questions.explanation: The client's machine is outside the server's control, so the client's own check cannot be the rule. The server keeps the authoritative record.

questions.prompt: Two copies of a value hold the same number. How can you tell which copy is authoritative?
options: By timing: the authoritative copy changes first
By comparing the values; the larger one is authoritative
By size; the copy stored in more bytes is authoritative
By location; the copy at the lower address is authoritative
questions.explanation: Matching values do not reveal which copy was read. The order in which they change does.

questions.prompt: A trace shows a game's authoritative value changing to 0 at tick 900, but the on-screen bar shows 0 only at tick 901. What explains the difference?
options: The bar draws from a copy that lags by one tick
The bar is the authoritative value, and it changed a tick late
The trace clock runs slow, so its ticks cannot be compared
The change at tick 900 was reversed and then made again
questions.explanation: A display is a copy updated after the simulation. Seeing 0 there confirms the value but does not show that the bar is where the change happened first.

questions.prompt: Event 41 (health reaches 0) is logged just before event 42 (mode becomes Downed). What does log order prove?
options: It fits damage causing the change, but a shared cause or flush timing also fits
It proves the health write directly caused the mode change that came after it
It proves the mode watch ran on a different thread from the health watch
It proves the two events happened in two different game ticks of the clock
questions.explanation: Log order is not cause. Lesson 13.2 adds correlation IDs to tie events to one action even when order misleads.

questions.prompt: What advantage do typed event fields have over free-text log sentences?
options: A test can check that a `HealthWrite` to 0 precedes the `ModeChanged` to `Downed`
Typed events take up less space, so the log never needs a size bound at all
Typed events are written to disk automatically in order of the entity ID number
Free-text sentences cannot contain tick numbers or entity IDs in any form
questions.explanation: Fields such as `before`, `after`, and `entity_id` can be compared by code, so the order can be checked automatically.

questions.prompt: Which transition is not in the Alive / Downed / Removed state diagram?
options: Removed to Alive
Downed to Alive by revive
Downed to Removed by timeout
Alive to Removed by despawn
questions.explanation: Removed leads only to the end of the diagram. Revive, timeout, and despawn are all listed as allowed transitions.

questions.prompt: For hook installation, what must remain true, and where does the health analogy break down?
options: A call sees a complete original path or a complete hook path; a hook changes bytes other threads use
A call sees only the hook path; health is a copy while a hook is the authoritative original
A hook may be half installed if telemetry records it; health is a value checked only once
The original bytes are overwritten at once; health is held in a register that no thread shares
questions.explanation: Health is one value, but a hook changes executable bytes that other threads may be running, which is why Lesson 6.10 handles concurrency separately.

questions.prompt: A log says only that a write was refused. Which of the four recorded things is missing?
options: The reason: which specific check produced the refusal
The identity: which process, build, and object was touched
The outcome: whether the write finally happened
The decision: whether the answer was allow or deny
questions.explanation: The log shows a decision, but without a reason you can never learn why. Dropping the outcome instead would hide whether an allowed operation completed.

questions.prompt: A log records that an operation was allowed, but nothing afterward. What can you not tell from it?
options: Whether it actually completed
Whether the operation was checked at all
Which operation was being considered
Whether a decision was made
questions.explanation: Allowed is not the same as completed. An outcome event is what separates the two.

questions.prompt: Events in log order: seq 10 corr A refused; seq 11 corr B allowed; seq 12 corr A state-changed; seq 13 corr B state-changed. Which action does the state change at seq 12 belong to?
options: Action A, which was refused
Action B, since it was allowed just before
Neither, since a refused action cannot change state
Both, since they happened close together
questions.explanation: Pairing by correlation ID shows that a state change followed a refusal, which is a contradiction worth investigating. Pairing by adjacency would call both actions successful and miss it.

questions.prompt: Why did the adjacency reading of that log reach the wrong conclusion even though no events were missing?
options: Two actions interleaved, and the reader assumed they had not
Sequence numbers were reordered so that 43 came before 42
The monotonic clock jumped between events 42 and 43
A dropped event hid the real decision for action 7
questions.explanation: The evidence was complete. Ordering alone misled, which is why detection rules join on the correlation ID, not on neighbouring lines.

questions.prompt: What is a correlation ID for?
options: Connecting the events of one logical action, even across threads
Counting how many events were lost when a queue overflowed
Recording how long each event took to produce, in microseconds
Naming the build so a reader can reject unknown schemas
questions.explanation: The ID ties decision and effect events together without pretending they happened on one thread. Dropped counts, durations, and schema checks use other fields.

questions.prompt: Why use a monotonic clock for event ordering and durations within one run?
options: Wall-clock time can jump, while a monotonic clock only moves forward
A monotonic clock is more accurate to the calendar date than wall time
Wall-clock time cannot be stored in a `u64` field
A monotonic clock records which thread produced each event
questions.explanation: Monotonic time is for measuring elapsed time and order inside a run. Wall time is useful to humans but can be adjusted.

questions.prompt: A log's events carry an increasing sequence number. What does that let a reader do?
options: Detect missing or reordered events
Join a decision to its later effect
Interpret fields whose format changed
Convert event times into calendar dates
questions.explanation: Sequence numbers run in order, so gaps and reordering show. A correlation ID does the joining, and a version field handles format changes.

questions.prompt: Why would a log record carry a format version number?
options: So readers can reject formats they cannot read
So newer records can overwrite older records in the log
So events can be ordered by their version numbers
So the log can be compressed more tightly on disk
questions.explanation: A reader that sees an unknown version can refuse the event instead of guessing what the fields mean.

questions.prompt: Why must denied operations be recorded too?
options: Logging only successes leaves a blind spot where refusals hide
Denied operations change some state, so they have to be written down first
A denial record is what makes the decision take effect in the game engine
Logs without denials cannot be compressed or normalized by the analysis tool
questions.explanation: A silent refusal can preserve state while leaving diagnosis and coverage testing blind, because nobody can see the control working.

questions.prompt: Why prefer build ID plus entity ID plus generation to a raw pointer as an identity?
options: Allocations move and addresses can be reused by something else
Pointers cannot be written into an event on a 64-bit build
Entity IDs are always smaller, which saves queue space
Generation numbers are the only value a pointer can verify
questions.explanation: A pointer may later name a different object. A build, an entity ID, and a generation keep naming the same thing.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a useful detection rule over explicit game events?
options: An entity's generation number decreases
A player's health goes down
An event occurs more than once per minute
The log file grows larger than yesterday's
questions.explanation: A useful rule is a query over explicit events that signals a contradiction. A generation number should only grow, while ordinary changes in health are expected.

questions.prompt: What does normalization do before comparing two traces?
options: Replaces unstable values such as addresses and timestamps so traces compare
Sorts all events by correlation ID value so that the two traces will match up
Deletes denied decisions, which would otherwise differ from run to run in a trace
Converts every event to the newest schema version that the reader currently uses
questions.explanation: Line-by-line text comparison is noisy because addresses and times differ every run. Normalizing exposes the first meaningful divergence.

questions.prompt: Fixture: an allowed command whose effect event arrives late, and the rule fires. How is it classified?
options: False positive: no invariant fails, yet the rule fires
True positive: the rule fired, so a real violation must exist
False negative: the late event somehow escaped the rule
True negative: allowed commands never fire this kind of rule
questions.explanation: A true positive needs the invariant to actually fail. Here the command was valid, only its event was delayed.

questions.prompt: The effect changed state, but the decision event was dropped, and the rule stayed silent. How is that classified?
options: False negative, or insufficient evidence
False positive, because the rule did not fire
True positive, because the effect changed state
True negative, because there was no decision event
questions.explanation: The invariant failed, but the rule could not see it. That is why dropped events lower confidence.

questions.prompt: A report says the rule 'detected 100%'. What is missing?
options: The counts and the exact fixture set that were tested
The wall-clock time at which the rule was written
The thread ID that produced each detection
The monotonic clock readings for every fixture
questions.explanation: A percentage means nothing without knowing what was tested. Report counts and the fixtures.

questions.prompt: A time-critical hook cannot wait when its log queue is full, so it must drop events. What is the right policy about the loss?
options: Never hide it: count the drops and lower confidence
Hide it, since gaps would only confuse analysts later
Block the hook until space frees up, whatever it costs
Overwrite old events silently to keep the log current
questions.explanation: Bounded queues need a deliberate policy, but any policy must record that events were dropped so that analysts can tell.

questions.prompt: What does a repair test built from the minimal regression trace need to show?
options: The effect stays unchanged after a denial while valid commands still work
Every event in the trace is written in a single frame, very quickly in order
The correlation ID is reused so that later runs can be compared to this one
The queue size is increased so that no event can ever be dropped in future runs
questions.explanation: A repair that disables everything would also pass the first half, so a separate valid-command test keeps the repair honest.

questions.prompt: Which of the five boundaries asks when bytes were measured and how long the result is reused?
options: Time
Bytes
Consumer
Failure
questions.explanation: Bytes asks what is covered, Time asks when and for how long, Identity asks which object, Consumer asks which operation trusts the result, and Failure asks what happens when verification cannot finish.

questions.prompt: A toy checksum is id × 3 + health + max × 10. What does it return for id 5, health 40 and max 100?
questions.explanation: 5 × 3 = 15, plus 40, plus 100 × 10 = 1,000 gives 1,055. Dropping the weight on max gives 155, and dropping the id term gives 1,040.

questions.prompt: Rotating a number left by 3 bits, when no set bit reaches the top, equals which operation?
options: Multiplying by 2^3, which is 8
Multiplying by 3, the number of bits moved
Adding 3, the number of bits moved
Dividing by 8, which is 2^3
questions.explanation: Moving bits three places toward the high end multiplies by 8 when nothing wraps around.

questions.prompt: A checksum covers some fields of a record but not its limit field. The limit is then lowered below the current value and nothing recomputes the checksum. What happens when it is verified?
options: It still matches, since the limit field was never covered
It fails, since any change to a record changes its checksum
It fails, since the limit is lower than the current value
It is skipped, since uncovered fields disable the check
questions.explanation: The check honestly reports that every byte it covers is unchanged. The record is still impossible because the damaged field was never looked at.

questions.prompt: A checksum id × 3 + health + max × 10 was stored as 1,055 for (5, 40, 100). Then max changes to 60 and nothing is recomputed. What does verification compute, and what happens?
options: 655, which differs from the stored value, so it is caught
1,055, the stored value, so nothing is noticed
115, which differs from the stored value, so it is caught
655, which equals the stored value, so nothing is noticed
questions.explanation: 15 + 40 + 600 = 655, which differs from the stored 1,055. A checksum that covers every field catches the edit.

questions.prompt: Why would a verifier test both a checksum and a sanity rule such as health <= max?
options: They answer different questions
Either test alone would be too slow to run
The checksum cannot be computed without the rule
Doing two tests makes each one more accurate
questions.explanation: A record can pass one and fail the other in either direction, so a check that asks only one question accepts states the game forbids.

questions.prompt: What kind of claim does the toy checksum make?
options: It signals accidental corruption; it is not cryptographic authentication
It proves that the record was written by the game itself, not by a tool
It prevents anyone from changing a record unless they hold the secret key
It encrypts the record so the health value stays secret from other programs
questions.explanation: Anyone who knows the formula can recompute it, so it detects accidents only. Defending against a deliberate editor needs an authenticated owner and key lifecycle.

questions.prompt: A hash of a byte range matches. What does that tell you?
options: Those bytes matched when measured, and nothing about anything outside them
The whole process stays unchanged for as long as the game keeps on running
Every operation that uses the object later on will see a valid state
The display cache and the simulation object hold the very same values now
questions.explanation: A hash proves something about the covered bytes and moment. It does not describe other objects, other fields, or later changes.

questions.prompt: A verifier approved version 17 of a record. The record changed to version 18 before another step trusted the old approval. Which repair fits?
options: Compare the approval's version with the current one
The verifier approves faster, so that less time passes
The approval is stored longer so that it can be reused
The record is made read-only for the verifier
questions.explanation: The approval was correct for 17, but nothing tied it to that version. Comparing at the last step catches the staleness.

questions.prompt: Why return an enumerated failure reason instead of a plain true or false from an integrity check?
options: Different failures would otherwise blur together
Enumerations run faster than boolean values do
A boolean cannot represent a failure at all
The compiler requires enumerations for checks
questions.explanation: Explicit variants make tests state exactly which promise failed, and they keep an unreadable record from passing.

questions.prompt: A guarded read fails because memory could not be read. What should the check report?
options: An unreadable result, which is never treated as valid
A valid result, since nothing contradicted the record
A mismatch, since unreadable memory means tampering
Nothing; the check is skipped this time
questions.explanation: The failure should say what actually went wrong. Treating an unreadable record as valid would be the worst outcome.

questions.prompt: Why is an operation that checks and changes the same object under one exclusive borrow easy to reason about?
options: Nothing else can change it between check and change
The compiler proves that the record is always valid
The check and the change run on separate threads
Exclusive borrows make the record immutable
questions.explanation: Check and effect share one mutable borrow, so nothing else can touch the record between them. Across threads or processes that guarantee no longer holds.

questions.prompt: Why is a remote read followed by a remote write not atomic?
options: State can change in between; use versioned snapshots, expected bytes, or the owner
The write always starts running before the read has completed on the other process
Remote reads return stale cached bytes, which the later write then overwrites for good
Remote writes are checked by a different checksum function than the one the reads use
questions.explanation: Another thread or process can change the state between the two calls. The lesson suggests tying the write to a snapshot, comparing expected bytes, or sending a command to the owner.

questions.prompt: A heal adds an amount to health and clamps the result to the maximum. Health is 70, the maximum is 100, and the amount is 50. What is health afterward?
options: 100, since 120 is clamped to the maximum
120, since the sum is stored as it is
50, since the amount replaces the old health
20, the amount above the maximum
questions.explanation: The sum is 120, and clamping with min(100) limits it to 100.

questions.prompt: A checksum covers only some fields of a record. What follows for a field outside its coverage?
options: Changing it leaves verification unaffected
Changing it makes the verification fail
Changing it is blocked by the checksum
Changing it is detected by a later checksum run
questions.explanation: Verification covers only the fields the checksum includes, so a change outside it does not affect the result. That is acceptable for display-only data.

questions.prompt: Why should a verifier still reject health > max even if the checksum was recomputed to match?
options: A matching checksum does not make an impossible value meaningful
A recomputed checksum is usually forged, so it cannot match
Checksums reject values larger than the maximum automatically
The checksum is optional once the rule has run
questions.explanation: Checksum and range answer different questions. A consistent but impossible record should still be refused.

questions.prompt: What does flipping one bit in each covered field, one at a time, prove?
options: That the test suite notices missing coverage
That the checksum is cryptographically secure
That the generation field never wraps around
That the display cache matches the simulation
questions.explanation: If flipping a field's bit goes unnoticed, that field is not covered. The mutation test exposes the gap.

questions.prompt: In a monitoring pipeline, what is an 'assessment'?
options: An interpretation of signals, like 'needs another sample'
The raw measurement itself, before anyone looks at it
The action that the system takes after a decision is made
The recorded ordinary behavior used as a comparison point
questions.explanation: A signal is measured data, an assessment interprets it, and a response is what the system then does. A baseline is the recorded ordinary behavior.

questions.prompt: Why is folding a signal, a conclusion and an action into one hidden boolean flag a poor design?
options: It hides false positives and cannot be explained
Booleans use more memory than separate types would
Booleans cannot be used inside automated tests
Booleans make the code run noticeably slower
questions.explanation: With separate types, a test can show what was measured, what was concluded and what was done. A single flag hides all three.

questions.prompt: A simple 'is a debugger attached?' API call mostly amounts to reading what?
options: A flag the system stored in the process at start-up
A live measurement of the processor's timing behavior
A count of the breakpoints that exist in the code
