A list of every debugging tool that is running
questions.explanation: The loader records that the process was started under a debugger, and the call reads that note. Nothing is measured.

questions.prompt: How can a program notice a software breakpoint placed in its own code?
options: A checksum over its code changes, since a byte was replaced
The processor refuses to execute the code at that location
Its memory usage suddenly doubles in size without cause
The stack starts to grow in an unexpected direction
questions.explanation: A software breakpoint replaces an instruction byte, which a checksum over the code can see. Hardware breakpoints leave no such change in the code.

questions.prompt: Why does a checksum over a program's own code miss a hardware breakpoint?
options: It changes no code bytes; it lives in debug registers `DR0` to `DR3` and `DR7`
Hardware breakpoints rewrite the checksum along with the bytes that they change
The checksum runs before debug registers are loaded, so it never sees their values
Hardware breakpoints are removed from memory whenever a checksum starts running
questions.explanation: The two kinds of breakpoint leave traces in different places. Checking only bytes never sees a hardware one, and checking only debug registers never sees a software one.

questions.prompt: A routine reads another thread's saved register state to look at its debug registers. For which thread can the result be trusted?
options: A suspended thread; a running one may give invalid data
A running thread, since its state is always current
Any thread, as long as the call reports success
Only a thread that belongs to a different process
questions.explanation: A call on a thread that is running can return success with an invalid context, so the return code alone is not evidence.

questions.prompt: Median 1.2 us, 99th percentile 8 us, maximum 412 us. What happens with a 10 us threshold?
options: Ordinary background activity trips it several times a minute
It flags only the single 412 us outlier and nothing else
It never fires, since 10 us is higher than the median
It fires only when a debugger is attached to the process
questions.explanation: The ordinary but unlucky samples overlap the paused ones. A low threshold makes false positives a constant occurrence.

questions.prompt: With the same numbers, what is wrong with setting the threshold above 412 us?
options: Almost nothing would trigger it, including the very condition you meant to catch
It would trip on ordinary samples several times each minute, just as 10 us does
It would change the median of the baseline measurements taken on the clean fixture
It would make the maximum value fall below the 99th percentile of the same samples
questions.explanation: No single number separates ordinary from paused cleanly. A very high limit is quiet because the rule is too blind to fire.

questions.prompt: Twenty slow samples in a row came from the same code path. What does that justify?
options: Evidence of a changed environment, though load or power policy may be the cause
A firm conclusion that a debugger must be attached to the game for the whole run
Proof that the game rules were violated by the player during these twenty samples
Permission to refuse every later command from the player after the twentieth sample
questions.explanation: Repetition is stronger than one sample, but it does not reveal intent. Persistent load, power policy, or an attached debugger can all do it.

questions.prompt: A function returns 'ordinary' when a delay is at or below a recorded 99th-percentile limit of 12 microseconds, and 'needs another sample' above it. What does it return for delays of 12 and 13?
options: Ordinary for 12, and needs another sample for 13
Needs another sample for 12, and ordinary for 13
Needs another sample for both of the delays
Ordinary for both of the delays given
questions.explanation: The check is delay <= limit, so 12 is ordinary and 13 is above the limit.

questions.prompt: Which description names a response precisely?
options: After two samples over p99 it enters `Diagnosing`; no game state changes
The game detects a debugger as soon as a long delay is seen in a sample
The anti-debug routine reacts whenever it spots something that looks suspicious
The detector decides the player is cheating after repeated timing signals
questions.explanation: A precise description lists the trigger, the state reached, the event emitted, and the effect. Vague statements hide the decision.

questions.prompt: When reversing an unfamiliar anti-debug routine, what does tracing forward from the branch find?
options: Every response and shared sink that the branch can reach
The signals and stored history that fed the branch before it ran
The ordinary variation seen across a set of several clean runs
Whether the routine happens to run on a suspended thread
questions.explanation: Backward from the branch finds signals and history; forward finds responses and sinks. Clean runs estimate ordinary variation.

questions.prompt: The test matrix has an invalid health command with no environment signals. What is expected?
options: The environment is ordinary, the command is rejected, and health is unchanged
The command is accepted, since the quiet environment shows no sign of a debugger
The command is accepted but a diagnostic event is written
The environment is reported as suspicious, and health is unchanged
questions.explanation: A quiet environment must not turn an invalid operation into a valid one. State validity is enforced at the state-changing boundary.

questions.prompt: In security design, what does 'fail-closed' mean?
options: When unsure, the risky effect is refused
When the system is unsure, the effect is allowed
The system stops itself whenever any error occurs
Failures are recorded but otherwise ignored
questions.explanation: Fail-open and fail-closed describe whether doubt permits or refuses an effect.

questions.prompt: Which situation is a false negative for an anti-debug detector?
options: The target condition occurs without the expected signal appearing
An ordinary slow frame is classified as suspicious by the detector
A clean run is accepted as normal behavior by the detector
A debugger is attached and the detector reports it correctly
questions.explanation: A false positive is an ordinary condition classified as suspicious. A false negative misses the target condition.

questions.prompt: Why should a game's state rules be enforced where the effect happens, rather than relying on a signal about the environment?
options: Signals are only evidence; the rule must always hold
Environment signals are always accurate, but they are slower
Rules cannot be enforced at the place where the effect occurs
Signals are impossible to measure in a running game
questions.explanation: The environment is evidence about the setting, not a verdict about the game state. The state rule must hold whether or not any signal is present.

questions.prompt: In a table of timing measurements, how should the maximum be treated?
options: As one extreme event to inspect, not to generalize from
As the best estimate of the typical duration of a sample
As the threshold that should be used for the detector
As proof that an observer was attached to the process
questions.explanation: The median gives the typical duration, percentiles give ordinary tail latency, and the maximum is a single extreme.

questions.prompt: Which pair of the five terms involves a secret?
options: Authentication and encryption
Obfuscation and encryption
Compression and obfuscation
Serialization and authentication
questions.explanation: Only authentication and encryption need a secret key. Compression, serialization, and obfuscation do not, which is why mistaking obfuscation for encryption sends you hunting for a key that was never there.

questions.prompt: A stored value looks random in a memory viewer. Why is it a mistake to assume encryption?
options: Obfuscation also looks like noise, and there may be no key to find
Random-looking bytes are always plain integers stored in hexadecimal
Encryption cannot be applied to a game value held in memory
Every transform that changes the bytes is a form of compression
questions.explanation: Looking like noise says almost nothing. Obfuscation is a reversible representation, so a hunt for a key can waste days.

questions.prompt: Why should an integrity tag be verified before the decoded value is used?
options: Edited bytes still decode to a plausible number, so a clean decode proves little
Decoding fails whenever the stored bytes were changed, so the tag adds nothing new
The tag holds the very key that is needed to decode the stored value
A tag checked after decoding would no longer match the stored bytes at all
questions.explanation: A value that decodes cleanly is not the same as one nobody tampered with. The tag check is what looks for modification.

questions.prompt: Why does applying the same key a second time undo the XOR step?
options: Because `x ^ k ^ k == x`, as each bit is flipped twice
Because XOR with a key always sets all bits back to zero
Because the key is removed from memory after the first use
Because a second XOR rotates the bits back by seven places
questions.explanation: XOR flips the bits where the key has a 1. Flipping them again restores the original.

questions.prompt: In hexadecimal, what is the 32-bit value 200?
questions.explanation: 200 = 12 × 16 + 8, and 12 is C in hexadecimal, so the value is 0xC8. Copying the decimal digits gives the wrong 0x200.

questions.prompt: What is 0x0F XOR 0xA5?
options: `0xAA`
`0xAF`
questions.explanation: Written in binary, 0000 1111 XOR 1010 0101 is 1010 1010, which is 0xAA. Addition, OR and AND give the other three values.

questions.prompt: How does rotating a 32-bit value left by 5 bits differ from shifting it left by 5?
options: Rotating brings the bits pushed off the top back in at the bottom
Rotating fills the bottom with zeros and shifting brings bits back
Rotating moves the bits right and shifting moves them left
They are identical for every possible value
questions.explanation: A rotate loses nothing, since bits that fall off the high end return at the low end. A plain shift drops them.

questions.prompt: A game stores a number only after XORing and rotating it with a secret key. A memory scan searches for the plain number's bytes. What happens?
options: Nothing matches, since the stored bytes look different
It finds the value, since XOR leaves the value's bytes intact
It finds the key instead of the value
It finds every copy, since rotation preserves all bytes
questions.explanation: A plain value would be stored with its own bytes. The encoded field has no such bytes, so a scan for the plain number misses it.

questions.prompt: A transform XORs a value with a key and then rotates it left by a fixed count. Two plain values that differ only in bit 0 give stored values that differ in one bit. What does that bit's position reveal?
options: The rotation count, since the key cancels out
The key's value, since the key appears in the difference
The plain values themselves, which are stored as they are
The number of times the transform was applied
questions.explanation: XOR cancels the key, so the difference between the stored values is the difference of the plain values rotated. A single flipped bit shows how far the rotation moved it.

questions.prompt: In a transform that XORs with a key and then rotates, why does encoding the value 0 expose the key?
options: Zero XOR key is the key, so storage holds the rotated key
Zero cannot be rotated, so the key leaks as an error
Zero is stored unchanged, which shows the key's length
XOR with zero reveals only the rotation count used
questions.explanation: The stored value is the key rotated left, so rotating it back right recovers the key.

questions.prompt: The same plain value encodes to different stored bytes after a restart. What does that suggest?
options: The key is not constant; it is made per session or per object
The rotation count changes after every restart of the program, from 7 to a new number
The value is compressed in a different way on each run of the game
The integrity tag is being computed over a different build of the game program
questions.explanation: A fixed key gives fixed output. Differences suggest the key (or a nearby key field) has to be recovered for each session or object.

questions.prompt: For a transform that XORs with a key and then rotates, what is the XOR of two encoded values?
options: The plain values' XOR, rotated, with the key cancelled
The key rotated by the difference between the values
The XOR of the plain values with the key still included
Always zero, since both used the same key
questions.explanation: Rotation only moves bits and XOR works bit by bit, so the key appears twice and cancels, since key XOR key is 0.

questions.prompt: Rotating the 7-bit value 90 left by 4 within a 32-bit word, where no bit reaches the top, gives what number?
questions.explanation: Rotating left by 4 with no wrap is a multiplication by 2^4 = 16, and 90 × 16 = 1,440.

questions.prompt: Why must a decoder reproduce operand widths exactly?
options: An 8-bit rotate is not a 32-bit rotate, and truncation or byte order matters
Wider arithmetic is always more accurate, so a decoder should always prefer it to the narrow one
Narrow widths are required to keep the key secret from a debugger that is attached to it
The width only matters for compression of data, not for any obfuscation of its values
questions.explanation: Machine arithmetic happens at a width. The example only comes out right because the rotation is 32-bit and the bytes are read lowest first.

questions.prompt: For multiplication modulo 2^32, which multiplier can be undone?
options: Any odd multiplier, because each one has a multiplicative inverse here
Any even multiplier, because two even numbers cancel each other out when divided
Only a multiplier that is an exact power of two, such as 128 or 256
Only multipliers that are smaller than 256, since they fit in one byte
questions.explanation: Only an odd multiplier has an inverse mod 2^32. An even multiplier discards information, so the transform cannot be reversed.

questions.prompt: Why is the toy tag beside an encoded value not cryptographic authentication?
options: Anyone who knows the algorithm and key can recompute it
It is stored in plain bytes, and plain bytes can be copied
It is shorter than a hash, so collisions are certain
It is checked after decoding rather than before
questions.explanation: A toy integrity relation catches accidental changes. It does not stop a party who can reproduce the relation.

questions.prompt: Which test checks that a decoder correctly reverses an encoder?
options: decode(encode(value, key), key) equals value for many inputs
encode(value, key) equals value, over edge values
decode(value, key) equals encode(value, key) for every value
encode(encode(value, key), key) equals the key
questions.explanation: A round trip must restore the original. Edge values such as 0, 1, the maximum, and carry boundaries make good test inputs.

questions.prompt: What should a mutation test do with the toy tag?
options: Flip each encoded bit and confirm the tag check refuses the changed sample
Flip each plain bit and confirm that the decode of it still works as before
Delete the tag and confirm that the value still decodes unchanged afterward
Change the key and confirm that the stored bytes stay exactly the same as before
questions.explanation: If a flipped bit is not caught, the tag does not cover it.

questions.prompt: Which row of the comparison table describes authenticated encryption?
options: Nonces make repeated values encrypt differently, and a built-in tag detects changes
Repeated values may reveal obvious patterns, and any tag is an optional ad-hoc add-on to it
No durable secret is needed, and the analysis recovers the transform itself from reading it
The purpose is to change the representation, with no promise of secrecy made at all
questions.explanation: Authenticated encryption keeps data secret and detects modification. Reversible obfuscation only changes representation.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a useful clue in a read path that a stored value is encoded?
options: A conversion to float or a clamp right after the value is decoded
A call that prints the stored value to the console right before every use of it
A branch that always accepts the value without ever comparing it to a limit
A single store of the value at the very start of the program run, with no reads
questions.explanation: Clues include XOR, rotate, byte-swap, add, subtract, and odd multiplies, a nearby key or generation field, duplicate calculations before a comparison, a rejecting branch, and a float conversion or clamp after decoding.

questions.prompt: A policy meant to enforce read-only mode blocks only a command named 'write'. A different command named 'patch' that also changes state is requested. What does the policy do?
options: Allows it, since the name is not on its list
Blocks it, since both commands change state
Blocks it, since unknown names are denied by default
Allows it, since patch commands are read-only
questions.explanation: The weak rule asks which command this is, and 'patch' is not on its list. It reaches the same state-changing effect that the policy claimed to stop.

questions.prompt: What is the weakness of a rule that blocks commands by their names?
options: It covers only listed names, not every command with that effect
It is slower than a rule that checks the real effect of commands
It blocks commands that have no effect on the state at all
It cannot be tested with any kind of automated test
questions.explanation: A deny list covers the spellings someone thought of. Another name with the same effect slips through.

questions.prompt: Why is adding more forbidden names to the denylist not a real fix?
options: There are as many names as commands, so the list is never complete
Forbidden names slow down the policy, so the lab would run too slowly
The compiler rejects an enum with more than three blocked names
Extra names make `Observe` look like a state-changing command
questions.explanation: A question about names has as many answers as there are names. A question about effect has a fixed number of answers and can be answered completely.

questions.prompt: Why is classifying each command by its effect on state (read-only or changes state) stronger than keeping a list of forbidden names?
options: A fixed set of answers lets the rule cover every case
Effects are cheaper for the computer to work out than names are
A list of names can be edited by players who read the game
Effects stay the same between all versions of the game
questions.explanation: A fixed, small set of answers means the rule can cover every case. A rule about names can never be complete.

questions.prompt: In Rust, a match over an enum must cover every variant. What does that do when a new variant is added to an enum that a classification function matches on?
options: The code fails to compile until it is classified
The new variant is treated as read-only by default
The new variant is ignored at run time
The compiler guesses a classification for it
questions.explanation: The match makes the classification decision unavoidable, so a list that would need extending forever becomes one decision made once per variant.

questions.prompt: A policy classifies commands by effect: read-only or changes state. In read-only mode, which commands should it accept?
options: Those whose effect is read-only
Those that change state but only a little
Those whose names do not contain 'write'
Any command that comes from a trusted source
questions.explanation: Only read-only effects pass in read-only mode. Every command that changes state is refused, whatever it is called.

questions.prompt: What should a regression test for an effect-based read-only policy do?
options: Check that every state-changing variant is denied
Test only the command named in the original bug report
Test that read-only commands are also denied
Test that the policy source file compiles
questions.explanation: Looping over every state-changing variant means a new variant has to be classified and tested, so the gap cannot silently return.

questions.prompt: A function checks a build number, then the build changes before the write happens, and the write still goes ahead. What is this kind of gap called?
options: A time-of-check, time-of-use gap (a stale decision)
An integer overflow, where a number wraps around
A privilege escalation, where rights are raised
A buffer overflow, where a write goes too far
questions.explanation: The decision was true when made and stale by the time it was used, so the write relied on an old check.

questions.prompt: Where does the repair for Recipe 2 put its validation?
options: Beside the write, checking both the build and the expected old byte
Before the program starts, checking the build only once for the whole run
After the write is done, undoing the change if the build ID differs
In the menu, so that the user can never select a stale command from it
questions.explanation: Checking right next to the write shrinks the gap and lets a changed byte be refused as `state changed`.

questions.prompt: Why can the toy's TOCTOU repair not fully close the gap in a real game process?
options: The target can still change between two calls, and another process cannot be frozen
Real processes ignore expected-byte comparisons for performance reasons in games
Real games encrypt the build ID, so that the check cannot read it at all
A real game has more than one build ID that must be compared at a given time
questions.explanation: So keep the interval small, compare expected bytes, report a mismatch as a normal refusal, and make the operation reversible.

questions.prompt: The old Recipe 3 code denies a write but records no event. Why is that still a problem?
options: A reader cannot tell 'nothing happened' from 'a request was blocked'
The denial lets the write go through without ever checking a policy at all
The event list overflows because every denial is counted twice in the lab
The policy returns `Allowed` for every later command that follows the denial
questions.explanation: It is a telemetry gap, not a control bypass: state is protected, but repeated mistakes are hidden and the control is hard to test.

questions.prompt: What is the fix for the missing denial event?
options: Compute the decision first, then log it whichever way it went
Log the command before the policy runs, then delete denied entries
Log only denied commands, since allowed ones are visible in effects
Return `Denied` early, then log in a separate cleanup step
questions.explanation: Both outcomes must produce an event, so decision and logging are separated.

questions.prompt: Which of these should an audit event not contain?
options: Raw memory contents, secrets, or giant payloads in events
The time and the operation category of the request, kept short
The allow or deny decision of the policy, kept as a short word
A bounded reason code that explains the decision made
questions.explanation: Useful events record time, category, verified target identity, the decision, and a bounded reason, while avoiding secrets, raw memory, keys, and huge payloads.

questions.prompt: A weak control promised to stop all state changes in read-only mode but checked only a single command's name. What did it actually check?
options: One command name, and nothing about the others
Every command's effect on state
The sink where every state change arrives
Whether the caller held the right permissions
questions.explanation: The promise was about state change, but the check covered one name, so an equivalent command reached the same sink.

questions.prompt: Why can a detector not read a player's intent?
options: It can only measure signals such as flags or timing and apply a rule
Intent is stored in a field that the detector is simply not permitted to read
Detectors run before the player ever acts, so that there is nothing for them to see
Intent can be read only for commands that the lab has already blocked earlier
questions.explanation: A detector observes proxies. A process name, timing gap, or flag often accompanies a violation without being the invariant itself.

questions.prompt: A detection rule fires on a harmless profiler. How is that classified?
options: A false positive: a compatibility bug to fix
A true positive: any attached tool is hostile
A false negative: the rule missed a real threat
A true negative: the profiler was correctly ignored
questions.explanation: A harmless tool producing the signal belongs in the false-positive row. It points to a rule that needs fixing.

questions.prompt: In the four-outcome table, which row is 'the prohibited effect occurs without the expected signal'?
options: False negative
False positive
True positive
True negative
questions.explanation: A true positive has both signal and prohibited condition. A false negative has the prohibited condition but no signal.

questions.prompt: Controls such as a greyed-out button or a one-field checksum check a stand-in for the rule. What weakness do they share?
options: They check something near the property, not the property
They are too slow to run on every single action taken
They cannot be tested with any automated tests at all
They depend on secret keys that could leak out someday
questions.explanation: A greyed-out button, a one-field checksum and a debugger flag are all easier to check than the real rule, and each can be true while the real property is false.

questions.prompt: What is the repair for all three weak controls?
options: Enforce the invariant at the effect boundary; keep the proxy as a clue
Add more proxy checks until every known path is covered by at least one of them
Make the proxy signal harder to change, so that it can be trusted as permission
Move the proxy check earlier in the frame, so that it runs before any input arrives
questions.explanation: The repair is never 'add more stand-ins'. It is to check where the effect becomes real and demote the stand-in to supporting telemetry.

questions.prompt: Why is a user-interface flag such as 'button unlocked' a poor basis for deciding whether the engine may change a score?
options: It describes how things look, not whether the engine may act
UI flags are stored in files that cannot be edited by anyone
UI flags are updated too slowly to be of any use at all
UI flags are not available to any game code that runs
questions.explanation: Presentation state is a copy used for drawing. Scripts, other inputs and restored UI state can reach the same engine operation without it.

questions.prompt: An engine's policy says an action is not allowed, but a function checks only a UI flag, which is set to true. The function is called. What happens?
options: The action is allowed and the effect happens despite policy
The action is denied, since the policy is checked second
The function raises an error, since the two values disagree
The action is queued until the policy changes
questions.explanation: The weak function reads only the UI flag, so it allows the action. An allowed event with a changed value while policy is false is the evidence of the contradiction.

questions.prompt: A repaired method no longer trusts a UI flag. In its regression test, what should the flag be set to, and what must the test prove?
options: Leave it true, and prove the action is denied by policy
Set it false, and prove the action is denied
Leave it true, and prove the action is allowed
Remove it from the test, and prove the action is allowed
questions.explanation: Keeping the old precondition true shows that the repaired method no longer trusts it. A second test shows that a valid policy still permits a bounded action.

questions.prompt: A weak checksum is computed from only the health field of a record that also has a maximum-health field. What question does it answer?
options: Only whether health has changed
Whether the whole record is valid
Whether health is within the maximum
Whether any field has been edited
questions.explanation: It answers only 'did the health field change?'. Changing the maximum can break the relationship while the stored checksum still matches.

questions.prompt: A record has health 80 and maximum 100, with a checksum covering only health. The maximum is changed to 60 and the checksum is not recomputed. Why does the weak check pass while a full relation check fails?
options: The full check tests health <= maximum; the weak one ignores it
The weak check recomputes the checksum with the new maximum
The full check uses a different checksum, so it must fail
The weak check ignores health and tests the maximum only
questions.explanation: This is a coverage bypass: the change falls outside the measured bytes but changes the meaning of the protected state.

questions.prompt: What is a meaningful change outside the data a control examines called?
options: A coverage bypass
A replay attack
A false positive
A race condition
questions.explanation: A coverage bypass is a change the control never measured. The effect boundary is the point where a change becomes canonical.

questions.prompt: Which fields does the repaired relation cover?
options: Player ID, health, maximum health, and generation, plus a separate range check
Health only, with a much stronger multiplier so that changes are noticed more
Health and maximum health only, because identity is already checked somewhere else
Every field, with the range check removed since the checksum already covers that
questions.explanation: Coverage and the range rule answer different questions. Specific failures such as `ChecksumMismatch` or `OutOfRange` should be reported separately.

questions.prompt: What does the regression suite for the checksum repair do?
options: Mutates each covered field in turn, expects failure, and keeps a valid record passing
Mutates only health, because that is the field the old checksum already covered
Mutates every field together at once and asserts one single combined failure
Replaces the checksum with a larger number and then tests only the valid records
questions.explanation: Keeping a valid record shows verification is not permanently closed, so a repair that rejects everything would fail the suite.

questions.prompt: If anyone can recompute an unkeyed checksum, what does a system need to defend against a deliberate editor?
options: Real authentication, not a more obscure formula
A longer checksum with many more digits in it
A more obscure formula, kept secret from everyone
A checksum computed twice with different seeds
questions.explanation: A checksum detects accidental corruption. Defending against a deliberate editor takes real authentication, not obscurity.

questions.prompt: A health-setting function refuses a request only when an 'environment flagged' signal is present. What does it do otherwise?
options: Stores any value, since the flag describes the environment
Checks the value against the maximum before storing it
Refuses any value that looks unusual or very large
Asks the engine to validate the request first
questions.explanation: Otherwise it stores any number. The flag describes the environment, not the command.

questions.prompt: Health is 80 and the maximum is 100. A function that checks only an environment signal is asked to set health to 500, with an 'ordinary' signal. What results?
options: Allowed, and health becomes 500, breaking health <= maximum
It is denied, since an ordinary signal means a suspicious value
It is clamped to 100, since the function enforces the maximum
It is allowed, but health stays at 80
questions.explanation: No signal is hidden or changed. The absence of one signal says nothing about whether the requested value is valid.

questions.prompt: The repaired health command creates two independent events. What are they?
options: An environment observation, and a decision validating `value <= maximum_health`
A snapshot event, and an effect event that records the changed health value
A denial event, and an allow event, so that both outcomes are always written
A checksum event, and a generation event for the record that was changed
questions.explanation: Keeping them separate means the environment record never grants or removes the health invariant.

questions.prompt: A repaired health command must hold whether or not an environment signal is present. Which test coverage follows?
options: All four combinations of signal and value validity
Only the flagged signal, tried with invalid values
Only the ordinary signal, tried with valid values
One test with a random signal and a random value
questions.explanation: The repaired rule must hold whether or not the signal is present, so each combination must give the expected decision.

questions.prompt: In the repaired design, what role does the observer flag still play?
options: It helps diagnose a run; it neither grants nor removes the health rule
It grants permission to change health once it has been recorded in a log
It replaces the maximum health check whenever the environment is flagged
It decides whether the decision event is written to the telemetry log at all
questions.explanation: The flag is a clue, not the invariant, and the health relation holds regardless of it.

questions.prompt: What must a complete regression pair prove?
options: The old case is denied, state unchanged; a valid case is allowed and changes only what it should
The old failing case is logged with a reason code, and the valid case is skipped as a result
The valid case still works, and the old failing case is documented in the test notes
Both cases give the same decision and the same event, so that behavior is consistent
questions.explanation: The negative test reproduces the old preconditions and expects a refusal with the canonical state untouched. The positive test shows the repair has not disabled the feature.

questions.prompt: In an unsigned 64-bit calculation that wraps silently, an offset is 2 below the largest value and the length is 8. What does offset + length evaluate to?
options: 6, so a check against a limit of 4,096 wrongly passes
2^64 + 6, which is larger than the limit and fails the check
A panic in every build, so the check never runs
The largest value, because the sum saturates
questions.explanation: The sum is computed modulo 2^64, so it wraps past zero to a small number. Nothing panics in a release build, and the comparison on the wrapped number is simply true.

questions.prompt: What does a checked addition do when the true sum does not fit in the integer type?
options: Reports failure instead of wrapping around
Wraps around silently, like plain addition does
Rounds the sum to the largest representable value
Switches to a larger integer type
questions.explanation: A checked operation returns an optional result: a value when the sum fits and nothing when it does not. A repair can turn that into a denial.

questions.prompt: A check allows any path whose characters begin with 'assets/'. Why does 'assets/../saves/profile' slip through?
options: It tests the string, but the string resolves outside assets
The check is case-sensitive, so capital letters get past it
The check runs on files only and never on folders
The dots are removed before the check ever runs
questions.explanation: The prefix test reads text, while the rule is about the resolved location. That path resolves to a spot outside the allowed root.

questions.prompt: A path resolver handles '..' by removing the last segment. What should it do when a '..' would climb above the root?
options: Return a clear 'escapes the root' answer instead of clamping quietly
Stay at the root and carry on as if the segment were not there
Ignore it and treat the rest as relative to the current folder
Wrap around to the deepest folder
questions.explanation: When there is nothing left to remove, the caller needs to know. Quietly clamping at the root would hide the escape attempt.

questions.prompt: A verification function returns a result that holds either a true or false answer, or an error. Which three outcomes does that represent?
options: Matched, did not match, and could not tell
Allowed, denied, and logged for review
Fast, slow, and failed with an error
Signed, unsigned, and revoked by a vendor
questions.explanation: True is a match, false is a mismatch, and an error means verification could not run. Turning the error into 'true' folds the third outcome into the first, which is the bug.

questions.prompt: A gate denies with one reason when a file changed and with another when verification could not run. Why keep them separate?
options: One means the file changed, the other the safeguard broke
Separate reasons make the log files shorter on disk
Two reasons are required before the gate can compile
The player must see both messages in the game window
questions.explanation: A mismatch says the asset changed, while an unavailable check says the safeguard is broken, which is a larger problem. People respond differently to each.

questions.prompt: A batch helper loops over items and calls a private writer directly, while the normal entry point applies a policy check and logs. What is wrong?
options: It routes around the guard, so no check or log happens
It runs the policy check, but too late to matter
It logs each write twice, so the log becomes unreadable
It weakened the guard so that it accepts everything
questions.explanation: The guard was never weakened, it was routed around. The batch path reaches the same effect without passing through the check, and the audit log shows nothing while bytes changed.

questions.prompt: What is the structural repair for a helper that bypasses a write guard?
options: Make it call the guarded entry point, so there is one door
Copy the guard's check into the helper as well, to be safe
Make the private writer public so everyone can check it
Remove the guard, since the helper is trusted
questions.explanation: One way in means one place to be correct. A second copy of the check is tempting but can drift out of step with the first.

questions.prompt: A command carries a valid integrity tag and awards 30 coins. A weak receiver accepts it each time it is submitted, and it is submitted 5 times. What is the balance, starting from 0?
options: 150, since a valid tag does not prove it was unused
30, since the receiver ignores duplicate commands
0, since a valid tag blocks any reuse of a command
5, since only the number of submissions is recorded
questions.explanation: A tag shows the bytes were not changed. It does not show the command was not already used, so each genuine copy pays out: 5 × 30 = 150.

questions.prompt: A receiver denies a command whose sequence number is less than or equal to the last applied one, and number 3 was just applied. Which command is accepted?
options: One numbered 4, with any tag
One numbered 3, with a fresh tag
One numbered 2, with a larger amount
One numbered 1, with the same amount
questions.explanation: Only a number strictly past the last applied one passes. Changing the amount or re-tagging does not change the number, so those are still stale.

questions.prompt: A design claims to stop replayed messages while remembering nothing between messages. What follows?
options: It cannot stop replay; it must remember a counter or window
It works if the key is long enough to resist guessing
It works because every message carries a valid tag on it
It works if messages travel over an encrypted channel
questions.explanation: The receiver has to remember something, such as a counter, a window of recent identifiers or a timestamp with bounded skew. A longer key does not tell it that a genuine message was already used.

questions.prompt: A tool reads 'writes allowed' once, caches the answer and reuses it. Writes are later switched off. What happens next?
options: It keeps writing, reusing the answer stored on the first call
It stops writing at once, since the setting is read again
It stops after the cache expires on its own
It raises an error because the cache disagrees
questions.explanation: The first call stores the answer, and every later call returns that stored value. The repair is to read the setting where the write happens.

questions.prompt: A teammate says, "We are single-threaded, so we can skip reviewing for cached-decision bugs." What is the best reply?
options: Nothing raced in the lab; a stale answer needs only an input that changed afterwards
True for most code, but the lab's cache is shared with a background timer thread
One thread is enough, as long as the cache is cleared whenever the program starts
Single-threaded code is safe here, though an optimised build can reorder the cache reads
questions.explanation: The answer simply outlived the input it was computed from. No unlucky timing or second thread is needed, so single-threaded code can have this bug too.

questions.prompt: The movement rule has a maximum step of 400 cm and a tolerance of 5 cm. A player takes 405 cm steps for 600 ticks. How much free distance has been gained beyond the maximum?
options: 3,000 cm, which is 30 metres, with every single tick passing its own check
300 cm, which is 3 metres, because most ticks are rejected as over the limit
5 cm, because the tolerance is only granted once for the whole run
240,000 cm, because the 400 cm maximum is also added on each tick
questions.explanation: Each tick passes, and the excess is 5 cm per tick: 600 x 5 = 3,000 cm. No individual check was wrong; the tolerance simply accumulated.

questions.prompt: Why does the window budget cost honest players nothing when their jitter averages out?
options: A step at or below the maximum spends zero budget, because the excess is clamped at 0
Jitter is filtered out of each step before the step length is measured against the rule
The budget refills in full after every tick, so only a single tick can ever exceed it
Each tick's unused tolerance is subtracted from the next tick's step, cancelling the jitter
questions.explanation: The repair computes `(step - MAX).max(0)` and spends only that. Steps under the maximum spend nothing, while a steady lean in one direction runs the budget out.

questions.prompt: A repair is tested only with inputs that must be denied. What risk does that leave?
options: It may be tightened until ordinary use breaks
It may drift back toward allowing denied inputs
It may be skipped when tests run in parallel
It may allow every input
questions.explanation: A negative-only test pushes toward ever stricter rules, so honest use starts failing. A positive-only test is what lets a rule drift back. Both are needed.

questions.prompt: A batch writes items in order and validates each one just before writing it. The second of two items is invalid. What do the result and the state show?
options: A denial, but the first item is already written
A denial, with no item written, since the batch is atomic
Success, since the first item was valid
A denial, with both items written anyway
questions.explanation: The first item is written before the second is rejected, so the denial is honest but the state is half-applied. A repair validates the whole batch first.

questions.prompt: What does the repair for a batch that fails halfway do?
options: It validates every item first and writes only once the whole request is known to be acceptable
It writes valid items as it goes and skips invalid ones, reporting `Allowed` for the batch
It validates only the first and last items, then writes the whole list in one pass
It writes every item, then tells callers in a comment to re-check the slots
questions.explanation: Two-phase apply means a denial genuinely means no change. Skipping bad items is tempting, but then the caller gets a state it never asked for. If atomic writes are impossible, the lesson wants an explicit rollback, not a comment.

questions.prompt: What shape do many bypass patterns share?
options: A control checks a stand-in that drifts from the real promise
A control is switched off, and then the effect happens freely
A control is too slow, so the effect happens before it
A control is guessed by an attacker, and the effect is blocked
questions.explanation: In every case the control measured something true, but something true was not the same as the thing promised. The repair moves the check to the effect itself.

questions.prompt: Why is asking a slice for a range with a checked getter better than comparing offsets by hand?
options: It knows its own length, so it refuses ranges it lacks
It widens the integers, so overflow cannot occur
It skips bounds checks in release builds for speed
It copies the range, so later changes are invisible
questions.explanation: Asking a value that knows the answer beats recomputing the answer yourself. The slice cannot be argued out of its own length.

questions.prompt: Which question does a debugger answer that a memory scanner cannot?
options: Which instruction just touched the value
Where might this value live in memory
Which value type the game uses for gold
How many copies of the value exist in RAM
questions.explanation: A scanner lists candidate locations for a value. A debugger pauses the program so you can see the instruction that accessed it.

questions.prompt: What does a write breakpoint on a memory location ask a debugger to do?
options: Pause when an instruction stores to those bytes
Pause when any instruction reads from those bytes
Block the write so that the value cannot be changed
Pause at the first instruction of the function that owns that memory
questions.explanation: A write breakpoint waits for a store to the watched bytes and pauses there. It does not stop the write, and plain reads do not trigger a write-only watch.

questions.prompt: Why should you perform exactly one gold-changing action while the breakpoint is set?
options: So the pause can be tied to that action
So the debugger records fewer registers in its log
So the gold address stays the same after a restart
So Windows keeps the thread's context from expiring
questions.explanation: If several actions happen, you cannot tell which one caused a given pause. One action gives one clean cause and effect.

questions.prompt: A write breakpoint fires on a purchase. What does that pause establish?
options: One execution; a later test shows if other actions use it too
That the instruction handles recruiting units and nothing else
That the instruction is the only code that ever writes the gold
That the instruction subtracts the unit price in every build
questions.explanation: The pause is evidence of one execution. The same instruction could also run for other gold changes, which a later test can check.

questions.prompt: Which item can you inspect when a debugger pauses a process?
options: The condition flags used by branches
The source-code variable names of the game
The next game turn's gold amount
The compiler settings used to build the game
questions.explanation: At a pause you can see the next instruction, registers, call stack, nearby memory, and flags. Source names and future values are not there.

questions.prompt: On x86-64, the register rax holds 0xAABBCCDD11223344. What does its 32-bit part, eax, hold?
options: 0x11223344, the low 32 bits
0xAABBCCDD, the high 32 bits
0x00000044, just the lowest byte
0x00003344, just the low 16 bits
questions.explanation: eax is the low half of rax, not a separate register. The low 16 bits are ax and the low 8 bits are al.

questions.prompt: On x86-64, an instruction writes to a 32-bit register name such as eax. What happens to the upper half of the full 64-bit register?
options: It is cleared to zero
It is left exactly as it was
It is set to all ones
It is copied into the lower half
questions.explanation: Writing a 32-bit register name also clears the upper half of the 64-bit register. Writing the 16-bit or 8-bit names leaves the rest alone.

questions.prompt: A register holds 0x7000 and an instruction reads memory at [register+20h]. Which address does it use?
options: 0x7020, since 20h is 32 bytes past the base
0x0020, since the offset replaces the base
0x7200, since the offset is appended to the base
0x6FE0, since the offset is taken away from the base
questions.explanation: The brackets mean base plus offset, and 20h is 32 in decimal. An offset is a distance, not a replacement address.

questions.prompt: A debugger stops on a subtract instruction that changes the watched value. What evidence best confirms it is the instruction behind the game action you triggered?
options: Its target and amount match the watched address and price on every repeat
It uses a subtract operation, which is what a spend has to look like
It was the first stop the debugger made, so it has to be the right one
Its register names match the ones that were shown in a tutorial online
questions.explanation: Recognizing an operation proves little. Matching both the address and the amount over repeated actions is strong evidence.

questions.prompt: What question does the call stack answer at a pause?
options: Which chain of function calls brought this thread here
Which values were stored in every register earlier
Which instructions will run after the next branch
Which memory addresses the thread has written so far
questions.explanation: A low-level update function may be called from a recruit action, an AI simulation, or a save loader. The stack shows which one led here.

questions.prompt: How does a debugger learn that a thread reached a breakpoint?
options: Windows sends it a debug event after the process pauses
The game sends its own message through a shared file
The debugger polls the registers in a loop between frames
The CPU notifies the debugger directly, skipping Windows
questions.explanation: The debugger is a separate process, and Windows remains the gatekeeper that reports debug events such as breakpoints and DLL loads.

questions.prompt: In debugger terms, what is a thread's context?
options: A snapshot of its registers, with the instruction pointer
A copy of the whole process memory taken when it launched
A list of every function that the thread has ever called
The source file in which the thread's code was written
questions.explanation: The debugger asks Windows for the context of the stopped thread. It can also copy memory separately.

questions.prompt: Why can audio and rendering stop while you inspect a breakpoint?
options: The debugger pauses the whole process so reads stay stable
Breakpoints always lower the process priority for good
The game switches off its media threads after any exception
Windows frees those threads' memory while the pause lasts
questions.explanation: Pausing other threads stops them from changing registers and memory while you read. The cost is that their work waits too.

questions.prompt: Which fact can live debugging establish that disassembly alone cannot?
options: The path actually taken, with concrete register values
Which instructions might exist elsewhere in the file
The branch targets mentioned in a function
The constants referenced by the compiled code
questions.explanation: Disassembly shows possible instructions and paths. Dynamic analysis shows which path a real event took, and with which values.

questions.prompt: A decompiler displays a friendly name for a value. How should you treat that name?
options: As a hypothesis until observed behavior confirms it
As a fact, since decompilers read the original source files
As the original name, since it is stored inside the executable
As unimportant, since names do not help in any way
questions.explanation: A decompiler guesses structure and names from machine code, which is the final record. Behavior is what confirms or refutes a guess.

questions.prompt: How could you gather evidence for the rule "subtract 25 only if gold is at least 25"?
options: Try one affordable and one unaffordable purchase, then compare
Run affordable purchases only, and read the registers each time
Read the source-level variable names shown in the decompiler
Place a breakpoint on the very first instruction of the game
questions.explanation: If the subtraction runs only in the affordable case, you have evidence for the proposed rule. Testing only one side cannot show the guard.

questions.prompt: What counts as success for the safe first debugger session?
options: Pausing and resuming, and knowing what each panel shows
Changing the gold value and seeing the new number on screen
Finding the instruction that spends gold on the first try
Writing a patch that survives a restart of the game
questions.explanation: The first session changes nothing in the game. You attach, pause, look at the CPU view, and resume.

questions.prompt: A hook sits at 0x00A1B07C and the displaced span is 7 bytes. What is the return address?
options: 0x00A1B083, since 0x7C is 124 and 124 + 7 = 131, which is 0x83
0x00A1B081, since a five-byte jump would return five bytes later
0x00A1B073, since the carry out of the last digit is dropped
0x00A1B07C, since the cave returns to the hook address itself
questions.explanation: Add the span to the hook address: 0x7C + 7 = 0x83, because 0xC + 7 = 0x13 carries a 1 into the next digit.

questions.prompt: How is the length of the span that a hook must cover worked out?
options: By decoding whole instructions until they total the jump's size
By subtracting the hook address from the address of the new code cave
By taking the size of the whole function that contains the hook
By counting bytes until the first zero byte is found after the hook
questions.explanation: The length comes from decoding instructions, not from guessing or subtraction. Whole instructions covering at least the jump's size give the span.

questions.prompt: A compiler inserts a harmless multi-byte instruction that does nothing useful, as alignment padding. How should it be treated when patching around it?
options: As a real instruction, to be covered whole and not cut
As empty space that can safely be overwritten in part by a jump
As data that the CPU skips over without decoding it
As a marker that shows where the function ends in memory
questions.explanation: Padding is still a real instruction. A jump that cuts it in half leaves a stray byte that the CPU would decode as something else.

questions.prompt: What do some tools call a small block that replays displaced instructions and then jumps back?
options: A trampoline
A hook site
A return address
A breakpoint
questions.explanation: Names vary, but a trampoline is that replay-and-return block. The hook site is where execution leaves, and the return address is where it resumes.

questions.prompt: With breakpoints on the hook, the first cave instruction and the return address, in what order should they hit?
options: Hook, then first cave instruction, then return address
First cave instruction, then hook, then return address
Return address, then hook, then first cave instruction
Hook, then return address, then first cave instruction
questions.explanation: Execution leaves at the hook, runs the cave, then resumes at the return address. Seeing that order once proves the path before any new logic is added.

questions.prompt: The game crashes before the cave's first instruction runs. Where does the symptom table point?
options: The hook bytes or the jump destination
The saved instruction or the return address
A register, flag or stack value changed by the cave
The trigger path running more than once
questions.explanation: A crash before the cave means the jump itself is wrong. Trouble after the cave points at what it replayed or where it returned.

questions.prompt: The detour works once, but the game behaves oddly several actions later. Which cause fits the table best?
options: Register, flag or stack state was changed and never restored
The hook was written over the wrong menu item in the game
The breakpoint at the first cave instruction was never reached
The original bytes were restored too early by the debugger
questions.explanation: Delayed failures come from state the original code still depended on. A crash right before the cave would suggest a bad jump, not this.

questions.prompt: A cave replays the displaced instructions twice before returning. Is that harmless?
options: No; the behavior runs twice, which is as wrong as skipping it
Yes; the second copy is ignored by the CPU when it runs it
Yes, as long as the return address is correct afterward
Yes, as long as the registers are saved and then restored
questions.explanation: The cave must replay the complete displaced instructions exactly once. A correct return address does not make up for doubled behavior.

questions.prompt: What can happen if a code cave changes the stack pointer and does not undo the change?
options: A later return can pop a wrong value and jump to garbage
The game runs slower afterward but is otherwise fine
The extra stack space is cleaned up automatically
The debugger refuses to attach to the game again
questions.explanation: A return pops its destination from the stack, so a shifted stack pointer makes it pop the wrong value. That is one reason hooks fail later than they were installed.

questions.prompt: Why start with a cave that only replays the removed instructions and jumps back?
options: It proves the round trip works before new logic can add faults
It makes the game run faster than the original code does
It lets the debugger skip the hook bytes check on retries
It hides the patch from the CPU so the cave is not decoded
questions.explanation: If the empty round trip fails, the fault is in the path. Adding behavior first would leave two suspects at once.

questions.prompt: A one-off experiment reuses empty-looking padding for a cave. What should a repeatable installer do differently?
options: Allocate its own cave, set protection, and release it on exit
Search the game for even more padding that it can reuse every time
Keep the cave stored in a file on disk between separate runs
Copy the padding once and then reuse it for every other game
questions.explanation: Padding that merely looks empty is fine for one experiment. A repeatable installer owns its memory and cleans up after itself.

questions.prompt: A five-byte relative jump (a one-byte opcode and a four-byte offset) is followed by one do-nothing byte. How many bytes does the hook cover?
options: Six: one opcode, four offset bytes and one do-nothing byte
Five: the opcode and the offset, since padding is not counted
Four: just the relative offset counts toward the span
Eight: one opcode and a do-nothing byte for each offset byte
questions.explanation: 1 + 4 + 1 = 6, which matches a span made of two whole instructions.

questions.prompt: When testing a hook, why trigger it with a harmless local action?
options: It runs the hooked code on demand without involving other players
Harmless actions are the just ones that can run hooked code
It makes the hook run faster than other kinds of action would do
Menus are the one place where hooks are able to work
questions.explanation: A harmless, local event lets you trigger the hooked path whenever you want without affecting anyone else.

questions.prompt: After the debugger-only round trip is restored, what is the lasting result?
options: Your map of the detour, not the temporary patch
The patched bytes saved permanently in the executable
A cave left in place for later labs
The breakpoints kept active for next time
questions.explanation: The patch is temporary and the bytes are restored. What carries forward to Lesson 6.4 is the understanding of each hop.

questions.prompt: How does a language that compiles ahead of time to native code reach the CPU?
options: It is translated into machine instructions for one target before it runs
A virtual machine reads bytecode and runs it when it is needed
The CPU reads the source words directly and follows them as it goes
The operating system translates it into instructions on every run
questions.explanation: Ahead-of-time compilation produces native instructions for one target. A bytecode and virtual-machine route works differently, translating or interpreting while the program runs.

questions.prompt: What is bytecode?
options: Instructions for a virtual machine, not the CPU's x86 code
The x86 machine code that is stored inside every EXE file
Source text with its comments and extra spaces removed from it
A table of addresses that the loader later fills in at launch
questions.explanation: A virtual machine understands its own instruction set, and bytecode is written in it. The CPU actually runs the virtual machine.

questions.prompt: Why are "compiled" and "interpreted" not mutually exclusive labels for Lua?
options: Lua compiles source to bytecode on load, then its VM interprets it
Lua compiles to a native EXE first, then interprets that file
Lua is interpreted on the first run and compiled on the second
Lua only interprets code, but a REPL compiles each typed line
questions.explanation: A Lua source chunk is compiled when loaded and the resulting bytecode is carried out by the VM, so both words apply.

questions.prompt: What do the four letters in REPL stand for?
options: Read, evaluate, print, loop
Run, execute, parse, load
Read, execute, patch, link
Resolve, evaluate, print, link
questions.explanation: A REPL reads a line, evaluates it, prints the answer, and loops for another line. It describes the interaction, not how the code runs underneath.

questions.prompt: A statically typed language rejects assigning a word to a variable declared as a number. When is the problem caught?
options: Before anything runs, when the compiler checks types
While running, at the moment the word is used in a sum
It is not caught, since the word is silently converted to zero first
When a player triggers that line for the first time
questions.explanation: In a statically typed language the compiler knows each variable's type and refuses the mismatch before anything runs.

questions.prompt: A dynamically typed language lets a variable switch from a number to a word. If the word is later used in a calculation, when is the mistake discovered?
options: At run time, when the calculation is attempted
When the code is first compiled, before any run
When the assignment happens, since variables keep one type
It cannot be detected, since the language has no type checks
questions.explanation: A dynamically typed language accepts the assignments and only fails when the arithmetic runs with a value that cannot act as a number.

questions.prompt: Does static typing tell you whether code runs as native code, bytecode, or in a REPL?
options: No; typing decides when a mismatch is caught, not how code runs
Yes; statically typed languages always become native code
Yes; dynamically typed languages always need a REPL
No; typing decides whether the code can be compiled at all
questions.explanation: The route to execution and the time a type mismatch is caught are separate questions.

questions.prompt: A C structure has a one-byte field followed by a four-byte field. Where does the second field normally start?
options: At offset 4, after 3 bytes of padding
At offset 1, directly after the first field with no gap
At offset 2, after one byte of padding to line it up
At offset 8, after seven bytes of padding to line it up
questions.explanation: Each field starts at an address suited to its type, so the compiler leaves 3 padding bytes: 1 + 3 = 4.

questions.prompt: A field sits 0x24 bytes into an object, and a register holds the object's base. How might a disassembler show an instruction that reads that field?
options: A read at the register's value plus 0x24
A read at the fixed address 0x24 itself
A read at the register's value minus 0x24
A read of the register, with 0x24 as a label
questions.explanation: Compiled code reaches a field using its distance from the object's base. Bracket notation shows base plus that distance.

questions.prompt: A release build shows no name for an internal game function in the debugger. What is the safest conclusion?
options: The binary may just lack source names that execution never needs
The author encrypted the names to hide what the function does
Windows deleted the names from memory when the game launched
The debugger is broken and cannot read any function names
questions.explanation: A binary without debug symbols is not necessarily obfuscated. Names that execution does not need are often left out.

questions.prompt: What does the linker do with a call to a function defined in another object file?
options: Matches the reference to a definition and lays out the image
Encrypts the call so that the loader cannot locate the function
Replaces the call with a copy of the function's bytecode
Leaves every reference for the debugger to resolve at a pause
questions.explanation: The linker matches references to definitions it has and records what the loader must finish later.

questions.prompt: Where does the Microsoft toolchain often keep debug information?
options: A separate `.pdb` file that the EXE does not need to run
Inside the import table of the EXE file itself, name by name
Inside the DLLs that the game loads when it starts up
In the preferred base address recorded for the module
questions.explanation: The EXE can run without its debug information, so the toolchain often puts it in a separate file.

questions.prompt: A debugger shows a system function by name but an internal game function only as a bare address. Why?
options: Imported functions must be named so the loader can find them
Internal functions are encrypted by the operating system when loaded
System functions are stored on disk, while internal ones exist just in memory
The debugger asks the game's developers for the names of system functions
questions.explanation: An import table has to say which library function the program needs, so those names stay in the executable. Names of internal functions are usually discarded during compiling.

questions.prompt: What does the linker record about where the module will be loaded?
options: A preferred base and a table of locations to adjust if it moves
The exact final address, which Windows must always use
Nothing, because Windows picks the layout from the source
A list of every DLL function address filled in at build time
questions.explanation: The linker cannot know the loader's choice. It records a preferred base plus a relocation table for the case that the base differs.

questions.prompt: What is the Import Address Table for?
options: Slots that the loader fills with real DLL function addresses
A list of every function that the game exports to other programs
A table of field offsets for each structure inside the game
A copy of the source names kept so the debugger can show them
questions.explanation: The linker knows which DLL and function the game needs but not their addresses. The loader writes them into the table, and the game's code calls through it.

questions.prompt: A module loads at 0x00500000 and an instruction sits 0x2A00 bytes into it. The next run loads the module at 0x00700000. What is the instruction's address then?
options: 0x00702A00, since the offset stays the same and only the base changes
0x00502A00, since an address recorded once cannot change later
0x00002A00, since an offset is already a full address
0x00700000, since the instruction sits at the start of its module
questions.explanation: The offset inside the module stays fixed, so the address is the new base plus 0x2A00.

questions.prompt: An object begins at 0x01000000 and a field sits at +0x18. A second object of the same kind is created at 0x01400000. Where is its field?
options: 0x01400018, since the offset counts from that object's base
0x01000018, since the field keeps the first object's own address
0x01400000, since the field is at the start of every object
0x00400018, since new objects are measured from the first object
questions.explanation: Each object has its own base, so add the offset to that object's base. The first object's field stays where it was.

questions.prompt: After restarting the same build of a game, which recorded location is most likely to still be correct?
options: An offset from a module's own base address
The raw address of an object that was created on the heap
The raw address of a variable that was kept on the stack
The number that a window handle had during the last run
questions.explanation: The linker fixed where things sit within a module image, so module offsets stay put. Raw addresses of runtime objects and handles are handed out fresh each run.

questions.prompt: A fixed-layout structure has 4-byte fields A at +0x00, B at +0x04 and C at +0x08. A new build inserts a 4-byte field between B and C. Where does C start?
options: +0x0C, which is 4 bytes later
+0x08, since offsets stay the same between builds
+0x04, since the new field pushes C earlier
+0x10, which is 8 bytes later
questions.explanation: Fields before the insertion keep their offsets, and every field after it moves later by the new field's size. Measure the new build rather than assuming the same shift everywhere.

questions.prompt: A function you expected is missing from the disassembly of a release build. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The compiler inlined it into its callers, so no call remains
The author hid it so that reverse engineers cannot find it
The loader deleted it from memory to save space at launch
The linker could not match it to a definition and dropped it
questions.explanation: An optimizing build may paste a small function into callers, keep variables in registers, and merge identical functions. A missing function is usually not a sign of hiding.

questions.prompt: Your match shows 100 gold and the recruited unit costs 15. What should you expect at the paused subtraction?
options: The destination is the gold address and the price register holds 15
The destination holds 115 and the price register holds 100
The destination is the price field and the register holds 85
The register holds the new gold, 85, and the destination holds 15
questions.explanation: The instruction subtracts the price from gold, taking it from 100 to 85. Use the actual numbers shown in your own match.

questions.prompt: Which x64dbg CPU-view area shows raw memory such as the gold bytes?
options: The dump
The disassembly
The registers
The stack
questions.explanation: Disassembly shows instructions, registers show scratch values, the dump shows raw memory, and the stack shows return addresses and temporary data.

questions.prompt: After attaching x64dbg, the game is paused in Windows system code. What should you do?
options: Resume it, since that is normal, then start your experiment
Restart the game, because attaching has clearly failed
Edit the system code so control returns to Wesnoth
Run the experiment while the process is still paused
questions.explanation: Attaching may stop in system code, which is normal. Resume the process before triggering the experiment.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit number 0x00001234 is stored in memory on an x86 machine. What bytes does a memory dump show?
questions.explanation: Memory on x86 is little-endian, so the least significant byte 34 comes first, then 12, then the two zero bytes.

questions.prompt: Why watch all four bytes of gold with the hardware breakpoint?
options: Gold is four bytes; one byte hides a partial write
Watching four bytes makes the breakpoint fire much less often
A hardware breakpoint cannot watch fewer than four bytes in total
Four bytes is the largest range that any breakpoint can cover
questions.explanation: One byte can still trigger, but it would not show whether the game wrote the complete integer or only part of it.

questions.prompt: In a debugger, a hardware data breakpoint is set with an access type and a width. What does a write breakpoint of width four on an address do?
options: Pauses when a four-byte store hits that address
Pauses when four different bytes are read from there
Prevents any four-byte value from being stored there
Pauses on every fourth access to that address
questions.explanation: The breakpoint asks the CPU to stop on a particular kind of access at a particular width. It does not block the access, and reads do not trigger a write-only watch.

questions.prompt: How does a hardware memory breakpoint work?
options: The debugger programs CPU debug registers with an address, access type, and width
The debugger replaces the first byte of the writing instruction with `0xCC`
The debugger copies the gold bytes and compares them each frame
Windows marks the gold page unreadable and waits for an error
questions.explanation: It does not replace any game bytes. The CPU raises a debug exception when an instruction writes the watched range.

questions.prompt: If three different functions write gold, what does a hardware write breakpoint on the gold address show?
options: It can reveal each of the three writers
Only the first function that writes gold
Only functions in the main executable
None of them, since it watches one fixed instruction
questions.explanation: It watches a data address, not an instruction. A software breakpoint on a code address answers the opposite question: when does this exact instruction run?

questions.prompt: A hardware data breakpoint pauses. Why might the highlighted instruction not be the one that wrote gold?
options: It can report after the writing instruction has already run
Hardware breakpoints always pick a random nearby instruction
The debugger highlights the previous function's call
Windows moves the instruction pointer forward by a fixed amount
questions.explanation: Use the access information and nearby disassembly to identify the triggering write, then confirm its destination is your gold address.

questions.prompt: A write-up shows a disassembly with one particular register and offset. Why should you not copy its exact register or offset into your own work?
options: Builds and runs differ, so read the instruction at your own pause
Registers are named differently on every computer that runs it
Write-ups use deliberately false offsets so that readers must guess
The debugger renames registers as soon as it attaches to a game
questions.explanation: A write-up shows what an instruction resembles. Confirm every detail against what you observe in your own pause.

questions.prompt: What is the complete effect of an instruction that subtracts a register from a memory location?
options: It reads the memory value, subtracts, stores it back, and updates the flags
It subtracts and keeps the result in a register, leaving memory unchanged
It just compares the two values and updates the flags without storing
It replaces the memory value with the register and clears the flags
questions.explanation: It is a read-modify-write on memory, and it also updates the arithmetic flags that later branches may inspect.

questions.prompt: In bracket notation such as [reg+offset], how is the memory address worked out?
options: Add the offset to the register's value, then read memory at that sum
Read memory at the register's value, then add the offset to what was read
Read memory at the offset, then add the register's value to what was read
Add the offset to the memory at the register, then read memory a second time
questions.explanation: The sum is formed first and the read happens at that address. Calculating an address is separate from reading the value stored there.

questions.prompt: A register holds 0x0B2E4400 and an instruction writes to [reg+48h]. The h means hexadecimal. What is the destination address?
options: 0x0B2E4448, since the offset is the hexadecimal number 0x48
0x0B2E4430, since the offset is read as the decimal number 48
0x0B2E4480, since the offset is appended after the address
0x00000048, since the offset replaces the register's value
questions.explanation: The offset 48h is hexadecimal, so add 0x48 directly: 0x0B2E4400 + 0x48 = 0x0B2E4448.

questions.prompt: An instruction is encoded as seven bytes. To neutralize it completely with one-byte do-nothing instructions, how many are needed?
options: Seven, one for every byte of the instruction
One, since a single do-nothing cancels an instruction
Two, one for the opcode and one for the operand
Zero, since erasing the opcode byte is enough
questions.explanation: The length comes from the encoding, so every byte of the instruction must be filled. The bytes column of a disassembly shows the count.

questions.prompt: A tester blanks out an instruction, and a game action stops costing gold. What does that show?
options: It takes the cost in that action, but may serve other actions too
It is the sole place where gold changes anywhere in the game
It was a bug that the developers accidentally left in the game
The gold is now being stored in some other place instead of there
questions.explanation: It supports the theory, but the same instruction may also run for other gold-changing actions. Restore the original bytes right away.

questions.prompt: Why should a repeatable tool confirm the expected original bytes before patching?
options: Refusing an unknown version is safer than a wrong write
Original bytes tell the tool which register it should use
Windows refuses to write bytes that it has not read first
Original bytes make the patch run faster than before
questions.explanation: A discovery made once on one build is not a safe constant. Verifying the bytes protects against writing into a different version.

questions.prompt: After finishing an experiment with breakpoints and patches, how should you clean up?
options: Remove them through the debugger, then verify the original instruction
Close the debugger window so that the game cleans everything up by itself
Leave them in place, since they just matter while a debugger is attached
Restart the computer, since breakpoints stay stored in memory permanently
questions.explanation: Removing a breakpoint through the debugger lets it restore the original bytes safely. Then check the instruction to be sure.

questions.prompt: When tracing how a game feature works, what is an anchor?
options: A verified starting point that you trace outward from
A breakpoint that freezes the game until you remove it
A guess about which function in the game is the largest
The first function that the game's main loop calls each frame
questions.explanation: The anchor is a known, confirmed starting instruction. You trace outward from it to understand the feature around it.

questions.prompt: Paused inside the function that writes gold, how does "run until return" help find who asked for the work?
options: It continues until the function finishes, back in its caller
It restarts the function so that it can be read from the top
It runs the whole game until the next menu has closed
It deletes the function so the caller reports an error
questions.explanation: After the current function returns, execution is back in its caller, which moves you one step from the low-level write toward the decision behind it.

questions.prompt: When the x86 call instruction runs, what does it do before jumping to the function?
options: It places a return address on the stack
It copies the whole function into the caller
It clears every register so the function starts fresh
It saves the return address in the flags register
questions.explanation: The return address points at the instruction the caller expects next. A debugger builds its call stack from these saved addresses.

questions.prompt: Why should you confirm an important caller instead of trusting the call-stack view completely?
options: The view is rebuilt, and inlining can leave out frames
