questions.explanation: Sixty steps remove 1.0, so the value needs 5 × 60 = 300 steps to reach 0. After 60 steps it has only fallen to 4.0.

questions.prompt: The time scale is 0.5 and an ability has a 5.0 second cooldown counted in game time. How long does the cooldown last in real time?
options: 10.0 seconds, because 5.0 ÷ 0.5 = 10.0
2.5 seconds, because 5.0 × 0.5 = 2.5
5.0 seconds, because the cooldown is measured in real time
5.5 seconds, because slow motion adds 0.5 second to each timer
questions.explanation: At half scale each frame adds half as much game time, so the timer takes twice as long to run out. Scale 2 would give 2.5 seconds.

questions.prompt: Why does a paused game still draw its menu and answer the mouse?
options: A pause sets game time to zero, but real time keeps running
A pause stops the frame loop, and the menu is drawn by the operating system
A pause only freezes the physics step while every other clock stops too
A pause slows the game by half, so the menu runs at its normal speed
questions.explanation: A time scale of 0 stops game time, which the rules use, while the wall clock used by menus continues. That is why two time values may exist in memory.

questions.prompt: A window is held still for 3 seconds and there is no clamp. A ball moves 150 pixels per second. What happens on the next update?
options: It jumps 450 pixels at once, and a fixed-step loop owes 180 steps
It jumps 150 pixels at once, and a fixed-step loop owes 60 steps
It jumps 450 pixels at once, and a fixed-step loop owes 18 steps
It stays put, since a stalled frame has no delta time to apply
questions.explanation: The delta is 3.0 s, so the ball moves 150 × 3.0 = 450 pixels, and 3.0 ÷ (1/60) = 180 steps are owed. A clamp prevents this.

questions.prompt: Each fixed step takes 20 ms to compute but advances game time by 16.67 ms. What does the clamp do to the spiral of death?
options: It throws away the excess, so the game slows down rather than freezes
It makes each step run faster, so computing drops below 16.67 ms again
It runs extra steps in parallel, so the lost 200 ms gets caught up again
It pauses the real clock, so the game never falls behind real time at all
questions.explanation: Each step leaves the game 3.33 ms further behind, and catching up only adds debt. The clamp discards the excess time so the game slows down and does not freeze.

questions.prompt: Reading a 3 MB file takes 30 ms. Why do engines hand such jobs to worker threads?
options: Waiting would miss about two 16.67 ms refreshes, so the loop keeps running
Waiting would make the file unreadable, since files expire after one frame
A worker thread reads files faster, because it ignores the display refresh
The main loop cannot read files, since only worker threads may touch disks
questions.explanation: 30 ÷ 16.67 = 1.8, so the update would miss two refreshes. A task runs beside the loop and sends its result through a channel that the main loop checks each frame.

questions.prompt: Four frames take 10, 10, 10 and 70 ms. Why should a diagnostic report the slowest frame as well as the average?
options: The 25 ms average hides the 70 ms frame that the player feels as a stutter
The average is quicker than the slowest frame, so the average is wrong
The slowest frame is the just one that matters to a player
Averages cannot be worked out for numbers that vary this much
questions.explanation: (10 + 10 + 10 + 70) / 4 = 25 ms, even though three of four frames were fine. A stutter is invisible in a plain average.

questions.prompt: A system takes 0.5 ms in an optimized build and 15 ms in an unoptimized debug build. What is a sound conclusion?
options: It is 30 times slower, so a timing means little until you know the build
It is broken in the debug build, so the debug code must be repaired
The optimized build must be skipping some of the required work
The debug time is the true cost that players will experience
questions.explanation: 15 / 0.5 = 30 times slower. Debug builds leave out most optimizations, so a number without its build is not very informative.

questions.prompt: In an entity component system, what is an entity?
options: Only an identity number, with a generation so a reused number is told apart
A function that runs on every update for all objects with certain data
A plain bundle of data such as `Position` attached to an object
A group of objects that can be loaded together from a file
questions.explanation: The entity is just the identity, the component holds data, and the system is the function. A scene is the loadable group.

questions.prompt: In an entity-component design, a movement system selects entities that have both a position and a speed. A wall has a position but no speed. What happens?
options: The wall is not matched, so it never moves, with no special case
The wall is matched and moves with a speed of zero on each frame
The game stops with an error, since the wall lacks a speed value
The system gives the wall a default speed so that it can move later
questions.explanation: What an entity does comes from which components it has, not from its kind. Nobody wrote a special case for walls.

questions.prompt: Why should a system queue commands instead of spawning or removing entities in the middle of a loop?
options: The loop could skip some entities and revisit others, so changes wait
Spawned entities are invisible at first, so the engine reveals them later
Commands run faster than direct changes, since they skip all memory writes
Removed entities must be saved to disk before the next update can begin
questions.explanation: Changing the set of entities during a loop disturbs the loop itself. The engine applies the queued spawns and despawns together between systems.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between disabling an entity and despawning it?
options: Disabling hides it from systems but keeps it in memory; despawning frees its identity
Disabling frees its identity, while despawning keeps it hidden in memory
Disabling removes its components one at a time, while despawning deletes them together
Disabling is permanent for the match, while despawning can be undone by a marker
questions.explanation: A marker such as `Disabled` makes queries skip the entity, but its data stays so it can come back unchanged. A despawned identity may be reused.

questions.prompt: A tank has a turret child and a barrel grandchild. What happens when the tank moves or is despawned?
options: Children follow it, since positions are relative; despawning removes them too
Children stay put, since each entity keeps its own world position only
Children follow it, but they survive a despawn as separate loose objects
Children are copied to a new parent, which the engine chooses for them
questions.explanation: A child's position is stored relative to its parent, so moving the parent moves everything below it. Despawning the parent despawns them as well.

questions.prompt: Why might an address found in one level mean nothing in the next?
options: The entities of a scene are freed when that scene is left
Every level stores its entities at a different fixed address in the file
A new level changes the numeric type of every value in memory
The loading screen encrypts addresses until the next match has begun
questions.explanation: States spawn a scene on entry and despawn it on exit. An address that pointed into the old scene's entity can be freed or reused.

questions.prompt: A game executable acts as an engine and loads content packages that hold the game's rules and art. What does that arrangement show?
options: Swapping the content package makes the same engine run a different game
The engine has to be rebuilt from source for each content package
The content package contains a complete copy of the engine itself
Content packages can just hold pictures and sounds, not rules
questions.explanation: The engine and the game are separate. Change the content and the same executable runs a different game, with rules often kept in data files.

questions.prompt: A game's rule lives in a script file loaded at run time rather than in compiled code. What should you study to change that rule?
options: The script itself, or what the host program lets scripts do
The compiled machine code just, since scripts are translated into it
The graphics driver, since it runs the script
The network layer, since scripts are sent over it
questions.explanation: Each place a rule can live has a matching technique. Scripts are examined as scripts, and data files as data.

questions.prompt: Debug drawing helpers draw a line for one frame and create no game object. What happens when code stops calling the helper?
options: The shape vanishes, since it was drawn per frame and no object holds it
The shape stays on screen until something else deletes it from the scene
The shape fades out slowly over the next several frames that follow
The game stops, since its drawing list was left incomplete by the helper
questions.explanation: Debug shapes are redrawn every frame and create no entity. That makes them easy to switch on and off while the game runs.

questions.prompt: A stress test draws 10,000 sprites and each costs 0.002 ms. Where does that leave the frame budget at 60 Hz?
options: 20 ms, which is already over the 16.67 ms budget
2 ms, which leaves most of the 16.67 ms budget free
0.2 ms, which is far under the 16.67 ms budget
200 ms, which is about twelve times the 16.67 ms budget
questions.explanation: 10,000 × 0.002 = 20 ms. A stress test finds where a game breaks down, and this one passes the budget before any other work.

questions.prompt: In the Breakout step, the ball is at x = 794 and moves 150 pixels per second right, with a step of 1/60 second, a width of 16, and a wall at x = 800. What happens?
options: It moves 2.5 pixels to 796.5, its right edge 804.5 passes the wall, and x returns to 792
It moves 150 pixels to 944, then the wall pushes x back to 800
It moves 2.5 pixels to 796.5, which is still before the wall, so nothing happens
It moves 2.5 pixels to 796.5, and x returns to 800, the wall position itself
questions.explanation: The move is 150 × (1/60) = 2.5. The right edge is 796.5 + 8 = 804.5, which is past 800, so velocity flips and x becomes 800 − 8 = 792.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a snapshot and an event?
options: A snapshot says what is true now; an event says what changed
A snapshot is stored on disk; an event is held only in memory
A snapshot comes from the game; an event comes from the player
A snapshot holds one field; an event holds the whole game state
questions.explanation: Keeping both ideas apart stops a bot repeating an action on every poll. A snapshot is a level; an event is the edge between two accepted snapshots.

questions.prompt: A tool polls a number five times and reads 50, 50, 50, 70, 70. How many change events should a responsive system produce?
options: One, for the move from 50 to 70
Two, one for each distinct value that was seen
Five, one for each of the polls that were made
Four, one for every poll after the first poll
questions.explanation: Only the transition is news. The repeated values before and after are the same level, so they do not create more events.

questions.prompt: Two snapshots differ in two separate fields, a number and a yes-or-no flag. What should a comparison function return?
options: One event for each field that changed
A single event that names just the first field it finds
An empty list, since two changes cancel each other out
One combined event that merges both of the changes
questions.explanation: A comparison checks each field and reports an event for every one that changed. An empty list is the result only when the two snapshots match.

questions.prompt: What should a comparison function return for two identical snapshots?
options: An empty list, so there is no new event to act on
An event saying that nothing has changed
The earlier snapshot again, for the caller to examine
An error, since the two snapshots are the same
questions.explanation: Nothing changed, so nothing is reported. This is what stops a bot from reacting again to a value it has already handled.

questions.prompt: Why name an event "value changed" rather than "value earned" when it comes from comparing two snapshots?
options: The endpoints show a change but not why it happened
Neutral names take up less memory than other names
The word earned can just be used for money
The compiler requires event names to be neutral
questions.explanation: If snapshots were missed, going from one value to another proves only the endpoints. Calling it earned would claim a reason that nothing else shows.

questions.prompt: The observer misses some snapshots and sees gold go from 120 to 145. What can it conclude?
options: Only the endpoints; gold may or may not have passed 130
That gold rose in one single step of exactly 25 points
That gold was earned, because gold can only ever rise by earning
That gold passed through every value between 120 and 145
questions.explanation: A gap in polling hides what happened in between. An event is an interpretation of two accepted snapshots, not raw truth.

questions.prompt: A rule says "if a menu is open, click". The menu is polled as closed, closed, open, open, open, closed. How many clicks does the rule make?
options: 3, one for each poll where the menu is open
1, since the menu opened just one time
2, one for the opening and one for the closing
6, one for every poll that was made
questions.explanation: A level rule fires on every poll where the condition holds, so one opening gives three clicks. An edge rule would act only at the change.

questions.prompt: A menu is polled as closed, closed, open, open, open, closed. On which polls does a rule that fires only on changes act?
options: Poll 3, when it opens, and poll 6
Polls 3, 4 and 5, while the menu is still open
Poll 1 just, since it is the very first poll
Polls 1 and 6, the first poll and the last poll
questions.explanation: An edge rule compares each poll with the one before it, so it fires where the value changes: an opening at poll 3 and a closing at poll 6.

questions.prompt: Why define events as an enum rather than identifying them by free text strings?
options: Each variant fixes its own data, and a typo will not compile
Strings cannot be compared with each other in a program
Enums need much less typing than strings do in a program
Strings are slower than enums in every possible case of use
questions.explanation: A misspelt string would silently be a new event type, while a misspelt enum variant fails to compile.

questions.prompt: During a scene change a read returns a number that was never a real game state. What is the likely cause?
options: The game is rebuilding the object, so the read hit a half-built one
The game saved the older value twice into the same memory slot
The CPU rounds large values when memory is under heavy pressure
The poll interval was set shorter than the length of a single frame
questions.explanation: The pointer may be briefly null or point at a fresh allocation whose fields are not yet filled in. The read succeeds, but the value was never a real state.

questions.prompt: A byte in memory reads 0xBE in hexadecimal. What number is that?
options: 190, since B is 11, E is 14 and 11 x 16 + 14 = 190
25, since the two digits are added: 11 + 14
1114, since the digits 11 and 14 are joined together
176, since just the first digit counts, as 11 x 16
questions.explanation: Each hexadecimal digit is worth 16 times the one to its right: 11 x 16 + 14 = 190.

questions.prompt: A debouncer accepts a value only after it repeats three times in a row. The accepted value is 100, then it reads 0, 0, and then 7. What happens with the 7?
options: It replaces the candidate and starts again at 1
It is added to the candidate's count, which makes it 3 now
It is accepted at once, since it is a brand new value
It is ignored, since the candidate was already 0 before
questions.explanation: Only a value equal to the candidate adds to its count. A different value replaces the candidate and starts again at 1, so a glitch never reaches three in a row.

questions.prompt: A debouncer holds an accepted value of 100, and a candidate of 80 with a count of 2. The next poll reads 100. What happens?
options: The candidate is cleared, and no event is reported
The candidate reaches 3 and is accepted as the new value
An event for the value 100 is reported again
The accepted value switches to 80 straight away
questions.explanation: A poll equal to the accepted value wipes the candidate, because the change did not last. Stability must start over from the next different value.

questions.prompt: Health really falls from 100 to 80, and three polls are required. On which matching poll does the debouncer accept 80?
options: The third, producing exactly one event
The first, to react as quickly as possible
The second, once the value repeats
Every poll in which 80 is read
questions.explanation: Counts go 1, 2, then 3, and on reaching the required number the candidate is accepted once. After that, 80 equals the accepted value and reports nothing more.

questions.prompt: Polls arrive 20 times a second and three matching polls are required. How late does a real change reach the bot?
options: 100 to 150 milliseconds
50 milliseconds
300 to 350 milliseconds
1 second
questions.explanation: Polls are 50 ms apart, so the third matching poll is two gaps (100 ms) after the first. That first poll can be up to 50 ms after the change, giving 100 to 150 ms.

questions.prompt: With the same three-poll rule at 100 polls a second, what is the delay?
options: About 20 to 30 milliseconds
About 100 to 150 milliseconds
About 3 milliseconds
About 300 milliseconds
questions.explanation: Gaps are 10 ms, so two gaps are 20 ms plus up to 10 ms of waiting. "Three polls" means nothing without the polling rate.

questions.prompt: Which value is best suited to a longer debounce?
options: "The match ended," where a delay is cheap
"An enemy appeared," where speed matters most
Every coordinate in a smooth animation
A value that never flickers
questions.explanation: A delay is cheap for "the match ended" and too slow for "an enemy appeared." Choose the requirement per value instead of once for the whole bot.

questions.prompt: The bot has just sent "end turn," and the next 50 ms poll still shows the old turn. What should it do?
options: Wait for a snapshot showing the turn changed, or a timeout
Send the request again, since the poll shows it failed
Close the menu and begin the bot again
Increase the turn number in its own record
questions.explanation: A pending action stops the bot sending anything while it waits for confirmation. Resending because of a stale poll risks ending two turns.

questions.prompt: A pending action waits for at most 30 polls, and polls arrive every 40 ms. How long does the game have to respond?
options: 30 ms, since the timeout is a count of polls
120 ms, since 30 x 4 = 120
questions.explanation: The timeout is a number of polls, so it becomes time through the polling rate: 30 polls x 40 ms = 1,200 ms.

questions.prompt: Which request is idempotent?
options: "Select entity 7," which has the same final result when repeated
"Move selection to the next entity," which repeats each time
"Add 25 gold to the player," which adds again
"End the turn," which advances to the next player
questions.explanation: Sending the same request twice has the same final effect as sending it once. That limits the damage if a timeout hides a successful first action.

questions.prompt: What does "AI" usually mean for a game character?
options: Code that picks the next action, often using a few quick rules
A neural network that has been trained on large amounts of player data
A human operator who controls the characters from a remote server
A script that records player moves and replays them later
questions.explanation: In games, AI is usually far simpler than the AI in the news: quick rules checked many times a second.

questions.prompt: A simulation runs at 20 ticks per second. How long is one tick?
options: 50 milliseconds, since 1000 divided by 20 is 50
20 milliseconds, since the tick rate is the tick length
200 milliseconds, since 20 is multiplied by 10
5 milliseconds, since 1000 is divided by 200
questions.explanation: 1000 / 20 = 50 ms. Every tick advances the simulation by the same slice of time, however fast the computer draws.

questions.prompt: Why does an NPC decide once per tick instead of once per drawn frame?
options: Behaviour follows simulated time, so 3 ticks is 300 ms on any computer
Ticks are drawn faster than frames, so the NPC looks smoother onscreen
A single frame can only carry one decision from the whole level
Deciding once per frame would let the guard see through the walls
questions.explanation: If it decided each frame, a machine drawing 144 frames a second would react faster than one drawing 30. Ticks also give bounded, repeatable cost.

questions.prompt: In a sense, decide, act update for a game character, why must sensing come before deciding?
options: Deciding first would use old information from the previous tick
Acting has to come first, so the others can use its result
Sensing needs the decision result before it can start
The order is arbitrary, since the stages not share data
questions.explanation: The character first senses and updates its memory, then decides, then acts. Deciding before sensing would work from stale information.

questions.prompt: Why might an NPC keep a remembered last-seen position instead of reading the player's true position every tick?
options: It knows the player only through senses, so hiding can work
True positions are not stored anywhere in the game's own memory
Remembered positions are more accurate than the true positions
Reading the true position would be slower for the game to do
questions.explanation: The separation between the world and what the NPC knows is the point. When a wall breaks sight, the NPC has only its memory of the last sighting.

questions.prompt: Why does the guard test distance and the view cone before line of sight?
options: The first two cost a few operations; line of sight tests every wall
Line of sight cannot run until the guard has finished moving
Distance and the cone must be built before the wall list exists
Walls only count when the player stands at the cone's exact centre
questions.explanation: Cheap checks come first so the expensive wall walk runs only when the target could possibly be seen.

questions.prompt: The guard sees within 60° of its facing on either side. How wide is the whole cone?
questions.explanation: 60° each side adds up to 60 + 60 = 120°. Everything behind the guard is outside it.

questions.prompt: A player stands 5 units straight behind the guard in the open. Why is the guard unable to see them?
options: They are outside the view cone, though within the distance of 10
They are farther away than the `VIEW_DISTANCE` of 10 units
A wall always sits behind a guard and blocks sight that way
The line of sight would be longer than the distance of 5 units
questions.explanation: Distance passes (5 is at most 10), but a direction 180° from the facing fails the cone check. Each check gives the player a way to stay unseen.

questions.prompt: In a state-based NPC, a low-health check runs before the current state is examined and forces a flee state. What does that ordering do?
options: It lets the health check override every other state
It skips the health check whenever the NPC is already fleeing
It delays fleeing until the end of the tick's work
It makes fleeing optional for the other states
questions.explanation: The early return happens before the state is looked at, so nothing can outrank it.

questions.prompt: In a simple state machine, the flee state has no rule that leads out of it. What happens once an NPC enters it?
options: It stays there until the simulation ends
It leaves after a single tick and returns to idle
It goes back to the state it was in before fleeing
It resets to idle as soon as its health recovers
questions.explanation: A state with no outgoing rule is a dead end. A fleeing NPC keeps fleeing for as long as the simulation runs.

questions.prompt: An NPC reacts once it has seen the player on 4 consecutive ticks, at 50 ms per tick. Roughly how long after the player steps into view does it react?
options: 150 to 200 ms, about three ticks plus a part of one
0 to 50 ms, since it reacts as soon as it sees them
250 to 300 ms, since each tick needs a further delay
400 ms, since every tick would take 100 ms
questions.explanation: The fourth seeing tick comes three ticks (150 ms) after the first tick that sees the player, and the player may have been visible up to 50 ms before that first tick.

questions.prompt: An NPC counts the consecutive ticks in which it sees the player. What happens to that count on a tick when it does not see the player?
options: It drops back to 0, so a quick glimpse starts no chase
It stays where it was, ready for the next sighting to add on
It drops by one, so that it fades away just slowly over time
It doubles, since the player is hiding from the NPC now
questions.explanation: The count measures consecutive ticks of sight, so one missed tick restarts it.

questions.prompt: A chasing NPC attacks once it is within 1.5 units. Its distance to the player goes 4, 3, 2, 1 on successive ticks. At which distance does it first attack?
options: 1, the first distance that is within 1.5
2, since distances are rounded to the nearest whole number
3, since that is half of the distance it started at
1.5, since an attack needs the distance to equal the range
questions.explanation: A rule that says within 1.5 triggers at any distance up to and including 1.5. Of the distances seen, 1 is the first that qualifies.

questions.prompt: On tick 8 the guard drops from Attack to Search. What is the cause?
options: The line from (4, 0) to (8, 0) crosses the wall, so sight fails
The player moved more than 10 units away from the guard's post
The guard's health had just dropped to 25, so it began to search
The view cone no longer covered the east direction the guard faced
questions.explanation: The wall spans x from 5.5 to 6.5 on the line y = 0. With no sight, a guard in Chase or Attack goes to Search at once.

questions.prompt: A search state starts at a count of 0, adds one each tick, and keeps searching while the count is at most 2. How many ticks does it spend searching?
options: Three, with counts 0, 1 and 2
Two, since it stops when the count reaches 2
Four, since it needs a tick to give up at 3
One, since it starts at 0 and then ends
questions.explanation: The counts 0, 1 and 2 each give a tick of searching, so three ticks pass before the count of 3 ends it. Check inclusive limits carefully.

questions.prompt: How do games usually split moving from deciding?
options: Decision picks where to go; navigation works out how and steers
Navigation picks the state, and the decision layer does the moving
Both are one single function, so that they can never disagree
Decisions walk the NPC in straight lines, and navigation draws it
questions.explanation: The lab's `move_toward` ignores walls. A navigation layer plans a route over a grid or navigation mesh and steers along it each tick.

questions.prompt: In your own toy, you write 4 (Flee) into the state byte mid-chase. What happens?
options: The guard flees until the program restarts; nothing leaves Flee
The guard returns to Chase next tick, since the player is in view
The guard crashes at once, because 4 is outside the valid range
The guard waits one tick, then returns to Patrol on its own
questions.explanation: `decide` keeps Flee as Flee, so the edit lasts. Only the Patrol edit is undone, because there the inputs still disagree.

questions.prompt: You write 0 (Patrol) while the guard is searching and the player is out of view. What happens?
options: The guard gives up early and walks home, so the edit lasts
The guard returns to Search on the next tick, undoing the edit
The guard turns to Chase at once, because Patrol means alert
The guard switches to Flee, because 0 is below the health limit
questions.explanation: The senses agree with Patrol because the player is not visible. An edit survives when the inputs agree with it.

questions.prompt: In a toy NPC whose rules make it flee when its health is low, what does changing its stored health value do on the next tick?
options: Behavior changes, since stored values are inputs the rules read
Nothing happens, since the rules ignore any stored health values
The NPC is removed from the game at once, with no warning to anyone
The NPC freezes in place until the value is restored to the old one
questions.explanation: Health is an input that the decision rules check, so changing it changes behavior for as long as the value holds.

questions.prompt: Why can't you change an online game's NPC by editing the client's memory?
options: The server runs the NPC, so its decisions are the ones that count
NPC data in client memory is always encrypted by the game itself
NPC values live only in video memory on the client's machine
The client stops receiving updates as soon as its memory is edited
questions.explanation: The server is authoritative. Your client receives what it needs to draw, and a client edit at most changes your own screen until the next update. Tampering with a live service is also out of scope.

questions.prompt: A game has a paddle, a ball and 40 bricks that all have a position component, plus one score resource. What does that mean for a memory scan?
options: The score is one record in one place, while positions form 42 values
The score has 42 copies, one for each entity that has a position
The positions are one shared record that all the entities point at
A resource cannot be found by scanning memory
questions.explanation: A resource exists exactly once per kind, so a scan finds a single candidate. Components have one value per entity that has them: 1 + 1 + 40 = 42.

questions.prompt: Why might a single-player game model its player as an entity instead of a resource?
options: The same systems can then handle the player and other characters
Resources are slower to read than entities in every system that uses them
Resources cannot hold numbers such as health or damage
Entities are required for a score to be displayed on screen
questions.explanation: The choice depends on how the data is used. A score or clock belongs to the game as a whole, while a player treated like other characters fits an entity.

questions.prompt: Two systems both read the same queue of events. How many times does each system see a given event?
options: Once each, since every reader keeps its own position in the queue
Once in total, so the two readers must share it between them
Twice each, since an event is delivered again each frame
The first reader sees it, because reading removes it
questions.explanation: An event queue is a list with a counter per reader. The sender never needs to know which readers exist.

questions.prompt: A game is paused, and the systems that read events stop running. What happens to an event sent just before the pause?
options: It can expire unread, so the reaction is lost for good
It waits in the queue and is delivered as soon as the game resumes
It is delivered to the nearest system that is still running
It is turned into a resource that the systems read after the pause
questions.explanation: Bevy keeps each event for at least two frames, and other engines choose differently. A system that does not run during that window never sees the event.

questions.prompt: A sender pushes an event during frame 10. A reader that runs earlier in the frame than the sender, when does it see the event, and how late is that?
options: In frame 11, one frame late, about 16.7 ms at 60 frames a second
In frame 10, at once, since the event is sent that frame
In frame 12, two frames late, as each reader needs a spare frame
It is not seen, since the reader has already finished with the queue
questions.explanation: A reader only sees what has already been sent. Running before the sender pushes the event to the next frame, adding one frame time.

questions.prompt: A game has 30 entities: a ball with position, size and velocity, a paddle with position and size, and 28 bricks with position and size. How many does a query for position and size, excluding velocity, match?
options: 29: the paddle and the 28 bricks, which lack velocity
30: the filter just removes components that do not exist
1: just the ball, since it is the one entity that is excluded
28: just the bricks, since the paddle is moved by player input
questions.explanation: The ball has velocity, so the exclusion filter removes it. The paddle and bricks have position and size but no velocity, giving 1 + 28 = 29.

questions.prompt: With 42 entities, how many pairs can a query that hands out every pair of entities produce, using n × (n − 1) ÷ 2?
options: 82, since each entity pairs with 41 others only once
questions.explanation: The formula divides by 2 because pair (a, b) and pair (b, a) are the same. For 1,000 entities it becomes 499,500.

questions.prompt: Testing every pair among N objects takes N x (N - 1) / 2 tests. For 200 objects stepping 60 times a second, how many contact tests is that per second?
options: 2,400,000, since each of 200 objects tests 200 others, times 60
12,000, since there are 200 pairs, times 60
23,940, since there are 399 pairs, times 60
questions.explanation: 200 x 199 / 2 = 19,900 pairs, and 19,900 x 60 = 1,194,000. That growth is why engines test only nearby pairs instead of all of them.

questions.prompt: The health-bar system last ran at counter 41. Entity A's health was written at 40, B's at 43, and C's at 44. Which entities are redrawn?
options: B and C, because their stamps are newer than 41
A and B, because they are the first two in the list
Only C, because it has the newest stamp of the three
All three, because a `Changed` query ignores the counter
questions.explanation: Each system remembers the counter from its last run, and `Changed` returns entities whose stamp is newer. A's write at 40 happened before that run.

questions.prompt: 5,000 objects each cost 0.004 ms to redraw, and only 10 changed this frame. What do changed-only queries save?
options: 20 ms down to 0.04 ms, about 500 times less
20 ms down to 10 ms, about half as much
20 ms down to 0.4 ms, about 50 times less
Nothing, since every object still has to be checked
questions.explanation: 5,000 x 0.004 = 20 ms, more than a whole frame, against 10 x 0.004 = 0.04 ms. 20 / 0.04 = 500.

questions.prompt: A system is skipped for 50 frames and then runs with a change-detecting query. Which changes does it see?
options: Every change since it last ran, using its own marker
The changes that were made during the current frame alone
The changes from the 50th frame that it was skipped
None, since skipped systems lose track of what changed
questions.explanation: Change detection compares against the system's own last-run marker, so a skipped system catches up. Events are different and can expire while a system waits.

questions.prompt: Why can a change-detection query not report a component that was removed this frame?
options: The value and its stamp are gone, so removals go in a separate list
Removed components still count as changed, but the query hides them
Change queries just look at whole entities, at components
Removal happens after the frame ends, so it cannot be seen yet
questions.explanation: A stamp lives with the value, so deleting the value deletes the stamp. Engines record the entities that lost a component separately.

questions.prompt: At 144 frames a second and a 60 Hz fixed step, how many steps run per frame, on average?
options: 5 of every 12 frames run one step; the other 7 run none
Every frame runs exactly one step of 16.67 ms
2 steps run on every frame, since 144 ÷ 60 is about 2
1 of every 4 frames runs one step, as at 240 frames a second
questions.explanation: A 144 fps frame lasts 6.94 ms, shorter than a 16.67 ms step. Time is carried over, so 60 steps spread across 144 frames: 60 ÷ 144 = 5 of 12.

questions.prompt: Bevy's default fixed step is 64 steps a second. How long is each step?
options: 64 ms, since the rate and the length match
questions.explanation: The step rate is a setting of the game. A value your tool watches can change once per step in one game and once per frame in another.

questions.prompt: Why might a system that runs early in the frame read yesterday's world position for an object?
options: The engine updates world positions in its bookkeeping phase near the frame's end
World positions are stored on the display and returned only by the next refresh
World positions are recalculated only when the player opens a pause menu screen
Early systems always read positions from the previous level's scene in memory
questions.explanation: The engine's own work is made of ordinary systems in the same phases. Anything reading the result before that phase sees the previous answer.

questions.prompt: Which condition must hold for a system to be ready to run?
options: No running system writes what it touches, and earlier-ordered systems are done
It was added to the schedule first, since earlier systems always run first
It touches no component at all, since any shared data forces strictly serial work
Its run condition is false, which tells the engine to hold it for a later frame
questions.explanation: Readiness depends on conflicts in declared reads and writes, order constraints, and run conditions being true. Systems touching different data can run at the same time.

questions.prompt: Two systems have no stated order between them. What may the engine do?
options: Run them either way round, and even change that order from one frame to the next
Always run them in the order in which they were added to the schedule
Refuse to start the frame until the order has been stated by the developer
Run them at the same moment even if they write the same data
questions.explanation: Without an order, the result can differ per frame. That is why two unordered writers can make a value flip.

questions.prompt: Four systems run on two threads with no other limits. R (4 ms) reads positions and W (2 ms) writes them, so W must wait for R. X (3 ms) and Y (1 ms) are independent. How long does the frame's work take?
options: 6 ms: the chain of R then W sets the minimum
10 ms, since all four systems run one after another
5 ms, since the writer can overlap with the reader
4 ms, since the longest single system sets the time
questions.explanation: R then W take 4 + 2 = 6 ms on one thread, while X and Y fit in 4 ms on the other. The longest dependent chain sets the minimum.

questions.prompt: Within each frame, a system that applies player input runs before the system that reads input. At 30 frames a second, how late is a key press applied?
options: One frame later, which is about 33.3 ms
No delay, since both systems run in the same frame
Two frames later, which is about 66.7 ms
One frame later, which is about 16.7 ms
questions.explanation: A key pressed during frame N is applied in frame N + 1. At 30 frames a second a frame lasts 1000 / 30 = 33.3 ms.

questions.prompt: What happens to a system whose run condition is false on a given frame?
options: It is skipped, and whatever it would have changed stays as it was
It runs anyway, but its writes are thrown away at the end of the frame
It runs at half speed, so it still updates every second frame
It is removed from the schedule and must be added again later
questions.explanation: The condition is a yes-or-no check made on every frame. A value that stops changing in a menu can simply belong to a skipped system.

questions.prompt: A system asks to change the game state from playing to game over. When does the change take effect?
options: At a fixed point in the next frame: exit work, the move, then enter work
Immediately, so the rest of the current frame already sees the new state
At the end of the current second, whichever frame that moment falls inside
Only after the player presses a key in the new state's own menu screen
questions.explanation: State changes are queued, not immediate. Exit work of the old state runs first, such as despawning the match.

questions.prompt: A bullet is spawned by a command in frame N. Which systems can see it, and from when?
options: Later phases in frame N, and systems that ran earlier see it in frame N + 1
Every system in frame N, since commands apply at the moment they are recorded
Only systems in frame N + 2, since commands wait two full frames
No system, since a spawned bullet lacks a Position until it is moved
questions.explanation: Commands apply at a safe point, usually the end of a phase. At 60 frames a second, the earlier systems get it 16.67 ms later.

questions.prompt: In table storage each component has its own column. If three components take 4, 4 and 8 bytes per entity, how many bytes do 5,000 entities that have all three take?
options: 80,000 bytes, since each entity needs 4 + 4 + 8 = 16 bytes
40,000 bytes, since just the largest component is stored for each entity
16,000 bytes, since entities share their components with each other
240,000 bytes, since every component takes a 16-byte slot
questions.explanation: A row is 16 bytes, and 5,000 x 16 = 80,000. Each component forms its own unbroken column.

questions.prompt: How does sparse-set storage compare with table storage when a short-lived marker is added to one entity?
options: Adding is cheap, as one record goes into a pool, but reads need an extra lookup
Adding moves the entity to another table, but reads are the cheapest possible
Adding and reading cost exactly the same as they do in table storage
Adding is impossible while systems are running, so the marker must wait
questions.explanation: A sparse set keeps its own pool and an index from entity to position. That suits a marker that comes and goes every frame.

questions.prompt: 10,000 bullets may each carry any of 8 optional markers. How many tables can that create, and what does it mean?
options: Up to 2⁸ = 256, so a scan for one component finds it in many pieces
Up to 8, one for each marker, so a scan finds it in eight pieces
Up to 80,000, one for each marker on each bullet, in separate runs
Exactly 1, since all bullets with `Position` share a table
questions.explanation: Each distinct set of components needs its own table. Eight on/off markers give 256 combinations, about 10,000 ÷ 256 = 39 bullets a table.

questions.prompt: Could adding more CPU threads make the five systems finish faster than 5 ms when the AI reads its own copy?
options: No, since the chain read_input, move_player, collide, play_sounds takes 5 ms
Yes, since each system could get its own thread, so the longest takes just 2 ms
Yes, since four threads divide the 8 ms total into four slices of 2 ms each
No, since the engine never runs more than two systems at any one moment
questions.explanation: A system cannot start before the one it depends on finishes. The longest chain of waiting systems sets a floor under the frame, whatever the thread count.

questions.prompt: One system sets speed to 100 and another sets it to 50, with no order stated. What might you observe in memory?
options: A value that flips between 50 and 100, with no input from you
A value that stays at 100, since the larger number always wins
A value that becomes 75, since the engine averages the two writes
A value that stays at 50, since the later system in the file always runs last
questions.explanation: The result depends on which system runs last, and an unstated order can change from frame to frame. An alternating number hints at two writers.

questions.prompt: Why does the engine drop events after a short time and not keep them until someone reads them?
options: A queue nobody empties would grow forever, such as 3,600 events a minute at 60 fps
Events carry timestamps that become invalid after exactly two frames of age
Reading an event more than once corrupts it, so each old one is removed at once
Events are kept in the display's memory, which is cleared on every refresh
questions.explanation: An event sent every frame and never read adds 60 × 60 = 3,600 events a minute. Dropping them bounds the queue at the cost of missed events.

questions.prompt: A system reads a value that always shows the previous frame's number. What is a likely cause?
options: The reader runs before the writer in the frame's order
A run condition on the writer is false, so it not runs
The value is stored as an integer instead of a float
The frame rate is too high for the value to update
questions.explanation: Order decides whether a reader sees this frame's data. A false run condition would freeze the value, not make it lag by one frame.

questions.prompt: A map is 4 columns wide and 3 rows tall, stored row by row. What flat index does tile (x = 1, y = 2) have?
options: 9, since 2 x 4 + 1 = 9
6, since 1 x 4 + 2 = 6
5, since 1 x 3 + 2 = 5
3, since 1 + 2 = 3
questions.explanation: Row 2 begins after two full rows of 4 tiles, so add the column: 2 x 4 + 1 = 9. Mixing up x and y or width and height gives other numbers.

questions.prompt: A map is 4 tiles wide and 3 tall, and tile (4, 1) is requested. Why must code check x against the width before computing an index?
options: Without it, (4, 1) silently lands on tile (0, 2), another tile
Without it, the index would come out negative for that tile
Without it, the code would try to divide by zero for the tile
Without it, the multiplication would run noticeably more slowly
questions.explanation: 1 x 4 + 4 = 8, which is the index of tile (0, 2) in a 4-wide grid. A bounds check catches it before any math.

questions.prompt: Why use checked multiplication when working out y times the width for an index from untrusted dimensions?
options: Absurd dimensions could overflow and wrap into a small, wrong index
Checked multiplication is required for every integer calculation
It rounds the result to the nearest tile on the grid
It turns the row number y into a negative number
questions.explanation: Bounds checks stop a bad tile, while checked arithmetic stops absurd dimensions from wrapping around into a small wrong index.

questions.prompt: A grid stores each row padded beyond its width. Why does y x width + x fail even if the first row looks right?
options: Rows start at stride intervals, not width, so later rows are misplaced
Padding changes the width of the first row, so x becomes negative
Padding makes every tile larger than the other tiles around it
Padding moves the whole grid to a different address on each run
questions.explanation: The address is base + y x row stride + x x element size. Verify with tiles on different rows and near both edges.

questions.prompt: Which fact belongs to the coordinate contract a grid needs before the formula can be trusted?
options: Which tile is `(0, 0)` and which way increasing `x` and `y` move
Which unit stands on the tile and which player owns that unit
How many frames the game takes to redraw the whole map
Which build number the Wesnoth executable reports in its title
questions.explanation: Origin, axis direction, stride, element width, layer, and owner must be recovered separately. Rows may even be stored bottom to top.

questions.prompt: Why might a cached visibility layer not be the source of truth?
options: The game rebuilds it from terrain, units, teams, and line-of-sight rules
It is stored in a compressed form, so changing it is impossible
It is held only by the graphics card, so memory never contains it
It is the same as the terrain layer, so it has no state of its own
questions.explanation: A derived view is recomputed. What matters is which system recomputes it and when, so an edit to the cache may be overwritten.

questions.prompt: Why verify an indexing formula using tiles on several rows and near both edges?
options: A wrong stride can look right on the first row and fail later
Edge tiles are stored in a different process from all the others
Edge tiles are the ones drawn on the screen of the player in the game
The formula changes over time while the game is still running
questions.explanation: One matching tile is a coincidence, not a proof. Different rows test the row math, and edges test the boundaries.

questions.prompt: A search for a tile's visibility value leaves a short list of candidates. What are you testing as you repeat it with other tiles?
options: Whether each belongs to one tile, one row, one player's layer, a cache, or the map
Whether each candidate is a pointer, since all visibility values are addresses
Whether each candidate equals the gold of the nearest player on the map
Whether each candidate is stored in UTF-16, since tiles are labelled with text
questions.explanation: Several kinds of memory can match a number. Repeating with other tiles tells them apart.

questions.prompt: A tile's raw stored value has every bit set (0xFFFFFFFF). Why not assume it means visible?
options: It might mean -1, a bit mask, or an uninitialized marker
All bits set is the standard code for true in every program
It is an invalid value that the game would not store
It means the tile is blocked and cannot be entered
questions.explanation: A raw value gets a name only after examples of every state have been collected. Otherwise the model is guessing.

questions.prompt: A decoder maps raw values to named states and keeps a variant that carries any unrecognized value. Why?
options: A surprise value stays visible and can be investigated
It makes the decoder run faster than a version that lacks it
Unrecognized values must crash a decoder that is built properly
It reduces the memory needed to store each decoded tile state
questions.explanation: The model only names states it has observed. Treating a new value as one of the known states would hide something the model lacks.

questions.prompt: A 6 x 5 layer stores one 32-bit value for each tile. How many bytes does reading the whole layer copy?
options: 120, since 30 tiles take 4 bytes each
30, since there is one byte for each tile
24, since 6 columns take 4 bytes each
480, since each tile takes 16 bytes
questions.explanation: The tile count is width x height = 30, and each tile takes 4 bytes, so 30 x 4 = 120.

questions.prompt: Why cap the total tile count (width times height) before reading a layer whose dimensions came from remote memory?
options: Corrupt dimensions could demand a huge read or allocation
Large maps cannot exist in any game that is made
A cap makes the bytes that are read more accurate
Remote numbers are rounded when they are copied over
questions.explanation: Remote numbers are untrusted. A cap on the total keeps one bad width or height from allocating or reading far too much.

questions.prompt: Why should a function that reads a layer return an owned collection of decoded values rather than a pointer into the game's memory?
options: The copy belongs to the tool and cannot dangle when the game changes
Owned collections update themselves as the game's data changes
A pointer into another process cannot be stored by a tool
The operating system requires every read to return a collection
questions.explanation: The function copies the bytes and decodes each value. The result belongs to the tool, so nothing in it can dangle.

questions.prompt: Why prefer an external text map or a separate window to patching a game when learning how a map is stored?
options: It observes state without altering rules and is easy to shut down
It runs much faster than the game that it is observing in real time
It gives the tool direct access to the game's own code and its data
It makes the map data permanent after the game itself has closed
questions.explanation: An external view reads state and presents it without altering the game. Patching is the harder and more fragile route.

questions.prompt: A game stores one visibility bit per tile and packs 32 tiles into a single 32-bit value. How does that change what the instructions look like?
options: Bit shifts and masks appear instead of plain array indexing
Floating-point instructions are used for visibility
Each tile becomes a pointer to a separate record
Nothing changes, since packing is invisible to the code
questions.explanation: That is why the instructions are bit-level, not simple y x width + x indexing. A different build may pack the same relationship differently.

questions.prompt: An instruction sequence shifts a 1 left by n, inverts it, and ANDs it into a stored word. What does it do?
options: Clears bit n and leaves the other bits as they were
Sets bit n and clears every other bit in the word
Sets every bit except bit n in the stored word
Flips bit n and leaves the other bits as they were
questions.explanation: The shift builds a single set bit, the inversion turns it into a mask that is 0 only at that position, and the AND keeps every other bit.

questions.prompt: What kind of stored state is fog of war in a strategy game?
options: A per-player view over shared map data, packed by each build
A single global flag that applies to all of the players alike
A picture drawn on the screen with no stored state behind it
A property of the terrain that does not depend on any player
questions.explanation: Visibility is derived per player from shared terrain and units. The exact bytes depend on the build.

questions.prompt: A simple bot presses a buy action whenever resources look high. What problem does that design have?
options: It could queue several buys before the first one shows up
It buys too slowly, since it waits for the next frame
It cannot see the resources, so it does not act
It stops after the first purchase and does not buy again later
questions.explanation: The bot does not know whether the game accepted the action. A useful macro tracks what was requested, what was accepted, and when to stop.

questions.prompt: What separates a closed-loop bot from an open-loop macro?
options: It observes the result of an action, then corrects or stops
It sends inputs faster, so the game has less time to change in between
It sends the same inputs with longer sleeps, so every action finishes first
It stores every input in a list, so the same sequence can be replayed later
questions.explanation: An open-loop macro sends inputs and assumes they worked. The closed loop senses, validates, decides, acts once, confirms, and corrects.

questions.prompt: Why does waiting between ticks not prove that an action succeeded?
options: Waiting only limits the rate; confirming means seeing state change
Sleeping erases all of the evidence that the action left behind
Waiting makes the action repeat itself again during the pause
Sleeping is not allowed inside any kind of loop in a game
questions.explanation: Menus or missed input can leave no outcome at all. A wait is a rate limit, not evidence.

questions.prompt: What does keeping "requested recruit" separate from "worker count increased" protect against?
options: Treating a sent request as proof that the game accepted it
Counting the same worker twice when two snapshots are compared
Reading the worker count while the game window is minimized
Sending a request before the macro has been told to start
questions.explanation: Menus, animation locks, pauses, and object replacement can make a request produce no outcome. Only the later snapshot shows the result.

questions.prompt: How can the decision logic be tested without launching the game?
options: Feed recorded snapshots through the decision function and compare decisions
Run the real bot with a shorter sleep, so the game reaches the end sooner
Press the keys by hand, so the bot logs each decision it would have made
Inject the bot into Wyrmsun with the stop flag cleared and watch the result
questions.explanation: The decision function takes a copied snapshot and returns a state. The same sequence should produce the same decisions each time.

questions.prompt: What does representing a controller's state as a single enum value, instead of several separate flags, guarantee?
options: It is in one state at a time, so contradictory combinations cannot occur
Each state runs faster than it would have done if flags were used
The state can not change once it has been chosen at the start
Every state is active at once and the code simply picks one of them
questions.explanation: Impossible combinations disappear because one variable holds exactly one variant. Each variant can also carry its own data, such as a countdown.

questions.prompt: A controller in a ready state moves to an acting state when resources reach a threshold. Why should it not jump straight to a cooldown state on that same tick?
options: Cooldown should begin only after a later snapshot confirms the action
Cooldown cannot follow acting in any kind of state machine design
Cooldown is just used when the user asks the controller to stop
Acting just starts after the threshold has been seen on two ticks
questions.explanation: The controller only requested an action. It must observe a later snapshot before it knows the action was accepted.

questions.prompt: In an automation state machine, a stop request arrives at the same moment an action would be taken. Which should win?
options: The stop request, since a user's stop outranks an action
The action, since it was already planned before the stop arrived
Whichever of the two is listed first in the code of the machine
Neither; the machine should wait one tick and then decide again
questions.explanation: A user stop must always be able to end the macro. A test can pin that priority without running the game.

questions.prompt: A controller is in an acting state, and the next snapshot shows that the action failed. Where should it go?
options: A recovery state that records why, then ready once state is valid
Straight back to acting, to repeat the failed action at once
Into cooldown, as if the action had actually succeeded in the game
Into stopped, which ends all of the automation from then on, for good
questions.explanation: A failed action takes the failure path. Recovery returns to ready only when the state is valid and the player is ready again.

questions.prompt: A cooldown state counts down from 3 and returns to ready only on a tick where the count is already 0. How many ticks pass before it is ready?
options: 4: the count goes 2, 1, 0, then one more tick
3: there is one tick for each number in the countdown
2: the countdown skips the first and the last numbers
0: it is ready as soon as the countdown has begun
questions.explanation: The count reaches 0 after three ticks, and the next tick, seen at 0, returns to ready. Checking the exact condition avoids an off-by-one error.

questions.prompt: A controller checks whether the match is active before looking at its own state. If the match stops while it is cooling down, what happens?
options: It falls back to waiting, since the global check comes first
It finishes the cooldown first and then notices the change
It keeps acting, since cooldown is already underway
It stops and exits, since the match is no longer there
questions.explanation: The match-active check comes before the state-specific rules, so any active state falls back to waiting.

questions.prompt: A loop design asks four questions: start, continue, progress and stop. Which one asks what changes so the loop does not repeat the same work forever?
options: Progress
Start
Continue
Stop
questions.explanation: In a macro, countdown ticks moving toward zero are the progress. Start is the first state, continue is what must stay true, and stop is the event that ends it.

questions.prompt: In a table that traces a state machine, one row lists two unrelated actions. What does that suggest?
options: The state owns too much work and should be split
The machine is efficient, since it does two jobs at once
The two actions are really a single action in disguise
Nothing in particular, since rows may list any actions
questions.explanation: A row should ask for exactly one action. Two unrelated actions in a row suggest the state does too much.

questions.prompt: In a design table for a looping automation, one state has no way to reach the stopped state. What does that mean?
options: The design is not safe yet, since a user must be able to end it
A fixed sleep covers it, because the loop pauses between all ticks
It is fine if that state just lasts for a short time
The state itself acts as the stop, so no path is required
questions.explanation: Every state needs a stop path so that a user can end the macro. A fixed sleep never replaces one.

questions.prompt: What does a fixed sleep inside an automation loop give you?
options: A bounded tick rate, but no proof the logic is correct
Proof that every action in the loop has succeeded
Automatic recovery from any action that has failed
A way for the user to stop the loop at any time
questions.explanation: A 100 ms sleep gives about ten observations a second. Correctness comes from the state machine and its snapshots.

questions.prompt: Before unloading an in-process library that runs the bot, what should happen first?
options: Set the stop flag, wait for the worker to exit, and restore any temporary state
Unload the library at once, since the worker stops when its code is gone
Restore the hooks, then set the stop flag after the library is unloaded
Clear the snapshot, then let the worker thread keep running in the background
questions.explanation: A worker still running code in an unloaded module would crash. The stop request is cooperative, so wait for it to finish.

questions.prompt: A game's module loads at 0x00E50000 on this run, and a target sits at module offset 0x1A30. Where is the target?
options: 0x00E51A30, since the base plus the offset is recalculated each run
0x00001A30, since an offset is already a full address
0x00E50000, since the module base is where the target sits
The same address as the previous run, since it was recorded then
questions.explanation: Module-relative offsets must be added to the current base on every run, because the module may be relocated.

questions.prompt: Why avoid calling an internal game function just because you saw it hit once at a breakpoint?
options: Several normal calls show its thread, arguments and checks
Internal functions can just be called one single time
Breakpoints change the addresses of the functions they stop in
The debugger hides the arguments of any function it stops at
questions.explanation: An action that works once under a debugger may fail at the wrong time. Watching several calls shows what the function needs.

questions.prompt: Why does the Wyrmsun port ask you to recruit one worker normally before gold passes 3000?
options: To capture one legitimate `0x110`-byte worker record that the bot can replay later
To raise the gold above 3000, since normal recruits grant resources
To unlock the recruit function, since the game blocks it before the first worker
To reset the module base, since the first recruit relocates the game's module
questions.explanation: The hook copies a real record into a local buffer. When gold is over 3000, the bot copies it back and calls the verified recruit function from the loop hook.

questions.prompt: In a layered automation design, which layer should not be tied to a specific game build?
options: The decision logic that works on validated, copied facts
The layer that reads values out of the game's memory
The layer that sends the actions into the game
The layer that finds addresses inside the game
questions.explanation: Low-level observation and action layers are tied to a build. Decision logic works on copied facts, so it can be reused and tested without the game.

questions.prompt: A point is at (1, 2) and another is at (7, 10). What is the straight-line distance between them?
options: 10, from the right triangle with sides 6 and 8
14, from adding the two differences together
100, which is the squared length of the arrow
8, the larger of the two differences
questions.explanation: The differences are 6 and 8, so the length is the square root of (36 + 64) = 10. Adding the differences forgets that the arrow runs diagonally, and 100 is the length squared.

questions.prompt: An arrow in 3D has the parts (2, 3, 6). What is its length?
options: 7, since 4 + 9 + 36 = 49 and its root is 7
49, which is the length before the root
6, since the longest part sets the length
questions.explanation: The same distance idea gains a third squared term: the square root of 49 is 7. Summing the raw parts overstates a diagonal.

questions.prompt: Why does subtracting an observer's position from a target's position give an arrow pointing from the observer to the target?
options: Target minus observer is the step you would take to get there
Subtraction points toward whichever position is larger
Subtraction gives the direction that the observer is facing
The order does not matter, so either order gives the same arrow
questions.explanation: Target minus observer is the step from the observer to the target. Reversing the operands would point the arrow backward while its length stays the same.

questions.prompt: Which expression has a useful meaning for positions and directions?
options: point + direction, which gives a new place after moving
point + point, which gives the place between the two
direction − point, which gives the distance travelled
point × point, which gives the area they cover
questions.explanation: Adding a movement vector to a position moves it. Adding two positions has no useful geometric meaning, because a position only says where something is, not an amount of movement.

questions.prompt: The axes of a game's coordinates are not documented. How can you find out which axis means up?
options: Move in one direction at a time and see which coordinate follows
Assume the third axis is up, since that is how it is written
Read the coordinates while standing still and look at the signs
Compare the numbers with those of a different game
questions.explanation: Games disagree about which axis is up, so you observe it. Changing one direction while the others stay put shows which field tracks the movement.

questions.prompt: What does normalizing the vector (6, 8, 0) return, and why?
options: (0.6, 0.8, 0), each part divided by the length 10
(0.06, 0.08, 0), each part divided by the length squared
(3, 4, 0), each part divided by 2
(1, 1, 0), each part divided by itself
questions.explanation: The length is 10, so dividing each part by 10 keeps the direction and gives a vector of length 1. Dividing by anything else changes the direction or leaves the length wrong.

questions.prompt: Why might a function that normalizes a vector return an optional result?
options: A zero-length vector has no direction, so nothing may be returned
Normalizing just works for vectors in two dimensions of space
Optional results make the calculation faster to run on a CPU
Normalized vectors cannot be stored in a plain variable
questions.explanation: When the two points coincide, dividing by a zero length gives no meaningful direction. Returning nothing stops bad numbers from spreading into later calculations.

questions.prompt: For two normalized directions, what dot product means they point in opposite ways?
questions.explanation: Normalized dot products run from 1 (same way) through 0 (perpendicular) to -1 (opposite). A value of 0 means a right angle, not opposite directions.

questions.prompt: A camera faces (0, 1, 0), and the unit direction to a target is (0.6, 0.8, 0). What does the dot product tell you?
options: It is 0.8, the cosine of about 37 degrees off-center
It is 1.4, the sum of the parts of the direction
It is 0.6, the first part of the target direction
It is 0, since the two vectors point differently
questions.explanation: Only the matching parts contribute: 1 x 0.8 = 0.8. That is the cosine of about 37 degrees, so the target is somewhat off-center.

questions.prompt: A rule says a target is visible within a 60-degree cone. How can you test it with the dot product of unit vectors, without computing angles?
options: Compare the dot product with cos(60 degrees), which is 0.5
Compare the dot product with the number 60
Compare the dot product with sin(60 degrees), about 0.87
Compare the dot product with 1 divided by 60
questions.explanation: Anything with a dot product above 0.5 lies inside the cone. Comparing cosines is cheaper than converting to angles.

questions.prompt: Why clamp a dot product to the range -1 to 1 before taking its inverse cosine?
options: Rounding can push it slightly outside the range the function accepts
Dot products are normally far larger than 1 and must be shrunk
The inverse cosine runs faster when its input is clamped
Negative dot products are invalid and have to be removed
questions.explanation: Floating-point rounding can nudge a value slightly past the mathematical range. The inverse cosine is only defined from -1 to 1, so clamping keeps it valid.

questions.prompt: Using linear interpolation, what value is one fifth of the way (t = 0.2) from a = 10 to b = 60?
options: 30, since that is the average of the two ends
70, since the two ends are added together
questions.explanation: Linear interpolation is a + (b - a) x t. Using b x t ignores the starting point.

questions.prompt: What is halfway (t = 0.5) between the positions (2, 6) and (10, 2)?
options: (6, 4), found by blending each coordinate separately
(12, 8), found by adding the two positions together
(4, -2), found by halving the difference of the positions
(8, 4), found by subtracting the starting position
questions.explanation: Each coordinate blends on its own: 2 + 8 x 0.5 = 6 and 6 - 4 x 0.5 = 4. Adding positions has no useful meaning here.

questions.prompt: After a fixed step, a quarter of a step's time is left over (t = 0.25). A ball was at x = 100 after the earlier step and at x = 108 after the later one. Where is it drawn?
options: 108, since the latest position is the best one to show
104, since the ball is shown halfway between the two steps
25, since the leftover fraction is used as the position
questions.explanation: The blend is 100 + (108 - 100) x 0.25 = 102. Using t alone, or taking the halfway point, ignores the real distance and the leftover fraction.

questions.prompt: An object moves from x = 0 to x = 200 using an ease-in curve that squares t. Where is it halfway through the time (t = 0.5)?
options: 50, since 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25 of the distance
100, which is the plain linear answer
150, which is what an ease-out curve would give
25, since half of a quarter is used
questions.explanation: Ease in reshapes t to t squared, so it starts slowly: 0.25 x 200 = 50. 100 is linear, and 150 belongs to ease out.

questions.prompt: A follower closes 25 percent of the remaining gap on each update, starting 16 units away. What is the gap after two updates?
options: 8, since the same four units are closed on each update
12, since just one update has been applied so far
0, since two updates close 25 percent twice over
questions.explanation: Each update keeps 75 percent of the gap: 16 x 0.75 = 12, then 9. The follower slows as it arrives because each step is a fraction of a shrinking gap.

questions.prompt: Why tie a follow fraction to the elapsed time instead of using a fixed fraction per update?
options: A fixed fraction closes the gap faster on machines that update often
Elapsed time makes the gap grow slowly, so it is safer to use here
A fixed fraction cannot be negative, which causes many problems
Time-based fractions are cheaper to compute than fixed ones are
questions.explanation: The follower would behave differently on fast and slow machines. A time-based fraction makes two short updates match one long one.

questions.prompt: A time-based follow uses a fraction k of the gap per update. If the update rate doubles, what should k do?
options: Get smaller, so two short updates match one long one
Double, so that each short update moves twice as far
Stay the same, since the fraction is already correct as it is
Drop to zero, since the follower would already be there
questions.explanation: Each shorter step needs a smaller fraction so the total movement over one second matches. Two small steps leave the same remaining gap as one big step.

questions.prompt: Updates report x = 50 at 0.00 s and x = 62 at 0.20 s. What does extrapolation guess for x at 0.30 s?
options: 68, continuing the same line to t = 1.5
62, the last value that was reported
56, the value halfway between the reports
74, the line continued to t = 2
questions.explanation: t = 0.30 / 0.20 = 1.5, so 50 + 12 x 1.5 = 68. Interpolation stays between known points, while extrapolation goes past them.

questions.prompt: A player stops at x = 106. How do interpolated and extrapolated views differ?
options: Interpolated lags but shows real places; extrapolated can overshoot and snap back
Interpolated overshoots to 111.4 then snaps back; extrapolated lags by 0.10 s
Both views lag by 0.10 s, but only extrapolated shows invented places
Neither view is ever wrong, because both use the same two known updates
questions.explanation: Interpolation draws a past state, so it is always behind but never invents positions. Extrapolation is never behind but overshoots when the guess is wrong, such as 111.4 before snapping to 106.

questions.prompt: A quadratic Bezier curve has control points P0 = (0, 0), P1 = (4, 8) and P2 = (8, 0). Where is the curve at t = 0.5?
options: (4, 4), pulled toward P1 but not reaching it
(4, 8), right at the middle control point of the curve
(4, 2), just a quarter of the way up to the point P1
(2, 4), found by halving the two ends of the curve
questions.explanation: The weights are 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25, so y = 0.5 x 8 = 4 and x = 2 + 2 = 4. The curve only rises to 4 even though the control point is at 8.

questions.prompt: Two circles have centers at (0, 0) and (6, 8), with radii 4 and 5. Do they touch or overlap?
options: No: 10 is more than 9, just as 100 is more than 81
Yes: 100 is bigger than 81, so the circles must overlap each other
Yes: each radius is smaller than 10, so the circles must meet
Yes: 9 is less than 14, the sum of the two center differences
questions.explanation: Circles overlap only when the distance is less than the sum of the radii. Comparing squares (100 against 81) gives the same answer as comparing 10 against 9, without a square root.

questions.prompt: Box A spans x 0 to 4 and y 0 to 3. Box B spans x 5 to 9 and y 2 to 6. Do they overlap?
options: No: x ranges 0 to 4 and 5 to 9 are apart, which is enough
Yes: the y ranges share 2 to 3, so contact is certain
Yes: both boxes lie inside 9 units of the origin point
No: box B is taller than box A, so they cannot overlap
questions.explanation: Axis-aligned boxes overlap only if their ranges overlap on every axis. One separated axis rules out contact, even though the y ranges share 2 to 3.

questions.prompt: When searching memory for a character's position, why move in just one direction at a time at first?
options: A single-axis change shows which candidates follow that axis
Scanners cannot detect a position change that is diagonal
Single-axis moves are faster for a scanner to process
Games just store one axis of a position at a time
questions.explanation: Each experiment changes only one coordinate, so the candidates that follow it identify that axis. Moving diagonally would change both values and blur which candidate is which.

questions.prompt: How should you test whether a memory address holds a position by writing a value to it?
options: In a disposable offline setup, nudge it slightly, then restore it
Write a large value in a live match so the effect is obvious at once
Write a new value and leave it there so that the effect stays on
Write to every candidate address at once to save a lot of time
questions.explanation: A tiny change confirms the candidate while risking little, and restoring the original value keeps the experiment clean. It belongs in an offline test area.

questions.prompt: The player's position offset has been confirmed. What should you do for an enemy object?
options: Confirm its offsets separately, since objects need not share a layout
Reuse the player's offsets, since every game object has the same layout
Add the player's offset to the enemy's base and trust the result
Copy the enemy offsets from the cursor position because both are floats
questions.explanation: Do not assume every object shares the same layout. An enemy, a cursor, and an alive flag each need their own confirmation.

questions.prompt: Why should a decision-making bot work from a copied snapshot and not hold live pointers into game memory?
options: Values captured together stay stable while it chooses
Copies are faster to read than live memory is to read from
Pointers into game memory cannot refer to enemy data
A snapshot updates itself as the game state changes
questions.explanation: The bot decides from local values captured together, and keeps no remote pointer alive. Remote memory can change under a pointer that is held.

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes the repeated jobs of a useful bot?
options: Observe, estimate state, choose an intent, act, observe again
Choose an intent, act, then observe once and stop
Estimate state, act, choose an intent, then observe
Act, observe, and repeat with no state estimate or intent
questions.explanation: The loop returns to observing after every action, because the action itself does not prove success. The estimate and the intent come before acting.

questions.prompt: A bot sent a movement request. Why shouldn't it assume the move happened?
options: It may be blocked or the target may vanish; wait for a confirming observation
The game ignores every request that arrives within a second of the last one
Requests are only accepted when the snapshot is older than about 500 ms
A request that returns no error code usually means the move failed
questions.explanation: An action requests something; only a later observation confirms it. After every request, wait for a specific observation that confirms or rejects it.

questions.prompt: Why record when an observation was captured?
options: Freshness matters: an old exact position can be worse than a noisy new one
Timestamps make the positions themselves more precise than before
The game refuses to accept any data that lacks a timestamp attached to it
Old data is cleaner than new data, so it should be preferred over it
questions.explanation: Time is part of the model. A bot should know how fresh its observation is and how long a confirmation stays valid.

questions.prompt: Why reject coordinates that are not finite numbers, such as NaN or infinity, before using them?
options: They poison comparisons, so a nearest-target search may be wrong
They take up more memory than ordinary numbers do in the game
They make every calculation run much more slowly than normal
They are negative numbers that the game cannot display on screen
questions.explanation: A NaN makes comparisons unreliable, so a nearest-enemy search could pick a meaningless target. Rejecting it up front keeps decisions sound.

questions.prompt: A coordinate passes a plausibility range check. What has been proven?
options: Only that it is plausible, not that it belongs to the right object
That it is the position of the player's own character in the game
That it is fully up to date with the current game state now
That it is the exact value that the game is using right now
questions.explanation: A range check cannot tell which object a number belongs to. Combine it with identity, alive flags, movement continuity and repeated reads.
