questions.prompt: A player is at (0, 0), and targets are at (6, 8) and (2, 0). Which does a nearest-target search choose?
options: (2, 0), at distance 2 rather than 10
(6, 8), since it is listed first in the targets
(6, 8), since larger coordinates count as closer
Neither, since the two targets are tied
questions.explanation: The distances are 10 and 2, and the search keeps the smallest. The order of the list does not decide the result.

questions.prompt: A player is at (0, 0), and candidates are at (9, 0) and (5, 5). Which is nearest, and why?
options: (5, 5), because about 7.07 is less than 9
(9, 0), because its parts add to 9, which is below 10
(9, 0), because it is listed first among the candidates
(5, 5), because 5 is smaller than 9
questions.explanation: The distance to (5, 5) is the square root of 50, about 7.07, which is less than 9. True distances are compared, not sums of the parts.

questions.prompt: A decision layer cannot trust the player's own position. What should it output?
options: A stop intent that comes with a reason
A wait intent, hoping that the next snapshot is fine
A move toward the nearest enemy anyway
Nothing, so the caller has to guess
questions.explanation: An invalid player position means the decision layer cannot trust any distance, so it stops and says why. A wait is for the case where no valid enemy exists.

questions.prompt: Why should a decision function return an intent value instead of sending an input directly?
options: The decision code knows nothing about how actions are carried out
Input events are slower than intent values in every kind of game
The operating system forbids any decision code from sending input
Intent values are encrypted, which also protects the decisions
questions.explanation: Keeping decision and action apart means the decision code touches no memory and can be unit-tested with made-up coordinates. A separate action layer carries the intent out.

questions.prompt: Which guardrail covers a player who keeps receiving move requests but never changes position?
options: Stop when the player has not moved after several attempts
Stop when the user requests a stop with the stop key
Stop when any base pointer in the snapshot becomes null
Stop when the target version check fails on startup
questions.explanation: The no-movement check catches a bot that is blocked or issuing useless input. The others cover different failures, such as an inactive level or a missing pointer.

questions.prompt: A module loaded at 0x00400000 on one run, and a call sat at 0x0040AB10. What is the module-relative offset?
options: 0xAB10, the address minus the module base
0x0040AB10, the absolute address of the call
0x0080AB10, the address plus the module base
0x00400000, the base of the module itself
questions.explanation: Subtracting the base leaves 0xAB10, which still works when the module loads elsewhere. The absolute address belonged only to that one run.

questions.prompt: Why can screen positions that a bot picks with a game-specific rule not be reused unchanged on another setup?
options: They depend on window size, interface scale and layout
They depend on the name of the player's character in the match
They are re-randomized by the game on every frame drawn
They are encrypted by the operating system when the window opens
questions.explanation: Screen numbers depend on the window and the interface, which differ between setups. Treat them as local calibration, not as universal constants.

questions.prompt: When the injected Flare library unloads, what comes first?
options: Stop the worker, then restore all three original five-byte calls
Restore the three calls first, since the worker only reads values
Free the captured addresses first so the worker cannot use them
Leave the detours installed so the next injection can reuse them
questions.explanation: The worker must stop and release the mouse input first, because it could still be using a captured value. Only then are the original calls restored.

questions.prompt: A wall lies between the player and a target. Why does moving straight toward the target fail?
options: A route must follow legal neighbouring tiles, so a direct line can get stuck on the wall
The target's coordinates change whenever a wall stands between it and the player
Walls reverse the direction of movement for any bot that approaches them
Straight-line movement is only allowed on grids wider than the player
questions.explanation: Coordinates give a direction, not a way around obstacles. Treating the map as a graph of legal neighbouring tiles lets a search find a route.

questions.prompt: When a grid map is viewed as a graph, what does a wall tile become?
options: A tile that no edge crosses
A node with a cost that is infinite
An edge that joins two neighboring nodes
A node that is visited last
questions.explanation: A wall means no legal move crosses that tile. Walkable tiles are nodes, and legal moves between neighbors are edges.

questions.prompt: A map stored row by row is 5 tiles wide. At which flat index is tile (x = 3, y = 2)?
options: 10, since 2 x 5 = 10
5, since 3 + 2 = 5
questions.explanation: The formula is y x width + x, so 2 x 5 + 3 = 13. Swapping the roles of x and y would read a different tile.

questions.prompt: Why must out-of-range coordinates be rejected before computing y x width + x?
options: The formula can turn a bad coordinate into an index in another row
The formula crashes whenever it receives a negative number as input
The result would be a decimal number instead of a whole number index
The formula just works on maps that are perfectly square in shape
questions.explanation: A bad coordinate can still produce an index that belongs to another row. Checking first, then using checked arithmetic, stops a corrupted width from wrapping into a valid-looking index.

questions.prompt: Why is the first route BFS finds to a tile a shortest one, on equal-cost moves?
options: Tiles leave the queue in the order they entered, so nearer tiles come first
The search always steps in the direction of the goal
The search remembers every tile and picks the cheapest after finishing
The queue sorts tiles by their estimated remaining cost
questions.explanation: First-in-first-out order examines everything one step away before two steps away. A shorter route would have come out earlier and got there first.

questions.prompt: Entering a swamp tile costs 8 and every other tile costs 1. A search finds a route through the swamp in 2 moves, while a route around takes 5 moves. Which is cheaper, and what does it show?
options: The 5-move route costs 5 against 9; fewest steps is not cheapest
The 2-move route, since fewer steps cost less in total
They cost the same, so the choice between them makes no difference
The 5-move route, but just because the search happens to prefer it
questions.explanation: The swamp route costs 8 + 1 = 9, while the longer route costs 5. Counting steps and counting cost are different things.

questions.prompt: Why can breadth-first search give the wrong answer on uneven terrain?
options: It guarantees fewest steps, not lowest cost, on uneven ground
Its queue forgets some of the tiles when the map is large enough
It cannot handle maps that contain any walls or other blocked tiles
It explores the goal tile last, after every other tile on the map
questions.explanation: Breadth-first search counts steps, so it is right only when every move costs the same. This is a limit of its guarantee, not a flaw in its queue.

questions.prompt: In A-Star, which value decides which tile comes out of the frontier next?
options: Cost already paid plus the estimated cost remaining
Estimated cost remaining, since it points at the goal
Cost already paid, as in BFS
The number of walls next to the tile
questions.explanation: The priority is the known cost so far plus the heuristic estimate. The estimate alone would chase the goal and ignore what has been spent.

questions.prompt: What is the Manhattan distance from (2, 7) to (6, 4)?
options: 7, from the differences 4 and 3 added together
5, from the straight line between the two points
25, from the squared straight-line distance
1, from subtracting the two nearest coordinates
questions.explanation: Manhattan distance adds the horizontal and vertical differences: 4 + 3 = 7. The straight line (5) is what diagonal movement would allow.

questions.prompt: When can Manhattan distance overestimate and break the cheapest-path guarantee?
options: With diagonals, `(0,0)` to `(1,1)` is one move yet Manhattan says two
Whenever any tile in the grid costs more than 1 to enter at all
Whenever the goal sits in the very same row as the start tile
Whenever the map is wider than it is tall, counted in tiles
questions.explanation: With diagonals the real minimum can be smaller than the estimate. The heuristic must match the movement rules, because an overestimate loses the guarantee.

questions.prompt: What does setting the heuristic to zero turn A-Star into, and why is that useful?
options: Dijkstra's algorithm, a debugging switch for blaming the estimate
Breadth-first search, a way to drop the cost field completely
A random walk, a way to test the input timing of a bot
Depth-first search, a way to shorten every route found
questions.explanation: With no estimate, only the cost so far orders the frontier. If that version works and the normal one does not, inspect the heuristic and cost assumptions before blaming the map.

questions.prompt: In a breadth-first search, what two jobs does a map from each reached tile to the tile it was reached from do?
options: It marks visited tiles and lets the route be rebuilt from the goal
It stores each tile's cost and the total cost of the finished route
It holds the order of the queue and the position of the goal tile
It records which tiles are walls and which of the tiles are open
questions.explanation: A tile already in the map is not added again, and the stored predecessor lets the route be rebuilt backward from the goal.

questions.prompt: A map header says 100 x 100, but the copied array holds fewer than 10,000 tiles. What catches this?
options: A checked lookup that returns nothing past the end of the array
The width and height checks, since they read the map's header
A checksum that is stored inside of the map header itself
The search algorithm itself, which stops at the very last tile
questions.explanation: The width and height checks only trust the header. A checked lookup uses the real length, so an incomplete snapshot gives nothing instead of a wrong tile.

questions.prompt: Why keep a tile's terrain, visibility and cost together in one record instead of in three parallel arrays?
options: Parallel arrays can drift apart, so one index may mean two tiles
Records are faster to read than separate arrays are
Arrays cannot hold values that have a named set of options in them
A record uses less memory because its fields all share the same space
questions.explanation: Keeping one tile's facts in one record makes that mistake hard to express. Parallel arrays can disagree about which tile an index means.

questions.prompt: Why should a path search function never read game memory or press keys?
options: It takes a copied grid and returns coordinates, so tests can run anywhere
Searching is too slow to be combined with memory reads on the same thread
The operating system blocks search code from reading any memory
Memory reads would change the map while the search is still running
questions.explanation: Observation, search and input are separate layers. Only an input layer turns a confirmed route step into an action.

questions.prompt: A route was planned from one snapshot. What should the bot do before taking the next step?
options: Check the current and next tiles are valid, and replan if not
Take every step at once so the map has no time to change
Trust the route, since the planner already checked every tile
Restart the game so that the grid is read again from scratch
questions.explanation: The observed grid can change after planning. A route is only as current as its snapshot, so check before acting and replan if a tile is no longer valid.

questions.prompt: A 4 x 2 grid has its start at (0, 0), its goal at (3, 0), and walls at (1, 0) and (2, 0). Moves are up, down, left or right. How many moves does the shortest route take?
options: 5 moves: down, across the lower row, then up
3 moves, going straight along the open top row
4 moves, cutting diagonally past the two blocked walls
3 moves, jumping over the two walls in the top row
questions.explanation: The route is (0,0), (0,1), (1,1), (2,1), (3,1), (3,0), which is five moves. The search rejects the wall tiles, and the grid has no diagonal moves.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the preferred image base and the live module base?
options: Preferred: where the file asks to load; live: where Windows put it this run
Preferred: where Windows put it this run; live: where the file asks to load
Preferred: a distance from the start of the module; live: a position in the file
Preferred: the final address the CPU uses; live: the entry-point RVA
questions.explanation: The preferred base is the address requested by the PE headers; the live base is the real location in this process run, which ASLR may change.

questions.prompt: What is an RVA?
options: Arithmetic describing a location inside one loaded image
A pointer stored inside the game's memory
The address where Windows loaded the module
A position counted in bytes from the start of the file
questions.explanation: An RVA is a distance from the module's beginning. It is not stored in the game, and it is not a file offset.

questions.prompt: An executable's preferred image base is 0x00500000 and an RVA is 0x2000. What is the preferred virtual address?
options: 0x00502000, the base plus the RVA
0x00002000, the RVA on its own
0x00520000, the RVA appended to the base
0x004FE000, the RVA taken away from the base
questions.explanation: Preferred address is the preferred base plus the RVA. It only matches a live address if the module loaded at its preferred base.

questions.prompt: Why is adding a live module base to a file offset compared with adding meters to seconds?
options: They are in different spaces, so the sum has no useful meaning
Both are measured in bytes, so the sum just breaks for large values
Both are addresses, so the sum is simply an address
The sum overflows, since both numbers are too large
questions.explanation: A file offset counts bytes on disk, while a live base is a location in memory. Mixing coordinate systems gives a number with no meaning.

questions.prompt: A section has virtual address 0x3000, a raw data pointer of 0x0800 and a raw size of 0x1000. Which file offset holds RVA 0x3450?
questions.explanation: The offset inside the section is 0x3450 - 0x3000 = 0x450, and 0x0800 + 0x450 = 0x0C50. Using the RVA as a file offset would look in the wrong place.

questions.prompt: The same section has a virtual size of 0x1400 and a raw size of 0x1000. RVA 0x4080 is 0x1080 into the section. Is there a byte for it in the file?
options: No: 0x1080 is past the 0x1000 raw bytes, so it is zero-filled
Yes: it is inside the virtual size, so the file stores that byte too
No: it lies outside the section, so it does not exist
Yes: it sits at file offset 0x1080 from the section's start in the file
questions.explanation: The mapping only works when the offset inside the section is below the raw size. Past it, but still inside the virtual size, the loader supplies zeros.

questions.prompt: What is special about RVAs that fall inside the headers, below the size of the headers?
options: No section covers them, and they commonly map to the same file offset
They map to the very end of the file, after all of the sections
They are not valid for any purpose in a loaded image of a program
They map to zero-filled memory that the loader supplies to the image
questions.explanation: Header RVAs are not covered by the normal section formula. They usually correspond to the same number as a file offset.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches how ASLR and a game update affect the numbers?
options: ASLR changes the live base; an update can change the RVA
ASLR changes the RVA; an update changes the live base
ASLR and updates both change only the preferred base
Neither affects the RVA or the live base
questions.explanation: Randomised loading moves the first term of base + RVA. Rebuilding the game can move the instruction inside the module, so the RVA is stable only for one exact build.

questions.prompt: An instruction was seen at 0x00A41234 when its module's base was 0x00A00000. What is its RVA?
questions.explanation: RVA is the observed address minus the observed base: 0x00A41234 - 0x00A00000 = 0x00041234. The absolute address was only valid for that run.

questions.prompt: An instruction's RVA is 0x00041234. In a later run the module's base is 0x00C00000. What is its live address?
questions.explanation: Add the new run's base to the same RVA: 0x00C00000 + 0x00041234 = 0x00C41234. The layout inside the module has not moved.

questions.prompt: You are debugging a run in which you measured a module's base as 0x02000000. For RVA 0x41234, which address should you use?
options: 0x02041234, since this run's base was measured
0x00A41234, since that was the address seen in an earlier run
0x00C41234, since that was the base used in another run
0x00041234, since the RVA already is the address
questions.explanation: Measure the module's base in the run you are actually debugging, and add the RVA to it. The base from a write-up or earlier run may not apply.

questions.prompt: Why wrap an offset-in-file and an address-in-memory as distinct types when both are integers?
options: Type names keep the spaces apart, so mixing them fails to build
Wrapped integers take up less memory than plain integers do
Wrapped integers cannot overflow when they are added together
Distinct types make the calculations run noticeably faster
questions.explanation: Both are numbers inside, but a function that wants one will not accept the other. That stops coordinate-space mistakes before runtime.

questions.prompt: A function turns an RVA into a live address by adding a module base. When should it return nothing?
options: When the RVA is outside the image or the sum overflows
When the module's base address happens to be an even number
When the RVA happens to be exactly zero in value
When the module has already been loaded into the process
questions.explanation: It has two proof obligations: the RVA belongs to this image, and the sum fits in the address type.

questions.prompt: A list of the modules loaded in a process is taken at one moment. What caution applies to it?
options: It is a moment-in-time view, so a module may unload later
It updates live, so it cannot be out of date at any point
It lists just the first module that was loaded in the process
It lists the modules of every process that is on the machine
questions.explanation: Reusable tools should handle a later read failure normally, since a module can unload after the list was taken.

questions.prompt: A tool is given an RVA that is not below the module's size. What does that most likely mean?
options: The RVA probably comes from another build of the module
The module has not been fully loaded into memory yet
The base address is wrong by exactly one single unit
The RVA is too small to be a real address of anything
questions.explanation: An RVA outside the module probably comes from a different build, so the tool should stop with an error. An overflowing addition is not a valid address either.

questions.prompt: Why is an RVA not a version check by itself?
options: A rebuild can move the code, so check the build and bytes too
An RVA changes every single time the game is started again
An RVA is identical for every program that runs on Windows
An RVA is stored in the file only when it is a debug build
questions.explanation: Keep all three checks: exact version, live base plus the version's RVA, and original bytes or a unique pattern at the final address.

questions.prompt: After printing the live address, what must you confirm in x64dbg before using it?
options: The bytes and disassembly match the lesson
The address is a multiple of 4
The live base equals the preferred base
The address is below 0x00400000
questions.explanation: The final address must show the expected bytes. That is why the code-cave installers reject unknown bytes instead of hoping the address is close enough.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly contrasts an export with an import?
options: An export says other images may ask this DLL for a name or ordinal; an import says this program needs one from elsewhere
An export lists the DLLs a program loads at startup; an import lists the functions the program offers to other images
An export is a function the game calls on itself; an import is a name that Windows creates when the loader starts
An export is stored only in executables; an import is stored only in DLLs that were built for plug-ins
questions.explanation: An import is a request for something provided by another image, while an export is a public offer. Swapping them is the common beginner mix-up.

questions.prompt: Which table in a DLL's export directory holds the RVAs of the public ASCII names?
options: The name pointer table, which lists name RVAs
The export address table, which holds the RVAs of code
The ordinal table, which maps names to code
The relocation table, which fixes addresses after loading
questions.explanation: The name pointer table lists name RVAs. The ordinal table gives small indexes, and the export address table holds RVAs of code, data or forwarder strings.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when a DLL exports a function by ordinal only?
options: The function has an address entry but no public name, so callers must ask for its number
The function is hidden from the loader, so even a call by number will fail with an error
The function name is stored in the ordinal table instead of the name pointer table
The function must be forwarded, because only forwarders are allowed to skip having names
questions.explanation: Not every export needs a name. That is why the tool reports the total number of address entries separately from the named ones.

questions.prompt: An export directory has an ordinal base of 10, and a caller asks for ordinal 13. Which index of the address table holds it?
options: Index 3, since 13 - 10 = 3
Index 13, since the ordinal is the index
Index 23, since the base is added to the ordinal
Index 4, since counting starts at one
questions.explanation: The real ordinal is the base plus the table index, so the index is 13 - 10 = 3. Using the wrong index is an off-by-one that returns a different export.

questions.prompt: A DLL's ordinal base is 10 and a named export sits at address-table index 3. What ordinal should the parser print?
questions.explanation: The printed ordinal is `ordinal_base + index`, so 10 + 3 = 13. Printing the bare index of 3 would not match what callers actually ask for.

questions.prompt: A section has virtual address 0x5000 and raw data pointer 0x400. The target RVA is 0x5180. What is the file offset?
questions.explanation: The distance inside the section is 0x5180 - 0x5000 = 0x180, and adding the raw start 0x400 gives 0x580. Reusing the RVA itself ignores the section shift.

questions.prompt: Why should a parser reject an RVA whose distance into a section is not smaller than that section's raw size?
options: It is zero-filled memory, with no bytes stored in the file
It points into a different section, which is not allowed
It points past the end of the file's own header data
The section is encrypted at that position in the file
questions.explanation: Virtual size can be larger than the bytes stored on disk. Without the check the parser would pretend padding bytes exist in the file.

questions.prompt: A parser handles both 32-bit and 64-bit executables. Why can it not hard-code where the data directories begin?
options: The optional header has different sizes in the two formats
The directories live in a separate file in the 64-bit format
Directories exist just in files of the 64-bit format
The position of the directories is random in every file
questions.explanation: The 64-bit optional header is larger, so the directories start at a different offset. A fixed shortcut belongs to one layout and is not reliable.

questions.prompt: Why is hard-coding "the export table is 0x78 after the PE signature" described as brittle?
options: It assumes one optional-header layout and mixes up header landmarks
It only works for DLLs, because EXE files always store their export table in a different section
It breaks whenever Windows picks a new load base, because the offset is added to the live base
It is too slow, because the parser must then scan the file twice for the PE signature
questions.explanation: PE32 and PE32+ place the directories differently, so a single offset from a screenshot fits only one shape. The magic value chooses the layout.

questions.prompt: Why does a parser check how many directory entries a header declares before reading entry zero?
options: An undeclared entry would lie outside the header's declared data
Entry zero is empty in most files, so reading it is wasteful of time
Entries can just be read in pairs, so a count is needed first
The count tells the parser which version of the format is in use
questions.explanation: Reading an entry the header never declared would cross the header's boundary. The check keeps the parser inside the data that the file claims to have.

questions.prompt: How does the parser decide that an address-table entry is a forwarder string rather than code?
options: The entry's RVA points back inside the export directory's own range
The entry's RVA is exactly zero, which the loader treats as a request to look elsewhere
The entry's name contains a dot, such as `KERNELBASE.VirtualQueryEx`, so it is a forwarder
The entry's ordinal is larger than the number of names stored in the name pointer table
questions.explanation: A forwarder is a text string stored inside the export directory range, so an RVA landing there is a string, not code. A dot in a name is not the test used.

questions.prompt: What does a forwarded export let the system do?
options: Keep a public name while the real code lives in another DLL
Run the exported function on a separate thread of its own choosing
Hide the exported function from debuggers and other analysis tools
Copy the exported function's code straight into the caller
questions.explanation: The loader follows the forwarder string to the named export in another DLL. Callers keep using the old name while the implementation moves behind it.

questions.prompt: An export directory spans RVAs 0x6000 to 0x6900. One function entry holds 0x6310 and another holds 0x2A40. Which entry is a forwarder?
options: The one holding 0x6310, which lies inside the directory range
The one holding 0x2A40, since it is the smaller of the values
Both of them, since every export entry can be a forwarder
Neither of them, since forwarders are stored somewhere else
questions.explanation: Only a value inside the export directory's range is a forwarder string. 0x2A40 lies outside it and points to code or data.

questions.prompt: In a file parser, why send every read through one checked helper?
options: Boundaries are checked in one place, so bad data gives an error
It makes the reads faster than separate checks would be
It encrypts the data so that nobody else is able to read it
It converts every value to the byte order of the machine used
questions.explanation: A bad table entry then reports a useful message instead of causing an index panic.

questions.prompt: Why use checked addition when computing offsets from numbers stored in a file?
options: A wrapped sum could turn a huge value into a small, valid one
Checked addition is faster than plain addition in most of the cases
File fields are negative, which plain addition cannot handle well
Plain addition can just add two values that are exactly the same size
questions.explanation: Numbers come from an untrusted file, so a wrapped sum could pass later bounds checks wrongly. A checked addition returns an error instead.

questions.prompt: Why must export strings terminate within 4096 bytes in this parser?
options: A corrupt file might omit the NUL forever, so the search needs an upper limit
Windows itself rejects any export name longer than 4096 bytes when it loads the DLL
The ordinal table can only address strings that fit inside one 4096-byte memory page
A longer string would be treated as a forwarder and followed to the next DLL in the chain
questions.explanation: The scan for a NUL byte is capped so malformed data cannot make the parser read endlessly. The limit is a teaching-tool guardrail, not a Windows rule.

questions.prompt: Why cap a count read from an untrusted file before using it to allocate memory or run a loop?
options: A damaged count could demand gigabytes of memory
Large counts are not valid in any file format that exists today
Caps make parsing faster than it would be without any of them
Counts above the cap would crash the whole operating system
questions.explanation: A fixed limit makes the tool fail with a message instead of consuming huge amounts of memory.

questions.prompt: In which order should a PE parser validate the file's structure?
options: From the outside inward: DOS header, PE header, directories, then exports
From the export table outward, since it is the only part of the file this tool must trust
Whichever order is shortest, because every later signature check can repair an earlier bad read
Sections first, because they decide the RVA mapping that every earlier header read depends on
questions.explanation: A later valid-looking signature cannot make an earlier out-of-bounds read safe. Each range is proven before the next field is read.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of distinct wrapper types for file offsets, RVAs and live addresses?
options: Mixing them up becomes a compile error, forcing one conversion
Conversions between the three kinds happen without any code
The need for bounds checks disappears for all three of the types
The values become unsigned, which is what makes them safer to use
questions.explanation: File offsets, RVAs, virtual addresses and table indexes are different things. Distinct types turn a mix-up into an error before the code runs.

questions.prompt: Why should a function that converts an RVA to a file offset return an optional or error result and not always a number?
options: Some mapped RVAs have no file bytes, and sections can overlap
File offsets can be negative, which a plain number cannot hold
RVAs are optional fields that are missing from many files on disk
Numbers cannot be returned from functions that read files from disk
questions.explanation: The conversion is a partial function. Inventing an offset for padding or broken section data would hide the problem instead of reporting it.

questions.prompt: An inspector reports that a game's main executable has no export table. What should you conclude?
options: That is valid, since many executables publish no exports
The file is corrupt and should be downloaded from the source again
The inspector has a bug that needs to be fixed before anything else
The game cannot run without an export table in its main file
questions.explanation: An executable may have no export table at all. DLLs are usually the more interesting files to inspect for exports.

questions.prompt: Why should you not call an export just because its name looks interesting?
options: A name does not reveal its signature, calling convention, or whether outsiders may use it
The name is only a nickname, so the real function behind it is picked at random on each load
Windows refuses to run any export whose name was not listed in the game's own documentation
Names are stored in the ordinal table, which is only accurate for the DLL's first ten entries
questions.explanation: The export table gives a name and an address, but nothing about parameters or intended use. Guessing could crash the host or misuse the API.

questions.prompt: A tool prints 120 address entries but only 95 named exports. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: Some exports have no name and can be reached only by ordinal
Twenty-five of the exports are duplicates of other exports
The file is damaged, since the two counts must match
Ninety-five of the exports are forwarders to other DLLs
questions.explanation: The address table can be larger than the name table when some exports are ordinal-only. The tool shows both numbers so the difference stays visible.

questions.prompt: A disassembler prints an instruction that loads a value from a register plus an offset of 0x30. Which fact can it NOT tell you from the bytes alone?
options: That the value at that offset is a player's score
That the instruction reads memory instead of only using registers
That the offset is the hexadecimal number 0x30
That the instruction is exactly as many bytes long as its encoding
questions.explanation: Names, comments and structure are normally gone after compilation. What a field means has to be learned by watching how the running program behaves.

questions.prompt: Which part of understanding an instruction does the decoder itself answer?
options: Mechanics: which registers, memory, and flags it can change
Data flow: where each input came from and where outputs are used
Program meaning: which game behavior the instruction implements
The programmer's intent, since the decoder knows the original source file
questions.explanation: The decoder answers mechanics; control-flow and data-flow analysis answer the second level; only the running target can establish the third.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a decoder and a formatter?
options: The decoder finds length and operands; the formatter chooses text spelling such as NASM style
The decoder prints assembly text; the formatter reads bytes from the target's memory
The decoder works on 32-bit code; the formatter handles only 64-bit instructions
The decoder is used for conditional jumps; the formatter is used for calls and returns
questions.explanation: A decoder answers structural questions. A formatter only spells the result, so tool logic should not depend on its string output.

questions.prompt: A tool must decide whether a decoded instruction is a jump. Why is checking a structured field better than searching its printed text for "jmp"?
options: Text depends on a formatter's style and spelling, while a field is a stable structured fact
Printed text is encrypted by the disassembler, so searching it is not allowed
Structured fields are always shorter, which makes the check a little quicker to type
A formatter never prints jumps at all, so the word cannot be found in its text
questions.explanation: Text is only a presentation of the decoded result. Reading the decoded data directly keeps the logic correct if the display format changes.

questions.prompt: In x86 instruction encoding, what is the role of a prefix?
options: It modifies a property such as operand size, repetition or locking
It selects which operation the processor performs, such as add or move
It describes how an index register is scaled when forming an address
It marks the end of an instruction, so the next byte starts a new one
questions.explanation: The opcode picks the operation and other bytes describe operands and addressing. A prefix adjusts how the instruction behaves, and most instructions have none.

questions.prompt: The bytes 89 D8 encode a register-to-register move. In 64-bit mode, what does placing a REX prefix byte 48 in front of them change?
options: It widens the move to a 64-bit operand size
It turns the move into a memory load instead of a register copy
It reverses the direction, so the source and destination swap places
It makes the instruction jump to the address held in the register
questions.explanation: A REX prefix extends the encoding, and its W bit selects a 64-bit operand size. Without it, the same bytes move a 32-bit register.

questions.prompt: A disassembler is given a block of copied bytes plus a starting address. What does that starting address change?
options: The addresses shown and the computed targets of relative jumps and calls
The bytes themselves, which are shifted to fit the new starting address
The number of instructions found, since a different start finds different code
The processor mode used to decode, which is chosen from the address range
questions.explanation: The bytes stay the same. The starting address only gives them a location, and relative branch targets are calculated from it.

questions.prompt: A 64-bit operating system is running a 32-bit program. In which mode should that program's code be decoded?
options: 32-bit, because the mode belongs to the code being decoded, not to the computer
64-bit, because the computer and the disassembler are both running in 64-bit mode
Either one, because modern disassemblers detect the correct mode from the bytes
16-bit, because 32-bit programs on 64-bit systems run in the oldest compatibility mode
questions.explanation: Bitness changes default operand sizes and which encodings are valid. The same bytes can mean different instructions in different modes, so the target's own mode must be used.

questions.prompt: Why should a disassembly helper refuse an unsupported mode setting instead of silently falling back to a default?
options: The same bytes decode differently per mode, so a guess can yield convincing but wrong output
Unsupported modes always crash the processor, so a default would stop the whole computer
A default mode would make the helper slower, since every byte must be decoded twice
Operating systems forbid running a disassembler in a mode they did not choose
questions.explanation: A silent guess produces output that looks real but is nonsense. Rejecting bad input up front is an honest error and a useful guardrail.

questions.prompt: Code bytes were copied from a running process into a local buffer. Which starting address should the disassembler be told?
options: The address they occupy in the target process, so branch destinations make sense
The address of the local buffer, since that is where the bytes are now stored
Zero, since a disassembler always counts positions from the start of the data
The address of the first jump in the bytes, so the targets are calculated against it
questions.explanation: Branch targets are computed from the instruction's own address. Using the target's real address keeps those destinations meaningful, no matter where the copy lives.

questions.prompt: What is a weakness of a linear sweep, which decodes one instruction after another?
options: It may decode data embedded in a code section as nonsense instructions
It cannot decode instructions that have prefixes, so it skips every prefixed opcode
It follows every call into other modules, which makes the output far too large
It needs a queue of addresses to visit, so it cannot run without a visited set
questions.explanation: A linear sweep treats every byte as code, so embedded data becomes meaningless instructions. A control-flow disassembler instead starts at an entry point and follows reachable branches.

questions.prompt: Which set of tools does a control-flow disassembler need that a linear sweep does not?
options: A work queue of addresses, a visited set, range checks, and branch-target extraction
A bigger byte buffer, since it decodes each instruction twice before printing them
A formatter for every CPU mode, since each branch might switch between 32 and 64 bit
A list of source variable names, since it must label each branch with its original name
questions.explanation: The lesson lists a work queue, a visited set, range checks, branch-target extraction, and a rule for following calls. It advises starting linear first.

questions.prompt: What is a basic block?
options: A straight run of instructions with one entry and a transfer at its end
A group of four instructions that the decoder reads together in one single call
A block of data bytes that a linear sweep must skip before it can continue on
Any function that has no conditional branches in it and also makes no calls
questions.explanation: Connecting blocks by possible jumps creates a control-flow graph. A conditional branch ends a block and starts new paths.

questions.prompt: Why should a control-flow graph mark unknown successors rather than pretend to be complete?
options: An indirect jump can get its target from a table or register, so some edges are unknown
Graphs with unknown edges decode faster, since the decoder skips the unmarked branches
Every jump in x86 code is indirect, so no graph can ever contain a known successor
The marks tell the formatter to hide the address of the instruction from the listing
questions.explanation: Exception handling and callbacks can also create edges that are not obvious. Claiming completeness would hide that uncertainty.

questions.prompt: The decoder reports an invalid instruction in the middle of a range. What must the tool never do?
options: Loop forever at the same bad byte
Show the invalid instruction clearly in the output
Stop and report an error to the learner
Advance by the decoder's reported length and continue
questions.explanation: The lesson says to show it clearly and decide whether to stop or advance by the reported length, but never enter an infinite loop at one bad byte.

questions.prompt: A test decodes the 32-bit bytes B8 05 00 00 00 C3 and expects exactly two instructions. What does that check?
options: That boundaries are found correctly: a five-byte instruction, then a one-byte one
That every byte in the buffer is a separate instruction, since each decodes on its own
That the processor will run the buffer without raising an exception at the second byte
That the immediate value 5 is stored in big-endian order inside the first instruction
questions.explanation: B8 with a four-byte value is one instruction and C3 is another. Getting two lines shows the decoder found the boundaries and sizes correctly.

questions.prompt: When disassembling around a known address, why decode only a small bounded range and stop on invalid bytes?
options: Starting mid-instruction or running into data gives garbage that looks like real code
Disassemblers can only read a fixed small number of bytes before the output is rejected
Invalid bytes are skipped by the processor, so a tool should stop to mirror that
Larger ranges decode into different code, because every byte changes the earlier ones
questions.explanation: A disassembler decodes whatever it is given, even data or a misaligned start. A bounded range from a verified address that halts on invalid bytes avoids inventing misleading output.

questions.prompt: Why is limiting a call logger to one code range and one moment more than a performance setting?
options: It makes the log a repeatable statement, such as which calls ran there in one action
It makes the logger run faster, which is the only practical reason to limit anything
It hides the calls outside the range so that other tools cannot record them
It guarantees that every call inside the range appears in the log exactly once
questions.explanation: A log of "calls from this range during this action" can be repeated and compared. A log of everything is mostly noise, and speed is only a side benefit.

questions.prompt: Which two jobs does a function call perform?
options: Remember where to continue afterward, and move the instruction pointer to the called function
Copy the called function into the caller's memory, and then erase the original function
Save every register to disk, and then reload the same registers when the call ends
Pause all other threads, and then unpause them when the called function returns
questions.explanation: The return address is remembered so execution can resume, and `EIP` is redirected to the target. Neither job copies or erases code.

questions.prompt: A 5-byte relative call sits at 0x00403000 with displacement 0x20. Where does it land?
questions.explanation: The displacement is added to the address of the next instruction, 0x00403005, giving 0x00403025. Adding it to the call's own address would give 0x00403020.

questions.prompt: A 5-byte relative call at 0x00405000 has the signed displacement -16 (0xFFFFFFF0). Where does it land?
questions.explanation: The displacement is measured from the end of the call, 0x00405005, and subtracting 16 (0x10) gives 0x00404FF5. A negative value means the target is earlier in memory.

questions.prompt: Why can a static look at the bytes not reveal a single destination for a call made through a register?
options: The register's value is set while the code runs and can differ from one call to the next
Register calls are always encoded as data, so no decoder can recognize them as calls
The operating system hides the target of a register call from every other program
Register calls only ever go to functions inside the operating system itself
questions.explanation: A direct call has its destination built into the bytes. An indirect call reads it from a register or memory at run time, so a separate technique is needed.

questions.prompt: Why is it unreliable to find calls by marking every byte equal to the call opcode?
options: That byte can sit inside another operand or in data, so decode whole instructions
Each call opcode is stored twice, so the second copy would be marked in error
The call opcode is different on every build, so a byte match is meaningless
Marking a byte changes its value, so later bytes would stop matching the opcode
questions.explanation: Bytes only have meaning at the correct instruction boundaries. Decoding complete instructions finds real calls and skips look-alike bytes.

questions.prompt: Instruction decoders report a flow-control kind for each instruction. What is that field useful for?
options: Telling calls, jumps and returns from other steps without hand-written opcode tests
Measuring how long each instruction takes to run on the current processor
Showing how many times each instruction has been run since the process started
Choosing which thread should run the instruction in a multithreaded target
questions.explanation: The decoder already understands the encodings, so it can label calls, branches and returns. That is more reliable than hand-written byte tests.

questions.prompt: How many bytes of the target instruction does a software breakpoint need to overwrite?
options: One, the trap byte placed at the first byte of the instruction
All of them, so that the whole instruction is replaced with traps
Two, a trap byte plus a byte that stores the instruction's address
One, but placed at the last byte so the instruction still starts normally
questions.explanation: Execution traps as soon as it reaches the first byte, so one byte is enough. The rest of the instruction, such as a call's distance, stays unchanged.

questions.prompt: Why does a debugger single-step the original instruction before it puts the trap byte back?
options: Re-arming at once would trap the same instruction again, so the thread never progresses
The processor ignores a trap byte until one instruction has passed since it was written
The single step is needed to flush the trap byte out of the instruction cache
Single-stepping is the only way to read the original byte before it is restored
questions.explanation: The trap sits on the instruction that must run. The debugger restores the real byte, steps once so it executes, and then re-arms the trap.

questions.prompt: A thread is single-stepped over a direct call instruction. What does the instruction pointer hold afterward?
options: The first address of the called code, because the call has just executed
The address of the instruction after the call, which is where it will return
The address of the call instruction itself, since a step does not move forward
Zero, because the processor clears the pointer after any trap
questions.explanation: A single step stops after exactly one instruction. After a call, execution is at the target, while the return address has been pushed onto the stack.

questions.prompt: Why is the stepping map keyed by thread ID?
options: Several game threads can hit different breakpoints, and one global slot would mix their state
Windows gives every thread the same stack pointer, so the thread ID is the only unique value
A thread ID is the only key that a `HashMap` can use when it stores a call site
The stepping map must hold one entry for every breakpoint that is installed in the process
questions.explanation: Each thread may be between restore and re-arm for a different call. Per-thread keys keep the two facts about address and thread separate.

questions.prompt: Which set of facts suits a compact trace entry for each call?
options: Time, thread, call site and target
The complete stack plus all memory that registers point to
The names of every local variable in the called function
A full copy of the called function's code and its data
questions.explanation: A small fixed record answers who called where, on which thread and when. Dumping whole stacks or arbitrary memory makes the log huge and hard to read.

questions.prompt: What does the logger do when the 1,024-slot channel is full?
options: It counts a dropped event with `try_send` instead of blocking the debug loop
It waits for the writer to catch up, so that no event is ever lost from the log
It grows the channel by another 1,024 slots, so the next event can be stored there
It stops the target process until the log file has caught up with all of the events
questions.explanation: Losing a counted event is better than holding every target thread suspended while a disk writer catches up. The bounded size is what creates backpressure.

questions.prompt: What does backpressure mean for a bounded channel?
options: The producer gets a fixed amount of space rather than letting logs use memory forever
The consumer sends a signal that makes the game run slower until the queue is empty
Events are stored in reverse order, so the oldest event is the first to be dropped
The channel pushes events through the kernel buffers back to the providers
questions.explanation: The size limit is a policy: `try_send` makes explicit what happens when space runs out. An unbounded queue could consume memory without limit.

questions.prompt: Why does the logger resolve module+offset names and symbols on a background worker?
options: Every target thread stays stopped until `ContinueDebugEvent`, so slow work must wait
Symbols can only be loaded after the target has exited, so the worker runs at the end
The debug loop is not allowed to read registers, so the worker copies them
Module offsets are encrypted in the paused thread, and only the worker can decode them
questions.explanation: The debug-event loop has a deadline. Copy the minimal register facts, re-arm and continue, then format and look up symbols elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Why is a location written as a module name plus an offset still useful without symbols?
options: It stays meaningful across runs, since it does not depend on where the module was loaded
It is the real address, since modules are always loaded at the same place each time
It lets the debugger read the function's name directly from the offset
It is shorter than a full address, so logs take up much less space
questions.explanation: The module's load address can change from run to run, but the offset inside it stays the same. Module plus offset therefore identifies a spot without needing names.

questions.prompt: Why does the CSV log start with a version header and a target hash?
options: So later analysis knows how to parse it and does not mix runs from different builds
So the file can be run by Windows Performance Analyzer without conversion
So Windows can recognize it as a debugger file and restrict who can open it
So the timestamps are made unique, since two rows would otherwise share a time
questions.explanation: CSV is boring on purpose. A version header explains the columns, and a target fingerprint ties the log to one binary.

questions.prompt: Why must a failed breakpoint restoration stop the logging experiment?
options: Continuing would leave the target running altered code whose ownership is uncertain
The log file would be unreadable, because restoration errors corrupt the CSV rows
Windows would end the process at once, since a failed restore raises a fatal exception
The event cap would no longer apply, so the logger could never stop by itself again
questions.explanation: The stop list includes the event cap, time window, target exit, drop threshold, user request, and a breakpoint that cannot be restored. The last one protects the target.

questions.prompt: When would you choose an ordered map over a hash map for a table of breakpoints?
options: When you want to walk entries in a repeatable sorted order, such as for stable output
When the table holds more than a few hundred entries, since hash maps stop working
When you need the fastest possible lookup, since ordered maps are always quicker
When keys are addresses, since hash maps cannot use numbers as keys
questions.explanation: Hash maps give quick keyed lookup but no promised iteration order. An ordered map gives deterministic order, which helps with repeatable output and restores.

questions.prompt: A debugger waits for an event from a target and receives one. What happens to the target's threads if the debugger never continues that event?
options: They stay stopped, so the target appears frozen
They keep running, and the event is dropped after a short timeout
They are terminated by the operating system for ignoring the event
They run, but only the thread that raised the event is paused
questions.explanation: Delivering a debug event pauses the target. It runs again only after a matching continue, so every successful wait needs exactly one, even when an error occurs.

questions.prompt: Why should a debugger restore any patched bytes before it detaches from a target?
options: A target left with trap bytes would raise an exception as soon as it reaches them
Detaching removes the original bytes automatically, so the patch would be lost
The operating system refuses to detach from a process that has any patched code
The trap bytes would slow the target down only a little, but it is good manners
questions.explanation: A trap byte only works with a debugger attached. If left behind, the target would hit an unhandled exception, so cleanup must put the original code back first.

questions.prompt: A call breakpoint is hit again and again at the same address. According to the troubleshooting table, what is the likely cause?
options: `EIP` was not rewound, or the call was re-armed too early
The thread ID was missing from the stepping map when the single-step arrived
The target exited, so Windows replays the last event for each breakpoint
The module range was wrong, so the breakpoint was set on a data section
questions.explanation: A repeated hit means the real instruction never got to run once. A missing thread ID produces an unhandled single-step instead.

questions.prompt: A static scan discovered 1,500 direct calls, but only 40 fired during a turn. What does that show?
options: Only 40 sites executed during that action; discovery does not prove a call ran
The other 1,460 calls were wrong, since a real call always fires during one turn
The logger lost 1,460 events, because the channel was full for the whole turn
The cap of 2,000 breakpoints was exceeded, so most of the sites were not installed
questions.explanation: Bytes found by a scan have not necessarily executed. A breakpoint hit proves the call ran during that experiment.

questions.prompt: Why might you choose ETW over a breakpoint debugger for a stutter?
options: Stopping a thread changes timing, while ETW records events with much less disturbance
ETW shows exact register values at each instruction, which a debugger cannot provide
ETW can single-step the game, so every frame can be examined one instruction at a time
ETW removes the need for a clean machine, since it never records unrelated programs
questions.explanation: A debugger is perfect when you need the instruction and registers, but pausing changes the behavior you want to measure.

questions.prompt: Which question is ETW suited to answer?
options: Which thread used most of the CPU during a slow frame
Which instruction subtracts the player's gold during a turn
What the original variable names in the game's source were
What value a particular heap address holds after a purchase
questions.explanation: ETW covers process, thread, image-load, CPU, disk, and similar activity. It does not tell you the meaning of an arbitrary `gold` field.

questions.prompt: What decides which events an ETW trace actually contains?
options: Which providers and keywords the trace enables
Which monitor resolution the game was running at when the trace began
Which compiler built the game, since each compiler writes its own event types
Which hex editor opened the `.etl` file after the recording had been saved
questions.explanation: The lesson says the exact events depend on the providers and keywords a trace enables. A different profile can leave out the event you wanted.

questions.prompt: In ETW's four roles, what does a provider do?
options: It creates events; Windows, a driver, or an application can be one
It starts and stops the session, and chooses which sessions are active
It receives chosen events into buffers and writes them to an `.etl` file
It reads the events live or from a saved file and builds a timeline
questions.explanation: The provider produces events, the session buffers them, the controller starts and stops, and the consumer reads. Each job is separate.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of tool and role is correct?
options: WPR is a controller and WPA is a graphical consumer
WPR is a consumer and WPA is a provider of kernel events
WPR is a provider and WPA is a controller that starts the session
WPR is a session buffer and WPA is the file it writes to disk
questions.explanation: Windows Performance Recorder starts and stops traces, and Windows Performance Analyzer reads them. Neither one creates the events.

questions.prompt: What is a keyword in ETW?
options: A bitmask used to select groups of related events from a provider
A word the game prints to its log, which a consumer then searches for
A password that the controller needs before it can start a session
The name of the `.etl` file that a session saves after it stops recording
questions.explanation: A trace enables some keywords and not others. That is how a session selects groups of events instead of everything a provider can emit.

questions.prompt: A system trace does not show an event you expected. What can you conclude?
options: Not necessarily that it never happened, since buffers can lose events under load
That it certainly never happened, because a trace records every event that occurs
That the trace file is damaged, since missing events always mean corruption
That the event happened but belongs to a different machine than the one traced
questions.explanation: If events are produced faster than the session can deliver them, records are lost. Check which providers are enabled and the controller's loss statistics before drawing conclusions.

questions.prompt: Why should you review a system-wide performance trace before sharing it with others?
options: It can contain file names, process names and activity from everything on the machine
It always contains the passwords typed during the recording, so they must be removed
It is always larger than the limit that sharing sites allow, so it needs trimming
It contains only the target program's data, so nothing else needs checking
questions.explanation: A general trace captures the whole machine, not only the program you care about. Record on a clean machine, for just long enough to reproduce the action.

questions.prompt: A recording tool is asked to save its output to a path that already exists. What is the safest default?
options: Refuse and report an error, so an earlier recording you may still need is not destroyed
Overwrite the old file silently, since the newest recording is always the better one
Append the new recording onto the old file, so both recordings share one file
Rename the old file at random, so that the name no longer collides
questions.explanation: Silent overwriting can destroy evidence that took effort to capture. Refusing is cheap, and the user can pick a new name or delete the file on purpose.

questions.prompt: Why is it safer to start a helper program with a list of separate arguments than to build one shell command string?
options: A path with odd characters stays plain data and is never read as shell syntax
Argument lists run faster, because no program file has to be found first
Shell command strings are blocked by the operating system when they contain paths
A command string cannot hold a path with spaces, so lists are required
questions.explanation: When a string is handed to a shell, characters such as quotes or semicolons can change what runs. Separate arguments are passed through as data and cannot add commands.

questions.prompt: Why does the helper ask WPR to cancel if reading Enter or stopping fails?
options: Starting a trace creates system state that outlives the first `wpr.exe` process
The cancel command saves the partial trace to disk, so no data is lost
A cancelled trace is the only kind that can be opened in Windows Performance Analyzer
The cancel restores the game's breakpoint bytes before the helper exits
questions.explanation: An error should not leave a forgotten recorder running. Cleanup is part of correctness, like restoring a breakpoint byte or closing a handle.

questions.prompt: A tool is already reporting a failure and runs a best-effort cleanup that also fails. Why report the original failure instead of the cleanup failure?
options: The first error is the most informative, and the cleanup error would bury it
Cleanup failures cannot be reported, because the tool has already stopped
The cleanup failure is always the same as the first error, so it adds nothing
Reporting two errors would crash the tool, so only one may be shown
questions.explanation: The first failure explains what really went wrong. A cleanup is only trying to leave things tidy, so its own failure should not hide the more useful message.

questions.prompt: Why record one short, repeatable action such as ending exactly one turn?
options: Repeatability makes two traces comparable, and a short window keeps the data focused
A longer trace would not open in WPA, since the viewer limits every file to ten seconds
One action produces exactly one event, which makes the timeline simple to read
Windows only keeps events for the most recent turn, so older ones are always lost
questions.explanation: The same short procedure can be repeated for AssaultCube startup or a map load. Comparable traces are how you spot a real difference.

questions.prompt: What is a sound way to begin reading a large performance trace?
options: Confirm the right process ran, find the busy threads, then zoom in on the action
Start from the single longest call stack and assume it explains everything that happened
Read every raw event in time order from the first one until the end of the trace
Search for one function name first and ignore which process produced it
questions.explanation: Start with broad questions and narrow down. Confirming the process, then busy threads, then the window around your action keeps the analysis grounded.

questions.prompt: Which WPA view answers "Which DLLs loaded while the game started?"
options: Image Load
Disk Usage
CPU Usage (Sampled)
Process Lifetimes
questions.explanation: Image Load lists modules loaded during startup. Disk Usage is for long reads that overlap a pause, and CPU Usage (Sampled) is for busy threads.

questions.prompt: A trace shows a stack frame as a module name plus an offset rather than a function name. What does that mean for the timing data?
options: The timing is still accurate, since symbols only translate addresses into readable names
The timing is unreliable, because frames without names have no recorded time
The timing belongs to a different process, because unnamed frames are not part of the target
The timing is doubled, since each unnamed frame is counted once for each module
questions.explanation: Symbols affect labels, not measurements. The recorded times are the same with or without matching symbol files.

questions.prompt: A diagnostic trace should be an honest record of what ran. Which action undermines that?
options: Suppressing providers or filtering events so real activity no longer shows
Closing unrelated programs before recording so there is less unrelated activity
Recording for a short time around the action that you are investigating
Saving each recording to a new file so earlier recordings are kept
questions.explanation: A trace is only useful if it reflects what actually happened. Hiding events corrupts the very evidence you are trying to read, while the other habits just keep it focused.

questions.prompt: A library's export list shows a function called Fetch. What does that name alone tell you?
options: Other code can look it up by name, but its arguments and ownership are still unknown
How many arguments it takes, since the name of an export lists them in order
Who must free the memory it returns, since exports always follow one fixed rule
Which thread may call it, since the loader records that next to each name
questions.explanation: An export name only makes a function findable. Its parameters, result meaning and ownership have to be recovered from the code or documentation.

questions.prompt: A machine-level function boundary involves what a value is, where it travels, who frees it, and how long it stays valid. Which list names these four parts?
options: Representation, transport, ownership, lifetime
Syntax, linking, scheduling, and naming rules
Encoding, caching, priority, and visibility
Alignment, padding, endianness, and bitness
questions.explanation: Representation is what the value is, transport is where it travels, ownership is who frees it, and lifetime is how long it stays valid. A boundary is only understood when all four are known.

questions.prompt: A function receives a valid pointer in the correct register, but the process later crashes because the caller released the buffer too soon. Which part of the contract was missed?
options: Ownership and lifetime, which a calling convention does not describe
Transport, because the pointer was placed in the wrong register
Representation, because a pointer cannot be passed through a register
Alignment, because the buffer did not start on a multiple of eight
questions.explanation: The pointer arrived correctly, so transport was fine. A calling convention says nothing about who frees data or how long it stays valid, and that gap caused the crash.

questions.prompt: Under the standard 64-bit Windows calling convention, how do the first four integer arguments and the return value normally travel?
options: In rcx, rdx, r8 and r9, with the result in rax
On the stack, with the result in rax
In rax, rbx, rcx and rdx, with the result in rcx
In rcx, rdx, r8 and r9, with the result on the stack
questions.explanation: The first four integer or pointer arguments go in registers rcx, rdx, r8 and r9, and the result is returned in rax. Mixing these up would confuse caller and callee.

questions.prompt: A caller runs "xor edx, edx", calls a function through a pointer, then runs "test eax, eax" and "je done". On 64-bit Windows, what does this suggest?
options: Zero is passed as the second argument, and it jumps to done when the result is zero
Zero is passed as the first argument, and it jumps to done when the result is nonzero
Zero is passed as the result, and it jumps to done when the argument is zero
Zero is passed as the second argument, and it jumps to done when the result is nonzero
questions.explanation: XOR of a register with itself clears it, and edx is the low half of the second-argument register. Test and je then branch on whether the result in eax is zero.

questions.prompt: In a foreign function declaration, what does naming a calling convention (such as the platform's system one) specify?
options: Where arguments and results go and who cleans up the stack, not whether the address is valid
That the function is safe to call, since the platform's convention is checked at compile time
That the function exists at the given address, since the convention names the loaded module
That the arguments are checked for correct types when the call is made at run time
questions.explanation: A calling convention picks the machine-level agreement between caller and callee. It proves nothing about the address, which is why calling through such a pointer is still unsafe.

questions.prompt: A callee reads four bytes through its pointer argument and never stores the pointer anywhere. What does this machine behavior suggest?
options: A short read-only borrow is enough; the data need not outlive the call
The caller must keep the data alive until the process exits
The callee takes ownership and will free the buffer itself
The argument is really a handle, not a pointer, because it is read
questions.explanation: A callee that only dereferences and does not save the pointer needs the data only during the call. Saving it in a global would instead demand a longer lifetime.

questions.prompt: When studying how a function handles a buffer, where does evidence of the buffer's length usually appear?
options: In bounds checks, loop limits and paired size arguments
In the function's name, since exports name the size of what they return
In the return value, since a function must give back the length it used
In global flags, since the length is stored where every function can see it
questions.explanation: Length shows up wherever the code limits itself to a size, such as a comparison against a bound, a loop count, or a size passed beside the pointer.

questions.prompt: Which machine-level clue best shows whether an export is safe to call more than once?
options: A global flag or counter, or an "already started" branch
Allocation and free calls made around the pointer argument
Whether the function's name appears in the importing caller's import table
Which register carries the first argument at the call site
questions.explanation: Repeatability is about state kept between calls, so a flag or counter that makes the second call behave differently is the evidence. Allocation calls speak to ownership.

questions.prompt: Why keep the conversion from a raw address to a function pointer inside one small function?
options: Each conversion is an unchecked promise about the ABI, so one place is easy to review
The compiler only accepts such a conversion inside functions that are very short
Conversions are slow, so doing one only once saves a lot of time while running
A function pointer can only be created once, or the second copy will be invalid
questions.explanation: A conversion asserts something the compiler cannot verify. Keeping them together makes the unchecked claim easy to audit.

questions.prompt: Foreign code reports results as small integers such as 0, 1 and 2. Why convert them into a named enumeration at the boundary?
options: Callers then match on readable names, and the meaning of each code is stated in one place
Integers cannot be returned from foreign code, so an enumeration is needed to transport them
An enumeration makes the foreign function run faster, since it avoids one comparison
The operating system requires every status to be an enumeration before it can be returned
questions.explanation: Raw numbers have no meaning for a reader. Mapping each documented code to a named value at the edge keeps the rest of the code clear and checkable.

questions.prompt: A wrapper maps foreign status codes to named values. Why keep a catch-all value for codes it was never told about?
options: A future version could add a status that must not be silently treated as success
The compiler would refuse to build a match that lacks a catch-all case
Unknown codes can only be produced by memory corruption, so they signal a crash
It allows the wrapper to retry the call until a known code is returned
questions.explanation: An unrecognized code means the contract has changed. Keeping it visible avoids mapping it to success and hiding the change.

questions.prompt: Two 32-bit functions have the same source-level signature, read(address). What can still differ between them?
options: The ABI, such as one expecting the address in a register and the other on the stack
The meaning of the address, which cannot be different when the signature is the same
The number of arguments, since a signature only lists a name and not a count
The size of a pointer, which changes from one function to the next
questions.explanation: An API says what a function accepts, while the ABI says where and how it arrives. Matching source signatures can still use different conventions, and a mismatch makes the callee read the wrong place.

questions.prompt: A call is made with the wrong stack-cleanup convention but seems to return normally. What is a likely later symptom?
options: The stack pointer ends up off by a few bytes, so a later return lands somewhere nonsensical
The loader refuses to start the process, because it checks the convention at load time
The function returns the wrong type, so the next comparison always fails
The call is run twice, since the processor repeats calls that return abnormally
questions.explanation: A wrong convention can appear to work in a small test. The damage shows up later as a shifted stack pointer or corrupted registers, not as an immediate error.

questions.prompt: In 32-bit x86 code, a function ends with "ret 12" instead of a plain "ret". What does that tell you?
options: The function removes 12 bytes of stack arguments itself, so the callee cleans up
The function returns the number 12 to its caller in a register
The function jumps twelve instructions ahead before returning to the caller
The function leaves 12 bytes on the stack for the caller to clean up
questions.explanation: The number after ret says how many bytes of arguments to pop on return. That reveals who cleans up the stack, which is one clue to the calling convention.

questions.prompt: A start function is designed so that calling it twice is safe. What should the second call do?
options: Report that the work is already running, and avoid starting a duplicate
Start a second copy of the work, so both can run side by side
Stop the first copy and restart it, so that the work begins fresh
Crash with an error, so the developer learns about the repeated call
questions.explanation: A well-behaved start function guards against double starts. Repeating it returns a clear status and leaves the existing work alone.

questions.prompt: You recovered a contract from the course DLL fixture. How far does that conclusion apply?
options: To that exact build only, not to other builds of the DLL
To every other DLL that also exports a function named `gha_start`
To every build of the course DLL, because names fix contracts
To any DLL compiled for the same architecture as the fixture
questions.explanation: The lesson says a contract recovered from the fixture applies to that exact build. A new build or other DLL could differ in arguments or ownership.

questions.prompt: While other threads keep running, what rule should a live hook installation satisfy?
options: Any thread sees it either completely absent or completely working, never half-written
The hook can be partly written, as long as the write finishes within a few microseconds
Only the thread doing the install must see a complete hook, since it is the one that wrote it
The hook may be half-written, since the processor ignores incomplete instructions
questions.explanation: A call landing on half a jump has no defined behavior. Short windows do not help, because another thread may execute those exact bytes.

questions.prompt: Which contract is broken when a hook's return lands in the middle of an instruction?
options: The instruction contract, which requires whole instructions to be displaced and relocated
The identity contract, which requires the module build and original bytes to match
The lifetime contract, which requires callback state to outlive every user of it
The ABI contract, which requires registers and stack alignment to survive the call
questions.explanation: Landing inside an instruction means a partial instruction was displaced. An ABI failure would instead hand the caller corrupted registers or stack.

questions.prompt: Removal frees the trampoline's memory while a callback is still running inside it. Which contract failed?
options: Lifetime: callback state and the trampoline must outlive every user
Concurrency: no thread may execute a partly written patch at any moment
Identity: the patch targeted a different version of the function entirely
Instruction: an operand that depends on its own address was left unrelocated
questions.explanation: The memory was released while still in use, which is a lifetime error. The concurrency contract is about partly written patches, which is a different mistake.

questions.prompt: Why is a hook that passes a single-threaded test not yet shown to be safe?
options: That test proves almost nothing about the concurrency and lifetime contracts under load
A single thread cannot execute the patched bytes, so the test never reaches the detour at all
Single-threaded runs skip the trampoline, so the displaced instructions never get executed
Passing once proves the bytes match, but it cannot show the right module build was loaded
questions.explanation: Races and use-after-free need other threads or removal during calls. A single thread does reach the detour; it just cannot expose these failures.

questions.prompt: Why decode complete instructions before deciding how many bytes to patch?
options: x86-64 instructions vary in length, and every displaced instruction must be kept for the trampoline
Every x86-64 instruction is four bytes long, so decoding only confirms the count of instructions
The branch encoding changes length depending on which game build is loaded into the process
Decoding lets the tool skip the saved original bytes, because the decoder can rebuild them later
questions.explanation: Cutting through an instruction would leave a fragment that later executes as garbage. The saved original bytes are still needed for removal.

questions.prompt: A 7-byte instruction at 0x3000 reads memory at its own end plus a displacement of 0x200, which is 0x3207. The same bytes are copied unchanged to 0x8000. What address does the copy read?
options: 0x8207, which has nothing to do with the original data
0x3207, since the displacement still points to the original data
0x8200, since the length of the instruction is no longer counted
0x5207, since only the distance of the move is added
questions.explanation: The displacement is measured from the end of the instruction, and the end moved: 0x8000 + 7 + 0x200 = 0x8207. The copy reads somewhere else entirely.

questions.prompt: A trampoline builder meets a relative instruction that it cannot relocate correctly. What is the reliable response?
options: Reject the site as unsupported, rather than copy the instruction unchanged
