Copy it unchanged, since the processor adjusts relative instructions
Copy it unchanged, and let the tests find a problem if there is one
Replace it with a no-op, so the trampoline still has the same length
questions.explanation: A rejected site is safe. A copied relative instruction points to the wrong target, and the damage usually appears much later.

questions.prompt: What does an unrelocated RIP-relative operand in a trampoline usually look like to the person debugging?
options: A wrong value or a jump into unrelated code that surfaces later, rarely a crash at the hook
An immediate crash inside the hook, because the instruction bytes no longer decode at all
A refusal by Windows to copy the bytes, since the displacement is invalid at the new address
A slowdown on the hooked function, because the processor must decode the copy a second time
questions.explanation: The bytes remain a valid instruction; they just read somewhere else. That is why the symptom is separated from the cause in time and place.

questions.prompt: Before a hook is published, the live bytes differ from the expected ones. What should the tool do?
options: Publish nothing, release the unused preparation, and report which check failed
Replace the expected bytes with the live ones, then publish the hook anyway
Publish the hook, but mark it as unverified so that it can be found again
Publish half of the hook, so the failing part can be tested on its own
questions.explanation: Verification happens before publication, so a failed check costs nothing. Changing the expected bytes would defeat the identity check.

questions.prompt: A hook has already been published, but verification afterward fails. What is the right move?
options: Roll it back with the same safe mechanism that installed it, and report the failure
Leave it in place, since a failed check does not mean the hook is faulty
Overwrite the bytes quickly with a plain write, since rolling back is simple
Restart the target, since a restart always removes the hook cleanly
questions.explanation: Once bytes are live, undoing them has the same concurrency hazards as installing them, so rollback must use the same careful mechanism.

questions.prompt: Making a code page writable before a multi-byte patch solves which problem, and which does it leave unsolved?
options: It allows the write, but does not make it atomic or synchronize other cores
It makes the write atomic, but does not allow the write to be made
It synchronizes other threads, but cannot make the page writable
It solves both, since a writable page is also protected from simultaneous execution
questions.explanation: Permissions and atomicity are separate problems. Making a page writable only permits the write, so a rendezvous or a transaction-capable library is needed for safe publication.

questions.prompt: In the publication sequence, what comes right after writing the complete detour and before restoring page protection?
options: Calling `FlushInstructionCache` for the modified range
Releasing the rendezvous so peer threads resume immediately
Freeing the saved original bytes since the patch is written
Rereading the original page protection from the target module
questions.explanation: The order is change protection, write the full detour, flush the cache, restore protection, reread the bytes, then release the rendezvous.

questions.prompt: A tool suspends all other threads before patching code. What risk comes with that?
options: A suspended thread may hold a lock the installer needs, so both wait
Suspended threads lose their registers, so they cannot resume correctly
Suspending threads is slow, but it can never cause a hang
The installer cannot suspend its own thread, so it always crashes
questions.explanation: A suspended thread cannot release the lock it holds. If the installer then waits for that lock, it never proceeds.

questions.prompt: When is a single aligned store a valid shortcut for publishing a patch?
options: Only when the architecture and exact encoding explicitly guarantee atomicity for that width
Whenever the patch is shorter than sixteen bytes, because short writes are always atomic
Whenever the game has fewer than four threads, because few threads rarely interleave
Whenever the page was just made writable, because permissions decide the write's atomicity
questions.explanation: An ordinary byte copy is not atomic by default. The shortcut needs documented guarantees; otherwise use a real rendezvous or a transaction-capable library.

questions.prompt: A logging callback calls related game code that enters the hooked function again. Which re-entry policy fits?
options: Bypass nested: the nested call uses the original path
Allow: the nested call runs the callback again every time
Reject: the nested entry returns a defined error to the game
Drain: the nested call waits until every active callback ends
questions.explanation: Observation code that may re-enter should not recurse into itself, so nested calls go straight to the original. Allow suits only pure recursion-safe callbacks.

questions.prompt: What is the stated limit of a thread-local depth counter used for bypassing nested calls?
options: It is not a substitute for process-wide lifetime tracking during removal
It cannot count more than one level of nesting in a single thread of execution
It only works in a fixture that has a single thread, so real games cannot use it
It prevents the callback from running at all unless the depth is exactly zero
questions.explanation: The counter is per thread, so it cannot say how many callbacks are active across the whole process. Removal needs that wider count.

questions.prompt: Which behavior suits a hook callback that runs on a time-critical thread?
options: Copy a small event into a bounded queue and return quickly
Write the event to a log file before returning, so nothing is lost
Wait for a worker thread to confirm the event, then return
Allocate a buffer as large as needed, and fill it with the event details
questions.explanation: The hooked thread has a deadline. Blocking input and output, waiting for other threads or unbounded allocation can stall the very frames being observed.

questions.prompt: A bounded event queue behind a hook is full. Which policy is preferred?
options: Drop the new event and count the drop, so overload stays visible
Block the hooked thread until there is room, so no event is lost
Drop events silently, so the hook never adds any extra work
Grow the queue without limit, so that every event is kept
questions.explanation: Counting drops makes overload visible. Blocking slows the thread being measured, and silent dropping hides the gap.

questions.prompt: Draining times out while some callbacks are still active. What should the tool do?
options: Keep the still-valid resources and report the incomplete shutdown
Free the trampoline anyway, since waiting longer will not change much
Restore the bytes and release callback state, treating the timeout as done
Retry by forcing the active threads to exit, so the count reaches zero
questions.explanation: Freeing memory that a callback may still use is not recovery. The tool keeps what is valid and reports the problem.

questions.prompt: Which two things does removal need to track before it frees anything?
options: Whether new callback work is accepted, and how many callbacks are currently active
How many threads the process has, and how many of them are currently suspended
Whether the original bytes were saved, and how many bytes the detour overwrote
How many times the hook was installed, and how many times it has been removed
questions.explanation: Setting the state to Draining stops new work; the active count reaching zero shows that it is safe to restore and free.

questions.prompt: An observer restores EAX but skips the displaced addition. Why is the original behavior still broken?
options: Restoring input does not execute the missing addition.
Restoring input automatically doubles the addition.
The original value no longer needs any continuation.
The caller must use a different decimal notation now.
questions.explanation: Preservation protects live state. The displaced operation still has to run with its original meaning before continuation.

questions.prompt: A trampoline executes the displaced bonus addition twice. What mistake does this demonstrate?
options: Replaying twice restores the original patch-site bytes.
Preserved state can still repeat the original side effect.
Two replays are required for every successful return.
Register saving makes repeated work have no effect.
questions.explanation: Saving machine state does not protect against duplicate replay. Original work must occur exactly once per intended path.

questions.prompt: The observer adds 10 to a live register and leaves it changed. What can fail even if the displaced addition runs once?
options: The object changes identity because its method is shared.
The process restores its disk snapshot automatically.
The original addition receives the wrong starting value.
The original addition loses its decimal representation.
questions.explanation: Temporary observer calculations must not leak into live values the original path expects.

questions.prompt: Restoring original patch-site bytes during removal serves which purpose?
options: Replaying a bonus for every previous caller again.
Choosing the target’s health-field offset for a call.
Clearing all inactive return addresses from memory.
Putting the original control-flow path back in place.
questions.explanation: Byte restoration removes the detour after entry and active users are safely handled. It differs from per-call preservation and replay.

questions.prompt: The toy’s final gold matches the original computation. What remains unproved for a real hook?
options: Relocation, live state, concurrent entry, and lifetime.
The meaning of adding a bonus once to starting gold.
The fact that a duplicate addition changes the result.
The difference between a register and stored field.
questions.explanation: A computation model omits instruction boundaries, address-dependent relocation, ABI details, threading, and lifetime contracts.

questions.prompt: A DLL can dereference a game address directly. Why does that not make the access automatically safe?
options: The address can still be null, stale, misaligned, or wrong for this game version
Direct pointer reads are slower than API reads and may time out on large objects
Windows blocks guest DLLs from reading memory that the game allocated itself
Pointers inside a shared address space are always encrypted until validated
questions.explanation: Sharing an address space removes a copying step, not the uncertainty. The game still owns the objects and may move or free them.

questions.prompt: Before dereferencing a remembered address in a running program, which facts should you be able to state?
options: Which build and state it belongs to, who owns it, which thread may change it, and how long it lasts
Its size in bytes, its color, its file name, and the time it was last printed
Which compiler built it, which linker joined it, how large it is, and who wrote it
Whether it is in hexadecimal, whether it is signed, how wide it is, and where it was copied
questions.explanation: A remembered address is only trustworthy while its assumptions hold. Version and state, ownership, threading and lifetime each limit when it can be used.

questions.prompt: How is a pointer to short-lived data safest handled?
options: Resolve it just before use, copy the needed fields into a local snapshot, and validate it
Resolve it once at start-up, keep it in a global, and reuse it for the whole session
Cache it in a file, so it survives the next run and need not be found again
Store it with extra padding, so it stays valid when the data is moved elsewhere
questions.explanation: Pointers go stale when the data they point to is freed or moved. Resolving late and copying a few fields means you rely on the borrowed view for as short a time as possible.

questions.prompt: Why should a library's load-time entry point do very little work?
options: It runs while the loader holds a global lock, so heavy work there can deadlock
The entry point is only allowed to run for a fixed number of instructions
Anything in it runs in every process on the machine, so it must stay small
The entry point cannot call any other function, so only simple code fits
questions.explanation: Code running during load is under the loader lock. Keeping the entry point tiny and doing real work later, after loading has finished, avoids deadlocks.

questions.prompt: Why might a function that starts a background worker return distinct codes for "started", "already running" and "failed to start"?
options: The caller can react differently to each outcome instead of guessing from true or false
Distinct codes make the worker thread run at a higher priority than usual
A function that returns numbers cannot also start a thread, so codes are needed
Three codes are required by the operating system for any function that creates threads
questions.explanation: A boolean hides why something failed or why nothing happened. Separate codes let callers retry, ignore or report each case properly.

questions.prompt: What is a once-only initialization guard, a flag that can be set successfully a single time, useful for?
options: Letting a later attempt notice that setup already happened, avoiding duplicates
Making setup code run faster, because the guard caches every result it sees
Letting several threads run the setup at the same moment, so that it finishes sooner
Undoing the setup automatically when the process exits, so it cleans up by itself
questions.explanation: Setting the guard succeeds only once. Later attempts see that it was already set and can return early instead of starting the work again, even if callers race.

questions.prompt: A function that reads from a raw address is declared unsafe, with a note describing what must hold. Whose job is it to make the read valid?
options: The caller, who must guarantee the address is live, aligned and of the right type
The compiler, which checks at build time that the address points to live memory
The function itself, which tests that the address is valid before every read
The operating system, which stops any bad reads and returns a clean error
questions.explanation: The unsafe marker moves the proof obligation to the caller. The function can only describe what it needs, not verify it.

questions.prompt: A value is reached through a chain: a fixed root address holds a pointer to object A, object A holds at offset 0x20 a pointer to object B, and the value sits at offset 0x08 in B. Which procedure reaches it?
options: Read the root pointer, read the pointer at that plus 0x20, then add 0x08 to it
Add 0x20 and 0x08 to the root address, then read the value from there
Read the root address itself as the value, then add both offsets to it
Read at 0x20 and at 0x08 as absolute addresses, then add the root to each
questions.explanation: A chain alternates reading a pointer and adding an offset. Every step moves to the next object, and only the last offset gives the value's address.

questions.prompt: In a pointer chain, which parts stay the same from run to run for a given build, and which change?
options: The root and structure offsets stay fixed; the objects the pointers lead to change
Every address in the chain stays fixed, because a build always loads in one layout
Only the offsets change from run to run, while the objects always remain in place
Nothing stays fixed, because every number in the chain is picked again at start-up
questions.explanation: The root and offsets are properties of the build, but objects are allocated while the program runs, so their addresses must be read live each time.

questions.prompt: Why must each pointer in a chain be checked for zero before it is followed?
options: A null pointer means the object does not exist now, and following it reads near zero
A null pointer is a valid address that always points to the start of the object
Zero is the pointer's size, so following it would read one byte at a time
Null pointers are fixed by the operating system, so the chain skips them on its own
questions.explanation: If the thing the chain describes is not active, the pointer is not set up yet. Returning an error is better than dereferencing zero.

questions.prompt: Why add a field offset to an address with a checked addition rather than a plain wrapping addition?
options: Overflow would wrap to a small bogus address, so checking turns it into an error
Checked addition makes the addition run faster, as the processor does less work
Wrapping addition always produces a negative number, which cannot be an address
Checked addition proves the address is properly aligned for the field being read
questions.explanation: A huge address plus an offset can wrap around and look valid. A checked addition reports overflow so the bad value never reaches a read.

questions.prompt: In a two-step startup of a library inside another process, what does the first step accomplish before the second begins?
options: The loader maps the library and finishes setup, so its exports are ready
The library's worker starts running, so the second step only has to stop it
The library is copied to disk, so the second step can find its path
The exports are renamed, so the second step can call them by number
questions.explanation: Loading comes first. Only after the loader has returned can the next step add an export's offset to the library's base and start work there.

questions.prompt: A library's setup needs to wait for another thread to finish. Why should that wait not happen in the library's load-time entry point?
options: The other thread may need the loader lock the entry point holds, so both wait forever
Threads cannot be created while a library is loading, so there is nothing to wait for
The entry point would finish before the thread starts, so the wait would end at once
Waiting in an entry point makes the processor skip every later instruction in that thread
questions.explanation: The loader lock is held during load-time code. A thread that needs it cannot proceed, and the waiting entry point never finishes, so the process deadlocks.

questions.prompt: A library with worker threads and patched code must be unloaded. Which order is safe?
options: Ask workers to stop, wait outside the entry point, restore patches, then unload
Unload first, then ask the workers to stop and restore the patches afterwards
Restore the patches, then wait for the workers from inside the entry point, then unload
Ask workers to stop, unload at once, then wait for them to finish and restore patches
questions.explanation: Threads or patches still pointing into the library would crash once it is unloaded, so they must be stopped and restored first. Waiting inside the entry point risks a loader-lock deadlock.

questions.prompt: What advantage does a lifecycle enumeration (not started, running, stopping, stopped) have over a single "started" boolean?
options: It can tell phases such as "cleaning up" apart and limit what each phase may do
It stores the exact time each phase began, which a boolean cannot hold
It makes the library start up faster, since the compiler removes the boolean
It proves that every address used in each phase is valid, which a boolean cannot
questions.explanation: A boolean has two values, but a real lifecycle has more phases. Separate states let the code reject new work while stopping, for example.

questions.prompt: Once a library reaches its final stopped state, what should it still own?
options: Nothing that points into its own code, since that code is about to be unloaded
A worker thread that waits for new work to arrive, so it can restart quickly
Patches it made earlier, so it can restore them when it is loaded again
Callbacks registered with the host, so the host can still call into it later
questions.explanation: By then workers are joined and patches restored. Anything left that points into the library's code would crash once the library unloads.

questions.prompt: How do you best show that code you loaded into your own test program really ran inside it?
options: A visible change in the target that only that code could cause
A success message that the loading tool prints when it finishes
The test program still being alive after the attempt has finished
The library file existing on disk at the path that was given
questions.explanation: A visible change in the target is evidence that the code executed there. A message from the loading tool proves much less.

questions.prompt: Why might a tool restrict itself to a short allowlist of known targets?
options: A mistyped or mistaken command cannot act on an unrelated process
The allowlist gives the tool access to protected processes it would otherwise be denied
The allowlist speeds up the tool, since it skips searching for addresses
Allowed targets are always loaded at the same address, so the tool can resolve them faster
questions.explanation: The list narrows the tool to the builds it was written for. It adds no access and has no effect on address resolution.

questions.prompt: Why use the operating system's normal loader to bring in a library rather than mapping its sections by hand?
options: The loader registers the module so tools can see it, and does relocations and imports
Hand mapping is blocked by the processor, so the loader is the only possible route
The loader makes the library run faster, since it maps sections in a smarter order
Hand mapping only works for libraries without any imports, so it is rarely useful
questions.explanation: A normal load leaves a visible, reversible record and does all the setup work correctly. Skipping the loader means redoing relocation, imports and TLS yourself.

questions.prompt: Which set of jobs does the operating system's loader perform when it loads a DLL?
options: Maps sections, applies relocations, resolves imports, sets up TLS, runs the entry point
Compiles the source code, links it with other code, and runs the library's tests
Allocates memory for the caller, writes the path text there, and starts a thread
Chooses the owner thread, copies the file to disk, and deletes it after use
questions.explanation: Those are the loader's responsibilities. Writing a path into another process and starting a thread are done by the caller, not the loader.

questions.prompt: In a load-by-remote-thread approach, why must the path string be written into the target before the thread starts?
options: The thread gets the string's address as its argument and reads it from the target
Threads cannot start until the target has some free memory to hold their stacks
The path must be checked by the target before the operating system accepts the thread
The thread copies the path back to the starting process as soon as it begins running
questions.explanation: The new thread runs inside the target and can only read what is in the target's address space. Its single argument is the address of the path.

questions.prompt: What kind of text does a wide-character Windows API expect for a path?
options: A zero-terminated UTF-16 string
A length-prefixed UTF-8 string
A zero-terminated ASCII string
A string of 16 bytes padded with spaces
questions.explanation: The wide variants of Windows functions take UTF-16 text that ends with a zero character. Missing the terminator would let the function read past the end of the string.

questions.prompt: Why is an absolute library path safer than a relative one when another process will do the loading?
options: A relative path is resolved from that process's working directory, not the file's
Relative paths are not accepted by the operating system when a file is loaded
Absolute paths load faster, since the loader never has to search any folders
Relative paths load the file twice, so the library's entry point runs two times
questions.explanation: The process doing the loading resolves a relative path from its own working directory, not the caller's. An absolute path points to one exact file.

questions.prompt: Why free a resource in a cleanup hook that runs automatically, rather than only at the end of the success path?
options: Cleanup then also runs on early error returns, so the resource is never leaked
Automatic cleanup runs sooner than manual code, which makes the code faster
The success path can never release resources, since it is already finished
Automatic cleanup is the only way to release memory that belongs to another process
questions.explanation: With only manual cleanup at the end, an early return would skip it. A hook that runs on every exit path leaves nothing behind.

questions.prompt: A call that writes into another process reports success but transferred fewer bytes than requested. Why check the byte count?
options: A short write still reports success, and would silently leave truncated data behind
The count reveals how fast the write ran, so slow writes can be retried
The count must be zero on success, so any other value means an error
Counts larger than requested are normal, because the system rounds up to pages
questions.explanation: Success only means the call did something. Comparing the transferred size to the requested size turns a partial write into an explicit error.

questions.prompt: A tool takes the address of a system library function from its own process and hands it to another process to use. What does that assume?
options: That the system library sits at the same base address in both processes
That both processes run with the same privileges and under the same user account
That the function is cached in the other process, so no lookup is needed there
That both processes were started at exactly the same time by the same parent
questions.explanation: An address from one process is only meaningful in another if the library is mapped at the same base. That often happens on one machine, but it is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: A reusable tool should not assume that a system library has the same base in the target. What should it do instead?
options: Find the real base in the target, verify the function is there, and refuse if unsure
Guess the nearest likely address and retry until the target stops complaining
Copy its own address and add a safety margin for any difference between processes
Skip the check and assume the system always loads libraries in a fixed order
questions.explanation: Starting a thread at a wrong address makes the target fault. A careful tool establishes the real address first, and stops if it cannot.

questions.prompt: Creating a thread in another process returns a handle. Why is that not proof that the intended work succeeded?
options: The thread may start and then fail, so you must wait for it and read its exit result
A handle only proves that the thread was created and finished successfully
The handle is valid only until the thread starts, so it says nothing afterward
The operating system returns a handle even if no thread was created at all
questions.explanation: Creating a thread and finishing its job are separate events. A start address that is wrong can still produce a handle before the thread faults.

questions.prompt: What shape must a function have to be used as a thread's start routine?
options: One pointer-sized argument and a 32-bit result under the platform convention
No arguments and no return value, because the thread starts with nothing
Any number of arguments, because the thread copies as many as it needs
Two arguments, a handle and a flags value, and a return value of one byte
questions.explanation: Thread start routines take a single pointer-sized argument and return a 32-bit number. Any function that matches that shape can be used as one.

questions.prompt: A thread-creation call has an option to start the thread suspended. If that option is not given, when does the thread begin?
options: Immediately, without waiting to be resumed
When the creating process calls a separate resume function
After the creating process exits, since threads wait for their parent
Only when the operating system schedules every other thread first
questions.explanation: With no suspend option, the thread is runnable right away. The suspended option exists for cases that need to prepare it before it runs.

questions.prompt: Why must a library's architecture, 32-bit or 64-bit, match the process that loads it?
options: A process can only load code built for its own instruction set and pointer size
The loader translates 32-bit code at run time, but only when the process allows it
The two kinds share one format, so a mismatch only changes how fast the code runs
Architecture only matters for the file's name, not for the code it contains
questions.explanation: A 32-bit process cannot execute 64-bit code and the reverse is also true. A mismatch makes the load fail.

questions.prompt: After a library is loaded, why would a launcher start the library's setup on a new thread instead of inside the load-time entry point?
options: By then the loader lock is released, and the new thread can do heavy work freely
Entry points cannot run any code, so a thread is the only way to get setup done
A new thread gets higher priority than the loading thread, so setup finishes sooner
The new thread reads the library's exit code, which tells it how large it is
questions.explanation: Code in the entry point runs under the loader lock. A thread started afterward is outside that constraint and can do real work.

questions.prompt: How can a tool compute the address of an exported function inside another process after a library is loaded there?
options: Add the export's offset, found in a local copy, to the base address the library loaded at
Read the address from the library's file on disk, which holds the final in-memory address
Use the export's address in its own process, because every process shares one layout
Search all of the target's memory until a function with the same name is found
questions.explanation: Offsets inside a library do not change, but the base address does. The loaded base plus the offset gives the real address.

questions.prompt: Why must a process handle stay open until remote memory that was allocated through it has been freed?
options: Freeing that memory is done through the handle, so it can be closed only afterward
Closing the handle first would free the memory by itself, so freeing again would fail
Handles are released in the order they were opened, and the process handle is last
The operating system closes the memory first, so the handle has to wait for it
questions.explanation: The free request names the process by its handle, so closing it earlier would make the free impossible. Thread handles do not have that dependency and can close first.

questions.prompt: One call returns a module handle, where null means failure. The next returns a status, where 0 means success. Which pair of results shows overall success?
options: A nonzero handle and a zero status
A zero handle and a zero status
A nonzero handle and a nonzero status
A zero handle and a nonzero status
questions.explanation: Different functions use different success conventions. A null module handle means loading failed, while zero from a status function means the work started.

questions.prompt: A library-loading call returns null. Which checks come first?
options: The target process id, both architectures, the exact path and the system error code
Whether the target was started as an administrator, before checking anything else
Whether the library is bigger than the target, since size limits apply
Whether the library's name starts with a capital letter on this system
questions.explanation: A null result means the load failed, and the basic facts usually explain why. Verify those before blaming permissions.

questions.prompt: A remote thread was started at a wrong address and the target crashed before any result came back. What is the right response?
options: Treat it as a failed experiment and find why the address was wrong before retrying
Run the identical attempt again, since crashes are usually random and temporary
Run it faster, so the target has less time to notice the problem
Run it with an administrator account, since that avoids crashes of this kind
questions.explanation: A bad start address faults the target every time. Repeating the same attempt repeats the failure, so find the cause first.

questions.prompt: Why describe a planned memory patch as plain data, with an address, expected bytes and replacement, before applying it?
options: It can be checked and reviewed without touching the target, so a mistake cannot modify anything
Plain data is written into the target automatically, which saves the work of applying it
A plan makes the patch permanent, so that it survives the target being restarted
A plan lets the replacement bytes be longer than the expected bytes without any problems
questions.explanation: A plan is just information. Building and validating it performs no raw memory access, so errors are caught before the target is changed.

questions.prompt: Why should a patch's replacement bytes be exactly as long as the bytes they replace?
options: A shorter or longer write would spill into the next instruction or leave stray bytes
The processor only accepts writes of one fixed size, whatever the instructions are
A longer replacement is slower to write, but would work the same way as an equal one
Different lengths change the file's checksum, which the operating system would reject
questions.explanation: Instructions sit back to back, so a write that is the wrong size damages its neighbors or leaves half an instruction. Equal lengths also keep the resume address fixed.

questions.prompt: How should the length of the hook span be chosen?
options: By decoding whole instructions with a disassembler, not by counting five arbitrary bytes
By using five bytes, since that is the length of every jump instruction
By copying the span length from another game version, which should be close enough
By picking the smallest span that contains the hook address, usually one byte
questions.explanation: A five-byte jump overwrites whatever lies there. If that lands in the middle of an instruction, the leftover bytes decode into nonsense.

questions.prompt: Why compare the live bytes with the expected bytes before writing a patch?
options: They work as a build fingerprint, and a mismatch means the patch was made for something else
The comparison speeds up the write, since matching bytes are skipped by the processor
The comparison makes a backup copy of the live bytes, which can be restored later
The comparison lets the tool choose a better replacement based on the live bytes
questions.explanation: If the running code differs from the profile, the planned patch could split a different instruction. Checking first turns that risk into a clean stop.

questions.prompt: A patch tool finds that the live bytes do not match the bytes it expected. Which behavior is best?
options: Stop and report, since a mismatch means the tool does not understand this build
Offer a force option, so the user can write anyway when they are confident
Write to the nearest address that does match, so the patch still happens
Skip the check from then on, since a mismatch is probably a false alarm
questions.explanation: A mismatch turns certainty into a guess. Writing anyway risks damaging unknown code, so a beginner-safe tool refuses.

questions.prompt: Why should the trusted core of a patch tool stay small?
options: More code able to validate a patch means more places for a bug to cause a bad write
Small code runs inside the loader lock without any risk of deadlock
The compiler refuses to inline functions that touch more than three structures
A longer core would cause the patch to be larger than the instruction span
questions.explanation: Menu themes, log formatters and hotkey labels should not be able to bypass byte verification. Fewer paths to a write means fewer places for a mistake.

questions.prompt: A restore function clears its "still patched" flag only after the write succeeds. Why?
options: If the write fails, the flag stays set so later cleanup knows the target is still modified
The flag has to be cleared last, since the processor reads it after the write
A failed write already clears the flag by itself, so clearing it again is optional
Flags can only be changed by the operating system, which does so after a write
questions.explanation: The flag records whether the target is still changed. Leaving it set on failure keeps the fallback cleanup alive for another try.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that an undo operation is idempotent, and why does it help cleanup?
options: Running it again has no further effect, so automatic cleanup after a manual undo is harmless
It can only run once, and a second call crashes, so cleanup must never repeat it
It runs faster each time it is repeated, since earlier work is stored in a cache
It undoes the previous undo, so a second call restores the patch to its patched state
questions.explanation: An idempotent undo does nothing once it has already been done. That allows explicit cleanup to report errors while a final automatic cleanup stays a harmless safety net.

questions.prompt: Why should automatic cleanup at scope exit not be the only way a patch gets undone?
options: It cannot hand an error back to the caller, whereas an explicit undo lets the caller react
Automatic cleanup runs before the patch is applied, so it can never undo anything
Automatic cleanup cannot access memory, so it can only print warnings and nothing else
Explicit undo is always faster, since automatic cleanup waits for a timer to expire
questions.explanation: Automatic cleanup is a last-chance attempt that can at most print a warning. Calling undo explicitly lets the program handle a failure while it still can.

questions.prompt: From which address does a 5-byte relative near jump measure its displacement?
options: The address of the next instruction, 5 bytes after the jump's own address
The address of the jump instruction itself, where its opcode byte sits
The start of the module that contains the jump
The address of the cave, which is subtracted from the hook address
questions.explanation: The CPU has already advanced past the five bytes when it applies the displacement, so `rel32 = to - (from + 5)`.

questions.prompt: A 5-byte near jump sits at 0x2000 and should reach code at 0x2210. What 32-bit relative displacement does it need?
options: 0x20B
questions.explanation: The distance is measured from the end of the jump, 0x2005, so 0x2210 - 0x2005 = 0x20B. Measuring from the jump's own address would give 0x210 and overshoot by five bytes.

questions.prompt: A cave lies at a lower address than the jump. What does the displacement look like?
options: A negative signed 32-bit value, which is perfectly ordinary
A value that wraps through the unsigned range and is rejected as an error
A positive value, because the CPU takes the absolute difference
Zero, because backward jumps use a different opcode and ignore the displacement
questions.explanation: The displacement is signed, so jumping backward just produces a negative number. The helper uses a wider signed type so no unsigned wraparound happens.

questions.prompt: A near jump encodes its distance as a signed 32-bit number. What should code do when the target is farther away than that can express?
options: Refuse and report it, since a truncated distance would land somewhere unrelated
Keep the low 32 bits of the distance, which still reaches the target by wrapping
Write the jump anyway, since the processor corrects distances that are too large
Switch to a shorter jump, which can always reach any address in the process
questions.explanation: A truncated displacement is a different number and leads to the wrong place. Detecting overflow and refusing is the safe answer.

questions.prompt: A working five-byte jump is copied to a different address. Why will it not land on the same target?
options: Its displacement is relative to its position, so the same bytes point somewhere else
The opcode `E9` changes meaning whenever it is copied to a different address
The CPU caches the old destination, so it keeps jumping to the first target
The displacement is absolute, so the new spot needs a different jump instruction
questions.explanation: The stored number is `to - next_instruction`. Moving the jump changes `next_instruction`, so the destination changes with it.

questions.prompt: A five-byte jump must replace whole instructions that total six bytes. What should happen to the sixth byte?
options: It is filled with a no-op, so no leftover half instruction is run as code
It is left as it was, since the processor ignores anything after a jump
It is deleted, and the code after the span is shifted back by one byte
It is filled with a second jump, so the first one has a backup
questions.explanation: The patch must cover whole instructions. A no-op fills the gap harmlessly, and the span length and resume address stay stable.

questions.prompt: A patch overwrites a 7-byte span starting at 0x00401000. Where should the inserted code resume the original flow?
options: 0x00401007, just past the span
0x00401000, the start of the span
0x00401005, right after the jump bytes
0x00401008, one byte past the span
questions.explanation: The span ends at start plus length, so resume at 0x00401007. Returning to the start would run the patch again forever.

questions.prompt: The cave ends by jumping to the resume address, not the hook address. Why does this not create a loop?
options: The function never returns to the hook address, so execution moves past it
The CPU remembers the cave was already visited and skips the second jump
The saved flags register disables the patch again after the first pass
`pushad` rewrites the resume address on every pass so the path differs
questions.explanation: Resuming after the span means the patched bytes are not executed again in the same pass. A jump back to the hook would run the patch again.

questions.prompt: A 5-byte jump at 0x00401000 should reach inserted code at 0x10002000. Which displacement is written?
options: 0x0FC00FFB
questions.explanation: The next instruction is at 0x00401005, and 0x10002000 - 0x00401005 = 0x0FC00FFB. Subtracting the jump's own address leaves a number that is five too large.

questions.prompt: A displacement is 0x1A2B3C4D. Which bytes follow the jump opcode in memory on x86?
options: 4D 3C 2B 1A, because the least significant byte is stored first
1A 2B 3C 4D, because bytes are stored in the same order as they are written
D4 C3 B2 A1, because each byte is stored with its digits swapped
4D 3C 2B 1A, but only when the displacement is a negative number
questions.explanation: x86 is little-endian, so the lowest byte comes first and the number reads backward in memory.

questions.prompt: Why would inserted code save the registers and flags at its start?
options: The interrupted code expects them unchanged, and the inserted code may overwrite them
The processor requires registers to be saved before any jump to a new address
Saved registers make the inserted code run faster, since they stay in the cache
The saved copy is how the inserted code learns which instruction it replaced
questions.explanation: The inserted code interrupts a function in mid-work. Saving and later restoring the state hides that interruption from the original code.

questions.prompt: Inserted code pushed the flags first and then the general registers. In which order should it restore them?
options: The registers first, then the flags, since the stack returns the last item pushed first
The flags first, then the registers, because the first item pushed comes back first
In any order, since flags and registers are stored in separate places
Only the registers, since flags are restored by the processor when it jumps back
questions.explanation: A stack is last in, first out. The most recent push must be the first pop, so the order is reversed.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit routine pushes eight general registers and one flags value, each four bytes wide. How many bytes of stack does it use?
questions.explanation: Eight registers of four bytes give 32, and the flags add four more, for 36 bytes in total.

questions.prompt: Is there one rule, "save every register", that is right for every inserted hook?
options: No, a hook should preserve only the live values its own code could disturb
Yes, because any unsaved register will always crash the original code
Yes, because partial saving is rejected by the processor
No, because registers never need saving once a jump has been made
questions.explanation: Saving everything is easy to understand in a small teaching example. A performance-sensitive hook preserves only what it can actually change.

questions.prompt: Why must inserted code re-execute the instructions it displaced before jumping back?
options: The patch overwrote them, but the original code still depends on their effects
The processor requires every displaced instruction to be executed twice
Displaced instructions hold the address to return to, so they are needed to jump back
Skipping them is fine, since the original code recomputes their results later
questions.explanation: The jump replaced real instructions. If they are skipped, registers and flow differ from what the original code planned for.

questions.prompt: After undoing a patch, what is the strongest evidence that the code is back to its original state?
options: Reading the bytes again and comparing them with the saved originals
The feature that the patch added no longer appears to be active
The tool reported that the undo call finished without any error
The target program is still running after the undo call has completed
questions.explanation: A feature looking disabled does not prove the bytes are back. Comparing the live bytes with the saved originals is direct evidence.

questions.prompt: Inserted code adds one to the first byte of a string every time that string is drawn. If the string starts with "A", what appears over successive draws?
options: "B", then "C", and so on, since the live string is changed on every draw
"A" every time, since the original string in the file cannot be changed
"B" every time, since the addition happens only the first time it is drawn
"A", then "C", then "E", since each draw adds two to the value
questions.explanation: The byte is incremented once per draw. That shows the inserted code sees the live string pointer while the original drawing still happens.

questions.prompt: A 5-byte call at 0x00500000 is replaced by a jump to inserted code, which first runs the original call. Where should execution continue afterward?
options: 0x00500005, right after the original call
0x00500000, the original call site
0x00500004, the last byte of the original call
0x00500010, the next multiple of sixteen
questions.explanation: The call is five bytes long, so the next instruction is at 0x00500005. The inserted code replays the call and then resumes there.

questions.prompt: How does the second hook display the second player's gold?
options: It caps gold at 999, makes up to three digits, and copies them into the live buffer
It writes a new string somewhere else in memory and replaces the text pointer in `edx`
It converts the gold to hexadecimal text and writes four bytes into the buffer
It changes the gold field itself to 999 and then redraws the whole description window
questions.explanation: Writing exactly three bytes into the existing buffer avoids overrunning it, and the cap keeps the number within three digits.

questions.prompt: A hook works on one build of a program. What should you do first when moving it to another build?
options: Start from what the hook is for, then re-measure its span, bytes, reach and resume point
Copy the same addresses and bytes, since the addresses stay the same across builds
Search for the replacement bytes in the new build and patch wherever they are found
Keep the old resume address, because only the jump distance changes between builds
questions.explanation: Addresses and bytes are evidence for one version. Each build needs its own measurements before the same idea can be applied.

questions.prompt: How does an import-table hook differ from an inline detour?
options: It edits one pointer in a table that calls already use, leaving instructions alone
It rewrites the call instruction itself, so no table needs to be involved
It replaces the whole function body, so the original code can no longer run
It works on any call in a program, even ones that do not go through a table
questions.explanation: A detour edits instruction bytes. An import-table hook edits the destination that an unchanged call already reads, so no jump distance is needed.

questions.prompt: After an import slot is redirected to a replacement function, which route does a call to the original function take?
options: Call site, then slot, then the replacement, which may forward to a saved original
Call site, then the original function, then the slot, then the replacement
Call site, then a rewritten call instruction, then the replacement directly
Call site, then the replacement, with the slot skipped since it was replaced
questions.explanation: The call instruction is unchanged and still loads its target from the slot, so it reaches the replacement. That function can then call the saved original.

questions.prompt: Why must a replacement for an imported function use the same arguments and calling convention as the original?
options: Callers follow the original's rules, so a mismatch can corrupt the stack
The loader rejects any replacement whose name differs from the original's name
The replacement must match in order to be placed in the same memory page
A mismatch only affects how quickly the replacement runs, not whether it works
questions.explanation: The call site was compiled for the original agreement. A wrong parameter size, convention or return type corrupts the stack or reads the wrong register.

questions.prompt: Why must a hook remember the original function pointer it replaced?
options: To forward calls to it, so the real behavior still happens
To compare it with the replacement, since the loader needs both to match
To keep the slot from being written to again by other code
To tell the operating system which module the replacement came from
questions.explanation: A hook usually wants to add to the original behavior, not remove it. The saved pointer is how the replacement reaches the real function.

questions.prompt: A PE file's import directory is a list of descriptors, one per imported library. How does a reader know where the list ends?
options: A final all-zero descriptor marks the end
The first descriptor holds a count of how many follow
The list ends at the next section boundary in the file
A descriptor with the name of the last library ends it
questions.explanation: The list has no stored length. It is terminated by an entry that is all zeros.

questions.prompt: Why does each imported DLL have two parallel arrays, a lookup table and the IAT?
options: The lookup table keeps which function each entry is; the IAT gets where it lives
The lookup table holds code and the IAT holds the data that the code uses
The IAT holds names for the loader, and the lookup table is a copy for debuggers
The two arrays hold different functions, so a name search needs both lists in turn
questions.explanation: Both start as identical name references. After loading, only the IAT contains live addresses, so you need the lookup table to know which slot is `MessageBoxW`.

questions.prompt: Why can't you find an imported function by name from the loaded import address table alone?
options: After loading it holds addresses, not names, which live in a separate list
The import address table is encrypted by the loader until the function is called
The table only lists functions that have already been called at least once
Names are stored there, but only for functions in the main module's own code
questions.explanation: Before loading the table points to names, but the loader overwrites those entries with live addresses. A parallel lookup list keeps the names.

questions.prompt: Why does the thunk loop run at most 2048 times?
options: A table with no zero terminator must not turn into an endless walk through memory
The Windows loader never allows more than 2048 imports from a single DLL
Each page can hold only 2048 four-byte slots, so the limit is the page size
The name hint is capped at 2048, so no further names exist beyond it
questions.explanation: The bound is a safety net for corrupt data. It is not a Windows rule about imports.

questions.prompt: In a 32-bit PE file, a function's name is found at index 5 of the lookup list. Each address slot is 4 bytes. How far into the address table is its slot?
options: 20 bytes: the same index, and each slot is four bytes wide
5 bytes, since the index is already measured in bytes
40 bytes, since every entry holds both a name and an address
9 bytes, since the slot is placed after the five name entries
questions.explanation: The two lists run in parallel, so the same index selects the slot, and 5 x 4 = 20 bytes from the start of the address table.

questions.prompt: Why change a memory page's protection before writing a pointer into an import table?
options: That page is normally not writable, so it is made writable for a moment
The page is hidden from other programs until its protection has been changed
Changing protection gives the page a fresh copy, so the write cannot be seen
The operating system only accepts a single write per page unless it is reset
questions.explanation: Import tables are usually read-only after loading. Making the page writable briefly allows the one change, and it is restored afterward.

questions.prompt: After writing the new pointer, what should the code do with the page's protection?
options: Restore the saved protection, so only the one pointer differs
Leave it writable, so later changes need no extra steps
Make it executable, so the replacement code can run from the page
Set it to no access, so other code cannot read the slot
questions.explanation: Putting the original protection back leaves memory as it was, apart from the single pointer that was meant to change.

questions.prompt: A pointer was written into a table, but restoring the page's protection then failed. What is the main concern?
options: The change is already in place, so the installer needs a way to retry or roll back
Nothing changed, because a failed call always cancels the write that came before it
The page is now locked, so the pointer can never be restored by anything
The pointer must be wrong, since an installation that fails is never complete
questions.explanation: An error later in the sequence does not undo an earlier write. The installer must keep enough state to recover from a half-finished change.

questions.prompt: A guard object that owns an installed hook goes out of scope. What should it do?
options: Put the saved original pointer back in the same slot, once
Leave the hook in place, so the process keeps behaving the same way
Put the saved original pointer in every slot of the table, to be safe
Delete the table entry, so nothing can call the function any more
questions.explanation: Cleanup follows ownership. The owner of the change restores the same slot exactly once, so the process is left as it was found.

questions.prompt: In the three-message-box proof, which text appears second?
options: "Hook reached the replacement IAT entry."
"The normal import runs first.", from the untouched call
"The original import is restored.", from the dropped patch
No box appears second, because the hook replaces the display
questions.explanation: Order is original, redirected, restored. The second proves interception and the third proves the slot was put back.

questions.prompt: Before planning an import-table hook, what must you first prove about the target function?
options: That the module actually calls it through one of its own import slots
That the function is the most frequently called one in the whole process
That the function's name is shorter than the table entry for it
That the function belongs to a library written in the same language
questions.explanation: If the call path is not an import slot of that module, there is nothing in the table to patch. Hooks should also stay small and avoid blocking.

questions.prompt: When would an inline detour be chosen over an import-table hook?
options: When the code path you care about is not reached through an import slot of the main module
When the function is imported, since a detour is always the better choice for those
When a module has no executable code, so only its tables can be changed
When the table is writable, since import tables never allow patches otherwise
questions.explanation: A hook should follow the real call path. If there is no import slot on that path, an instruction detour is the tool that fits.

questions.prompt: What should happen to a game IAT slot before the injected DLL unloads?
options: It should be restored to the original pointer
It should be left on the hook so the game keeps the feature
It should be zeroed so later calls fail safely
It should be rewritten with the DLL's own export address
questions.explanation: If the slot still points into the DLL's code after it unloads, the next call would jump to unmapped memory.

questions.prompt: In a typical game engine, in what order does input travel before it affects the game?
options: Device events, input state, bindings, then actions used by the game rules
Bindings, device events, game rules, then input state used for drawing
Input state, actions, device events, then bindings that decode the keys
Game rules, actions, bindings, then device events from the keyboard
questions.explanation: The device reports a fact, the engine records it as state, bindings map it to a named action, and the rules react to the action without ever naming a key.

questions.prompt: Why can one game accept a keyboard, a controller and a remapped key for the same jump?
options: The rules read an action, and bindings from the player's settings decide which input produces it
The operating system converts every device into the same key press before the game sees it
The game polls each device in turn and picks whichever one pressed first this frame
Controllers send keyboard scan codes, so the rules only ever read key positions
questions.explanation: The action layer is the only one that knows the player's settings. Rules refer to actions such as jump rather than a physical key.

questions.prompt: How does an engine compute that a button was just pressed?
options: It compares the current state with last frame's copy: down now, not down before
It asks the hardware whether a new key-down event arrived this millisecond
It checks that the key has been down for at least one whole frame
It waits for the operating system to send a repeat key-down event
questions.explanation: An edge needs two states: this frame's and the previous frame's. Down now and up before means just pressed.

questions.prompt: At 60 frames a second, a key goes down at 105 ms during frame 6 and the game first reports it as just pressed on frame 7. About how long after the press does the game notice?
options: About 11.7 ms, since frame 7 starts at 116.7 ms
About 16.7 ms, since a full frame always passes first
About 5 ms, since frame 6 already sees events during its run
About 105 ms, since the game counts from the start of the run
questions.explanation: Events are collected at the start of each frame. 116.7 - 105 = 11.7 ms, and the delay is never more than one frame.

questions.prompt: A game polls the key once per frame at 60 frames a second. A tool presses a key for 10 ms at a random moment. What is the chance a poll lands inside the press?
options: About 60%, since 10 ms divided by 16.67 ms is 0.60
About 30%, since 10 ms divided by 33.3 ms is 0.30
About 100%, since any press longer than 1 ms is seen
About 16%, since one frame is 16.67 ms and only one in six presses are seen
questions.explanation: The probability is D divided by the frame time. A 5 ms press would be seen about 30% of the time, and 16.67 ms or longer always, if frames are steady.

questions.prompt: Why does a game that collects events see even a very short press, while one that polls may not?
options: Events wait in a queue until the next frame; a poll looks at one instant
Event-based games run at a higher frame rate than polling games
Polling games ignore the keyboard unless a window message arrives first
Events are kept for 16.67 ms and discarded, but polled values persist
questions.explanation: A press's down and up both sit in the queue until collected. A poll samples only the moment it runs, so a press between two polls can be missed.

questions.prompt: Suppose two fixed steps run on the same frame as a just-pressed edge. What happens if each step reads the edge?
options: Both see the same press, so a jump could happen twice
Only the first step sees it, because the edge is cleared after it is read
Neither sees it, because edges only exist outside fixed steps
The second step sees a released edge instead of the press
questions.explanation: The edge belongs to the frame, not to a step, so every step on that frame sees it. That is why queued intents consumed exactly once are the fix.

questions.prompt: What does the repair for missed edges do with a press?
options: Records it as an intent, such as "jump requested", queued until a step takes it
Holds the key down artificially for several frames so every step sees it
Raises the fixed step rate until a step always lands on the edge frame
Moves the edge test inside each step so steps read the keyboard directly
questions.explanation: An intent decouples the press from the frame it happened on. A step takes it from the queue once, so it is neither missed nor handled twice.

questions.prompt: Why do engines apply a dead zone to a stick?
options: A resting stick rarely reads exactly 0, and without a fix the character would drift
A dead zone makes a stick report a larger range so it feels more sensitive
A stick reads 0 at rest but briefly reports 1 when it is moved, which must be filtered
A dead zone limits how many axis values can be sent per second
questions.explanation: Springs and sensors are imperfect, so a resting stick might read 0.06. The dead zone treats small values as 0.

questions.prompt: A stick filter uses a dead zone of 0.2 and rescales so a full push still reaches 1. What does a reading of 0.6 become?
options: 0.5, since (0.6 - 0.2) divided by 0.8 is 0.5
0.4, since subtracting 0.2 is all that rescaling needs
0.6, since readings above the dead zone are left alone
0.75, since 0.6 divided by 0.8 is 0.75
questions.explanation: Rescaling is (value - dead zone) divided by (1 - dead zone). Subtracting without dividing would leave a full push unable to reach 1.

questions.prompt: A stick resting slightly off center reads 0.05, and the dead zone is 0.1. What should the filtered value be, and why?
options: 0, because the reading is smaller than the dead zone and is treated as drift
0.05, because a filter must never change a reading that is not zero
0.5, because values inside the dead zone are scaled up to fill the range
0.1, because values inside the dead zone are raised to the zone's edge
questions.explanation: Small readings below the dead zone are treated as noise or wear and ignored, so the game does not drift on its own.

questions.prompt: A stick is pushed to 0.12 on both axes with a dead zone of 0.15. How do the two dead zone styles differ?
options: Per-axis gives (0, 0); radial sees a distance near 0.17 and keeps a small output
Per-axis keeps a small output; radial gives (0, 0), since 0.12 is below 0.15 alone
Both give (0, 0), since each reading of 0.12 is below the zone of 0.15
Both give a small output, since the stick is pushed along a diagonal direction
questions.explanation: Per-axis checks each axis alone, so the diagonal feels dead. Radial checks the distance from the centre, 0.12 x 1.414 = 0.17, which is above the zone.

questions.prompt: Pressing W and D together gives the vector (1, 1). Why does a game normalise it?
options: Its length is about 1.414, so unnormalised diagonal walking would be 41% faster
Its length is 2, so unnormalised diagonal walking would be twice as fast
Its length is 1, so normalising keeps the speed the same for all keys
It would make the character turn instead of walk
questions.explanation: The length is the square root of 2, about 1.414. Dividing by it gives (0.707, 0.707) and length 1.

questions.prompt: Why does movement code scale down input vectors that are longer than 1 but leave shorter ones alone?
options: Diagonals would be faster than straight moves; short ones are gentle pushes
Short vectors are invalid input, so the code ignores them to avoid errors
Scaling short vectors would make the character move in the wrong direction
Long vectors only come from broken devices, so they are reduced to be safe
questions.explanation: Scaling everything to length 1 would make a gentle half push as fast as a full one. Only too-long vectors need limiting.

questions.prompt: What are the two identities of a keyboard key?
options: Its position, reported as a scan code, and the character it types, which depends on the layout
Its label, set by the manufacturer, and the scan code, which depends on the layout
Its virtual-key code, which is fixed, and its scan code, which depends on the layout
Its character, which is fixed by the board, and its position, which depends on the layout
questions.explanation: The physical place is fixed, but the layout decides what it types. The virtual-key code follows the layout, not the position.

questions.prompt: A scan code names a key's physical position, while a virtual-key code names the character it gives under the current layout. Which is better for movement keys on the left of a keyboard, and why?
options: The scan code, because the keys keep the same positions on every layout
The virtual-key code, because every layout puts the same letters in the same places
Neither, because positions and letters are identical on all keyboards
The virtual-key code, because scan codes differ between keyboards of the same model
questions.explanation: Position-based controls should follow physical position. Layouts such as AZERTY move letters around, so a letter-based binding ends up on a different key.

questions.prompt: Why do games usually bind movement to key positions rather than letters?
options: The four keys under the left hand keep their roles on any keyboard layout
Letters are slower for the operating system to translate than scan codes are
Key positions let the game ignore the focus state of its own window
Letters are only valid inside text boxes, and not while a game is running
questions.explanation: On AZERTY the letter W moves to a different key, so a letter binding breaks. Positions keep the same hand shape.

questions.prompt: What is an input method editor (IME) for?
options: Typing languages with thousands of characters by composing text, then confirming
Remapping keys so scan codes match the layout the player selected for typing
Converting controller buttons into text characters for a chat box
Sending keyboard shortcuts directly to the game without using its window
questions.explanation: While composing, keys go to the IME rather than to the game as ordinary key events, which is why text boxes enable it and gameplay must not.

questions.prompt: A display is set to 150% scaling. How many physical pixels correspond to 800 logical pixels?
questions.explanation: Scaling multiplies logical pixels by 1.5, so 800 x 1.5 = 1,200. Dividing instead would give about 533.

questions.prompt: On Windows, one notch of a traditional wheel is 120 units. How many lines does a game read for 360 units?
options: 3 lines, since 360 divided by 120
120 lines, since the units count lines
360 lines, since each unit is a line
30 lines, since 360 divided by 12
questions.explanation: Three notches report 360 units, which a game reads as 3 lines. Touchpads report small smooth pixel amounts instead.

questions.prompt: Why do many engines move the cursor back to the centre after every read when looking around?
options: Windows has no built-in lock, so recentring keeps the cursor off the window's edge
The cursor must be at the centre for the mouse to report any motion at all
The operating system requires the cursor to be recentred after every single read
Recentring converts window coordinates into physical pixels on a scaled screen
questions.explanation: In locked mode the cursor is hidden and cannot hit the edge. Some engines read raw movement instead.

questions.prompt: In a 1280 x 720 window, the centre is (640, 360) and the engine reads the cursor at (652, 357). What is the motion?
options: (+12, +3), since the engine takes the absolute change
(-12, +3), since the centre is subtracted from the reading
(652, 357), since the cursor position is the motion
questions.explanation: Motion is the reading minus the centre. The sign of y shows the cursor went up, since y grows downward.

questions.prompt: When a player switches windows while holding a key, what do engines do?
options: Watch for the focus-lost event and clear their input state
Wait for the key-up and ignore other events until it arrives
Keep the old state so that the key is still held when the player returns
Pause the game and ask the player to press the key again
questions.explanation: The game never receives the key-up. Without clearing, the key would look stuck held.

questions.prompt: A tool must (a) learn whether a key is held right now, (b) make the system act as if a key was typed, and (c) notify one specific window. Which pairing of job to mechanism is right?
options: Sample the key state; inject an event into the system input stream; post a window message
Post a window message; sample the key state; inject an event into the system input stream
Inject an event into the system input stream; post a window message; sample the key state
Sample the key state; post a window message; inject an event into the system input stream
questions.explanation: Sampling answers "is it down now", injection feeds the system input stream, and window messages go to one window. Mixing the three up is a common source of tools that seem to do nothing.

questions.prompt: What question does sampling the keyboard state answer?
options: Is this key down at the moment I check?
Which keys were pressed since I last checked, in order?
Which window received the last keypress?
How long has this key been held down?
questions.explanation: Sampling reads the current state of a key. It does not wait for an event, and it does not keep a history of earlier presses.

questions.prompt: A key-state function returns a 16-bit signed number in which the top bit means "down right now". What does a held key look like?
options: A negative number, because the top bit is the sign bit
A positive number, because the top bit is the largest value bit
Always exactly 1, because a held key is reported as a single flag
Zero, because a held key reports no change since the last check
questions.explanation: In a signed 16-bit value the top bit is also the sign bit, so a key that is down right now shows as a negative number.

questions.prompt: A shared key-state function has a "pressed since the last call" bit. Why is it unreliable for detecting a single press?
options: Another caller can clear it first, so keep your own previous sample instead
It is set for every key at once, so it cannot tell one key from another
It is only valid for letters, so special keys never set it
It is reset by the display refresh, so it is only correct at 60 times per second
questions.explanation: State that other code can consume is not dependable. Keeping your own previous sample and comparing it with the current one gives a reliable press detector.

questions.prompt: A rising-edge detector returns true only when a key is down now and was up at the previous poll. Successive polls report: up, down, down, up, down. What does it return for them?
options: false, true, false, false, true
false, true, true, false, true
true, false, false, true, false
false, false, true, false, false
questions.explanation: Only a change from up to down counts. The second and fifth polls qualify, while the third is still held from the previous poll.

questions.prompt: Why is a hotkey polling loop usually written with a short sleep, such as 10 milliseconds, instead of a tight loop?
options: A tight loop wastes a whole core, and a short sleep is fast enough for humans
A tight loop is more accurate, but the operating system forbids it
A sleep makes the key state change more slowly, which avoids false presses
A short sleep lets the keyboard buffer fill up, so no key is missed
questions.explanation: Polling constantly burns processor time for no benefit. A modest interval catches normal presses, though a very short tap between polls can still be missed.

questions.prompt: A key-state query returns zero for every key. What can you conclude?
options: Not that it is broken: the desktop may be inactive or security rules block it
That the keyboard is broken, because zero is the code for a missing device
That every key is currently up, so the query is certainly working
That the query has been run twice, because the second call always returns zero
questions.explanation: Desktop state and privilege rules can produce zeros, so a zero is not evidence of a hardware fault.

questions.prompt: Synthetic input is injected into the system input stream without naming a window. Which window receives it?
options: Whichever window currently has keyboard focus
The window under the mouse pointer when it is sent
The window that was created most recently
Every window on the desktop at the same time
questions.explanation: Injected events go to the system's normal input path, so the focused window gets them. That is why a tool should check focus before sending.

questions.prompt: Before injecting synthetic input, why should a tool verify that the intended window is in the foreground?
options: Events go to the focused window, so keys could land in an unrelated one
Windows in the background never exist, so the injection would fail with an error
The foreground window decides how fast injected events may be sent
Foreground windows are the only ones whose titles can be read by tools
questions.explanation: Injection does not name a destination. Checking that the focused window belongs to the target process keeps keystrokes from reaching something else.

questions.prompt: Why should a tool that sends a synthetic key press always send the matching release too?
options: Otherwise the key stays held as far as the target is concerned, even after an error
The target ignores presses that are not followed by a release within a second
The release is what actually delivers the press, since a press alone is only a request
A release is needed to tell the operating system which window to deliver to
questions.explanation: A synthetic key that is never released remains down in the target. Good tools release it on error and cancellation paths as well.

questions.prompt: An injection function returns the number of events it accepted. Why compare it with the number you tried to send?
options: A smaller count means some events never entered the stream, so it is a failure
A larger count means the target pressed extra keys, which should be released
The count is the number of windows that received the events, so one is expected
The count tells how many milliseconds the injection took, so lower is better
questions.explanation: The return value says how many events were accepted. If it is lower than sent, part of the input was lost and the tool should report an error.

questions.prompt: In a bit-flags field, what does the value zero mean?
options: No optional flags are set, so the default behavior applies
Every flag is set, so every optional behavior applies at once
The field is invalid, so the whole structure is rejected
Only the lowest flag is set, so a single option applies
questions.explanation: Each flag is one bit that switches on an option. With all bits clear you get the default, which for a key event is a press.

questions.prompt: Two option bits, 0x0004 and 0x0010, are combined with bitwise OR. What is the value?
questions.explanation: The bits do not overlap, so OR gives the same result as addition: 0x0004 + 0x0010 = 0x0014.

questions.prompt: Why might a game ignore an event that carries only a virtual-key code?
options: Some games read scan codes, so a virtual-key event does not reach them
Virtual-key codes are valid only inside the lab window
Games read the `time` field and reject zero timestamps
Virtual-key events are delivered only to games running as administrator
questions.explanation: `wScan` and `KEYEVENTF_SCANCODE` give the key's position instead. A game that reads positions would not respond to a virtual-key event.

questions.prompt: What does User Interface Privilege Isolation (UIPI) do?
options: Blocks input from a lower-integrity process into a higher-integrity window
Blocks every `SendInput` call made from a process that owns a hidden window
Stops a process from reading the messages sent to its own windows
Encrypts input events so that only the game's own window can read them
questions.explanation: A game running as administrator will not accept injected input from a normal tool. The mechanism protects the more trusted window.

questions.prompt: Why is a privilege-level block on synthetic input hard to diagnose?
options: It fails quietly, and looks the same as a wrong key code or an unfocused window
It always crashes the sending tool, which hides the cause of the failure
It sends an error message to the target, which is never seen by the sender
It slows the input down, so it looks like a slow computer
questions.explanation: The operating system simply drops the input without naming the reason. Several unrelated problems produce the same symptom of nothing happening.

questions.prompt: Synthetic input silently does nothing. What is a sensible response?
options: Check whether the target has higher privileges, log it, and stop
Send the same input many times in a row until the target accepts it
Raise the tool's own privileges blindly until something changes
Assume the keyboard is broken and replace the key mappings
questions.explanation: Silent failure often points to a privilege mismatch. Diagnose it rather than flooding the target with retries or escalating without understanding.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between sending a message to a window and posting one?
options: Sending waits for the handler's result, while posting queues the message and returns
Sending queues the message and returns, while posting calls the handler and waits
Sending works only inside one process, while posting works only between processes
Sending carries a single number, while posting can carry a pointer as well
questions.explanation: Sending is synchronous, since it waits for the handler to finish. Posting is asynchronous, since it only places the message in the owning thread's queue.

questions.prompt: Why prefer a send-with-timeout call when messaging a window in another process?
options: A bounded wait stops your tool from hanging on a stuck window
A timeout makes the message arrive earlier than one without a limit
