Messages to other processes are dropped unless they include a timeout
A timeout lets the call carry a larger message than normal
questions.explanation: A synchronous send waits for the other window. If that window is hung, a limit returns control to your tool instead of blocking it.

questions.prompt: Why should a message to a window in another process not carry a pointer from your own address space?
options: Each process has its own address space, so the pointer means nothing there
Pointers are too large to fit inside a message, so the system truncates them
The operating system encrypts pointers in messages, so the receiver cannot read them
Pointers in messages are always accepted, but they are slower than numbers
questions.explanation: An address is only meaningful inside the process that owns it. Cross-process messages should carry plain integers that both sides agree on.

questions.prompt: A game reads raw device state, and a tool sends it window key messages. What is the likely outcome?
options: Nothing: the game never reads that path, so the wrong abstraction was chosen
The game accepts them, since every key message is turned into device state first
The game crashes, since window messages cannot be sent to a full-screen process
The game repeats each key forever, since it never sees the matching release
questions.explanation: Messages and device state are separate paths. If the target reads only the second, the first has no effect, and the fix is to study how it consumes input.

questions.prompt: In a standard window message loop, what does the dispatch step do?
options: It hands a retrieved message to the window's handler
It waits until the next message arrives in the queue
It turns key presses into character messages
It checks the queue without blocking and then returns
questions.explanation: The loop retrieves a message, may translate key presses into characters, and then dispatches it to the handler. Waiting and non-blocking checks are separate retrieve calls.

questions.prompt: Why does a game loop check its message queue without blocking?
options: It must keep updating and drawing even when no message arrives
Blocking calls cannot read keyboard messages, so only non-blocking ones work
Non-blocking calls make the window run at a higher priority than others
A blocking call would remove messages from the queue before they were read
questions.explanation: A blocking wait suits a window with nothing to do. A game has to advance its world and draw frames even if the player does nothing.

questions.prompt: A window procedure spends a second reading a large file. What happens to other messages on that thread?
options: They wait until it returns, so the window may stop repainting or responding
They are processed by another thread in parallel while the file is being read
They are dropped by Windows once the queue has been waiting for a short delay
They are handled first, ahead of the slow file read that is already running
questions.explanation: One thread handles one message at a time. A slow handler delays movement, repainting and close.

questions.prompt: A client area must be 1280 x 720 and the borders and title bar add 16 across and 39 down. How big is the outer rectangle?
questions.explanation: Adding the frame to both sides: 1280 + 16 = 1296 and 720 + 39 = 759. The system works the exact sizes out with `AdjustWindowRect`.

questions.prompt: A game keeps the aspect ratio for a 1280 x 720 client area after the window becomes 1000 x 720. What happens?
options: The picture is squashed: the old ratio is 1280/720, but the window is now 1000/720
The picture is drawn correctly, since the aspect ratio only matters at start-up time
The picture is drawn stretched wider, since the old ratio is smaller than the new one
The game crashes, since `WM_SIZE` is not allowed to change the client area width
questions.explanation: On `WM_SIZE` a game should recompute the ratio from the new width and height.

questions.prompt: The game's client area starts at screen point (100, 100) and a tool window's at (1400, 100). What is screen point (1500, 200) in the tool window's client coordinates?
questions.explanation: Subtract the tool window's origin: (1500 - 1400, 200 - 100). Subtracting the game's origin gives (1400, 100), which is off by a constant.

questions.prompt: Why is it better to identify a game's window by its owning process than by its title?
options: A title can change or be shared, while the owning process is a stable identity
Titles cannot be read by other programs, but process identifiers can be read
A process always owns exactly one window, so its identifier is easy to match
Titles are unique, but they take longer to compare than process identifiers
questions.explanation: Titles are just text that may change with the game state or match other windows. The process that owns the window does not change.

questions.prompt: What should an input tool do when the user switches focus away from its target to another application?
options: Pause instead of typing into the wrong window
Carry on typing, since the target will still receive the keys
Bring the target window back to the front at once and keep going
Close itself, since focus loss means the session has ended
questions.explanation: Synthetic input goes to the focused window, so the tool must stop when focus is lost, and resume only when the target is in front again.

questions.prompt: Which four questions should a game-tool menu answer clearly?
options: What features exist, each one's state, what reached the worker, and how shutdown restores normal
What features exist, how fast each runs, which key toggles it, and how often it was used
Which game is running, which build it is, how large the window is, and how to quit
What colors are used, which fonts apply, where the panels sit, and how the theme changes
questions.explanation: The four questions cover features, per-feature state, what actually reached the worker, and how everything returns to normal.

questions.prompt: Why does the tutorial build a separate desktop window as the first menu?
options: It is easy to debug, avoids loader lock, and can sit beside a local target
It can draw directly into the game's renderer with no extra work
It gives the menu write access to the game's memory without a worker
It avoids needing a channel because the window shares the game's thread
questions.explanation: Integrating the same widgets into an injected renderer is a later graphics-backend problem.

questions.prompt: Why use one enumeration for an overlay mode instead of three booleans named off, team and all?
options: One value is exactly one variant, while three booleans could all be true at once
Booleans cannot be copied or compared, so only an enumeration can be stored
An enumeration runs faster, because booleans must be converted before every check
Booleans can only be used for yes or no questions about files, not about menus
questions.explanation: An enumeration makes contradictory states impossible to represent. Three separate flags allow combinations that mean nothing.

questions.prompt: What advantage does grouping a tool's options into one settings value have over a separate global flag for each option?
options: The group can be copied, compared, validated, saved and sent as a unit
Each option in a group is automatically kept safe by the compiler
The group makes each option run faster, since it is stored together
A group removes the need for default values, since every option is optional
questions.explanation: A single value can be cloned into a command and compared with the last one sent. Scattered globals have to be gathered by hand each time.

questions.prompt: Why should a tool's riskier capabilities start switched off?
options: The tool begins harmless, and the user must make a deliberate choice
Switched-off features use less memory, so the tool starts faster
A feature that starts on cannot be turned off again later
Users prefer menus that begin with fewer options visible
questions.explanation: A safe default is part of the design, not a warning to remember. Opting in to anything active is a conscious step.

questions.prompt: What is different about immediate-mode UI compared with a retained toolkit?
options: The `ui` function describes the interface again each frame, and the app stores the settings
The framework keeps a checkbox object that the app asks later whether it was clicked
The UI draws once and updates only when a thread sends a redraw message
Each widget stores its own value and the app never sees it
questions.explanation: The checkbox borrows `show_names` for the call, draws it, and changes it on a click. The `MenuApp` keeps the value between frames.

questions.prompt: A menu is redrawn every frame, and a slider's code writes a value into another process each time it runs. What is wrong?
options: It repeats a side effect because the menu repainted, not because the user acted
The write is too slow, since sliders cannot write to other processes
The write happens only once, so the slider will not follow the user
The slider can only show values, because writing is a job for buttons only
questions.explanation: Painting the menu should not cause side effects. The change should be tied to an explicit user action, such as pressing an apply button.

questions.prompt: Why plan a table of events, commands, results and feedback before drawing widgets?
options: Each control gets a clear request, an owner of the side effect, and a truthful result
So the widgets can be drawn faster, since layout is the slowest part of a menu
So the menu can run without a worker, since results are computed from the table
So all features share one button, since the table lists only a single event
questions.explanation: Without a plan, a button can change its label before anyone knows whether the work finished. The worker owns the effect, and the menu reports its true result.

questions.prompt: Why would a menu send a worker thread its own copy of the settings rather than a shared reference?
options: Each side keeps its own copy, so editing in the menu cannot race with the worker
A copy is faster to send than a reference, since references need a lock
A shared reference cannot be sent to another thread under any circumstances
A copy lets the worker change the menu's settings directly afterwards
questions.explanation: Passing owned data avoids sharing one mutable value between threads. The menu can keep editing while the worker uses the copy it was given.

questions.prompt: A menu remembers the last settings it sent. Why compare new settings with that copy before sending?
options: To avoid resending unchanged settings, and to tell the user nothing changed
To check that the worker has applied the earlier settings and finished
To make sure the settings are valid, since only new values can be validated
To undo the last change, since the copy is what the worker will restore
questions.explanation: Comparing with the last sent copy lets the menu skip a pointless command and give honest feedback.

questions.prompt: Why update the remembered "last sent" copy only after the send succeeded?
options: It then reflects what was really submitted, so a failed send can be tried again
Sending is always successful, so the order makes no difference at all
The remembered copy is the worker's confirmation that it applied the settings
Updating it earlier would erase the settings the user is still editing
questions.explanation: The copy tracks what the menu knows it submitted. If the send failed and the copy were already updated, the change would never be retried.

questions.prompt: A menu toggles when a hotkey is pressed. Why toggle on the rising edge rather than whenever the key is down?
options: Held down, it would toggle every frame, so the menu would flicker open and shut
A held key sends only one signal, so the rising edge is the only one that exists
The rising edge is the only point at which the key state can be read
Toggling while held would use up the keyboard's buffer of waiting keys
questions.explanation: A single press lasts many frames. Acting on the change from up to down makes it count once per press.

questions.prompt: Should a tool keep forcing the target window to the foreground?
options: No: let the user choose focus, and pause active input when it is lost
Yes, since a tool can only work correctly while its target stays in front
Yes, but only every few seconds, so the user does not notice
No, because the operating system forbids any tool from changing focus
questions.explanation: Fighting the user for focus is rude and risky. If the target loses focus, active input features should simply pause.

questions.prompt: Which guideline helps keep a status menu readable and honest?
options: Do not use color as the only sign of success or failure
Show every setting at once, so nothing is ever hidden from the user
Keep status text so short that errors are left out
Restore every active feature automatically at the next start
questions.explanation: Some users cannot tell certain colors apart, so text or symbols should carry the meaning too. Unsafe active features should not be remembered across runs.

questions.prompt: Why does the full example set a minimum window size?
options: A narrow window can wrap Restore defaults into a column of one-letter lines
The OpenGL backend refuses to create windows below a certain width in pixels
The worker needs a minimum window size before it will receive any commands
Narrow windows lose keyboard focus and stop responding to the Escape key
questions.explanation: The button is still technically present but unreadable.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches the worker's shutdown order?
options: Stop new commands, release input, restore changes, unhook, close handles, report
Close handles, release input, stop new commands, restore changes, unhook, report
Restore changes, close handles, release input, unhook, stop new commands, report
Report, restore changes, stop new commands, close handles, release input, unhook
questions.explanation: Shutdown is the reverse of setup.

questions.prompt: Why does the main thread join the worker before returning?
options: A vanished window does not prove cleanup finished; joining makes the program wait
Joining makes the worker run faster during the shutdown stage of the program
The window cannot close until the worker has sent its first status message back
Joining releases the channel's sender so that the worker can notice it closed
questions.explanation: Without the join, the process could end while cleanup is still running.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a module to be cohesive?
options: Its pieces all serve one job, and related work lives together
It shares its private details with the modules next to it
It is as large as possible, so everything is in one place
It has no functions of its own, only data that others use
questions.explanation: Cohesion means the contents belong together. Sharing private details with neighbors is coupling, which is the opposite of what splitting code aims for.

questions.prompt: A new build of the target ships, and only its addresses and module facts change. Which part of a well-organized tool should mostly change?
options: The part that identifies the build and holds its addresses
The entry point that connects all the other parts together
The part that draws the menu and reports status to the user
The part that owns the worker thread and its command channel
questions.explanation: Build identity and addresses belong together in one place. The code that merely connects pieces should not need to change for a new build.

questions.prompt: Why might two features share one copied observation instead of each reading the target separately?
options: They describe one moment, and the copy stays valid if the source is freed
Copies are the only way to read from another process, so sharing is required
A shared copy pauses the target, so both features see the same state
Reading twice is not allowed, so the second feature would be refused
questions.explanation: A copy is an owned value, so features agree on one moment and keep a valid view even after the original is gone. It does not pause anything.

questions.prompt: A tool labels each observation with a counter that it increments itself. What does the counter tell you?
options: Which pass of the tool it came from, not that the target was paused
Which update of the target the observation came from, since the counter follows the game
That the target was paused while it was read, since the counter only changes then
How long the observation took, since the counter is a clock
questions.explanation: A counter owned by the tool only labels the tool's own passes. Only a tick or generation number supplied by the target could say anything about the target's own updates.

questions.prompt: The target exposes a tick counter that changes whenever the game updates. How can the observer use it?
options: Read it before and after copying the fields, and retry the capture when the two values differ
Write a larger value into it before copying, so the game waits until the observer has finished reading
Store it in place of health and gold, since the tick already summarises the state of the player
Skip range checks on the copied fields, because a matching tick proves every value is reasonable
questions.explanation: If the counter changed mid-copy, the fields may mix two moments, so retry. A matching counter still does not replace validating what was captured.

questions.prompt: A feature interface requires start and stop methods, but a feature that only reads and logs values has nothing to start or undo. What does it do?
options: It implements them to do nothing and report success, as its work happens elsewhere
It leaves them out, since a read-only feature cannot be given those methods
It starts a worker thread in them, so the feature has something to stop later
It reports failure from them, so the tool knows the feature is passive
questions.explanation: An interface asks every implementer for all of its methods. A passive feature gives trivial answers for the lifecycle ones and does its work in the update method.

questions.prompt: A display can show health, gold, both, or nothing, and exactly one choice is active at a time. Which representation matches that rule?
options: One value of an enumeration with four variants
Three booleans named health, gold and both
Two booleans named health and gold, plus a counter
A text string that holds the name of the active mode
questions.explanation: The type should follow the real rule. One enumeration value is a single variant, so impossible combinations cannot be represented.

questions.prompt: Which options belong in separate booleans rather than as variants of one enumeration?
options: Activities that can run at the same time, which are independent switches
Choices that exclude each other, which are best stored one per variant
Options that have more than four possible values, which a boolean can hold
Settings that never change after start-up, which an enumeration cannot store
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive choices become an enumeration. Activities that may overlap stay separate switches.

questions.prompt: A setting cycles Low, then Medium, then High, and then wraps around to Low each time a command is applied. Starting at Medium, two commands are applied. What is the result?
options: Low
High
Medium
Low, then High
questions.explanation: Medium moves to High, and High wraps around to Low.

questions.prompt: A command handler returns a boolean meaning "stop after this command". What should it return for a stop request and for an ordinary setting change?
options: True for the stop request, and false for the setting change
False for the stop request, and true for the setting change
True for both, since each command ends the current pass
False for both, since the loop ends by itself
questions.explanation: The boolean tells the loop whether to leave. Only the stop request asks for that, and ordinary changes let the loop carry on.

questions.prompt: Why might an input thread send a command through a channel rather than edit a feature's settings directly?
options: The worker alone owns the settings, so no shared state is touched mid-update
Channels are faster than direct edits, since settings are slow to change
The operating system forbids input threads from changing any settings
A channel makes the settings permanent, so that they survive a restart
questions.explanation: A key press requests a change and the owner applies it. The reason is ownership and safety, not speed or an operating-system rule.

questions.prompt: A command enables a patch. When should the worker send the acknowledgement to the menu?
options: Only after the patch owner reports success, so the menu can tell requested from applied state
As soon as the command is received, so the menu updates quickly and the user sees no delay
Just before the patch is written, so the menu is ready if the write finishes very quickly
Only when the game process closes, so the menu can summarise every patch in one message
questions.explanation: Acknowledging early would show a checked box for a patch that may have failed. Acknowledging after success separates what was asked from what happened.

questions.prompt: One feature gets malformed input while another feature's input is valid. What is a sound response?
options: Treat it as that feature's problem, stop it, and let the valid one carry on
Stop the whole tool, since one bad input means every feature is untrustworthy
Ignore the error silently, so that the feature keeps running on bad data
Restart every feature, since a bad value is shared by all of them
questions.explanation: First decide whether the error belongs to one feature or to something shared. A closed target would affect everything, but one bad field does not.

questions.prompt: A feature's update fails, and then its own cleanup fails too. What should the tool do next?
options: Report the error, enter shutdown, and keep resources so cleanup can be retried
Mark the feature disabled and carry on, since the failure has been recorded
Unload at once, since a failed cleanup means the resources are already gone
Ignore the second failure, since the first error was the one that mattered
questions.explanation: A failed cleanup must not hide behind a disabled flag, because a hook may still be live. Unloading would be worse, so the tool shuts down carefully and keeps what it needs to retry.

questions.prompt: Why mark a failed feature as disabled before attempting its cleanup?
options: So the next update pass cannot run the broken feature again while cleanup is unresolved
So that the cleanup is certain to succeed, since a disabled feature has nothing to undo
So the other features are disabled as well, since failures spread between them
So the flag can be saved to disk, where it will be read after a restart
questions.explanation: The flag guards against re-running a broken feature. It does not make restoration succeed, and it does not affect other features.

questions.prompt: Which shutdown order is safe for a tool with input handling, workers, features, patches and handles?
options: Stop input, signal workers, wait, disable features, restore patches, close handles
Close handles, stop input, signal workers, restore patches, disable features
Restore patches, close handles, stop input, then signal and wait for workers
Disable features, close handles, wait for workers, stop input, restore patches
questions.explanation: Workers must be finished before the things they use go away. Closing handles first would leave a worker using handles that no longer exist.

questions.prompt: After the user presses Stop, the tool's window disappears. What does that prove about cleanup?
options: Nothing: a vanished window is not proof, so a restoration failure must remain visible
That every patch was restored, because the window can only close after the cleanup finishes
That the workers have exited, because Windows waits for threads before it removes a window
That handles are closed, since the window owns every handle the tool opened during its run
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that the UI going away says nothing about restoration. Separate logs and error reports show whether the patch bytes were restored.

questions.prompt: Why keep build-specific offsets and locations together in one profile that is checked against the target's fingerprint?
options: An offset is a fact about one build, so a different build is rejected, not guessed
One profile loads faster than several scattered constants, since the compiler merges them
A profile makes the offsets valid for all builds, since it adjusts them while running
Offsets in a profile are encrypted, so other tools cannot read the target's layout
questions.explanation: Addresses only mean something for the build they were measured on. Keeping them with a fingerprint check makes a wrong build fail loudly.

questions.prompt: Before enabling a feature that patches an address, what should the tool compare?
options: The live bytes at that address against the expected original instruction signature
The address against the previous run's address, since a stable value proves the same build
The size of the executable file on disk against the size recorded in the tool's log
The feature's name against the profile, because the name identifies which bytes are present
questions.explanation: Matching bytes show that the instruction is the one the profile describes. A mismatch should produce a clear rejection, not a value from the wrong field.

questions.prompt: A test gives a fake memory reader bytes that differ from the expected signature and asserts that patching is refused. What does this show?
options: The refusal logic works, and it can be tested without a real running target
The real read call works, since the fake reader exercises the real operating system
The signature is correct for the real build, since the fake bytes were checked
Handles are released properly, since the test finishes without any errors
questions.explanation: A fake reader makes the comparison rule testable anywhere. It does not exercise handle ownership or the real memory read.

questions.prompt: Why does searching a library's export table for the name of a COM interface method find nothing?
options: COM hands out objects, so methods are reached through a vtable, not an exported name
The method names are encrypted, so they must be decoded before they can be found
Exports are only listed for functions that are called from outside the process
The method names are shortened by the compiler, so the full name does not appear
questions.explanation: The public exports are mostly creator functions. Methods live behind an object's vtable, which is how COM exposes functionality, not obfuscation.

questions.prompt: What does COM, the Component Object Model, mean for how you reach a Direct3D method?
options: Start from an object and follow its table of function pointers, not a name
Call each method by its exported name, but with an extra hidden first argument
Search the module's byte patterns for the first instruction of each method
Read each method's address from the import table of the game's executable
questions.explanation: A COM interface pointer begins with a vtable pointer, as a published ABI contract rather than something inferred from disassembly.

questions.prompt: Given a pointer to a COM object, how many memory reads reach the code behind one of its methods?
options: Two: the vtable pointer, then the function pointer from the method's slot
One: the object pointer already holds the function's address
Three: the object, the type description, and the function pointer
Two: the function's name from the object, then its address from the export table
questions.explanation: The first read gets the vtable from the object, and the second reads the slot at the method's index to get the function.

questions.prompt: Why does using 4-byte slot steps in a 64-bit process misplace every vtable index above zero?
options: Slots are 8 bytes wide there, so 4-byte steps land partway between entries
Slots are 4 bytes wide there, so 8-byte steps would be the ones that are wrong
Slots are skipped in pairs there, so the index is doubled before it is used
Slot zero is reserved there, so every index must start one place later
questions.explanation: In 64-bit code, slot 6 is at offset 6 × 8 = 48. Using 4 bytes would land at 24, which is in the middle of slot 3.

questions.prompt: An interface's own methods begin at slot 4, in declaration order: Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta. Which slot is Delta?
options: Slot 7
Slot 6
Slot 8
Slot 3
questions.explanation: Alpha is slot 4, Beta is 5, Gamma is 6, and Delta is 7. Slots are assigned in declaration order, after the inherited methods.

questions.prompt: A COM interface inherits only from the base interface with three methods. At which slot do its own methods begin?
options: Slot 3, right after the three base methods in slots 0, 1 and 2
Slot 0, since each interface has its own table
Slot 1, since slot 0 is only a marker for the end of the table
Slot 4, since one slot is kept spare after the base methods
questions.explanation: A derived interface's table begins with the base methods, so its own methods follow, counting on from 3.

questions.prompt: A hook is installed at an index copied from a forum post that was counted for another interface. What happens?
options: It replaces whichever method actually lives in that slot
It safely does nothing, because the interface name is checked at install
It hooks `Present` anyway, since vtables are sorted by method name
It fails to compile, because the index belongs to a different type
questions.explanation: Confirm each index against the SDK header for the version you are targeting before relying on it.

questions.prompt: What is the idea of creating a small hidden window, device, and swap chain inside your own process?
options: Its vtable gives a candidate `Present` address, without finding the main swap chain
It gives you a handle to the game's main swap chain, which you can then use directly
It lets the hidden window draw over the game, so that no hooking is needed
It copies the game's textures into your process so that they can be inspected there
questions.explanation: Objects of one implementation commonly share a vtable. Confirm the real swap chain uses the same method entry before relying on it.

questions.prompt: Why should you not copy an absolute function address from a helper process into a target process?
options: Each process has its own address space, and libraries may be loaded at different places
Absolute addresses are encrypted, so only the process that made them can read them
Addresses are only valid for 60 seconds, so a copied one would already be too old
Helper processes always use 32-bit addresses, so they cannot fit in a 64-bit target
questions.explanation: An address is meaningful only inside its own process. A module-relative offset can be translated only after confirming the same module build and the same code in both.

questions.prompt: Several runtimes can implement the same interface. Which approach reveals the implementation used by one particular object?
options: Reading the method's address from that object's own vtable
Looking up the interface's name in the library's export table
Reading the method's address from the interface's documentation
Copying the address from the same method on another machine
questions.explanation: Only the object itself knows which implementation it uses. Even then, the address still needs a compatibility check against the actual runtime.

questions.prompt: A table of function pointers sits on a read-only page. Which sequence replaces one entry and leaves the process tidy?
options: Make it writable, save the original, write the replacement, restore the protection
Write the replacement, make it writable, restore the protection, save the original
Save the original, write the replacement, make it writable, and leave it that way
Make it writable, write the replacement, leave it writable, save the original later
questions.explanation: The page must be writable before the write, the original must be saved before it is replaced, and the old protection should be put back afterward.

questions.prompt: A replacement for a COM method leaves out the implicit first parameter, the pointer to the object. What happens?
options: Every argument shifts by one position, so each parameter reads the wrong value
Nothing, since the object pointer is only used by the compiler and not by the call
The call fails at once with an error, since the signature is checked when it is made
Only the last argument is wrong, since the missing parameter is always read last
questions.explanation: The object pointer is passed like any other argument, so leaving it out shifts the rest. The call still runs, so it looks like a glitch rather than a signature mistake.

questions.prompt: Why should a hook on a function that returns a status code pass back the status it received from the original?
options: Callers check it, and the call can really fail, so swallowing it changes behavior
The status is only used for logging, so a different one makes no difference
Returning the status makes the original run faster, since it can be cached
Hooks that return a constant success code are the ones the caller prefers
questions.explanation: A real failure, such as a lost device, is something the game expects to handle. Hiding it changes the game's behavior.

questions.prompt: A tool installs its hook twice. What goes wrong on the next frame?
options: The second install saves your own replacement as the original, which then forwards to itself
The second install restores the runtime's function, so the first hook silently stops running
The two replacements run one after another, so each frame is drawn twice over
The slot is locked by the first hook, so the second install blocks forever
questions.explanation: Refuse a second install by checking whether the slot already holds your function.

questions.prompt: Another tool hooked the same slot after yours. What goes wrong if you restore your saved pointer blindly?
options: You remove their hook and leave them forwarding to a function that is gone
You restore only your own bytes, and their hook keeps working unchanged afterward
The restore fails with a protection error, so nothing changes in the table
Their hook is saved and runs after yours on every call from then on
questions.explanation: Restore only when the slot still holds your own function.

questions.prompt: Why should a hook copy the original pointer out and release its lock before calling the original?
options: The original may re-enter the hooked path, and holding the lock across it can deadlock
The lock would slow the original, so the game would drop below sixty frames a second
The original pointer is only valid while the lock is released
Locks cannot be held by functions that return an `HRESULT`
questions.explanation: A deadlock means two paths each wait for something the other holds, and neither continues.

questions.prompt: When a graphics device is reset or its buffers are resized, what should code holding cached device resources do?
options: Drop and rebuild them, since they were created against the old state
Keep using them, since resources survive any reset or resize
Copy them to a new location, since they only need to be moved
Resize them in place, since the device updates them automatically
questions.explanation: A resolution change or an alt-tab can invalidate everything allocated against the old device. Such calls are the signal to rebuild.

questions.prompt: A hooked function runs on the render thread many times per second. What is the advice for its replacement?
options: Copy a small fixed-size sample, return quickly, and analyze the data elsewhere
Analyze everything on the spot, so that no data has to be copied anywhere
Wait for a lock, so the data is always consistent before the call returns
Write each sample to a file straight away, so none of them can be lost
questions.explanation: Locks, allocations and file writes on this path are a frame-time cost paid again and again. Do the minimum there and move the rest to another thread.

questions.prompt: Hooking the call that presents a finished frame tells you what, and what does it not tell you?
options: That a frame was submitted, not what it holds or if the GPU finished
Which objects the frame holds, but not that a frame was submitted
Whether the GPU finished it, but not which frame was submitted
Everything about the frame, since presenting is the last step of drawing
questions.explanation: To learn the contents you need the draw calls and the state bound around them.

questions.prompt: In a 32-bit process, each vtable slot is 4 bytes wide. At which byte offset from the start of the table is slot 10?
options: 40 bytes
80 bytes
10 bytes
44 bytes
questions.explanation: The offset is index × slot width, so 10 × 4 = 40. Using the 64-bit width of 8 would give 80.

questions.prompt: A character in a scene is drawn with its body, weapon, and shadow. What does that show about draw calls?
options: One object can take several draws, and one draw can cover many objects
Each draw call always matches exactly one game object in the scene
Draw calls name the object by an ID that is passed as the first argument
A draw is only issued for the local player, while others use another path
questions.explanation: A draw call asks the GPU to consume indices using whatever is bound. It does not say "draw the player."

questions.prompt: In an indexed draw call with arguments for index count, start index and base vertex, what does the start index choose?
options: Where in the bound index buffer to begin reading
Which object in the game the draw belongs to
Which vertex in the vertex buffer is drawn first
How many triangles are drawn from the buffer
questions.explanation: The three numbers choose geometry within the bound buffers. They do not identify a game object by themselves.

questions.prompt: Two indexed draw calls in one frame have identical arguments. Why can they produce different images?
options: The bound textures, shaders and depth settings can differ between them
The second call always draws on top, so it replaces the first one
Identical arguments are randomized by the driver, so results differ
The calls run on different processors, so each makes a different image
questions.explanation: The arguments say which indices were submitted. The bound buffers, shaders, textures and depth state explain how they are used.

questions.prompt: A signed 32-bit field is logged as unsigned and shows 4,294,967,286. What is the likely true value?
options: -10, a valid negative value read as unsigned
10, the same number with its sign dropped
4,294,967,286, a very large positive shift
2,147,483,638, half of the unsigned value
questions.explanation: The bits never change, only how they are read. 2³² − 4,294,967,286 = 10, so the signed value is −10. Such a field is signed so several meshes can share one buffer.

questions.prompt: A triangle-list draw submits 1,200 indices. How many triangles were submitted?
questions.explanation: A triangle list uses three indices per triangle, so 1,200 ÷ 3 = 400. These are submitted triangles, not necessarily visible ones.

questions.prompt: Why is the index count of a draw not the same as the number of unique vertices drawn?
options: Indices can name the same vertex more than once, so shared vertices repeat
Each index names a vertex that is used only once, but some are skipped
Indices count the triangles, while vertices are counted separately
The driver removes duplicate vertices, so the counts differ after the draw
questions.explanation: Index count divided by three gives submitted triangles, but it is neither the visible triangle count nor the unique vertex count.

questions.prompt: A draw submits 300 triangles, but none appear on screen. Which explanation fits?
options: They may be culled, clipped, degenerate or covered by something nearer
They were never submitted, since the draw call itself is only a request
They are on screen, but the count must be above a limit before they show
They are hidden, since a draw call only shows triangles after the next frame
questions.explanation: Submitting a triangle does not guarantee that pixels change. It can still be back-face culled, clipped, collapsed to a line, or hidden behind nearer geometry.

questions.prompt: In an older graphics API the draw call passes the primitive type, such as list or strip, directly. In a newer API the draw call does not mention it. Where does the newer API keep it?
options: As state bound before the draw
Inside the vertex data itself
In the shader that is running
In the texture that is bound
questions.explanation: The newer API treats topology as bound state, set on the context before drawing. The draw call only says how much to draw.

questions.prompt: Inside a hook on a draw call in an API that binds state to a context, how do you learn which blend state is currently bound?
options: Ask the context for its current state object and read the description
Read it from the draw call's arguments, which always carry the state
Read it from the device, which keeps a single global copy of all state
Wait for the next frame, since state objects are only readable between frames
questions.explanation: In this style of API, immutable state objects are bound to a context. A hook queries the context and reads what it returns.

questions.prompt: A "Get" call on a COM object returns an interface pointer. What must the caller do with it?
options: Release it on every path, because getting it raised the reference count
Nothing, since the pointer is borrowed and the count is unchanged
Free it with the normal memory deallocator when the call has finished
Keep it for the whole session, since releasing it would destroy the object
questions.explanation: A hook that runs thousands of times per second leaks steadily if even one release is missed. A wrapper that releases when it goes out of scope covers early returns too.

questions.prompt: Querying several state objects on every draw call inside a hook is expensive. What is a sensible approach?
options: Sample, for example one draw in a hundred or only draws within a range
Query everything on every draw, since correctness matters more than speed
Query only on the first draw of the process, since state never changes
Query on a separate thread, since state objects cannot be read inside a hook
questions.explanation: The hook runs on a thread with a frame deadline, so recording everything costs real time. Sampling keeps the cost small.

questions.prompt: Which observable best suggests UI drawn without regard to the world, rather than world geometry?
options: A depth-stencil state with depth testing disabled
A large index count, since big meshes are always interface elements
A pixel shader that is shared with the world geometry nearby
A bound texture that contains a repeating tiled pattern in it
questions.explanation: Depth-stencil state often separates world geometry from UI. Each of these is a proxy, a clue that correlates but does not prove the category.

questions.prompt: A pixel shader is shared by characters and crates. What is the right way to treat it as a label?
options: As a proxy, tested by changing something you control and watching the group
As proof, since one shader always means exactly one kind of game object
As noise, since shaders can never correlate with any particular asset
As a fixed ID, which stays identical between frames and between sessions
questions.explanation: A label that matched in one frame can be an accident of what that frame happened to draw.

questions.prompt: Why tag each sampled draw with a frame number taken from the hook on the presentation call?
options: Draws repeat within a frame while presents mark its end, giving order meaning
The frame number tells how long the draw took to run on the graphics card
Without a frame number, the driver refuses to store the draw call
The frame number identifies which object in the game was drawn
questions.explanation: With a boundary, the position of a draw within its frame is meaningful. Without one, you cannot tell where one frame's order ends and the next begins.

questions.prompt: In the frame 412 example, draws 191 to 201 are UI with depth testing disabled. How many UI draws is that?
questions.explanation: 191 to 201 inclusive is `201 - 191 + 1 = 11`, matching the "last eleven draws" statement.

questions.prompt: Why bound both the samples per frame and the frames retained?
options: An unbounded recorder eats memory and skews the frame times
The GPU refuses to draw more than 256 samples in a single frame
Retained frames are deleted automatically by the swap chain over time
More than one frame in memory prevents `Present` from running at all
questions.explanation: This is the same discipline as the per-frame recorder in Lesson 4.11.

questions.prompt: Why does a single Direct3D 12 submission hook not show you individual draws?
options: Commands are recorded into lists and queued, so a hook sees a batch, not each draw
Direct3D 12 has no `Present` call, so no frame boundary exists to use
Direct3D 12 draws are only ever issued from a single thread in a game
Command lists are encrypted by the driver, so their contents cannot be read
questions.explanation: `Present` still works as a frame boundary, and the vtable reasoning transfers; the assumption that one hook sees one draw does not.

questions.prompt: Why must the positions and the camera used to project them come from the same captured update?
options: Otherwise a well-organized tool can still draw markers for a different moment than the camera shows
Otherwise the projection function would refuse to run, since it checks the frame number
Otherwise the positions would be drawn in a different colour from the camera's own markers
Otherwise the camera matrix would be stored in the wrong byte order for the game
questions.explanation: Rendering adds a timing constraint on top of the tool architecture: features must describe the same update.

questions.prompt: The radar reads the player list in one pass, and the overlay reads the camera matrix a few milliseconds later. What can go wrong?
options: Markers can land where enemies used to be, since the features describe different updates
The radar and overlay will both crash, because two features cannot read at different times
The matrix is replaced by the player list, so projection returns no points at all
Nothing, since every feature already shares the same captured values
questions.explanation: Bundling fields into one snapshot means both features use the same captured values.

questions.prompt: A snapshot struct bundles the players, matrix, and viewport. Does that make the reads atomic?
options: No: the game can update an entity mid-copy, so validate and check a tick counter
Yes: once the values are copied into one struct, the game can no longer change them
Yes: the struct locks the game's memory until the whole snapshot has been built
No: but only the matrix can change during the read, never a player record there
questions.explanation: Bundling makes every feature use the same captured values. It does not freeze the game while the copy is made.

questions.prompt: Positions captured this frame are projected through the previous frame's camera matrix. How does that look?
options: Slightly behind where things belong, worst when turning quickly
Perfectly aligned, since a one-frame difference is too small to see
Mirrored left to right, since the old matrix reverses the horizontal axis
Randomly scattered, since an old matrix gives a different result each time
questions.explanation: The result looks almost right, which is why people blame the projection math instead of the timing.

questions.prompt: Why should a snapshot own copied values rather than hold references into the target's memory?
options: The target may free an entity, leaving a stale reference, so copy and read the copy
References are slower to read than copies, so owned data is always the fastest
The compiler forbids references to memory that belongs to another process
Copied values update themselves, so they always match the target's latest state
questions.explanation: A reference to something the target later frees becomes a stale-pointer failure. Copy once, then let every feature read from the copy.

questions.prompt: Each feature must provide start and stop methods. Which kind of feature needs real work in them?
options: One that patches or hooks, since it must install and later restore its changes
One that only reads values and prints them, since printing needs a setup step
One that draws text on screen, since text is always created at start
Every feature, since an empty method is not allowed by the interface
questions.explanation: Only patching or hooking features have something to set up or undo. Read-only features can implement the methods trivially.

questions.prompt: An overlay has four choices, and exactly one is active at a time. What is the danger of storing them as four separate booleans?
options: They could all be set at once, a combination that has no meaning
Booleans cannot be changed after they are first set, so the choice would be stuck
Four booleans take four times the memory, which is too much for a menu
Booleans cannot be shown in a menu, since they have no text
questions.explanation: One enumeration value holds exactly one choice, so impossible combinations cannot be represented.

questions.prompt: A setting cycles Off, then Low, then High, then Max, then back to Off each time a command is applied. Starting at Off, where is it after seven commands?
options: Max
High
Low
Off
questions.explanation: Four commands return it to Off, so seven commands are the same as three: Low, High, Max.

questions.prompt: In a worker loop, a command handler returns true for exactly one command. Which command, and what does the loop do?
options: The stop command, so the loop leaves its frame cycle and runs cleanup
Any setting change, so the loop restarts with the new settings
The first command, so the loop begins processing frames
The toggle command, so the loop pauses until the next key press
questions.explanation: The boolean means "stop after this command". Only the stop command returns true, and every other command returns false after changing a setting.

questions.prompt: Why does the input thread send commands through a channel instead of reaching into a feature directly?
options: The update loop owns and changes the settings, avoiding shared mutable globals
Channels make key presses arrive faster than direct function calls ever could
The game does not allow tools to read the keyboard outside of a channel
A channel lets two threads write to the same setting at once, with no care
questions.explanation: A key press should request a change, not modify a feature while the update loop is using it.

questions.prompt: A feature's update fails because there is no valid projection matrix this frame. What should the owner do?
options: Record the error, disable that feature, and restore it while the others continue
Print a message and let the feature run again next frame, in case it recovers
Stop every feature, since one failure means the whole tool is unreliable
Ignore the error, since a missing matrix will be fixed by the next frame
questions.explanation: A message alone leaves the feature running again on the next frame. Containing the failure to one feature lets the rest keep working.

questions.prompt: Which failure stops every consumer instead of only one feature?
options: A closed process or an invalid entity list
A missing camera matrix for the current frame
A failed overlay projection for the current frame
An unavailable debug-value display for the current frame
questions.explanation: A missing camera may disable only screen projection. The local decision is valid only when the rest of the snapshot is sound.

questions.prompt: A failing feature cannot restore its hook. What is the right response?
options: Keep the failure visible and enter the shared shutdown path
Mark the feature as disabled and carry on as if it were clean
Retry forever on the same thread until the restore succeeds
Unload the tool at once, since nothing more can be done
questions.explanation: A disabled checkbox is not a successful cleanup if the hook was never restored. The failure must stay visible while the shared shutdown handles the rest.

questions.prompt: Which order does the shutdown diagram give?
options: Stop input, signal workers, wait for them, disable features, restore patches, close handles
Close handles, restore patches and hooks, signal workers, wait for them, then stop input
Disable features, close handles, stop input, wait for workers, then restore every hook
Restore hooks, stop input, close handles, disable features, then wait for the workers
questions.explanation: Do not unload code while another thread may still execute it; a render callback may still be running after the menu closes.

questions.prompt: A per-build profile has no known address for one capability on the current build. What should the tool do?
options: Keep that control unavailable, not borrow an address from another build
Use the address from the nearest known build, since it is probably close
Search memory at random for a matching value, until one looks right
Fill in zero, so the capability is called without any address
questions.explanation: An offset is a fact about one supported executable. A missing entry is not an invitation to borrow another build's value.

questions.prompt: Why would a tool include one dedicated key that stops its worker and restores every active patch?
options: One dependable exit that undoes all changes leaves the target as it was found
Several keys are not allowed to be bound, so a single one is required
The key hides the tool's activity, so the target cannot tell it ran
The key saves the tool's settings, so they are restored at the next start
questions.explanation: A single, always-available way out makes cleanup predictable. It restores active changes, so the target ends up in its original state.

questions.prompt: Why keep a log of target, build, feature, address, expected bytes, found bytes, action, and restoration result separate from the menu?
options: A failed cleanup stays inspectable even after its UI closes
The menu cannot display text longer than one line
The log lets the DLL stay loaded after the game exits
The game reads the log at startup to find the verified addresses
questions.explanation: These records are separate so a failure can be reviewed after the visible menu is gone.

questions.prompt: Why is calling the game's own print function the cheapest way to put a menu inside the game?
options: It already knows the font, scale, screen size, and the right moment in the frame
It runs outside the render path, so the game cannot slow it down or delay a frame
It can draw directly into the GPU without any strings having to be supplied
It lets the menu run in its own separate window while still showing in the game
questions.explanation: The hard graphics work is done and you only supply strings. The trade is that your code now runs inside the game's render path.

questions.prompt: Which of these inside the in-game menu hook delays the game's next frame?
options: A file read, a sleep, or a blocking channel receive
A call to the game's text function for one menu line
A comparison of the previous key state with the current one
Reusing a buffer that was already allocated
questions.explanation: The hook sits in the render path, so it must finish quickly. Lesson 4.11 measures the same cost in a per-frame recorder.

questions.prompt: A glyph atlas draws "Gold" one quad per letter. The advances of G, o, and l are 12, 9, and 4 pixels. How far to the right of the G's start does the d begin?
options: 25 pixels
13 pixels
21 pixels
16 pixels
questions.explanation: Each letter moves along by its own advance width: `12 + 9 + 4 = 25`. The d's own width is not added until the next letter.

questions.prompt: A 300 by 40 pixel box is anchored to the bottom-right corner of a 1920 by 1080 screen with a 16-pixel margin. Where is its top-left corner?
In a 600-pixel row, three boxes have flex weights 1, 2, and 1. How wide is the middle box?
options: 300 pixels
200 pixels
150 pixels
400 pixels
questions.explanation: The weights total 4, so each unit of weight is 150 pixels and the weight-2 box gets 300. Equal sharing would give 200 each.

questions.prompt: An interface designed for 1920 × 1080 is shown on a 1280 × 720 screen. How wide is a 300-pixel button drawn?
options: 200 pixels, because the scale is 0.6667
300 pixels, because the layout ignores screen size
450 pixels, because the scale is 1.5
100 pixels, because the scale is 0.3333
questions.explanation: The scale is the smaller of `1280 ÷ 1920` and `720 ÷ 1080`, both 0.6667, and `300 × 0.6667 = 200`.

questions.prompt: A button picture with 16-pixel corners is drawn as a 200 × 60 nine-slice. What size is the stretched centre?
questions.explanation: The centre loses a 16-pixel corner on each side, so `200 - 32 = 168` wide and `60 - 32 = 28` tall. The corners themselves stay 16 × 16.

questions.prompt: How does clipping make a scrolling list work?
options: Items move by the scroll amount, and only the part inside the box is drawn
Items outside the box are deleted from memory until they are scrolled back in again
The whole list is scaled down until every item fits inside the list's own box
Each item is redrawn in a separate window that follows the position of the scroll bar
questions.explanation: Clipping hides whatever falls outside a box, which is also how popups can be cut off at an edge.

questions.prompt: A 200-pixel-wide context menu is opened at x = 1800 on a 1920-pixel screen. Where is it placed if it must stay on the screen?
questions.explanation: If the menu would run off the screen, it is moved back until it fits: min(1800, 1920 − 200) = 1720.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an immediate-mode and a retained-mode interface?
options: Immediate mode redraws all elements from state each frame; retained keeps a tree
Immediate mode keeps a tree of elements; retained mode redraws all of them each frame
Immediate mode works only for text, while retained mode handles buttons and sliders
Immediate mode draws once at startup, while retained mode draws on each user click
questions.explanation: Lesson 6.8 contrasts the two ways such code is written.

questions.prompt: Why is a call that runs once per frame near the end of the game's own drawing a good place to draw extra menu lines?
options: Lines drawn there share a pass with the game's HUD, so they appear on top of the world
Lines drawn there are hidden from the player, so they cannot be seen by mistake
Lines drawn there are cached for the next frame, so they never need to be redrawn
Lines drawn there use the world's depth buffer, so they appear behind objects
questions.explanation: Drawing there means your lines inherit the HUD's ordering and do not end up underneath the world.

questions.prompt: Which question about a function that draws a string must be answered before the first call?
options: Whether it copies the string or only keeps the pointer for later
Whether the string is stored in uppercase or lowercase letters
Whether the string is longer than the width of the screen
Whether the function is called by the game's menu or its HUD
questions.explanation: A function that only keeps the pointer will read the string later, so the string must stay alive that long. The arguments, where they go, and what it returns also need to be known.

questions.prompt: A drawing function stores a string pointer and draws the string later in the frame. Why is passing a pointer to a temporary local buffer a bug?
options: The buffer is freed when the scope ends, so the game reads stale memory
Local buffers are too small, so only part of the string would be shown
Pointers to local data are always zero, so no text would be drawn
The game copies strings on its own, so the buffer is made twice
questions.explanation: Keep an owned buffer alive for at least the frame, so that the pointer stays valid until the game has finished with it.

questions.prompt: A text renderer treats a control byte followed by a digit as a color change that is not drawn. The word "Menu" is prefixed with that marker and one digit. How many bytes are there, and how many characters are visible?
options: 6 bytes, 4 visible characters
4 bytes, 4 visible characters
6 bytes, 6 visible characters
5 bytes, 4 visible characters
questions.explanation: The marker and its digit take two bytes that the renderer consumes without drawing, plus four letters. A menu that lines up columns by counting bytes will be crooked.

questions.prompt: Why should you confirm a colour marker byte by drawing a string that contains it?
options: The exact marker is a fact about one build, not a general rule
Colour markers are chosen at random each time the game starts
The renderer only accepts marker bytes that are typed on a keyboard
A wrong marker byte makes the text function crash right away
questions.explanation: The mechanism, a marker byte followed by a palette index, is common, but its value should not be trusted from a lesson.

questions.prompt: A menu cursor is an unsigned index sitting at row 0. Moving up computes cursor minus 1. What happens?
options: It underflows: a panic in debug builds, a huge wrapped number in release
It stays at row 0, since an unsigned number cannot go below zero
It becomes -1, which the menu then treats as the last row
It wraps to the last row, since the list length decides the result
questions.explanation: Unsigned subtraction below zero is an error or a wrap, never a clean -1. Handle the boundary explicitly, for example by jumping to the last row when the cursor is zero.

questions.prompt: A key-state check says a key is down on every frame of one press. How does a menu turn that into one move per press?
options: Act on the edge: down now and not down on the previous frame
Act on the level: move on every frame in which the key is down
Act on the release: move only when the key goes back up
Act on a timer: move once every few frames while it is down
questions.explanation: Acting on the level would scroll the whole list in a fraction of a second. Acting on the edge gives one move per press.

questions.prompt: Why clear and reuse one string buffer each frame instead of allocating a new one?
options: It runs thousands of times a second, so allocation cost adds up
A new buffer would always be larger than needed, so memory would run out
The old buffer must be cleared, or the game will draw stale text
Allocating is forbidden in code that runs inside another process
questions.explanation: Reusing a buffer avoids paying the allocation cost on every frame, which matters on a path with a frame deadline.

questions.prompt: Why should the menu only produce settings and commands, and not write into game memory while the render thread draws?
options: That would put a second writer on the same data
The menu is not allowed to hold any strings
Game memory is read-only while a frame is drawn
Commands are faster than direct writes by about a hundred times
questions.explanation: The worker reads the menu's settings and does any writing, keeping the split from Lesson 6.8.

questions.prompt: A render hook is **draining** while unloading. What does that mean?
options: No new calls should enter, but the call in flight must finish before its code goes
Its memory has been emptied, so the hook returns before any work gets done at all
The hook is waiting on a lock that another thread holds forever and never releases
The displaced bytes are already restored, so the hook can no longer be called by anyone
questions.explanation: Stop the worker, wait for it to leave the hooked path, restore the displaced bytes, then release the DLL.

questions.prompt: An object is on screen in the game's logic, but no draw call is submitted for it. Which stage should you inspect first?
options: Culling or entity selection, because the work stops before a call exists
The depth test, because fragments from the object may be failing against a wall
The fragment shader, because it may be producing a colour that matches the background
The blend state, because the object's alpha may be set to zero by the material
questions.explanation: Find the earliest stage where output goes wrong. Depth, blending, and shading only apply once a call exists.

questions.prompt: What is a fragment in the rendering pipeline?
options: A pixel-sized candidate produced by rasterizing a primitive, which tests may still reject
A broken triangle that clipping has cut into pieces too small to draw anywhere
The final pixel value stored in the framebuffer once all of the tests have passed
One vertex of a mesh after the vertex shader has moved it into clip space
questions.explanation: Several triangles may produce fragments for the same pixel, and depth, stencil, or blend rules decide what is stored. A fragment is not yet a final pixel.

questions.prompt: An indexed draw of triangles submits 18 indices. What does that tell you?
options: Six triangles were submitted, though some may be clipped, culled or hidden
Eighteen triangles were submitted, and every one of them is visible
Eighteen different vertices were used, since each index names a new one
Six triangles are visible, since the draw only counts what appears on screen
questions.explanation: Three indices make one triangle, so 18 ÷ 3 = 6 were submitted. Indices may repeat vertices, and some triangles may never reach the screen.

questions.prompt: What does a material add to a mesh?
options: How the surface looks: base colour, wrapped image, and how it answers light
Where the surface is, by listing vertices and the indices that connect them
Which camera may draw the surface, through a mask of render layers
How far away the surface is, as a value that the depth test compares later
questions.explanation: A mesh says where the surface is; a material says how it looks. Layers and depth belong to other parts of the pipeline.

questions.prompt: A vertex has texture coordinate (u, v) = (0.5, 0.25) on a 512 by 512 texture with its origin at the top left. Which pixel does it point at?
questions.explanation: Multiply each coordinate by the texture size: 0.5 × 512 = 256 and 0.25 × 512 = 128. Which corner counts as the origin depends on the graphics API.

questions.prompt: A surface with normal (0, 0, 1) and color (100, 200, 50) is lit from direction (0.8, 0, 0.6). With simple diffuse lighting, where the color is scaled by the dot product of normal and light direction, what color results?
questions.explanation: The dot product is 0 + 0 + 0.6 = 0.6, and 0.6 times each channel gives (60, 120, 30). A dot product of zero or less would mean no light.

questions.prompt: Transparent objects often keep the depth test on but turn depth writes off. Why is that different from turning the test off entirely?
options: The test still hides them behind solid objects, but they do not block later transparent layers
The test is only used when writes are enabled, so turning writes off already disables both
Turning writes off makes them draw first, while turning the test off makes them draw last
The test and the write are one operation, so there is no real difference between the choices
questions.explanation: The test compares a fragment with the stored depth; the write replaces the stored depth. Disabling them separately gives different results.

questions.prompt: What can happen if the depth comparison is changed to always pass?
options: Later fragments can appear on top of nearer ones, even when their geometry is behind a wall
Fragments are drawn in a random order, but the nearer surface still wins at each pixel
The depth buffer is cleared, so every pixel is redrawn from the farthest layer again
Back faces are culled automatically, because depth no longer separates front from back
questions.explanation: The test no longer rejects farther fragments. Depth is a per-fragment comparison, not a flag stored with the entity.

questions.prompt: What can cause two nearby surfaces to alternate visibility, called z-fighting?
options: A near plane extremely small compared with the far plane wastes depth precision
A fragment shader that discards pixels, which hides one surface and then the other
A texture whose `v` axis points the wrong way, which swaps the surfaces' colours
A frame rate below 30, since slow frames make surfaces swap places in the buffer
questions.explanation: Nonlinear perspective depth concentrates precision near the camera. A tiny near plane relative to the far plane leaves too little for distant surfaces.

questions.prompt: A green fragment (0, 255, 0) with alpha 0.4 is drawn over a background (100, 0, 0) using source × alpha + destination × (1 − alpha). What is the result?
questions.explanation: Red is 100 × 0.6 = 60 and green is 255 × 0.4 = 102. Adding the colors without weights would be additive blending, which is a different rule.

questions.prompt: In what order do engines draw solid and see-through objects?
options: Solid objects first with depth writes on, then see-through ones far to near
See-through objects first from nearest to farthest, then the solid objects on top
All objects in the order they were created, since blending is independent of order
Solid and see-through objects together, sorted by texture to reduce state changes
questions.explanation: Blending mixes with whatever is already stored, so swapping two layers changes the result. That is why order matters.

questions.prompt: A camera at the origin looks along +x with a 90 degree view, so the visible wedge is |y| ≤ x. A sphere of radius 2 is centered at (10, 14). What happens?
options: It is culled, since its center is about 2.83 beyond the edge, more than its radius
It is culled, since its center is exactly 4 beyond the upper edge
It is drawn, since its center is about 2 beyond the edge and the radius is 2
It is drawn, since any object in front of the camera is always inside the wedge
questions.explanation: The distance beyond the edge line y = x is (14 − 10) ÷ √2 ≈ 2.83, which exceeds the radius of 2, so no part of the sphere reaches the visible wedge.

questions.prompt: The direction from a triangle toward the camera has a negative dot product with the triangle's normal. With back-face culling on, what happens?
options: The triangle is skipped, since its back is turned toward the camera
The triangle is drawn, since a negative result means it faces the camera
The triangle is drawn, but only when its normal has length zero
The triangle is skipped, but only when the camera is closer than one unit
questions.explanation: A negative dot product means the normal points away from the camera, so the camera sees the triangle's back. Back-face culling skips such triangles.

questions.prompt: A camera's layer mask is 6 (binary 110) and an object's mask is 3 (binary 011). Does the camera draw the object?
options: Yes, since 6 AND 3 is 2, so the masks share a layer
No, since 6 AND 3 is not 6, so the masks are different
No, since 6 AND 3 is not 0, so the masks collide
Yes, since 6 plus 3 is 9, which is larger than either mask
questions.explanation: A bitwise AND keeps only the bits both masks have. A nonzero result means at least one shared layer, so the camera draws the object.

questions.prompt: A tank is set to hidden, and its turret and barrel are set to inherit. What happens to the turret and barrel?
options: They are hidden, because an inherited setting follows the parent
They stay visible, because each object's own setting overrides its parent
They are hidden only if they share a render layer with the tank
They are drawn, but only by cameras that look at them from the front
questions.explanation: Settings are combined from the root down, so an inherited object under a hidden parent is hidden.

questions.prompt: An object lies beyond a camera's far limit. What happens?
options: It is outside the view volume, so that camera never draws it
It is drawn at lower quality, since far objects use simpler models
It is drawn, but it is hidden by fog until the camera gets close enough
It is drawn only when no other object is blocking it in the view
questions.explanation: Beyond the far limit an object is outside the view volume, so it never reaches a draw call. Moving closer brings it back.

questions.prompt: A surface point is 7.50 from the light, and its stored shadow-map depth is also 7.50. With a bias of 0.05, is it in shadow?
options: No, because shadow needs a stored depth below 7.50 − 0.05 = 7.45, which is not the case
Yes, because the stored depth equals the point's depth, so something is at the same place
Yes, because the bias is added to the stored depth, giving 7.55, which is greater than 7.50
No, because shadow maps only compare the first digit of each depth value
questions.explanation: Without a bias, rounding could make a surface shadow itself. The bias requires the stored depth to be clearly nearer.

questions.prompt: Fog begins at distance 20 and is complete at 60. A surface at distance 50 keeps a share (60 − 50) ÷ (60 − 20) of its own color, and the rest is haze. For a surface (200, 100, 40) and haze (100, 120, 160), what color results?
With the simple tone-mapping rule c ÷ (1 + c), what does the HDR value 3.0 become?
questions.explanation: 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75. The rule squeezes bright values into the displayable range, and always gives a number below 1.

questions.prompt: A sunlit wall comes out at 1.4 and a lamp at 12.0. Why do they look equally bright in an 8-bit picture?
options: Each channel tops out at 1.0, so both are cut off at the same value
Both values are rounded down to the nearest multiple of 256 in the framebuffer
Tone mapping is skipped in 8-bit pictures, so brightness is stored as a difference
The lamp's higher value is stored in the alpha channel, where the display ignores it
questions.explanation: An 8-bit channel can't exceed 1.0. HDR uses wider floating-point pixels so the difference survives until tone mapping.

questions.prompt: A 1920 × 1080 picture has 4 channels. How much memory does it take at 2 bytes per channel instead of 1?
options: About 16.6 MB, which is twice the 8.3 MB of the 1-byte version
About 33.2 MB, which is four times the 8.3 MB of the 1-byte version
About 8.3 MB, because wider channels reuse the memory of the narrower ones
About 4.1 MB, because the extra bytes replace the alpha channel's space
questions.explanation: 2,073,600 pixels × 4 channels × 2 bytes = 16,588,800 bytes. Doubling the bytes per channel doubles the total.

questions.prompt: With 4 samples per pixel, a green triangle (0, 200, 0) covers 1 of the 4 samples of an edge pixel over a white background (255, 255, 255). About what color does the pixel get?
What is the price of FXAA's low cost?
options: It blurs text and fine texture detail too, since it cannot tell edges from sharp lines
It uses four times the colour memory, because it stores extra samples for every pixel
It only smooths triangle edges, so shader-drawn patterns inside triangles still look jagged
It needs motion vectors, so it leaves ghost trails behind objects that are moving
questions.explanation: FXAA works on the finished picture. The other options describe MSAA's memory cost and TAA's motion vectors.

questions.prompt: What causes the ghost trail that temporal anti-aliasing can leave behind a moving object?
options: Wrong motion vectors, such as behind a transparent surface, so old colours linger
Too few sample points per pixel, so edge pixels flicker between two colours
A blur applied to the whole picture, which smears every sharp line it finds
A shadow bias that is too large, so the stored depth sits behind the surface
questions.explanation: TAA blends each pixel with the colour from earlier frames, and needs motion vectors to find where it was. Wrong vectors leave old colours.

questions.prompt: Simulating a frame takes 6 ms and drawing it takes 8 ms. With the stages overlapped, what is the time per frame and the frames per second?
options: 8 ms, which is 125 frames per second, set by the slower stage
14 ms, which is about 71 frames per second, from adding the two stages
6 ms, which is about 167 frames per second, set by the faster stage
7 ms, which is about 143 frames per second, the average of the stages
questions.explanation: Overlapped, the slower stage sets the pace: 1000 ÷ 8 = 125. One after the other would take 6 + 8 = 14 ms.

questions.prompt: A game keeps a main world and a render world. What happens if you edit a position in the render copy?
options: The picture changes only until the next extract overwrites it from the main copy
The change lasts forever, because the render world is the one the rules read
The game's rules change with it, because both copies share the same memory
The edit is rejected, because the render world is read-only once drawing starts
questions.explanation: The extract step copies from the main world each frame. Editing the main copy changes the rules and the picture together.

questions.prompt: A 512 by 512 sheet holds 8 by 8 frames of 64 by 64 pixels. Frame 10, counting from 0 in rows left to right, covers which u range?
questions.explanation: The column is 10 mod 8 = 2, so u runs from 2 × 64 ÷ 512 = 0.25 to 3 × 64 ÷ 512 = 0.375. The row is 1, which sets v rather than u.

questions.prompt: Why is restoring the exact value that was present better than setting a state back to the usual default?
options: Another legitimate render pass may enter with different state, so a guessed default can break it
Defaults are slower to set than saved values, so saved values keep each frame within budget
Defaults can only be set from the game thread, but saved values work on any worker thread
A saved value is always the default, so the two approaches really give the same result
questions.explanation: Treat a temporary change as a transaction: capture the old value, apply the experiment, draw, and restore, on the same thread and context.

questions.prompt: A flag in memory is expected to hold 0 or 1, but a reader finds 7. Why treat that as an error rather than as true?
options: An unexpected value suggests a wrong address or layout, so it is rejected
Any nonzero value is invalid, since a flag must always hold exactly zero
Values above 1 are rounded down, so seven would be read as one anyway
A flag with the value 7 means seven different options, so it needs a list
questions.explanation: A flag is expected to hold only 0 or 1. Any other value is a sign that the address or the layout may be wrong, so it is safer not to guess.

questions.prompt: A transparent observer wraps a drawing call, records one of its arguments, and forwards the call. What should the player see?
options: An identical picture, with only the separate observation log changing
A slightly darker picture, since the observer takes some of the work
A picture with the recorded objects highlighted, so the data can be checked
No picture at all, until the observer has finished recording
questions.explanation: A transparent observer preserves the contract of the call. If the picture changed, the measurement could no longer be trusted.

questions.prompt: How does hooking one instruction inside a function differ from wrapping the whole call?
options: It has no clean before and after the call, so changed state cannot be restored
