It is always faster, since fewer instructions run than with a wrapper
It sees every argument as a typed value, which a whole-call wrapper cannot do
It needs no saved original, since the instruction is replaced in place
questions.explanation: A wrapper surrounds one typed call and can tidy up right after it. A cave in the middle of a function has no such moment, so cleanup waits for a later point.

questions.prompt: An index buffer holds the twelve indices 0 1 2 2 1 3 3 1 4 4 5 6, drawn as triangles. How many triangles and how many different vertices?
options: 4 triangles and 7 different vertices
4 triangles and 12 different vertices
12 triangles and 7 different vertices
6 triangles and 7 different vertices
questions.explanation: Twelve indices make 12 ÷ 3 = 4 triangles, and they refer to vertices 0 to 6, which is seven. The index count is not the number of vertices.

questions.prompt: When an element buffer is bound, how should the indices argument of an indexed draw call be read?
options: As an offset into the bound buffer, not a process pointer
As a pointer to an array of indices in the process's own memory
As the number of indices that the call will draw
As the identifier of the buffer that the call will use
questions.explanation: With a buffer bound, the value points into state managed by the graphics driver. Treating it as an ordinary address would fault or give nonsense.

questions.prompt: A hook runs when the game calls a draw function. What does it observe?
options: Submitted work: it runs when the CPU queues the draw, not when the GPU finishes its pixels
Finished pixels: the call returns only after the GPU has completed the frame it drew
Only the final framebuffer, because commands are not visible until they have been executed
The GPU's timing, because the hook runs on the graphics card's own processor
questions.explanation: The CPU usually records commands faster than the GPU runs them, so a returned call does not mean the pixels are done.

questions.prompt: In the two-rate design, what belongs on the capture path inside the hook?
options: Copying a tiny fixed-size sample and returning immediately
Grouping samples by model name and counting them for a summary
Saving the sample to a file so that nothing is lost if the game crashes
Labelling each sample with the entity it probably belongs to
questions.explanation: Aggregating, labelling, and saving all happen later on a worker. The hook only has time to copy and return.

questions.prompt: A hook on a rendering thread uses a bounded queue, and the queue is full. Why prefer dropping the sample and counting the drop over waiting?
options: Waiting would slow the frames being measured, while a counter keeps the gap visible
Dropped samples are never missed, since later samples contain the same data
Waiting is not allowed on a rendering thread, since the operating system forbids it
Counting drops makes the queue larger, which prevents it from becoming full again
questions.explanation: Losing a sample leaves a gap, but blocking would distort what is being measured. Counting drops makes the gap visible instead of hidden.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't the hook write each draw to a file synchronously?
options: Draws occur thousands of times a frame, so file output wrecks performance and risks re-entry
Files can only be opened from the game's main thread, so the render thread would be refused access
The operating system limits a process to a few hundred writes per frame, after which they fail
File output changes the draw arguments, so the logged `count` would no longer match the real one
questions.explanation: The render thread has a deadline. Use a bounded channel and let a worker do slow work.

questions.prompt: Where should the function type for a hooked graphics call come from?
options: The documented API, with its types and calling convention, not register guesses
Whatever the disassembler shows first, since registers reveal the true signature
A test run of the target, since the types are decided only while it runs
The names of the exported function, since a name encodes its argument types
questions.explanation: The calling convention matters, and the signature is part of the documented API. Guessing from register contents risks an immediate crash.

questions.prompt: Why must the real function pointer be resolved and stored before the wrapper is installed?
options: If it pointed at the wrapper, calls would recurse forever and no call would reach OpenGL
OpenGL refuses to draw until the pointer has been stored in a `OnceLock` on the main thread
The wrapper needs a pointer to find the game's textures, which are looked up through it
A pointer resolved late could be removed by the driver, so it must be cached early
questions.explanation: The cycle game → wrapper → stored 'original' → wrapper never returns.

questions.prompt: A wrapper is meant to forward to the original function, but its saved pointer accidentally points back to the wrapper itself. What happens?
options: It calls itself again and again until the stack overflows
It forwards to the original, since the saved pointer is only used for logging
It stops after one call, since the second call is blocked by the operating system
It runs forever without any error, since each call returns before the next one starts
questions.explanation: Each nested call keeps a stack frame, and with no base case the stack eventually runs out.

questions.prompt: What is a good first milestone when building a wrapper around a drawing call?
options: A transparent wrapper that forwards every call and leaves rendering unchanged
A wrapper that records every argument before forwarding any of the calls
A wrapper that changes the output, to prove that it is really being called
A wrapper that skips the original, so the new code has full control
questions.explanation: Prove first that the wrapper is invisible, and only then add the code that copies samples.

questions.prompt: Why is a single number, such as the index count of a draw, a fragile way to recognize a particular model?
options: Different objects can share a count, and updates to a model can change it
A count is hidden by the graphics driver, so it differs from the real value
A count only changes when the player moves, so it never describes the model itself
A count is the same for every model, so it carries no information at all
questions.explanation: A rule built on one number describes what you happened to see, not the concept. Collect more features and change one thing at a time.

questions.prompt: What is a limit of using the return address of a draw call, its call site, as a feature for identifying objects?
options: Inlining or updates can move it, so it is not stable across builds
It changes with every frame, so no two draws ever share one
It can only be read by the graphics driver, which does not share it
It is the same for all draws, so it cannot tell two paths apart
questions.explanation: A call site can separate different submission paths in an engine, but it is not stable across builds. A feature should only be trusted after experiments.

questions.prompt: When can an observed feature, such as which texture is bound, be trusted to identify a category of objects?
options: After controlled one-at-a-time experiments show it still tracks the same objects
As soon as it is seen on one object, since a feature is always unique
When it has the largest value of any feature measured, since larger is more reliable
When it matches in a single test with every setting changed at once
questions.explanation: Skins, quality settings and texture atlases can change a value. Only controlled changes show whether it holds.

questions.prompt: Which description matches the two central shader stages?
options: A vertex shader produces clip-space position per vertex; a fragment shader produces a colour for covered samples
A vertex shader produces the colour of each pixel; a fragment shader moves each vertex into clip space
A vertex shader runs once per frame; a fragment shader runs once for each object in the scene
A vertex shader reads textures only; a fragment shader reads matrices only for the whole mesh
questions.explanation: Vertex shaders transform vertices, and fragment shaders run for candidate covered samples. Values like texture coordinates are interpolated between them.

questions.prompt: What is a uniform?
options: A value that is the same for every shader invocation in one draw, such as a matrix or the time
A value that differs for each vertex and is blended across the triangle for the fragment shader
A texture sampled at a `(u, v)` position, which every invocation reads from a different place
A list of vertex indices bound to the draw, which says how to connect the vertices
questions.explanation: Interpolated inputs vary across a triangle; uniforms stay constant for the whole draw.

questions.prompt: A greyscale shader computes the dot product of a pixel's color with the weights (0.299, 0.587, 0.114). For the pixel (100, 200, 50), which value results?
options: About 153
About 117
About 200
About 350
questions.explanation: 0.299 × 100 = 29.9, 0.587 × 200 = 117.4 and 0.114 × 50 = 5.7, which total 153. The weights reflect how bright the eye finds each channel, so a plain average (about 117) would be different.

questions.prompt: A shader has three on/off switches such as 'has a normal map' and 'has fog'. How many variants can be compiled?
options: 8, because 2 × 2 × 2 covers every combination
6, because each of three switches adds two programs
3, because there is one program for each switch
9, because each switch has three states: on, off, and default
questions.explanation: Each combination compiles to a separate program, which is why a game can hitch the first time something new appears.

questions.prompt: A game draws 1,000 trees with one instanced call. Each instance has a 4 × 4 matrix of four-byte floats. How many bytes of transforms are needed?
options: 64,000, since each matrix is 16 floats of 4 bytes, or 64 bytes
16,000, since each matrix is stored as 16 bytes per instance
4,000, since one four-byte float is stored for each instance
1,000, since a single byte is enough to place each instance
questions.explanation: 16 × 4 = 64 bytes per instance, and 1,000 × 64 = 64,000. Instancing is the deliberate version of one draw holding many objects.

questions.prompt: What is a compute shader's job?
options: A general GPU program run once for each item in a grid of work, not part of drawing
A fragment shader that runs over a full-screen rectangle to apply bloom or grading
A vertex shader that moves each corner of a model into clip space before rasterization
A shader that compiles other shaders into variants, so the driver can pick the right one
questions.explanation: Engines use compute shaders for particles, culling, mesh deformation, and post-processing.

questions.prompt: Suppose one draw costs 5 microseconds of CPU time. What do 10,000 draws cost, compared with a 16.67 ms frame budget?
options: 50 ms, about three frame budgets, with the GPU waiting
5 ms, well inside the frame budget, so many small draws are cheap
500 ms, because each draw also adds the time taken by the GPU
16.67 ms, because the driver caps the CPU cost at one frame
questions.explanation: 10,000 × 5 µs = 50,000 µs = 50 ms. Instancing, merged meshes, atlases, and culling all cut the number of draws.

questions.prompt: 1,000 cubes take 4 ms and 4,000 take 16 ms. Roughly how many cubes fit in a 16.67 ms budget?
options: About 4,167, since each cube costs 0.004 ms
About 1,667, since each cube costs 0.01 ms
About 16,670, since each cube costs 0.001 ms
About 4,000, since the budget matches the larger test

questions.prompt: You halve the window's pixel count and the frame time does not change. Which processor is the limit?
options: The CPU, because the pixel work that shrank was not the bottleneck
The GPU, because fewer pixels should always speed up its fill rate
The monitor, because it refreshes at a fixed rate whatever the window size
The driver's shader compiler, because variants are rebuilt at each resize
questions.explanation: Fewer pixels reduce GPU shading work. No change means the time is spent elsewhere, such as in submitting draws.

questions.prompt: A rule marks every object with more than 300 vertices as a "vehicle". It marks a large rock but misses a small car. Which labels fit?
options: The rock is a false positive and the car is a false negative
The rock is a false negative and the car is a false positive
Both the rock and the car are false positives
Both the rock and the car are false negatives
questions.explanation: A false positive is something the rule caught that does not belong. A false negative is something that does belong but was missed.

questions.prompt: Why does the middle-of-function cave restore normal depth state on the next non-highlighted draw and when the feature is disabled?
options: It cannot surround one typed call, so it has no point right after the highlighted draw
OpenGL resets depth state by itself at each draw, so the cave is only repeating that
The next draw is always the same model, so the state is restored for the same object
Restoring on the next draw is quicker than restoring after each call, with the same effect
questions.explanation: A cave inside the function can't wrap one call, so it fixes up state at later moments. A whole-call wrapper could restore right afterwards.

questions.prompt: Why does pressing End disable the graphics mode before removing the code patch?
options: So the game is not left with `GL_ALWAYS` active after the cave stops running
So the patch can be removed faster, because the graphics mode holds the original bytes
So the cave runs one more time, which lets it save the registers before it is removed
So the DLL can unload before the game, because modes are freed in reverse order
questions.explanation: Once the cave is gone nothing can restore the depth function, so the mode must be switched off first.

questions.prompt: Why does the cave save the flags and all general-purpose registers before calling the helper?
options: The original function expects them to hold particular values when it resumes, and the helper may change them
The helper needs every register for its own work, so none can be left free for the original function
The game checks the registers at the end of the frame and exits if any have changed since then
The saved registers are logged with each sample, so the worker can see the state of the CPU
questions.explanation: Saving and restoring makes the helper almost invisible to the interrupted function.

questions.prompt: A five-byte jump replaces a six-byte instruction. Why fill the extra byte with a no-op?
options: So no fragment of the old instruction remains behind the jump
So the jump executes faster, since the processor skips no-ops
So the sixth byte stores the address of the saved original code
So the instruction after the patch moves up by one byte
questions.explanation: The inserted code returns after all six bytes, so the no-op never runs. It only keeps a leftover piece of the old instruction from being misread as code.

questions.prompt: What is a temporary solid colour (chams) used for in this course?
options: As a visual debugger that shows which draw calls a classification rule actually catches
As a way to hide models from the screen, so that the scene can be read more clearly
As a permanent skin that replaces the game's textures for every model in the level
As a measurement of how many triangles each model submits during one frame of play
questions.explanation: The question it answers is whether the filter caught player models or unrelated geometry.

questions.prompt: Why is 'set the colour to red' not the whole story for the final framebuffer value?
options: Vertex colour, sampled texture, lighting, blending, and display conversion can all contribute
The framebuffer ignores the colour that was set, and keeps the value that the game wrote first
Red is not a colour the GPU can store, so it is converted to the nearest supported one
The colour is applied only after the frame is shown, so the player sees the previous colour
questions.explanation: Multiplication is one common model, and a shader can compute anything. Disabling selected arrays and textures reduces the active contributors.

questions.prompt: A debug colour has alpha 0.5, but the object still looks solid. Why might that be?
options: Blending must be enabled with a specific source and destination rule, so alpha alone does nothing
Alpha only applies to textures, and a colour that is set directly never carries an alpha value
The framebuffer treats every alpha value below 1 as 1 when the display is in sRGB mode
Alpha is read only for objects drawn first, and later objects ignore it for depth reasons
questions.explanation: Alpha does not automatically mean transparency, and draw order still matters once blending is on.

questions.prompt: A classifier rule matches none of its known categories for a sample. Why return an explicit "unknown" rather than the nearest category?
options: A confident-looking wrong label is harder to diagnose than an honest unknown
Unknown results are faster, since the classifier stops checking after the first rule
Every sample must belong to a category, so unknown can only be a temporary state
The nearest category is always right, so reporting it never leads to mistakes
questions.explanation: Making uncertainty visible is the point. A count of unknowns shows how many samples the rules could not place.

questions.prompt: Why should the classifier not call OpenGL or change memory?
options: A pure function is easy to test with recorded samples
OpenGL calls are not permitted outside the render thread's main loop at any time
Memory writes made by a classifier are blocked by the operating system's protection
A pure function runs faster than an impure one because it never needs a stack frame
questions.explanation: Keeping classification separate from styling lets a new rule be scored against the same samples.

questions.prompt: A non-player model gets coloured by the classifier. What is this outcome called?
options: A false positive
A false negative
A true positive
A true negative
questions.explanation: It was labelled as a player, but is not one. A false negative would be a player left unchanged.

questions.prompt: On a labelled capture, 6 player draws are coloured, 2 non-player draws are coloured, and 3 player draws are left unchanged. What is precision?
questions.explanation: Precision asks how often 'player' is right when the rule says it. The 3 missed players affect recall, not precision.

questions.prompt: Using the same capture (6 player draws coloured, 2 non-player draws coloured, 3 player draws left unchanged), what is recall?
options: About 0.67, from 6 ÷ (6 + 3)
About 0.33, from 3 ÷ (6 + 3)
questions.explanation: Recall asks how many of all player draws the rule found: 6 of 9. The 2 wrongly coloured models affect precision.

questions.prompt: In a labelled test set, a rule marked nothing as positive, so true positives plus false positives is zero. How should precision be reported?
options: As undefined, rather than inventing a score
As 100 percent, since no mistakes were made
As 0 percent, since nothing was found
As 50 percent, as the middle of the scale
questions.explanation: Precision divides by that total, so a total of zero means the metric cannot be computed. Reporting it as undefined avoids a misleading number.

questions.prompt: What usually happens when you change a count threshold?
options: It trades false positives against false negatives
It removes false positives while leaving false negatives unchanged
It changes only the display colour, with no effect on which draws are caught
It fixes both kinds of error at once, as long as the threshold is a round number
questions.explanation: Raising or lowering a threshold shifts which draws are caught. Add independent features only when experiments show they help.

questions.prompt: Why keep recorded samples separate from the classifier implementation?
options: A new rule can be scored on the same samples, so a change in precision or recall comes from the rule
The samples take less memory when stored apart, which keeps the hook inside its time budget
The classifier can then change the samples as it runs, so they match the rule's output
OpenGL reloads the samples at each frame, so they must live outside the classifier's module
questions.explanation: If each rule used a fresh capture, differences could come from the capture, not the rule.

questions.prompt: A color channel is 0.4 of full brightness. What 0 to 255 value would a paint program show?
questions.explanation: Each channel is a fraction of full brightness, so multiply by 255: 0.4 × 255 = 102.

questions.prompt: Why is capturing only the visible colour not enough before applying a debug colour?
options: The draw may take colour from a bound client array, so those flags need restoring too
The visible colour is stored on the GPU, and no OpenGL function can read it back
The colour is reset by the driver after each draw, so any capture of it would be out of date
Arrays are only used for depth values, so they have no effect on the colour of a draw
questions.explanation: State covers server-side values such as enable flags and client array state such as colour or texture-coordinate arrays.

questions.prompt: What does the exact-build fallback assume when it restores state on the next ordinary draw?
options: Texture and colour arrays are on, colour is white, and depth is `0..1` with `GL_LEQUAL`
The previous state was saved by a guard, so the next draw can read it back and restore it
The draw is always a whole-call wrapper, so the old state can be restored right afterwards
Every render pass uses the same state, so the values never differ from one pass to another
questions.explanation: The fallback assumes engine defaults, which a renderer may legally change. A reusable tool should query or track the prior state in a typed guard.

questions.prompt: An object shows the expected color in a mirror pass and a shadow pass but not in the main view. What should be recorded with each sample to investigate?
options: Which render target, shader and pass position the sample came from
Only the object's name, since the same object always has the same color
Only the frame number, since passes are decided by timing alone
Only the screen position, since passes differ in where things are drawn
questions.explanation: The same object can be drawn in several passes. A rule that matches in one pass does not automatically match the object everywhere.

questions.prompt: Why classify draws by several independent properties instead of by one number such as a vertex count?
options: One number is a rough filter, and independent properties that agree cut false matches
Several properties make the rule run faster, since each one is cheaper to compare
One number cannot be stored for a draw, so more than one has to be recorded
Any single property is exact, so extra ones only add noise to the result
questions.explanation: Different objects can share any single value. Requiring several independent properties to agree reduces mistaken matches.

questions.prompt: A scope guard that restores graphics state is dropped on a different thread from the one that changed it. What is the problem?
options: It is not equivalent cleanup, because restoring needs the render thread and its context
Nothing is wrong, because a guard restores CPU state and graphics state in the same way
The guard restores the state twice, because both threads run the same drop code
The guard fails to compile, because Rust forbids moving a guard across a thread boundary
questions.explanation: OpenGL state belongs to a current context. Scope guards help with CPU state, but graphics restoration must run where the context is.

questions.prompt: A ray is written as point(t) = origin + t × direction. When is t a distance in world units?
options: When the direction has length one
When the origin is at the center of the world
When t is a whole number of units
When the direction points along an axis
questions.explanation: With a normalized direction, t counts world units. Otherwise it is only a scale parameter, so hit distances must be compared consistently.

questions.prompt: What extra step does a crosshair away from the screen centre need?
options: Unprojection: send near and far screen points back through the inverse view-projection, divide by `w`, normalise
Projection: send the target forward through the view-projection, then add the camera position to it
Translation: add the crosshair's pixel offset to the camera position, then cast the ray from there
Rotation: turn the camera's forward direction by the angle between the screen centre and the crosshair
questions.explanation: A centred crosshair simply uses the camera's forward direction. Off-centre ones must undo the projection to find a direction.

questions.prompt: Why might the ray origin for a crosshair query differ from the weapon's visible muzzle?
options: Many games aim from the camera but spawn a projectile at the weapon, then reconcile them
The muzzle is always farther from the screen than the camera, so rays from it would miss targets
The muzzle's position is stored in screen space, which cannot be used to cast a ray
Rays must start inside the player's collision shape, and the muzzle lies outside that shape
questions.explanation: The aiming ray and the projectile path can differ; this is why recreating a ray from partial data is risky.

questions.prompt: What is the job of the broad phase in a ray query?
options: Quickly reject distant regions using trees or bounding volumes, leaving a small candidate set
Compute the exact intersection points with every triangle that lies along the ray's path
Apply team and alive checks to the nearest hit before the result is returned to the game
Convert the hit parameter into screen pixels so the nametag can be drawn at the right place
questions.explanation: The narrow phase then tests shapes or triangles, and semantic filters apply last. Testing every triangle directly would be too slow.

questions.prompt: A ray meets a sphere at two parameter values, and the nearer hit comes from the smaller one. What if the ray starts inside the sphere?
options: The smaller value is negative, so the larger one is the first valid hit
There are no hits at all, since a ray cannot meet a sphere from inside it
The smaller value is still the first hit, even though it lies behind the start
Both values are equal, since the ray crosses the surface at a single point
questions.explanation: A negative parameter lies behind the ray's origin. Starting inside means the exit point is the first valid hit.

questions.prompt: The discriminant for a ray and a sphere comes out below zero. What does it say?
options: The ray passes wide of the sphere, so there is no hit
The ray grazes the sphere's surface at exactly one point
The ray enters and exits, so there are two touch points
The ray starts inside the sphere, so the hit is behind it
questions.explanation: The discriminant compares how close the ray passes to the centre against the radius. Zero means a graze, and positive means a pass-through.

questions.prompt: In ray and sphere math, let m be the vector from the sphere's center to the ray's origin, and c = |m|² − r². What does a negative c tell you?
options: The ray starts inside the sphere
The ray misses the sphere completely
The ray touches the sphere at one point
The sphere is behind the ray
questions.explanation: |m|² is the squared distance from the center to the origin. When it is smaller than r², the origin lies within the radius.

questions.prompt: On a 1000 by 500 pixel window, the cursor is at pixel (250, 125) with y growing downward. What are the normalized device coordinates, with y growing upward?
questions.explanation: x is 2 × 250 ÷ 1000 − 1 = −0.5. y is flipped because screen y grows downward, so it is 1 − 2 × 125 ÷ 500 = 0.5.

questions.prompt: How does picking with an orthographic camera differ from perspective?
options: Every ray points straight forward, and the origin is the world point under the cursor
Every ray starts at the camera position, and its direction depends on the field of view
Rays are not needed, because the cursor position is already the object's world position
Each ray points at the screen centre, and the origin moves with the cursor's distance
questions.explanation: With no division by depth, the ray direction does not vary. For the pixel `(600, 180)` the origin is the world point `(5, 3)`.

questions.prompt: A ray from (0, 0) heads along (2, 1). A box spans x from 6 to 10 and y from 2 to 4. Where does the ray first hit it?
options: At t = 3, the point (6, 3)
At t = 2, the point (4, 2)
At t = 4, the point (8, 4)
It misses, since the x and y ranges do not line up
questions.explanation: The x slab gives t from 3 to 5 and the y slab gives t from 2 to 4. The ray is inside both only from the later entry, 3, to the earlier exit, 4, so it first hits at t = 3.

questions.prompt: The same ray and a box spanning y from 3.5 to 5 give y range t from 7 to 10 and x range t from 4 to 6. What is the result?
options: A miss, because the ray would enter at 7 but has already left at 6
A hit at t = 4, because the x range alone decides whether the box is crossed
A hit at t = 7, because the ray reaches the box once the y range begins
A miss, because the y range starts after the box in the x direction
questions.explanation: Entering after leaving means the ray never is inside both ranges at once.

questions.prompt: In color picking, object number 1000 is drawn in a flat color, using base 256 with red as the high part and blue as the low part. What are the three channel values?
questions.explanation: 1000 = 0 × 65536 + 3 × 256 + 232. Reading the pixel back decodes the object, already corrected for whatever is in front of it, at the cost of an extra pass.

questions.prompt: How does a game drag an object with the mouse using this ray query?
options: It picks on button down, recasts the ray each frame to move the object along a plane, and drops it on button up
It picks once on button down, then freezes the ray so that the object keeps the same distance from the camera
It casts a ray only on button up, then moves the object to the point where that ray finally ended up
It picks again on every frame, so the held object changes whenever the mouse moves across another one
questions.explanation: The same query is repeated as the mouse moves, which is why debug views that draw the ray help to see wrong picks.

questions.prompt: Foliage is visible on screen, but shots pass through it. What explains this?
options: Render and collision visibility differ: the foliage may be set not to block shots
The depth buffer is wrong, so the foliage is drawn although the renderer should skip it
The weapon's ray is normalised, so it passes through any object that looks visibly thin
The foliage has a different level-of-detail mesh, and the ray tests only the nearest mesh version
questions.explanation: The renderer and the gameplay ray use different data. The reverse can also occur: something invisible may still block shots.

questions.prompt: Which data source most likely decides which entity gets a nametag?
options: A UI selection result
A physics collision query for shots
The depth and render buffers
The weapon's damage logic
questions.explanation: The four questions use different sources, and they may agree most of the time without being the same variable.

questions.prompt: Why model "the thing under the crosshair" as an optional value?
options: Looking at empty space is a normal state, so there must be a way to say "nothing"
An optional value makes the lookup run faster, since empty results are skipped
Looking at nothing is an error, so the optional type is used to report it
Entities have no identity, so an optional wrapper is needed to name them
questions.explanation: Many frames have no target. A missing value is normal, not a failure, and the other fields only describe a target when there is one.

questions.prompt: A rule produces a candidate only when a target is alive, visible and an opponent. For a living, visible teammate, what does it produce?
options: No candidate: all three conditions must hold, and one fails
A candidate, since two of the three conditions hold
A candidate, since alive and visible are the only checks that matter
An error, since a teammate is not an expected kind of target
questions.explanation: The rule needs every condition to hold. It only returns a decision and never acts by itself.

questions.prompt: Why name a boolean field after the exact check that produced it, rather than just "visible"?
options: It can mean a game query, a ray hit or an on-screen point, which differ
Short names are not allowed for booleans, so a longer one is needed
The name is read by the compiler to decide how to store the value
Visible is a reserved word that cannot be used as a field name
questions.explanation: Different definitions of visible give different results. A precise name stops readers from treating them as the same thing.

questions.prompt: What does the worker's edge detection achieve?
options: Only a change of state sends input, instead of thousands of repeated down events
It sends a mouse-down on every frame while the target is held, so firing stays smooth
It waits for three matching frames before sending any input at all, to reduce flicker
It sends a mouse-up first on every change, so the button can never stay held down
questions.explanation: The worker remembers whether it previously pressed the button and compares it with what is wanted.

questions.prompt: A tool sends a synthetic button press. Why must it also send a final release when the feature is turned off or unloaded?
options: A press with no release leaves the button logically held down
A release tells the target which tool sent the press, which it needs for cleanup
Presses expire after a few seconds, so the release only confirms that fact
A release is sent automatically, so the extra one just doubles the effect
questions.explanation: Input state is part of what must be restored, not only code bytes. A missing release leaves the state stuck.

questions.prompt: A debouncer reports a stable target only after the same target appears on 3 consecutive frames, and an empty frame resets its count. The frames are A, A, A, none, A. What does it report for the fifth frame?
options: Not stable: the empty frame reset the count to start again at 1
Stable, since A has appeared four times in total
Stable, since the empty frame does not break the run
Not stable, since a target can only be reported once per run
questions.explanation: Three consecutive matches are needed. The empty frame reset the count, so the fifth frame starts again at 1, which is below 3.

questions.prompt: In a multiplayer game, a client reads a crosshair result. Why doesn't that decide what the server accepts?
options: A server may own hit and firing decisions, so the local result is not its decision
A local client cannot read any crosshair result while it is connected to a server
The server always uses the client's result, so the local value is the final one
The crosshair result is hidden by encryption, so the client cannot read it
questions.explanation: The lab is tied to an offline bot match. A client-side value is local game state.

questions.prompt: A target appears selected through thin walls. Which causes should be checked first?
options: A query that ignores a collision layer, or a stale cached result
A wrong field of view, since walls only block part of the screen
A wrong aspect ratio, since walls are measured against the screen width
A wrong sign in the projection, since walls are checked after unprojection
questions.explanation: Selection through walls suggests the query ignores a layer or reuses an old value. Unprojection errors show up as off-center misses instead.

questions.prompt: Removing the camera kick from a weapon is tested and the view stops rising. What may you conclude?
options: Only that the camera kick is gone; projectile spread may still be there
That spread is removed too, since both read the same recoil number
That the weapon animation has stopped, because the model follows the camera
That the player's mouse aim has been disabled for the whole weapon
questions.explanation: Kick, spread, shake, and model animation can look alike but are separate systems. The lesson's diagram gives view and shot direction separate paths.

questions.prompt: Why can the camera's visible motion and the actual direction of a shot differ in a game?
options: The view may include visual-only effects, while the shot is base aim plus spread
The shot always follows the exact picture on screen, so the two cannot differ
The camera is drawn one frame later than the shot, so they differ by that frame
The shot ignores aim entirely, since spread is computed from the world alone
questions.explanation: What the player sees can include effects that do not change the shot. That is why changing one of them does not necessarily change the other.

questions.prompt: Why give each recoil sample a monotonic timestamp rather than a wall-clock time?
options: A wall clock can jump, while a monotonic clock measures elapsed duration reliably
A monotonic clock is more accurate to the nanosecond than any wall clock
A wall clock stops while the game is paused, so samples would never differ
A monotonic clock records the exact frame the game assigned to the shot
questions.explanation: Recovery behavior depends on elapsed time between samples. A tick or frame number can be added when the game exposes one.

questions.prompt: Why should each sample also record the weapon, fire mode, and whether the shot was accepted?
options: A reload or dry-fire sample could otherwise be mistaken for a weapon with zero recoil
The game only writes its recoil value when the weapon name is stored beside it
Fire mode decides how many bytes each logged sample must occupy
Accepted shots are the only ones that the debugger lets you breakpoint on
questions.explanation: Without that context, a missing kick could mean no recoil or simply no shot. Context keeps the series honest.

questions.prompt: Why check that a floating-point value is finite before using it?
options: NaN and infinity spread through later math and break comparisons
Finite values are always within the game's limits, so no further checks are needed
Infinity is the largest valid value, so the check removes it to save space
NaN equals every other value, so it is always safe to compare
questions.explanation: A single NaN or infinity contaminates every calculation it touches, and comparisons with NaN are always false. Range limits are only a sanity check, so real units still have to be measured.

questions.prompt: A recovery constant is applied once per frame instead of per second. What happens when the frame rate changes?
options: It behaves differently, unless the engine runs that update on a fixed simulation tick
Nothing happens, because degrees per frame and degrees per second are the same quantity
The recovery is always faster at lower frame rates, in every engine and build
The kick amount itself changes, since the impulse is multiplied by the frame count too
questions.explanation: A per-frame constant ties the speed to how often frames are drawn. Name samples with their units to keep this visible.

questions.prompt: An exponential recovery removes half of a kick in each 0.1 s. A kick of 8 units starts at the shot; how much remains after 0.3 s?
options: 1 unit, because half is lost three times: 8, 4, 2, 1
2 units, because half is lost only twice by that time
0 units, because the kick ends after losing 4 units per 0.1 s
4 units, because only the first interval removes half of the kick
questions.explanation: With `x(t) = x₀e^(-kt)`, equal fractions disappear in equal intervals. Linear recovery removes equal amounts instead and would reach zero.

questions.prompt: You fire the same shot many times and compute the mean and the spread around it. What does each tell you?
options: The mean exposes a fixed pattern, and the spread around it exposes randomness
The mean proves the random-number source, and the spread shows the unit used
The mean shows the recovery time, and the spread shows the game's frame rate
The mean gives the engine's exact formula, and the spread fixes the weapon's offset
questions.explanation: Variance describes observed variation only; it does not prove which random source or distribution produced it.

questions.prompt: After a temporary patch, the weapon animation still moves but the camera no longer kicks. What does that suggest?
options: You may have isolated the view kick from the weapon animation
The patch removed all recoil, including spread on the shots
The animation and camera are always controlled by one shared instruction
The patch must have failed, because a real recoil store stops the animation too
questions.explanation: If accuracy changes as well, the instruction controls more than presentation. Compare the observables separately.

questions.prompt: On the x87 floating-point unit, a store-and-pop instruction removes a value from the stack. Why can't it be replaced with plain no-ops?
options: The pop is a needed side effect, and skipping it leaves a stray value
No-ops are not allowed inside floating-point code, so the processor would fault
The no-ops would be longer than the original instruction, so the code would shift
The processor treats no-ops as stores, so the value would be written anyway
questions.explanation: Discarding the pending value keeps the stack balanced. A replacement must keep the original stack effect while only removing the store.

questions.prompt: How can you find the instruction that changes a known memory field, such as a view angle?
options: Watch writes to that field during the action, then follow the writing instruction
Search the target's code for the field's name, since the compiler keeps names
Scan for the field's value, since the writing instruction stores its own address
Pause the target at random, since the writer is always running at that moment
questions.explanation: The writer is found by observing the field change during the action, not by guessing from nearby code. Then you follow that instruction back to the code that triggered it.

questions.prompt: Why does picking a random distance r = R × u, with u uniform between 0 and 1, bunch points near the center of a disc?
options: Half the values fall below half the radius, which holds a quarter of the area
The random values are biased toward zero, so smaller radii are picked more often
The disc has more area near its center, so more points are placed there
Random numbers repeat after a while, so the same inner radii are chosen again
questions.explanation: Area grows with the square of the radius. Using r = R × √u makes the points spread evenly over the disc.

questions.prompt: A spread uses radius r = R × √u and angle = 360° × v. With R = 4 degrees, u = 0.25 and v = 0.25, what is the offset (x, y) in degrees?
Two runs of a game seed their pseudo-random generator with the same number. What happens to the spread?
options: Both runs repeat the same sequence, which lets replays and networked games agree
Each run still differs, because the generator mixes in the clock on every call it makes
Only the first shot matches, since later shots depend on the camera angle at the time
The spread vanishes entirely, because identical seeds cancel each other out
questions.explanation: Different seeds do not repeat. A fixed seed is a deliberate way to make 'random' values reproducible.

questions.prompt: A shake has an amplitude of 4 pixels that fades linearly to 0 over 0.5 s. What is its largest offset at 0.25 s?
options: 2.0 pixels
3.2 pixels
1.0 pixels
4.0 pixels
questions.explanation: `4 × (1 - 0.25 ÷ 0.5) = 2.0`. The 3.2 pixel value belongs to 0.1 s.

questions.prompt: An orbit camera looks at the origin from distance 20 with yaw 0° and pitch 60°, with z up. Where does it sit?
questions.explanation: The position is 20 × (cos60 × cos0, cos60 × sin0, sin60) = 20 × (0.5, 0, 0.866) = (10, 0, 17.32). The height comes from sin(pitch).

questions.prompt: A perspective camera goes from a 90° to a 60° field of view. What happens to the picture?
options: It is scaled up by about 1.732, since a narrower field of view zooms in
It is scaled down by about 1.732, since a narrower view shows less area
It is scaled up by exactly 1.5, the ratio of the two angles
It is unchanged, because only an orthographic camera responds to zoom
questions.explanation: For an orthographic camera, zooming shrinks the visible world box instead; halving its width doubles the pixels per unit.

questions.prompt: Why does the order of combining yaw and pitch matter for full 3D orientations?
options: Large rotations do not commute, so yaw-then-pitch can differ from pitch-then-yaw
Pitch must always be added first, because yaw is always stored as a quaternion
Rotations are only valid when each is smaller than 1°, so order is hidden
Engines apply yaw and pitch at the same instant, so the order cannot be changed
questions.explanation: Adding small angle offsets is a common approximation, but identify how the engine combines matrices or quaternions first.

questions.prompt: A tester says: "the weapon model stopped bobbing after my patch, so my shots no longer deviate." Why is that unjustified?
options: The model transform and the shot direction are separate observables; check impact points too
Model movement is always driven by spread, so the shots must still deviate
Weapon models are drawn after the frame, so they cannot reflect any change
A patch that stops the model also stops the shot, so the claim needs no more evidence
questions.explanation: The lesson's table lists this directly: animation of the weapon model does not tell you whether the aim direction changed.

questions.prompt: If the shot number inside a burst matters for recoil, how should the samples be analyzed?
options: Group them by shot index, rather than averaging the whole magazine together
Average every shot in the magazine, so the burst pattern cancels into one value
Keep only the first shot of each burst, because later shots repeat it exactly
Sort the shots by size, so that the largest kicks are always listed first
questions.explanation: Averaging across indices hides a per-shot pattern. Repeat the same burst and compute mean and spread for each index.

questions.prompt: In the radar pipeline, which stage decides whether a valid entity is allowed on this radar at all?
options: Filtering, which applies the radar's rules such as team
Enumeration, which visits each entity record in the list
Validation, which checks that a record is active and usable
Projection, which works out where the marker should appear
questions.explanation: Enumeration, validation, filtering, projection, and drawing answer different questions. Keeping them apart shows which stage rejected an entity.

questions.prompt: An opponent never appears on radar. What should you not conclude immediately?
options: That its position is missing, since the loop may read it and skip it at the filter
That its team field must be stored in a different byte order from teammates
That the radar is drawn before entities are read in each frame
That the opponent's marker was drawn off-screen by the scaling step
questions.explanation: A read breakpoint on the team field helps locate the decision that skips the opponent.

questions.prompt: Which coordinate space comes right after world space on the way to a radar marker?
options: Local-relative space, made by subtracting the local player's position
View-aligned space, made by rotating so the local facing becomes radar-up
Radar space, made by scaling into pixels or normalized marker units
Clipped space, made by clamping or rejecting markers outside the radar shape
questions.explanation: The order is world, local-relative, view-aligned, radar, then clipped. Naming each space and unit in variables helps catch sign and unit errors.

questions.prompt: A radar rotates every marker by the negative of the local player's yaw, so the player's forward direction always stays at the top. Which radar convention is that?
options: Heading-up, where the map rotates as the player turns
North-up, where the map stays fixed and the player icon turns
Range-clamped, where far markers are pinned to the edge
Zoom-to-fit, where the scale changes to keep every marker visible
questions.explanation: Applying the negative yaw is an inverse rotation. It undoes the player's orientation, so coordinates are expressed in the player's own axes.

questions.prompt: A rule shows an entity only when every one of several checks passes. An entity passes all checks except that its position holds NaN. What happens?
options: It is hidden, since one failing check is enough
It is shown, since most of the checks passed
It is shown, since NaN compares equal to any number
It is hidden, but only if its team differs
questions.explanation: The checks are joined with AND, so any one failure rejects the entity. A bad position is invalid data and must not be drawn.

questions.prompt: Why keep "allowed to appear" separate from "has a drawable marker"?
options: One merged boolean hides which rule rejected an entity when its marker is missing
A drawable marker is always allowed, so the second check only repeats the first
Separate checks let the radar draw an entity that the filter has rejected
Merging them stops the game from calling the drawing function twice
questions.explanation: An entity can pass team and alive filters but still fail coordinate validation, be out of range, or lack an icon.

questions.prompt: With no rotation, a radar offset is the difference between the entity and local positions, multiplied by a scale. The local position is (50, 20), the entity is at (60, 20), and the scale is 4. What is the offset?
questions.explanation: The difference is (10, 0), and scaling by 4 gives (40, 0). Multiplying the raw positions instead of their difference would give (240, 80).

questions.prompt: A marker's distance from the radar centre changes while only the player's yaw changes. What does that indicate?
options: The transform or units are wrong, since rotation preserves length
The marker is really moving, because rotation alone changes distance
The scale factor is too small, which makes the distance grow with yaw
The radar is north-up, so distance is expected to vary a bit
questions.explanation: Rotation keeps the basis orthonormal, so `x'² + y'² = x² + y²` apart from rounding. A degree/radian mix is a common cause.

questions.prompt: A radar has a radius of 80 pixels and shows 4 pixels per world unit. What unclamped world radius does it display?
options: 20 world units
320 world units
84 world units
76 world units
questions.explanation: The displayed world radius is the pixel radius divided by pixels per unit: 80 ÷ 4 = 20. Multiplying instead would give 320.

questions.prompt: A circular radar has a radius of 13 pixels, and a marker lands at (30, 72) pixels. If it is pulled in along the line to the center, where does it go?
questions.explanation: The length is √(30² + 72²) = 78, which exceeds 13, so scale by 13 ÷ 78 = 1/6, giving (5, 12). Clamping each axis separately would bend the direction.

questions.prompt: Diagonal markers stick to the corners of a circular radar. Which cause does the failure table suggest?
options: A square clamp is used for a circular radar
The yaw sign is inverted in the rotation
Two snapshots from different frames are mixed
No height policy is defined for the floors
questions.explanation: Clamping x and y independently clamps to a square, distorts direction near corners, and makes diagonals look farther from the centre.

questions.prompt: A near conditional jump is encoded as two opcode bytes followed by four more bytes. What do those four bytes hold?
options: A signed relative distance to the jump's destination
The absolute address of the destination
The condition that decides whether the jump is taken
The number of bytes to skip, as an unsigned count
questions.explanation: Near jumps store a signed offset relative to the next instruction. That is why copying such an instruction elsewhere changes where it goes.

questions.prompt: A conditional jump skips a block of code when a comparison is not equal. What happens if the whole jump is replaced with no-ops?
options: Execution falls through into the block, so only that decision changes
The block is never run, since a missing jump means it is removed
The process crashes, since a jump cannot be replaced by no-ops
The comparison runs twice, since the no-ops repeat the previous step
questions.explanation: Without the jump, the code simply continues into the next instruction. The decision the jump made is gone, while everything else stays the same.

questions.prompt: Which check would catch a subtraction-order or mixed-snapshot error in the radar math?
options: Move the local player and entity equally and confirm the marker stays fixed
Double the radar radius and confirm the marker stays on the same pixel exactly
Rotate the camera in place and confirm each marker's angle never changes at all
Move the entity farther away and confirm its pixel distance halves as it goes
questions.explanation: The relative position is a difference, so equal translations cancel. Doubling world distance should double the unclamped pixel distance.

questions.prompt: A marker flickers on and off at maximum range. Which cause does the failure table list?
options: Noisy distance and no hysteresis at the cutoff
A yaw sign that undoes the local orientation wrongly
A missing height policy for different floors
A degree/radian mix inside the rotation
questions.explanation: Tiny distance changes keep crossing the edge. A margin between show and hide thresholds stops the flicker.

questions.prompt: A radar shows a fixed pixel radius, with s pixels per world unit. What happens to the visible world range if s doubles?
options: It halves, so the radar zooms in
It doubles, so the radar zooms out
It stays the same, since the radius is fixed
It quadruples, since both axes scale
questions.explanation: The visible world radius is the pixel radius divided by s, so a larger s fits fewer world units inside the same circle.

questions.prompt: Why compare a teammate that appears with an opponent that does not, instead of looking at one entity?
options: One example cannot show a rule, and two similar entities differ mainly by team
The game only stores the team field for entities that appear on radar
Two entities are needed because the radar can draw only a pair of markers
The opponent's record is always read first, so it has to be compared with another one
questions.explanation: Matching every other property isolates the team as the likely input to the filter.

questions.prompt: How can a TCP stream carry one game message?
options: It may be split across segments, or share one with other messages
Each message travels in a TCP segment that carries that message alone
Each message becomes one IP packet whose size equals the message
The capture shows one row per message, so rows equal messages
questions.explanation: Packet rows are not game-message rows. The application needs its own framing rule, such as a length prefix or delimiter.

questions.prompt: What identifies one TCP connection?
options: Source address, source port, destination address and destination port
Source address and destination address, since ports only name services
The destination port alone, since each service has exactly one connection
A connection number, which is assigned by the network card
questions.explanation: The same connection reads the other way round for each direction, with source and destination swapped.

questions.prompt: A trace shows bytes after you click "send". What can the trace not tell you by itself?
options: Which UI action caused a packet, or any variable names
How many bytes crossed the one capture point in total
The moments at which the bytes were recorded by the trace
Which port each of the two endpoints happened to use
questions.explanation: A capture records bytes and timing. The link to an action comes from changing one thing at a time.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of capturing a quiet baseline first?
options: To see what traffic appears with no action at all
To measure how quickly the server compresses outgoing data
To encrypt the later capture before it is compared
To force the client to send a login frame to the server
questions.explanation: The method is baseline, one distinctive action, one changed input, then comparing directions and repeats.

questions.prompt: Client and server run on one machine, but the capture of the physical Wi-Fi adapter shows nothing. Why?
options: Traffic to `127.0.0.1` stays on the loopback path
Wi-Fi adapters are not able to capture any TCP traffic
Wireshark hides every packet that uses port 15000
The server compressed the data too small to be seen
questions.explanation: Pick the loopback adapter and start capturing before connecting. A wrong interface makes an empty-looking experiment.

questions.prompt: Why is a display filter preferable to a capture filter while you are still learning a protocol?
options: Everything is recorded, so the filter can be changed later without losing packets
A display filter makes the capture run faster, since fewer packets are saved
A capture filter cannot be changed, so it is never useful while learning
A display filter hides packets from the network, so they never reach the computer
questions.explanation: A capture filter drops other packets for good. A display filter only hides rows, so the full record is still there to be examined.

questions.prompt: In one connection, which port is typically stable and which is temporary?
options: The server's listening port is stable; the client's is ephemeral
The client's port is stable; the server's port is ephemeral
Both ports change with every packet that is sent
Both ports are fixed by the system for all programs
questions.explanation: In the lab, the server stays on 15000 while Windows picks a temporary local port for the client.

questions.prompt: When the server accepts a client, what happens to its listening socket on port 15000?
options: It stays open while another socket serves the client
It becomes the connected socket and stops listening
It is closed until the client disconnects again
It moves over to the client's ephemeral port number
questions.explanation: Accepting creates a new connected socket. The listener stays so other clients can still connect.

questions.prompt: Follow TCP Stream shows the reassembled bytes of a connection. What must your client still handle?
options: Partial reads, because `read()` may return fewer bytes than requested
Nothing, since reassembly fixes message boundaries for the client too
Retransmissions, because the stream view repeats them
Port numbers, because the stream view hides them
questions.explanation: Reassembly is for inspection. Your program still reads from a stream with no built-in message boundaries.

questions.prompt: When is it appropriate to read an exact number of bytes from a stream?
options: After a validated length says how many bytes belong to the next piece
Before any length is known, to see how many bytes the stream holds
At the start of a connection, since every message has the same size
Whenever the stream is quiet, since all pending bytes can then be read
questions.explanation: Without a validated length, waiting for an exact count could mean waiting for bytes that never come.

questions.prompt: Why keep the original capture alongside an exported stream fixture?
options: Reassembly picks an order and drops overlap; timing is lost
The exported stream is larger than the original capture is
Fixtures cannot be loaded unless the capture sits beside them
The capture holds the source code of the parser you use
questions.explanation: The stream view loses information that the packet-level file still has.

questions.prompt: What should a stored frame fixture avoid containing?
options: Secrets, account tokens, or other people's traffic
Direction and timing labels for each frame in it
The bytes of one clearly labeled action
The protocol and game version it was made with
questions.explanation: Fixtures are for parser tests and use invented data. Redact or avoid anything private.

questions.prompt: Capture A sends "red" and capture B sends "blue". Only one small byte range differs. What does that suggest?
options: That region may hold the text
The whole payload is compressed
The frame header was damaged
The length field has changed byte order
questions.explanation: If the whole payload changed instead, compression or encryption may be involved.

questions.prompt: Why is it worth capturing a connection from its very first packet when studying a protocol?
options: The opening messages show the handshake that later messages depend on
The first packets are the only ones that contain readable text
Later packets are always encrypted, so only the opening can be read
The first packet holds the protocol's complete specification
questions.explanation: Negotiation, version checks and login usually come first, and later messages only make sense in that context.

questions.prompt: A captured frame begins 00 00 00 1E followed by compressed data. What do the first four bytes say?
options: The data that follows is 30 bytes long
The whole frame is 30 bytes long, header included
The protocol version is 30
Thirty more frames will follow this one
questions.explanation: 0x1E is 30, and the length counts only the payload after the header. Many such formats do not count the header itself.

questions.prompt: A captured connection shows negotiation, then a version check, then a login, then the lobby. What does this ordering tell an implementer?
options: The server expects the stages in sequence, so a message sent early may be rejected
The stages can be sent in any order, since the server sorts them
Only the login matters, since the other stages are for the client's benefit
The order is chosen at random by the client at the start of each connection
questions.explanation: Each stage builds on the one before. Observing the order tells you what a conforming client must do.

questions.prompt: Why add a filter for the TCP push flag when looking for application data in a capture?
options: It shows packets that carry data, not every bare acknowledgement
It shows only encrypted packets, which hold the application's messages
It hides packets from other hosts, so only your own traffic is left
It shows packets in the order that they were sent, instead of arrival order
questions.explanation: The filter cuts down noise, so the packets that carry data are easier to match with the actions you performed.

questions.prompt: Why keep a raw capture log unchanged and rebuild the session state from it by replay?
options: A fixed rule can replay the same frames, so changes in its behavior show up
Replay is faster than reading state, since the log is smaller than the state
The log is encrypted, so it is safer to rebuild than to store the state itself
Stored state cannot be saved to disk, so only the log can be kept
questions.explanation: The log stores frames, not states. Editing a stored state by hand would lose the history that replay reveals.

questions.prompt: A session machine moves from Idle to Open on "hello" and from Open to Busy on "start". A "note" message is accepted in Open and Busy without changing the state. Starting in Idle, the messages are hello, note, start. What is the state right after the note?
options: Open, since the note is accepted but changes nothing
Busy, since every accepted message moves the machine forward
Idle, since a note resets the machine to its start
Closed, since a note without a start is not allowed
questions.explanation: A note is accepted in Open and leaves the state as it was. Busy only arrives with the start message.

questions.prompt: What separates a snapshot from a delta?
options: A snapshot stands alone; a delta edits a named baseline
A snapshot holds changes; a delta repeats the full state
A snapshot is sent by clients; a delta is sent by servers
A snapshot confirms a command; a delta asks for a command
questions.explanation: A delta applied to the wrong baseline can parse perfectly and still be nonsense, so its baseline ID must travel with it.

questions.prompt: Why store direction, sequence identifiers, and timing with each captured frame?
options: Duplicate bytes can then be told from duplicate actions
They shorten each frame so that the replay runs faster
They let the parser skip the length prefix of each frame
They take the place of keeping the exact frame bytes
questions.explanation: A retransmitted request and a deliberate second request can look identical. The extra labels let you tell them apart.

questions.prompt: A state machine accepts a "chat" message only in its lobby and match states. A well-formed chat arrives while the machine is in its greeted state. What happens?
options: Rejected as an illegal transition, though the message is valid
It is accepted, since a well-formed message is always allowed
It is queued until the machine reaches a state that accepts it
It is accepted and moves the machine to the lobby state
questions.explanation: Whether a message is legal depends on the current state. The parser can accept a message that the state machine still refuses.

questions.prompt: A greeting message with an unsupported version arrives in the initial state. What is the best result?
options: An error naming the unsupported version, with the state left unchanged
A silent acceptance, with the machine moved to the greeted state
A silent drop, with the machine left to wait for the next message
A crash of the whole session, since the version cannot be used
questions.explanation: A precise error explains what was wrong, and leaving the state unchanged lets the session recover or close cleanly.

questions.prompt: Why might a "goodbye" transition be drawn from every state of a session machine?
options: Ending a session makes sense at any point, so it is always a legal message
Goodbye is the only message that every state can understand
A session cannot be ended from the start, so every state needs one
Goodbye resets the machine, so it must be added to each state in turn
questions.explanation: A close is legal whatever the session is doing, so a catch-all rule for it matches any state, including the closed one.

questions.prompt: A replay contains a greeting as its first frame and another greeting as its second, but the machine has no greeting transition out of the greeted state. What does replay report?
options: An illegal transition error at the second frame
Success, since the second greeting repeats the first and does no harm
An error at the first frame, since a greeting cannot start a session
Nothing, since replay only reports errors that appear at the end
questions.explanation: After the first frame the machine is greeted, and no greeting arrow leaves that state, so the second frame is the one that fails.

questions.prompt: A transition has a guard that requires a non-empty name. A message with an empty name arrives in that state. What happens?
options: The guard fails, and matching falls to the catch-all illegal transition
The guard passes, since an empty name is still a valid value
The name is replaced by a default, and the transition goes ahead
The message is dropped without any error, and the state is unchanged
questions.explanation: The guard only lets non-empty names through. When it fails, matching continues and ends at the final arm.

questions.prompt: Why would a replay function check recorded timing data without actually sleeping for it?
options: Waiting is slow and machine-dependent, so timeouts use a virtual clock
Sleeping is not allowed inside functions that are tested by replay
Timing data is not accurate enough to be waited for in a test
Replay is meant to run faster than real time, so waiting is skipped
questions.explanation: Waiting in real time makes tests slow and machine-dependent. A virtual clock lets timeouts be tested deterministically.

questions.prompt: The same recorded input sometimes ends in different states. What should you conclude?
options: Some input, such as a clock or a setting, is still hidden from the model
The recording is corrupt, since the same input must always give the same state
The state machine is random, since real protocols include random choices
The replay is running too fast, since the timing of messages affects states
questions.explanation: Deterministic replay needs every input to be controlled and passed into the model, not read from a real clock or setting inside it.

questions.prompt: A rule closes a connection if no hello arrives within 3 seconds. A test feeds the hello at 3,200 ms on a virtual clock, and again at 2,900 ms. What results are expected?
options: Rejected at 3,200 ms, accepted at 2,900 ms
Accepted at both times, since the hello did arrive
Accepted at 3,200 ms, rejected at 2,900 ms
Rejected at both times, since a test clock is not real
questions.explanation: 3,200 is past the 3,000 ms limit and 2,900 is inside it. Reading a wall clock would make the result depend on machine speed.

questions.prompt: A frame's header promises 12 payload bytes, but only 5 follow. How many are missing, and what should the parser do?
options: 7 bytes; return an error instead of reading past the end
7 bytes; read what is there and pad the rest with zeros
5 bytes; wait forever, since more bytes will surely arrive
17 bytes; ignore the frame and move on to the next one
questions.explanation: 12 − 5 = 7 bytes are missing. Trusting the length would read past the end of the data, so a checked slice must turn it into an error.

questions.prompt: A client resends a request because the reply was lost. How can a server make a repeat safe?
options: Give each request an identifier, remember handled ones, and refuse repeats
Compare the bytes with the last message, and ignore any that look the same
Process every request again, since repeated requests do no harm
Close the connection when a repeat arrives, since it is a mistake
questions.explanation: The identifier is what makes "same request" testable. Matching bytes is not safe, since two identical chat lines may be two real messages.

questions.prompt: A server runs at 60 ticks per second. About how long is one tick?
options: 16.67 milliseconds
60 milliseconds
1.67 milliseconds
0.6 seconds
questions.explanation: One second divided by 60 is about 0.01667 seconds, or 16.67 ms.

questions.prompt: A scan finds a coordinate that is correct, but later the value "snaps back". What is one likely explanation?
options: It may be a predicted or drawn copy that a later server snapshot replaced
The scan found a corrupted value, which the game repaired from a backup
The coordinate is stored twice, so the second copy always wins
The game rolled back the clock, so all coordinates were reset
questions.explanation: Several copies of a value coexist, such as confirmed, predicted and interpolated ones. A newer server state overwrites the predicted one.

questions.prompt: Which fact helps tell the predicted copy of a coordinate from the confirmed one?
options: Whether updates follow local input or incoming packets
Whether its value is stored as a signed integer type
Whether the number holds an even or an odd value
Whether it lies inside the first megabyte of memory
questions.explanation: The lesson lists three clues: which thread writes the field, whether updates follow input or packets, and which tick travels beside it.

questions.prompt: A wrapping 8-bit sequence counter last accepted 250, and the next packet carries 3. What does a modular distance test conclude?
options: Distance 9, so the packet is newer and is accepted
Distance 247, so the packet is older and is rejected
Distance 253, so the packet is a duplicate and is rejected
Distance 3, so the packet is accepted only if it equals the last
questions.explanation: (3 − 250) mod 256 = 9, so it is nine steps ahead, which is newer. A plain "greater than" test would wrongly reject it, and every later number as well.

questions.prompt: With a wrapping sequence counter, why is a forward distance of exactly half the counter's range ambiguous?
options: It is as far ahead as behind, so the numbers cannot say which is newer
Half the range is always a duplicate, since it equals the last number
A distance of half the range is too large to store in the counter
Half the range only happens when packets arrive in the wrong order
questions.explanation: At exactly halfway, the new number is equally far ahead and behind, so the sequence numbers alone cannot decide.

questions.prompt: A delta is applied to a different baseline than the one it was built from. What is the likely outcome?
options: It parses fine yet produces nonsense state
The parser reports a length error before decoding
The delta is automatically converted to a snapshot
The server tick counter resets to zero
questions.explanation: Nothing in the bytes alone warns you. Robust tooling keeps the baseline ID with the bytes and refuses missing dependencies.

questions.prompt: In game networking, what is interpolation of remote objects used for?
options: Drawing remote objects smoothly at a time between two received snapshots
Predicting where a remote object will be before the next snapshot arrives
Confirming that the server has accepted a request from the client
Compressing snapshots so that they use less bandwidth
questions.explanation: Interpolation draws remote objects at a render time between two snapshots. Prediction, confirmation and compression do other jobs.

questions.prompt: A client sends the coordinate (3, 8) in a move request, and later the server replies with (3, 8). What is the difference in meaning?
options: The request is a desired destination, while the reply is what was accepted
There is no difference, since the same bytes always mean the same thing
The request is what the server accepted, and the reply is only a wish
The reply is only valid if the request was sent twice
questions.explanation: Equal-looking bytes can carry different authority depending on the kind of message that holds them.

questions.prompt: What is the job of a session state machine, compared with the parser?
options: The parser gives bytes a meaning, and the machine decides if that message is legal now
The parser decides if a message is legal, and the machine gives bytes a meaning
Both do the same job, but the machine runs after the connection closes
The machine reads bytes from the network, and the parser stores the state
questions.explanation: The parser produces message values. The machine pairs the current state with each value and accepts or refuses it.

questions.prompt: Why must a client's handshake follow a fixed order, reading each reply before sending the next message?
options: Each reply confirms a stage is done, and the server expects the next only then
Replies are only readable in the order the client sent its messages
The network delivers messages in a random order unless they are sent slowly
The server needs the whole handshake in a single write to work out the order
questions.explanation: A handshake is a conversation in stages. The server expects each message only after the previous stage has finished.

questions.prompt: How is the first message, the four zero bytes, different from later messages?
options: It is sent raw, with no gzip and no length prefix
It is gzip-compressed but has no length prefix on it
It is a length prefix whose payload is empty WML text
It is sent over UDP before the TCP connection opens
questions.explanation: Later frames are a big-endian length plus gzip-compressed WML. The negotiation bytes are written directly with `write_all`.

questions.prompt: Why would a practice client refuse any address other than the local loopback and one fixed port?
options: It keeps the exercise on the local test server, away from other hosts
Loopback addresses are the only ones that the operating system can resolve
Other ports are slower, so the client would be too slow to use
A fixed port makes the client faster, since it skips address lookups
questions.explanation: The lab is meant to talk only to a local course server. Refusing anything else is a safety limit, not a technical requirement.

questions.prompt: What does the 5-second read timeout protect the bot from?
options: A stalled server or parser leaving it waiting forever
The server sending frames that are larger than `MAX_FRAME`
The gzip decoder producing invalid UTF-8 text
The nickname containing a quote character
questions.explanation: With a finite wait, a read that gets no data ends with an error instead of hanging the bot indefinitely.

questions.prompt: Why write a whole frame with a "write all" helper instead of a single write call?
options: One write may send only part of the buffer, leaving the rest unsent
A single write always sends everything, so the helper only checks for errors
A write all call encrypts the frame, which a single write cannot do
A single write sends one byte at a time, so the helper makes it faster
questions.explanation: TCP writes can be partial. The helper keeps going until the whole frame has been handed to the socket.

questions.prompt: What are the steps for reading one length-prefixed frame, in order?
options: Read the length header, check it against a cap, then read that many bytes
Read as much as is available, then search for the end of the frame
Read the body first, then read the header that follows it
Check the cap, then read the header, then read an unknown number of bytes
questions.explanation: Only the header is trusted at first. After the length passes the cap check, exactly that many bytes are read before decoding.

questions.prompt: Why does the assumption "one read call equals one message" fail on TCP?
options: TCP can split or join messages, so reading has to follow the length
TCP always sends one message per packet, but the receiver may miss some
Messages are only separated if the sender waits between writes
TCP sorts the bytes, so a read shows the messages in size order
questions.explanation: TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries. A reader must loop until it has the number of bytes the length promised.

questions.prompt: A reply has no length marker and no terminator. How might a client decide that it is complete?
options: By waiting for a short quiet period with no more data
By reading until the buffer is exactly one kilobyte long
By assuming that every reply is a single read call long
By waiting until the server closes the connection
questions.explanation: With no length to follow, silence is a last-resort signal. Once messages have a length field, the length should be used instead.

questions.prompt: A read call on a socket succeeds but returns zero bytes. What does that mean?
options: The peer has closed its side of the connection
No data is available yet, so the caller should read again immediately
The read timed out, so the caller should wait a little longer
The message was empty, so the connection should be kept open
questions.explanation: A zero-length successful read signals the end of the stream. A timeout shows up as an error instead.

questions.prompt: A helper collects an unframed reply using a read timeout. A "would block" or "timed out" error arrives. How should it treat that?
