options: As the end of the quiet period, stopping with the bytes it has
As a fatal error, discarding everything it has collected so far
As a sign that the connection closed, closing its own side
As a request to retry the same read forever
questions.explanation: The helper decides the reply is complete when silence lasts for the timeout. The timeout is a signal, not a failure.

questions.prompt: How many bytes did the historical capture of the server's negotiation reply contain?
options: 41 bytes
4 bytes
250 bytes
512 bytes
questions.explanation: The lesson notes 41 bytes. The 4 is the zero bytes the client sent, 250 is the quiet period in milliseconds, and 512 is the chunk size.

questions.prompt: Why cap how much data a collecting loop will accept from a peer?
options: A misbehaving peer could otherwise make the buffer grow without bound
Larger replies are always invalid, since the protocol forbids them
A cap makes reading faster, since smaller buffers are cheaper to fill
The cap decides when a reply is complete, so it is part of the format
questions.explanation: Without a cap, a peer that keeps sending would make the collecting buffer grow until memory runs out.

questions.prompt: A server rejects a client's version message. What is a sound way to debug it?
options: Compare it with an official client's, fix the document, and recompress
Edit the compressed bytes directly until the server accepts them
Resend the same message with a higher version number each time
Change the server's settings, since the client must be right
questions.explanation: The compressed bytes are a product of the document inside. Changing them blindly cannot fix a wrong document.

questions.prompt: Why validate a user-supplied name before inserting it into a quoted field of a message?
options: A quote or newline could break the field's structure and alter the message
Names must be shorter than the field, or the message becomes invalid
The server only accepts names that were validated by the client
Validation makes the message smaller, which the server prefers
questions.explanation: A name is placed inside quotes. A character that ends the quote or the line would let the value change the message.

questions.prompt: A bot reacts only to one specific message pattern. What should it do with all other messages?
options: Log them if useful and keep reading, since only a match triggers a reply
Reply to them with an error, so the sender knows they were ignored
Stop running, since an unexpected message means something went wrong
Queue them for later, since each one will be needed in a moment
questions.explanation: Only a matching message triggers a reply. Everything else leaves the connection running.

questions.prompt: What does keeping transport, decoding, session meaning, and behavior as separate layers buy the bot?
options: A malformed frame fails before it reaches command logic
Frames no longer need a length prefix at the front
The gzip step can be skipped for short chat messages
The server stops validating the login of the client
questions.explanation: Behavior works with decoded events rather than raw bytes, so bad input is stopped at an earlier layer.

questions.prompt: A client hits a parse error. What does well-behaved behavior look like?
options: Report the problem and stop cleanly, not reconnect in a storm
Reconnect at once and retry, since errors are usually temporary
Ignore the error and continue, since the next message may be fine
Send the same message faster, so the server notices it
questions.explanation: A good client uses bounded replies, a send rate limit, and a clean stop when something goes wrong.

questions.prompt: A client sends a command and sees the expected reply appear in the lobby. What does that show?
options: Negotiation, login, framing and commands all work together
Only that the command was formed correctly
Only that the connection was opened successfully
Nothing, since a reply can appear without any layer working
questions.explanation: A visible reply depends on every layer working together. A valid message by itself is not a complete client.

questions.prompt: A client reading frames hits an unexpected end of stream because the local server closed. What should it do?
options: Leave its loop and exit cleanly, rather than reconnect
Reconnect straight away, since a closed stream is a temporary condition
Keep reading in a loop, since more data may arrive later
Crash, since an end of stream is an unrecoverable bug
questions.explanation: An unexpected end of stream means the server closed the connection. The client should stop instead of reconnecting.

questions.prompt: A helper reads a frame that has a 4-byte length header. Why check whether it returns the payload alone or the header and payload together?
options: Code that assumes the wrong one is off by the header length, four bytes
The header is always dropped, so only the payload could ever be returned
Returning the header makes the helper slower, so it is avoided
Only the header is checked by the network, so the payload is the same either way
questions.explanation: A helper may return either form. Parsing code that expects the other one would read every field four bytes out of place.

questions.prompt: A client connects to a local proxy, which opens its own connection to the server. Why does reaching the server's lobby this way prove something?
options: Both directions are being relayed correctly
The proxy has decoded and understood every message
The client is talking to the server directly, without the proxy
The proxy has changed the messages without anyone noticing
questions.explanation: The proxy listens on its own port and opens a separate connection onward. A working session through it proves that bytes flow both ways.

questions.prompt: Why start a proxy as a transparent relay before adding any decoding or editing?
options: A failure before any change points at the relay itself
A transparent relay is faster, so it is used for all later work
Decoding cannot be added to a relay that was started without it
A transparent relay is not allowed to be used for debugging
questions.explanation: With no decoding or editing involved, any failure must come from the relay. Only later does the proxy switch to a message-aware path.

questions.prompt: Why check that both endpoints are local addresses before opening any connections?
options: A copied address could send traffic to the wrong service
Local addresses are the only ones that proxies can open
Remote addresses are slower, so the proxy would time out
A local check makes the proxy faster, since it skips address lookups
questions.explanation: The proxy is meant for a local lab and not as a general interception tool. The check keeps both ends on the local machine.

questions.prompt: A relay copies bytes from a source stream to a destination stream. When does the copy end?
options: When the source reaches the end of its stream
When the destination has received exactly one message
After a fixed number of bytes, such as one kilobyte
When the destination sends a reply back
questions.explanation: The copy forwards one direction until the source side ends, then reports the number of bytes it copied.

questions.prompt: Why does a proxy run two relays on two threads, one for each direction?
options: TCP is full duplex, so each direction needs its own copy loop
Each relay can only read from one socket, so two sockets need two relays
Two threads encrypt the data twice, which makes it safer
A single thread cannot read from the network and write to it
questions.explanation: A single copy loop would be stuck waiting on one direction while the other side has data to send.

questions.prompt: A socket is needed by two relays, one reading from it and one writing to it. How can they share it?
options: Each thread gets its own handle to the same socket by duplicating the handle
Both threads share one handle and take turns, since sockets cannot be duplicated
Each thread opens a new connection to the same address
The relays swap handles after every message
questions.explanation: A duplicate handle refers to the same underlying socket, so each relay can own a handle without opening a second connection.

questions.prompt: One relay direction reaches EOF while the server still has replies to send. What should the proxy do?
options: Call `shutdown(Write)` on the destination; let the other relay run
Close both sockets at once so the two sides cannot lose sync
Wait until the client sends more data before doing anything
Restart the connection to the server and replay the log
questions.explanation: A half-close says "no more bytes from me" while leaving the other direction open for the remaining game messages.

questions.prompt: Which log line fits good advice for logging proxied traffic?
options: client to server: 142 bytes in one frame
client to server: every byte of the frame, in hexadecimal
client to server: the account's saved login details
client to server: the whole conversation so far
questions.explanation: Log bounded metadata such as direction and size. If you preview frames, cap their length and avoid secrets by default.

questions.prompt: A transparent proxy fails a handshake. What is a good first diagnostic approach?
options: Compare direct and proxied captures for lost or changed bytes
Add decoding to the proxy, so it can explain what went wrong
Restart the proxy several times, since failures are usually temporary
Raise the proxy's buffer sizes, since the bytes may be too large
questions.explanation: Comparing both captures shows whether both directions started and whether the relay altered or lost any bytes.

questions.prompt: A protocol uses TLS with a certificate tied to a hostname, and a proxied handshake fails. What is the right approach?
options: Do not bypass the check, and use a test setup with certificates you control
Turn off certificate checking in the client, since it is only a test
Copy the real server's certificate into the proxy, so the names match
Ignore the failure and retry, since certificates are checked only once
questions.explanation: Certificate validation is a protection, not an obstacle. Encrypted protocols get a lab configuration with certificates that you own.

questions.prompt: In the tee design, what happens to the bytes the proxy reads?
options: A copy goes to a bounded parser or log; originals pass unchanged
They are parsed first and then forwarded when they decode cleanly
They are rewritten by the parser before they are forwarded
They are dropped whenever the parser falls behind the stream
questions.explanation: The tee only observes. Keeping parsing off the critical path means a slow parser drops log entries rather than blocking the connection.

questions.prompt: Why can a tee not decide where to insert a new message?
options: A TCP read does not show where a frame ends
A tee has no access to the bytes of the connection
The bytes seen by a tee are encrypted before parsing
Insertion needs the server's port number to be known
questions.explanation: A read may end mid-frame. Insertion must wait for a complete, bounded frame and handle parse errors explicitly.

questions.prompt: Why must one task own the upstream writer when injecting a message?
options: Two threads writing to the server could interleave their bytes
One thread at a time may read the client's incoming frames
TCP refuses a second writer on the same listening port
The injected frame must be larger than the original frame
questions.explanation: If the original and injected frames were written by different threads, their bytes could be mixed together and corrupt both.

questions.prompt: Why must a message-aware proxy read whole length-prefixed frames instead of arbitrary chunks?
options: A plain read could split one frame or combine several
Chunks are always one frame, but they might arrive in the wrong order
Whole frames are smaller than chunks, so they travel faster
Plain reads only work on the first message of a connection
questions.explanation: A hook needs one complete message at a time before it can decode it.

questions.prompt: A proxy adds an extra message after seeing a particular one. What should it forward first?
options: The original message unchanged, then the added one
The added message first, then the original
Only the added message, in place of the original
Neither, until the server asks for them
questions.explanation: The proxy preserves legitimate traffic exactly as it was captured. An addition is not a replacement.

questions.prompt: A message-aware proxy fails to decode a frame. What should it do?
options: Report an error and not forward the frame
Forward the frame anyway, as a transparent relay would
Guess the missing parts and forward the repaired frame
Drop the error silently and continue with the next one
questions.explanation: Unlike a transparent relay, this path depends on parsing. A frame that cannot be decoded stops it with a clear error.

questions.prompt: Why does the proxy need a small state flag at the start of a connection?
options: The first four zero bytes are not gzip; forward them directly
The flag counts the number of frames that were injected
The flag stores the nickname that the user logged in with
The flag chooses between port 15000 and port 27015
questions.explanation: Only after the negotiation bytes pass can the upstream parser switch into framed mode.

questions.prompt: Why is a simple substring check for a message's text only a shortcut?
options: It could match that text inside an unrelated field
Substring checks are slower than parsing, so they can miss messages
Substring checks cannot read compressed data, so they never match
Substrings only match at the start of a message, so many are missed
questions.explanation: A general proxy should parse the message structure and look at the real field and session state before reacting.

questions.prompt: Why might a proxy parse and edit only one direction and keep the other as a plain relay?
options: Fewer places for bugs, since one hook cannot rewrite both ways
One direction is always empty, so there is nothing to parse
The other direction is encrypted, so it cannot be parsed
Parsing both directions would use the same thread twice
questions.explanation: Keeping the other direction a plain copy limits where a bug can appear and keeps the hook's scope small.

questions.prompt: How can you confirm that a proxy can go back to a plain, transparent state?
options: Remove decoding and injection, and check it behaves as a plain relay
Restart the proxy, since a restart always returns it to transparency
Check that its code has no comments about decoding
Compare the proxy's log with the server's log, since they are the same
questions.explanation: Direct and proxied sessions should behave the same, with byte counts that agree with a packet capture.

questions.prompt: Two processes both use the address 0x00400000. What does that tell you about the storage they refer to?
options: Nothing, since each process has its own virtual address space
They refer to the same physical storage, since the numbers match
One of them has copied the other's memory to that address
They are sharing data, since only shared memory uses fixed addresses
questions.explanation: Addresses are per-process virtual numbers. Sharing memory needs a mapping object that both processes connect a view to.

questions.prompt: The writer's view and the reader's view of one mapping object can have what relationship?
options: Different virtual addresses over the same underlying bytes
The same virtual address in both of the processes
Different bytes that Windows copies between the views
Pointers that lead into each other's private memory
questions.explanation: Windows connects both views to one file-mapping object, so the two address numbers need not match.

questions.prompt: After a shared memory object is mapped into a process, which item tells you where this process's view begins?
options: The pointer returned by the mapping call
The handle used to open the shared object
The name of the shared object
The size given when the object was created
questions.explanation: The handle names the shared object, while the pointer names where this particular process sees it.

questions.prompt: Releasing a shared memory mapping involves two separate steps. What are they?
options: Unmapping the view and closing the object's handle
Clearing the memory and deleting the object's name
Closing the process and unloading the object
Flushing the view and locking the handle
questions.explanation: A view and a handle are different resources. Closing the handle does not unmap the view, so each needs its own cleanup.

questions.prompt: A writer creates a shared memory object without naming any file. What backs the storage, and what must be given?
options: The system paging file, and a nonzero size
A temporary file in the current folder, and a name
The writer's own stack, and a pointer
A hidden section of the disk, and a password
questions.explanation: With no file handle, the operating system backs the memory with its paging file, and a nonzero size is required.

questions.prompt: Why might a shared object's name be placed in a per-session namespace rather than a global one?
options: A narrower scope suits the need, while global names can need extra privilege
Per-session names are faster to look up, since the table is smaller
Global names are never allowed, since the system keeps them for itself
Per-session names are shared between all users, which is more convenient
questions.explanation: Keeping a name local limits who can reach the object. Global names widen the scope and can need more privilege.

questions.prompt: The mapping is 4096 bytes and the header takes 4. How many UTF-8 bytes can the longest message have?
questions.explanation: The writer rejects any message longer than `MAPPING_BYTES - HEADER_BYTES`, which is 4096 - 4 = 4092.

questions.prompt: A writer stores a 300-byte message and a 4-byte little-endian length header in front of it. Which header bytes does it write?
questions.explanation: 300 is 0x12C, and a little-endian number stores its lowest byte first, so the bytes are 2C 01 00 00.

questions.prompt: Why store a length for a message instead of reading until the first zero byte?
options: A length makes embedded zeros clear and lets the reader check the size first
A zero byte is slower to find than a stored number, which costs time
Messages can never contain zero bytes, so a length is just for tidiness
A length is shorter than a zero byte, which saves space
questions.explanation: The length gives an exact boundary, and the reader can reject a size that does not fit before slicing anything.

questions.prompt: What does the reader verify before slicing the payload?
options: That the length fits in the mapping after the header
That the writer's process is still running right now
That the text is shorter than eleven bytes in length
That the mapping name starts with the `Local\` prefix
questions.explanation: The length must be at most `bytes.len() - HEADER_BYTES`. UTF-8 is validated after that, before the bytes are treated as text.

questions.prompt: The writer stores a new length of 11 before copying the payload, and a reader arrives in between. What does it likely get?
options: The new length with the old message's payload bytes
A clean error from the length check of the reader
The complete new message, copied across in full
A zero-length message with nothing at all inside
questions.explanation: The length check passes and the old bytes may still decode as valid UTF-8, so the text is wrong or partly old.

questions.prompt: A writer updates the length field first and only then copies the new bytes. A reader looks in between. What can it see?
options: The new length with partly old bytes, a message nobody published
The old message complete, since the reader always sees the last finished write
An error from the operating system, since reading during a write is blocked
Nothing at all, since shared memory is hidden while it is being written
questions.explanation: Shared memory has no built-in ordering between writer and reader. Without an agreement on timing, a reader can see a mixture that passes simple checks.

questions.prompt: Why does writing the payload before the length only narrow the race window?
options: The CPU and compiler may reorder the two stores
Readers read the payload before they read the length
Lengths are kept in the paging file, not in memory
Payload bytes cannot be changed once the header is set
questions.explanation: Order in the source does not guarantee the order other processes see. Closing the race needs a real synchronization rule.

questions.prompt: Which design closes the partial-write problem?
options: A sequence number checked before and after the copy
A longer mapping name that the reader must match exactly
Zeroing the whole buffer after a reader has finished
Switching `Local\` for `Global\` in the mapping name
questions.explanation: A reader that sees the same sequence value both times knows no write happened during its copy.

questions.prompt: Why might a writer clear a shared buffer before writing a new, shorter message?
options: To remove leftover bytes of an older, longer message
Clearing the buffer lets the reader know a write is about to start
A buffer must be zeroed or the operating system refuses the write
Zeros make the new message compress better in memory
questions.explanation: Only the length marks the current boundary, but stale bytes past it would be confusing leftovers if someone looked.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer wait for Enter before exiting?
options: Dropping the last handle destroys the mapping and its name
Windows needs a keypress to flush the paging file contents
A reader can start when the writer has already ended
The writer must unmap its view before it can write bytes
questions.explanation: The named object exists only while a handle is open. A reader started later gets a clear error.

questions.prompt: What does mapping a view as read-only and exposing it as an immutable slice express?
options: The reader may look at the bytes but may not change them
The reader owns the memory and may free it when finished
The reader sees a private copy that updates are not shown in
The reader may change the bytes but the writer may not
questions.explanation: Mutability in the types shows which side may change data. The writer gets a mutable view of a writable mapping.

questions.prompt: Why wrap raw pointer code in a small type that exposes safe slices?
options: The wrapper fixes the pointer's bounds and lifetime once
Raw pointers are slower than slices, so the wrapper makes them faster
The compiler rejects raw pointers unless they live inside a wrapper
The wrapper makes the pointer valid after the memory is unmapped
questions.explanation: A raw pointer from a mapping call carries no length or lifetime. The wrapper records both once, so everything outside it is checked by the compiler.

questions.prompt: A reader opens a named shared object before any writer has created it. What should happen?
options: The open fails, so the reader reports a clear "start the writer first" error
The open succeeds with an empty object, so the reader waits for data
The open creates the object itself, so the writer can connect to it later
The open blocks forever, until the writer happens to create the object
questions.explanation: Opening a name that does not exist fails. Adding context to that error tells the user what to do next.

questions.prompt: Why should passwords or secret tokens not go in a mapping protected only by a convenient name?
options: A name alone is not real protection for the bytes
Names longer than 20 characters leak the data inside
Shared memory cannot hold any text at all
Secrets can be stored in `Global\` mappings and nowhere else
questions.explanation: A name is easy to guess or reuse. The lesson says the contract and its protections should be designed deliberately.

questions.prompt: A game asks for an asset and the engine hands back a handle at once. What is true at that moment?
options: The handle exists, but the file may not be read, decoded or uploaded yet
The asset is fully loaded, since the engine returns a handle only when it is ready
The handle holds the asset's pixels, so they can be read straight away
The handle is the file itself, so it can be edited like any other file
questions.explanation: A handle is a small ID standing for an asset that a background task still reads and decodes. Assuming the data exists already is a mistake.

questions.prompt: A 256 × 256 PNG takes 40 KB on disk. About how much memory do its decoded red, green, blue, and alpha pixels use?
options: 262,144 bytes
40,960 bytes
65,536 bytes
questions.explanation: Each pixel takes 4 bytes, so 256 × 256 × 4 = 262,144. The 40 KB file size is the compressed form, which is not what memory holds after decoding.

questions.prompt: How much does a mipmap chain add to a texture's decoded size?
options: About one third more, as the half-size copies shrink geometrically
About double, because every smaller copy repeats the full image data
About one tenth more, because only a few small copies are ever kept
Nothing extra, because the smaller copies are made fresh on every draw
questions.explanation: Each copy has a quarter of the pixels of the one before, so the chain adds 1/4 + 1/16 + ... which is about a third. That turns 262,144 bytes into about 349,525.

questions.prompt: A level loader holds one strong handle to a bullet texture, and 12 bullets each hold one too. How many strong handles keep the texture alive?
questions.explanation: The loader's 1 plus the bullets' 12 gives 13. Forgetting the loader gives 12, but the loader's handle counts as well.

questions.prompt: When does the engine free the decoded data of an asset?
options: When the count of strong handles reaches 0
When the first user of the asset despawns
When a weak handle to it is created
As soon as the pixels reach the graphics card
questions.explanation: Strong handles keep the asset alive, so it is freed only when none are left. Uploading to the graphics card does not free it, and a weak handle never held it alive in the first place.

questions.prompt: What is a weak handle used for?
options: Naming an asset for lookups without keeping it alive
Keeping an asset loaded until the game exits
Marking an asset that failed to decode
Counting how many bullets still draw the texture
questions.explanation: A weak handle names an asset but does not add to the strong count, so lookups do not delay freeing. Keeping something loaded is the job of strong handles.

questions.prompt: In the bullet texture example, the loader holds 1 strong handle and 40 bullets hold 1 each. After all 40 despawn, what is the state?
options: 1 strong handle remains, so the texture stays in memory
0 strong handles remain, so the texture is freed
40 strong handles remain until the next level loads
1 weak handle remains, so the texture is freed
questions.explanation: The loader still holds its own handle, so the count is 1 and the texture remains. It is freed only when the level unloads and the loader lets go.

questions.prompt: Two systems ask for the same path. What does the engine's asset cache do?
options: Returns the same handle, so no second copy is loaded
Loads a second copy so each system can edit its own
Returns a weak handle to the first requester only
Rejects the second request until the first finishes
questions.explanation: The cache maps a path to one asset, so repeated requests share it. This is why one texture can serve many separate bullets.

questions.prompt: Why does replacing a file on disk never change an embedded asset?
options: It is compiled into the executable, so no file is read at run time
It is cached by a search index that ignores modification times
It is stored only in graphics card memory and never in a file
It is encrypted, and the game rejects any file that differs
questions.explanation: An embedded asset travels inside the executable. Nothing reads the folder for it, so a replacement file has nothing to override.

questions.prompt: What does a game with hot reloading do when a watched file's modification time changes?
options: Decodes it again, swaps the data behind the same handle, sends an event
Restarts the game so every handle is created again from scratch
Deletes the asset and waits for the next player request to load it
Sends a modified event but keeps showing the old data until restart
questions.explanation: The same handle now points at new data, so everything holding it shows the new version on its next draw. A restart is exactly what hot reloading avoids.

questions.prompt: A shipped game reads each texture once when its level loads. When does your replacement texture show up?
options: The next time that level loads
On the next frame, as in a development build
Never, because it is compiled into the executable
As soon as the file's modification time changes
questions.explanation: Without a watcher, nothing notices the changed file until the level reads it again. Showing on the next frame describes a development build with hot reloading.

questions.prompt: A model file holds 3 meshes, 2 materials, 1 texture, 2 animations, and 1 scene. How many assets does it give the engine?
questions.explanation: Each part gets its own handle: 3 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 9. Counting only the file as one asset misses that the engine splits it up.

questions.prompt: A mesh takes 5 seconds to load and a system checks every frame at 60 frames per second. How many checks does that cost, compared with reacting to one asset event?
options: 300 checks, versus a single run on the event
60 checks, versus a single run on the event
5 checks, versus a single run on the event
3,600 checks, versus a single run on the event
questions.explanation: 5 seconds × 60 frames = 300 checks, all to learn one fact. An asset event runs the system once, when the mesh finishes.

questions.prompt: Why does scanning process memory for a PNG's own file bytes find nothing?
options: Memory holds the decoded pixels, not the compressed PNG data
The PNG is stored in graphics memory in its original form
The engine encrypts every asset before it leaves the disk
The PNG's bytes are moved to the page file as soon as it loads
questions.explanation: Loading decodes the file into raw pixels, so the original compressed bytes are not what sits in memory. A scan would find image data, not the file.

questions.prompt: Why must a replacement texture keep the original's name, folder, and format?
options: The game finds the asset by its path and expects that format
The graphics card matches textures by file size alone
The cache refuses any file whose modification time is newer
The handle stores the original file's checksum and compares it
questions.explanation: A request names a path, so a file under a different name or in a different folder is never asked for. The format must also match what the loader decodes.

questions.prompt: How can you find which file holds a game's save, using a disposable character?
options: Monitor the game's file activity and look for a write just after you save
Scan the game's memory for the character's name to find its file
Open the first file in the game's folder, since saves are always listed first
Look for the largest file in the folder, since a save is the biggest file
questions.explanation: A file-activity monitor records operations per process, so a write right after the save click is a strong candidate. A memory scan cannot name a file.

questions.prompt: A backup routine finds that a backup file already exists. What should it do?
options: Return an error and leave the earlier backup alone
Overwrite the old backup, since the newest copy is the best one
Delete the old backup first, so the folder stays tidy
Append the new copy to the old one, so both are kept in one file
questions.explanation: The first backup is your way back. Silently overwriting it could replace a good copy with an already edited one.

questions.prompt: A helper is asked for the first 16 bytes of a file that is only 10 bytes long. What should it return?
options: Just the 10 bytes that really exist in the file
16 bytes, with the last 6 filled with zeros
An error, since fewer bytes than requested can never be returned
Nothing, since a partial answer is the same as a failed one
questions.explanation: A read reports how many bytes it got, and the helper should cut its result to that. Returning unused zeros would pretend the file held data it does not.

questions.prompt: A file named data.bin begins with the bytes 89 50 4E 47. What is it most likely?
options: A PNG image
A ZIP archive
A gzip-compressed file
A plain text file
questions.explanation: The bytes 89 50 4E 47 are the PNG signature. ZIP begins 50 4B and gzip begins 1F 8B, so the file extension was only a hint.

questions.prompt: A save line looks like "stats=5,1,1,2". Why parse it by its format instead of searching the file for the digit 5?
options: A 5 elsewhere would match the search, but not be the same field
Searching for a digit is slower, since every byte has to be compared
A parser can only find numbers that are written in hexadecimal
The first digit in a file is never part of a field
questions.explanation: Format rules say where the field and its parts are. A matching digit in another place proves nothing.

questions.prompt: A save is well-formed, but it names a unit type the game has never defined. Which stage of validation fails?
options: Meaning validation, because the bytes parse but the ID is not legal
Byte validation, because the offsets and lengths are wrong
Neither stage, because the file loaded without a parse error
Encoding validation, because unknown names are not valid text
questions.explanation: Byte validation covers offsets, lengths, counts, and encoding. Whether an ID refers to something real is a question about meaning.

questions.prompt: Which statement about ZIP is correct?
options: It bundles named entries and normally compresses them, yet one can be stored as is
It only compresses a single file, so many entries need a separate container
It encrypts each entry, which is why the contents look unreadable in a viewer
It compresses every entry, since storing without compression is not allowed
questions.explanation: An archive is a container and compression is a separate idea, though ZIP normally does both. An entry can still be stored as is.

questions.prompt: What does a cryptographic signature add that a checksum does not?
options: A key, so it shows who produced the data rather than only that bytes changed
A faster comparison, so large files can be checked in one step
Protection against accidental corruption, which a checksum cannot catch
Compression of the data, so it can be sent in fewer bytes
questions.explanation: A checksum detects accidental changes in other bytes. A signature uses a key to prove the producer, and renaming or recompressing a file does not recreate one.

questions.prompt: Why should a game be closed before you edit its save file?
options: The game may hold state in memory and overwrite your edit on exit
A running game locks every save file, so edits are always refused
Editing a file while a game runs makes the file's checksum wrong
The operating system only allows edits to files that are not in use
questions.explanation: A running game may write its in-memory state back over your change at shutdown, which undoes the edit.

questions.prompt: A game keeps a character's values in one file and a shared stash in another. What should you do before changing either?
options: Copy both files first, so there is a way back
Change the stash first, since it affects fewer values
Delete the stash, since the game rebuilds it when it starts
Change only the character file, since the stash cannot be damaged
questions.explanation: Related files can depend on each other. Backing up both gives you a way to return to a known-good state.

questions.prompt: When isolating a game's file activity in a monitoring tool, why filter by process name first?
options: It shows all the game does, and narrower filters could hide writes
It makes the monitor run faster, since fewer processes are watched
It is the only filter that the monitoring tool supports
It hides all operating system activity, so only saves remain
questions.explanation: A broad filter on the game itself leaves the full picture. Narrower filters can exclude the very write you are looking for.

questions.prompt: A save line holds four numbers whose meaning is not documented. How should you find out which is which?
options: Change one value at a time in a throwaway save and watch what moves
Assume they are in the order the game's menu shows them
Assume they are sorted from the smallest to the largest value
Change all four at once, and see whether the game still loads
questions.explanation: Guessing the order would put a value in the wrong place. Controlled experiments tie each number to a visible change.

questions.prompt: Why compare two saves made with exactly one intended change between them?
options: A real field follows that one change; other differences are background state
Two saves of one character always differ in exactly one byte, the changed one
The comparison proves that every changed byte belongs to the chosen field
The game refuses to load a save that was made without a matching second copy
questions.explanation: Saves may also change play time, random state, or timestamps. Only a difference that follows the chosen change consistently is a field.

questions.prompt: A helper compares two files by pairing their bytes with a zip-style iterator. What does that leave unchecked?
options: Extra bytes in the longer file, so the two lengths need a separate check
Bytes in the middle of the files, since zipping skips every other pair
Bytes at the start of the files, since a pairing starts at the second byte
Bytes that differ, since a pairing only finds those that match
questions.explanation: Zipping stops at the shorter input, so a longer file's tail is ignored. An inserted field or newline needs a separate length check.

questions.prompt: Two saves from one small change differ at almost every offset. What is the most reasonable guess?
options: Compression, encryption, a timestamp, or a checksum may be involved
The game is storing the file as plain text with different line endings
The hex editor has numbered the offsets from a different starting point
Flare writes its attributes in random order on each save
questions.explanation: A small cause should touch a small region. Differences everywhere suggest the whole file is transformed or covered by an integrity field.

questions.prompt: Parsed key=value lines are collected into a map. What does that hide?
options: Repeated keys, since only one value per key survives
Keys with empty values, since a map cannot hold an empty string
Keys in a different order, since a map sorts them
Keys that are too long, since a map limits their length
questions.explanation: A map holds one value per key, so a duplicate silently overwrites its twin. A careful editor counts the matching lines and refuses unless there is exactly one.

questions.prompt: An editor expects exactly one line with a given key but finds zero, or three. What should it do?
options: Stop with an error and leave the original file untouched
Edit the first match it finds, since the others are probably copies
Edit every match it finds, since all of them need the same value
Create the missing line at the end of the file
questions.explanation: Zero means the field is missing, and several make the edit ambiguous. In both cases the tool should report the count and change nothing.

questions.prompt: Why is writing a new version of a save file directly over the original risky?
options: Writing truncates the original first, so a crash can leave half a save
Direct writes are always slower than other methods, which risks a timeout
Direct writes keep the old data, so the file ends up twice as large
Direct writes are blocked by the operating system when a game is open
questions.explanation: Writing in place uses the original as scratch space. Preparing a temporary file next to it keeps the old one whole until the new one is complete.

questions.prompt: What does asking the operating system to flush a temporary file's data to disk before replacing the original achieve?
options: It makes it likelier that the finished data survives a crash
It locks the original file, so nothing else can change it
It performs the rename, so the replacement is complete
It checks the contents, so a damaged file is detected
questions.explanation: Flushing improves durability. It does not lock the original or perform the rename, which are separate steps.

questions.prompt: Why close a temporary file's handle before replacing the original with it on Windows?
options: An open handle can block the swap with a sharing conflict
A closed file is smaller, so the replacement is quicker
Open files cannot be flushed, so the data would be lost
The handle holds the checksum, which is only valid once closed
questions.explanation: On Windows an open handle can block the replacement. The close is about sharing, not about size or checksums.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between atomic and durable?
options: Atomic: old or new file, never a mixture. Durable: finished data survives failures
Atomic: the file is encrypted. Durable: the file is also compressed before saving
Atomic: the file is flushed to disk. Durable: the file has been renamed
Atomic: the save is backed up. Durable: the backup is then signed as well
questions.explanation: Atomic is about never showing a half-written mixture. Durable is about surviving failures, and no single call makes the whole save set one transaction.

questions.prompt: What does crash consistency require beyond the normal path completing once?
options: After any interruption, the files show an old, new, or recoverable state
The editor must have run at least twice in a row without any failure
Every file in the saves folder must share the same modification time
The game's cloud sync must be switched off for the whole duration of the edit
questions.explanation: The property is about every point where execution could stop, not only the case where nothing goes wrong.

questions.prompt: You find the original save plus a leftover temporary file from an editing tool. What is the safe response?
options: Check or remove only the temporary; the original is still good
Use the temporary file, since it is newer than the original
Delete the original, since the temporary file replaces it
Merge the two files, so no data is lost from either
questions.explanation: A leftover temporary means preparation was interrupted, so the original is intact. Choosing by newest time could install a half-written file.

questions.prompt: A game's original save file is missing, but a backup of it exists. What should happen?
options: Restore the backup, after checking it, before launching the game
Launch the game, since it will create a new save by itself
Delete the backup, since a missing original means it is out of date
Rename the backup silently, since the game cannot tell the difference
questions.explanation: A missing original with a backup means recovery is needed. Check the backup's name, format and contents, and ask before replacing the only known-good copy.

questions.prompt: What advantage does a single operating-system replace call have over separate rename and copy steps?
options: The new file is installed and the backup made in one filesystem action
It checks the file's format, so a damaged file is never installed
It edits the line inside the file, so no separate parser is needed
It works on files that are open, so the game need not be closed
questions.explanation: Using one call means replacement and backup creation happen together. Parsing and editing are separate steps done before it.

questions.prompt: Why does the editor reject a new value that contains a newline character?
options: A newline would start a second field, turning a value edit into a structure change
A newline makes the file larger than the maximum size Windows allows for a save
Newlines are not valid in the ASCII subset that the Flare loader accepts
A newline would make the editor erase the backup that is already stored
questions.explanation: A value must stay on one line, or the edit could inject extra lines into the save. Size limits and character sets are not the reason.

questions.prompt: When is the edit considered successful?
options: Flare loads it and a later normal save keeps the value
The editor prints that it changed the field in the original file
The temporary file has been deleted again after the swap finished
The backup has been created next to the save in the same folder
questions.explanation: A game's own loader and serializer are the real test. Messages from the editor only show that its own steps ran.

questions.prompt: Which question should you answer before patching a save that seems to contain a checksum?
options: Which bytes it covers, its algorithm, its location, and byte order
Whether the file's extension matches the name of its folder
Whether the save is older than the game's most recent update
How many characters the player's character name contains
questions.explanation: The checksum must be recomputed correctly, so you need its coverage, algorithm, location, and byte order. If a secret key is involved, use supported tools.

questions.prompt: A game ships its content in files with an unusual extension, yet ordinary ZIP tools can open them. What explains this?
options: The extension is only a label; the bytes inside are a normal ZIP archive
ZIP tools decide the format from the file size, not from its contents
The game converts each file to ZIP in memory every time it is opened
The files are ZIP archives protected by a password that tools skip
questions.explanation: A container format can be reused under a custom extension. Because the bytes are standard ZIP, standard tools can list and extract them.

questions.prompt: A game finds files inside an archive by their path from the archive's root, such as `env/sky.png`. You zip an edited work folder by selecting the outer folder itself, which is named `work`. What goes wrong?
options: Every path gains a `work/` prefix, so lookups of `env/sky.png` fail
Nothing changes, because engines search every folder level for a match
The archive grows past the size limit the engine allows for content
The files inside are compressed twice and can no longer be read
questions.explanation: Archive paths are relative to the archive root. An extra wrapping folder changes every path, so lookups by the original path fail.

questions.prompt: A patch tool is meant to replace exactly one entry in an archive. Why should it confirm that exactly one entry was replaced before installing anything?
options: Zero means the target was missing and two means a duplicate path
It makes the install faster by skipping the compression step afterwards
It proves the new file is a valid image that the engine will accept
It confirms the archive was produced by the original game developer
questions.explanation: Checking the count of matches turns a silent wrong result into a clear failure. A missing or duplicated target means the patch is not doing what was planned.

questions.prompt: Why does the PK3 tool rebuild every ZIP entry rather than patch bytes inside the old archive?
options: Only the `UP` entry gets new bytes; the rest are copied into a fresh file
ZIP files can be changed only by rewriting them from the first byte onward
Patching in place would also rewrite the backup file that sits beside it
Rebuilding makes the new sky image compress smaller than the old one did
questions.explanation: The lab writes a new archive, so the original stays whole until the atomic swap. Entries other than the sky face are copied unchanged.

questions.prompt: A tool reads an image header and reports its width, height and color format. What can you conclude from that alone?
options: Whether they match the original image, which is one check but no guarantee
That the game will definitely load it, since the header holds all the engine needs
That every pixel matches the original, since both have equal dimensions
That the file has no corruption anywhere in its pixel data
questions.explanation: A header describes only a few properties. Matching them is one check among several, and it says nothing about the pixel data or the engine's other requirements.

questions.prompt: You change a picture's extension from .png to .tga without converting it. What is the file now?
options: Still PNG data under another name, since renaming changes only the label
A real TGA file, since the format is determined by the extension
A corrupted file, because the system rewrites the header on rename
A TGA file that is compressed in the PNG style
questions.explanation: Extensions are labels. Only conversion by a program that understands both formats changes the bytes into a different format.

questions.prompt: A routine draws a square marker whose side is limited, on each axis separately, to the smaller of 12 pixels and the image's own size on that axis. For an image 40 pixels wide and 5 pixels tall, what size is the marker?
options: 12 wide and 5 tall
5 wide and 5 tall
12 wide and 12 tall
40 wide and 5 tall
questions.explanation: Per axis, min(12, 40) is 12 and min(12, 5) is 5. Clamping to the image's size keeps the marker from drawing outside the image.

questions.prompt: Why mark only a 16-pixel corner instead of repainting the whole texture?
options: It proves which image loaded while keeping the change small and reversible
The game rejects any texture where more than 256 pixels have changed
A larger change would alter the file's width and height in the header
The mipmaps are built from the corner pixels of the full-size image only
questions.explanation: A small, obvious mark answers one question: does the game use this file? It also keeps the diff against the original easy to inspect.

questions.prompt: You replace one wall texture and see changes in several other places. Why can that happen?
options: UV coordinates map surfaces to an image, so one texture can cover many surfaces
The engine copies every texture into one shared file when it loads a level
Mipmaps spread edits to neighbouring textures stored in the same archive
A replaced file is also applied to every other file that has the same size
questions.explanation: One image can repeat or be reused across surfaces, so changing it may affect more places than the first one you noticed.

questions.prompt: A replacement texture appears upside down in the game. What is a likely cause?
options: The file and the engine disagree about which edge `v = 0` names
The texture's alpha channel was set to 0 instead of 255
The texture was saved without mipmaps, which flips the image
The archive was compressed with the wrong method
questions.explanation: Some formats put `v = 0` at the top and some at the bottom. A mismatch flips the picture without changing any pixels.

questions.prompt: What is the basic structure of a glTF 3D model file?
options: A JSON graph of scenes, nodes and meshes that refer to each other by index
A flat run of vertex coordinates with a fixed byte count and no description
A ZIP archive holding one text file for every mesh in the model
A compiled script that the game runs to build the model at load time
questions.explanation: The JSON is a graph of named parts that point at each other by position, and the bulky vertex and index bytes live in a buffer that those parts describe.

questions.prompt: A buffer view holds vertex data described as 2-component vectors of 4-byte floats, with a count of 5. How many bytes does it span?
questions.explanation: Each vector is 2 × 4 = 8 bytes, and five of them take 5 × 8 = 40 bytes. Forgetting the 4-byte size gives 10, and forgetting the component count gives 20.

questions.prompt: A model file's header claims it holds 2,000,000 items of 12 bytes each, but only 48 bytes of data actually follow. How should a careful loader behave?
options: Compare the claim with the bytes present and reject it before allocating
Allocate 24,000,000 bytes first, then read until the data runs out
Trust the header and read past the end, since model files are not hostile
Read the 48 bytes and pad the rest with zeros so the model still loads
questions.explanation: A file is untrusted input, so its claimed sizes must be checked against reality before any large allocation or read. Doing the arithmetic first prevents crashes and memory exhaustion.

questions.prompt: CD-quality audio takes 44,100 samples a second for 2 channels at 2 bytes each. How many bytes is that per second?
questions.explanation: 44,100 × 2 × 2 = 176,400. Forgetting either the channels or the sample size halves the answer.

questions.prompt: Why is music usually streamed while a short sound effect is decoded once and kept in memory?
options: A song decodes to about 30 MiB, while a short effect is cheap to keep
A sound effect cannot be stored compressed in any format at all
Music is stored in mono, so streaming is the only way to play it back
The sound card can play effects only when they are held in memory
questions.explanation: Music is stored compressed and decoded a chunk at a time. A small effect is cheap to hold, and it plays often.

questions.prompt: Two sounds with samples of 0.7 and 0.6 are mixed by adding them. What happens, and why?
options: The total is 1.3, past the limit, so it is cut to 1.0 and distorts
The total is 0.65, since mixing takes the average of the two sounds
The total is 1.3, which the sound card simply plays back louder
The total is 0.1, since each sound is subtracted from the other one
questions.explanation: Mixing adds samples scaled by volume, and the range ends at 1. Engines lower volumes or add a limiter to avoid clipping.

questions.prompt: A sound card asks for buffers of 1,024 samples at 44,100 samples a second. About how long does one buffer last?
options: 23 ms
44 ms
1 second
0.23 seconds
questions.explanation: 1,024 ÷ 44,100 is about 0.0232 seconds. If the next buffer is not filled in time, the listener hears a click.

questions.prompt: A listener faces +y, so their right side is +x. Pan is the dot product of the unit direction toward a sound with the right vector, so a negative pan means left. A sound sits at (-8, 6, 0). What are its distance and pan?
options: Distance 10 and pan -0.8, toward the left
Distance 10 and pan 0.6, toward the right
Distance 14 and pan -0.8, toward the left
Distance 10 and pan -0.6, toward the left
questions.explanation: The distance is √(64 + 36) = 10, the unit direction is (-0.8, 0.6, 0), and dotting with (1, 0, 0) gives -0.8. The 0.6 is the forward part, not the sideways part.

questions.prompt: At a distance of 10, what do the inverse and linear falloffs (full at 1, silent at 50) give?
options: Inverse 0.1 and linear about 0.82
Inverse 0.82 and linear 0.1
Inverse 0.2 and linear about 0.92
Both give 0.1
questions.explanation: Inverse is 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1, while linear is 1 − 9 ÷ 49 ≈ 0.82. Linear stays loud nearby and reaches 0 only at 50.

questions.prompt: Why does a game set a distance beyond which an inverse-falloff sound is not mixed at all?
options: Inverse falloff never reaches silence, so the cutoff saves the work
Inverse falloff goes negative at long range, which sounds wrong
Linear falloff needs that cutoff to find where to start
The sound card cannot play a volume below 0.1
questions.explanation: 1 ÷ d is small but never exactly zero. A cutoff skips mixing sounds nobody can hear.

questions.prompt: What should a replacement sound match, as a replacement texture does?
options: The same path and format, usually the same sample rate and channels
The same duration to the millisecond and the same size in bytes
The same position in the game's archive listing as the original
The same checksum as the sound that it is replacing in the game
questions.explanation: The game finds the sound by path and decodes it with an expected format. A changed sample rate or channel count can break playback.

questions.prompt: Halfway through a 2-second cross-fade between two music tracks, what are the volumes?
options: Old track 0.5 and new track 0.5
Old track 1.0 and new track 0.0
Old track 0.25 and new track 0.75
Old track 0.0 and new track 1.0
questions.explanation: A linear blend halfway through gives each track half volume. The lesson compares it to an animation blend.

questions.prompt: What should a small texture mod folder contain?
options: Only the changed file and a short manifest
The full original game archive plus the changed file
Every texture in the game, to keep paths consistent
A copy of the game's executable, patched to load the file
questions.explanation: Ship a small patch, not copyrighted original assets. The manifest records the target, source path, original hash, and how to uninstall.

questions.prompt: A game loads several data packs in a fixed order, and each pack can replace files that earlier packs provided. Where should a pack that must win any conflict be placed?
options: At the end, since each later pack can replace data from earlier ones
At the start, since the first pack loaded is protected from replacement
In the middle, so both earlier and later packs can see its data
At the end, but only if its files are larger than the originals
questions.explanation: When packs are applied in sequence, the last one to supply a given file is the one the game ends up with. Putting a pack first would let everything after it override it.

questions.prompt: A base pack has `units/goblin.txt`, and a later pack adds `units/goblin2.txt`. The game replaces data only when the relative paths match exactly. What happens to the original goblin?
options: It is unchanged; the new file is a separate extra entry and replaces nothing
It is replaced, because the two names are similar enough to count as a match
It is deleted, because a newer goblin file now exists in a later pack
It is merged with the new file, field by field
questions.explanation: Overrides work by matching the relative path. A different path creates a new, independent entry rather than replacing the existing one.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't a mod copy the entire base data folder?
options: It would freeze and override unrelated files, cutting them off from updates
Flare refuses to load any mod folder that holds more than ten files
The copied folder would be loaded before the base game and then lost
It makes the mod folder unreadable to the list in `mods.txt` entirely
questions.explanation: A small mod makes it obvious which file wins. Extra copies override files you never meant to touch.

questions.prompt: A game defines a monster in two layers: a shared base file describes its animations, and a specific file adds its display name and combat numbers. To change the displayed name, which file should you override?
options: The specific file that holds the name and combat numbers
The shared base file, since everything else inherits from it
Both files together, or the game rejects the monster
Neither file, since displayed names live inside the game's executable
questions.explanation: Change the layer that actually holds the data you want to alter. Overriding the shared base would affect every record that inherits from it.

questions.prompt: A data file for a monster starts with a line that includes a shared base file, then sets only a new name and health. What does the include achieve?
options: The record inherits shared fields, so only the differences are listed
It downloads the base file from the game's server every time it launches
It locks the base values so the new file is not able to override them
It merges the two files into one permanent file stored on the disk
questions.explanation: An include lets a record reuse shared data and override just a few fields. This keeps files short and consistent with the base definition.

questions.prompt: Why might a data-file validator accept only a short allow-list of characters in identifiers instead of rejecting a list of known bad characters?
options: Anything not on the allowed list is rejected, including characters nobody thought of
Block-lists are slower to check than allow-lists in every programming language
Games cannot store identifiers that use more than a few kinds of characters
Allow-lists make the data files compress better when stored in the pack
questions.explanation: A deny-list only stops what its author remembered to include. An allow-list fails closed, which is safer for untrusted or beginner-written data.

questions.prompt: A validator accepts a health value from 10 to 90 inclusive. Which set of test values best probes its edges?
options: 9, 10, 90 and 91, just outside and just inside each end
10, 50 and 90, the two ends and the middle of the range
0, 100 and 1000, far outside the range on either side
11, 12, 88 and 89, comfortably inside the range at each end
questions.explanation: Range bugs usually sit at the boundaries, such as using less-than where less-or-equal was meant. Testing each end and the value just beyond it catches those off-by-one mistakes.

questions.prompt: A validator only checks that a floating-point speed is greater than zero. Which value still slips through and could break later calculations?
options: Infinity, which is greater than zero but is not a usable finite number
Negative three, since negative numbers can compare as greater than zero
Zero, since zero counts as positive in floating point
A tiny value like 0.000001, since tiny values fail greater-than checks
questions.explanation: Infinity is greater than zero, so a bare greater-than test accepts it. A validator should also require the value to be finite, which also excludes not-a-number.

questions.prompt: A config file has several lines that start with the same key but carry different values. Why is loading them into a map keyed only by that key a problem?
options: A map holds one value per key, so later lines overwrite earlier ones
Maps can only store numbers, so any text values cannot be kept
The keys get sorted, which scrambles the order of the lines
Maps are too slow to handle more than one line per key
questions.explanation: When a key can repeat, collect the entries in a list, or key them on more than the name alone. A plain map silently keeps just one.

questions.prompt: Why verify the case of asset paths?
options: Windows may accept a path that Linux rejects
Flare reads only upper-case file names
Case changes how many bytes the file takes
Mixed-case paths are always rejected on Windows
questions.explanation: A name like `Zombie.PNG` can load on a case-insensitive system and fail on a case-sensitive one.

questions.prompt: Why paint a blue background behind the zombie's frames without resizing the sheet?
options: The animation file selects fixed rectangles, so a new size breaks frames
Flare rejects any PNG that is larger than the original sheet was
Resizing the sheet would also change the zombie's HP in the file
A bigger sheet would be loaded from the base mod and not from yours
questions.explanation: The chain runs from `zombie.txt` to the animation file to the sheet. Frames are fixed rectangles, so moving or resizing them shows the wrong pixels.

questions.prompt: You copy an existing game record to make a variant of it. What is the most reliable way to build up your edits?
options: Change one thing, test it in the game, then change the next
Make all the planned edits first, then test once, since testing is slow
Edit several files at once so the game reports every error together
Change the fields you are least sure about first, all at the same time
questions.explanation: Small steps tie any new problem to the one edit that just changed. With many edits at once you cannot tell which one broke it.

questions.prompt: A mod's manifest records which game version it was tested against. What is that for?
options: Letting an installer warn when versions differ, since layouts can change
Locking the mod so it runs only on one particular player's computer
Making the game update itself automatically to that exact version
Proving that the mod's author is the game's official developer
questions.explanation: Layouts and asset paths can change between builds, so recording the tested version lets tools check compatibility before installing.

questions.prompt: Why is a supported data-file mod better than a live memory patch when both reach the goal?
options: The diff is readable, the game can validate it, and players can uninstall it
It runs faster, because the game skips every check on plain data files
It cannot be undone afterwards, which is what keeps each unit stable
It works on any game, since all of them share the same data file names
questions.explanation: File-based mods are inspectable, versioned, and removable, and no raw process memory is touched.

questions.prompt: An installer builds a destination by joining an archive entry's name onto its mods folder, then checks that the resulting string starts with the mods folder's name. Why can an entry containing `..` components still escape that folder?
options: The string still begins with the folder name; each `..` is resolved later
Operating systems ignore `..` components inside names that come from archives
The check is skipped whenever the entry name contains a backslash
Joined paths are cut to a fixed length, so extra components are dropped
questions.explanation: Joining is plain string concatenation, so a prefix check passes. The climb out of the folder happens later, when the operating system resolves each `..`.

questions.prompt: In many path libraries, what happens when an absolute path is joined onto a base folder?
options: The absolute path replaces the base, so the result ignores the base folder
The absolute path is appended after the base, giving a longer combined path
The join fails with an error, so nothing is produced
The drive letter is dropped and the rest is placed inside the base
questions.explanation: Joining an absolute path discards the base. That makes absolute entry names in an archive even more dangerous than `..`.

questions.prompt: Starting from the folder `D:\Games\Arena\Content\mods`, how many `..` components in a row are needed to reach the root of drive D:?
questions.explanation: Each `..` climbs one level: mods to Content, Content to Arena, Arena to Games, Games to the drive root. That is four.

questions.prompt: To make archive entry names safe, why is parsing a path into components and accepting only plain names better than deleting suspicious text such as `..` from the string?
options: Removing text can leave an escape behind, or even create a new one
Component parsing is faster, and speed is the main risk of text removal
Removing text changes the archive's checksum, so the file cannot be extracted
Suspicious text only occurs in compressed archives and not in plain folders
questions.explanation: Deleting text from `....//` leaves `../`, and odd separators, drive prefixes and links offer other disguises. Allow only an explicitly safe relative form instead.

questions.prompt: A path inside the destination folder is validated, but just before writing, a folder on that path is swapped for a link that points elsewhere. What kind of problem is this, and what reduces it?
options: A check-then-use race; a private staging folder and refusing links
A hash collision; switching to a stronger hash function would help
A buffer overflow; using a longer buffer for each path would help
A compression bug; switching to a different archive format would help
questions.explanation: The thing that was checked is not necessarily the thing that is written to. A fresh private folder, no links, and a final inspection leave far less room to swap anything.

questions.prompt: A ZIP library offers a helper that returns nothing when an entry name would land outside the extraction root. How should an installer treat that result?
options: As an error that stops the install, because the entry is unsafe
As an empty name that can be skipped while the rest installs
As a hint to rewrite the name by removing the `..` parts
As a sign that the entry is a folder and needs no further check
questions.explanation: Failing closed is the safe policy. An archive with one escaping entry is not trustworthy, so the installer rejects it instead of repairing it.

questions.prompt: ZIP entry names conventionally use `/` as the separator. Why might an installer on Windows reject names that contain a backslash?
options: A name that looks like a flat file elsewhere could be a folder path on Windows
The ZIP format reserves the backslash to mark encrypted entries
A backslash makes the entry's recorded size unreliable
Windows quietly turns backslashes into forward slashes, so they are redundant
questions.explanation: Different systems read separators differently. Rejecting the ambiguous name removes the chance that a harmless-looking name means something else on the target.

questions.prompt: When copying an archive entry with a size limit of N bytes, why read up to N + 1 bytes instead of stopping at exactly N?
options: The extra byte reveals an oversized entry instead of silently truncating it
The extra byte is a terminator that marks the end of the file
Reading one more byte makes the copy faster by aligning to the buffer
Counting starts at zero, so a limit of N really allows N + 1 bytes
questions.explanation: Stopping at exactly N would write a cut-off file that looks fine. Reading one more byte lets the check notice the entry was bigger than allowed.

questions.prompt: An entry declares 10 bytes but produces more while it is copied. What catches this?
options: The count of bytes actually written, compared with the declared size
The declared size in the header, since it is checked before copying
The file extension, which has to match the content of the entry
The magic bytes found at the very start of the entry's data
questions.explanation: Declared sizes are claims by the archive. Only the counted bytes are trusted.

questions.prompt: An archive holds 200,000 tiny files, all with safe paths and small sizes. Why might an installer still cap the number of entries?
options: Huge counts can exhaust time, memory or disk, even if each file is small
Each path becomes automatically unsafe once an archive has many entries
A large entry count means the archive must be encrypted somewhere
The ZIP format cannot record more than a handful of entries at once
questions.explanation: Size caps on each file and the total do not stop a flood of tiny files. Limits on counts are part of treating archives as untrusted input.

questions.prompt: A per-entry limit is written as 32 * 1024 * 1024 bytes. How many bytes is that?
questions.explanation: 32 × 1,024 × 1,024 = 33,554,432, which is 32 MiB. Writing 32,000,000 mixes up decimal megabytes with binary mebibytes.

questions.prompt: What does opening an output file in a mode that fails if the path already exists protect an extractor against?
options: Overwriting an existing file or writing through a planted link
Writing a file that is larger than the limit set for the archive
Running out of disk space during a long extraction
Extracting an entry whose name uses uppercase letters
questions.explanation: The open call fails if anything is already at the path, so a duplicate entry name or a planted link cannot be written through.

questions.prompt: In the nine-step transaction, which step comes right before moving validated files into place?
options: Backing up the affected original files
Hashing every one of the staged files
Parsing the mod manifest in the package
Creating the new staging directory
questions.explanation: The order is: show the replacement plan, back up originals, move, and record an uninstall manifest. The backup is the way back.

questions.prompt: A multi-step installer extracts into a temporary staging folder, and validation fails midway. What cleanup is correct?
options: Delete only the staging folder it created, leaving player files alone
Delete the whole mods folder to be sure nothing partial remains
Leave the staging folder in place so the next install can resume
Delete any game files whose names match the staged files
questions.explanation: Staging exists to keep a half-installed mod away from the real game. Cleanup must be limited to what the installer itself made, or it risks the player's own files.

questions.prompt: A file-format signature begins with a byte above 127, such as 0x89. Why is that a good design?
options: Plain text never starts with it, and stripping the top bit breaks the signature
Bytes above 127 are faster for a decoder to compare than ordinary text bytes
It tells the decoder that the image is larger than 127 pixels in each direction
It marks the file as encrypted so only the right program opens it
questions.explanation: ASCII stops at 127, so a high first byte separates binary files from text. If a transfer strips the top bit, the signature no longer matches and the damage is noticed.

questions.prompt: Why do some file signatures include a carriage return and line feed pair among their first bytes?
options: Line-ending conversion changes the bytes, so damaged files stop matching
They tell the decoder to begin a new row of pixels in the image data
They let text editors display the signature on a line of its own
They mark where the compressed data begins inside the file
questions.explanation: Converting between line-ending styles adds or removes bytes, so the signature no longer matches and the damage shows up before any decoding.

questions.prompt: A file named `photo.png` is actually an executable. Which check is most likely to catch this?
options: Comparing its first bytes with the signature of the claimed format
Checking that the extension is lowercase and three letters long
Checking that the file is smaller than one megabyte in size
Checking that the file name contains no spaces or odd symbols
questions.explanation: Extensions are only hints. Magic bytes expose an obvious mismatch, though a full decoder should still check sizes and limits.

questions.prompt: What is a manifest in a mod installer?
options: A machine-readable receipt of what the install changed
A compressed copy of every file in the game folder
A list of the game's known cheat codes and offsets
A password that unlocks the mod folder for writing
questions.explanation: It records the mod, version, destination paths, hashes, backup location, and status, so the installer knows exactly what it did.

questions.prompt: Why avoid absolute paths in a portable manifest?
options: The game root is kept apart, and enclosed relative paths resolve under it
Absolute paths are always longer than the hashes stored beside them
Only relative paths can be hashed with SHA-256 by the installer
Absolute paths cannot be written into a JSON file by the installer
questions.explanation: Relative paths work on any machine and, once enclosed, cannot point outside the game folder.

questions.prompt: An installer records two kinds of changes: files it created, and files it replaced. How is each one undone?
options: Delete the created file; put back a saved copy of the replaced file
Delete both, since the game recreates its own files on the next launch
Restore both from backups, since a backup is made for every change
Keep both, since removing files might break the game
questions.explanation: A created file did not exist before, so removing it is the undo. A replaced file needs the original restored from its backup.

questions.prompt: Why would a reversible installer track 'new file' and 'replaced existing file' as separate kinds of change?
options: So uninstalling never deletes a file that existed before the mod
So that replaced files install faster than brand new files do
So that the change record stays under a size limit on disk
So that two mods can never touch the same path in the game
questions.explanation: If every change looked the same, an uninstall might delete something that belonged to the game rather than to the mod.

questions.prompt: An installer planned to replace a file and recorded that file's hash at planning time. By install time, the file's current hash is different. What should the installer do?
options: Stop with an error, since overwriting could destroy an unexpected change
Go ahead, since the mod's file is newer than whatever is on disk
Replace the file but skip the backup, since the recorded hash is stale
Quietly update the recorded hash and continue with the install
questions.explanation: The plan was made against a different file than the one now on disk. Comparing hashes right before acting prevents acting on stale assumptions.

questions.prompt: The check that compares a file's hash with the one recorded at planning time is an example of what?
options: An optimistic concurrency check, assuming no change and then verifying
A checksum repair, which rewrites a damaged file until the sums match
A signature verification, which proves who published the game file
A compression test, which checks that the file would shrink in an archive
questions.explanation: It assumes nothing changed and verifies that assumption before acting. A mismatch means the file no longer belongs only to the recorded transaction.

questions.prompt: The installer crashes after making a backup but before copying the mod's file. How does recovery know what to do?
options: The manifest records the stage reached, so the original needs restoring
Recovery compares the modification times of the backup and the game file
Recovery deletes every file in the mod folder and starts the install again
Recovery asks the player which of the two versions they would prefer
questions.explanation: The status is stored durably, so recovery reads `BackedUp` and knows the replacement was not completed.

questions.prompt: What is the safe way to update the manifest?
options: Write a temporary file, flush it, check it parses, then replace the old one
Edit the manifest in place so that no extra file is ever created
Delete the old manifest first so that only a single copy of it exists
Write the new manifest only after the install has fully finished
questions.explanation: The receipt is part of the modification. A half-written manifest would hide what state the install reached.

questions.prompt: To uninstall a created file, the current hash no longer matches the mod's installed hash. What should the uninstaller do?
options: Report that someone changed it and leave it alone
Delete it anyway, since the mod was the one that created it
Replace it with a copy of the mod's original file instead
Mark it `Restored` and move on to the next file in the list
questions.explanation: A different hash means a later edit. Deleting it would erase someone's newer work.

questions.prompt: When uninstalling a replaced file, what is verified before restoring?
options: The file matches the installed hash and the backup matches the original
The backup is older than the current file in the game folder
The mod's version number is the newest one listed in the manifest
No other program currently has the game folder open on the system
questions.explanation: Both hashes confirm that the file is still the mod's and that the backup is the true original, so the restore is safe.

questions.prompt: Two mods each replace the same game file, and each works fine alone. What should a mod installer do when both are selected?
options: Report the clash before installing, rather than letting one silently win
