Install both in alphabetical order, since order does not matter
Install whichever file is larger, since it probably has more changes
Install neither mod and delete both of their records
questions.explanation: Each mod expects its own version of the file, so combining them is a real conflict. Showing it first lets the player choose instead of getting a surprise.

questions.prompt: To find clashing mods, a tool builds a map from each file path to the mods that touch it. What should it keep to report the clashes?
options: Only the paths touched by more than one mod
Only the paths touched by exactly one mod
Only the paths with the longest names
Every path, with the mods sorted by name
questions.explanation: Paths with a single owner are harmless. Filtering the map down to entries with several owners leaves exactly the real clashes.

questions.prompt: In the recovery test, you edit one installed file by hand and then uninstall. What should happen?
options: The edited file is kept, with a warning
The edited file is deleted, since it came from the mod
The edited file is replaced silently with the backup
The uninstall stops and all files are removed
questions.explanation: The hash no longer matches, so the policy is to avoid erasing the user's later work and to say so.

questions.prompt: Why does the recovery test interrupt the installer after the backup step?
options: To confirm the original survives and recovery finishes from the status
To make sure the mod's files are larger in size than the backup is
To measure how long the hashing step takes on a large texture
To check that the mod keeps working on two different game builds
questions.explanation: The crash point between backup and install is where an unrecorded install would lose the original.

questions.prompt: Which tool is reversible and needs no secret?
options: Encoding, such as Base64
A hash, such as SHA-256
A MAC, such as Poly1305
Encryption, such as XChaCha20
questions.explanation: Encoding only represents data in another form, so anyone can undo it. A hash cannot be reversed, and MACs and encryption need a key.

questions.prompt: What does a MAC give you that a plain hash does not?
options: Detection of changes made by someone without the secret key
A way to read the original bytes back from the fingerprint
A fingerprint that is the same size as the original file
A guarantee that nobody can ever copy the file
questions.explanation: Anyone can recompute a hash, but a valid MAC needs the key. A MAC does not hide the data.

questions.prompt: Why is AEAD a sound starting point for a new encrypted file?
options: Secrecy without tamper detection is incomplete, and AEAD adds the check
It makes the key shorter, so the key is simpler to store safely
It compresses the plaintext first, which makes every save smaller
It removes the need for a nonce, since the key is always fresh
questions.explanation: AEAD hides the plaintext and authenticates it and its context, so a flipped bit is caught.

questions.prompt: With symmetric encryption, what problem remains?
options: The shared key has to reach the other side unseen
The ciphertext is always larger than the plaintext it came from
Only public data can ever be encrypted with a shared key
It is far too slow to use on large files such as saves
questions.explanation: One key both locks and unlocks, so both sides need the same secret. It is efficient for large payloads.

questions.prompt: The open-padlock picture explains public-key encryption. What does it leave out?
options: Whose public key you received, since identity needs a separate check
How to make the padlock stronger by choosing a longer key
Why the private key may safely be shared with a trusted friend
How a padlock manages to lock a file that is stored on disk
questions.explanation: The picture does not tell you who owns a key, or explain key agreement.

questions.prompt: Which question is part of a threat model's trust boundary?
options: Which program, account, or server may hold the key and decide?
Which of the cipher names is the longest one to type out?
How many bytes does the nonce take up inside the envelope?
Which compression method does the save file happen to use?
questions.explanation: The four statements are asset, adversary, property, and trust boundary. The cipher comes after them.

questions.prompt: Why can encryption alone not create a server-like secret for an offline save?
options: The same PC must decrypt it, so an owner can watch the key in use
The save is too small for a cipher to protect in any useful way
A single-player game is unable to use a MAC on its save files
Encrypted files cannot be copied to a backup location at all
questions.explanation: The player controls the machine that holds the key. Encryption can still protect against casual disclosure or accidental edits.

questions.prompt: An encryption scheme stores a 12-byte nonce, then the ciphertext (the same length as the message), then a 16-byte authentication tag. How long is the stored result for a 50-byte message?
options: 78 bytes
66 bytes
62 bytes
50 bytes
questions.explanation: 12 + 50 + 16 = 78. Leaving out the tag gives 62, and leaving out the nonce gives 66.

questions.prompt: What is true of the 24-byte nonce?
options: It need not be hidden, but must not repeat under one key
It must be kept secret in the same way that the key is
It can be reused freely as long as the plaintext changes
It is derived from the save's file name every single time
questions.explanation: The decryption code needs the same nonce, so it is stored in front of the ciphertext. A repeated nonce under the same key breaks the guarantee.

questions.prompt: An authenticated-encryption seal covers a note that is stored in plain view, such as 'slot 3'. What happens if someone tries to open it while supplying 'slot 4' as that note?
options: Opening fails, since the note is covered by the tag though it is not encrypted
It opens normally, since a note that is not encrypted is ignored
It opens, but returns garbage because the wrong note acts as a wrong key
It opens and silently relabels the data as belonging to slot 4
questions.explanation: Associated data is not hidden, but it is part of what the tag authenticates. Changing it breaks verification, so the data cannot be moved between contexts.

questions.prompt: What should the opener do when authentication fails?
options: Return an error and no partly decrypted data
Return the bytes already decrypted, along with a warning message
Retry the decryption with a different nonce until it works
Delete the envelope from the disk and then continue on
questions.explanation: Fail closed means a failed check yields nothing usable.

questions.prompt: Why return one generic failure instead of saying which part was wrong?
options: Detailed errors could become an oracle for an untrusted caller
The tag is nearly always the wrong part when a failure happens
Rust is unable to define more than one error type per program
The player would be confused by the longer error messages shown
questions.explanation: Telling an attacker whether the key, nonce, tag, or context failed gives them a way to learn from the errors.

questions.prompt: Perfect encryption code ships with its key committed to Git. What is the verdict?
options: It is still broken, since anyone with the repository has the key
It is fine, since the key is only 32 bytes long in the source
It is fine as long as the repository happens to be small in size
It is broken only if the nonce is also reused with that key
questions.explanation: The key is the hard part. Where it is created and stored matters as much as the algorithm.

questions.prompt: Each extra bit in a key does what to the number of possible keys?
options: Doubles it
Adds one more
Multiplies it by ten
Leaves it unchanged
questions.explanation: 128 bits gives 2¹²⁸ keys. Every 10 bits multiply the count by about 1,000.

questions.prompt: A billion computers each test a trillion keys per second against a 128-bit key. About how long to try every key?
options: About 11 billion years
About 11 days
About 11 million years
About 11 minutes
questions.explanation: That is 10²¹ keys per second, about 3.2 × 10²⁸ a year, against 3.4 × 10³⁸ keys, about 1.1 × 10¹⁰ years.

questions.prompt: How many six-letter lowercase passwords exist, and how long at a billion guesses per second?
options: 308,915,776, about a third of a second
17,576, a few microseconds
308,915,776, about 11 billion years
26, less than a millisecond
questions.explanation: 26⁶ = 308,915,776, so all of them take about 0.3 s. That is why passwords need a slow key-derivation function.

questions.prompt: Why run a password through a deliberately slow key-derivation function?
options: So that every guess costs the attacker real time
So that the key it produces becomes shorter than the password
So that the original password can be recovered from the key
So that the ciphertext that is produced becomes smaller on disk
questions.explanation: A small secret falls to brute force quickly. A slow derivation multiplies the cost of each guess.

questions.prompt: After a key is rotated, what must the design provide?
options: A way to tell old envelopes apart and read or migrate them
Nothing more, since every old save is deleted at the rotation
A copy of the new key stored inside each of the old envelopes
A fresh nonce written into each of the old files on the disk
questions.explanation: Rotation needs version metadata or similar, so old envelopes stay readable or are migrated.

questions.prompt: Why does a key lifecycle need a recovery path?
options: Without one, a lost key means the player's save is gone for good
Recovery makes the decryption step run a lot faster than before
Recovery lets anyone who finds the file read the save contents
The nonce stored in each envelope depends on the recovery path
questions.explanation: Availability is part of the design. A correct authenticated file still needs backups, version metadata, and a way back.

questions.prompt: Why does an unkeyed checksum not prove who created a save?
options: Anyone who can edit it can recompute it; a tag needs a key
It is always longer than the authentication tag would be
Checksums can only be computed by the game's own code
It encrypts the file using a weak key before it is saved
questions.explanation: A checksum detects accidental damage. A MAC or AEAD tag makes a different promise because it needs the key.

questions.prompt: The same byte value 5 can mean coins or status flags. What establishes that meaning?
options: The order of the debugger’s window tabs.
The format and code that use the byte.
The number of set bits in the byte alone.
The address’s final hexadecimal digit.
questions.explanation: A numeric representation does not label its role. The consuming code and declared format establish the interpretation.

questions.prompt: Why use AND with a one-bit mask to inspect an alarm flag?
options: It reverses all selected and unselected bits.
It moves the flag into a different process.
It isolates that selected bit’s current value.
It sets every other position to a known one.
questions.explanation: AND produces 1 at a position only if both the byte and mask contain 1 there, isolating the selected flag.

questions.prompt: A mask selects two flags, but the AND result equals only one selected bit. What is true?
options: Both flags are set because the result is nonzero.
No flag is set because the result is below the mask.
The selected flags have moved to different addresses.
At least one selected flag is set, but not both.
questions.explanation: A nonzero result tests any selected bit. Equality with the mask tests that all selected bits are set.

questions.prompt: Why use OR rather than XOR when the request is to turn a lamp on?
options: OR leaves an already-on lamp bit on.
OR always switches an already-on bit off.
OR clears all bits outside the lamp mask.
OR moves the lamp bit toward the byte’s edge.
questions.explanation: OR sets selected positions to 1 regardless of their previous state. XOR would toggle an already-set bit off.

questions.prompt: Why does clearing one flag use AND with an inverted one-bit mask?
options: The target gains a new address for every operation.
The target becomes zero while other bits survive.
The target becomes one while other bits disappear.
The target moves left while other bits rotate right.
questions.explanation: The clearing mask has 0 at the target and 1 elsewhere. AND clears that target and preserves all other input bits.

questions.prompt: What happens when the same XOR mask is applied twice to a byte?
options: Every unselected position becomes permanently zero.
The byte grows by twice the numeric mask value.
The flipped positions return to their initial state.
The mask’s positions become permanently set to one.
questions.explanation: XOR toggles each selected bit, so a second identical toggle restores it. Unselected positions remain unchanged.

questions.prompt: Why must you record the width when interpreting NOT?
options: It changes one bit for every decimal digit shown.
It rotates the highest bit into a new memory page.
It only reverses flags named by the source program.
It flips every bit within the operand’s type.
questions.explanation: NOT on u8 flips eight positions; a wider integer has more positions to flip and therefore a different numeric result.

questions.prompt: When does shifting an unsigned value left once double its value without losing information?
options: When the doubled value fits the chosen width.
When its original value has exactly two set bits.
When every incoming position is filled with one.
When the mask points at the least significant bit.
questions.explanation: A valid left shift introduces zero on the right. If a high bit leaves the width, it is discarded and doubling no longer fits.

questions.prompt: An eight-bit 10000001 is shifted left once. Why does the result equal 2?
options: The decimal digits are rearranged into a smaller value.
The high bit is discarded and the low bit moves left.
The high bit wraps around and replaces the low bit.
The byte expands into a new sixteen-bit storage field.
questions.explanation: A logical shift retains the chosen width. The outgoing high bit is lost, leaving 00000010.

questions.prompt: Why can unsigned right shift produce 2 from decimal 5?
options: It adds a high bit to keep the original value odd.
It changes the stored type into a fractional number.
It discards the low bit, like division rounded down.
It preserves the low bit by wrapping it to the top.
questions.explanation: Unsigned logical right shift fills the left with zeros and discards low bits, matching integer division by two for a one-bit shift.

questions.prompt: What does Rust checked_shl check for an eight-bit value?
options: Whether every outgoing bit would have been zero.
Whether the input has exactly eight set bits.
Whether the result uses the same decimal digits.
Whether the shift count is less than eight.
questions.explanation: checked_shl returns None when the count is at least the width. A valid count can still discard high bits.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a rotation from a logical shift at the same width?
options: Outgoing bits wrap to the opposite edge.
Outgoing bits are replaced by new random bits.
The result always has the same numeric value.
The operand grows by one byte at every step.
questions.explanation: Rotation retains the bits by wrapping them around. A logical shift discards outgoing bits and introduces zeros.

questions.prompt: A rotation changes a byte’s numeric value. Which property does it preserve?
options: The decimal sum before the operation began.
The number of positions containing one.
The weight assigned to every original one.
The identity of the least significant bit.
questions.explanation: Rotation moves bits without creating or discarding them, preserving the count of set bits while their weights may change.

questions.prompt: Why does rotating a byte by eight positions return its starting value?
options: Every numeric value has eight decimal digits.
Every flag handler stores an extra backup byte.
Every bit travels once around the eight positions.
Every bit is discarded and restored from the mask.
questions.explanation: Rotation wraps within the byte width. Eight steps place every bit back at its starting position.

questions.prompt: A format puts quantity in the low four bits. Why mask with 00001111 to read it?
options: To shift the quantity into the upper four positions.
To turn every quantity position into a set flag.
To combine the fields into one decimal digit each.
To preserve those bits and discard the upper field.
questions.explanation: AND with the low-four-bit mask keeps the quantity and removes contributions from the upper field.

questions.prompt: A field occupies the upper four bits of one byte. What does shifting right four accomplish?
options: It moves the field down to weights starting at one.
It preserves the field at exactly its former weights.
It replaces the field with its original byte address.
It toggles the field while leaving its position fixed.
questions.explanation: The low four bits are discarded; the upper field moves down so its value can be read using ordinary low-bit weights.

questions.prompt: Why is Rust’s numeric bitwise AND different from boolean &&?
options: One uses decimal values; the other uses hexadecimal only.
One combines bit positions; the other combines conditions.
One always returns true; the other always returns a byte.
One reads remote memory; the other rewrites the source file.
questions.explanation: Numeric & operates on corresponding bit positions. Boolean && combines true/false operands and has short-circuit behavior.

questions.title: Calculate before reading
questions.prompt: Code calculates the address of a player field but performs no load there. What has it learned?
options: A candidate location, without learning the field value yet
The field value, because every address calculation reads it
The object lifetime, because a calculated address is valid
The source variable name, because field offsets encode names
questions.explanation: Address arithmetic calculates where bytes would be. A separate memory access is needed to learn their contents, and validity and lifetime still require evidence.

questions.title: Step through records
questions.prompt: A player record is 24 bytes wide and health is eight bytes into it. How should the next player be reached?
options: Advance the record base by 24, then add the field offset
Advance the record base by eight, then reuse the old value
Advance the record base by four, since health has four bytes
Advance the record base by one, because the index is a count
questions.explanation: Record stride and field width are different. Each next record begins 24 bytes later; its health field is still eight bytes into that record.

questions.title: Separate two overflow questions
questions.prompt: A 32-bit value holding all one bits receives one more. As unsigned it exceeds its range; as signed it is minus one plus one. Which interpretation fits?
options: Unsigned carry occurs, while this signed sum still fits
Signed overflow occurs, while this unsigned sum still fits
Both sums exceed their ranges because the stored bits wrap
Neither sum exceeds its range because the result is zero
questions.explanation: The stored result is zero. CF reports the unsigned carry beyond 32 bits; signed minus one plus one equals zero and does not set signed overflow.

questions.title: Interpret the signed boundary
questions.prompt: Adding one to the largest positive signed 32-bit value sets signed overflow but no unsigned carry. Why?
options: The signed sum is too large, but the unsigned sum fits
The unsigned sum is too large, but the signed sum fits
A positive input disables carry until a negative one arrives
The result width grows automatically to keep the sum exact
questions.explanation: The same bits have different ranges under signed and unsigned interpretations. OF and CF report those separate boundary questions.

questions.title: Know who wrote a flag
questions.prompt: A count increases by one using an operation that preserves the carry flag. Carry was already set. What does carry now prove about this increase?
options: Nothing new; it still records the earlier flag producer
That this increase overflowed the unsigned count exactly
That this increase overflowed the signed count exactly
That this increase stored zero in the destination register
questions.explanation: A preserved flag is old information. The increment may update zero, sign, and overflow flags, but its preserved carry is not a fresh carry result.

questions.title: Read the chosen width
questions.prompt: An instruction stores one byte into a four-byte game field. What should you check before treating the whole field as replaced?
options: Which remaining bytes were left unchanged by that store
Which register became four times wider after that store
Which field name was encoded inside the stored byte value
Which page acquired execution permission after that store
questions.explanation: A one-byte store replaces only its selected byte. The remaining bytes can keep older contents, so the complete four-byte value may differ from a simple reading of the new byte.

questions.title: Keep the full product in mind
questions.prompt: Signed multiplication keeps only the low 32 bits and reports that the exact product did not fit. What is safe to conclude?
options: The stored bits are truncated, so the reward needs handling
The stored bits are exact, because multiplication never wraps
The source field was erased, because multiplication consumes it
The zero flag proves success, because every product sets it
questions.explanation: A low-width product can differ from the exact mathematical signed result. Overflow reporting needs handling; undefined result flags cannot establish success.

questions.title: Prepare the whole dividend
questions.prompt: A signed divide instruction reads a double-width dividend from two registers. The low register is correct but the high one is stale. What is the problem?
options: The combined dividend can differ from the intended value
The stale high register is ignored for every small divisor
The quotient is correct but its decimal display is reversed
The divisor automatically replaces the stale high register
questions.explanation: The implicit high half is part of the dividend. Preparing only the low register is insufficient; signed division normally needs the appropriate sign extension.

questions.title: Understand rounding toward zero
questions.prompt: A signed coin adjustment of minus seven is divided by three using truncation toward zero. What quotient and remainder result?
options: Quotient minus two, with a remainder of minus one
Quotient minus three, with a remainder of positive two
Quotient positive two, with a remainder of positive one
Quotient minus one, with a remainder of positive four
questions.explanation: Truncation toward zero gives minus two. The remainder makes the identity hold: minus seven equals minus two times three plus minus one.

questions.title: Guard division before it runs
questions.prompt: A sharing rule has a valid coin total but zero participants. What should a division-based implementation do?
options: Handle the zero-participant case before attempting division
Divide first and inspect the carry flag for the missing result
Divide first and treat the previous quotient as the new share
Use the zero divisor as a request to divide the total by one
questions.explanation: Integer division by zero raises a divide-error exception. The game rule must define and guard the zero-participant case before invoking the instruction.

questions.title: Check the quotient range
questions.prompt: A divisor is nonzero, but the exact signed quotient cannot fit the destination register. Is the divide automatically safe?
options: No; a quotient-range failure can raise divide error as well
Yes; every nonzero divisor guarantees that the quotient fits
Yes; the processor silently returns a wider register result
No; the processor always clears both input registers first
questions.explanation: A nonzero divisor removes only one failure case. A quotient that does not fit the instruction result width can also raise divide error.

questions.title: Widen an unsigned field
questions.prompt: An unsigned eight-bit count has all eight bits set. It is widened by filling new high bits with zeros. What is preserved?
options: Its numeric value of 255 in the wider representation
Its numeric value of minus one in the wider representation
Its original memory address as the wider numeric value
Its original bit width while only its variable name changes
questions.explanation: Zero extension preserves the numeric value of an unsigned smaller field. Eight one bits become a wider value with zeros above them, still 255.

questions.title: Widen a signed field
questions.prompt: A signed eight-bit movement delta represents minus one. Why repeat its top bit when widening it?
options: Repeating the sign bit preserves the signed numeric value
Repeating the sign bit turns the delta into an unsigned count
Repeating the sign bit validates the pointer to the game object
Repeating the sign bit preserves only its least significant bit
questions.explanation: Sign extension fills the new high bits with the old sign bit. In two-complement representation this keeps minus one as minus one rather than interpreting it as 255.

questions.title: Separate address from lifetime
questions.prompt: Address arithmetic gives a plausible field location. What additional evidence is needed before reading it?
options: That the mapping and intended object are valid for the access
That the address has the same final digit as the field offset
That a previous run once used an object at the same location
That the instruction calculating it left the zero flag clear
questions.explanation: A plausible location does not establish a live object or accessible mapping. Bounds, lifetime, mapping permissions, and the intended layout still matter.

questions.title: Inspect without deleting
questions.prompt: A status word contains several independent bits. You want to inspect one bit while keeping every status value intact. What operation is needed?
options: A temporary masked comparison that discards its bit result
A masked store that keeps only the selected status bit alive
A complement of the entire status word before inspecting it
A shift that permanently removes every bit below the target
questions.explanation: A masked test can update flags from a temporary AND without changing the original status word. A stored AND would clear unselected bits.

questions.title: Choose the intended ordering
questions.prompt: The same 32 bits represent minus one as signed and a very large value as unsigned. Can comparisons with a small positive number choose opposite paths?
options: Yes; signed and unsigned ordering interpret those bits differently
No; the flags store the source language type along with each result
No; all ordering comparisons must use the same highest-bit test
Yes; only because the comparison also rewrites the original value
questions.explanation: A signed less-than condition uses sign and overflow; unsigned below uses borrow. Their different interpretations can produce opposite ordering for identical operand bits.

questions.title: Keep comparison results live
questions.prompt: A comparison is followed by arithmetic before its conditional branch. What needs checking?
options: Whether the arithmetic replaced flags that the branch will read
Whether the branch restored the original source-code field names
Whether the arithmetic resized the branch into a new CPU register
Whether the comparison automatically froze all following flags
questions.explanation: Flags are current processor state, not a permanent attachment to the earlier comparison. A later arithmetic instruction can replace the condition that the branch reads.

questions.title: Distinguish a jump from a call
questions.prompt: A control transfer enters a helper without saving a return address. Which expectation is unsafe?
options: Expecting an ordinary return to know where the transfer came from
Expecting the instruction pointer to change to the helper location
Expecting the helper to execute instructions at its own location
Expecting earlier game memory to remain available in the process
questions.explanation: An ordinary jump does not save a continuation. A return consumes an existing stack address; the surrounding code must deliberately establish it.

questions.title: Save the correct continuation
questions.prompt: An ordinary near call saves a return address. Which point should that address identify?
options: The instruction immediately after the call in the caller
The first instruction of the helper that was just entered
The most recent memory field read before the call occurred
The end of the entire program regardless of which helper ran
questions.explanation: The saved continuation lets the helper return to the next instruction in its caller. It is neither a pointer to the helper start nor a game-data field.

questions.title: Know who made the result
questions.prompt: A helper calculates a number in a result register and then returns. Which action actually produced the numeric result?
options: The helper calculation, with the calling convention choosing its register
The return instruction, which computes a new number from the stack bytes
The call instruction, which always initializes all result registers to zero
The saved address, which changes into the numeric result during the return
questions.explanation: Return transfers control using the saved address. The helper instructions produced the result; the calling convention explains where the caller expects it.

questions.title: Reverse temporary saves
questions.prompt: Code saves two registers on a last-in, first-out stack. How should it restore those saved values?
options: Restore the last saved register first, then the earlier one
Restore the first saved register first, then the later one
Restore both into whichever register currently contains zero
Restore only one because both saves share one stack address
questions.explanation: The last pushed value is at the top. Reversing the save order restores the intended registers and avoids leaving an extra slot above the return address.

questions.title: Distinguish active storage from leftovers
questions.prompt: A stack value is popped, but inspecting the old memory slot still shows its bytes. What does that mean?
options: The bytes can remain even though that slot is no longer active
The pop failed because successful removal must erase the bytes
The popped register still borrows the slot instead of holding a value
The return address must have moved into those leftover bytes automatically
questions.explanation: Popping changes the active top and copies the value. It normally does not overwrite the old slot, so leftover bytes alone do not prove live stack data.

questions.title: Handle a zero effective count
questions.prompt: A bit-shift instruction receives an effective count of zero. What happens to the operand and its arithmetic flags?
options: Both keep their prior values rather than producing a new shift result
The operand keeps its value while all arithmetic flags become zero
The operand becomes zero while its earlier arithmetic flags survive
Both become undefined because a shift requires at least one position
questions.explanation: A zero effective shift count preserves the value and flags. For nonzero counts, specific flags change, and overflow is only defined for a one-bit shift.

questions.title: Compare shift and division rounding
questions.prompt: A negative odd integer is shifted right while repeating its sign bit. Why can that differ from signed division by two?
options: The shift rounds downward while signed division truncates toward zero
The shift rounds toward zero while signed division always rounds upward
The shift converts the number into a float before moving any of its bits
The shift uses an unsigned divisor even though the input remains signed
questions.explanation: Arithmetic right shift of a negative odd value rounds toward minus infinity. Signed integer division truncates toward zero, so minus three becomes minus two by shift but minus one by division.

questions.title: Set a state consistently
questions.prompt: A control may request the same enabled state twice. Which bit rule keeps the state enabled on both requests?
options: Set the bit with an OR mask instead of toggling it each time
Toggle the bit with an XOR mask each time the request arrives
Complement the whole word each time the request arrives
Clear the bit with an AND mask before treating it as enabled
questions.explanation: OR with a one-bit mask sets that bit whether it was previously zero or one. XOR toggles it, so two identical requests would undo each other.

questions.title: Read the entire selected width
questions.prompt: A 32-bit word is complemented, but an illustration displays only its four lowest bits. What happens to the unseen high bits?
options: They invert too, because the operation uses the full selected width
They stay unchanged, because unseen bits are outside the bit operation
They become undefined, because the drawing omits their numeric labels
They move into the low four positions before the complement is applied
questions.explanation: The displayed boxes are a partial view. A full-width bitwise complement inverts every selected bit, including the high bits absent from that illustration.

questions.title: Keep following the path
questions.prompt: An instruction performs no data operation and execution advances. Does that prevent the next instruction from spending ammo?
options: No; the next instruction still runs unless another control transfer stops it
Yes; doing no work stops all later writes until the program restarts
No; but it automatically restores any ammo spent by the next instruction
Yes; doing no work is equivalent to returning from the current function
questions.explanation: A no-op does not pause, return, or undo later work. Execution continues to the next instruction, which can still perform the ammo update.

questions.title: Inspect the state before the action
questions.prompt: A deliberate one-byte breakpoint instruction precedes an ammo subtraction. The debugger pauses on its exception. Has the later subtraction executed?
options: No; the saved continuation follows the breakpoint and precedes that action
Yes; breakpoint handling always executes the next instruction before pausing
No; because the breakpoint permanently removed that action from the function
Yes; because a breakpoint is simply a data-neutral instruction with no exception
questions.explanation: The breakpoint transfers through exception handling. In this deliberate breakpoint case, the saved next instruction is after the breakpoint byte, and continuation is a separate debugger decision.

questions.title: Check the exact copy form
questions.prompt: Two legacy scalar float copies have the same low value, but one loads from memory and one copies another XMM register. Why inspect their forms?
options: Their rules for the destination upper bits are different
Their low values must use opposite byte order in memory
Their source values both become zero after a successful copy
Their integer zero flags always disagree after the two copies
questions.explanation: Legacy movss from memory clears destination XMM bits 127:32, while the register copy preserves them. Stores write only the selected four-byte scalar.

questions.title: Keep bits and value separate
questions.prompt: An integer score is needed as a floating-point numeric value. Why is merely copying its four bytes insufficient?
options: Integer and float formats assign different meanings to the same bits
Integer and float formats require different physical memory address sizes
Every integer occupies eight bytes while every float occupies four bytes
A byte copy consumes the score before its new representation can be read
questions.explanation: Numeric conversion constructs a floating-point encoding of the integer's value. A copy instead preserves the integer bit pattern, which usually has a different meaning as a float.

questions.title: Do not read an old carry
questions.prompt: A scalar floating-point multiply is followed by an integer carry branch. What can that branch reveal about this multiplication alone?
options: Nothing reliable; that arithmetic did not make a new integer carry result
Whether the float multiplied past its unsigned 32-bit integer maximum
Whether the float result is zero because carry always becomes its zero test
Whether the float has a fractional part because carry records discarded digits
questions.explanation: Scalar SSE arithmetic uses floating-point control/status in MXCSR and preserves integer comparison flags. An integer carry branch can therefore read an earlier operation's carry.

questions.title: Allow for representable values
questions.prompt: A signed 32-bit integer fits its integer register but becomes slightly different when converted to a single-precision float. What explains this?
options: The float format cannot represent every such integer exactly
The conversion always keeps only the last decimal digit of the input
The integer register lost its low bits before the conversion was selected
The source value was unsigned because positive integers have no signed form
questions.explanation: Binary32 has limited significand precision. Some larger 32-bit integers need rounding even though they fit the integer source register.

questions.title: Know truncation direction
questions.prompt: A float value of minus 2.75 is converted to a signed integer by truncating toward zero. Which value results?
options: Minus two, because the fractional part is discarded toward zero
Minus three, because every negative fraction must round downward
Positive two, because integer conversion removes the sign bit first
Zero, because a negative fractional value has no integer representation
questions.explanation: Truncation toward zero gives minus two for minus 2.75 and two for 2.75. It differs from rounding down on negative values.

questions.title: Know what a masked invalid conversion does
questions.prompt: An out-of-range float-to-integer conversion has its invalid-operation exception masked. What can happen?
options: An indefinite integer is written and floating-point status records invalid
A larger integer register is automatically allocated for the exact answer
The source float is clamped to the largest valid input without reporting it
The zero flag becomes the exact count of missing destination bits afterward
questions.explanation: For the 32-bit cvttss2si form, masked invalid returns the indefinite integer 0x80000000 and records invalid operation in MXCSR. This is not an ordinary valid conversion result.

questions.title: Recognize the exception path
questions.prompt: A numeric conversion encounters invalid input and the corresponding floating-point exception is unmasked. Which expectation is unsafe?
options: Assuming a normal converted integer was produced before the exception path
Expecting exception handling to interrupt the ordinary conversion path
Expecting the caller to define how invalid numeric input should be handled
Expecting the result width and input range to matter when validating the value
questions.explanation: An unmasked invalid-operation condition raises an exception. Code must not assume that the normal conversion result and following store have completed.

questions.title: Validate more than the returned bits
questions.prompt: A conversion output has the same bit pattern as the valid minimum signed integer. Does that pattern alone prove conversion succeeded?
options: No; an invalid masked conversion can return that same indefinite pattern
Yes; the minimum signed integer is reserved exclusively for successful conversion
No; every successful conversion clears all destination bits before returning
Yes; invalid conversions always choose a pattern outside the integer bit width
questions.explanation: The indefinite output of a masked invalid 32-bit conversion is 0x80000000, which also encodes the valid signed minimum. Validation or appropriate status handling is needed to distinguish them.

questions.title: Leave room for unordered values
questions.prompt: A speed field contains NaN and is compared with a numeric limit. Which description is accurate?
options: Its comparison is unordered rather than less, equal, or greater
Its comparison is equal because both values occupy four bytes
Its comparison is less because every NaN represents negative infinity
Its comparison is greater because every NaN represents positive infinity
questions.explanation: NaN represents a not-a-number case. It is unordered with numeric values, and instructions define specific flag and exception behavior for that fourth outcome.

questions.title: Do not confuse unordered with equal
questions.prompt: After a completed float comparison, the zero flag is set. Why may an equality-only check be insufficient?
options: Unordered comparison can set that flag as well as true equality
Floating-point registers store the zero flag inside every value
Every less-than result sets all comparison flags to the same state
The zero flag always describes a previous integer operation instead
questions.explanation: A completed comiss comparison with invalid masked sets ZF/PF/CF to one for unordered. ZF alone therefore cannot distinguish equality from a NaN case.

questions.title: Handle invalid order first
questions.prompt: A completed float comparison offers an unordered marker plus less/equal/greater indicators. What is a sound decision order?
options: Handle unordered first, then use ordering or equality for valid numeric cases
Handle equality first and accept it whenever its indicator is present
Handle greater first and treat every remaining value as a valid smaller number
Ignore the unordered marker because it only describes unused register bits
questions.explanation: The unordered case overlaps some equality/ordering flag tests. Handling it first prevents invalid numeric input from entering a path intended for valid ordered values.

questions.title: Use the producer's flag contract
questions.prompt: Why can signed-integer branch conditions give misleading ordering after a floating-point comparison?
options: That comparison uses a different flag contract for numeric ordering
Every floating-point comparison first converts both operands to signed integers
Signed branch conditions require the source to occupy more than one XMM register
Floating-point comparison destroys the instruction pointer before any branch runs
questions.explanation: For completed comiss, SF and OF are cleared while ZF/PF/CF encode ordering and unordered. Signed-integer ordering formulas therefore do not express this comparison's intended ordering.

questions.title: Know where arithmetic rounding comes from
questions.prompt: A scalar floating-point addition must round an inexact result. In the ordinary legacy SSE form, what controls that direction?
options: The floating-point rounding setting in MXCSR
The integer carry flag from the previous arithmetic step
The number of letters in the instruction's destination name
The last memory address used to store the player's score
questions.explanation: Ordinary scalar SSE addition and multiplication round according to MXCSR. Integer flags and register names do not choose the floating-point rounding direction.

questions.title: Keep the source available
questions.prompt: A numeric conversion reads an integer source and writes a float destination. What happens to the source in that conversion alone?
options: It keeps the integer value while the destination receives a converted value
It becomes the rounded float because every conversion rewrites both operands
It becomes zero because conversion consumes its original representation
It becomes the destination address so a later conversion can find the result
questions.explanation: The source is read, not consumed. The conversion writes its destination; the source can still be used in its original numeric representation afterward.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A successful lookup is followed by another lookup that can also be absent. Which composition avoids a nested optional value?
options: Chain the fallible lookup and keep one optional layer.
Map the second lookup and keep two optional layers.
Copy the first value and ignore the second lookup.
Replace both missing cases with an invented value.
questions.explanation: Chaining an operation returning Option keeps its success or absence in one Option layer.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A parser returns either a value or a reason for failure. A transformation of success should leave that reason intact. Which behavior fits?
options: Transform failure and pass an existing success along.
Transform success and pass an existing failure along.
Transform both cases into the same success value.
Retry the parser until it produces a success value.
questions.explanation: Result mapping applies its closure to Ok and preserves an existing Err.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A successful parse feeds a conversion that can fail. What should the composed result represent?
options: A success containing both success and failure cases.
Only the parse outcome, discarding conversion failure.
The conversion outcome, or the earlier parse failure.
A default conversion value whenever parsing succeeds.
questions.explanation: Fallible chaining propagates the first failure and returns the next Result without nesting.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: An error-mapping closure translates an error into a library-specific description. What happens on success?
options: The success value becomes the translated error text.
The closure runs to validate the success value again.
The closure supplies a replacement default result.
The success value passes through without that closure.
questions.explanation: map_err changes the error side only; it does not transform success.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A function uses question mark on a failed operation. What follows inside that function?
options: It returns the compatible failure before later work.
It continues after substituting a default success.
It restarts the whole function with the same inputs.
It automatically unwinds through a panic instead.
questions.explanation: Question mark propagates a compatible failure with an early return; it is not a retry or panic.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: An optional amount becomes a Result with a chosen missing-value error. What happens to a present zero?
options: It becomes missing because zero has no positive value.
It remains successful zero; presence is the decision.
It becomes an error unless the amount is increased.
It becomes a successful default chosen by the caller.
questions.explanation: Some(0) contains a value. Absence and a numeric zero have different meanings.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: Two failures become the same missing-value marker. A caller now needs to distinguish them. What must change?
options: Give the shared marker a longer diagnostic message.
Convert every failed operation into a success value.
Preserve distinct failure causes in the return type.
Add a larger integer type to the successful value.
questions.explanation: Once causes are collapsed into one absence, later code cannot recover which cause occurred.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: An action can be ready, or cooling with a remaining duration. Which representation prevents a ready flag and duration from contradicting each other?
options: Two independent fields holding flag and duration.
A string whose spelling describes the next action.
A duration using zero to mean every possible state.
An enum whose cooling variant owns the duration.
questions.explanation: A data-carrying enum stores only the fields appropriate to the selected state.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A match arm has a guard. The pattern fits but the guard is false. What happens?
options: Later matching arms can still be considered.
The guarded arm runs with its data cleared.
The entire match returns an absent value.
Earlier matching arms are tried a second time.
questions.explanation: A guard adds a condition to that arm; a false guard lets matching continue.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A function needs the value inside a particular variant and returns immediately for other variants. Why use let-else?
options: Make every variant contain the same default value.
Bind the matching value on the continuing path.
Hide all failures without ending the current call.
Evaluate every alternative before binding a value.
questions.explanation: let-else makes the successful shape available after a branch that must leave on mismatch.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A program asks whether a value fits a pattern but needs no newly bound fields. What is the result of that test?
options: A borrowed reference to the value that matched.
A new enum containing every possible alternative.
A boolean indicating whether the pattern matched.
A replacement value chosen from the matched fields.
questions.explanation: A pattern predicate such as matches! answers true or false; it does not export pattern bindings.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A function returns Result with a custom error type. It uses question mark on another error type. What relationship is required?
options: An identical display message for both error types.
A matching integer representation for both errors.
A shared default success value for both functions.
A supported conversion into the returned error type.
questions.explanation: Propagation must convert the source error into the error type promised by the enclosing function.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: Mapping an optional value returns another optional value inside the closure. What does ordinary map produce?
options: An outer optional value containing the inner option.
One flattened optional value regardless of absence.
A failure reason copied from the lookup operation.
The original value without calling the new closure.
questions.explanation: map wraps the closure result; use and_then when the closure already returns Option and one layer is desired.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A checked subtraction returns absence when a charge is too large. Why is that useful?
options: The caller gets an automatically wrapped balance.
The caller can refuse a balance it cannot represent.
The caller gets a balance clamped to a game limit.
The caller learns the reason for every lookup failure.
questions.explanation: checked_sub reports an unrepresentable result. It does not wrap, clamp, or explain unrelated failures.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A query keeps values matching a condition, transforms them, and combines them into one answer. Which sequence fits?
options: Map, then discard the accumulator, then copy values.
Filter, then map, then fold over the kept values.
Fold, then repeat each item, then restore all values.
Copy, then sort the source, then ignore the condition.
questions.explanation: Filtering selects, mapping transforms, and folding accumulates; their order changes what each operation sees.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A filter predicate receives a borrowed item. Why can that be useful?
options: The predicate can always replace the original item.
The iterator must copy every item before checking it.
The iterator can still yield that item after checking.
The predicate must take ownership of the whole source.
questions.explanation: The predicate can inspect an item while the iterator retains it for possible output.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A parser compares each sample with its immediate successor. What distinguishes windows from fixed chunks?
options: Adjacent windows discard every final complete pair.
Adjacent windows always own copies of the source.
Adjacent windows need no length or size boundary.
Adjacent windows overlap; fixed chunks do not.
questions.explanation: A window advances by one element; complete chunks advance by their group size.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A buffer contains complete fixed-size records plus a short tail. What should a strict whole-packet parser check?
options: Inspect the remainder before accepting the packet.
Decode complete chunks and silently discard the tail.
Treat the tail as a record filled with invented bytes.
Repeat the final complete record to replace the tail.
questions.explanation: chunks_exact exposes incomplete trailing bytes. The parser must choose whether to reject or retain them.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A grouping size comes from input. Why must zero be rejected before windows or chunks_exact?
options: Zero always selects the largest possible grouping.
Those operations require a positive group size.
Zero tells the iterator to copy all existing groups.
Those operations use zero only for empty buffers.
questions.explanation: A zero size panics for these APIs; validate a variable size before calling them.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A field requires four bytes, but only three arrived. What should a checked decoder do?
options: Read a fourth byte from outside the provided slice.
Choose a fourth byte using the previous field value.
Return missing or failure before interpreting the field.
Interpret three bytes as the required four-byte field.
questions.explanation: Length validation precedes interpretation. A partial field is not a complete value.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A file specifies that the lowest byte comes first. Which decision makes decoding portable?
options: Use whichever byte order the current CPU prefers.
Copy the bytes into any integer-shaped allocation.
Reverse the bytes every time the program is loaded.
Use the format’s explicit little-endian conversion.
questions.explanation: from_le_bytes follows the format rather than relying on host byte order.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A checked four-byte prefix was decoded successfully. What has that alone not established?
options: That the whole record has no unexpected trailing bytes.
That the borrowed prefix contained at least four bytes.
That the chosen conversion used four bytes for a value.
That the prefix range was inside the provided buffer.
questions.explanation: Checking a prefix verifies that field; an exact whole-record format needs its own total-length check.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: An eight-bit counter intentionally cycles after its maximum. Which arithmetic policy expresses that?
options: Checked arithmetic always returns the maximum value.
Wrapping arithmetic keeps the low destination bits.
Saturating arithmetic automatically resets to zero.
Plain arithmetic promises the same build behavior.
questions.explanation: Wrapping explicitly chooses modular behavior; plain overflow behavior depends on enabled checks.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: A buffer-size calculation exceeds its integer type. Which policy makes rejection possible?
options: Wrapping arithmetic returns an always safe small size.
Saturating arithmetic preserves the exact requested size.
Checked arithmetic reports an unrepresentable result.
Plain addition proves that the allocation will succeed.
questions.explanation: A failed checked calculation lets the caller reject the size before using a truncated value.

questions.title: Reason about the concept
questions.prompt: Health is stored in an eight-bit integer, but a game caps it at ninety. What does saturating_add alone guarantee?
options: It discovers the game cap from the variable name.
It rejects every increase beyond the current health.
